A dungeon crawling RPG and "Average RPG Item Shop" clerk sim combined into one humorous game. No single part of the game is really amazing or innovative but put together you have a lot of things to juggle. It reminds me of Persona in how your day is broken up into time slots where you have to manage your store, shop at the market, do quests to recruit mercs, and dungeon crawl for more loot to stock your store. The game's main objective is making weekly payments to clear your family's debt. They really ramp up in cost quickly which is where most of the difficulty comes from. However, the last payment is really high and most people don't manage it on their first playthrough. While there is a NG+ mode, the second time through was way too easy and got boring without the dungeon crawling.
Despite some balancing issues, this is a great JRPG and worth picking up. Just try to remember to keep multiple save games. Oh yeah, and the boss fights are pretty cool.

General Gameplay:
It's a more or less typical incremental playstyle: Grind for *Gameplay element XY* that boosts your progress next reset, rinse, repeat.
It is however one of the better idle/incremental games I've played. Clicking is mostly an optional mechanic, that feels rewarding most of the time if you decide to utilize it.
Progress is mostly semi idle: You need to check in every 30-45 minutes and be active for a minute or two to level your character(s) for optimal progress. You do however get a currency and damage bonus from time spent completely idle. Harder missions/objectives may require you to be active throughout.
The mechanics are more or less easy to learn, easy to master until you get to the point of crafting legendary gear where it's probably best to rely on external sources to see if you'll want the item in queston later on.
Specific gameplay:
There is a *ton* of characters (ingame name=Crusaders) you will not have at the beginning each with his/her/its unique abilities/ability combination (which do follow certain schemes so it's really not hard to get a grasp of all important mechanics after a while). So if you like to collect stuff you'll have a grand time. Downside of that is that you'll not have *the best* crusaders and their equipment at the start (you get a chance to recruit new crusaders and improve their gear outside of date based events through missions).
Freemium aspect:
As in almost every F2P game nowadays there are microtransactions;
Here's the good news though:
While at times not too subtle about you being able to buy stuff you are by no means forced to spend cash on anything to advance and have fun with the game. The way the game is structured now you'll reach endgame far more quickly (still talking about months of semi active playtime, as usual with idle/incrementals) than those who started earlier. You can also opt in to the newsletter (which only yields you bonus loot and no spam). As a strictly not paying player I regard their model of microtransactions as pretty fair. You do get a boost out of spending cash on the game (and supporting the devs) but not so much that you'd need to grind for days on end to get the same result.
Development/technical:
The developers of this game are very active and constantly working on adding new stuff (up to this point and mostly in accordance to known mechanics; still new content is new content, right? :p).
They have an amazing community manager (weekly ama on reddit), do consider player feedback/suggestions and clear up support messages quickly.
Obligatory Praise/Nitpicking:
+The game is "cross platform" (android, steam/desktop, browser [afaik]) and actively maintained/playable on each
+There's a nice little community that has grown around the game
+Months of (semi idle) playtime until you reach anything resembling endgame
-It is "always on" which sometimes can suck as sometimes there are some server hiccups (mostly for 15 minutes but I have experienced up to 1.5 hours [at most though])
-There are some balancing issues where you need to get lucky to get some crusaders/specific pieces of equipment that are *leaps and bounds* better than anything else you could get
~I feel that there might a bit of performance optimization left to be done, the game has its phases where it runs slower than *I* think is necessary

In summary:
I have had and still have fun playing the game after such a long time (at least with the game open in the background), especially events and newly added content. It is at (most) times a mindless idle grindfest but then again I'm not playing these games to focus 100% on them and have action packed adventures either. If you are an impatient completionist and/or violently allergic to microtransactions I'd say hands off. If you like idle/incrementals give it a go, at the very least it's a nice long term timewaster without that much active play required. Do check it out it's free and you won't have to spend money to play efficiently either.

As a game in general, I suggest you spend your time doing something else, as it would be better spent doing something besides playing a clicker game. But, as a clicker game, Crusaders manages to keep things interesting by changing objectives, limitations, and interactions. That aside, sometimes the jokes inside are genuinely hilarious. Skeletons called Baqfurmor? Gold.
I'll try and keep it brief, since I have issues with rambling on and on.
The most interesting/unique system in this game is the squad/positioning mechanic. Certain crusaders support filling your squad to the brim, others support having as little as possible. Some even support being overwhelmed on purpose so that they get a DPS/Gold boost, or being close/far away from other crusaders. I could give more examples, but I'm sure you understand the point: position and other miscellaneous factors are keeping each of the many runthroughs fresh here, and it's the different conflicting, sometimes synergizing interactions that do so.
There are very few downsides to playing this game, to be perfectly honest. The only issue I've had with nearly 200 hours (and only 150 of them idling, I think), is that some things are unclear. Take for example, the Hermit's legendary backpack. When he is the only crusader on the lonely trek, there is still a symbol marking him as getting a 200% bonus for each empty spot. However, I have no idea if the game thinks there are any empty spots. Problems like this could be solved with a current effect on the crusader. In fact, this is already implemented with idols and the various horns. A similar problem arises with talents. Yes, I get 1% for each percent of cooldown, but how much is that as of right now?
Also, syncing to your mobile account can be somewhat difficult. There are guides detailing how it's done, so I won't bother describing it here.
In summary:
+Game manages to stay fresh though the, what I would call unique, positioning system.
+Also does this through some of the limiting factors in objectives here and there.
+Pretty funny at times.
-Very minor issues with clarity
-Somewhat complicated to get game synced up to mobile

I'm quite surprised that I kinda liked a game that not only had Square-Enix's filthy logo on it, but also had a protagonist with a fedora.
I found the story compelling enough to play the entire game despite being almost completely lacking in any originality. You're playing as a rough and tumble man with a troubled youth who finds his way into becoming a police officer only to be MURDERED and has to find the SOLE SUSPECT responsible (I feel ashamed for that one but it was practically screaming at me to make that "joke"). Except, you have to do it as a ghost! I'm only dissapointed that this game didn't feature more Whoopi Goldberg ( insert unfunny movie reference here).
I won't go so far as to spoil the story, but needless to say I wasn't really surprised by anything that happened. I think Scooby-Doo has had more surprising plot twists if I was gonna be honest. The characters are actually likeable enough, my favorite being Joy.
Onto the gameplay, it's...alright. It's mostly just finding and collecting stuff, which I would've actually been fine with if that had been all it was. But they just couldn't reisit themselves and decided they had to add my absolute least favorite game mechanic, half-a*sed stealth sections. By far the biggest issue with the game are the parts where you have to deal with demons by sneaking up on them and quick-time eventing them to death (or I guess "super death" cause they're not alive). I don't fully understand why development teams add these kinds of things. Game developers, if you're not gonna put much effort into a mechanic, then don't bother programming it. No one will think you're lazy for NOT putting in something that isn't vital to the core gameplay in, but they will if you barely do anything with it. Also, the puzzles are a little too easy but I wasn't expecting much of a challenge in story with Square-Enix attached to the project.
In terms of graphics, the game looks pretty good. Facial animations are well done and they do a good job of conveying the emotions of the characters. The voice acting is pretty decent, too. Though there's this weird thing I've noticed where when you read someone's thoughts, sometimes the voice in their head won't match the one coming out of their mouth. I know in real life, you don't exactly hear your voice the way everyone else does, so if that was done deliberately then that's actually kinda clever. If not, then that's just dumb.
In short, a pretty decent game IF you get it on sale like I did.

This is the best Assassin's Creed since Brotherhood.
I stand by that statement despite the various shortcomings other reviews have already mentioned. The story sometimes feels conjointed (mainly due to timejumps) and inconsequential which doesn't bother me so much though. The game does not portray world shaking events or an artifact that can bring nations to their knees, because of that the story can focus on the work of an Assassin who still does assassiny things. Aveline is conflicted between following the creed, serving her mentor, who has largely become self absorbed and self righteous, and the Templars whose ideas are presented as tempting but extreme. Aveline is a well rounded character who is likeable, relatable and badass. The fact that she is a woman, a perfect opportunity for showcasing Ubisoft completely feministic and open mindset, is not showcased at all, which I think is the strongest argument for feminism you can make. It presents the facts without agenda.
And lastly the reason I would have recommended this game no matter the story is the persona system. While it requires a bit of time until you fully get the hang of it (I think the tutorial didn't do a great job) it is worth it. It allows for actual infiltration and secrecy (something both Unity and Syndicate tried and failed at) As well as a certain amount of planning for your missions. There are unique equipments for every persona that you can use to upgrade their capabilities like a hidden pistol or a parasol with a dartlauncher build in.
Equipment for the Assassin persona is fun as well, I especially like the whip both for it's capabilities and the symbolism.
Lastly worth mentioning is that future you is not working for the Assassins or the Templars you are literally just a bloke who plays a videogame but get interrupted by some ominous voice that doesn't try to convince you to do anything (or ask you to press A to join the Assassins) but simply chimes in after a cutscene and says "Yeah that's nice but just take a look at the uncut version and make up your own mind". It gives you perspective on how the perception of history changes how we view both it and the present.
Definitely worthy of your attention and the direction Ubisoft should have taken the franchise.

Before I begin, I want everyone to know that I've been waiting on this game for years now. Ever since we were told they began development. I knew exactly what I was going to get, so I'm basing my review on that.
____
When you first see the game, it looks exactly like Euro Truck Simulator 2. The only differences include it being in the United States, having vehicles driven in the United States, trailers that are used in the United States, and a couple states in the United States.
After you get past the $20 price tag and actually get in the game, it's exactly as it seems. Just a reskin of ETS2. But what was to be expected? It's the same engine used to rebuild ETS2 for a different region. That's what we were told we were going to receive and that's what we got. I am not at all upset that we only get 2 states at release with Arizona coming a little later for free and 2 trucks. I knew I was getting that and I paid the price for that.
The developers wanted to go the correct route with the game and get licensing for the vehicles used so the lack of vehicles is okay. As time goes on, we'll get loads more. As far as states go, 3 might not seem like much. With the scale, it definitely seems lacking in content. But you have to remember. If they went to a more in-depth scale and added more content, then it'd take years for a single state to come out. I don't know about you, but I'd like to have 48 states before I turn 70 years old. :P
And the game is called American Truck Simulator. American. The United States is only one of dozens upon dozens of countries in America. Canada and Mexico are 2 more countries in NORTH America. Meanwhile, there's still South America that has to be scaled in. By the time we get all of that(if we ever do, the plans could change), we'd have so much map, we wouldn't be able to explore it all in a reasonable amount of time. Sure, California and Nevada might not seem like much, but they are comparable to Great Britain and France in ETS2 when you talk about size. Now add the equivelent amount of states as there are countries in ETS2 and you have the United States completed. UK and France might not seem like much on ETS2, but when you travel from one to the other, and then all the way to Poland and then up to Sweden, you start to realize that even though the map is small now, it will be much bigger later on when we have more content to play.
Not much of a regular review that you'd see on Steam, but these are my opinions on the game so far. It's a reskin of ETS2 and that's what we were told and what we paid for. No complaints here. Still a billion times better than most simulators out there.

Everything is perfect as the Euro Truck SImulator except the map is too small, I hope they can expand it for free in the future.

Going into Liberation, I knew three things: that it was a port from the Vita, that it took place at the same time as AC3, and that it had a female protagonist. I had never played an Assassin's Creed game seriously before this one - I dabbled about a bit with Assassin's Creed II, but stopped playing after I found Ezio and Desmond to be thoroughly boring and unlikeable. Since this game was supposedly not tied into all the silly meta-narrative and didn't include a single appearance of Desmond or cartoonishly-evil Abstergo employees, I figured it was as good a time as any to stop laughing at the series from afar and play one of these games myself to see what all the fuss was about. Plus, it was five bucks on sale - what have I got to lose?
As it turns out, I ended up enjoying myself. A lot. More than I thought I would, and more than I was expecting based on the reviews it's been getting. The parkour system, even though it's been used as the framework for this series since the start, is still tons of fun, and I often just fire up this game sometimes and run around just to relax myself. Every animation is incredibly fluid and seamless - with just the push of a button, Aveline can scale wooden buildings, swing around a tree trunk as she runs across its branches, use lampposts and hanging signs as stepping stones to cross a street ten feet below you...it's all so much fun to watch and it's even more fun to be the one doing it. Sure, there are times where you can't grab a ledge you can clearly reach (the Bayou in particular is a bad offender in this regard) but for the most part, the free-running is sublime.
As the first female Assassin, and thanks to both her African and French heritage, Aveline is capable of changing between different personas with nothing more than a dressing chamber, each with a different set of strengths and weaknesses. The default Assassin persona is always at least a little notorious, but it's the best suited for combat and can use any and all weapons. The Slave persona limits the weapons and health, but allows you to blend in with groups of slaves - and since this is set during the American Revolution, slaves are in no short supply. The Lady persona has a massive hat and dress that allows Aveline to be seen as a respectable member of the nobility, but the hem of the skirt makes it impossible to do any kind of free-running and makes combat incredibly difficult. Each one is used throughout the story at different times, and all feel well-balanced and rounded - it's a great example of a game telling a story through it's mechanics alone.
Combat, however, is a different story. Enemies are really fickle and trigger happy, and guards will be more than willing to fire a musket as soon as you come within line of sight. And when you get a high enough notoriety, they practically send the whole force after you - and if you're in the Lady persona with just a hidden blade and no smoke bombs, you're gonna have a bad time. There are plenty of ways to approach an encounter, however - the hidden blade is the standard Assassin weapon of choice, but Aveline also has access to swords, axes, slave tools, guns, and assorted gizmos to work with in combat. Not all weapons are available for all personas, of course - you can't swing around an obsidian axe as a lowly slave, for instance - but as long as you keep on top of upgrades and stay stocked up on supplies, you'll have everything you need to get out of a situation alive. Most of the challenge in combat comes from timing your counters to do special instant-kill moves - it's a quick-timed event, but the animations look REALLY good.
Overall, I'm having a lot of fun with Liberation. It's substantial enough that I can play it for fifteen minute bursts to ease some stress in between classes with free-running and trading, but still engrossing enough that I can sit down and play it for hours on end. If all Assassin's Creed games are like this one, then I can see why people are getting tired of it after a while - but as for me, it's easily becoming one of my favorite games that I played this year.

Judging Fable’s qualities as a video game, both then and now, is a relatively easy thing to do. But trying to come to a conclusion about this game as a whole is a lot more difficult. Playing the original game again the raw ambition is still obvious, but inevitably many of its best ideas have now been appropriated by other games. And, equally inevitably, most of those other games have managed to fashion a more consistently enjoyable experience out of them.
I got this game mainly due to the fact I like RPGs and there are little available for the 360. Part of my gripe with Fable is largely due to the emmulation of the 360 console as opposed to the game itself however, Fable still has some irritating aspects which I'll cover first.
On the subject of the actual emmulation, the game requires at least 2 or 3 updates to be installed every time I put the game on which is a bit annoying although undertstandable. However, the emmulation at time causes my game to freeze which takes me onto my next point regarding the game.
The save procedure can be infuriating. While for the most part you can complete a "world" save which stores everything you've done you can't do this mid quest. All you can complete is a "hero" save which stores you're experience but not how far you are in the quest. Bearing in mind some quests are very long winded, and during this you do a lot of battling. What really annoyed me was getting half way through one, then going into a different area of Albion only to find my game freezes on the load page leaving me to restart the console. That also meant that I was back to square 1 with the quests.

Every time I play Fable I'm pleasantly reminded as to just how timeless it really is. It's so damn good in my opinion that at least every 2 years I find myself playing it again, just to re-experience it and all of its stellar contents. In my opinion it's way up there in what I'd consider one of the best RPG's - if not one of the best games - of all time. If you haven't played it before, buy it and find the time to. You won't regret it if you're interested in good video games. I'll preface in saying that I've played this game far more outside of Steam, on both PC & Xbox, so I've more hours played this than what my profile suggests.
The amount of dynamic freedom Fable offers you is unprecedented anywhere else even now. 10 years on, I'm still surprised by how much I'm allowed to do. Infiltrating a bandit camp? You can either shoot the guards to pass, or sneak in-between them. Further in, you then need to retrieve a uniform; which then allows you access to the base camp. But how do you proceed to the Boss's location? You can choose to kill all the bandits in sight, drawing out the elites, opening your passageway. How about you release captive slaves as a diversion, hire a group of assassins to do the work for you, OR acquire a pass from a shady bandit hiding in a dark corner for 1000 gold pieces. Which you can then kill him to retrieve your money. Or just skip giving the part where you pay him. And it doesn't indicate to you these options - it leaves it for you to find them.
You've got all of the game's tight mechanics, and then on top of that it shoves this titanic amount of meta-content. Visit bars to play games like Blackjack, Pairs and a table-top golf-esque game called Coin Flick. Assist traders with their passage through the woods, seek out silver keys to open locked chests or pursue a treasure trail. Go fishing. Dig up some loot. ♥♥♥♥ some ♥♥♥♥♥es that you pick up from your nearby Inn. Oh, and CHICKEN KICKING, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
There's just so much to love. The sense of culture is hilarious; the attention to detail, consuming. The story, soundtrack and characters are memorable ones, too, and after finishing The Lost Chapters - the game's rather large and only expansion, from which this edition gets its namesake - for my first time this weekend, I can easily say Jack of Blades is certainly one of the most appealing antagonists I've seen in a video game.
I could write about this game for ages. One of the highest recommendations I could give for any video game out.
TL;DR: If you are one of the few that haven't played Fable, go out and buy it. It's a ♥♥♥♥ing awesome game. Period.

Mass Effect 2 is a great game in many respects.
It boasts memorable locations. Be it the crime hub of Omega, Asari corporate haven of Illium or the Citadel Wards, all of them feature meticulous attention to detail, making all of them believable, lively and interesting to explore.
It boasts great characters, each with their unique custom-tailored missions. No longer it feels like tedious shoot 'em up of ME1 in the same three-template outposts (underground base, two-story warehouse or a cave). Surroundings, goals and flow of those missions will make almost all of them stand out as much as Noveria or Feros did. While custom (!) tense brooding music (and rightly so - a lot of plots are about something very messed up and troubling) only sharpens the experience.
The combat itself was greatly improved too. The highlight is probably the sniper rifle wielding Infiltrator experiencing a massive positive change compared to ME1.
Some notable gameplay changes worth mentioning include weapon heat, bullets, weapon and armor customization. ME2 introduces bullets (you have to worry about picking clips up, particularly if you rely on a sniper rifle or a pistol in the scenario involving fighting waves or simply a large host of enemies) and removes all customization and overheating. I can understand the reasons well enough - let's admit it, 99% of the people were using the same mods and bullets anyways, the console interface of ME1 was extremely uncomfortable to navigate while outfitting each of your companions, and having to worry about bullets does change the combat somewhat. Yet still it feels too streamlined and sterile.
Exploration in Mako was completely removed, replaced with planet scanning. Personally, I've always found Mako roaming tedious and needlessly time-consuming, but a lot of people seem to miss it.
ME2 also features a new system of gaining experience. You are now rewarded for completing missions, which means that you don't have to worry about doing something gamey to milk maximum experience.
I have only two personal gripes with new features. The first one is about purchasing new abilities. Each ability has only 4 levels, each subsequent one costing more. By the end of the game you get to spend your points to purchase new levels very rarely - once every 2-3 missions. And no, they don't feel rewarding enough to justify the wait. The second one is that the number of available weapons is reduced to 2-3 per slot (which could be augmented with DLCs, but DLC weapons usually suffer from being OP, so no joy anyways).
(What's interesting is that ME3 managed to find a great middleground between streamlining of ME2 and overabundance of ME1. Weapon mods and weapon variety are back, missions consist of subobjectives, each rewarding you with xp, and you have more abilities with more levels in each. All of it smoothes out the gameflow.)
Mass Effect 2 isn't without its flaws of course. And the biggest one in my opinion demolishes the idea that Drew Karpyshyn would've definitely made a huge difference for writing ME3. The main plot of the second game is shambles. Worse yet, it was made even more pointless by the Arrival DLC and ME3. Fortunately it is comprised of only a handful of missions, and the last one at least gives you tense rewarding action and cinematics. But as long as you can turn off your brain (fortunately Shepard displays this capacity all too often already :p ) and just blindly do whatever the Illusive Man wants you to - you'll be fine. The rest of the game is totally worth it. So much so I'm currently riding ME1 one more time to get a lvl 60 import just because I enjoyed ME2 immensely and want more of it.

So the Mass Effect series is amazing, The third Mass Effect, due to EA's continual flighty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting, is only available on Origin, so those of you looking for that solid 10 out of 10 (well, except for the ending) will not be finding it here.
HOWEVER, I can inform you that Mass Effect 2 is still worth your time. It is relatively easy to pick up the series at this game and still know what the heck is going on without having to play the first game, which is often stated as being pretty "meh" compared to the rest of the series.
Perks of this game are good character customization, the new ability to romance some of the alien crew, good combat gameplay, non-linear storytelling, excellent voice acting (especially from Femshep), and AMAZING story / lore, whether you chose to play as paragon or renegade.
The gameplay great for a game from 2010, even though I now laugh at how Shepard runs in the second game (it is pretty comical). Keep in mind, though, that if you choose to play as a Sentinal (my choice in class) your raised shield matrix DOES NOT automatically activate at the beginning of combat, as it does in the third game. Make sure you do that, folks, or you are wasting class perks!
The fact the storyline changes based upon Shepard's critical decisions in the game gives this game HUGE replay value and the story / avatar are importable from the first game and completed files of the second game.
The main missions were excellent, but some of the necessary loyalty missions are a touch dry, but I found that Amara's and Thane's were very refreshing, especially when I got some renegade point-free oppertunities to go all badass and theaten to chop off a guy's balls and sell them to a Krogan.
I may not run like a cheetah or fight like a Krogan but I sure as hell can dance, flirt, and hold my liquor better than Commander Shepard!!

Mixed Review - not for everyone.
The key thing to understand is that this is more a *simulation* than a game.
It is incredibly detailed and open ended.  Your most likely problem starting a game will literally be having no idea what to do or what your options even really are.
I must confess, I love complexity (I've a doctorate and read technical papers for fun), but the barrier of this game has been too high for me to do more than peruse its systems.  It's incredibly dense and not organized for easy access.
That doesn't make it bad -- far from it -- it's quite impressive, but it is an opposite of the elegeant simple but deep game play we often asssociate with more cerebral ventures.
If any of the subject matters interests you at all (in particular diplomacy and politics as strategy) I recommend getting it just to see the kinds of systems the designers are using -- they're neat.  But unless you are willing to put a fair bit of study time into the game you are unlikely to get much out of it.

Ahh...  I hate to be this guy.
You know, that guy that hates on a game because it didn't live up to it's name.  Even with the knowledge that it was a completely different game in the same storyline.
That said.  This game was nothing but irritating for me.  I was expecting a comparable continuance of the Metro storyline.  What did I get for my hard earned money?  Something that was far less.  Lots of storyline, but not of the same quality.  In fact, so much that it interfered with my gameplay.  I'd have to estimate that at least 20 percent of the game is cutscenes that are not nearly as interesting as they should have been.  In fact, at least half of those cutscenes were worthless drains of time that did nothing for the storyline.
Without spoiling the plot, I have to say that this game felt more like I was trying to watch Alien Resurrection and watch the child friendly favorite, E.T. at the same time.  It was badly presented and did not do Metro 2033 justice.
So, how was the gameplay?  Easy.  Way easier than Metro 2033.  You had everything you needed, conservation of resources was not ever an issue.  And yea, I was playing on Ranger.  On the most difficult setting you should feel a hell of a challenge.  You should feel like every shot counts and that any mistake you do is punished with the most unpredictable of consequences.  Maybe you should suffocate due to not packing enough filters.  Maybe you should run out of all your best ammunition and be resorted to using some stray weapon you found on a corpse.  No.  None of that.  I don't know about you, but I'm not really here for a walk in the friggin park.
Instead of difficult gameplay concepts, you know what we got?  Resident Evil style bosses.  "Oh, superboss...  just shoot it in the flashing red areas to do damage."  I'm sorry, wtf did you just say??? Did you just tell me IN GAME that I had to shoot a difficult adversary in the red flashy areas?  You didn't expect that to be immersion breaking? Gtfo.
Nothing about this game lives up to Metro 2033.  The only saving grace it had was a couple moments of intense gunfights.  I cannot recommend this game.
I completed this game in less than 10 hours.  It was a painful 10 hours.

Best racing game ive played in years. Finally finished the career mode after about 12 hours, still lots to do though. A solid racing game. The pros outweigh the cons but in my opinon they are:
Pros:
- great graphics for its time, still holds up.
- realistic physics and car handling.
- Fast pace racing and varying difficulty.
- realistic car body deformation. (like Wreckfest or BeamNG)
- fun racing mechanics. (gain nitro by raming opponents/props etc.)
- very high play hours/price ratio. (paid $1 but game is worth whatever theyre asking)
- Bonus mini games are kinda fun.
Cons:
- brutally unforgiving reset-to-track will cause infuriation and frustration when you spin out.
- vehicle upgrades will take quite a while to save up for. (grinding required to 100%)
- no custom races, only career mode races with set amount of laps.
- menues are very basic.
- music. the tracklist is ok at best but my problem with it is that the developers decided to increase the run time of every song by abruptly replaying the song again from someplace near the beginning. This is extreamly distracting and does not improve the music at all. Id rather listen to 2 or 3 songs during a 5 minue long race than listen to a 2 minute long song played in a loop...
But after all the game is terrific and id recommend it to anyone who likes casual racing games.

Is the game scary? No I would not say it is scary, maybe creepy or atmospheric. The Dev does a good job of making you feel and realize that you are not among the living. There is the occassional disappearing ghosts and scary music but nothing like silent hill, dead space, or amnesia. The point of the game is not to scare or freak you out. It's to tell a great story and for you to solve a mystery.
On top of figuring out your own mystery there are about 6-10 little side quests. None are very long, but they are each enjoyable and have a little story of their own. There are also hundreds of little collectables to find and to keep you busy. I am not usually a fan of finding and hunting for hidden objects; but for some reason in this game it does not seem to tedious or difficult. The style of game just seems to lend itself towards finding lost or hidden items.
All that being said I would recommend this game overall score 8/10. I picked it up at 75% off and am not disapointed. I think for me even %50 off would justify the purchase. If it's on sale and you are a story driven gamer I would strongly urge you to pick this one up at some point.
Oh and if that's not convincing enough did I mention you have the ability to posses cats, and you have a never ending cigarette?! Yup see I knew that would help you make the right decision!

As a long time fan of the Assassin's Creed series, I have had mixed feelings about some of the games. Liberation is a mobile port so the graphics are not quite as sharp as others, but the story and gameplay are fun. Liberation is riddled with bugs and can sometimes be hard to make it do what you are trying to do, but it's gripping enough that can't stay away for long.
The division of personalities was a brilliant, if somewhat underused concept. Sometimes you are locked into one personality, or you randomly change from wanted status. Switching to Lady mode, you can finally run around the city without fear of accidently climbing on top of a crate or lamppost.
Each personality has collectables and mini missions hidden around the different zones, encouraging you to explore in all roles. But the game often prevents you from having the freedom it needs you to have. This leaves you frequently frustrated, trying to please the game rather than have assassins creed style fun.
At the end of the day, with the multiple zones, personalities, story and collectables, this was a very good addition to the series and I recommend it. Just try not to let the bugs get to you and keep going!

This game shows it's age. Not just in graphics, but in plotline. Maybe the voice acting and side quest mechanics were interesting at the time, but now? Meh. Specific points:
Marketed as a game where you could have influence in the world, but....
-You can be mayor. What does it mean to be mayor? Nothing. You don't do anything, noone reacts.
-You can own property. What does it mean to own property? Not much. You can upgrade the furnishings, hang trophies on the wall, and collect rent. And then never go back, because why would you?
-You can get married. Find one of the many nameless NPCs and stand in front of them to show off your manly pectorals. Then throw a ring at them. You now have access to the sex scene, which is a fade to black with suggestive voice acting. Never interact with your wife again.
-You can be good or evil. What's the difference? Halos or demon horns. You could slaughter the innocent one day, vanquish the wicked the next, and that's totally fine.
The running theme is that none of these decisions impact the story greatly. You can occasionally choose: "kill this dude" or "don't kill this dude." That'll affect 2 or 3 scenes. Basically doesn't matter.
Not sure what to say about the core gameplay. I found it very easy, but YMMV.
======================================================
Response to first comment:
I am skeptical of your rebuttal, and examined faqs and forum posts to investigate.
Are you sure about that mayor thing? Everything indicates that it does nothing. I did learn that I COULD purchase and rent out buildings and businesses other than the marital homes in each town, but you have to kill the tenant to do so. Which...geez. Talk about a hostile takeover. *rimshot*
Anyway, nobody reacted to me as mayor. And no new properties became available for rent. All signs point to violent death being the only way other property becomes available.
Still not sure what the point of renting things out is. It'd take an awful lot of time just making the rounds accumulating rent to earn the money back, and what is there to spend the money on? There's some legendary sword you can buy with it I guess, but there's dozens of legendary weapons sitting around everywhere anyways. You can pour it into the temple of Avo to shift alignment over to good. That's something I guess, but getting good alignment just happened as a natural result of going through the main quest, since every monster or bandit killed gave some good alignment points.
Didn't realize the spouse would give gifts. So that's something.
All indications also point to never having a child of one's own, that was added in Fable 2.  If you marry the right person in Bowerstone, and they happen to be a single parent of one of the children in the school, then the child may be brought along. No sign that the child would eventually act like you. The aging mechanic gets weird here too, since you might get married at age 30, get married, meet your stepchild, then advance levels to age 65 and the stepchild is still the same age.
Good and evil have more result than most of these other effects, but...eh. Complaining that I'm not locked in? Hm. Perhaps I would like to be locked in a little bit. Redemption and corruption stories are interesting, and I don't want to always have to be the stupendously good-aligned butterfly-attracting goodly hero of goodness just because I ate some Tofu one time, but yeah. When I decided to try the other alignment, it was unsatisfying. Swapping the extremes is just too easy, and too without consequence. It doesn't seem the game particularly cares. Townsfolk alternately run away from me or come around to applaud me, and both are kind of annoying. Big clusters of sound files all being played at once either way.
I don't know what your last comment is supposed to imply. Do you mean I shouldn't have needed to spend that much time to complete the main storyline? I could have dropped the sidequests and paid even less attention to the economy, I guess. Do you mean I should have realized that I could kill townspeople and buy their houses? I was definitely surprised to learn that, but I don't see why I would.

My initial thoughts after 2 hours of play.  This is an alpha release survival game.  It isnt complete yet so this review gives some space for a few niggles.  I do have a high spec pc and have seen no framerate or lag problems that some others are seeing:
On first logging on I didnt see any servers in the multiplayer list but apparently it is an issue because so many people are playing it. However I started in coop mode (server on your own pc). The start sees you crucified on a cross completely naked. I laughed in the creation screen as you can actually increase the size of your manhood (i did say completely naked). Died loads - thirsty, hungry, creatures, NPCs. The initial survival is very much along the lines of 7DTD in that you create an axe, make clothes build a house. Not that I have the house built yet and there are no shotguns or waves of zombies. There is no starter guide or intro quests which I quite like, its explore and click everything yourself. So far so good seeing it is an alpha early release. My only dislike is that the map in that it doesnt have markers for your bedroll (spawn point), the fact that it seems a little small and not randomly generated which may bore me after a month or so because I will know where everything is.  I will update this as I play more of the game or Funcom do updates.
Top tips:
Make a bedroll as soon as possible
Pick up everything
Put some trousers on!
Make a spare bedroll - they get used up when you die.
Dont get in a fist fight with a crocodile.
Look for water as a priority.
[Update] 46 hours in and I am still playing.  I have actually now played this more than I have played Skyrim.  I am playing on a server with some friends so it has been good fun. I still like it.
We have built a couple of little communes.  Captured some thralls, explored, gathered, hunted, built and been on a slaying rampage.
Dont let these put you off, but the problems I have encountered have been:
1) Cant find the server - patched very quickly by Funcom
2) Click to join a server and then end up on a different one - fixed
3) Items disappearing - a work bench and severall cook thralls.  I suspect they were eaten by Hyenas.
4) Our little village can take ages to render when you login or port back there after death.
5) You can sometimes get attacked by invisible hyenas.
6) the UI sometimes freezes so you cant see that you are starving or dying of thirst.
7) Signs lose their text
8) Reboots occassionally required to fix the above.
9) I have now seen some rubber-banding and lag on occassions.
Some respect to Funcom team here in that they have been patching every day so far.  Mostly these have been fixes around servers.  Reading the Dev Blogs they have some great plans for the future.
Even though I would question us having to pay full price to test the game for Funcom, I do feel I have already had my £26 worth of entertainment even with the early access issues.  This is going to be a great game providing it isnt turned into a pay to win Funcom special.
Even more tips:
- Build a bed as a permanent spawn point
- Move your camp nearer to where there is iron ore
- Capture archer thralls to defend your base from nasty wildlife
- Put some more trousers on!

The combat is heavily skill based, relying on you learning how to ' Get Gud '. While this is usually perfectly fine, and I enjoy a challenge, it does not work well when most of the rest of the community has two bodies, and a spare leg and a head above you in experience.
You will rarely find other players that are at the start of the leveling tier. Why? Because most are turned away by the sheer cliff of difficulty when it comes to learning the moves of the game, and actually being able to combat people who have done it for far longer than you, of which is little to impossible.
It gets worse when most of these high level players stack on their own team, making it impossible to make a dent, and ending with the match being steamrolled.
I had fun at times, but overall, there's more rage than fun to be found here.
I cannot reccommend this game, at this time.
I'd more than happy give this another shot, if some sort of rank matchmaking system were implemented, placing you in games with people of your own level of skill. This needs to be fixed. Hopefully, someday it will.

Murdered Soul Suspect has quickly jumped to my list of most underrated games of 2014.  A solid mystery yarn with great atmosphere and a gripping story, it's a sure bet for any gamers looking for more story-driven fare.
Like similar titles (Beyond Two Souls, LA Noire, The Walking Dead), MSS operates on the philosophy that story trumps action.  The gameplay consists almost entirely of investigating scenes to piece together the central mystery, with some stealth elements wedged in for good measure.
Everything is fairly well-done gameplay-wise, though the investigations can become a little repetitive later on into the game.
The story is the focus here, though.  The plot (which I won't spoil here), is like Patrick Swayze's "GHOST" had a baby with LA Noire.  Overall, enough to keep you going through the game.
Not that it needs to keep you going for long.  I finished the game in just over 5 hours.  I don't, however, feel cheated.  If purchased at sale price, it's a great game that's worth your time and money.  I'm going to be revisiting it eventually because replaying would be so quick.
So if you're looking that's light on action and heavy on story, check this one out!  I really enjoyed it.

Very fun game with unique aesthetics and a addictive loot system for new warframes ( characters ) and weapons.
BUT why did I give it a thumbs down you ask? Well let me explain:
Firstly and most importantly the monetization. You can technically play and experience pretty much anything in the game without paying. Of course that doesn't tell the whole story though. You see the game has this nasty thing called limited inventory space. Which applies to pretty much anything that isn't a resource or consumable.
So after playing with a few frames you got into the game and just finished building a new warframe. Well tough luck you need to either pay us or destroy one of your previous warframes.
What's that a new batch of weapons got introduced and they seem awesome. Don't forget you hit your inventory limit a while back and all those older fully upgraded weapons still have decent stats. Oh the agony of having to choose. And DE then comes in and says "You don't need to choose just pay us".
Fanboys will come in and defend the devs saying "But you can trade for platinum and thus not pay for anything". And it's true there is a trading system that let's you trade for that currency. But that's a deflection from my original point. Those inventory slots NEED TO BE PAID FOR. And it's either going to be your money or someone else's money.
There are other things that come in and scream for you to pay them. Like some of the frames or weapons have pretty hefty time constraints when it comes to grinding. Coupled that with the crafting time some of them have. One frame I recently build took 3 DAYS of sitting and looking at the progress bar all the while in the corner the platinum cost was visibly reminding me I could just rush it.
But really time wasting requirements are a standard for F2P and aren't really that big of an issue. The slots are though.
They are a inevitability if you keep on playing and not want to destroy older equipment you spend weeks upgrading. And either you or someone else WILL pay for them.
If you are fine with the mindset the devs have and are ok with the possibility of needing to continuously open slots ( sometimes new inventories appear like the dogs not sharing the older sentinels inventory ) be it through paying yourself or grinding for someone else to then by all means enjoy the game.
But it's definitely not for me.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a pretty good game, as long as you recognize it for what it is and what it isn't. It's essentially a mystery adventure game but entirely lacking in inventory. The game play is fairly simple and most of the game is fairly easy and can be finished rather quickly. A lot of it is going from point to point, looking for clues, answering a few questions based on the clues, and moving onward. In that sense its got a lot of "novel as game" elements. It has a small semi-stealth-like action element that crops up a few times, but it is in no way an action game.
While in some sense there's not much to the game play, it has a pretty good story and a lot of atmosphere. In addition to the main plot, there are a few side quest mysteries to solve, and a large number of collectables to find if you enjoy that aspect of games.
Because the game play is fairly simple, moderately short, and its almost more of a game novel at times, the game is likely not worth full retail price, but if you can get it on sale and enjoy supernatural murder mysteries, it's a worthy pick up.

For what it is worth, this game is not bad. In fact, it has a decient story to it.
It is clearly unpolished in many ways, from the fact that Ronan always enters an area the same way, even if the story should indicate a sense of urgency to the fact that many of the ghosts you come across are merely 2D, and fade to prevent you from being able to tell easily. At one point you are wandering through a quarantined area and you can talk to a ghost of someone who had caught TB. For the time of the event you should expect her to be dressed in early 1900s style clothing, but she is wearing something clearly modern.
i really want to like this game, but it is unsatisfying.
Pros would be that the game does have a decient story, the main characters are developed enough to be believable, even if at times they do act very out of character in attempt to push the story forward.
Cons, the gameplay gets seriously repetative. Every area is exactly the same things. Collect this, investigate this, guide this person, find a way around this, rinse, wash, repeat. Areas involving the demons are simply annoying. The puzzles are overly simplistic and many of the clues are difficult to find. Do not be surprised if you find yourself looking over the same room half a dozen times because they made things exceptionally obscure.
For what it has, i am glad the game is short. Anything more than 7.5 hours and it would have become far to repetative and annoying to bother with. That and this game has little replay value.
Why am i still recommending this game? Because if you can get it on sale for something under 10 dollars, i think the story alone is worth it. Anything more, and it would be best to pass this up for something a bit better.

This game is heavily story driven. It's so story driven that you can't even call it an adventure game!
Monkey Island has more gameplay in it than this game.
All you do is walk around and press X where needed (I use an Xbox 360 controller). It's not a third-person action/adventure game or hell, it isn't even a "detective" game like L.A Noire (another epic game) is.
Nope, in here you just walk around and press X. You don't solve puzzles, you don't shoot, you don't...you don't do anything but walking, really.
It has an "open world" sandbox city that you're free to roam but there's nothing to do in it. Sometimes you stumble on a collectible and press X. That's all there is to it.
The minimap shows you where you need to go in order to "progress" in the game and well, just walk on over there and you get a new cutscene.
Other games that lack in gameplay, such as The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, let you choose what to say or do in certain situations. This adds some replay value to both games.
However, the story in this game is linear and you can't make any choices. No choices at all!
So why am i recommending this game ?
It has a good story! A very good story! If you don't mind watching a movie with a controller in your hand or sitting in front of your PC/laptop then this "game" is for you.

After the “third” game, the Animus stars getting used for slimmest of excuses, with nary a scant of modern-day story. This is rather significant, since as the player character is actually the user of the Animus (or, in this case, the Animus-derived video game), this basically removes all rationale for why they should even keep playing. Why try for high synchronisation? Why finish side quests? Previously, this was justified by Desmond working through the motions to discover what he needs to know, but now it feels like I could take it or leave it.
The game itself is rather short and half-baked. The story seems quite far removed from the central themes of the series, and while there are some neat little mechanics that make it feel like more than just a filler -- the different roles Aveline can assume, and the introduction of the whole trade fleet mechanic, off the top of my head -- it definitely seems like the work of the studio B or C team.

A short and fun game with few flaws, Liberation is one of the most enjoyable entries in the AC series and well worth playing.
The lead character, Aveline, is written and performed well. The plot is interesting, but the storytelling is at times weak. Interesting and relevant parts of Aveline's life (such as why and how she became an Assassin) are not covered in any detail. Unlike earlier games in the series, I sometimes ended up killing a large number of people purely because it was the objective, without really knowing why. I didn't connect as emotionally with the story as I did in ACII and Brotherhood.
The voice acting was generally strong, but a few of the minor characters were a little overdone. The soundtrack is brilliant and well worth listening to on its own.
A couple of the bosses (first swamp boss and tower) were pretty tough if you tried to kill them using conventional means, but all were entirely trivial if using a smoke bomb or a chain kill.
I'd reccomend this game if you like the AC series, but not as an introduction to it.

Look, this isn't a bad game. But for the love of god, don't play it. It's all afk, you just let it play by itself, you think if you wait a few hours and let it idle, you'll have money to level  up and progress. Nope, you'll get enough money to take you for a few levels, but because the levels and items get more expensive as you level up, the money goes away really quickly. But hey, thats not a problem, you can just pay for money, idles, and chests, right?
That brings me to problem number two, its pretty much all pay to win. They know it takes forever to level up by idling, they know its time consuming and you'll ultimately get nowhere. They want it that way, so that you spend money on microtransactions and DLC. As a disclaimer, I got the DLC I have for free, and let me tell you, I would never pay real money for it. The DLC is basically worthless, you get items that aren't even useful until waaay later into the game.
Problem number 3, the idles. You get so far in the game and you can reset which you get rewarded with idles. But you'll get VERY few, I'd be suprised if you get over twenty. Doesn't seem like too much of a problem right? Wrong. It takes HUNDREDS of idles to get the upgrades for them. So you have to sink hours and hours into the game to even get there. They want you to pay for the microtransactions however.
In the end this all comes down to personal preference, If you're a fan of (in my opinion) wasting your money by playing a completely pay to win game, go right a head. I wouldn't recommend it, I've sunk many hours into, and I've only been able to reset ONCE, and got twelve idles. Not worth the time, or the electricity to play. Avoid it, please.

A fairly good game, if you can forgive the obvious, outrageous cash grabs. Elsword is a 2.5D MMORPG priding itself on its anime/manga stylised visuals, both in how the characters appear, the cutscenes (intros) and if enabled: the combat effects.
Elsword has a fairly poorly established storyline throughout the game, one which is clashed with if you choose to play any of the characters who are not of the original cast: Elsword (Swordsman), Aisha (Mage) and Rena (Archer). However, the storyline presented in textual summaries and elsewhere (which I have yet, nor inclined to find discovered) seems fairly dramatic and compelling, especially the 'dark characters'.
The game is split into two main components: Dungeons (PVE) and The Arena (PVP), outside of which is notably bare.
Combat in early game, as the unspecialised character is notably bland, with generalised abilities branching from three drastically different styles, lack of completed flowing combos and particularly tame visuals. This does not pose as much of an issue as it is fairly easy to reach the first specialisation within a single session, after which the character follows a chosen theme, has decent combat flow and the visuals become more over the top.
The biggest criticism I have of the game, as mentioned earlier is its cash grabs. A character has initially access to only 4 active ability slots which is dreadfully small, however they can rectify this by paying around $3 to have access to another 4 slots; as far as im aware, there is no other way to obtain this otherwise (permanently atleast). The game also makes certain abilities have very long winded quests to obtain but allow the player to easily purchase them for $2 also.
The cash shop in the game is also terribly expensive, to obtain a full, permanent set of base cosmetic items costs close to $30, the items are also character bound thus are unable to be given to others were one to change characters.
Other then these flaws, the game in my opinion is enjoyable, of course I also copiously waste money so some of the issues may not have been a problem for myself. While not to Maplestory scale (2DMMORPG) It is a fairly enjoyable game.

It's alright for an Assassin's Creed spin-off. It functions fine and feels like an AC game, specifically AC III, so if you enjoy AC games then this is perfectly serviceable for no more than the $5-$7.50 sweet spot. If you like AC multiplayer then you're SOL with this game, but me personally I always enjoyed the single player aspect over the multiplayer so that didn't bother me too much. The story is kind of interesting for the first half of the game but then falls apart toward the end before finishing with a completely unsatisfying ending. The worst part is since this is a spin-off you're left with the feeling that Aveline's story didn't mean much of anything in the grand scheme of things regarding the overall AC mythos, but I still need to play Black Flag, Rogue and Unity so perhaps they reference it in any of those games. This is a spin-off, though, and much like Altair's PSP sidestory was lost in the ether I get the feeling this is the last we'll ever hear of Aveline and the First Civilization mystery disc that this game is about. I thought the graphics were fine considering this is just an upscaled Vita game. The graphics and resolution options are barebones so look elsewhere if you're looking for a game to make your rig purr. As it is, it's a serviceable spin-off or "expansion pack" to AC III.
I'll recommend this to only people that enjoy the Assassin's Creed games and only if you get this for $7.50 or less. It's a decent time-waster if you're waiting on the next AC release.

This isn't really a PC game - sure, it runs on PC, but it's not accomplishing anything that the puzzles in the newspaper do, or a puzzle book.  It's not telling a story, or providing you with a journey, like Myst and other such games, it's just providing Sudoku and word puzzles.
Some people may really like such games - you can play them for free over the web, this is something HTML can provide, without spending a cent.   So what's this game doing, asking for money on Steam?   Asking for thumbs down, that's what.
Existential issues aside, the other reasons not to buy this:  The interface isn't really aimed at PC, you can't change the resolution (although it does have a handy handwriting recognition capability, because presumably the developers didn't know about keyboards).   So it runs at about 800x600 whether you like it or not.   As I said - it's not even a PC game.

It's a space RPG where you play as the ships. You start on the outside of a galaxy and fight your way through worlds and space police checkpoints to get to the center og the galaxy where everyone prospers. There's a decent backstory behind it.
At times the game really feels like a grind, but thats okay, it's an RPG. You fight, gain exp, and upgrade your stats. The usefulness of stats are: small passive bonuses (aka armor bonus, % health increase, etc) and your skill level allows you to slot the different parts (weapons, armor, etc) onto your ship. There's like 12 -15 different areas to level up in i believe. Like shields, armor, hull (general structure integrity once armor is gone, aka ship health), engines, reactors, beam weapons, etc. It's pretty in depth.
If you like games like atom zombie smasher, you'll like this. You are given a top down view of where you fly in space. There's hot keys to do various things, and you can switch between any ship flying with you in the same sector at any time. Say, your ship gets destroyed or sent to repair, you can control another one in live battle. There's factions, whether they like you or not in each sector gains you access to parts, or you can try to take them down yourself. They act as bosses bt provide decent xp.
Yeah, just get the game. ESPECIALLY if it goes on sale. Right now it's 80% off so it's $2 ($1.99). There's no reason not to buy this at such a steal. They're currently making Spaz 2. Can't wait. Oh, TB does some voice acting. The character voices kinda suck, but it's cool.
Downsides:
Can be a grind regardless of skill/ level (its an RPG)
Sometimes too much reading (i get lazy)
Voice acting sucks (this doesn't affect gameplay)

I really want to like this game, but I just can't.
Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube (Electric Boogaloo) looks like a game of the walking-sim puzzle-block variety, but looks are deceiving. The puzzles here aren't really puzzles at all, only mild inconveniences. The only reason the game is challenging is you're trying not to fall off of tiny ledges as you jump around with a modest interface.
I'll give you a concrete example. One of the levels gives you seventeen cubes, but you can beat everything in the level with only ten cubes. The "puzzles" are using cubes to make ledges in obvious places, but whoever made the game was not a puzzle person at all. They included way too many cubes because they weren't able to do the puzzles themselves, and the puzzles are neither inventive nor interesting as a result. The only "challenge" is to find a slightly-harder-to-reach game element in every level.
I like hard puzzles and I was very disappointed, because the game had so much potential! The game music is airy and pleasant, the visuals are pretty, and the controls are relatively smooth. But the puzzles simply aren't puzzles, there aren't any true challenges, and "try not to fall" becomes repetitive almost immediately. This could have been a great game with each level introducing new ideas and tricks to doing things with fewer cubes, but they should have employed at least one puzzle person in its design, because the design sucks. The game is very boring, and I can't recommend it.
Maybe if they do a sequel they'll put some effort into the game design next time. One can hope!

Heroes Tactics is a mobile/browser port that you definitely shouldn’t play......
If you’re a fan of the turned-based strategy/RPG genre then you’ve probably played classics like Heroes of Might and Magic III. You should buy that instead, or get one of the newer versions (V or VI). There are also the excellent King’s Bounty games to play. Both series have better visuals and creature designs than HT and even feature innovative 3D graphics!
(My first impressions video)
They also have exploration and stories with numerous characters (KB even has dialogue options and choices). HT has no exploration, basic visuals and simple animations. Story and dialogue are almost none existent.
HT also has less satisfying turn-based combat than the aforementioned games, with what appears to be less unit variety and no spell mechanics. Base building seems lightweight too, and is tied to resource gathering which can be speeded up with; you guessed it, micro transactions. I didn’t play enough of the game to hit a paywall (if there is one), but it seemed apparent that real money could be used to speed up unit recruitment, item collection and levelling up. These are all signs of a Pay to win game.
This takes away from the games only positive, that it’s free to play. Spend a little money on a more in depth turned-based game like those mentioned above. Don’t waste your time playing this on a PC, it really isn’t worth it.
Finally, Steam needs to add a stipulation to its store that you can’t release a game (even in early access) if it doesn’t have a full screen option. I have a dream….

Crank your noir machine up to an 11!  This game has more noir atmosphere and characters then any game in the history of videogames!  Too bad it has a ridiculous amount of problems as well.  Before I go into those problems, I just want to reiteriate that I lovedddddddd the noir atmosphere and did really enjoy my time with the game. From the creepy haunted house to the crazy insane asylum this game just drips with noir atmosphere (but seriously wtf I wanted to go to that lighthouse the whole game and it never happened, why have a creepy lighthouse that I can't go to!)  It's almost exactly what I wanted "Wolf Among Us" to be.
First of all it's important to know that this is an adventure game through and through.  It has no combat (it has a couple of extremely easy stealth puzzles), it kind of has 1 quick time event, but really it's just you walking around.  In fact I'm not even sure if the "puzzles" qualify as puzzles.  The main game mechanic is searching for clues to solve the mystery.  You do this by examining the environment until you come across a button prompt showing you it's a clue, you then take those clues and try and put them in the right order to solve the current "puzzle."  It has no fail state, so you can just click on things until you get the right order.  I'd say that is one of the games biggest failings.  It would have been great if you didn't know how many clues you need and could come to the wrong conclusions as you went through the game eventually causing you to solve the ultimate mystery incorrectly.  However, everything is rather straight forward.
I'm also very confident that this game was simply unfinished.  You more or less have an open world to walk around in, yet the game only has about 4 or 5 side quests.  I can't imagine that this is all they wanted to have when they set out to make this game.  The fact that the game also ranks you on how you solve the "puzzles" also leads me to believe originally their was more to it and you could solve the puzzles incorrectly without the game just stopping.  The plot also starts to come apart towards the end.  The cast of characters seems just silly small for a murder mystery and almost none of these characters are developed at all.  I can only assume they wanted to go more into these characters if they had time.  Despite all that, I enjoyed the central story and loved the atmosphere and the mechanic of searching for clues, and I just really wanted more of everything.  The fact it ends in 7 hours is just ludicrous and unforgiveable at a price of $50, I bought it for $12 which I thought was way too much.  #Worth $5

All since I purchased the game I've found myself playing it for a few hours each day. I love the competition in it, because a lot of people who play it tend to have good sportsmanship. Occasionally there are a few angry players who decide to throw fits, but overall the community is pretty splendid.
One thing I especially like about the game is the league system. It trys to group you up with people of your same league, meaning that you will fight against people who have the same skill as you. This encourages the player to try to get better in order to proceed out of their league and into the one afterwards. Also with the smaller community this game has, I often find myself being paired up with some of the same people, which over time has made me gain friends.
The only real down sides I see to this game are some glitches and some unfair advantages some players are granted at certain times. I do realize this game is still in beta so I'm not going to hit it hard when it comes to glitches, but they can get annoying some times. Also the game crashes for me often unlike the majority of games I play. I'm not sure if that is just me or the game. An unfairness in the game I tend to witness is the bomb and the golden grappling hook. The bomb is a lot of the times completely unavoidable and can make you go from first to last or even die. If you are climbing along walls and someone throws it down below, everyone below is sure to die. I say the golden grappling hook because it can sometimes be very unfair. If you are a few (theoretical) feet behind a player and you grapple, it is a 99.9% chance it will succeed no matter what the grappled player tries to do. This can be instantly fatal when in a tightly condensed box and can make someone who is really good at the map and has been leading for quite some time do very badly in a way that is out of their control.
Although the game has a few downsides right now, I still have incredible amounts of fun playing it and think you will too.

Bioware did some big favours for themselves with this release.
The combat has been completely redone which was my biggest complaint about ME1, and while it still isn't as satisfying as a dedicated TPS like say, Resident Evil or Max Payne, its an admirable effort for a hybrid RPG, and most especially from a studio that's usually stuck to D&Desque rules for combat.
The graphics, style and presentation have all been kicked up a notch, and the world and scope of the game has been vastly expanded.
The story however, is a little underwhelming, and almost insignificant compared to the first game. Where ME1 was concerned with the almost extinction of all sentient life in the galaxy by an ancient evil force, ME2 is about some kind of splinter remnants kidnapping a few hicks on the outskirts of space AND ONLY YOU CAN STOP THEM.
More than that though, the structure of the story is a bit too straightforward. The game is about recruiting people in your team, and then going to kill the bad guys. That's basically it.
It's a bit unfair to simplify the game as such, as there is some decent writing concerning your ship mates (some of which return from ME1). And the presentation and emotional investment of the final mission in the game really is quite an experience.
There's plenty of content to be had, with my blind insanity playthrough being almost 50 hours. However this is including all the side missions, which consists of exploring lots of boring empty space for a blip on a radar, that leads to an underwhelming and somewhat pointless mission (usually just give you some negligable amounts of money and xp)
As a sequel, the game is a fantastic continuance of Shephard's journey, but on its own merits as both a TPS and an RPG, it may leave some people wanting.

I used to play this game on Xbox when it was just Fable. The extra storyline in this version just blows away any other RPG i have played in quite a while. The only new-ish RPG that comes close to this game that has the same style of play would be Fable 2, yes i know its the same people but thats the thing noone else makes a game quite as good as this IMO. So lets go over the 4 categories I like to write my reviews on (other than Combat Arms, doesnt even deserve the time anymore, yes it used to deserve it). Now onwards,
1) Graphics 8/10
Obviously the graphics are going to look and seem old, but thats one fo the tings i love about this game. It gives the game a classic feeling. If you prefer older textures that dont look all 8-bit then this game has just the right graphics for you. (I would do 10/10 but I do have to take in to account some glitchy textures like your hair looking wiry, etc.)
2) Storyline 12/10 (HOLY SH#T)
This games storyline will suck you in and make you feel as if you were living it. The narration is just amazing giving you in depth background and current information on whats happening. In the very beginning you start off as a boy trying to get a present for your sisters birthday so you go around doing good deeds so your father will pay you for them (1 gold piece per good deed). *SPOILER ALERT* If you havent played skip to the next rating, After your sister gets her present she knows something is not quite right. You hide in a field while the entire village you knew and loved is being burned and its people slaughtered. A guild master comes and rescues you and you start training as a hero from there on out the story gets more complex and interesting. By far, one of the best storylines I have EVER had the PRIVILEGE to play.
3) Character development 7.5/10
Yeah this game is slightly lacking in chracter development. You get more famous, you get good or evil, and you choose all your skills. This might sound incredibly amazing but the way they chose to lay it all out is slightly boring. You doo good or bad deeds your alignment changes (obviously). As your alignment changes you get horns and red mist if your evil and butterfllys and a halo if your good. You skills are Strength, Skill, and Will. Stregth is your health, damage and damge taken. Skill is speed, guile(sneakyness), and damage you do with cross/bows. Will is actually the main thing I loved as far as the character development go's hence the 7.5, You are able to choose skills that heal you, damage your foes, make you do more damage, make you take less damage, among an array of other spells you can buy all of them (eventually) for your experience. You earn experience based on which attack you use to deal with enemies and general experience that can be used for all three (skill,strength, and will) trees at your disposal. The alignment and renown is a little clunky but the Skills are very in-depth (if you dont like spending alot of time figuring out what works for you and what you like just stop playing RPGs their not for you)
4) Gameplay 9.5/10
This games gameplay is amazing as well. I cant give it a 10/10 however because of one tiny detail that I cant get over. When your stealing stuff and noone is looking at you but since they are in the same area you still get caught. THat is so unrealistic. If they didnt see you do it HOW ARE YOU IN TROUBLE. >:(I Anyways other than that the games mechanics and fighting are all very well thought out and its runs great on pretty much all computers (because its an older game).The fighting is in depth yet still easy to control and the other controls for just moving and using spells etc, are well thought out because you dont ahve to use complicated keyboard controls to kick a$$. Its that simple great mechanics make for a great game.
OVER ALL RATING
Should you play it: If you dont you should blow up your computer.
Do I recommend this: YES but only to those people who are serious about RPG's because its a little in deptha and challenging if your not a RPG lover.
Rating out of 100: 92.5/100 ( As far as im concerned no game will ever earn 100/100 from me (EVER)

So, I have played the game for about two hours in total. I've gotten to the point I have a house and not near to the point I can start gathering thralls. However, I felt it necessary to post a review of the game at its current point with what I have played and noticed.
First, the game is beautiful. The scenery is refreshing and the way things break apart are realistic and definitively more appealing than the dissolving rocks of Ark.
Second, the amount of customization for your character is already leaps ahead than I would expect for an Early Access game and you have really catered to the community in allowing players to really customize their character from what they wear to how they look and to what they prefer to wield.
This leads straight into the issues I see with this game so far. The animal and NPC AIs are pretty wonky and half the time they stand there while I kill them or they just lag out of view. Friendlies (clan mates) are extremely difficult to distinguish from other people. While this makes for an immersive Roleplay experience it doesn't appeal to players more interested in the PVP aspect of the game. Perhaps having a server setting would be appropriate that adds color to players names but can be turned off to maintain your immersive RP experience (this is more of an opinion than a real issue with the game but I have already heard some complaints regarding this from players in game). There are definitely a few more bugs that I haven't noticed or just forgot to mention but the enemy AI is the most glaring of them for me and what really brings the game lower down in my review. It is my hope this will be repaired in patches to come.
For those of you reading this review and are curious of whether or not you should purchase it. It IS similar to Ark but another comparison I would make to it would be  Life is Feudal with the primitive medieval aspect. However, a vast majority of survival games have very similar mechanics and while each one boasts a unique take on the genre in the end, they all are along the same vein of game. I would recommend checking it out for sure! I've enjoyed my gameplay so far besides some of the glaring bugs but it is an early access game and bugs are to expected on its release. I think it shows a lot of promise for what the game can be with more biomes, the ability to get mounts, more religions (avatars), and more building tiers/textures. The mods for this game will be very interesting and you'll definitely see me hitting end game content soon!

I bought this awhile back based on the storm of positive buzz surrounding it and my own passionate love of the free market in its many forms. What I found was not only a most excellent simulator of that strange and wonderous machine known as the marketplace, but also cleverly interwoven simulations of the murder-and-riches-filled hole in the ground and the confusing morass that is society. Recettear is a game for our era. It explores all the great questions of our era through the saga of that iconic hero of the West, the starving entrepreneur. It touches upon such themes as love, loss, homelessness and hunger while also seeking to transcend them through good and honest capitalism. Yet most importantly, it touches upon the most wonderous power of free exchange, namely that two people can each better their lives through the simple modicum of trade. My inner poet wept, my inner economist exulted and my whole self basked in the divine joy of commercial success.
