Dost thou knowest how good this game is? Nay you say, then I shall tell thee in but a single word - LOTS!!
Yes, this game is 'lots' of good. The premise is essentially a civil war between two rival factions - the Agatha Knights and the Mason Order.  Each of the two groups has the same 4 classes to choose from: Archers, Man-At-Arms, Vanguards and Knights.  Archers have the least amount of armor whereas the knights have the most; vanguards make use of the ultimate Zweihander sword as well as polearms and the m-a-a's make use of maces and lighter/shorter swords than those that the vanguards and knights have access to, so there's a decent balance between the classes and they all have their pros and cons, so some are much better for certain situations than others.
What's more, the voices/laughs, etc. for a knight of the Agatha Knights is different from that of the Mason Order, which really keeps things fresh.  On top of that you also have different game modes to choose from and spanning a decent number of maps, such as Team Objective (when one team is defending the other is attacking), Free-For-All (classic deathmatch type gameplay, but there is also a team deathmatch associated with the Team Objective mode, which is lots of fun), Duel and One-On-One type matches and even some custom types like infection mode.
So you have different classes with many different weapons to choose from, a decent number of maps and unique game modes, unique voices/laughs which are often hilarious, especially when dudes are screaming whilst on fire (yes, in real life this wouldn't be funny, but it is in this game.....don't judge me!) and loads of gore to keep it real medieval style.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is easily one of the more enjoyable multiplayer games on Steam and I'd recommend getting it even when not on sale.  So grab an axe or a sword, or something else of the sharp/pointy persuasion and prepare thine selves for ye olden times smiting!!
P.S. team kills happen a lot in this game as would be expected, so watch yourself (too much team damage, even a high ping, is likely to get you vote kicked). In the end you'll likely say to yourself "Man, if only I had a dollar for all the times I got team killed...I'd be rich indeed!!"

Recettear is an absolutely endearing jrpg / item shop sim in which you play as Recette on her quest to erase the huge debt that her father amassed before he left her.
You try to accomplish this task by selling items that you bought from different merchants or found in dungeons.

All since I purchased the game I've found myself playing it for a few hours each day. I love the competition in it, because a lot of people who play it tend to have good sportsmanship. Occasionally there are a few angry players who decide to throw fits, but overall the community is pretty splendid.
One thing I especially like about the game is the league system. It trys to group you up with people of your same league, meaning that you will fight against people who have the same skill as you. This encourages the player to try to get better in order to proceed out of their league and into the one afterwards. Also with the smaller community this game has, I often find myself being paired up with some of the same people, which over time has made me gain friends.
The only real down sides I see to this game are some glitches and some unfair advantages some players are granted at certain times. I do realize this game is still in beta so I'm not going to hit it hard when it comes to glitches, but they can get annoying some times. Also the game crashes for me often unlike the majority of games I play. I'm not sure if that is just me or the game. An unfairness in the game I tend to witness is the bomb and the golden grappling hook. The bomb is a lot of the times completely unavoidable and can make you go from first to last or even die. If you are climbing along walls and someone throws it down below, everyone below is sure to die. I say the golden grappling hook because it can sometimes be very unfair. If you are a few (theoretical) feet behind a player and you grapple, it is a 99.9% chance it will succeed no matter what the grappled player tries to do. This can be instantly fatal when in a tightly condensed box and can make someone who is really good at the map and has been leading for quite some time do very badly in a way that is out of their control.
Although the game has a few downsides right now, I still have incredible amounts of fun playing it and think you will too.

Don't play this! Currently, the game is online only, and the server is located far enough away that not all sprites load when you play. It used to be able to be fixed by dropping to low quality and restarting the game, but recently there are just far too many assets needed to be loaded. As such, you cannot drag the Crusaders around to make use of their formation bonuses. Hopefully this gets fixed in the future, but the devs are seemingly focused on creating new content for the game rather than fixing these issues...ironically, that new content aggravates the problem, making it even more unplayable for us!
Don't let the tag of "clicker" fool you - this is a great idle game that quite easily beats games such as Clicker Heroes and Adventure Capitalist.
The formation strategies and swappable heroes add a dimension of thought and difficulty that feels far more rewarding than other idle games. Often, I've found myself having to abandon an objective simply because I hadn't thought out my strategy and I wasn't quite ready for that challenge yet; the time sink would not have been worth the rewards essentially.
Crusaders are seen as Supports, Tanks, DPSes, Healers, Gold finders etc etc - managing your formation is vital!
As an example: some supports may offer a buff to all male crusaders but that will be reduced for any non-Royal Crusader. You'd need to assess whether the buff offered by a female, non-Royal Crusader would counter-act that.
There are also Events where you can "win" event specific Crusaders. There are also special buffs that only occur for those few days - this adds a level of excitement and freshness to the game fairly frequently.
The biggest drawcard for me is the idler nature - I can leave this running in the background while I work, or play other games.
Quite a big drawcard for me here! The artwork is good, the characters feel different and fairly fleshed out compared to the Heroes from Clicker Heroes. In particular, the Event Crusaders and objectives come across as having thought put into them.
This game possibly wins the Most Monty Python References in a Game award...which is awesome.
Great community and devs that actually get involved! Great stuff!
There is a store which provides players willing to drop some cash with a huge advantage in terms of how quickly they can progress through the game.
However, I feel that the base level of the game is not that punishing to new players - there is a large roster of Crusaders to keep you busy and interested.
As mentioned, the game is online only - this is fantastic as it means that there is no way for the game to be hacked or cheated. It does, as in my opening paragraph, create a severe issue for us South Africans; a problem that will no doubt be experienced by other players across the globe as well.

I've been following this game since it was announced, and I was really excited it got released. I know there isn't much of a map yet, and there are only two trucks, even though dozens of ETS2 truck mods have been seamlessly transferred over to ATS, this game is worth $20. I go back to the 18 WoS games, starting out with Hard Truck and Across America, good old days. Back then we only had one or two major cities and a highway leading out. Now, we only have Cali and Nevada, and things are looking great already. If they are truly planning on adding that much detail to each section of the USA, then it is worth the wait.
I've been known to pay close attention to small details, and ATS has some really nice features so far. The map detail is amazing and the roads look great. So much potential here. There are, however, some things that I think could improve or be changed.
- Speed limits: You see a sign that says 35 but yet the speed limit is actually 30 (very strange).
- Police: I have to admit, I disabled them with a mod. If you go over the limit at all you get a hefty $1,000 fine. A cop could be tailing you and the speed limit will suddenly change, and boom, instant ticket. Do you guys remember the system in 18 WoS American Long Haul and Haulin' in which there was a meter, and when you did something wrong, that meter grew? For example, you are speeding, and the meter grew slowly, and at a certain point, like 40-50%, if a cop saw you or went by you, you got a ticket. They had cops on the side of the road in that game, and driving around, just not nearly as much as you see in ATS. It's ridiculous really. Every 5 cars is a cop, needs to be fixed.
-AI Vehicle Behavior: I really enjoy the AI vehicles, in ETS2 and ATS. You feel like you are a part of the system. One thing that I have noticed in ATS, when you are merging into the highway, AI vehicles don’t really get over like they are supposed to. I’ve seen it a few times, not sure if it is programmed and just not very effective, or what. Here in America, if you are merging onto the highway, vehicles will switch into the left lane to clear a lane for you to merge, and if they cannot, they slow down and give the merging traffic space to get on. I hate trying to get on the highway and a damn camper or something doesn’t give a crap, and I have to stop, making it really hard to get on because I’m in a semi, not a lambo.
-Weight Stations: In America, weigh stations aren’t open 24/7 and have hours that they operate on. There is almost always a light of some sort that says whether you have to go in or you can bypass the weigh station, or a sign will say closed/open. In ATS, you just get a message on your GPS right before you are about to blow past the exit for the station. They need to add these signs/lights to signal the status of the station or make the GPS message happen sooner. Also, I haven’t seen any AI trucks use the weigh station, which was present in earlier games.
These are just some things I have noticed so far, I will probably discover more as time goes on, but I really think these issues need to be addressed before the game grows any more. Less work on the end of things really. Regardless, it is a great start to something that could grow to be the biggest trucking game ever. I enjoy it now, and will keep enjoying this game into the future, and I recommend getting it.

Crusaders of the Lost Idols is a clever game that is far too hard core and far too grindy to really be enjoyable.
The premise is simple, use a group of characters, in a certain ‘formation’ to complete a goal, say level 350. Each ‘crusader’ has slot with equipment as well as powers. By placing certain ones next to other ones you might gain more damage or more gold. Each level has a goal, when it’s met you move on to the next one. Then you ‘reset’ the game which gives you idols. The idols in turn, permanently give you more dps and gold.
The problem is that game is so complex, there are so many different talent and builds, that people have tried to make spreadsheet to figure it out. Those are so complex you need an MBA just to figure out where to spend your idols. You can try just any combination, but you will hit a wall and accomplish nothing.
The devs have certain bases campaigns that are available all the time, and then 2 weeks a month, a special event. The difficult with the game comes with the grindy nature of the game. To finish the last mission of the first world you realistically need about 100k idols. Idols are earned at best at around 100-300 / hour. That means doing over 300 hours of mission just to be able to win it.
You will notice a lot of people have thousands of hours in it. Don’t be fooled. They just let it run, probably with an auto-clicker to farm idols. Unlike AdCap you can’t just turn it off for months and get a haul of idols. Turn efficiently grind, you have to babysit the game, and is the most time intensive idle/clicker game I’ve played. The last mission I did I let it run for four days straight, to reap a stunning 280 idols.
Bottom Line: Nice game if you have 20,000 hours to spare

So, Youtubers Life. It came out when Youtubers were/are a really popular thing, so it's understandable why people, including myself, were drawn to it while it was in early access. I enjoyed the gaming channel until... It got repetitive. Then the music channel came out and I was excited until I realized the gameplay mechanics were basically the same and the intstruments really did not match up with the music type. Then cooking came out, and.... It was repetitive.
Do you see the pattern here?
Pros:
Fun in short bursts.
Striving to reach your goals can be fun and challenging.
Hiring people and managing rent is a difficult but fun task.
Cons:
Not something you can play for hours on end.
Once you reach the end of the game, there's literally nothing else to do.
Not being able to study at a house after a point is upsetting because it makes more sense to max out skills when you have others to do the managing and recording for you.
They promised Fashion and Lifestyle as part of the base game, did not deliver, said it will be DLC. Still yet to announce anything.
As they updated more stuff, it became INCREDIBLY easy to miss things that could help you out, such as demos and product releases, etc.
In conclusion:
Get it while it's on sale. It's a fun game, again, in short bursts, but part of me does regret spending money on this.
If it's on sale for less than $10, get it.
If it's not on sale, don't get it.
Since I regret spending money on this game, that is why I do not recommend it.

Pros:
-Characters and their interactions with each other. As you build your team, you stumble upon some very interesting people. The best aspect of the game was getting to know everybody between missions, hearing their stories, and delving deeper into the Mass Effect universe. Especially Garrus with all of his calibrations, which is everything he wants to talk about.  Then there’s the fact that you’re able to romance some of the crew members. I really felt like I was invested in and torn between some of them. Whether it was flirty Kelly, shy Tali, or (insert your description of) Miranda.
-Loyalty and crew missions. One of the reasons why you do care about the crew is permadeath. In order to get all of the crew out alive, you have to go on some loyalty missions. As you get to know everybody, crewmembers will tell you that there’s some personal problem they would like solved. Loyalty missions were the best kind of side mission because they weren’t random things to do. There was a sense of purpose—gaining a more meaningful understanding of the crew. All of them played out like a good movie should, with everybody gaining some type of character growth and a solid resolution.
-Combat is decent and can be challenging. While it reinvented the wheel, I wasn’t bored senseless. In fact, there were a few parts that I had a difficult challenge. This one part of saving Garrus took me at least ten or so tries. Mostly due to the fact that enemies will use cover effectively, (generally) work as a group, and at times actually attempt to flank you.
Mixed Bag:
-Dumbing down of rpg elements. It really seemed like there was much less of a focus on weapon diversity and putting together your gear. While it doesn’t kill the game, it certainly does make it more confusing when you buy upgrades. The upgrades tell you that it will do XYZ% more damage, but there’s no indication of how much that would be.
-Interiors seem a lot smaller. The Citadel is pathetically tiny compared to the original. And the same could be said of a lot of the places you visit. They felt small and often very linear. I really wanted to explore some of these places, but to no avail.
-No Mako, scanning only. The Mako is totally gone, which also felt like exploration was severely curtailed, and has been replaced with scanning planets. While this may on paper sound like getting resources has been streamlined—it isn’t. I did have this Minecraft mentality of collecting everything everywhere, but It’s downright boring a tedious after the fifth or so planet that you’ve scanned in the same system. By the time that you’re done with scanning every planet you’ll have an astronomically huge collection of resources.
Overall:
Mass Effect 2 is a masterpiece. There was not a lot of time that I felt like I was disengaged from the story or that I was bored doing ho-hum quests. The mythos of the universe, the strength of the characters, and the story is what elevates this game into what I consider to be near legendary. 9.5/10

Let me start by saying this review's seriously biased: I had this game on the XBox OG and it blew my mind all over my poor mom's upholstery. Nostalgia may factor in here, but I'll try to maintain some sense of objectivity.
The good:
The gameplay of the original Fable was very unlike a lot of the RPGs in 2004. The mechanic utilized every decision you made to influence the story in some way or another. As enemies land hits on you, scars appear on your body. Do good deeds, the town loves you and a little halo appears on your head. Lay waste to all who stand in your way, and the potato-scrubbing plebians run in fear as little horns sprout out of your head. Your choices seriously affect your weapon stats, skill set, appearence, plot- every nuance of the game begins at day 1.
And remember, this is back in 2004. The DS was hot off the factory when this came out. Outkast's "Hey Ya!" was not yet overplayed and annoying. Bush was still in office. That's impressive.
The music is also pretty impressive. Danny Elfman (yeah, THAT Danny Elfman) helped write the main score, while Russel Shaw, the compser for a majority of Molyneux's games, actually used a small orchestra to do the majority of the game. Not the first or the last time a group of live people was responsible for a VG score, but again, an impressive feat for an RPG of this scale considering we were still using Windows XP. It's atmospheric, and suits the naturally light-hearted nature of the game.
The game itself has bits and pieces of humor around. It's a game that tries to not take itself too seriously. The dry, snarky sort of humor only a crazy Brit could come up with. The animation and graphics, as well, are bright with just a touch of cartoony.
Still, the selling point here is that Fable set the standard for all the open-world RPGs that follow. Some of Fable's mechanics were borrowed, sure, and some it invented, but I have to argue that it's really the first single player RPG that put it all together to make something that feels this open and massive in scale, where your decisions and style of gameplay seriously affect the game. Really, the closest relative I can think of is Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion in 2006, a full two years after.
(Maybe there's a hidden gem I missed, but I'm sure someone will point it out if I'm wrong about this.)
The ugly:
Oh, sweet jesus, the graphics have aged. It takes some getting used to. Even in 2004, she wasn't winning any pagents, but now, even with my GPU's antialiasing cranked up as far as she goes, it's pretty bad. Low poly, pre-HD res, and cheap modeling.
It's not a dealbreaker by any means, unless your idea of a good game rests solely on whether or not your dog's character model looks like a real dog. Like I said, it does take a bit getting used to, but the game is still so immersive, you'll ignore it after a few minutes of real gameplay.
The contols are a bit awkward, as well. Maybe it's just me, or maybe it's from playing some more modern RPGs, but, it feels like the red-headed stepchild: the controls are still reasonably well-laid (at least it's still using WASD), but there's just some modern conventions that are missing. You can remap the controls, though, which helps somewhat, but it's still a little clunky.
The bad:
The avatar-to-enviroment ratio isn't linear. At all. You can get some pretty powerful magic and weapons early on in the game. There's a couple of spells that are just straight up unfair- notibly the spell that slows down time, and the "Heavenly Whatever/Infernal Thing" spells. Even late in the game, it's way too powerful. Together, all you need to do is slow down time for a bit, and whack all the enemies in a 40-block radius with your Heavenly Thingamabob before they can land a single hit. Mix that with the fact that enemy strength barely goes up after 10 hours, and an open-world, well-designed RPG turns into a hack-and-slash. The game does offer a chance to tack on challenges to your quests, like no damage, fists only, no armour, but it doesn't actually add challenge to a quest itself- it's just a bet. If you take damage during a no damage run, you just lose a few gold, and the quest continues as normal.
Basically, after a while, it becomes waaaaay too easy to just blast your way though a quest if you have the right upgrades. It's really a major oversight. It certainly doesn't ruin the game, but it is a nasty blemish that's hard to overlook.
Final verdict:
Go for it. It's ten bucks, and it's, well, not the grandpa of RPGs, more like the weird-uncle-your-mom-doesn't-like-to-talk-about of RPGs. Okay, so it's got some flaws, and aged like hell, but it's still a pretty solid game. Like most Molyneux projects, it feels planned and thought-out. It's smart, clever, and a lot of fun, and still has a few surprises left in her sleeve.

Excellent puzzle platformer with minecraft-y level design where you have to use a combination of 4 different kinds of cubes to get from point a to point b. you place cubes on special tiles in the level which accomplish different tasks (red is just a block, blue is a key/activates things, purple reduces gravity in a set area and green moves a limited distance) all on levels which are surrealist and floating high up in the stratosphere. the style of the levels almost remind me of the temples from Journey or Abzu and the soundtrack is a nice mellow ambient that is repetitive but manages to not get obnoxious (minus one or two levels.) some of my favorite parts of the game would have to be the shadow underneath your character, which, for anyone who has played a first person game where you can't see your feet, this is a godsend when dealing with narrow ledges. another great part about it is the ability to "break" the game as i call it, or manage to escape the bounds of what the developers intended to be the playing field by finding a way on top of the level and finding all sorts of easter eggs or finding new ways to bypass entire parts of the levels just by using a little creative thinking.
all in all a great game, and plenty of community levels if you're into that. give it a shot if you're a puzzle platform fan

Very slow movement speed, "puzzles" based on parkour and dexterity rather than actual thinking (and no quicksaving, so if you fail you're set back about five minutes), and puzzles based on finding hidden objects rather than actual thinking.
The game does a poor job at communicating the puzzles to players:
* Very unclear connections, SO MANY "mystery buttons".
* You can look on the ground (sometimes) for connections leading into devices, but they don't change color when the device is activated (like an antline in Portal), so it's hard to tell whether the button is actually pressed. They're also nearly the same color as the walls and floors anyways, so you really have to squint to follow them.
* It doesn't help that the game intentionally hides buttons.
* ...as well as the cubes you require to solve them. It's possible to look at a puzzle, find it to be impossible, but then look in a random crevice you didn't think to look into before and find like fifteen red cubes that would have trivialized the puzzle.
* A number of puzzles have BLATANT unintended solutions.
* A number of puzzles don't even use anywhere close to all the cubes.
* Buttons look exactly the same as a completely different puzzle element (red cubes)
* World 2 is very dark for no discernible reason. I could hardly see what I am supposed to do.
* Because there's no quicksaving, few checkpoints, and very very long screen transitions (why?), it's really hard to justify experimentation in the puzzles.
Breaks a number of like, Puzzle Design 101 things:
* Red herrings.
* Trapping situations.
* Hiding stuff.
* Execution-based puzzles.
* Experimentation discouraged.
* No difficulty curve - the harder levels are hard because they have more parkour and hidden objects, not more thinking.
Took a look at the level editor.
* It's a grid/voxel based game, but nothing snaps to the grid by default?
* Doors have the complete wrong origin - if you use grid snap on them they either hover half a unit above the ground or sink half a unit below it.
* Very hard to sketch out puzzles with the ease of something like Portal 2's Puzzlemaker. It takes forever to even get a room set up, never mind an actual puzzle. Controls are very clunky.

It's a decent though albeit short RPG with a flexible leveling system, and a flexible alignment system to look good or evil. HOWEVER there are several downers that will prove annoying quickly.
CONS
1: The flexible leveling system causes your character to age quickly. This means that if you went and maxed out everything, your character turns from 18 to 65, which is not very fun for the gameplay perspective.
2: The aging kills continuity, your character ages, but nobody else does. This means that your spouse(if you married) is suddenly younger than you because you went from 20 to 65.
3: too many visual personal touches than are incorrectly modifying your alignment. Long hair should mean you become more attractive, and baldness a neutral or scary point.
4: It's all too easy to skip something when it sets clicking to further the diologue.
5: There's no controller setting, which is a downer since it could have been mapped or formatted to use a controller which is more ideal for RPGs than a keyboard and mouse.
6: Certain story events force your character to change visuals suddenly(IE getting locked up in prison can get you shaved bald, and the one year passage on the ghost ship in the post game causes you to grow a beard and your hair is changed needlessly even if you have longer hair like the ponytail)
7: difficulty decline. This issue is a pain for any RPG, and a killer of the fun factor. The endgame is supposed to have lengthy battles with insane damaging final bosses. Side quests tend to have an increasing difficulty that scales better than the final boss or bosses in game.
PROs
1: you can define your own sexuality freely. This means you can go around marrying or killing suitors as you please.
2: the flexible leveling system lets you max out your offensive and defensive perks at your leisure, allowing you to max them all out to make the perfect character.
3: Alignment is easy to adjust. If you focused on doing evil deeds and want to turn good, it's easy. If you went good and want to be evil, just kill a bunch of guards until you have had your fill of turning evil.
4: Weapons are up to personal choice! As someone who loves swinging a sword, I like swinging a blade, it's more fun and more epic than lugging around a mace.
5: Customizable character visual. Tattoo vendors, barbers, armor and weapon vendors allow you to pick your ideal style(despite limitations).

Boy how do I describe Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube? I guess the best place to start is  with the objective of the game. Your overall objective is to find cubes throughout the level which are needed to not only traverse the levels  , but also to complete puzzles in each of the levels. There are 6 worlds each with 6 levels in them for a total of 36 levels. In each level there are only certain places you can put the cubes marked by golden squares on the floors, walls, and chillings in each level. Now some of the cubes are hidden while others are in the open. Also the cubes themselves come in variety of colors such as red, blue, purple, green, and occasionally white. Each cube having a unique property except the red cubes. The blue cubes open doors, the purple ones have a gravity less field around them when place them, and finally the white cubes are used to activate portals. Now you use a combination of these cubes to traverse the world and solve puzzles. There is a secondary objective to find the  golden pyramid hidden in each level. The pyramids themselves don't do anything, but you will need to find them if you want to complete the game.  Next is the Story.
There is no story. No I am serious. I have looked everywhere and I can't find anything about any kind of story in the game or on the internet. This isn't like a Soulsborne game either where you have to piece the story together. There just isn't one. Which is said since I really enjoyed the many of the aspects of the game such as the soundtrack and atmosphere of the game,  but I'll take no story in place of half backed one any day of the week. With the being said this game isn't going long for you to complete it, and while I enjoyed the puzzles. Trying to find the golden pyramid pieces gave me an extra incentive to keep playing the game. With that being said not matter what you choose to do this game isn't particularly long. I complete the game can be completed in 40 hrs, and beat in 20 hrs. Overall I did enjoy my time with this game, but don't be looking for a deep or hard game. I would recommend it to anyone who likes puzzles games that aren't to challenging or looking for a nice game to chill out with

I recommend this game to anyone that has an interest in shooters like this game.  It is very casual, fun, but still requires a bit of skill to play.
there are 4 modes:  free for all, team free for all, chase the rabbit, and invasion.
In my opinion invasion mode is the bread and butter of the game.  The objective is to fight waves of enemies and survive as long as you can.  As you advance higher in waves, the enemy count and difficulty gets higher as well.
The gameplay in my opinion is pretty solid, i use a xbox1 controller, you fly automatically, there is no acceleration or stop button.  The other button is to shoot.  The skill part comes into play here in that your bullets travel slow, so you have to predict where your enemy might end up at and shoot in that direction.  Or here is where the dog fight comes into play and you chase the enemy and shoot them from behind point blank-ish.  Both ways are viable.
Another interesting mechanic is that you can fly off screen and end up on the opposite side, for example: you fly towards the left of the screen and then you end up on the right side.  This brings in some tactical play because as you progress higher into the levels you will need to utilize this tactic.
There are occassional item drops as you play that grant you weapons and shields.  So this gives you some variety in gameplay.
As for cons, the gameplay is a bit slow for my tastes, but is kind of necessary for a game like this.  Would like it if there was an option to increase gameplay speed.  Not much in the variety of weapon drops either, I would love to see more.
From a singleplayer standpoint it is a fun game, but can get boring, this is somewhat remedied with AI allies.  This game was really meant for multiplayer because I can see a lot of fun and excitment with friends.
As for pricing, id say it is a bit high if youre playing by yourself, id wait for a future sale.  But for multiplayer it is definitely worth the price.
overall game is very fun.  I hope this review helps you decide.

Deadfall Adventures is a fairly by-the-numbers shooter. You can only hold two guns, you can only take so much damage before BLOODY SCREEN takes over, and there's puzzles that are sometimes so obtuse I had to resort to YouTube videos. Thankfully there's a difficulty for combat *and* puzzles so you could probably put the puzzles on easy so you can get back to shooting the various baddies you fight throughout. There's also an interesting mechanic of using your flashlight to take out mummies in the latter parts of the game, which is cool but sadly done much better in Alan Wake.
The Farm 51 clearly made Deadfall with influences from not only Uncharted, but adventure fiction as a whole. Like one part involved the player riding minecarts through a lava-filled ruins shooting baddies, which made me think The Farm 51 *really* liked Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. I mean, the protagonist is a descedent of Allan Quatermain, which is a bit on-the-nose here.
The problem is this game has the patented Eurojank(tm) technology, where the game will bug out in many ways, such as weird ragdolls, getting stuck in places, having 3 guns when you're supposed to only have two, and lots of non-native English speakers saying English with awkward accents. Bonus: this is an Unreal Engine 3 game, so hope you like texture pop-in when you load from checkpoints!
In terms of Uncharted derivatives, where Tomb Raider 2013 is on top and Unearthed: Trail of Ibn Battuta is at the very bottom, Deadfall Adventures is squarely in the middle. It is not awful, but it's certainly not *great*. Only get it if you have a soft spot for Eurojank(tm).

I haven’t had this much fun playing a game in a long time. Seriously. Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a FPS with a medieval twist from the great minds at Torn Banner Studios. Lets’ get rocking.
The Good
I first played C:MW a few years back and, honestly, I wasn’t too impressed. However, it has come a long way since then and is easily one of the funnest online games I have played in recent memory. The controls are easily mastered and that, I feel, is the key to making Chivalry as good as it is. It keeps things simple and let’s you put more energy into decapitating heathens than into figuring out what damned button pulls out your throwing axe.
The maps are downright amazing. There are no maps in Chivalry that outright dislike. Sure, there are maps that I like more than others, but, you’ll see that with every game won’t you? If you’ve played Mount & Blade you’ve got an idea of how cool medieval themed battle maps can be. Picture that, only 100 times better and with far better graphics. Voila! You’ve got the maps from Chivalry.
The weaponry is great and (for the most part) feels really well balanced. Until you’ve experienced the unbridled joy of hurling a javelin through the face of a roid raging knight in full plate armor and watching him die writhing, you have not really lived. Apart from that, killing people with a flail is also absurdly satisfying.
The playable classes are all fun and all of them are well balanced. You’ll have access to different weaponry depending on what class you choose and your level of armor will vary as well. I personally favor the Man-at-Arms or the Knight, but I occasionally get my Archer on and javelin some fools.
The graphics are good. On low settings, they look just fine. On high settings, they look beautiful.
Chivalry also incorporates Steam Workshop. This gives you access to weapon skins that are player made and a whole new range of maps for every mode of play. Replay value just went through the roof.
The Bad
I don’t have any major gripes about Chivalry at all.
The Meh
Some items can only be unlocked by purchasing them. With little more than a cosmetic change made to your character with  said purchasable items, I’m not really digging the in-game transactions there.
Verdict: Yea
If you’re looking for something new, absolutely check into Chivalry. I guarantee you’ll have fun. It’s not even frustrating when you die because it usually ends up being hilarious. As always, thanks for reading.

This is a weirdly compelling idle game, at least in part due to the various "new game" goals you get when you acheive objectives and reset the world, and the fact that there's more things to do when you're feeling more like actually playing the game. (Triggering buffs and skills at the right time can definitely affect the difficulty of clearing a map or beating a boss.)
The game is fairly generous with premium currency (rubies), and while they'll always encourage you to spend real money to acquire chests for loot (along with dangling a chance at epic gear), it's definitely not a necessity, which is nice.
The variety of formations and character placement within them gives a welcome depth to the game, as placement becomes crucial for certain characters' long-term viability.
Gear can be a game changer, as an epic piece of gear, or a new piece (of any tier) in a previously-empty slot can suddenly change a warrior from an afterthought into a major piece of your strategy.
On top of that, any duplicate gear you find gets consumed and applied as a permanent buff to your character in all playthroughs, which again feeds into their overall viability on playthroughs. No loot is ever really "junk".
To top it all off, the devs regularly (roughly every 1-2 weeks) run some sort  of special event (many of which are more for people who've reached total end game, though not always) or a multi-day buff to a handful of specific warriors, which again makes things worth changing up for people who enjoy the strategy of tinkering with their formations.
This is definitely an idle/clicker game though, and so you'll find yourself actively playing it in short bursts, then either leaving it to run in the background, or closing it entirely (and you'll still gain XP and gold for your game when you do) and coming back to it the next day to optimize your party, then leaving it alone again for awhile.
That's not a bad thing. The fact I'm not bored with this one after a few hours/one completion of the world is pretty amazing to me, and I find myself regularly checking in on my current run.
If you've never tried an idle/clicker style game, this one is really the pinnacle of the entire genre, and worth trying, if you're curious.
I can't recommend this one highly enough.

Noticed that even as an early access, the devs don't seem to care about player feedback. The game is choppy, and graphics poorly drawn (I've seen better jobs done in Microsoft Paint). The engine and server are prone to glitches and drop outs, meaning players experience up to several seconds worth of delays when competing (even on a 100mb/ps cable plan, it still has issues with ping/MS). LAN mode is a nightmare to navigate for the newer players, and there's no "learning curve," just sink or swim. The small amount of fame brought to it by well-known youtubers seems to be the only cash-cow, and a go-to when the game fails to meet expectations (DLC can be purchased for $2.99, and you have a choice of two youtube teams. The winning team has proceeds donated to charity, and they keep the rest...clever, if not disgusting.) As for the gameplay itself, it is fun. It's a great way to kill time for half an hour or so, but the obvious niggles and bugs that haven't been fixed in 10+ updates seems wrong. Random lazer deaths, missed jumps, getting caught on ledges that don't exist, and some smaller issues such as the tackle option being unlimited (to the point a player could lay on the ground and bring everyone to a grinding halt) make the game a throw-away. However, the grappling concept is a lot of fun, and the weapon system seems specifically thought out with help-or-hinder in mind, which I give props to.
At this point, I don't recommend purchasing the game. Maybe wait until they've cashed in their half a million "charity" check, and see what the devs decide to fix?

I've been following this game since it was announced, and I was really excited it got released. I know there isn't much of a map yet, and there are only two trucks, even though dozens of ETS2 truck mods have been seamlessly transferred over to ATS, this game is worth $20. I go back to the 18 WoS games, starting out with Hard Truck and Across America, good old days. Back then we only had one or two major cities and a highway leading out. Now, we only have Cali and Nevada, and things are looking great already. If they are truly planning on adding that much detail to each section of the USA, then it is worth the wait.
I've been known to pay close attention to small details, and ATS has some really nice features so far. The map detail is amazing and the roads look great. So much potential here. There are, however, some things that I think could improve or be changed.
- Speed limits: You see a sign that says 35 but yet the speed limit is actually 30 (very strange).
- Police: I have to admit, I disabled them with a mod. If you go over the limit at all you get a hefty $1,000 fine. A cop could be tailing you and the speed limit will suddenly change, and boom, instant ticket. Do you guys remember the system in 18 WoS American Long Haul and Haulin' in which there was a meter, and when you did something wrong, that meter grew? For example, you are speeding, and the meter grew slowly, and at a certain point, like 40-50%, if a cop saw you or went by you, you got a ticket. They had cops on the side of the road in that game, and driving around, just not nearly as much as you see in ATS. It's ridiculous really. Every 5 cars is a cop, needs to be fixed.
-AI Vehicle Behavior: I really enjoy the AI vehicles, in ETS2 and ATS. You feel like you are a part of the system. One thing that I have noticed in ATS, when you are merging into the highway, AI vehicles don’t really get over like they are supposed to. I’ve seen it a few times, not sure if it is programmed and just not very effective, or what. Here in America, if you are merging onto the highway, vehicles will switch into the left lane to clear a lane for you to merge, and if they cannot, they slow down and give the merging traffic space to get on. I hate trying to get on the highway and a damn camper or something doesn’t give a crap, and I have to stop, making it really hard to get on because I’m in a semi, not a lambo.
-Weight Stations: In America, weigh stations aren’t open 24/7 and have hours that they operate on. There is almost always a light of some sort that says whether you have to go in or you can bypass the weigh station, or a sign will say closed/open. In ATS, you just get a message on your GPS right before you are about to blow past the exit for the station. They need to add these signs/lights to signal the status of the station or make the GPS message happen sooner. Also, I haven’t seen any AI trucks use the weigh station, which was present in earlier games.
These are just some things I have noticed so far, I will probably discover more as time goes on, but I really think these issues need to be addressed before the game grows any more. Less work on the end of things really. Regardless, it is a great start to something that could grow to be the biggest trucking game ever. I enjoy it now, and will keep enjoying this game into the future, and I recommend getting it.

The game is pay to win. There is no end game, and only endless chests or hours of mindless grinding will get you real progress.
The problem is the loot system which works on a 5 tier system: common, uncommon, rare, epic and golden epic. The loot is progressive so uncommon is a better version of common, rare is a better version of uncommon, and so on. There is no choice of equipment - they simply keep the highest tier available and disenchant the rest.
Common, uncommon and rare drop from silver chests, the game's currency which each contain 3 items. VERY rarely a silver chest will be upgraded for free (about one in a hundred?) from a silver chest to a 'Jewelled' chest.
These jewelled chests contain 5 items one of which will be rare or above. EPIC gear can only be had from these chests. These chests are sold 3 for $4.99. Buying chests is the difference between 'I might get the achievements this week' and 'See you in 2025'. Chest purchases also grant you a 24 hour 100% damage increase. Cheap, eh?
What's worse is the Golden Epics. They come with 'flash sales' which appear periodically to try and pressure you into buying them within a 8-10 hour window. They are ridiculously powerful. Many grant 150% bonuses when common items might be 5%. There are ALOT of these golden epics. You'd have to spend hundreds of dollars just to get those that exist right now, and more to get those they add with each update. Power creep is inherent here - they bring out new characters and gear to outdate the stuff you paid for so you'll buy more stuff. It's a hamster wheel of pay to win crap.
What's worse is the dev's have had bugs with the Golden Epic system awarding the wrong things - and refusing to correct all of it even though it's their fault. Even if you give them REAL MONEY for a in-game digital benefit which costs them nothing, they'll still give you the short end of the stick if their crap system glitches.
This is nothing but a mobile phone quality java game that rewards continuous spending and excessive playtime over any semblence of logic, skill, or ability. This isn't a game, it's a money pit.

This game is very similar to Assassin's Creed III in gameplay. If you enjoy that or other AC games you'll likely enjoy this too. In fact I was pleasantly surprised how much it resembled the other games even though this was originally a game for handhelds. Steam doesn't mention it, but this game does have (Xbox 360) controller support. I played it with controller nearly exclusively and it works very well.
It took me 16 hours to beat this game, that includes a lot of getting full synchronizations, collecting stuff, doing all missions. I haven't finished everything yet, so I'd say this game takes about 15-20 hours if you do everything and get every achievement. Compared to the other AC games, which all took me about 30-35 hours to complete everything this is quite decent for a game originally intended for handhelds! The graphics mostly look quite good as well, most textures in particular are really good looking. Faces are still not the most visually impressive but this has always been a 'problem' with AC games. Some of the locations are just gorgeous, particularly the Bayou and the Mayan Ruins.
I liked the soundtrack, though it did get slightly repetitive after spending a lot of time with this game. But I think that is a problem with a lot of games so I can't fault this game too much for it, there is enough variety between locations.
I encountered only a few glitches during my running time and nothing game-breaking, the game was generally playing quite smooth on my computer.
The weakest parts of this game is the writing. The story, characters and dialogue all feel jumbled. It was hard to make sense of it and there's not a lot of depth to be found. In some ways this too is similar to the other AC games but I'd say this game is worse. The characters and voice acting are kind of bland, a lot of people had issues with Connor as the protagonist in ACIII, I never had a problem with him but I did feel like Aveline could have been more interesting. The story also doesn't add anything to the main story arc of the series, which I guess has been screwed up anyway with ACIII (haven't played Black Flag and later entries yet).
All in all I'd recommend this games to fans of the Assassin's Creed series. If you've never played any of those games before this will likely be a decent starting entry, the story stands on its own with perhaps a few references here and there. If you don't like the AC games this game most likely won't change your mind.

On Steam I have been looking for an RPG worth playing. Divinity Original Sin 2 being this RPG.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is a fun and interesting game to play. In comparison to other RPGs its mechanics are both complex yet simple to understand.
One of the pros for Divinity being the combat. The combat has great environment interactions, for example; Fire spells could light oil and create some explosions creating AoE dmg, etc. Which is really an interesting concept I haven't seen in many games.
The customization is also very well done providing multiple options for you to display your character as. However, if creating characters is not your thing there are origin characters which provide great backstories which give you optional dialogue options as well.
However, one thing I find annoying is trying to play the game solo. This is because in my opinion I prefer to play solo (Means I have no friends still ;P). This is really hard to do, however I've still managed to become a lvl 8 rogue but not any further.
In short, Divinity Original Sin 2 is a great interactive RPG and I hope for it's release to be better and more than what we have so far. Thank you for such a great Larian Studios ;)

I love games with an interactive story to them, and this game delivers. While the game will start up with timed scenarios, such as the Mongol invasions or the the 1st Crusade, the interactions in the game are all determined by how you do things.
In this game, I am Emperor Daniel Badass VII, the Christian Viking king who's dynasty has conquered half of Europe, all the Middle East, and most of India for the great Scandinavian Empire. As you go about and make your own country, all the other players will react to your actions, and will influence your family's story through marriages, assassinations plots, crusades/jihads against you, and lots more.
As you get larger, you can set up your dynasty members as the kings of other nations, or as vassal kings/dukes/counts in your mighty empire. Careful though, as they may some day seek your throne.
If you don't like someone, just throw an assassin at them, although if it fails your reputation will be ruined and they'll probably try to kill you now...
Make sure your vassals like you, or they'll join plots against you.
The story isn't just interactive, it's really created by the player in a way no big title game on the market allows.

Out of the different FlatOut titles, while the original is the most simple, looks okay at best and is quite outdated, I always find myself going back to play it. Not out of nostalgia, as I mostly played FlatOut 2 when the games were new, but because the game has elements of realism not found in it's more arcade-y sequels. Your car's alignment will get screwed up, the cars handle relatively realistically and you can't just power around every corner. That being said, this game is quite difficult, and I feel the primary reason for that is the camera. The camera is the biggest competitor here, not the other cars, not your lack of skill, but the camera. To put it bluntly, it sucks. It's either too far away, too close or too low, and regardless of which you choose, the camera's movements will screw with your depth and make recovering from accidents much more difficult.
Good game, awful camera.

This can be an extremely addicting game, if you give it enough time to do so. Right in the beginning, you choose from a decently large variety of characters. To be honest, it's not really that great until you hit level 15 and can start your job change. A job change basically means you get more skills, a new look, and better stats. There are, however, both pros and cons to this game which I will also review.
> Lots of potential time to put into it
> Variety in characters
> Different playstyle, even in just one character
> PvP can be based more off of strategy than pure strength
> Lots of people - lots of friends
> Community is, for the most part, pretty good. Better than most.
> CAN be pay to win (The game's gold currency (ED) can be used to buy items that normally cost real money)
> Trading could possibly make you lose your ED
> Broken economy
> Unbalanced characters (Though, there are character rebalances every so often)
> PvPers who rage when they lose
It's a great game and definitely worth a try. Try not to be too discouraged by it being a bit slow in pace up until level 15 (which you could easily get in 30 minutes) and the broken economy. The variety in characters and even variety within each character should keep you busy for a LONG time. It's easy to make friends, because a lot of people are pretty friendly.

I've been following this game since it was announced, and I was really excited it got released. I know there isn't much of a map yet, and there are only two trucks, even though dozens of ETS2 truck mods have been seamlessly transferred over to ATS, this game is worth $20. I go back to the 18 WoS games, starting out with Hard Truck and Across America, good old days. Back then we only had one or two major cities and a highway leading out. Now, we only have Cali and Nevada, and things are looking great already. If they are truly planning on adding that much detail to each section of the USA, then it is worth the wait.
I've been known to pay close attention to small details, and ATS has some really nice features so far. The map detail is amazing and the roads look great. So much potential here. There are, however, some things that I think could improve or be changed.
- Speed limits: You see a sign that says 35 but yet the speed limit is actually 30 (very strange).
- Police: I have to admit, I disabled them with a mod. If you go over the limit at all you get a hefty $1,000 fine. A cop could be tailing you and the speed limit will suddenly change, and boom, instant ticket. Do you guys remember the system in 18 WoS American Long Haul and Haulin' in which there was a meter, and when you did something wrong, that meter grew? For example, you are speeding, and the meter grew slowly, and at a certain point, like 40-50%, if a cop saw you or went by you, you got a ticket. They had cops on the side of the road in that game, and driving around, just not nearly as much as you see in ATS. It's ridiculous really. Every 5 cars is a cop, needs to be fixed.
-AI Vehicle Behavior: I really enjoy the AI vehicles, in ETS2 and ATS. You feel like you are a part of the system. One thing that I have noticed in ATS, when you are merging into the highway, AI vehicles don’t really get over like they are supposed to. I’ve seen it a few times, not sure if it is programmed and just not very effective, or what. Here in America, if you are merging onto the highway, vehicles will switch into the left lane to clear a lane for you to merge, and if they cannot, they slow down and give the merging traffic space to get on. I hate trying to get on the highway and a damn camper or something doesn’t give a crap, and I have to stop, making it really hard to get on because I’m in a semi, not a lambo.
-Weight Stations: In America, weigh stations aren’t open 24/7 and have hours that they operate on. There is almost always a light of some sort that says whether you have to go in or you can bypass the weigh station, or a sign will say closed/open. In ATS, you just get a message on your GPS right before you are about to blow past the exit for the station. They need to add these signs/lights to signal the status of the station or make the GPS message happen sooner. Also, I haven’t seen any AI trucks use the weigh station, which was present in earlier games.
These are just some things I have noticed so far, I will probably discover more as time goes on, but I really think these issues need to be addressed before the game grows any more. Less work on the end of things really. Regardless, it is a great start to something that could grow to be the biggest trucking game ever. I enjoy it now, and will keep enjoying this game into the future, and I recommend getting it.

Deadfall Adventures plays like a real solo campaign based game of late 90's / early 2k'.
Took me around 8-9 hours to finish, which is "nowadays" considered a long run.
The game has a nice adventure vibe to it, like a mix between Call of Duty, Tomb Raider and Indiana Jones. The scenery and atmosphere is very palpable and immersive.
The engine shows capable of displaying great panoramas with modern technical features. Honestly it's a good looking game even for a 2013 production. The camera movement, the FXs and the weaponry makes it very cool to play and look.
All-in-all, gameplay wise Deadfall is a success, maybe simple, but perfectly executed. There is exploration elements for collectionnist, and it doesn't feels weak, it's part of the game essence. Finally, a skill tree is a nice addition even if it could have affected the game more with better ideas.
Deadfall has its proper identity in my opinion.
Now the game has its many flaws, starting with the terrible characters acting, especially the main one. And not only does he sounds aweful, the dialogs are cringy af, and that actually goes for the whole cast.
Also the animation of characters during cutscenes is mediocre and remind games of 10 years ago.
But those issues aren't a big deal compared to the main problem :
Deadfall Adventures struggles to handle a good rythm of progression because of the puzzles & traps system. Actually those are great gamedesign ideas, but most of the time they are unclear and mistaken for bugs. The pace is totally broken, and the gameplay flow as well because it can take some time to figure out what to do.
Yet we can use Quatermain's journal for help to solve riddles, but they are still confusing even with the hints. The game lacks of guidelines to tell you wether you're doing the right thing or completely lost.
And i'm not mentionning the actual bugs occuring in-game (stuck in environnement elements, keybinding temporarly ineffectiv, fps view weapons doing absurd animations etc) which makes it a doubtful adventure.
In the end, the game isn't all that bad if you ignore the glitches and the horrible puzzles, but even with its strong identity, you wont miss anything by avoiding this game. It's a correct and beautiful adventure fps with a weird rythm approach, a good lenght and some punch!
If you like old shooters with firefights, exploration and riddles, you should consider this game at low price. But expect to encounter times of disappointment.
Deadfall Adventures had potential and ends up being nicely entertaining but frustrating, just like a good hiking ♥♥♥♥s your feet up.

Veteran player of ETS2, and now have played ATS for 18 hours, so I'm updating this review.  Reason for buying: simply because I greatly prefer to sim-drive on US roads, as I despise German highway interchanges and the entire French guardrail industry.
If you have ETS2 and wondering how this differs...well, it doesn't, much.  The new map great by my standards (it's in the US) but it is small.  As others have said, it's probably about 1/3 the size of the standard, non-DLC map of ETS2.  The scenery is far more variant and interesting, but it won't take you long to explore the whole map.  You'll also be doing it in one of only two trucks for now due to licensing issues (third truck is imminent, btw).
Let me add that the scenery is much more alive than in ETS2.  While the map is smaller and I've definitely covered at least half the map over and over again, the scenery is really, really good.  I'm inclined to go back to ETS2 to quantify why I like ATS so much more.
There is a new parking mechanism for job delivery, allowing you to select either the previous hard method, or a "middle of the road" method that pays half the XP (and you can of course still skip for 0 XP bonus).  I'm liking this a lot, and now have even done a few hard parking jobs now that I've had practice with a bunch of the easier ones.
So, if you own ETS2, I recommend this pretty highly.  If nothing else, it gives you some cool new places to drive.  If you don't own ETS2 and have never played this kind of sim, download the demo and give it a try.  A lot of people, including myself, never thought they'd like this sim until they tried it.
Edit:  They've expanded the scale to match ETS2 at 1:20, which makes the map absolutely spectacular.  I've played a whole lot of this game now, and I like it much more than ETS2--as I said previously, ATS' scenery is better, and the guardrails of ETS2 absolutely suck.  There's none of that in ATS, thankfully.

Since there is no inbetween on whether I should recommend this game, so I'll keep this brief.
Two years ago, I stopped playing the game since my laptop died and I couldn't play Elsword. So I come back to the game, two years later with my laptop repaired, and realize there was this balance patch event.
'Balance' with quotations.
And a new character, Ainchase Ishmael -who is now on my list of cool characters-.
So I got back to the game, and realize they got rid of Fossil Readers (you know, the thing that gives you mounts for cheaper).
So I compiled a few things that I don't like and like about the game.
Pros:
- The characters have english voices, Bryce Papenbrook voices Add though you can barely hear him.
- The story quests give you a lot of ED and EXP. Also some dialogue exchanges between characters if you choose whether or not to skip the quest dialogue screens.
- Secret Dungeon Bosses were buffed (especially in Bethma's SD) and some were made shorter (Hamel's SD)
- Added HA Skill Slot which is unlocked with the skill if you do the quest.
- Getting a character to 2nd promotion is easier, so you don't need to grind as much as before.
- Transcendance, comes with an open skill slot and a 15 day B-Slot upon completion. Also, MORE SKILLS!
- Can get a 30-day B-Slot in Monthly Quest supplied by Ariel.
- Can get a Quick Slot Expansion in Monthly Quest supplied by Ariel.
- Get an Adult pet from the start with 15-day Fetch Aura.
- Story Quest in Elder (?) gets you another 15-day Fetch Aura.
- You can now skip Story Quests if you are too high of level for it (but pay attention to the quest rewards and wonder if you should get them or not).
- Levelling up is now a lot more faster (my sister got to level 90 in five days)
- Event Dungeons can become permanent (like Halloween Hide and Seek)
- Character customization poses are cheaper now.
- Achievements were added, you can now get more stuff just by doing random stuff.
- HA quest is easier now.
- Transcendance just requires you to do dungeons several times, mostly Secret Dungeons.
- 3rd Promotions have been announced and yes, we are finally getting Dreadlord the throwing knives!
- The sh*tpost community is baaaack.
- They also made an anime of this game.
Now for the Cons:
- Dungeon line ups are dead, best to party with a friend or guild member.
- Some Event Dungeons require a ticket that can be bought from the Item Mall
- PvP is still broken, I don't bother with it anymore.
- Certain Secret Dungeons open for each day and it's restricted to two dungeons open a day.
- Field Bosses have a low spawn rate.
- We don't have Unlimited Stamina Weekends anymore (because someone spammed an event dungeon like no tomorrow)
- Can't party in Arena (someone abused that too)
- Can't use public chat during PvP.
- Aisha (Elemental Master) can't use Ice Spells anymore.
- Lag spots in Field, makes it hard to do quests in a field.
- Game still uses Item Mall as the Hidden MVP.
- Can no longer buy a costume in IM for 30-days, accessories are excluded.
- Ice Burners still have impossible odds of getting a costume piece (Pro: but they have cubes for costume items now)
- Everything Costume Related in the market is still overpriced.
- Guild Hall upgraded... it now looks rather simplistic.
- Luto's Secret Keys do not count as Secret Dungeon Passes anymore.
- Characters made before Ain have smaller inventory slots than newly made characters (kids these days will never understand the true meaning of (Raven) PAAAIN...)
- Ariel still won't give you that 8+ ammie, even so it's practically useless under the might of 13+ gear.
- "I see you broke your gear, pay us two dollars to repair that." I lost 31 Dark El Shards for that!!!
- Fossil Readers... were removed, PAY FULL PRICE FOR A MOUNT YOU CANNOT AFFORD! [-$24]
However, the game is still fun. Just bring a friend along, make a new character and just mess about in dungeons. Make a guild, make friends... even in the most weird of places and in the most awkward of situations. Because I sure did!

TL;DR: Addictive as hell, not really fun. Get out while you still can. Read summary at the bottom.
Is it fun? I guess. Is smoking/pot/worse drugs fun? In Steam reviews, addictive is often equated to fun. It is not.
Firstly, it's not really a clicker. Your first crusader levels by clicking, but unless you're an even bigger zombie than me, spend your time playing actual games and leave this on in the background. After your first "reset" you will find there is a "auto progress to next area" button, meaning you only have to come back once an hour to spend your money.
And it is this resetting which is the backbone of your gradual enstrongerment. Resetting gives you the titular Idols, each increasing DPS by 3% and gold found by 1%. Linearly. So while the first reset gets you a ~20% increase, this gets worse every reset. But the amount of idols is dependant on you crusader levels at time of reset, so you get more every time. Linearly. Eventually, you have to wait longer and longer for a satisfying shot of "progress", which takes an exponential amount of time.
These Idols can be further used (but not expended) on talents, which do things like "increase your DPS by X% for every critical % chance you have." Ultimately, they are another linear increasing buff to keep you hooked.
The game lures you in by there being "quests", so there must be interesting stuff to do right? The quests appear as that area's flavor text at the top of the screen. They are either downright "kill X creatures", or "get X items", which is just "kill X" in disguise. There's not even a drop chance. Every "quest item" has a value Y so that it drops every Yth monster kill. So it's just "Kill X times Y".
Well, at least you kill them quicker every reset, right? After a few resets, you find that the monsters in the first areas die the same frame they are targetable. Which makes the next one spawn faster! But whether you can kill it in one frame or in one tenth of a frame doesn't matter. Eventually after a reset, you don't need to bother with making the correct formation, your lvl 1 lumberjack can clear everything up to area 50.
Other than quests, there are Campaign Objectives. Every reset, you pick one, which defines the formation layout, which crusaders you may use, what enemies spawn, or other various limitations. Every layout has 11 different objectives, and a "free play" mode. The free play mode gives you Idols, but not rubies, as the other objectives give. Completing objectives is the only real progress you can feel, but some are simply "hard as nails", like "get to area 650".
Every setup(being area + whatever modifiers that mission may have), I decide in five minutes what the optimal formation would be, and then don't deviate from that ever. Subsequent runs aren't influenced at all. All crusaders have the ability "For every 25 levels over and including 200, <Name>'s DPS is multiplied by 4x. This multiplier stacks." Multiplicatively! At level 300, the multiplier is 1K!
Crusader costs are also exponential though, and every 25 levels costs about 5 times as much as the 25 levels before it. And monster keep getting harder (though their gold dropped seems to be linearly dependant on their health). So there is a "limit area" where you're stuck, the monsters beat your♥♥♥♥♥
For this there are XP points! For every 5 hours a crusader is in formation, it gets an XP point, increasing its damage by 100%, linearly. XP points are lost on reset. So if you wait 5 hours, you can get a few areas further! You can theoretically get any objective by waiting long enough! You know, just really, really, really long. We're talking months. The optimal way is thus to simply reset as soon as you reach this limit area. But then you won't beat the objective :'(
Because now we get to what every game needs, money. There's an ingame shop where you can buy gold chests. These reward random drops, hopefully a gear upgrade for your crusaders. But if the gear is equal or worse it gets disenchanted, giving enchantment points to the crusader the gear was for. Which give a 20% dps buff. Linearly.
Other things in chests are Buffs, such as "increase crusader DPS by 100% for 150 seconds". If your limit area is 200 while you want to reach 300, it is nearly useless. You progress a few areas with the Buff, then lose it, and monsters beat you back to the previous area. The only thing to do is keeping yourself buffed all the way to the target area. And if you run out of Buffs halfway? Well, that's what the shop is for! So that you can abuse the Gambler's Fallacy of not having "wasted" those 100 Buffs, you buy 200 more! Ah, but just that one buff isn't enough, a DPS increase simply increases your limit area by about 10 areas. Activating multiple of the same buff lengthens its duration, but doesn't increase its effect. Though you will probably need that anyway, as you can't beat those 10 areas in 150 seconds. So you also use the common 200% buff, the rare 400% buff, and the epic 800% buff. And then your limit area is still below the target area. Too bad. Clicking with the Clicker crusader in formation might get you what you need, but there are simply a lot of objectives always out of reach.
The game 'gates' the objectives for this reason, to not overwhelm new players. Objectives have "must have 15k+ idols" in their unlocking requirements. But then you check the forums. And see that you need at least four million idols to reasonably do this. Imagine all the people with 15k idols futilly trying this objective.
But at least there's a goal post, right? Eventually, you must have finished everything, right? Don't count on it. There are 8 campaigns and counting, and there is an event campaign up about every month for two weeks. Also, most campaign objectives have a level 2, and even level 3 version, unlocked by talents. The idea is mostly always pretty simple, raise the numbers! Did you have to reach level 400 in the level 2 objective? Reach level 600 in the level 3 one! And have a few extra debuffs as well.
In an event campaign, you can unlock new crusaders that can switch places with existing ones, picked so that there aren't overly OP combo's. The event campaigns have level 2 objectives as well. Event objectives require a resource which you get automatically during the event. As such, you can usually finish a campaign level and about 6 free plays. Getting you X golden and Y silver chests. Which contained only crap gear for the event crusaders. Bummer. But you can buy these Event chests during the event in the shop too! Just buy an arbitrary number and hope you get the gear you wanted! Available only in this limited time! Buy now!
There are more timed offers, giving unique items that are not otherwise attainable. These bring a 40% buff to that specific crusader compared to the best possible non-paid item. Such "golden epic" items are also given when purchasing any number of gold chests with real money. But again, a linear buff can only get you so far. Like 2 areas further. Woop woop.
Also, there are Daily Quests and Missions. Daily quests are either "kill X monsters/bosses/progress X areas/Level up X times" which you do automatically, or "click X times". They reward rubies. Usefulness is thus not so big.
Missions let you send off up to half of your crusaders. They all have a bunch of flags, and mission succes chance is dependant on which crusaders you send. Seldom gives you gear upgrades, but you have no control over what missions you get. You just go with the flow.
---
Stuff being addictive isn't bad per se, if fun. (South Park ho!) It has a buttload of mechanics, way more than other games in the genre "incremental games", but they all offer linear increases in the onslaught of exponentialness. The ever increasing amount of content is rife with mechanics made to either addict you or pressure you into spending money.
And it's Always Online. Downloads lots.

Major cons: those of a direct console to PC port.

In sum, a great experience which I hope Square Enix will renew.  Intelligent ghost based games not focused on blowing everything away are scarce. The foundation of this game has a lot of potential.

What we have here is a failure to communicate... with the simulation timer.
The story in Assassin's Creed: Liberation HD is incredible, I honestly don't understand how they started it off at such a low price originally. The persona (character) options also make for an interesting, realistic experience.
The problem is the simulation timing is off. There is a dizzying, herky-jerky, pause every other second, almost as if the frames are being rendered faster than the game mechanics can react. Every minute or two, it gets so backed up that it even loses input response. Many times I had my kill or jump timed perfectly, only to have the controller become unresponsive momentarily, leaving me able to do nothing but watch Aveline's ragdoll corpse jostle about.
It is worth noting that the story kept me playing all the way through, but it was only my 30 years out of 35 in gaming experience that kept me from hurling up my lunch evertime I played. Suffice it to say, a controller was nearly laid to rest from the frustration of this unlikely game engine glitch.
And before you blame my hardware... An MSI GT70-2PE Dominator Pro, with its NVidia 880 and 8GB of Video RAM, should be able to hand this 1 year older game, with the ease of pilfering confectionary treats from a prepubescent child (like taking candy from a baby).
Addendum (One week later):
Having completed the game, I can guarrantee that the story is wonderfull, however the game suffers from egregious annoyances such as enemies attacking before they can be targetted, attacks from literally invisible enemies, random hangs when reloading guns, random roof edges in open, flat areas, and the previously mentioned severe lack of smooth simulation timing. These annoyances continue throughout the game.

When they say "adventure game", you expect puzzles there. This one's gameplay consists entirely of hunting the scenes for interactive objects and then picking one of them by guessing the scriptwriter's logic. This is not a puzzle game, this is a casual time-waster. A shame, because the characters weren't bad.
