I wanted to give this game a positive review but I can't bring myself to.
For how I'm one all for unpolished games and raw gameplay, this is just clunky and unfun.
Full of invisible walls and obstacles, graphic glitches, unforgiving bugged traps that force you to repeat the same section of the level countless times, the lack of a saving function; the artificial intelligence, even at the hardest difficulty, leaves A LOT to be desired (and ALOT to desire too), in a way that the enemies will often hide with half their body popping out from the "cover".
The weapons are imbalanced in a way that whether you're using a luger or sniper rifle, you can kill an enemies on the other side of a stadium with a super accurate headshot in one hit, no matter what difficulty level you're playing.
Furthermore, which I don't really care for but other people do: coop means coop survival, there is no longer the possibility of playing the campaign in cooperative mode with a friend.
The graphic is okay for a 2013 game, the sounds and the music too, the voice acting isn't the best one but is acceptable; even though some lines are cheeky on the paper but fail to have the same verve due to a rather amateurish voice acting, they still add up to the improbable story about nazist and supernatural forces.
The puzzles and the slight customization of the character add up to the total value of the gameplay, motivating the player to look for secret areas and such, but a worse-than-mediocre gameplay shatters everything positive that this game has to offer.
If you need votes:
Graphic: 6/10
Sounds: 6/10
Gameplay: 5/10
Longevity: stillhavetofinishit/10
Overall: 5/10
I do not recommend this game, perhaps only if you're a casual gamer who wants to have some relaxed fun with a very easy FPS; even then, be prepared to tolerate sporadic glitches and unfair forced repetitions.

You’re cast as one of these survivors, a ranger named Artyom, the hero of Metro 2033 returned for another valiant adventure. Artyom, along with his group of survivors -- and innocent bystanders in general -- find themselves caught with increasing frequency in the middle of warring factions in the metro, a situation made all the more dangerous and untenable by the mutated creatures that live both in the tunnels and on the surface.
Metro’s world is tangibly dangerous and rife with terror, with a feeling of risk and foreboding around virtually every corner. The political thread that connects everything – how surviving factions lucky just to be alive could still be at each other’s throats -- makes the situation that much more interesting. + Amazing setting.
+ Strong story / storystelling.
+ Considerable production value.
+ Good Gameplay.
+ Survival horror has returned.
+ Immersion.
+ More than 1 ending.
+ Unique enemies


- Questionable enemy AI
- Awkward addition of nudity
- Stereotypical shooter boss battles
- Occasional technical hiccups

This game almost takes pysical strain to make progress.
1. There are invisible walls everywhere. Try jumping up onto a low rock. Invisible walls everywhere.
2. It is obtuse. There will be a crate that you could climb onto and move on. However you can't climb onto a crate. You have to do a puzzle to move on. Most of the time, the puzzle clues mean nothing. Either you trial and error them or google them.

7. Almost every room needs a puzzle to get out of. Almost every puzzle is really aggravating.
8. It looks like a shooter with a few puzzles. Wrong. It's all puzzles and less shooting. The relatively noce graphics do not lift the game enough.
9. Checkpoints are far from fair.
10. The character has very little stamina unless upgraded. Upgrades come by finding treasuers which you use for upgrading. Meaning you have to scour everywhere. Some treasures will be left after just getting fed up trying to collect them. It really means that you are in a constant pushing wrangle with your keyboard to get character moving when needed.
It feels as if this game is physically pushing you back, while you're just trying to play it. All you want is a cool adventure with some shooting. I thought OK give it a go. Why would you want this game?
It's a galaxy-wide RPG. You progress, and you can really feel how you and your ship get better and stronger. You can explore unknown planets, and that's very thrilling to discover an 'anomaly' and land on the surface, not exactly knowing what you'll find there. You mine resources, and it's easy and fun. You hack sophisticated systems and get money. You build relationships with people, basing upon your speechcraft and charisma. And, you fight with constant confidence in your strength. There's no enemy you can't defeat. You're a hero.
It's hard to find balance between traditional RPG style and casual gaming. Bioware has found it. The game is not too difficult, and it's not too easy. Result: absolutely comfortable experience. You can play for hours and not get tired. Add fine graphics to it, and here you get the recipe for a game that just won't let you out.
For such an absorbing thing, it's just painful that it is so extremely short. I tried as hard as I could to extend my being in there, but it still ended after 33 hours of gameplay. Suppose we take good old Skyrim for comparison, which has the same open-world structure and shares ME's approach to quest lines; it's about 150 hours per character. I really wish I could stay that much in the game I'm reviewing now.
I'll sum up my recommendation as follows: having played this one, I will definitely buy Mass Effect 3.

This is an idling game that seems to have a lot more strategy than other idling games.
You will typically, unwittingly at first, pick out a character to be the DPS unit. Then you will position buffing characters around them, and other buffing characters where they fit. Then you take them through different tasks which are semi-difficult to get through. After each task, you soft reset while gaining 'idols' which grant you 3% more DPS each and 1% more gold each globally.
Each weekend/holiday they implement a themed event, which is great for peaking everyone's interest. The new events will often grant buffs that will help you to push through an area you were having difficulties on, or even have new characters you can win. The winning of new characters really gives the feeling of progression.
Each character can hold 3 pieces of equipment, and each item is a better version of the previous item. There are plans set in the future for new rules on crafting items you are having trouble finding, and even crafting those items into Legendary items which can be upgraded to infinity.
This game is a great distraction. But I have found that after I set up my formation after a reset, that I do other things and come back to this game to spend gold on my DPS character every 30 minutes or even a few hours.

First-person puzzle game.
You have to get from the beginning to the end of the level using the different features of several different types of cubes. Unlike DOOM (1993), in which you had to fight enemies while activating switches and getting colored keys to open like-colored doors to access more of the level until you reached the end of the not-really-3D levels, Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube levels exist in a fully-3D world in which you must use cubes to construct platforms to reach other areas, approach bird-like structures which unfurl their "wings" (I'm unsure about the function of these bird-like or spaceship-on-the-ground-like structures at this point), and, eventually find your way to the shining white exit region.
Instead of baddies, your primary enemy (other than the puzzles themselves) in this game is gravity; the levels (at least in the first world, the last level of which I'm close to finishing) are constructed of stone cubes and other structures suspended in a void of some kind. The lighting and shadows are really beautiful, but falling through a gap or off a ledge will restart the level or load the last save point.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys first-person games, and especially to those who enjoy solving puzzles.

I bought this game noticing it was on sale recently on Steam, as I'm a fan of good endless runner arcade style games (the last one I got was Race the Sun - which is MILES better).
The story is awful, and the English translations (I sincerely hope English is not your first language as a dev) are deplorable. There is nothing more to say here.
The graphics look alright, but that's not what I look for in an arcade style game like this - I want something quick and fun for when I have 5-10 minutes to kill waiting for someone, or want a game to pass the Steam Controller around with while talking with friends.
The music and sound effects are a pretty bad fit too. The cannon doesn't feel like it has weight when fired - it sounds like a pop gun. The music sounds like someone just pirated some random instrumentals and threw em' together. I'll never forget infiltrating the prison of 'Windopolis' - a situation one would expect to be fairly tense - to.... Luau music???? I thought I was sitting on a beach in Hawaii.
The gameplay is slow, and more importantly, BORING. Your airship will control like it is flying through molasses rather than air. Every level in the story mode is extremely repetitive.
The Endless Mode, which really should be the bread and butter of this game, manages to be even worse than the story mode. I don't know if the difficulty never increases, or if it just takes a really long time, but 15 minutes of just dodging the same floating walls/debris over and over again collecting gears and speed up power ups that barely make a difference is... well, it's not interesting to say the least.
To put it simply - the only way I could end Endless Mode was to ram myself into obstacles repeatedly and die after I was bored to tears. If this game really has this positive of a reception, people must have really low standards - be wary of the positive reviews here.

I'm only two worlds into the game but, well, there's already a laundry list of problems.
First off, the game is barely a puzzle game. It tries to act like one, but a lot of the game is jumping, and a lot of the jumps are kind of terrifying, since you can barely make them, and a good number of them are over death pits where falling means back to the last checkpoint.
That's the thing, what's up with the checkpointing? Why are there so few per level, why are they so far apart? It really makes no sense. You end up having to redo a lot of stuff if you die between checkpoints, and it's just... really tedious. Really unfun.
The game also seems to want to make you explore to find secrets, but also punishes you for exploring by killing you a lot if you try to explore? It doesn't work out.
The puzzle design itself feels really clunky; I'm rarely sure whether or not what I did was the intended solution or not because it feels so janky and off. Sometimes I feel like I'm breaking a puzzle and I actually am, other times I do a similar type of puzzle-breaking that turns out to be the right solution? It's so confusing.
The game also has a major oversight where it tries to make you lose cubes by having indentations where you have to put a cube in, but a lot of the time you can stand on the ledge above it, go just far enough out, and grab the cube from inside the indentation, thus generally giving you an extra cube to work with. And I doubt this was intended, but, hey, it works.
There was one puzzle where the solution was literally just a hidden passage that let you skip a door that would otherwise require a blue key block to open. So that's... something.
Also, there's fall damage for some arbitrary reason. Another one of those anti-exploring things as it's never been relevant in a puzzle yet.
The basic mechanic of this game, even, is just... kind of dumb. There's an arbitrary limit on how far away you can grab stuff, where it's too far to be "realistic" but too close to be "useful". It feels like an arbitrary limitation that only exists to make puzzles more tedious.
Another arbitrary mechanic. It's really picky about where you can put blocks. You can't stack blocks down, at all, unless you have a deep enough angle under the blocks. Not just "a bit below" but "standing under". So sometimes you'll end up needing to stop what you're doing, go back down and put a block under another block, then come back up to continue onward, because of this completely pointless limitation.
You also can't place blocks in a bridge in front of you, so yep, go back down, walk to the other side, stretch the bridge out... doesn't this sound tedious as heck? Believe me, it is.
And even then... the game runs out of interesting things to do with its basic block building mechanic about one world in. Yet still continues to reuse the same slow building puzzles over and over, for... some reason or other, I really don't know.
This is just two worlds' worth of experience and I highly doubt it's going to get better but I'm inevitably going to end up playing more so I'll update this later... I just, already had a lot I wanted to say and definitely wouldn't recommend this game based off what I've played. There's starting out on the wrong foot, and then there's not having a right foot to start with, period, and this game... seems to be the latter.
World 3 update: The game introduces a low-gravity hi jump mechanic... that's horribly inconsistent and I can't figure out why jump height varies so much. Getting stuck on ledges also becomes a thing. The rest of the game is pretty much the same tedious schlock. I'm not sure I can keep playing much further, honestly, this game is just a special kind of unpleasant.

To recommend or not, that is the question. I really enjoyed parts of this game, but it has some major issues. I recomend this only if you get it for less than $5. On the plus side - visuals are wonderful as is the fun ways to upgrade and get new ships. You can expand into the galaxy and explore to your hearts content. You also have factions that will attack you depending on how your relationship is with them. You can even bribe the UTA faction to get past gates. The simplistic gameplay is easy to figure out and fun to swap out with different ships to see what works better. One small paragraph about how fun this game can be.
Now here is the bad news. It's grindy. VERY grindy, from factions to currency, to getting new ships, to upgrades. Lets start with faction grinding - the only (well main) reason why you would want to get to positive is to buy ship upgrades. I am in act 3 of the game in the inner core world area and so far it makes no difference if you leave a sector with the Civ's or UTA positive or negative. Later in the game you meet the bounty hunter faction. In certian areas (seems like all of them really) if you kill anyone, enemies or friendlies, you will get a bounty for it. About 1/4 of the missions also have bounties attached. What does this mean? It means that if your bounty gets high enough, you may get surprised in a mission with a bounty hunter attack on top of regular guys on that map. It also means that as you leave a sector, if your bounty is high enough, you may be asked to pay a ransom of sorts to not be attacked. If you don't pay you will get ambushed and attacked. To prevent this you have to pay off your bounty at any of thier HQ's in a direct Rez to bounty conversion. You can also buy 'respect' which is basically a level of friendliness toward them. That costs twice as much rez and is not worth it. Civ and UTA factions, once you are neutral, allow you to gain faction by paying with 'goons', or your spare crew. Regaining your crew generally takes a long time. Sometimes a quest allows you to gain faction rep. However, I have found that in some sectors, I needed UTA rep, but no matter how long I kept jumping around in that system hoping for a quest that would give me their rep, it never came. TL;DR - lots of factions as worthless mechanics in the game and are nothing but grindy.
Now the next is ships and ship upgrading. The different ships available and weapons you can use are pretty big. However, you cannot get new ship modifications unless you buy them. Some plans are in 5 diffferent parts scattered all over the galaxy. So you are forced to explore. You have no idea where specific plans are or which faction sells them so you gotta look everywhere. It takes a long time. Some plans you will never use, but it is not until you have gone through a hefty number of hours in the game when you will figure out what upgrades are actually useful. All ship upgrades cost Rez
Next is getting new ships. Some are worthless and some are quite the tanks. Some have lots of firepower but have less crew and hull strength. The problem is that you have to destroy a new ship to get 'plans' for them. Bigger ships take more plans. Once you have enough then you can make them. This is fun, but still a bit grindy. Sometimes those bigger or newer ships kick your butt and you cannot get the plan on that mission. Sometimes those ships do not appear in the same sector after many missions.
Next up is the leveling. First aspect is that unless you are at least 5 levels above what that area is, you will have major trouble.  You HAVE to stay above the curve or you will get destroyed. Which means more grinding for rez and crew to rebuild your fleet. The other aspect is the points per level you gain. You always get 3 research points for every level up. Early on, the points roll in and you can get new research for your ships quickly. Each research upgrade (like shields or engines) costs 1 research point per level. So a level 1 Cannon costs 1 point, a level 2 costs 3 points (1+2) and a level 6 costs 21 points. It takes a ton of leveling to get a research area maxed out. The problem with this is that you cannot be a 'jack of all trades'. You have to stick to one type of research upgrade. So it is cannons or beams, not both. Bombs or launchers. Shields or stealth, etc. The last aspect is the leveling points themselves (called data). This is like every other game where each level you gain takes a little more points than the previous one. However, coupled with the research leveling, getting a strong ship takes a long, long time.
Next up is the main currency (Rez). If you make mistakes and run out of currency, you have to go back to a mining facility and gather, gather gather. Unless you have a ship with a huge cargo hold and preferably 2 large tractor beams to gather the rez, it will take a long time. Later in the game you have a reserve of 10,000 rez and it can get depleted quickly. Regaining Rez, even at a mining facility that is close to your beacon (cargo drop off point), will take at least 10 minutes with a very good ship.
So in short - you have to scour the galaxy, stay ahead of the curve as far as ship levels, ship modifications, and research levels. And make sure your Rez and Goons are consistently topped off. The main questline is fun, but the monotony of the grinding makes this annoying at the very least. So I bought this for about $3 and it was worth it. Any more than 5 and I would not recommend.

Mudered: Soul Suspect left me wanting in almost every aspect of the game. I expected an engaging story focused 3rd person game with puzzles and minimal to no combat and in a way thats what you get here, just not well executed.
Graphical Fidelty is mediocre as you would expect from a Console Port and i wouldnt mind if the mechanics and story were up to compensate for that. This almost plays like a hidden object game and its really not interesting. At the end you are supposed to select some of the clues to conclude your investigatoin into a story and a little cutscene tells you what you gathered from that.
Sometimes you can possess a witness where you can peek through his eyes to find a clue on a screen or notepad, influence his memory by selecting a clue you found so that he reveals more information about that or you can eavesdrop on a conversation. The Problem with all this is that you do it maybe 5 times in the game with some effect while the rest of the time, it doesnt do anything at all. Mindreading in Salem is really boring and i hope the real inhabitants have more going though their head than these NPCs.
The Game has two types of collectibles which reveal some lore about your former life or a criminal story. The lore bits about your former life or you girlfriend reveal information one at a time which you can access by going into a horrible menu where you have to click on each piece individually to see what it says. And the Navigatoin of the Menu is horrible, the most basic pc-conversion where using your mouse is a pain, they put no effort into adjusting a system for pc which is badly designed from the start. Why dont you let me just click on this! You just dont want to navigate through this to get 2 sentences about the meaning of your tattoos, or how you met your deceased wife.
The second tye which reveals a little story is even worse, because these are collectibles in a major areas which only reveal their story after you collected all of them. This means you can run around the levels for ages looking for that last piece which extends the game time in a very boring and artificial way. Only some true OCD guys will suffer through that.
And they even have more ideas how to prolong their game time. Sometimes there are areas with demons which can end your undead life unless you sneak up behind them and press a button+mouse combination to ban them. So you jump from hiding point to hiding point to get behind them and banish all of them. This is neither challenging nor interesting, its only annoying because you want to get through this part which adds nothing to the game.
All in all i am very disappointed and if i had payed full price for this i would be furious. It's a turn-based isometric RPG which attempts to do what Sword Coast Legends never did: make a computer game that captured the essence of PnP, complete with campaign editor (not tried yet, since this is an EA review), GM mode and true RPG-freedom-of-choice. It is very similar to RPG's of old, like Neverwinter Nights, Baldurs Gate etc.
I have only completed Act 1 so far, since that's all that exists in the early access version, but I am hooked. The game is a joy to play. Difficult at times, yet rewarding too. It offers true freedom of choice in the way you play and create your character. It features a classless character system so you are free to do whatever you want with your character. It also features various "origin" characters which are kind of pre-generated characters with fleshed out backgrounds (the kind of thing you do yourself in a D&D campaign). You can choose to play one of those or alternatively make up your own and recruit them in game.
There are many ways to solve the quests in game, offering a lot of replay value. Race, "tags" (such as Outlaw etc.) all make NPC's treat you differently and offer various other ways to do things. The co-op gameplay (up to 4 players) has also been specifically designed with this in mind, meaning your party may not always see eye-to-eye on things. This creates the potential for some interesting RP scenarios.
Although the version I played does not yet feature a GM mode or level editor, this looks to be the icing on the cake and could significantly increase play-time. They will also offer Steam Workshop support for "click-and-play" modding.
Now all they need to do is offer the ability to import/export characters...
Overwhelming to begin with, but once you get to grips with the game mechanics you realise just how well crafted this game is. Gorgeous graphics, wonderful sound and music, solid turn-based tactical combat and endless replay value.

I really tried hard to like this game.  I love Portal and The Swapper and tons of other puzzle games, but ultimately this game failed me because the platforming elements vastly overwhelmed the puzzle elements.  I would say that this game is 90+% dexterity, which is way too high for an ostensible puzzle game.  Much of the dexterity consists of precise jumps, which, if you fail, mean you have to restart at the previous checkpoint.  You can't save the game just before a jump; the checkpoints are fixed, and very far between, so missing a jump means redoing a big chunk of the game, which gets really boring really fast.  Also, when you have made a structure out of blocks and are standing on it, very often you have to add a block right next to the block you are standing on, which requires extremely precise control or you will fall off the structure, requiring you to start over, which is just bad game design.  The puzzles (such as they are) are usually pretty trivial; most of the time if you can't solve one it's because you didn't see some place where a cube could go.  Finally, the game is just plain monotonous, and finishing a level feels like a chore.  The graphics are gorgeous and the music is nice and serene (though I ended up turning it off anyway), but the flaws in this game make it not worth your time.  This isn't a Zen-like game at all; it just looks like one.  It's actually aggravating and frustrating.  Perhaps if you consider walking on a tightrope over a canyon to be Zen-like, you will like this game.  Otherwise, look elsewhere.

Metro 2033 takes place in the year 2033 in a world where a nuclear war has occurred.
The only survivors now are living inside the giant metro of Moscou.
Over time Metro’s stations transformed into citys with their own politics.
In this metro there is 2 big factions the Reds and the Fascists their ideologies are basicaly the same as the one of the USSR and the Third Reich.
And also dangerous mutant creatures are living outside and inside of the Metro.
You play as Artiom a young man who lived  peacefuly in the station of ВДНХ until the Dark ones appeared out of nowhere, their regular attack are threatening the survival of the station.
A friend named Hunter gives you a mission before intering a tunnel to check it, in case he don’t come back after 24 hours you will need to contact Sparta a group composed of the best warriors of the Metro to help you and your station to get rid of those Dark ones.
Hunter didn’t come back so you will need to get to Polis to get there it will not be easy of course, but you will see the rest by yourself.
And I will not talk about the story of Metro Last Light because I don’t want to spoil you the ending of Metro 2033.
Because I don’t want to spoil you the games’ characters I will not talk about each individually I will say in general.
They all looks nice you can easely guess their personality only with the visual, they don’t do things that are out of theirs character and they are interesting not everyone but a lot of them.
This is all.
The game’s graphics are realy good I am not talking about 11K textures resolution but the environment’s composition, god it’s gorgeous if you want to see some amazing post nuclear environments try this game.
I love the musics this is just incredible the feelings of loneliness, sadness and hope that are given only by the main menu music...
The overall sound design is magnificent it immerse you completely in the univers, the sounds of the wind outside, the "cave" sounds in the tunnels, just wow.
So obviously I think that the ambiance is outstanding.
The gameplay is realy good the fighting is realy satisfying in this game.
The game have a lot of weapons and some nice customisation possibility.
It’s interesting that when you are against humans (it’s more rare with monsters) you can do it stealthy and it’s fun to try even if sometimes it’s pretty hard.
The game itself is in my opinion "too easy" even on the highest difficulty I din’t get much problem to finish those two games but it was still a lot of fun and the the fact that you can’t see your HUD  (Spartan mod) is an original and cool idea.
Also you will need to be a little patient you will not fight humans every five seconds there is a lot of dialogue that you can’t skip, if get interested by the story it goes pretty fast and it’s enjoyable to listen but I can’t imagine how boring it is if you don’t get in.
During every loading screens Artiom is explaining where he is going and why, it’s a realy good way to easely keep the track of the story and so be more easely immersed in the universe.

All in all a game with great detective story and voice acting, that is poor on usability. The story is also really predictable, to the point when every single "build up" for the next turning point in the story practically has the revelation written all over it from the start. But the detective story mechanics are good, locales are good, there is a lot to explore and a good reason to do it and overall I would recommend this game - at a discount. 50% off or more and a certain buy. You probably won't play it more than once, but you will remember this dark story with a smile.

Elsword is a Korean MMO beat 'em up in 2&1/2D. Here the player controls one out of nine (as of now) characters to level them up and defeat hordes of monsters while progressing through the story.
Unfortunately, I already ran into problems at the level of trying to register an account. Apparently their confirmation emails can only reach certain domains, like GMail. Before I figured it out, however, I already linked my Steam account to the one that I couldn't activate and had to wait a few days for it to expire before being able to re-link it to a working one. During that time my enthusiasm for this game died out completely and it basically set the tone for my playthrough of this. If the creators fail on the level of account creation... That's just not a good sign.
Once we enter the game, the first thing that comes to us is the fact that the English localization team decided to leave the Korean voice acting intact, which is quite unusual for most English versions of Asian games. I personally don't mind them, it's just that it was kinda hard to understand what they were actually saying, me being used more to Japanese.
Speaking of that, I usually like to mod my games to some extent, so I managed to find (by complete accident) a mod which replaces the voice packs with those from different languages, so for example I could try getting Japanese ones into the game, which would keep it somewhat climactic yet I would be able to make out some words out of it... eeexcept the NA version (which is apparently the Steam one) changed the voiceover format from .wav to .ogg. For no reason.
Another thing that stroke me as kind of odd is the fact that you need to name your characters. I mean, it would be okay if they were just classes to be chosen from and you could customize their appearance to some extent, but they are all named characters with unique backstories. Why do you have to call yourself something like "Eve Clone no. 99"? Why can't you just give your account as a whole a single nickname to use for all of your characters?
I stretched out this rant long enough, so let's get to the main part of the review.
The anime-style cell-shaded graphics look okay. They aren't anything spectacular, and can kind of make your eyes tired, especially the low-res textures. While it did take over three years for the game to leave Asia, it still came out later than for example
.
In the sound department, it's honestly mediocre. None of the music felt memorable to me, and you will get tired of your characters saying the same thing over and over again during their combos or victory poses.
When it comes to gameplay, it's pretty much just your standard 2&1/2D beat 'em up but with RPG elements. You level up your character, your skills, obtain better gear, power it up... At level 15 you can advance into one of the three possible paths for your character, each possessing different skills and abilities, and at level 35 you can achieve the final form of your chosen path. And here's where the bad things begin to pop up: even the normal mooks are often tanky damage sponges with heavily-telegraphed attacks, turning at least the early game into a button mashing contest of you just wearing down their HP using the same combos over again. Your chances of dying at anything that isn't at least a mini-boss are basically nonexistant provided you do dodge their blows. You can use special skills which are usually very powerful hits or autocombos akin to supers from fighting games, burning MP in the process which can be gained back by hitting enemies and slowly replenishes itself over time. Also, you get only three item quickslots and four skill quickslots. You can double those amounts... by paying real money. Imagine if in an MMORPG, you had a very limited quickbar for skills and items and had to pay for another quickbar.
Oh, and guess what: after reaching certain levels, you get two new skills... to choose from. Yes, you can get only one of those two. Considering you are already limited to taking a maximum of eight skills with you to any given battle, four if you didn't pay up, this kind of thing heavily limits the level of versatility your character can achieve. Of course, you
get the other skills via a different skill tree...
The worst part is,
Only later did the creators realize that they can grab money off of that new possible restriction.
Also, the costume pieces you get in this game only last so long. After that, you are switched back to regular, unimpressive, plain clothes. I dislike limited-time stuff like this in games in general, since they're just one huge bait. You get used to them, and then they are taken away, like that. If you want me to earn my cool looks later on, then don't showcase them early on, so I will actually be able to see how my character progresses from plain clothing to divine-level armor or something.
The quests are also disappointing. They have the standard story dialogues, with the only difference being that your character isn't a soulless mime who just listens to what others have to say. Most of the quests are your basic "kill X enemies", "collect X items" or "beat X dungeon". Heck, some quests even outright tell you to beat the same dungeon multiple times. Let the obvious grind begin!
What also bothers me is the fact that higher difficulties, for the most part, count as Numerical Hard, i.e. enemies' stats are inflated to higher levels but they fight the same way and it only takes longer to beat them down. Besides that, higher difficulties sometimes add an additional miniboss for you to fight, and that's about it.
Another thing is that, despite it being technically a beat 'em up, it still has accuracy and evasion stats. Why does the RNG get to decide whether or not you hit the monster when your weapon visibly makes physical contact with it?
Since this is a beat 'em up, I wanted to play it on a gamepad, but this game's support for it is honestly pretty mediocre. You still need your mouse to get through menus, and the number of skill and item quickslots (
buying the additional ones!) already exceeds the number of buttons a PS controller (which I'm using) posseses. So you'll have to reach your hand out to the keyboard often.
I can't say much about PvP since I'm not interested in it, but I can already tell that it's not fun. The game allows you to take your gear and its stat boosts into PvP matches, and while it does get "normalized" to not allow min-maxers to build something ridiculously broken and impossible to counter, it doesn't apply to everything. While skill obviously allows you to overcome challenges, the gear is still an important part of it. You'd think that it being a beat 'em up will have some kind of way of purely skill-based play, at least as an option, but no.
Okay, so until now it was only the negatives. What are the positives? Well... the wide variety of characters and their possible classes allow for a lot of experimentation. The bosses are still pretty fun to fight against. There is also a Stamina system which is supposed to lock your character out of dungeons for the duration of the day if their Stamina gets completely depleted, but it shouldn't happen unless you've been playing for a few hours straight. The character arts also look absolutely amazing.
My final verdict? The cons far outweigh the pros. There are restrictions on things that shouldn't even be restricted and certain solutions to things that are just plain stupid. I can't recommend it
you play it more as a side thing for fun, not taking it too seriously and ignoring all of the limitations induced upon you.

The direct sequel to the blockbusting science fiction RPG hit by Bioware, Mass Effect 2 picks up on and improves everything that made ME1 so memorable.
Just like the first game, Mass Effect 2 has a very high immersion factor thanks to givin the player every opportunity to step into the shoes of the now legendary Commander Shepard, a completely customizeable protagonist in whom the player can all but become the savior or the scourge of the galaxy. Thanks to the save-file transfer system, all the major and even a few minor choices the player made in the first game will carry over into this game and change how the galactic community views you and the human race.
The story has evolved quite a bit and at this point in the series is beginning to unfold into something grand and sinister, upon learning that your quarry from the previous game was nothing more than a mindless puppet being used by an even greater threat, the Commander has had difficulty convincing the council of this looming presence (ah yes, "reapers") and is instead being sent out to clean out the remaining synthetic soldiers used by Saren. Until a massive twist in the form of what looks suspiciously like a floating space turd attacks your ship and kills you in the process, but fear not, because you are revived at no small cost by Cerberus, an extremist pro-human organization that is officially labelled as a terrorist group. They explain that the space turd that killed you is related to a systematic series of abductions of human colonies, they believe something greater is at work and that you are the only one who can do anything about it.
The combat mechanics have improved tenfold since the previous game, the cover system is much more fluid and dynamic and gunfights are intense, fast paced and mind boggling. The gameplay factor has also been completely amped up by the removal of the Mako and the horrendous inventory management system that plagued the first game, simplifying the inventory system and adding resources to collect via exploring the galaxy that can be used to research upgrades for your ship, armor, weapons and abilities.
Like the previous game, the dialogue is highly varied, offers different outcomes based on your behavior and adds a good replay factor to the game. Being respectful or a complete jerk adds to a "paragon and renegade" score that can unlock further dialogue options that can make certain missions go a lot smoother, as well as adding a paragon-renegade interrupt indicator during conversations which can make the commander perform a heroic deed or a reckless decision. The choice, and consequences, are completely up to you.
The squad has increased dramatically, with DLCs maxing out at 12 squadmates to choose from on missions. Each squadmate also offers their own personal mission which when completed earns you that particular squadmate's undying loyalty and unlocks a new ability and outfit for them.
However, Mass Effect 2 also has more than it's fair share of graphical bugs that can break the immersion, as well as the occasional game-breaking glitch where the commander floats up to and gets trapped in the ceiling for no expliciable reason, forcing the player to reload their game and avoid the area where it occured. The level design is also far more linear than the previous game, and feels like a bit of a hand holder throughout as a result.
All things considered, with a large experience that can easily max out at over 15 hours per playthrough depending on how much you want to experience the game, Mass Effect 2 is a deserving addition to the series and remains one of the best games I've played. Highly recommended.

Assassin's Creed Liberation (ACL) HD adalah game pertama Assassin's Creed Series yang berada di luar garis keturunan experiment 17 (Desmond) yang juga game hasil port dari PSVita.
Cerita (7/10)
Cerita tentang Aveline yang mencoba membebaskan penduduk kulit hitam dari perbudakan di New Orleands AS. Aveline adalah karakter wanita pertama di Assassin's Creed Series. Semua cerita ada di masa lalu (masa awal kemerdekaan AS), tidak ada Animus, Abstergo, dll, seolah membuat kita sebagai pelaku utama yang memasuki animus itu sendiri hingga selesai permainan.
Cerita Aveline terbilang cukup membosankan karena semua cerita ada di masa lalu, tak ada hubungan dengan masa kini apalagi tujuan utama kita memasuki ingatan Aveline.
Kuil ala peradapan pertama yang sudah jadi ciri khas AC memang dapat kita temui sepanjang cerita, namun artefak yang diperoleh tidak dijelaskan sama sekali untuk apa tujuannya.
Connor Kenway (AC III) muncul sebentar membantu Aveline, namun keberadaannya seakan cuma numpang lewat beberapa menit.
Salah satu yang menarik mungkin adalah plot twist yang muncul di akhir cerita. Biarpun sudah bisa ditebak sih.
Gameplay (7/10)
Dalam menjalankan misinya, Aveline bisa berganti kostum yang mempunyai fungsi khas di setiap kondisi. Lady Persona memiliki tingkat notoriety yang rendah di mata pasukan dan bisa mengakses banyak tempat namun pergerakan dan senjatanya terbatas. Slave Persona memiliki memiliki notoriety yang cepat naik di mata pasukan namun memiliki pergerakan dan senjata yang lebih baik dari Lady Persona. Yang terkhir adalah Assassin Persona yang memiliki noriety yang selalu tinggi (dan mewajibkan kita menghindari pasukan) dengan pergerakan dan senjata terbaik selayaknya seorang assassin.
Aveline dapat menggunakan senjata unik yang tidak dipakai sebelumnya, seperti pecut untuk menarik musuh dan menghabisinya sekaligus bisa dipakai untuk mengayun di dahan pohon ala Tarzan. Selain itu Lady Persona Aveline dipersenjatai dengan payung yang dapat dipakai untuk menembakkan poison darts secara tersembunyi.
Grafis (7/10)
Bila dibanding dengan game terbaru Ubisoft yang lain, ACL mungkin memiliki tingkat grafis yang pas2an tapi mengingat ini adalah port dari PSVita yg notabene adalah handheld game, grafis yang ditawarkan tergolong baik apalagi melihat ukurannya yang cuma 3,2 GB.
Ubisoft membuat ACL HD dengan menambahkan graphic setting dan kualitas yang kalau saya bilang di antara AC Brothehood dengan AC III, ini membuktikan kalo Ubisoft tidak setengah2 dalam mengerjakan versi HD ini.

My first review on Steam is actually a ramble.
I bought this game mainly to complete the collection. It turns out to be the worst I've EVER played.
It's a port from PS Vita; really obvious from the monotonous music.
The first thing that frustrates me is the controls. Aveline, though slimmer than her male counterparts, is much more clumsier. Freerunning through the trees in the Bayou is a pain. Somehow the system can't detect another branch on the other side of the trunk unless you press left or right. The leaves can be hard like walls and nothing can get through. Some of the gaps can be slid under while other gaps, much higher, are simply see-through walls.
Another really annoying thing about the game is the environment sounds and Aveline's sounds. Everytime she hops, or just getting onto a barrel, she grunts or groans. Freerunning through rooftops comes with a series of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ from her. The most irritating sound in the game is the questioning "enh?" from the passerbys. In the end I just stab them when they issue such a sound.
The dialogue in this game is really illogical. No wait, they're ILL-logical. Take, for example, sequence 3. Aveline and Elise both crashed through the fort and "wrecked" the slaves' "chance for work" (more likely to be sold). But somehow the slaves had grudge only on Aveline, and Elise is able to take the slaves back, not to mention giving Aveline a sarcastic sneer of her "incurring gratitude" when she herself had a hand in this. The mentor Agate questions Aveline's loyalty when she came to him instantly upon receiving his message, and then he stole her idea to assassin the governor and gave her an order that apparently she was going to carry out, regardless the order.
The quests themselves are just unreasonably difficult. Guards can detect you with their backs to you. Cutscenes are long, boring and unskippable, and the checkpoints are scarce. Don't even hope for the fast-travel: the "fast-travels" marked on the  map means "ship from New Orleans to the Bayou".
The innovative aspect of this game is the personas. BUT don't get you hopes high about changing persona whenever you want in the quest - impossible.
Don't waste your money on this. This is even worse than AC3. The only game in the series worse than this is AC3 DLCs.

SPaZ is kind of a throwback.  Flying 2D spaceships and accepting missions is a lot of fun, and I have fond memories of other games of this type.  This one, though, feels a little lacking in some areas.  You get a decent variety of ships and weapons, plus a tech tree to spend your upgrade points on as you level up.  There's a big galaxy map, except that all the systems feel kind of the same.  There's only 4 factions (military, civs, and bounty hunters, plus the titular zombies that come in later on).  Oh, and your reputation with 2 of these factions, instead of being global, is system-by-system, and randomly determined.  So, you could hop into a new area wanting to do business with one of them, only to find out they hate your guts, and you'd have to take missions for them (or bribe them) in order to turn that around.
There are plenty of randomly generated missions to undertake, but aside from a few plot-related side missions these are all repeatable and repetitious.  The main obstacles standing in your way are the warp gate blockades, preset enemies you have to fight to proceed to the next system, so a lot of what you're doing is just knocking these guys down to get from A to B.  Sometimes you have to train up and get more resources to take on a tough outpost, but other than that..
The big draw here is the combat, and customizing your ships, outfits, and tech the way you want them.
If you like 2-D spaceship-flying games, this'll be right up your alley.  If not, there isn't a whole lot here that'll change your mind.

The game is fun, and builds up from where ETS leaves off. The only thing that is unclear to anyone looking to buy or anyone that has already bought it is if the additional states will need to be paid for individually, or if they will come in packs like "Midwest". It is still a pretty cheap game for what it offers, and I would recommend it if you are looking for a bit more of the same that ETS2 had, but in a beautiful and vibrant US setting which will be expanded on very soon with the free Arizona expansion. Perfect game for Truck enthusiasts or people who want a relaxing driving game in general. I didn't play a whole lot of ETS2, but will be playing more of this since it's in the US.
Pros:
-New Location to Explore! (The US, the place where trucking stereotypes thrive)
-Finally be able to relieve your fantasies of being an American Truck Driver
-You can do this without the fatigue or stress of being a real truck driver.
-A skill system taken from ETS2, but works well nonetheless.
-You can manage your own trucking company.
-You can customize your trucks and make them the way you want them to be.
Cons:
-Tickets for traffic offenses can be a bit too high and penalizing. (SERIOUSLY, $700 FOR GOING 4 MPH ABOVE THE LIMIT, COME ON!)
-The Traffic AI loves to troll you whenever you are trying to yield onto a road, and as such you could be prone to damage, 10 miles before your destination.
-Hard to get money in the beginning compared to ETS2, but understandable (The US has a bad economy).
-Cops everywhere like its second nature. (Really? You have nothing better to do than stalk a truck driver? Get back to work protecting banks or racial profiling or something)
All in all though, it's a pretty fun game and would recommend anyone who is on the fence to pick it up and try it out. You will almost certainly like it for what it is, especially when you start to mod the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out of it.

Delivers that old-school skill based freeflying space shooter gameplay (say that three times fast) just like the developers wanted and manages to combine it with fast paced naval style tactics in a 2 dimensonal battlefield to keep things interesting. On top of that they shift gears at the end game and throw in a light turn based strategy system on top of it.
Resource mangement can be a grind and a drag at times as your progress comes to an almost literal deadstop because your enemies are simply way too strong for you to even make a dent in their armor. Time has to be spent collecting resources to build ships while buttering up the factions for each system you visit for the tech upgrades they have unless you want to blow their stations to pieces so you can just take it instead, either way you're going to have to stop and smell the roses a few times, more than a few if you lose a lot of ships.
The plot is a throwback to the classic days as well, no "deep" triple A slop here, just a decent story to keep the action going with a predictable unfolding if you pay any attention at all and a great ending to lead into the second game which I am now highly anticipating. Overall an excellent title for anyone who likes classic action, tactics and maybe a small sense of conquest and conquering at the same time.

Originally, this game was made as an exclusive title for the Playstation Vita, but was later ported to other systems, like the PC. Yes, it's a port, and it shows.
It's supposed to be a HD game, but don't get fooled by that. Though the graphics are not ugly, there's loads of examples of low res textures everywhere. But the worst part, is that the FPS seems to be locked at some very low value, which gets VERY straining on the eyes. And that's my #1 issue with this game, it's painful to play it.
The new feature that makes this game different from other AC games, is that the main protaganist can change between 3 different "roles", each with a suitable outfit for that role. The roles are Lady, Slave and Assassin. When playing a certain role, there are restrictions to what you can do, or extra things that role can that no one else can. For example, as a Slave, you can pick up crates and walk past guards unnoticed, if you don't take too long.
Sounds interesting? Well it isn't. It's a good idea that ends up being a barrier, and restricts you.
Else it's just more of the same. This game is often considered as a standalone addition to AC3, so if you've played that one, you already know a lot about what you're getting. Though it isn't nowhere near the size of AC3.
The low FPS is the main reason I'm not recommending the game. But apart from that, the rest is pretty much "meh..." and not really worth spending much money on. If you're still interested, pick it up on sale, do not buy it at full price.

On Steam I have been looking for an RPG worth playing. Divinity Original Sin 2 being this RPG.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is a fun and interesting game to play. In comparison to other RPGs its mechanics are both complex yet simple to understand.

The customization is also very well done providing multiple options for you to display your character as. However, if creating characters is not your thing there are origin characters which provide great backstories which give you optional dialogue options as well.
However, one thing I find annoying is trying to play the game solo. This is because in my opinion I prefer to play solo (Means I have no friends still ;P). This is really hard to do, however I've still managed to become a lvl 8 rogue but not any further.
In short, Divinity Original Sin 2 is a great interactive RPG and I hope for it's release to be better and more than what we have so far. Thank you for such a great Larian Studios ;)

'Deadfall Adventures' could be summed up as a budget Indiana Jones fps, an attempt to do the swaggering setpieces of 'Uncharted' in a genre that usually only the likes of 'Call Of Duty' attempt.
Bear in mind this isn't a full price release, because those games I just namechecked would no doubt give most people unrealistic expectations - which DA can't quite manage, and it also has some flaws while its at it. On the other hand - its quite good fun, tries some different things to most fps, and does have some nifty setpieces.
You play as the great grandson of Alan Quatermain - a fictional character from the victorian times, who was basically the template for a certain hat wearing, whip wielding adventurer with a hatred of Nazi's and snakes....It's a nice setup to the story, as its a "new" character but also one that draws from an established source.
There's ancient civilisations, supernatural doohickeys / creatures, and nazi's to deal with - so far its nothing most people haven't seen before. As a shooter DA is passable - the guns are okay, and the action handles well enough to be reasonably exciting albeit not top notch. Taken as just a run of the mill fps, well...its, er, run of the mill.
But....it has two things that make it stand out. The first is nicked from 'Alan Wake' - supernatural enemies in the game require use of a focused flashlight beam to make them vulnerable to your weapons. As the enemy numbers ramp up later in the game it does get tricky having to switch between powering up the flashlight, and then blasting them once weakened.
The second feature that stands out is...puzzles. Yes - its that rare breed (unicorn levels of rare) of fps - one with a smidgeon of brains to it. Joining the hallowed ranks of King Kong, Singularity and, um, er....maybe a few others, DA likes to mix blasting with reasonably engaging braintwisters. Though in all honesty you don't exactly have to be a mensa member to solve them, but its still a nice change of pace.
Add in a really cool setpiece of a shootout while riding a minecart (can't recall the last game where I did that...dayum, I can actually - it was Metro Last Light LOL), temples filled with traps and a bit where you have to dodge between swinging blades - and you get a flavour thats absent from most fps.
Is it an amazing game? not quite. As I said before: the shooting is acceptable but nothing more, and the story whilst okay is nothing spectacular either. Taken as a whole I found the game to be quite enjoyable, and although it starts off slowly it does get pretty decent as it goes on.
Its a flawed little gem, and worth the price. It looks nice enough, handles fairly well, has alright voice acting, and gets reasonably challenging. I haven't finished it yet, but have enjoyed my time with it (9 hours so far) and would recommend it to anyone who wants something a little different from the very played out COD / Battlefield formula.

Chivalry: medieval Warfare is a multiplayer game, so it basically does not have any storyline, although the creators have added
a small prologue to explain the rivalry between the two sides. In my opinion that was better story than Call of Duty ones (except Modern Warfare and Black Ops).
This game has amazing graphics, beautiful shaders and a perfect quality in particles, all thanks to Unreal Engine's technology. Yes, this game runs with the Unreal Graphics Engine, so you can't have any doughts on the quality of the Graphics. The color pallete is realistic and doesn't bore the eye, unlike other medieval games (for example I didn't personally enjoy the inside of the buildings in Assassin's Creed).
The game's sound effects are perfect, they are like the sound you would hear if you were actually watching a sword fight before your very eyes (and ears in this case). There is not a big variety of music tracks, but A: They are really epic. B: You don't need them, you are playing an online game, which explains the lack of a rich story line, as well. (Read Story)
When you play games like this you really want to have the best controls to use. That's why the Chivalry's controls are what you need. Unlike other games, like Darksouls, in this case the keyboard is your best friend. The controls are perfect and they are exactly placed with the order of usefulness and amound of clicks per match (at least considering my personal play style). There are numerous options to change and the menu is easy to navigate at the same time. I can guarantee you will have no problems choosing your prefrenses. There is only one drawback: there is always a small delay between your action and the knight's response. I believe this is totally normal, because back then they were carrying f*cking HEAVY stuff, but it might take you a little while before you get used to it.

I absolutely love this game.  I'll get the bad parts out of the way first.  Regrettably, I've had to revert to the 2.0.4 version as they release game breaking patches seemingly every month.  I don't know about you, but I can't play a full game that quickly.  In fact, I've never played a full game.  I rarely got more than 50 years in before a patch either broke the game or made it impossible to continue.  Thankfully, since reverting, I'm almost 80 years in and going strong.  It's nice to not worry about a patch undoing all my hard work.
The patches change the base game, usually to bring it in line with whatever DLC they've most recently released.  Which would be fine, but you need to buy the DLC to use the new features (which the AI can use, putting you at a severe disadvantadge).
If you've made it through my rant, wondering how I can recommend this game, it's nearly perfect.  There's nothing like collecting the fruits of a well laid plan.  Marrying the right person at the right time can yield benefits well in excess of the money used to kill those in your way.  Why conquer a kingdom when you can inherit it?  It's far cheaper, and depending on your target (say, Russia) it can take the same amount of time.
Want to breed a dynasty of super diplomats?  You can!  Great generals?  Sure!  Stewards with a golden touch?  Of course!  It just takes a lot of time and patience to find the right people, bring them together, hope they breed, and give the kids the best education possible.  I have two gripes with dynasties.  1. They're all or nothing, either you're a member or not.  And 2. There's no dynastic feuds besides the ones you wage, which isn't as much fun as the AI doesn't feud back.
If you like politics, Medieval Europe, and the Black Death, this game is for you.
Edit: With much regret, I've changed my recommendation to no. Every patch adds DLC only content to the game, effectively breaking it if you don't own the DLC. Oh, retinues? Sounds fun, I can't wait to stop relying on vassals to... wait, everyone else can use retinues but I can't? That's dirty way to incentivse DLC purchases. Features which are game breaking if you don't own it, wonderful. And the newer DLC are even worse, adding vastly different game mechanics that make it impossible to play unless you have the DLC.
It can be somewhat avoided by reverting to a previous version, but it's a hassle. And I find it to be a horrible business practice. Deliberately breaking your product to sell the fixes? What happend to the days when you released a game and patches actually improved it?
I will not be buying any more DLC for this game. The sad thing is I really do enjoy it. But I will not support a game which needs DLC to be playable. Games should be playable in their base state, and stay that way throughout the patching of actual, non-intentional bugs.

A positive review with a major caveat: This is not quite the worthy spiritual sequel to STALKER that it is made out to be.
If you're coming from STALKER, as I am, prepare to be underwhelmed. The game is nowhere near as hard as it's made out to be. I played on hardest difficulty + Spartan + ranger mode and never had more trouble than an average map in STALKER (and to the degree it *is* hard it's usually due to poor design, such as sudden scripted rushes of enemies (especially bad in Last Light), or poor checkpoint placement (also especially bad in Last Light). Anomalies are there, technically, in the DLC, but certainly aren't a real part of the game. The maps are linear. The world is also unexpectedly bright--ambient light abounds. On the surface during the day it's almost sunny--certainly not the oppressive atmosphere I was expecting--and underground it's as if the developers couldn't hold themselves back from placing glowing mushrooms in every corridor. Consequently, though the game was certainly tense, I never felt afraid the way I would exploring a lab in STALKER.

Is this game well-made and one of the best of its kind? Absolutely. However, I do not recommend it. This entire genre of games is designed to be addictive, and these games usually include gambling using real money to buy treasure chests in-game, containing various prizes. I'd imagine these kinds of games have legal verbage that keeps it from being called "gambling," but the premise is basically that of a slot machine. You spend real money for a treasure chest and get random rewards. Considering the entire game is essentially an endless cycle with no true way to win, this is a huge trap for certain people.
Rather than be part of the problem, please refrain from insulting the kinds of people who would spend money in these games, and blame the ugly business practice of preying on people vulnerable to this form of gambling (or whatever the lawyers call this obvious gambling in legalese).
Also, before saying "the developer needs a way to make money because the game is free! Derp derp!" keep in mind that the developer could simply sell the game if it was good enough for people to pay money to own. Also, Patreon is there for donations/backing, and Kickstarter is there if a developer doesn't know if they'll be able to fund their game and get by afterward if the game sells poorly, because Kickstarter will cover the development costs, much like having a publisher does.
Back to the people who fall victim to this, keep in mind that everyone has a weakness. No matter how arrogant and prideful a person may be, whether they realize it or not, they have a weakness. Imagine your own addiction or temptation that gnaws at you. For some people, it's gambling in these games, and indie companies as well as big companies like Electronic Arts know that there are people with this weakness, and it's such a powerful addiction that some folks will spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on these games.
Heck, even more than that. Here's an article about an accountant who ripped a company off and used $1 million of the money he stole to pay for that Game of War mobile game's in-game gambling:
Granted, some idiot is going to focus on the fact that he's a criminal and state that makes this irrelevant, but the fact that someone can spend a million dollars on these games when they're addicting, is evidence that they are unethical to make, as developers are
aware of people who fall victim to this sort of thing, and are hoping to get those players to play their game.
So in closing, although this game is well-made and as good or better than most of the other games of its ilk, it is designed to prey on people with certain addictions to take them for as much money as possible, instead of a developer using donations (Patreon), Kickstarter, or selling the game for a flat price with direct DLC to purchase specific things you want vs purchasing "chances" at things you want (i.e. these chests with random items in them). This is a business model companies use because it nets them heaps more money that selling a game of similar quality ever could, because people weak to this type of game can spend more than it costs to buy a thousand games on Steam.

A very solid turn-based RPG that is inspired by a hybrid of early Fallout series and Metro universe.
Combat is very unforgiving and challenging and forces the player to give a lot of thought to the way they build thieir characters, and the way they approach combat. Since player will often find himself vastly outnumbered and outgunned, quests and combat often offer at least one alternative to a frontal assault, favoring more stealthy and tactical approach including traps, ambushes, psionics or just pure charisma.
While the game can sometimes be tedious with quite a lot of backtracking with bags of loot or series of bad RNG, combat and character progression makes the gameplay rewarding. Finding a unique gun, a stash with good ammo and meds or just winning a fight against all odds by using your brain, patience and all available tools makes the experience really enjoyable.
Learing game mechanics helps enormously in the long run. Since the tutorial covers only the bare minimum the player has to explore most of the features of the game on his own, often quite painfully. For instance, enemies' level and difficulty doesn't scale with the player (like in Skyrim or new Fallout series), so it is possible to wander to a more difficult sections of the caves by mistake (or while exploring) and die immediately to a single trap, a poisonous monster or a stealthed slasher bandit on drugs with a knife.
The game shows a convincing vision of a post-apocalyptic world where violence is lingua franca, crime is prevalent and poverty rampant, however writing and dialogues tend to get dull from time to time and need some improvements. Also, music score could be expanded as it gets repetitive after several hours, but it gets the job done and adds to the dark atmosphere.
To sum up, if you are a turn-based games fan who likes a challenge, or you enjoyed the old Fallout series I strongly recommend this game. For its' price and the content it has, Underrail is a strong pick for long rainy/snowy nights to sink into the world and explore what if has to offer.

I write this recommendation with a caveat:  I don't recommend this game to everyone.  I wish I could put a neutral rating.  Since I can't, I will recommend it for some people.
Puzzler World is a collection of puzzles, such as crosswords and sudoku, similar to the variety puzzle books you find at a grocery store.  There are quite a lot of puzzles, and two modes you can play in.  One mode has all of the puzzles listed in a certain order (like pages in a puzzle book), the other randomly selects a puzzle for you.  Because it's a simple idea, its pretty well implemented.  There's no problem whether you want to go through sequentially, pick out specific puzzle types (like just word searches), or do a random puzzle.
The problem is that the puzzles are very, very simple.  Someone I was talking to looking at the game commented one of the puzzles looked like something you would use to teach a child to use a mouse.  So if you're looking for serious brain puzzlers, don't look here.
For casual gamers who aren't great with puzzles, or for children, it's a great game.  I'd totally recommend it.  I enjoy it because even though there's no difficulty, it takes my mind off things.  But it is very simple, even things like sudoku are sometimes simplified by removing some of the squares.  This is not for serious puzzle enthusiasts.
The interface has some odd features due to the fact that this game was ported.  It is designed to work with handwriting recognition, as well as mouse and keyboard, however the handwriting doesn't work very well with a mouse.  There are also a few minor glitches in the puzzles (such as math puzzles ignoring order of operations).  It's minor stuff, however.
Summary:  Recommended for children and some casual players, not recommended for serious puzzle-solvers.

Although the metascore for the game is similar to the first part in the series, I did not have high expectations for this game, mostly due to the comments on various forum boards. It appears a lot of players did not like the second part and were dissapointed with it.
I, however, enjoyed the gameplay. It took me some time to adapt to slightly changed fight system (which in the end turned out to be better than in Mass Effect). A lot of micromanaging - changing rounds, checking which weapon is better, was removed, and the player is thrown straight into the action, yet still having a full control of his and teammates' actions.
The story is so good, and the characters develop in such a beautiful way - you cannot wait for another mission to end to advance with the story and hear their backgrounds. I imagine it'd be hard to match the quality of storytelling found in the original, and I was delighted to see that the momentum was not lost and that game designers were able to continue this magnificent journey.
The only bad critique that I have to give is regarding textures. While the character faces look absolutely wonderful, some textures look like they were created in Paint. Luckily, these do not show often and it's just a slight annoyance.
Not to speak about some truly humourous stories between NPCs that you can find around the galaxy. Hopeless Turian trying to get it on with the Quarian, Scottish guy down in the engineering making funny comments about current events and mission progress, Garrus talking about his adventures...
I've enjoyed the game thoroughly and cannot wait to get the 3rd installment in the series. Too bad it's not available on Steam.

UPDATE - AFTER A FEW DAYS OF PLAY
ATS does a great job of being ETS2 in the US, which some added features and complications. I enjoy the optional parking challenges, and navigating the complicated terrain, but although the game is a lot of fun, there is one main difference between it, and ETS2. That difference is that ETS2 is relaxing to play, while ATS I feel like I'm on the edge of my seat worrying. Why? Well there are two issues that I feel need to be fixed to change this.
1) SPEED CHANGES
While an accurate depiction of the US, where the speed limits frequently change and aren't always clearly communicated, this game has a condensed version of the map, so the changes happen too frequently, and too quickly. I'll be doing 55, then without a sign, it suddenly drops to 35, and a few seconds late back up to 55. This is just an example, but the problem is, as soon as the speed changes, I slam the breaks... but usually get a fine as a cop is always behind me when it happens. I'm not driving badly, there was just no notice. What happens is I don't watch the road, keep missing turns on the route, and instead focus most of my attention on speed and speed limit.
There is also a speed limiter in ETS2, so you can happily hit max speed on the freeway and enjoy the drive. ATS doesn't allow you to relax like that.
2) FINES
Speeding fines, running red lights, etc. are annoying, but it encourages better driving and works well in ETS2. You advanced notice of speed cameras, so can usually slow in time, but if you don't manage to slow, the fines don't break the bank. In ATS, the fines happen so frequently due mainly to speed issues above, and they are far too high for the early game. For example, you can usually go 5mph over the speed limit in the US without a problem, but if you go 6mph over, in ATS, a cop will slap a $1000 fine on you. Roll not quite far enough into an intersection when turning left at a light and the light changing, and you get a $1400 fine. This is for a job paying only $5000, so many times I barely make a profit.
SUMMARY
I still think the game is great, but I am continuing to due quick jobs instead of buying my own truck, because I'm worried I'd go bankrupt otherwise. Once I have enough funds to hire a couple of drivers, I think it'll improve as they will provide funds to pay my fines.
===================================================================
FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW: American Truck Simulator.
After I set up my company, I was all set to make my mark on American soil. This I did fairly quickly, when I went off-road after missing a turn! The trucks handle very differently than the European trucks I'm used to driving, in terms of power, turning radius and braking ability. Even the mirrors seem awkwardly positioned at first. It takes some getting used to, but after 3 quick jobs with random trucks, I'm getting the hang of it. At launch, we only have California and Nevada, with Arizona coming soon, but it doesn't feel limiting, and is plenty of space to begin with.
Some of the excellent points so far:
- There are police, and I found out the hard way that they are not just for decoration. I sped past one who immediately put on his lights and I got dinged for double speeding fine ($1,000!).
- There are hidden speed traps, cameras and police hiding behind bushes, so you really need to watch your speed.
- It's much harder to watch your speed because your truck can go up to 80mph (so far), but just like real life, the speed limit can drop from 70 to 30, and catch you unaware if you aren't careful.
- You can turn right on a red! I am very happy they added this rule.
- Weight stations are scattered around, and sometimes you get a message requiring you to pull in for inspection. I only had this once so far, so I'm not sure what happens if you ignore it.
- Tumbleweed blows across the road and at first I almost swerved to avoid it. Makes you jump when you first see it.
- New parking options. The locations where you pickup and drop off deliveries are much more complicated to navigate, but when you pull in to make your delivery, you now have three options: Skip parking (no bonus), Relatively easy parking (small bonus xp), and complicated parking that will take a lot of skill, but gives a decent xp bonus.
Overall, loving the game so far, and I intentionally haven't taken the loan to buy my own truck yet, as right now, damages are not my problem on the loaners :) If you enjoyed ETS2, get ATS.

Space Pirates and Zombies. Remember Starscape? This feels a lot like a very well-done and much-improved sequal to Starscape. You fly around different space zones collecting resources that you use to upgrade your mothership, unlock new fighter chassis and build fighters.
So how does it hold up? I think very well. A word about control: Don't bother without a mouse. Personally, there are very few games that require both mouse and keyboard that I will play with a laptop touchpad. This is not one of them. It's a very twitchy game, and the awkwardness of having one hand under my other wrist and having to click both buttons with my thumb is just too clumsy for me.
The graphics are fun. The fighter/shuttle designs are different enough to be interesting, and the effects are flashy enough to be from a JJ Abrams movie.
They make a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at realistic physics, which is not really the rule with space games. That is to say: inertia is a thing, but not the infinite thing that it really ought to be. If you cut your engines, you will keep going but eventually stop. Is it always impressive when a game DOES have realistic physics? Yup. Is it always fun? Nope.  To that point, SPAZ makes it fun.

This game is great.
It's basically a Minecraft Parkour Map, but with:
- Amazing Graphics
- Amazing Music
- A calming feel
I normally hate platformers (except for VVVVVV), but this is one of those exceptions.

THE GOOD
Murdered: Soul Suspect has a fantastic atmosphere and environment design and it is all supported by a good story and each collectible (of which there are 242 in the game) also comes with a flavour text. It creates an really immersive experience. You also get to do some detective work, both in the main plot and for a couple of NPC ghosts in Salem, but...
THE SO-SO
...Murdered's core gameplay is more akin to a visual novel, but in 3D. You look at stuff, you collect information and you solve "puzzles" by putting piece A and piece B together. It's nothing spactacular and probably not for everyone. Also while the game does have 242 collectibles, there is no way to tell if you missed one or have collected everything in an area. People that like to explore may like that, people that just want to collect everything may not.
THE UGLY
The Stealth gameplay where you have to have to evade demons feels incredibly tacked on and unpolished. You go up behind them and kill them with a QTE. If you mess up or get spotted you have to jump between hiding places with a button press until they calm down, at which point you can try again. There is no grace period for getting spotted so you might as well reload from checkpoint because it's faster than waiting for the demons to go back to lurking.
SUMMARY
If the sudo-Stealth segments don't turn you off and you don't expect some action-oriented gameplay, Murdered Soul Suspect is a great experience. It's a little frustrating because had they spent just a little more time on the gameplay, this game would get a blind recommendation, but as it stands this game is still
RECOMMENDED FOR FANS OF SUPERNATURAL MYSTERY STORIES AND PLAYERS WHO WANT TO GET IMMERSED IN A WORLD
