Think 3D puzzle maze and you've got a fairly decent description of this game, but you'd be missing on a few key aspects
Qbeh-1 is a first person puzzle platformer that places the player on a structure floating in the upper atmosphere with only one goal: reach the doorway at the end of the area.  In order to get there, you'll use various cubes to open doors, reduce the effects of gravity, or raise yourself to new heights.  There is no narrative to this game so you'll not find any purpose to your level progression and puzzles really aren't that complicated, but the levels themselves are extraordinarily fun to explore.
Each world is set over a gorgeous sky scape that changes from level to level.  Some levels show bright blue of mid-day, others the darkness of night, and still more the orange hues of sunrise and sunset.  The lighting within each level is built to reflect the setting outside, so you really feel like you're immersed in the level.  It all combines to make a very peaceful game-playing experience.
I felt every level could have been more difficult.  The game practically throws cubes at you, so you never actually have to worry about using your cubes judiciously and picking them up when you're done.  I'd say the puzzle aspect of this game could have been much improved if the game actually made you think about how to build a stairway with 4 cubes, rather than giving you 10 cubes to make your way up.  One or two levels early on actually did make you build stairs with only 3 cubes, and that proved to be a fun and challenging puzzle.
The first world starts you off with only one type of cube that you will use to add to the structure of the world, enabling you to progress to the exit.  Subsequent worlds slowly introduce new cubes and you're ability to affect your surroundings slowly begins to expand.  The difficulty ramps up smoothly as you progress, but never reaches a point that casual players would find frustrating.
I would say that I had more fun exploring the levels than I did actually solving their puzzles.  This game gives you a lot to explore, and it rewards exploration with secrets that you can find in every level.  I was constantly looking for gaps in the wall that were at least 3 cubes tall (that's the size you can fit through) or for ways to jump to higher levels.  I often found myself standing on the wall of a level looking down on where I previously trekked just to see if I somehow missed the hidden pyramid.
Of the secret pyramids I found, my favorite was probably the one that had a switch underneath the floor right before the exit.  There was a small crack in the ground that was barely noticeable, but if you put a cube on the switch, a platform would lower and you could get the pyramid.  However, you couldn't get back up to the exit unless you saved all your cubes earlier in the level, so I felt doubly rewarded for being observant and for being stingy on my cubes!
The checkpoint feature in each level is a bit too unforgiving.  Rather than remember the farthest you've reached, the checkpoints reset to the most recent one you pass, so a small slip off a platform could force you to restart a level if you land near a checkpoint but left all your cubes above you. (This happened to me more than once!)
One caution I would say about exploration is that the game not often but occasionally punishes you for exploring.  A few times I ended up on a platform that I couldn't jump out of simply because all the walls were 2 cubes high (you can only jump up 1 cube height).
Qbeh-1 features a level creator in case you want to try your own hand at creating some levels, or if you want to try what others have designed.  I tried a handful of community-made levels, but didn't like any of them.  Seems like people just want to make levels ridiculously complicated or are just trying to create the minimum amount necessary to get the Steam achievement.  I don't know if I'll ever come back and make my own, but I probably won't play any more anytime soon.
The level selection map has probably the poorest design I've ever seen in a game.  Each world is represented as a cube, and you have to rotate the cube until you find the side that corresponds with the level you want to play, but the cube faces aren't numbered.
There is also a glitch that allows you to use the effect of the purple low gravity cube without actually attaching it to a wall.  I stumbled across this early on but played through the game without it because let's be honest, cheating your way through a game on the first play really isn't all that fun.
The later levels have a lot of empty hallways that serve no purpose to the level other than to increase the time you spend walking in circles.  I like to explore, but a boring circular hallway isn't what I'm looking for.

This game is entirely about discovery, and the developers put a lot of creativity together to present you with a fantastic world to explore.  This game was definitely created with casual players in mind, but I'd say anyone who wants to play a relaxing game with beautiful atmosphere and puzzles nearly reminiscent of Zelda would enjoy Qbeh-1 immensely!

I picked Metro Last Light and Metro 2033 redux versions on a Steam sale for dirt cheap ($4.99 each) and actually didn't boot up Last Light for almost a year because I was preoccupied with other games. On the one hand, I could kick myself for not playing it earlier -- on the other, this game was a really pleasant surprise.
Simply put, Last Light is much, much better than I expected it would be. There are so many games set in dark, dystopian futures, with the same muted colors and razor-thin plots that, if you've come late to the Metro franchise as I have, it's easy to look at the gameplay vids and screens and wave them off as a jaded gamer.
But this isn't a game that takes its setting for granted, or uses a post-apocalyptic setting for shallow purposes. There's a real story here, real world-building, real lore. Everything you see and encounter is there for a reason -- including the Metro stations themselves, the radiated surface, the factions and the personalities.
Pros:
- Well-written characters with distinct and amusing personalities
- Exceptional graphics: Metro Last Light looks better, as a 2014 redux, than many major 2016 titles
- The combat and gunplay is fun, smooth and intuitive
- Even in English, the dialog is peppered with interesting Russian slang and colloquialisms
- Likewise, the voice acting is top notch
- The game guides you, but it never feels like it's pushing you. It's a nice balance
- Last Light accommodates not only several difficulty levels, but also playstyles: You can play a more low-key, survival-style version with stealth mechanics, or you can play a more direct action-oriented shooter style which still gives you the option to be stealthy
Cons:
- The gun swapping and upgrading system isn't as intuitive as the rest of the game. Some of the guns don't behave the way you'd expect them to based on the type of weapons they are, and the store/purchasing system is a bit odd
- I don't like it when games, especially shooters, hide items in obscure places and force you to stalk around every map, looking in every nook and cranny lest you miss something important. Last Light isn't as bad as some games in this respect, but it's an element of game design I dislike.
- Lack of Vladimir Putin
- No MetArt girls. This is Russia. There should be amazing MetArt girls!
Overall: Highly recommended

I got into the Metro series a little late, but I've thoroughly enjoyed Last Light.  If I were to paraphrase my experience: frustratingly fun. Last Light feeds into my love for FPS games, as all you're doing is shooting people or creatures. There is an option to knife/melee, but other than that, it's primarily gun play.  The atmosphere of this game is dark, and I don't mean the story.  For the most part, you're playing in some part of the map that is dark and difficult to see.  This element was done to help make the player on edge and "scared" of what may be around them.
When you start the game, you're given two options which are either the game gives you more ammo and isn't as punishing if you just unload your weapon, or, essentially, hardcore, where ammo is scarce.  Even if you choose the former, ammo is still scarce.  There were a few times where I ran out of ammo and non was around, so had to reload an earlier check point.  Personally, I'm not a fan of this.  I know a lot of people are, but I don't want to spend five-ten minutes just trying to gather supplies.
Unfortunately, I made the mistake of playing Last Light first, as I didn't know 2033 was the first game.  It is highly advised to play 2033 first to help you understand the story characters better/  Eventually you
figure it out, but you're still left confused about certain characters.  As this is the redux version, we can go back into the story and play from another character's perspective.  This is a fantastic option!  I've not seen many games offer this.
There were some parts in the game that I felt weren't helpful and were meant for raging.  It's bad enough when you have an invincible demon in the sky trying to swoop you up, but to make matters worse, there are these water creatures that come out of the water, shoot things at you, and/or just follow you and are invincible.  Oh, and if you go in the water, there's a creature that insta-kills you.  I raged..hard.
Gun wise, I felt the developers did a fantastic job differentiating between the guns and accurately depicting their power.  For example, my favorite gun to use was the Revolver.  It packed quite a punch, and was pretty accurate.
One element I hadn't been expecting that I enjoyed very much was that we could use our lighter to burn up cobwebs and/or light wall torches. This is probably one of the best mechanics I've seen in a while!  It's not often you see a game which actually has your lighter burning things when you're near/touching them.  Brownie points to the devs!
Finally, I took the time to explore this game.  Explore the surroundings, the people.  Today we don't see this as ever happening, impossible, right?  But to imagine it. To imagine that something happens and we're forced underground like they are.  I may be in the minority here, but games like this really make me think about something that
happen, albeit a very far fetched chance.
All in all, and raging aside, I quite enjoyed this game.

Short Review
Crusaders of the Lost Idols is a great game with a few vital flaws:
-You don't progress while offline.
-There is a 5s transition between levels which, with most objectives having 200 levels or more adds up to almost half an hour
-Levels take about 30s when they're strong enough to instant kill and going by the relatively short objective of 200 levels this means 100 minutes of actively playing the game(plus other things such as transitions)
-Even if you have it on in the background it's not good enough since it adds a 15s delay(see more below) which means to save 50 mins you need to be actively playing for roughly 2 hours...
-All that aside it is a good game so play it if you whish to
________________________________________________________________________________
You know I really like this game, it's well made, has good visuals, interesting gameplay and is probably the best idle's I've ever played expect for a few things...
First off my impressions of the game were as above, I love strategy games and idle games and this game really hit the sweet spot, however as I played more though I started to get really frustrated for multiple reasons, those being:
-You don't automatically progress
Unlike clicker heroes, Crusader of the Lost Idols requires you to be running the game in order for you to get anywhere, this wouldn't be a huge deal if it wasn't for the following reasons
-There is a delay in chaging levels
This slight delay is not the slight delay from other progressive idles, I mean a roughly 5 second transition for the arrow to go to the next level to be clickable and the level to transition. This adds up, most mission average you requiring to traverse 200 levels, 200x5 is 1000s which is almost half an hour of wasted time!
-The levels take forever
Each level is about 30s long if your crusaders are strong enough to instant kill the enemies. Once again over the course of 200 levels this adds up to 100minutes, and this wouldn't be a problem if you could progress while offline but there is more to get you to constantly focus on the game...
-Even if it's running in the background it's not good enough
If your not familiar with how you progress, most level goals require you to collect a certain amount of items that drop from monsters walking across the screen(there are other mission but there less common and don't apply to this).
Once your crusaders reach the items they pick collect them automatically but there is always a huge delay of about 15s when you've finished the objective for this to happen and you to automatically progress.
This means that to save on average 50 minutes on time you need to constantly be focusing on the game which is usually not something you want to do for about an hour or two

Elsword first time impressions
Having completed the first quests and made it to the second town I can say I see where the game has its pluses and potential problems later on in the game.
For starters the fact that all of the characters start off unlocked is a great bonus.  Unlike most games where you see them all but need to unlock them, having them all there at the beginning is VERY welcome.  I look forward to playing them all over time ^_^
the combat system of the game is also pretty simple [but might change based on other characters, I have only played the primary protagonist so far so I dont know if the combat remains as simple so far] featuring the use of mostly the arrow keys, Z and X buttons.  In fact the game even shows you what combos you can do depenind on your situation.
Ex
ZZZZ  or ZZZX when standing
XXX and XXZ is the secondary combo when standing.
You also have yoru special attacsk you can que to different Keys it looks like and it all flows really well so far. the cool down time for skills doesn't seem that bad and its really easy to recharge MP if you need to.
The animation of the enemies and characters are also  VERY well done and fantastic.  I only saw a few glitches so far but those where in towns with many players running around.
Double edged help
In many areas of the game in between towns other players can run around with you, and in some cases can help you in the middle of dungeons and combat.  thankfully It looks like the items you SEE are the ones for you to get so It doesn't look like you need to worry about item theft of hogging.  [if im wrong let me know please.. cause then id feel bad]
However the down side of this is that dungeons with multiple players in some towns can have wait times, and Even when you pick a certain difficulty for a dungeon, when the QUE comes in it might send you to the wrong one.   [I almost entered a very hard dungeon by mistake even though I picked normal on the screen].
All in all the game is alot of fun so far, and I definatly plan to play alot more later on when I want to play a simple multiplayer hack and slash side scroller.
Oh yeah at the moment my character is Elsword with the nick name AlexanderRed so feel free to say hello or whatever if ya see me around.

Many people are of the mistaken opinion that Mass Effect is an RPG. This may be forgiven, as the developers themselves were under this delusion while developing the first game. By the sequel, they had realized their error and switched genres. Mass Effect 2 is actually one of the slickest Adventure games around, joining the ranks of Monkey Island and Same & Max.
Running around talking to people remains the central gameplay mechanic outside of missions, but the fiddly half-baked RPG systems have been removed. Characters are colorful, interacting with them is enjoyable, and the gunplay is fun.
The story is even more episodic than the first and third games, with semi-mandatory self-contained side-quests as you assemble and gain the loyalty of various members of Shephard's team. The writing and acting isn't fantastic, but it's quite adequate. I've seen worse from the likes of Star Trek, which this game oozes from it's pores. Family members watching gameplay have briefly thought that it was a movie.
Combat can follow the static “stay safe behind barriers and shoot things occasionally,” pattern but it doesn't have to. The Infiltrator class has a lot of freedom to flank enemies, and the Vanguard class in particular mixes up the formula a lot.
This being said, seeing everything in the game takes a long time, you're almost certainly going to want see everything to get the best ending if you're playing through the series, and ME3 gameplay is significantly better. The ME2 time investment is akin to sitting through three seasons of a (British) TV show sequentially. I don't know that the replay value is very high.
Note that the the game provides you with an Origin cdkey as well. I would somewhat strongly recommend playing it there, as the Origin version has online save game backups. I lost 32 hours of playtime on the Steam version right before the final mission when my HD died. Shame on Bioware for not enabling Steam Cloud on this game.

UPDATE - AFTER A FEW DAYS OF PLAY
ATS does a great job of being ETS2 in the US, which some added features and complications. I enjoy the optional parking challenges, and navigating the complicated terrain, but although the game is a lot of fun, there is one main difference between it, and ETS2. That difference is that ETS2 is relaxing to play, while ATS I feel like I'm on the edge of my seat worrying. Why? Well there are two issues that I feel need to be fixed to change this.
1) SPEED CHANGES
While an accurate depiction of the US, where the speed limits frequently change and aren't always clearly communicated, this game has a condensed version of the map, so the changes happen too frequently, and too quickly. I'll be doing 55, then without a sign, it suddenly drops to 35, and a few seconds late back up to 55. This is just an example, but the problem is, as soon as the speed changes, I slam the breaks... but usually get a fine as a cop is always behind me when it happens. I'm not driving badly, there was just no notice. What happens is I don't watch the road, keep missing turns on the route, and instead focus most of my attention on speed and speed limit.
There is also a speed limiter in ETS2, so you can happily hit max speed on the freeway and enjoy the drive. ATS doesn't allow you to relax like that.
2) FINES
Speeding fines, running red lights, etc. are annoying, but it encourages better driving and works well in ETS2. You advanced notice of speed cameras, so can usually slow in time, but if you don't manage to slow, the fines don't break the bank. In ATS, the fines happen so frequently due mainly to speed issues above, and they are far too high for the early game. For example, you can usually go 5mph over the speed limit in the US without a problem, but if you go 6mph over, in ATS, a cop will slap a $1000 fine on you. Roll not quite far enough into an intersection when turning left at a light and the light changing, and you get a $1400 fine. This is for a job paying only $5000, so many times I barely make a profit.
SUMMARY
I still think the game is great, but I am continuing to due quick jobs instead of buying my own truck, because I'm worried I'd go bankrupt otherwise. Once I have enough funds to hire a couple of drivers, I think it'll improve as they will provide funds to pay my fines.
===================================================================
FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW: American Truck Simulator.
After I set up my company, I was all set to make my mark on American soil. This I did fairly quickly, when I went off-road after missing a turn! The trucks handle very differently than the European trucks I'm used to driving, in terms of power, turning radius and braking ability. Even the mirrors seem awkwardly positioned at first. It takes some getting used to, but after 3 quick jobs with random trucks, I'm getting the hang of it. At launch, we only have California and Nevada, with Arizona coming soon, but it doesn't feel limiting, and is plenty of space to begin with.
Some of the excellent points so far:
- There are police, and I found out the hard way that they are not just for decoration. I sped past one who immediately put on his lights and I got dinged for double speeding fine ($1,000!).
- There are hidden speed traps, cameras and police hiding behind bushes, so you really need to watch your speed.
- It's much harder to watch your speed because your truck can go up to 80mph (so far), but just like real life, the speed limit can drop from 70 to 30, and catch you unaware if you aren't careful.
- You can turn right on a red! I am very happy they added this rule.
- Weight stations are scattered around, and sometimes you get a message requiring you to pull in for inspection. I only had this once so far, so I'm not sure what happens if you ignore it.
- Tumbleweed blows across the road and at first I almost swerved to avoid it. Makes you jump when you first see it.
- New parking options. The locations where you pickup and drop off deliveries are much more complicated to navigate, but when you pull in to make your delivery, you now have three options: Skip parking (no bonus), Relatively easy parking (small bonus xp), and complicated parking that will take a lot of skill, but gives a decent xp bonus.
Overall, loving the game so far, and I intentionally haven't taken the loan to buy my own truck yet, as right now, damages are not my problem on the loaners :) If you enjoyed ETS2, get ATS.

Also you will probably find it easier if you change the keyboard layout to buttons that suit you, rather than the ones that are pre-programmed. The great thing though is everything is fully customizable, from the colours of the suit for your character to the colours of the ship you fly. The players also seem, at first glance anyway, to be helpful to new players, but its always better if you can play with friends in a clan.
If you are one of those players that want the best in the game then expect to pay real money for the "Prime" characters, though if you are patient you can get the blueprints to start building your own "Prime" warframes. You can also get a free "Prime" bundle, I got the Frost Prime, just by signing up to Twitch Prime and in turn Amazon Prime. You can also get freebies from the game by watching the Devs run around on Twitch, which is always worth while doing.
So all in all, its a great game and worth getting, especially considering its a FTP.

It's a turn-based isometric RPG which attempts to do what Sword Coast Legends never did: make a computer game that captured the essence of PnP, complete with campaign editor (not tried yet, since this is an EA review), GM mode and true RPG-freedom-of-choice. It is very similar to RPG's of old, like Neverwinter Nights, Baldurs Gate etc.
I have only completed Act 1 so far, since that's all that exists in the early access version, but I am hooked. The game is a joy to play. Difficult at times, yet rewarding too. It offers true freedom of choice in the way you play and create your character. It features a classless character system so you are free to do whatever you want with your character. It also features various "origin" characters which are kind of pre-generated characters with fleshed out backgrounds (the kind of thing you do yourself in a D&D campaign). You can choose to play one of those or alternatively make up your own and recruit them in game.
There are many ways to solve the quests in game, offering a lot of replay value. Race, "tags" (such as Outlaw etc.) all make NPC's treat you differently and offer various other ways to do things. The co-op gameplay (up to 4 players) has also been specifically designed with this in mind, meaning your party may not always see eye-to-eye on things. This creates the potential for some interesting RP scenarios.
Although the version I played does not yet feature a GM mode or level editor, this looks to be the icing on the cake and could significantly increase play-time. They will also offer Steam Workshop support for "click-and-play" modding.
Now all they need to do is offer the ability to import/export characters...

As a fan of Metro 2033 Redux, I was disappointed by this game. TL;DR at the end.
It's not Metro. At least not the Metro I played in the first game. And no, adding a survival mode option does not alleviate that issue. You see, this game was tailor-made to be an action game first. The more subdued, desolate, and isolating 2033 felt real. It felt grounded. I was terrified of losing my life, and in effect letting my world go to waste as a result of my failure.
In Last Light, I just felt like I was moving through a shooting gallery. The only difference being, instead of flat wooden targets, I had 3D creature/human models at my mercy. I believe this is partly the result of the more obvious emphasis on stealth/moral gameplay in the human sections (making each room feel like a piece of a slideshow), partly the result of a linear good/bad ending system that essentially forces players to play a certain way to achieve their desired goal, and partly the result of a loss of plain and simple STAKES; There were none. The game simply places you in the middle of a narrative you really don't care about:
1. You are introduced to about 50 (exaggeration) new characters at once, with no real investment or proper development of any of them.
2. You are introduced to a threat that you can't even ascertain, and when you finally do, the issue is resolved a short while thereafter. It has no lasting ramifications or effect on you whatsoever. While the walkthrough level related to the said threat was a bit jarring, I got over the feeling quickly, as the game simply shimmied me to the next corridor of gameplay (while apparently making an unwritten agreement with me to never speak of it again). I honestly didn't care, and you won't care.
3. The ending is extremely anti-climactic, and I'm not just talking about the cinematic. Even the final battle feels like a drag.
It feels like an iteration of Call of Duty with a small helping of its requisite set-piece moments, with peak creativity at maybe three meager moments
.
TL;DR
A bad Metro game. A lackluster game in general. Just play 2033.
I genuinely believe 4A Games can do better, and honestly they did a lot with the means they had. Metro 2033 is testament to that opinion, and I hope to see better and original titles from them in the future.

Although far from being a masterpiece, Deadfall Adventures feels like a step forward when compared to The Farm 51's previous "budget" titles such as NecroVision and Painkiller HD.
POSITIVES
- The main menu theme setting up an adventuresque feel
- 3 exotic settings
- A badass hero
- Dual-wielding guns
- Deadly traps and mechanism
- Interesting puzzles
- Tips are given through the notes
- Upgrade system
- Many secret areas and collectables
- Mummies!!!
- Alan Wake-esque combat mechanics
NEGATIVES
- Some cringeworthy dialogues
- Predictable plot
- Transition between gameplay and cutscene is not always coherent
- Some texture popping issues
- Gunplay against human enemies feels more tedious than fun
- Strategy to defeat the undead is too simple and repetitive
- Some hitbox issues
- Player movement is slow
- Grenade throwing arc is inconsistent and unintuitive
- Can carry only 2 weapons
Despite its cheesiness and low production value, Deadfall Adventures has enough personality to make the experience worthwhile.

I just finished my Spartan Ranger Hardcore campaign, and needless to say it was awesome. I wasn't a fan when the original game came out but I can assure you that the Redux Versions of Last Light and the original Metro, are worth every penny.

There are points in the game that you will get tempted to just shoot the place up to be done with it, as doing a stealthy (and usually the morally sound route) to be more tedious. Any way gets the job done. (if you aren't as obsessive with earning stealth achievements.)
What fascinated me the most is the setting and the sense of urgency and realism. The greatest challenge really was in conserving ammo (though the Spartan Mode is there to remedy that) and making every second on the surface count since you can die from the environment and asphyxiation. Non-combat portions of the game are as tense as those moments you face bandits, Commies, Nazis, and even mutant wildlife.
The additional missions were also quite entertaining. Bite-size in nature but also provides their own challenge and flavor, having to fill the shoes of different characters in the actual campaign. (among others) I did this however, in Normal Spartan mode so the experience may be quite different for you.
Worth a second playthrough, if you're the type that's into perfecting game achievements like me. This one is easily in the bag.

In the challenge mode you can play 560 main puzzles and always when you solved one you are able to play an other mini puzzle. So the amount of puzzles in this mode is 1.120. There is also a Quickplaymode but the puzzles in this mode are so easy that you very probably won‘t play it. Anyways for so many puzzles I give
points because the most puzzle magazines have like 100-200 puzzles.

The possible languages which you can choose are: American English, British English, German, Spanish, French and Italian. Of course this is a great selection but maybe they should add also Russian and I can’t give the full points because there are sometimes little spelling mistakes in the game, e. g. I have had a hangman puzzle where I had to search a „panet“ (correct word would be planet) and the result was „merker“ but the planet is called in German „Merkur“ (english = Mercury). Such mistakes are really rare and don’t disturb the game too much so I can give for the languages and ortography
points.

The controls are really easy. You can use the keyboard or you click on the letters with your mouse. There is also a handwriting recognition function.

There are 15 achievements which you get easily. No bugged ones. The only con is that there are no leaderboards.
The normal price for this game is 4,99 €. For so many puzzles this price is okay but I advise to buy the game on a sale. I bought it at Steam Summer Sale for 0,79 € (valuta calculator says: 1,08 Dollar ^^) and for this price I am really happy with this game.

More than just a loveletter to the isometrics and Fallout titles of yesteryear, Underrail is honestly no different than any other  crpg you would have found on the shelf during the mid 90s and that's why I love it. The game is no cargo cultish retro experience which is so common in the modern crpg, rather for good and bad it plays just like the classics.
It also means no map to guide you and no hints to hold your hand as you wander into highly dangerous areas filled with newcomer slaughtering monsters. Combat itself can come down to who gets in the first crossbow bolt to the head and many reloads of frustration depending on how you play.
The character system demands specialization which goes against the modern day "see it all and do it all" sandbox style so common now and as such it provides the chance to create really bad characters that force you to restart hours after you've made the fatal error.
The story can get a little out there, but I appriciate the fact that it makes no attempts to be philosophically deep and meaningful, it gets the job done and in this day and age that's a tall order for a crpg to make. It's also quite the long game, sure to keep your busy for a time even if you don't need to reroll. So if you've let this one slip by you and you consider yourself a fan of the old isometric style crpgs then this one is worth checking out. Also keep in mind that an expansion is in development as of this writing.

I really, really wanted to like Underrail.
But apparently, it didn't want me to, because it greeted me with a kick to the happy place, and proceeded to stomp on my face repeatedly while I was laying on the ground in pain. For 80 hours.
I got this game for free after backing Wasteland 3, the sequel to one of my favorite RPGs of all time, on the crowndfunding site Fig. I'm a lover of post apocalyptic RPGs like the classic Fallouts and Wasteland, so Underrail seemed right up my alley, but life got in the way, and the game sat around in my Steam library for over a year without ever being touched. During a vacation where I only had access to my laptop, I completed the first Witcher game and thought
Lo and behold, Underrail fit the bill perfectly.
It's a top down, isometric RPG with turn-based combat, and it's very reminiscent of Fallout 1 and 2 in both its atmosphere, which is top notch, and presentation. In terms of substance, writing and overall enjoyment however ? Forget it. Underrail was an absolute chore to play from start to finish, with only small exceptions that I wish had been much more frequent. Don't believe me that this game scared a huge part of its playerbase away ? Just look at the achievements and, based on the time I got some achievements with my main weapon, I can easily deduce that over 85% of players stopped playing before getting past the junkyard, which is the second town. 85% of an audience that would normally be willing to put up with a few shortcomings if it meant the game underneath was worth it. Unfortunately, Underrail has more than just
.
The game has so many more problems and I could rant about it for hours. It has its moments, sure, but it is such a slow, tedious and unrewarding experience in the end that I cannot recommend it. In fact, I'd actually suggest avoiding it. Spend your money, and more importantly your time, elsewhere. I got this for free, but the 80 hours I spent playing through Underrail, hoping it would all be worth it in the end, those I'll never get back.
Underrail hates you, and you should avoid it at all costs.

UPDATE - AFTER A FEW DAYS OF PLAY
ATS does a great job of being ETS2 in the US, which some added features and complications. I enjoy the optional parking challenges, and navigating the complicated terrain, but although the game is a lot of fun, there is one main difference between it, and ETS2. That difference is that ETS2 is relaxing to play, while ATS I feel like I'm on the edge of my seat worrying. Why? Well there are two issues that I feel need to be fixed to change this.
1) SPEED CHANGES
While an accurate depiction of the US, where the speed limits frequently change and aren't always clearly communicated, this game has a condensed version of the map, so the changes happen too frequently, and too quickly. I'll be doing 55, then without a sign, it suddenly drops to 35, and a few seconds late back up to 55. This is just an example, but the problem is, as soon as the speed changes, I slam the breaks... but usually get a fine as a cop is always behind me when it happens. I'm not driving badly, there was just no notice. What happens is I don't watch the road, keep missing turns on the route, and instead focus most of my attention on speed and speed limit.
There is also a speed limiter in ETS2, so you can happily hit max speed on the freeway and enjoy the drive. ATS doesn't allow you to relax like that.
2) FINES
Speeding fines, running red lights, etc. are annoying, but it encourages better driving and works well in ETS2. You advanced notice of speed cameras, so can usually slow in time, but if you don't manage to slow, the fines don't break the bank. In ATS, the fines happen so frequently due mainly to speed issues above, and they are far too high for the early game. For example, you can usually go 5mph over the speed limit in the US without a problem, but if you go 6mph over, in ATS, a cop will slap a $1000 fine on you. Roll not quite far enough into an intersection when turning left at a light and the light changing, and you get a $1400 fine. This is for a job paying only $5000, so many times I barely make a profit.
SUMMARY
I still think the game is great, but I am continuing to due quick jobs instead of buying my own truck, because I'm worried I'd go bankrupt otherwise. Once I have enough funds to hire a couple of drivers, I think it'll improve as they will provide funds to pay my fines.
===================================================================
FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW: American Truck Simulator.
After I set up my company, I was all set to make my mark on American soil. This I did fairly quickly, when I went off-road after missing a turn! The trucks handle very differently than the European trucks I'm used to driving, in terms of power, turning radius and braking ability. Even the mirrors seem awkwardly positioned at first. It takes some getting used to, but after 3 quick jobs with random trucks, I'm getting the hang of it. At launch, we only have California and Nevada, with Arizona coming soon, but it doesn't feel limiting, and is plenty of space to begin with.
Some of the excellent points so far:
- There are police, and I found out the hard way that they are not just for decoration. I sped past one who immediately put on his lights and I got dinged for double speeding fine ($1,000!).
- There are hidden speed traps, cameras and police hiding behind bushes, so you really need to watch your speed.
- It's much harder to watch your speed because your truck can go up to 80mph (so far), but just like real life, the speed limit can drop from 70 to 30, and catch you unaware if you aren't careful.
- You can turn right on a red! I am very happy they added this rule.
- Weight stations are scattered around, and sometimes you get a message requiring you to pull in for inspection. I only had this once so far, so I'm not sure what happens if you ignore it.
- Tumbleweed blows across the road and at first I almost swerved to avoid it. Makes you jump when you first see it.
- New parking options. The locations where you pickup and drop off deliveries are much more complicated to navigate, but when you pull in to make your delivery, you now have three options: Skip parking (no bonus), Relatively easy parking (small bonus xp), and complicated parking that will take a lot of skill, but gives a decent xp bonus.
Overall, loving the game so far, and I intentionally haven't taken the loan to buy my own truck yet, as right now, damages are not my problem on the loaners :) If you enjoyed ETS2, get ATS.

Murdered: Soul Suspect - Spoiler Free Review
First off, I'd like to point out that I like both pulp noir and ghost stories both of which are heavy influences on the general feel of this game.  If you do not like either the cinematography stylings of pulp noir (in which case, you won't like the cut-scenes and may dislike the characters on occassion) or think ghost stories are dull, then this is not the game for you.
For those of you still with me and looking at potentially buying this game a bit of background is in order.  The studio that released M:SS closed down despite really ploughing everything into this game.  Part of it is odd in places, which I'll get to, but mostly they'd been struggling for a while due to releasing a couple of games which were bombs a while back.  Any future updates to the game will have to be community driven but that at least is one piece of good news - after multiple playthroughs I only came across one minor glitch, once, and it was a graphical one that I couldn't replicate.  The game runs really well so future patching should not be necessary.
So, where to start?  How about the story.  It's pretty standard fair, almost straight out of a "Randall & Hopkirk: Deceased" episode.  You're a detective in Salem when a call is put in about a strange hooded man breaking into an apartment building.  As you are an emotional loose cannon after your wifes' death (it's actually nice to play a character who's irrational behaviour gets some explanation for once) you chase after him alone only to find that he's too strong for you, the eventual fight resulting in your death.  Your purpose is to stop the killer from beyond the grave so that your spirit can move on and be reunited with your wife.
This opening is actually really impressive as it's almost entirely done using the in-game engine and graphically looks superb, the sweeping camera shots and the slow-motion work really well giving a strong movie quality feel but rather than just have you as a passenger watching the opening the developer makes you take part in it, trying to first catch the killer and even trying to survive the attack.  The sound is excellent too and is nicely understated, something that carries throughout the whole game.
After this you're left, dead, in Salem trying to figure out how you can stop this killer.  There's a tutorial which covers the controls and then you're given objectives to complete but you are left to wander through reasonably large parts of Salem without being stopped.  As you're dead you come across other spirits and left over memories of Salem in it's past, which just helps to make the world more interesting and full and the contrast in design is really well realised, especially when it ties in with the sidequests and main stories.  The more you progress the more of Salem opens up to you, allowing you to find out more about Salems past and revisit areas you have already explored.  The team have been as historically accurate as possible, considering that the game is a work of fiction, and you'll get to pick up on a real flavour of Salems darker past as you wander town.
Character design suits the mood of the town too and there are characters in period dress in certain areas, although they are very few and far between, I'd have liked to have seen more of them.  They are reasonably realistic to look at - not ultra-real - which would feel out of place in a ghost story, but real anyway with very good motion capture and facial expressions especially on the main ones.  One that stood out to me is a point where a character manages to pretty much lie with just their face for a split second near the end, you'll know it when you see it, but the technology is well utilised without being overdone, it does not take you out of the story or gameplay very much if ever.
As a ghost you get to travel through walls but presumably due to hardware limitations this pretty much is only really used within enclosed spaces, though this is explained within the game-worlds mythos itself well enough and it can be quite good fun.  These sections really can make you feel like a running, screaming spirit.  I felt less like a spirit and more like I was going to have a seizure due to swoosh noise everytime you select a conversation topic.  It's fine in short conversations but they can be long and a little grating if you want to find out everything.
There's some disturbing bits in this game too.  Some pretty nasty deaths of young women, some ghosts have some surprisingly harrowing and well-acted lines, almost mini-stories, of their own if you come across them and there are collectables that unlock urban legends, a couple of which are genuinely quite creepy.  There are places with a lot of extra details added in which build up a wonderful sense of dread and oppression too, a lot of which can easily be missed and overlooked as it is just there for scene-setting.
Controls are pretty tight, the camera is good but can be a bit awkward when you are possessing something or trying to get through a wall slowly.  But there are two elephants in the room and these are what most reviewers scored the game so harshly on.
1) Pointless Sort-of Forced Combat/Stealth Sections.
You do combat, you either have to go for it whole-heartedly or just don't do it.  In for a penny, in for a pound!  M:SS feels like it's dipping it's fingers into the collection bowl and wondering if it can get away with giving a two Christmas old chocolate coin.  You get an enforced stealth section, taking you out of the more interesting portion of the game which feels jarring, so you can try to sneak past these demon-monsters which look like the Nozghul if they'd been drinking sheep-dip.  It hardly ever works so you have to try to stealth kill them, which is only a temporary fix.
2) Escort Mission
The escort is at least useful but these are really badly designed - it barely matters if you get spotted because the spotter sub-routine is so badly programmed.
Both of these things feel tacked on and out of place.  I have a sneaking suspicion that they received orders from their publisher that if they wanted a Triple A advertising budget then it had to have those things in it because they feel completely at odds with the rest of the game.  And yes, I will be doing a video rant I am that annoyed about it.
Mercifully, there's only a handful of those sections and apart from that and one point with a truly stupid portrayal of mental illness (completely different to an earlier scene with a ghost in a bath), the rest of the game is pretty much excellent.  If you can stick out those few parts you will find a good to look at, engaging murder mystery, with an excellent twist and interesting backdrop and characters.
I recommend it, but have to dock it marks for 1) & 2)
Total Score:  7.5/10

First off, ignore all reviews made by professional critics. For some reason or another they have given this game a bad rap that it does not deserve.
This game is a 'good' game. Nothing groundbreaking but it is definately worth playing. I found myself immersed in the story and constantly guessing "who is the murderer?" This to me is one of the most important thing in a mystery driven game; it keeps you guessing. The gameplay is simplistic and the investigations are very straightforward. In my opinion, this is moreso used as a vehicle for the story and not meant to give a significant challenge.
Murdered: Soul Suspect has a story to tell and I must say it does it well here. Dont walk into this expecting an action packed skill gauntlet, because it simply doesnt occur here. It's asking price is quite steep for what the game is. I would wait till it gets down to $20-$30. The game took me around 6 hours to complete so it is not very long at all. However, I came away from this like after watching a good film at the movies. Expensive for something short, but so enjoyable.

I beat this game and was disappointed that there was no plot. The game throws a bunch of plot hooks all over the place, but none find purchase. Things just happen and Aveline has no real agancy, which for a large part of the game I thought would be the theme. One gets a vague sense that interesting things might be happening in-between playable segments, but nothing is resolved. The game even throws in a meta story element by framing itself as an entertainment product developed by the Assassins' enemies, Abstergo. At three or four points in the game, you are told to kill game abstractions to unlock cinematic sequences Abstergo removed from the narrative. These sequences add nothing to the plot or explain character motivations. One is inclined to ask, "Why would Abstergo cut these segments where people advocate more action against the slave trade?" In addition to these cinematics, your sparse journal entries on some of the characters you encounter are changed, but not in any surprising or meaningful ways.
tl;dr - What would have saved this game for me would be if it had Shaun or some Shaun analoge to give context to this mess of a story.

I'm enjoying the heck out of this game. It's top-down 2D space combat primarily, with some exploration and slight RPG-ish aspects. The game features pretty good AI, has lots of outstanding ship customization options, a fun story, and it's got a pretty small hard drive footprint. SPAZ can get somewhat repetitive if you generate a large galaxy to explore, but a big galaxy also allows you plenty of areas to grind for levels or items to beat down a story mission or particular system. After playing most of the Afrika Korps campaign I must say that I am positively impressed with this game.
Short Story:
At first glance this game may look as just another Panzer General clone, in reality there are a number of well designed features in the game that offer a lot more options for stategic decision during the campaign. Potentially the game has a solid re-playability value.
More in details:
Unit customisation. First you can buy battalion or brigate size units which have different cost and different combat statistics, then you can attach sub units (companies) to change some of the statistics of the parent unit and so customise your units to fit better for specific tasks. The units gain experience if they win battles. Of course more experienced units perform better; as a rule of thums a unit with 3 exp. levels has a performance ca. doubled compared to a green unit.
Leaders. Each unit must have a leader attached to it. Each leader has different stats that can significantly alter the unit performance in many ways. Leaders are class specific and limited in number so your army composition is somehow determined / limited by their availability (e.g. you can not buy an artillery unit if there is not an artillery leader available).
The leader themselves evolve with the game. If they perform well they increase their statistics (thus making more powerful the units under their command), on the other hands, if a unit under a leader command takes a significant beating or is destroyed, the leader stats. may be reduced.
During the campaign, either by effect of player decisions or by taking on map objetives, you get more leaders. You can reassign the best leaders as you see fit, however this cost a lot of points (resouces), so between the campaign scenarios you really need to make deciosions such as: do I buy a new Tank or I replace that crappy leader of that high experience fighter?
Combat mechanics. Many factors are considered in the determination of the combat outcome, and these are presented as a table before (as predictor) and after the combat (as detailed result) so you can look at which factor(s) contributed most to the loss ratio you had. That is a nice way to learn how to better use your equipment.
OKW Favour points. In each mission you get a special task such as capturing a location, destroying enemy units,  saving your own units etc. When you get 3 points you can decide if you want to change them for more resources, get more leaders or just skip the decision later when you accumulate 6 or 9 points. Of course, with 6 and 9 points you can get far better rewards. I think this is very intersting because makes the campaing varying based on that you decide.
Maps. Looks well drawn and clear, however, IMHO they do not blend well with the Nato counters and I prefer to see the tiny soldiers on the ground.
Area for improvement;
Note: the game is just released and most of the points below can be easily fixed. Consider also that most of this game is almost a one man effort, so it is quite impressive the quality level at launch.

Unit sprites. I find the units too small and sometimes it is hard to see the differences between e.g. mountain inf. vs regular inf. or similar tank units. It looks that not much effort has been put on this aspect.
Unit roster and Game interface. Same as above, the game offers a lot of options for the unit management/refit/upgrade but is a real pain look at all the small symbols at least for my old eyes :-)
Manual. There is one and contains useful info but there is no reference of its existence either in the product page or in the game menu. You have to find the PDF doc in the game root.
Overall the game needs some polishing (spelling) and have some naive things that ruin the immersion, however nothing that can not be fixed or modified in due course.

Acronimowww did a good review in the forums. Most of what he said I am repeating here, with additional info about modding.
With the Gamersgate 20% discount and a few "blue coins," I bought the game for $20, and after about four hours I am happy with it. However, if one is pretty sure they will NOT be using the editor, at $30 it may be a tough decision.
Once again, the file management required to use the editor is not well-documented, but it works like the dev's first game. I would be happy to help anyone in that area.
I find the first few missions - even the one locked on "easy" - to be far from it, for me at least. I'm guessing they will require an ideal plan of attack/defense that will take a few losses to learn. Some will enjoy this challenge.
The game is very easy to understand and play (why couldn't Matrix Tigers on the Hunt have such a UI? ), and all the data (and possibly more) found in Panzer Corps and Order of Battle is here and immediately available to the player with no clicking around. The AI can be very aggressive - seems more so than PC and OOB - and it does flank.
Almost all the 1939-1942 military equipment is here, and the dev has seen fit to add the M4 Sherman (circa 1943 in North Africa?) and Panther D as chrome. But again, to access this good stuff requires using the editor. With that utility, you can pretty much build anything. You can currently mod five historical scenarios, and about 10 templates are also available. I have not figured out how to create or modify campaigns yet.
Other bits of chrome available in the regular game includes the attachment of up to eight(?) BN assets that add 5 strength points each and enhance a unit's capabilities. So if you are defending an objective against an infantry force, you might want to add an MG or mortar company. Against tanks, there are a variety of assets available. These can be attached to all types of units.
In addition, unit sizes vary from Bn to Div (although most are Reg in strength) with strength points as high as 100. This is where the game soundly beats PC and OOB. The added strength points give the units more resilience. They will retreat into the FoW, but count on them coming back due to the ability of the players to resupply and equip their forces to full strength using "resources" given at first turn, and every turn, depending on the scenario settings.
Also, the pre- and post-battle reports can be set to "detailed," which gives a long list of nice data in a box that does not interfere with game play. PC and OOB give loss estimates only. AG goes much further. There is also experience levels and gains, units that carry over, and other things you might expect.
As I have spent more time in the editor, I can not vouch for campaign balance, etc., but am eager to find out. The dev's first game was good, but I always felt a bit "generic." This game offers a wealth of tactical detail and graphics that (in my mind) are fully sufficient if not exactly up to OOB's standards.

I liked underrail, for the most part its a very awesome game. However, it does suffer quite a bit from a few key points. The level cap is 25, so don't expect to get to do everything you want on a single play through of the game. You just won't have the points to be able to put into it all, and you can NOT respec your character. You'll have to start a new character and a new game to get to do some of the crafting or whatever you leave out in the first play through. Character builds are important, but in Underrail they're... all important. As in, it is absolutely vital to build your character properly. If you make a mistake in building your character, that's it. There is no going back, unless you have a great many saves and you don't mind redoing a lot of what you've already done, in order to be able to put those leveling points elsewhere in order to correct your mistake. Some kind of trainers in the game (say an NPC that you can pay or quest for) that could teach you and give you some skill points, would have been an excellent addition to this game.
But there is nothing like that, and I can't stress enough with how stuck you are with your decisions. Again, there is no going back, ever. Another thing has already been covered by everyone, but there is no map and a map is REALLY called for in this game. Best you've got is online maps, from which you can work things out, but its something of a hassle and you're still going to be working a lot of it out on your own. Don't expect to not have to consult the internet on where to go, or how to find that difficult location. Because there is no map in game. Those are the only 2 real problems I had with the game. Given its release date, better graphics would have been appreciated, but the game doesn't suffer too much without them. You can imagine a slightly improved Fallout 2 in terms of graphics, and you'll have what this game looks and feels like. Despite these issues, Underrail is well worth playing, and well worth the money. If you like old school turn based RPG's, you should not skip Underrail. I'm so very glad that I bought it and played it, and you won't be disappointed.

Adorable loli + economics = fantastic.
Taking control of a young girl left with a large debt by her father, you strive to squeeze every penny out of the customers who visit the store and the monsters who inhabit various dungeons.  The mechanics are pretty simple, both in town and in the dungeons.  When manning your shop, you try to propose the ideal price based on the customer and the item.  Customers will pay base cost + X%, and it's your job to figure out what each customer's range is.  In dungeons, you control one of many eager adventurers, killing monsters, trying to avoid their attacks, and looting items to sell in your shop.  There's a decent amount of content for the dungeons and adventerers, making it unlikely that you'll complete that aspect of the game before you repay your debt, but with NG+ available you'll be able to jump back in pretty quickly.
All in all, the game is simple, sweet, and very much worth the price.

I thought this game was really cool at first... until one gameplay mechanic pretty much brought everything to a halt.
Unlike in Fallout 1 & 2, there is no healing skill that can be used for free without expending limited resources.  All resources are extremely precious and limited.  However, you can go back to town and get a medic to heal you completely for free, without limit.  Pair this with the fact that you can often escape a fight by entering an area transition zone, and you can leave every fight as soon as you take damage, walk back to town, get healed, go back to where you fought that enemy, and continue fighting them, and they haven't healed at all, and that becomes obviously the easiest way to progress in much of the game, and it is *not fun*.  The developers should implement a healing skill (like in Fallout 1 & 2) that can be used without expending any limited resources (or perhaps a healing skill that can be used if the player character has a healing kit, and maybe there's a small chance of that healing kit being expended or partially expended).  That seems like it would be an easy fix to this serious game-breaking problem.

Yet another FPS game where Americans eventually kills everybody they meet on the scene. Well, maybe except for a few Arabs in the prologue. I'm not here to sound all pollutical, and I have to say, despite being the very unoriginal, the story itself isn't the problem of the game. In fact, it's fun. Yeah, people loves Indiana Jones type of archeology, and, even being all that repetitive, the stories of some Nazi looking for over the world for powerful ancient artefacts - and some daredevils trying to stop them - still don't get old. After all those years. The game authors sinks even deeper and binding to the game the spirit of the famous book adventurer, Allan Quatermain, even if feels a bit of a necromancy.
Yet, I repeat, the story is ok. Trivial, stupid - but ok, fitting the current standards. The sounding is lacking, the scripts are sometimes really bad, but all that is not making the game awful. The visuals are not bad, for the consoles in the year 2013. The jungles, snows, and sands are colourful, all playing the part, you know. Graphically, that's acceptable game.
Now, what is really disappointing - is how it plays. It's on-the-rail first-person view shooter, see? And... it goes worse than the very first Call of Duty. The process of the shooting is so annoying, that I really suggest everyone to play (if you decide to play it) only on the easiest difficulty. It's really not the game where you'll be enjoying with the gunplay. Were the Deadfall a 2-d sidescroller - that would suit it much better. You know, with all those big white bubbles, coming out of the rifles, and dummy enemies, running towards you no matter what?
I must admit, the riddles in the game process were not all that easy (at least for me, I've played on the hard setting). And I'm really happy that there's the possibility to tune the game difficulty for the riddles and shootouts separately. If you decide to try the game, no matter what, please, use the difficulty choices wisely.
Finally, as an obvious and predictable downvote point, there is a dead multiplayer. And about 20 achievements tied to it (for those of you who collect achievements).

It's a reasonably fun diversion, but there are a few things that make it so that I can't recommend it. First and foremost being that it's not too hard to find puzzles of a similar ilk online for free -- and often with better interfaces. (Just compare the Link-a-Pix in the game to the same found on Conceptis's own website.)  The second problem is that some of the games aren't really puzzles per se... showing the user a picture and asking them to memorize it for three questions isn't a puzzle, it's just a memory test. It's not a puzzle unless one has to puzzle something out. Memorization is just an irritation. There's also a staggering difference in apparent audience between puzzles; the Codeword puzzle is clearly meant for advanced puzzlers, while Silhouette is obviously set for the grade school crowd, but they're all mixed in together.
Finally, though it's a minor element, it bothers me quite a bit that the Equate "puzzles" don't follow the proper order of operations. The only thing worse than a puzzle that's stupidly simple is one that's only challenging because the desired answer is actually wrong.

At the end of a stressful day, one of the most relaxing things is a nice drive on the open road. That is why I have spent hundreds of hours playing ETS2, and at the time of this review, I've spent 75 hours on ATS.
I'm not going to go into an extensive comparison of the two, because they are essentially the same, just different driving conditions. Basically, in America, everything is bigger. Bigger roads, bigger trucks, bigger loads.
I don't really have any complaints about gameplay. The graphics in the game are incredible, if your pc can handle the higher settings. On the other hand, it doesn't look too bad with the graphics settings turned down, and it's nice that even low end computer can run the game decently.
My only issue is when it comes to SCS releasing dlc for the game. After a year and a half, we still only have 3 states. At this rate, don't expect to ever have the entire country to travel. Sure, it's nice to have more variety in loads and truck customization, but the modding community has created lots of that type of content already. I would really like to see SCS focus more on the map at this point. The fact is that when you are driving, what the truck looks like on the outside doesn't change the fact that you are still looking at the same scenery on the same few roads. It gets kind of repetitive after a while.
I would still recommend the game for winding down after a long day, but SCS really needs to step up the release of additional states if they want to keep people interested.

This game is the best $20 you could spend if you like driving and/or traveling. Even if you don't like to drive semi trucks, there are plenty of mods for smaller vehicles like sedans, pickup trucks, and SUVs.
What I like about the game:
-Same scale as ETS2, which is 1:20. This is the perfect balance that both lets you explore places faster than IRL but includes most of the details.
-Deep truck customization.
-Even with just the current 3 states (soon to be 4), it takes at least 200 hours to fully explore them. The developers put a lot of detail into the game world.
-The graphics are great. The scenery is fairly realistic (more so if your PC can handle High-Ultra settings) and the trucks are very detailed.
-The developers listen to the community for the most part. If they hadn't we would still be stuck with a much smaller map.
What I don't like about the game:
-New map DLCs take quite a long time to come out
-Even with top-notch PCs, driving in cities can be laggy especially in 1st person view.
-There are minor innaccuracies in the map, such as roads that don't exist (that highway that goes from Fresno all the way to US-395) or completely missing areas (like the Silicon Valley).
-Pickup trucks are non-existent, and all car/pickup/SUV mods have truck physics (abnormally high center of gravity, terrible low-end acceleration)

With the level editor FINALLY being implemented after so long, I can definitely recommend this game.
Even with the base content, it's definitely worth the $9.99 USD price tag. There are a total of 36 levels spread out around 6 'worlds', each with their own theme such as spring, winter, fall, summer, etc. Each level has a secret, which is a golden triangle, and if you manage to find all of them in worlds 1-5, world 6 will then unlock. In addition, there are a few extra secrets for achievements as well.
The gameplay is typical of puzzlers, starting out easy and getting progressively harder. However, it is also VERY fun, with four (technically five, but the fifth is a portal key to unlock the next world only found in the last level for each world) block types. The red cube, which is a structure block. The blue cube, which is a power block. The purple cube, which is a cube that reduces gravity in a certain range. And the green cube, which is a motor device that deteriorates after a certain distance. Typically, each world introduces a new block type, making the levels and designs more and more complex and challenging. Expect to fall out of the world to your death many times, this can be a very challenging puzzler.
The sounds and music are also superb. Each level has its own special music track, each as equally entrancing as the last. The musical score for this game is honestly amazing, and they also have the soundtrack available for purchase, which I will provide the link to
.
I can't leave out the graphics. For as simple as this game is, the visuals are honestly breathtaking. Lighting and shadowing are definitely the biggest strong points of this game graphically, and they never disappoint. Everything from the soft lighting on the blocks, the varying skyboxes, the flowing trees, and the glistening water all look the very best. If you're a sucker for that kind of thing, you might find yourself like I was, anticipating the next levels to see what lighting and graphics tricks they would apply next.
The only thing that's really any kind of drawback is the lack of a story whatsoever. There isn't necessarily an obvious point to the puzzling madness, but imo it's nothing major. It isn't what the selling point is anyway in any case.
Amazing game, definitely a must-buy for puzzle fans, particularly if it's ever on sale, and I'm very excited to play and build community levels.

I have to admit, that I like Assassin's Creed series and enjoy each AC game. The same was with Liberation, which is not a 'normal' game as e.g. Black Flag, but a port of a PSP's version. However I have enjoyed the time spent with Aveline. Liberation offers the same as the other games, but everything is just smaller. There are the same pros and cons as in other AC games. It offers us canonical for series: story similar to the previous ones; impressive fights, parkour great as always. There are also three different locations, which I prefered more than the ones in ACIII. On the other hand we find here a very  stupid ending, sporadic camera problems and a few frustrating missions. Also the visual side of this game could be better - it is clearly seen, that the game was not made to work on the powerful computers.
The items collectors will also have fun - there are many chests to be looted and diary pages or alligator eggs to be found.
The game is smaller by all means. You should include the time needed to complete it - it took me 6,5 hours to complete 86% of Liberation (including the items, mini missions etc).
I recommend this game as much as I recommend any other AC game. Even if it is not perfect, it still makes fun and does not cost a fortune.

Beautiful little gem, really feels like a new world instead of a puzzle game with puzzle levels... Even though it really is just that.
The world is formed around blocky architecture with "natural" assets added to give it a more friendly and inviting environment. There's no story, dialogue, or text except for the main menu/chapter titles. Everything is presented in a manner that teaches the player what to do, instead of holding their hand/letting them walk around blindly.
The best aspect about this game is the... everything. As I said, it has no story, but with what it has (instead of what it's missing); the level design, the atmosphere, the music, the sound design, the HUD, the graphics, it hits the right note on every one of these.
I found myself smiling and feeling a sense of wonder and calmness throughout the levels, but it knows how to be a tad more serious/somewhat challenging at times as well.
As I mentioned, the game is missing something that's keeping it from being even more. I could probably say that a story would improve the experience for me, but if it weren't done correctly, it may ruin the already wonderful experience it gives.
For such a short game, I'm probably writing too much or more than such a simple game warrants, but I think everyone should consider playing this for its atmosphere and sound design. The water sounds really wet, the wind sounds really windy, and the cubes sound really cubey. Just play it for the experience, not for challenge or story.

I Love this game!  Its great for anyone who likes a mix of arcade style action and elaborate Indiana Jones Style puzzle solving, minus the whip.  Didn't play the multipler, and I only really bought this game for single player campaign, so I will not touch on the multiplayer in this review.  However, that doesn't mean that I won't try the multiplayer eventually.   You can only get so much out of the single player campaign, especially since there isn't much that seems to be randomized in this game.  I have only played the game on its easiest settings, but it was enough of a challenge for me.  Perhaps that would be too easy for you, but you can play the game on a higher difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty.  You can set both the combat difficulty and the puzzle difficulty, to determine how much you want to improve your shooting and mental skills.
There are a ton of puzzles in this game, and some of them can be a bit of a challenge even on the lowest setting.  A few will kill you instantly if you make a mistake.  I may still choose to raise the puzzle difficulty the next time I play, since most of them were pretty easy.
In addition, in some cases you can use the traps to kill your enemies, but your timing has to be right, otherwise they will escape unscathed.   It is still a plus through, becouse it adds a bit more stratagy to the game.
All of the weapons are great and I really loved how they set it up so that you need to focus the light from your flashlight, ( or "torch" as people in the UK call them ) on the mummies in order to kill them.  If you don't, your bullets will not harm them.  You will just keep shooting them until they manage to kill you instead.  That is a pretty unique game play mechanic that makes the mummies far more challenging than they otherwise would be, even though it took me a little while to figure it out.  It was a bit embarrassing given the fact that it kept telling me to use the "alt key" to focus the beem.
There are also a few plot twists, one of which may shock you.
I usually prefer the old school "look for med kits to replenish your health" system in video games, particulary first person shooters.  I was a bit disappointed that it had a modern regenerative health system rather than something like the health system in Duke Nukem 3D or Half Life.  Regenerative health systerms usually make games too hard for me, since they tend to really pile on the enemies, assuming the playing is always going to be at full health. However the health system worked well for this game, and I don't think I would change it too much.  It would be really cool through if they added a special hardcore mode where health didn't regenerate and the player had to look for healt packs to restore their health.
I also really enjoyed the treasure hunting mechanic.  Its also really nice how you can use the treasure to uprgrade Quertermane's abilities.  However, it would have been better in my opinion if you could have used the treasures to upgrade his abilities in anyway you wanted, instead of having to search for specific treasures for specific abilities.
There are a few other improvements they could have made to this game.
Although the weapon design was good, and the choices made sense for the time period that this game takes place ( around World War 2 ) it was a bit of a let down for me that you didn't have any melee weapons.  You can't even use your guns as melee weapons.  Luckily you do have a pistol that has infinate ammo.  You can however swicth pistol with other weapons, but weapons in the pistol slot tend to have infinate ammo.  Weapons in the second gun and explosive slots do not have unlimited ammo. It would have been more realistic if none of your weapons had infinate ammo and instead you could use them as melee weapons when you were low on ammunition.

Deadfall Adventures is a first person action/adventure game developed by The Farm 51 and published by Nordic Games. In Deadfall Adventures you play as James Lee Quatermain, an adventurer who struggles to live up to his legendary adventurer of a grandfather, Allan Quatermain
Quatermain's new job is to escort a US agent called Jennifer Goodwin through an Egyptian temple to find an ancient treasure which will eventually lead you all across the world killing mummies and chasing Nazis and it looks like Deadfall Adventures is inspired by Indiana Jones and Naughty Dog's Uncharted
Deadfall Adventures has some good graphics with good visual effects yet some poor character animations. Surprisingly, good puzzles, they are challenging and often take a lot of thinking to solve but never feel too hard and the combat difficulty and puzzle difficulty can be changed independently via the settings menu

The game has an Interesting mix of genre with an overall mediocre gunplay apart from an interesting mechanic involving mummies and flashlights which seems to copy Remedy's Alan Wake. There are some cool and pretty big locations with lots of hidden collectibles to find
There is a relatively wide variety of weapons with a good variety of enemies to fight however they can become rinse and repeat nearing the end of the game and there are some great atmospheric settings in the game
Surprisingly, Deadfall Adventures performs well on high settings with little to no framerate drops with simple controls. However, all of the humour in the game is very cheesy and cringy, and I hardly laughed at the supposed 'funny' dialogue
Deadfall Adventures does suffer with bland and terrible voice acting and I noticed a fair few typos and occasionally missing words in the subtitles
There is an uninteresting story based around uninteresting characters taking references to other better movies and games such as Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and the Uncharted series and the game is riddled with bugs and glitches
The puzzle hints are almost entirely useless and the checkpoints are few and far between. As mentioned previously, Deadfall Adventures suffers with some very clunky animations
Despite some issues I had fun playing Deadfall Adventures with its good graphics, good puzzles and its interesting genre combination. If you're a fan of Indiana Jones and Uncharted style of things then I suggest you pick this one up while it's on sale however not at full price...

tl;dr - Overall, American Truck Simulator (ATS) is a great game and worth the $20!
ATS, the successor to SCS' European Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2) and their many other trucking-based titles is, in many ways, more of the same: drive your truck, constantly threading a moving needle, finding your Zen as you explore the world (without hitting anything). However, it is something new, expanded, and GREATLY improved from the predecessors.
Gameplay is much the same - Create your company, do quick jobs in the trucks of others, earn some money, research the map, and try not to hit stuff. When you have enough money - or feel like going to the bank, buy a truck (or two) and start taking your own jobs across the American Southwest. Maybe expand your garage and hire someone to drive with you - It does help to pay the bills. Wash, rinse, repeat until you have pimped out your ride.
Some of the improvements I have noticed are better graphics (more easily readable dash panels, reflections in the rain-soaked asphalt), MUCH improved AI drivers, and all of the touches that make you really feel you are in America - not just an Americanized version of Europe. The on and off ramps are wider (that I have seen).
The hard work SCS went to in order to give the feeling that you are actually in the Southwest is obvious. I have driven a LOT of this region and they really give you a feel for it. As one major review for the mentioned - this seems more Fallout than Fallout. (Can't wait to have a garage in Primm...) One of my major issues with ETS2 was that I always felt like I was driving in a valley between hills. ATS shows the scenery and vistas of the wide-open spaces. I can't wait to see what they do in Arizona - a former home state for me. I wonder if I can stop off at the Perkins in Flagstaff... or get some biscuits and gravy in Mesa Verde... or maybe stop off at Mag's Ham Bun...
One thing that will catch up MANY players - especially old ETS2 drivers - is the increased punitive fines. Not only is there an increase in the dollar amount of the fines (I did always feel ETS2 fined you too little), The presence of patrol cars ANYWHERE is a bit jarring. Hiding on the side of the road or in a parking lot? expected. Cruising up behind and catching you for going a mile over? maddening on occasion. In my first half dozen jobs, I think I lost $3700 between a few speeding tickets and one red light... But, you do the crime...
One complaint from others regards the minimal environment (CA and NV only) and only having two trucks (Petes and KWs). While I can understand this to a point, it is a non-issue after playing for awhile. By the time a driver gets around the area, Arizona will be out. By the time a driver levels up to a top truck/engine, new trucks will be in the game (pleasebealonestarpleasebealonestarpleasebealonestarpleasebealonestar).
So, yeah. Pay the $20. Play the game. Find your Zen.
