Some of the best damn character creation I've ever seen in a game. Plenty of games promise wide character creation, this game delivers. Pure psionic mindcaster? Pistols and riot shield? Sniper? Stealthy ninja? Dude with a giant hammer? Trapper? These are all viable, all play distinctly, and can be mixed with each other to make unique characters. Combat is an engaging experience, with plenty of options every turn. This also one of the few games to get crafting right. Instead of acting as a smalltime craftsmen and churn out dozens of identical weapons to rake in some cash, you instead slowly collect high-quality ingredients that can be combined into a supremely powerful item, such as a weapon, armor, or psionic headband. I probably crafted only a dozen items throughout my playthrough, and each one felt like a significant achievement by my character, this was also reflected in the stats of the item. Going room to room, fighting monsters and developing your character is where the game shines the most.
Some people dislike the story. The overall story is fairly dry for most of the game, but it is told competently. Slowly, through reading computer logs, an overall picture of what is happening forms. It feels very natural, and I enjoy games that tell a story that way. But there are very few memorable characters, the world, while having a few unique and interesting parts, generally feels bland, and the writing is merely servicable (although thankfully not too long).
Also, this is not a game that respects the player's time. Walking is slow, even though I wore speed-boosting boots. Selling off all your items can require ferrying around to multiple different cities to completely cash out. The player house takes a long time to get to.
Ultimately, this game is either absolutely incredible to a certain kind of gamer, and boring and unfair to another. I don't know how to differentiate these groups, as it is not simply a hardcore/casual divide. For what it's worth, I found it very enjoyable.

I do really love elsword, and I have been playing since about almost 3 years now. Although this game is very good,
there are flaws too. Let me get started.
Graphics.
The graphics in this game are VERY well done. Very clear looking, and I don't get bored
from fighting either. They put well detail into the graphics which is definatly one of my favorite
things about Elsword. Although, if you don't have a very strong PC, it can get laggy. If your PC
is strong enough to handle the graphics, you will enjoy the game. Lagging can eventually lead
to crashing, (which I have experianced before) So in dungeons it can be very annoying because
you will have to start the dungeon all over again if you crash. Depending if the dungeon is very long
that is. if you also have bad internet that increases crashing. (from experiance)
Characters.
All the characters are very interesting in their own way. There are approximatley 7
characters in the game. Elsword has a story line to it, which is why every character comes with
their own backstory which is a cool detail to add about the characters. There is a new character
coming in the future, so there are gonna be about 8.
Although, there are more female characters then male characters in the game. There are 5
female characters and 4 male characters. Not much of a difference, but I still feel like they
should balance out male and female characters, so the amount is equal.
About the fighting animation on the characters. I absolutley love this part! The animation is soooo
well done in the fighting/Action parts of the game! Very cool to look at, and it's not easy to get bored.
The cool thing I like about the fighting, is that there are loops you can learn on each character. So if you are
a beginner and are just starting out, don't worry because you can look at many tutuorials on youtube for looping
on each character. If you are unsure of the term "looping" in Elsword, it's basicly a combo that you can learn that
can be done over and over again once mastered on your keyboard. Here's an example on the keyboard : zzz < > zzz
(and repeat over and over again) These loops can help you become better at fighting in the game. Learn combos
and become creative!
So far the character design is very well done. Put well detail into the characters which is very good about them.
The characters don't look deformed in places, and it looks like the creaters actually put the effort in making a game
that can look and feel cool to their players that play the game.
Item Mall / Cash Shop
The item mall can be a very cool place to buy things from. You can buy costumes, Pets, accesorys, ect.
You need something called "K-ching" to buy things from the item mall. But, to get K-ching you need to pay
with your real money. I have had an experiance with their credit card system about a year back, maybe a little
more then that. Of course, I was purchasing KC (k-ching) like I always do, when it stopped excepting the credit
card I was using. And I have asked players if some of them had the same problem. And some of them have. I had
to download Elsword on steam as well for it to actually work for me again. Luckily it works on steam, so I reccommend
getting KC from here then from the original Elsword. Other then that, the item mall is very fun. But one more thing is
that things can be kind of expensive in the item mall. Usually, for example getting a costume peice permanatley
would be, 500-KC and sometimes 600 KC. The price goes higher too. And the options for how much KC you can get
are:

5$ = 500 k-ching
10$ = 1000 k-ching
20$ = 2000 k-ching
50$ = 5000 k-ching
100$ = 10,000 k-ching.
If you wanted you could save your Kc to get more also. but for me, I think these prices for KC can be a little
pricy for the amount of K-ching you get. Other then that, I love buying from the item mall and probably won't stop.
Customer service/ Support
Before I dowloaded the steam version of Elsword, I was asking for help on the original Elsword website.
Remember that K-ching problem I had? Yup,  I had to go through sooooo much with them just to fix some
dumb k-ching problem. They kept telling me that my card must have been with no money on it, when there
was exaclty enough! I kept telling them it was their system that was causing the problem, because  absolutley
nothing! was wrong with my credit card. I told them it stopped excepting my credit card number, so they told
me to wait 48 hours to try again. Nothing. Still did not work. They told me to try AGAIN. Nothing. Then they
told me they'd contact someone to help me which still DID NOT do anything! I got very angry with them, and
eventually stopped asking them for customer service. I definatley don't think they know what their doing in
customer service so I don't recommend coming to their original website for help. Come to steam instead.
Villages/Towns
Since there is a story line to Elsword their is an amount of towns you go through when leveling. Right now
there are about 8 towns right now which I think is pretty good. There will also be new towns coming soon
and a new level cap. They do a good job putting a story to each town. Not dissapointed with this. I will name
the towns below from top to bottom in order, of when you start till' your'e done leveling.

Conan Exiles has a solid start in the early access system, but still has massive work left in it.
Video:
Text:
Visually the game has a very nice art-style that fits thematically immensely well with the settings, but the developers have also created a lush and diverse environment - even when the basic premises seems to be "Sand, Sand everywhere". Sadly the animations leave quite a bit of room for improvement with there being some missing animations, some floaty transitions and quite a few weird movement / physics bugs.
Crafting and exploration are the games main draws, and those two elements are very well fleshed out - with a good balance between "Survival" and sandbox fun, the game has a slew of interesting progression tiers tied into its crafting mechanics that allows for a very fluid expansion of your hovel, house and homestead.
The drawback is that the combat is non-existent in terms of development time. You can swing a sword and shoot a bow and there it ends, Dodge is buggy, movement is fiddly, animations are clunky, blocking is buggy and there is no depth to combat in any shape. Also the monster and NPC Ai is very weak overall and needs massive work.
All in all, Conan exiles has the solid foundation for a great multiplayer experience if you enjoy cooperative building and exploring, and lacks the depth if you enjoy PvP.
Servers can be hosted by players with an extensive set of rules and options, and while the admin tools are very "alpha", they are also reasonably robust and allow on the fly rule-changes and customization from Food & Hunger requirements all the way to day/night cycle times. Pretty good.
Depending on your gameplay goals, PvE or PvP the game is worth your time in many scenarios.... but not all.

* Level design is uninspired and sometimes unneccisarily confusing. Also, at least one of these makes absolutely no sense whatsoever within the game universe. Who in their right mind would rig a line of bells ringing all around the place when enemies are attracted by noise?
* Player-style: The game kind of hints there are alternatives to how you play. Quiet or loud. But really, the way the game ramps up difficulty as the story progresses, it forces you to be non-sneaky (as mentioned above, this is at least sometimes against the game's own premise).
* Representation: There's nowhere near a reasonable female to male ratio and those few women that did survive the appoxolypse have insanly wobbly and large breasts. Further, the game thinks it is very smart and clever with this bright and never before seen use of women as sexualized objects.
* Story: The lack of representation and fully kills what does start out promising. It's not the only issue I have with it. It doesn't really bring anything new and interesting. Just go here, get caught or similar go somewhere else. Chase some bad people, oops fall down into a monster's den. You all know this story. I must admit I got so fed up with the whole game that I decided it ended about three quarters through where I decided my Artyom died. On the surface. Suffocating. The most suitable ending to a disappointing experience.

I wasn't really sure what to expect from this game going in. The PS Vita version got some pretty mixed reviews, so I was skeptical. Ultimately, Assassin's Creed: Liberation HD won me over. It's pretty short compared to the main Assassin's Creed games, but for only $20 it's ultimately a solid deal. The game plays mostly like Assassin's Creed 3, with the exception of the cool, new kill chain feature, which allows you to quickly target up to 3 enemies at once and kill them all in quick succession. It's fun. There's also a new take on the notoriety system called personas. Aveline, the game's protagonist, may change between 3 outfits that change how guards treat her. The standard Assassin getup allows for full mobility and equipment usage, but you always have your notoriety meter at least a quarter filled. Her slave disguise also allows free-running, but she's restricted to blow darts, her hidden blade, and a machete. She can sneak right into restricted areas as long as she looks like she's working, but socially unacceptable actions carry a much higher noteriety penalty than usual. Aveline's Lady persona, aside from making her look pretty attractive, makes her nearly impossible to discover in restricted areas, but the dress she is wearing prevents her from climbing at all, and allows her to move on foot at a jog at the fastest. She is also limited to just her hidden blade and a parasol gun. It was an interesting new idea that was mostly successful, but could have used a bit more freedom and variety in practice.
On the story side of things, the game is pretty irrelevant. I couldn't help but often question why Aveline was going through any of the scenarios I was playing. There's no sense of urgency to the game that drives the plot forward, unlike the main series. Visually, the game is pretty impressive. Again it's roughly on the same level as Assassin's Creed 3 in that regard. The game world itself is a decent size. Over the course of the game, you visit New Orleans, the Lousiana bayou, and Chichén Itzá: a templar controlled colony in Mexico. New Orelans is similar in size to AC3's Boston, while being a fair bit more colorful and varied. The Bayou is dwarfed by the Frontier, but it's still farily expansive and takes some time to fully explore. Overall, If you're looking for a little bit more Assassin's Creed to tide you over while you wait for Unity, Liberation is a worthwhile buy.

This wasn't a game at the top of my wishlist, but I have been eyeing it since it came out, and when I found it on sale at the HB store for $15 I jumped at the opportunity.  I wasn't disappointed - personally I really enjoyed the game.  The story is engaging, the acting is very good, the visuals and mood of the game are great.  I think a lot of people hating on it are either bandwagon-jumpers who haven't played it, or were just expecting a different kind of game.  A lot of complaints seem to revolve around a lack of action - you just sort of walk around and click where it tells you to.  And in reality there's not too much more to the gameplay, so if you want more then you probably won't like it.  I went in treating it as more of an interactive story - a glossed-up point-and-click adventure, if you will, and I wasn't let down.  The game does have legitimate problems, but for me none of them were deal-breakers, and were outweighed by the pros:
Cons:
- suffered from performance issues and fairly frequent frame rate drops, which got worse as the game went on
- no ability to remap keys
- the mouse didn't work for all the menu items
- no chance to go back and finish collecting items once you've entered the final level, meaning you'd have to play through the game again in order to try and get everything.  As much as I like the game, I'm not interested in playing it all again just to finish up a few achievements
- the demons were really more of an annoyance than anything - they should have played more of a roll or just been pulled altogether
- a lot of the investigations were far too simple to solve, while a small few were unreasonably obscure
Pros:
- Great voice acting
- Great camera work
- Great atmosphere
- Great story
- NOT too short - I put 12-13 hours into the game by taking my time, doing the side missions, collecting artifacts, and generally immersing myself into the really good story.  I'd rather play a really enjoyable 8-12 hour game than spend 2 or 3 times that on something I end up barely able to finish because I've gotten so sick of it (L.A. Noire springs to mind).  Besides, at 12 hours I spent barely over a buck per hour on it - that's pretty good value in my book.
So overall it's probably not worth full price, but easily worth $15-$25, as long as you enjoy story-driven adventure games.

Writing this review as of the Plains update, as someone who has played since the game came out.
Warframe seems to be getting farther and farther away from the formula that made it entertaining to begin with, which is mindlessly killing things in fun and fast ways. While new concepts in Warframe have always started off rough and gotten polished over time, the latest additions are doubling down on concepts that many players resent.
First, the story in Warframe has become mandatory. Early Warframe you barely had to worry about any story, which is what many people look for in a somewhat mindless shoot and loot game. Now, you are forced to partake in story quests if you don't want to severely limit your potential. And why they still don't allow you to skip cutscenes is beyond me. Being forced to sit through the entirety of what I find to be an uninteresting story is painful.
The grind in Warframe has also become insane with the newest Plains patch. I enjoyed knowing I could log on, do a sortie and maybe an alert or two, and then I could choose what to do with my time. Maybe that is farming materials, maybe it is void missions to get parts for a new weapon or frame, maybe its a credit farm, but whatever it was, its because I wanted to do it. With the current update, accessing any of the new content requires that I now force myself to run bounties and kill the same enemy over and over for the new reputation gains. If I want to use my archwing, I am forced to fish. Because thats why I play a game about space ninjas... to go fishing. And in what is basically like a big middle finger to their players, you can spend 45 minutes doing a high-level bounty, and assuming a bug doesn't ruin it, the reward at the end can be a common item found in a 5 minute alert.
I could go on and on about things that don't make sense to me... why are they forcing operators down our throats which just feels completely uninteresting after we have spent years working on frames and weapons. Why do riven mods require  such stupid tasks to unlock, instead of something fun like kill 300 enemies. Why is the Plains patch described as an open world and completely new way to play Warframe, when ultimately it is just the same map over and over with a slightly larger tileset, and really not open world at all.
It seems like the devs need to hire someone who listens to every idea that they pitch or discuss, and then asks "but is it fun?" Because many of their current designs seem to be lacking in that. The game has become more of a chore for me than something I can play at my own pace and in my own way. It is days after the release of a major new patch and I find myself uninterested to log on at all.

I saw this game at E3 of last year, thought it looked pretty interesting, then forgot all about it until it came out. I was going to wait until the price went down, because I had heard mixed reviews about it. I bought it for $25 bucks off of Ebay, and don't regret it one bit. I'll go over the gameplay aspect, but also the PC version side of it as well. I also think that with most of my reviews, rather than peppering the things I don't like in the different sections, I'll just save everything that I don't like for the end, so that you know what I'm talking about.
Gameplay and Story: Gameplay is incredibly intuitive, but not what you would expect. It is a very laid back, calming game. There isn't a lot of action, and when there is it comes in short bursts. As I've read on other reviews, this is a thinking man's game. And, as I have been more of an intellectual versus athletic person, it fits my type of game perfectly. I haven't finished the game yet, I would hazard a guess that I'm about 3/4 of the way through, but so far I have really enjoyed it.
What the game consists of is walking around crime scenes, collecting evidence and slowly picturing together the scene, with each investigation leading you closer to solving your murder, which is the entire point of the game. There are some little side investigations, helping lost souls "find their purpose" for still being on earth even though they're dead. They provide a little bit of depth to the world, but nothing crazy.
Sound and Dialogue: The sound is pretty standard as far as games go, it's not a spectacular soundtrack but the music fits the mood and always sounds good. The voice acting isn't amazing, but it doesn't suck either. Pretty standard.
Environment: The developers did a really nice job at portraying a really dreary, kind of depressing Salem. That could also be the ghost world though, I'm not totally positive which they were going for, but it's really awesome.
Interface and controls: One thing that's nice about not having any real sort of combat is that there isn't anything to clutter up your UI. No bullet counters, no health bars, it's just you. Controls are pretty standard as far as PC games go, shift to run, E to interact, stuff like that. No real difference between games, but if it ain't broke, don't fix it, right?
PC Version: I haven't played the console versions, so I can't compare the quality of the build, but as far as PC ports go it's rock solid. I downloaded it through Steam, didn't have any hiccups installing or booting it up for the first time. The game looks good, it's not next gen quality obviously, but it still looks awesome. One cool thing is that it is not very graphics intensive at all. I have a gtx 770 and could completely max the game out, AA and v sync included, and I still got over 100 fps. If I did that on a 770, I would hazard to guess that you could completely max it out on 600 series cards, or maybe even late 500 series cards. (It was on 1080p, so obviously account for the difference if you have a different resolution).
One odd quirk that I experienced was when I walked by a police car, it dropped and capped at 30 frames per second. As soon as I turned the screen and walked away, it jumped back up to 60. I tried turning everything on low, and it still did it. So that was one weird quirk in the gameplay, but it only happened once and hasn't happened since! If you guys want, I actually did a video demo of the graphics on the 770, you can check it out here if you feel so inclined :D
[...]
So now for the dislikes:
- The length. It's not a long game at all, but I give a little more explanation down below.
- In the menus, and when choosing dialogue options, you can obviously use the mouse, but the button options are the number buttons 1,2,3, and 4. Like what? Who's bright idea was it to make those buttons the switching/choosing dialogue buttons? They deserve to be fired. Lol.
All in all it's a great game, but definitely not for everybody. It's a slow paced, thinking game. I don't think it's worth the $60 price tag, but as I stated earlier I got it for 25 and felt that that was a good deal. I would have even paid 30 for it. The only reason that I feel it's not worth the price tag is merely for the length. I'm only a few hours in and almost done with the game. I explore, but I don't look for every single nook and cranny on every single level, unless it will benefit me in-game somehow. There are a ton of collectibles, but they don't really benefit you in any other way than to say that you've gotten them. So I look, but I don't scour the map for them.
I'm pretty sure that's everything, if you guys have any questions or and corrections, comment and let me know!
**Update 6/15**
So I finished the game, and I loved it. I have 9 hours logged, with what I would put as pretty extensive exploring. I kind of tapered off towards the end, just because I wanted to finish the game lol. I loved the story, atmosphere, the characters, it was great. I would pay up to $30 for it and not regret it. Anything more than that and I think that it wouldn't really be enough, but that's just my opinion!

I've got to say, I rarely write reviews for anything, but I think that in this case, I just have to. So let's get started!
Qbeh-1 is a prequel to game Qbeh (which you can download via Desura). Qbeh was a student project, practically a demo containing 6 levels. This '-1' (minus one) standing next to Qbeh tells that this is a prequel. So, getting back to Qbeh-1: This is a
You will meet several game genres here.
The game contains 5 (or maybe 6? I won't spoil it) worlds, each with 6 levels.
It's an exploration game, so you will not be told practically anything except key bindings (in options).
a) Your goal
Your goal is simple: find the portal to the next level. Simple but difficult.
b) Environment
As you probably saw in the trailers, Qbeh-1 is inspired by Minecraft -
In every level, you will be placed in... well, locations floating somewhere high in the sky. The sky is both above you and below you. On your way, you will encounter several kinds of cubes you can pick up, each one with a unique ability.
c) No violence
For some it's an advantage, for some it's a disadvantage. The only dangers you face is falling, being crushed by a door and touching poison.
d) Soundtrack

Once a 4-level mod made as a puzzle platformer, Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube has gained a dash, a colon, and even a tagline.  The remarkable thing about this mod-to-game is how polished and professional the entire package looks.  Inspired by games like Portal and Minecraft, this game has carved itself a niche that makes it both familiar enough for players to try out, yet unique enough to keep players intrigued and interested.
One of the strongest things Qbeh-1 has going for it is the simplistic gameplay.  It's very obviously inspired by early games, and eschews many of the trappings of modern gaming's superfluous complexities.  Because of this streamlined gameplay loop - find block, place block, move on - it allows the puzzle design to shine.  Rather than throw a substantial number of complicated puzzle mechanics at you, this game instead chooses to give you four basic concepts - building, powering, jumping, and traveling - and by combining them in various ways, can deliver challenges as simple as building a basic set of stairs to a complicated maze with no floor that must be travelled using synchronized floating paths, complete with a white-knuckled jump at the end after placing a power block near the end of the path.  Puzzles start as being simple - its a tutorial that doesn't feel like a tutorial at all, which is commendable - but build and combine in ways where you end up scaling a tower with only a handful of blocks and a deep sense of satisfaction when you reach the top.
The art design is commendable.  One of the most interesting art projects I ever had was to draw a still life using a single color - brown, and two shades, one light brown, and one dark brown.  The point of the exercise was to force you to make your choices more meaningful, rather than rely on an explosion of various colors.  In a way, Qbeh-1 replicates this exercise.  Rather than rely on flashy explosions, the latest and greatest shader effects, models with tens of thousands of polygons, and other graphical gimmicks, it focuses on a narrow band of artistic effects, and then pulls it off with great success.  The colors - stark whites and greys accented with bursts of vibrant colors - not only are visually appeasing next to each other, but also contrast nicely with the amazing skies; some of the best I've yet seen in games.  I got distinct feelings of Mirror's Edge and how they used color to guide the player through the levels.  The color palette here is similar, and I think Qbeh-1 pulls it off better due to how uncluttered the worlds appear compared to Mirror's Edge.
The sound and music design for Qbeh-1 is amazing, as it's simplicity not only fits the thematic elements perfectly, but because of the simplicity, it manages to achieve depth.  Rather than attempt to wow you with orchestral suites or generic dub-step wub-wubs, the music is airy, dreamy, and light.  It fits in perfectly not only with the levels - large buildings floating high in the atmosphere - but it also hits a sweet spot that so much of game music misses; it's unique enough to be noticed, but not catchy enough to become so immediately recognizable (much of World of Warcraft's music suffers from this) that it becomes quickly tedious.  It serves its purpose precisely - as ambient background sound to draw you in, but never to distract you.  It's almost childlike sound and instrument choices help to draw you into the exploration motif, and even still, some tracks have almost a dark feel to them, suggesting there may be more under the surface than what first seems to be the case.
As someone who does level design, the design of the levels was something that impressed me immensely.  Visually, the levels were stunning - floating monolithic structures that combined the comforting feeling of symmetry along with enough asymmetry to still remain visually interesting.  Each world has its own theme, and the themes blend perfectly into the levels - icicles hang overhead in the winter levels, empty calcareous shells of molluscs lay in pools in the water levels, dead leaves lay in corners in the wind levels.  Because everything was uniformly scaled (and the borders on the cubes helped reinforce this), there was never a feeling of having to make ridiculous trick-jumps.  You immediately got the sense of what was possible and what was not, based on distance and the world's physics.  Rather than try to cheat the puzzles using tricky jumps or falls, the solutions felt fair, and ultimately felt rewarding by using your brain rather than trying to exploit the physics, jumping, or collision.
The story and theme is something that I specifically wanted to touch on, as I had seen some posts about there not being a story or anything resembling it.  I'm not entirely sure that's the case, as there definitely feels like there's something going on below the surface.  I think it might be safer to say that rather than a storyline, I felt like there was some overarching theme to the game.
Qbeh-1 feels like a dead world, in a lot of ways.  There is beauty here, but also sadness.  Presumably it was inhabited once - something or someone had to create those owl and elephant statues - but whoever it was is now gone.  The player feels like, as he is exploring, he is inadvertently bringing this world back to life through his actions, either by literally building with red cubes, or by powering up devices with blue cubes.  The notion of power - or the importance of it at least - is reinforced with the windmills and fans in Chapter 4.
Something else that is striking is the feeling and sense of an entropic world.  An extremely basic (flawed, but works here) definition for entropy is the lack of order or structure - that in a closed system, energy flows out of organized and structured systems to leave them in a disordered and chaotic state.  Qbeh-1 really has an entropic feeling to it - the idea that the world is gradually falling into an entropic state of disarray.  Rooms are missing walls, floors, and ceilings, where blocks literally fall into the atmosphere.  Even in areas where walls and floors are straight, the occasional cube will be out of place - sticking out a few cm, or perhaps tilted just a few degrees; clearly done on purpose by the designer for effect.  Floors crumble beneath you as you walk on them.  Perhaps the fans and windmills were an effort to make sure energy remaining in the system, holding it together as best as it could.  And perhaps by our actions, and how we (in a way) organized the system, there is hope for this world after all.
Qbeh-1, overall, is an amazing example of a non-typical game that easily surpasses much of what would be considered more mainstream games, by virtue of the fact that everything is does, it does really, really well.  Rather than be a jack-of-all-trades to attempt to appeal to everything while exceeding at nothing, Qbeh-1 excels at the simplistic gameplay that leads to complicated puzzles, stunning artistic theme, amazing music and sounds, and incredible level design that pulls all these elements together into a cohesive unit.  It's a peaceful game that alternates some degree of timing puzzles with the slow and methodical exploration that allows you to play at your own pace. For those who enjoy exploration, each level also contains a golden pyramid pickup which are usually hidden in fiendishly clever places.
Developed using the Unity game engine, this is a game which is highly recommended, but I fear that it will slide under the radar for most gamers which I think is a tragedy.  It's a great example of the ability to marry the puzzle genre with a more  traditional first person genre, and still be successful without resorting to violence, being spoon fed a storyline, or the overly scripted gameplay which creates the illusion of cerebral choice, but actually offers none at all.  Rather this game celebrates choice, exploration, and emergent problem solving in an environment which nutures it.

This is the second part of the Mass Effect trilogy, picking up where the first left off.  If you haven't played the first game yet, you should play it before starting this one.  The entire universe of the series is laid out in ME1, and this second game loses a lot in the story department (the series' strongest part) if you don't have the backstory and characterization that the first game brings.  Also, there are a number of major decisions that you make in the first game which carry over with your save into the second.
On a technical level, this game is better in most respects than the first installment.  The shooting and controls are improved, the galaxy map is massively improved, the graphics are much better, certain things which were overly complicated are simplified, etc.  They have improved the overall accessability and playability of the game greatly
Unfortunately, Bioware also seems to have decided that if something didn't work right in the first game, it's better to just tear it out instead of improving it.  So they practically removed weapon customization from the game for example.
Another case in point - the first game allowed you to explore huge sandbox style spaces on dozens of different planets throughout the galaxy.  Although this was tedious at times and the controls for exploring were wonky, the one thing this mechanic did perfectly was SHOW the vastness and variety of the galaxy you were flying around it.  In Mass Effect 2, they remove this mechanic entirely save for a couple of DLC missions which pale in comparison.  So now you play almost entirely on small map spaces with many corridors and indoor sections and makes it just feel like you are flying from airport to airport like a business traveller.  You don't get the feeling that you are really exploring the great expanse of the galaxy, and the overall feel of the game suffers for it.
Still, this is a great game, and I think more fun to replay than the first game because of the simplication measures that were done.  Taken as an overall package it's probably the best game of the trilogy.

I can appreciate this game going for the old school isometric thing that was big back in the day. Games like Fallout and Fallout II come to mind. While those games were somewhat difficult, Underrail is insanely difficult even on easy (easy is actully very hard and normal is nightmare).
Combat is grueling and I mean extremely grueling. You will always be outnumbered. All enemies get their full move. All enemies get full attacks. Your enemies will always use special attacks and they are always succesful. If you are outnumbered 5:1, every enemy will get 5 attacks which means 25 attacks to your 3. If you move at all, only 2 attacks. Have to reload? Only one attack for you. You may have a 95% chance to hit but be prepared to miss every single attack. I often tabbed out of the game to let combat play out so I could do some surfing. I would come back to the game to find my character almost dead and stunned meaning hit the space bar and let them attack 25 more times. I often would forget to come back to Underrail after alt-tabbing out to surf while combat played out hence my many hours in the game. I'm sure I left in running many nights after going to bed.
It's one thing to be difficult but there has to be some balance.
You have to wait 2 (or 4) turns to heal. Not your enemies.
You have to wait 2 or 3 rounds to use a grenade. Not your enemies.
Miss a key shot? - hit F9, you probably won't survive combat.
Weapons and armor degrade very fast and repair kits are extremely expensive.
Levels are very samey and there's no map so be prepared to wonder aimlessly trying to find things for hours.
Combat will wear you down. Everyone has a certain level of tolerance. I probably have a fair amount for stuff like this but I got to the last area and that was it. I just couldn't stomach any more F5, F9, F9, F9, F9, F5, F9, F9, F5, F9, F9, F9...
If you are considering this, just start searching for Underrail and difficulty. Read some of the negative reviews.

If you want to know weather or not you're going to enjoy Deadfall Adventures, you have to ask yourself one question:
"Can I look past the absolute worst dialogue in the history of modern video games?"
That is the key part where Deadfall... falls dead. The story is nothing special but it's interesting enough. The action is good, the music is well-done, and the puzzles are challenging. There is a lot to like here.
Unfortunately Deadfall Adventures has numerous setbacks. The biggest one being the abysmal dialogue. The writing is average, but the voice acting is awful. Characters are loud when they should be quiet, and quiet when they should be loud. There are odd pauses throughout conversations, and some of the voice lines are just downright delayed beyond belief.
The other big issue is the widescreen support (or lack thereof), and the FOV. While I praise Deadfall Adventure's FOV slider for offering the player an unusually large variation (up to 140), the weapon view models are unaffected by this FOV. Thus, although you can set the FOV to a high number, you cannot remove the visual sensation that your character is holding his gun right in front of his eyeball.
However, with some tweaking this can be fixed. An excellent (and free) program called
will allow you to tweak the weapon FOV to be more acceptable.
Fortunately, this fix is a trivial one. And once you have completed it, you should have no trouble enjoying the game's unique blend of shooting and puzzle-solving.
My only other problem with Deadfall Adventures was its difficulty. And I don't mean the game was too hard. Rather, I think it was far too easy. In my first playthrough, I set both the puzzle and combat difficulty to their highest (Hard), and had little trouble with it. Bare in mind that I also restricted myself from using any of the upgrades throughout the game, in order to try and increase the game's challenge. I think the difficulty on the puzzles was a good balance, but the combat was far too forgiving.
The culprit behind the easy combat is likely the game's rather stupid AI. The enemies will often walk slowly towards the player with no regard for their safety. Or sometimes they'll pop up from behind cover, aim at the player, and take several seconds before they actually pull the trigger. This gives the player plenty of opportunities to eliminate them.
However, do not let these faults detract from the game too much. In spite of the above, there is much to like in Deadfall Adventures. I found the puzzles (for the most part) to be challenging and just frustrating enough to keep me going. The weapons were also surprisingly satisfying. Couple that with an interesting story, and a chance to play what is essentially the Indiana Jones FPS we never got, and Deadfall Adventures is a fun, albeit flawed, gaming experience.

If you are offended by foul language, steer clear. It isn't just enemy pilots about to die; it isn't just in dialogs with lowlifes; it is in the ambient sound for the game itself (presumably intercom chatter aboard your own vessel). Totally unnecessary, and adds no value to the game.
Now, after turning the noise completely off, and ignoring the dialogs (which you can probably get away with, since the in-game indicators tell you what you need to do next), you can get around that objection, so what is left?
A lot of grinding. I don't mind grinding, generally, but I appreciate some sort of appreciable reward for grinding. Admittedly, I didn't go far in the game, but the whole time I felt behind.
Regrets that I can't give a positive comment. Building and maintaining a small space task force is right up my alley, so I thought it would be great. It isn't.

I got this after completing the Ezio trilogy, thinking nothing could top how much I liked them. This absolutely does. It runs 100x smoother, has more longevity, and above all, feels more realistic.
I've thought time and time again that Ezio (and the other assassins) stick out like sore thumbs in their robes, and finally, it got addressed. Aveline can dress as a Lady, to blend with the elite crowd and charm/bribe guards into letting her in restricted areas. She can dress as a Slave, to blend with other workers and get in to places only slaves would be allowed, as well as being able to free run and climb in this persona. And thirdly, we can dress as an Assassin, but the attire looks more pirate/sailer in my opinion. The only downside is that in Assassin persona, you're always slightly notorious.
Another issue I've had with previous AC's is that you can't climb trees...the one thing even most regular people could climb. Aveline not only climbs trees, but can take advantage of hanging vines to swing from tree to tree. You also get a whip some 1/4 way in to swing from things with, and to catch and drag back enemies that might be running from you.
There are plenty of side missions, a large amount specific to each persona, which means you can switch as you please to do missions you're in the mood for. You make money in Liberation by using the ship trading system, which is pretty fun and easy to use.
My only qualm with this game is that it uses the newer fighting system, and I find it a bit player unfriendly.

This game is all about trial and error. Messing up is a party of the game. Yes, this game sucks sometimes, but what it does well, it does great. Stealth, crafting and combat in particular.
Infiltrating enemy base, looting containers for oddities, killing just the boss, that you have a contract on... It just works.
Crafting loses some fun when you start mix-maxing, but being able to craft almost anything in the game makes it much more believable.
And combat is what makes or breaks the game. Yes, rng plays a big role and some fights are frustrating. But what really works is a feeling, that you are fighting characters, similar to your own, not gimped losers, who are only there for you to feel good about yourself. Enemy snipers, crossbow hunters, melee, rogues, psionics can kill you in 1 turn in 1-on-1 fight. Killing a group of such enemies due to planning and execution (and save-load abuse sometimes) feels very good.
If this game has some appeal to you, it's definitely worth trying.

Recettear is an interesting game with Zelda-style dungeon scrolling with a twist. You are NOT the hero/adventurer! You're the bloody shopkeeper.
Recette is a young girl who inherited her father's debt and must now pay a collection agency umptybajillion dollars or have her house reposessed. Helping her with this is Tear, a small fairy girl who works for said agency and helps her run an item shop to earn enough money to pay off the debt.
To stock the shop you team up with several different heroes, at first just a swordsman but eventually a mage, thief, elven archer, and so on and crawl through dungeons to find weapons, food, armor, and so on. You then put this stuff up for sale in Recette's shop and sell it to said adventurers, regular people, and so on.
Given that my REAL JOB is working as a register monkey this game should have had me running in terror... but damn if I didn't get a kick out of playing it. If you like RPGs its definately worth a try.

This is game is excellent. Simply put, I don't know of a game that offers so much replay value. As you'll see from others' (as well as my own) review, this game can be played for literally hundreds of hours (and that's without indulging in the multiplayer, I'd say). Each religion offers a fairly different style of gameplay, as does playing in each individual empire. If you're looking for a good deal in grand strategy, look no further. This game often goes on sale with much of its DLC included for $10, and at that price it's a steal. Paradox also adds content about every 4 months, and while some of it is DLC (usually $10-$15), I've always found it's worth it, and they release a bunch of free content with each DLC release anyways. I really cannot recommend this highly enough. If you want a good write up of the game, I recommend reading T.J. Hafer's Crusader Kings Chronicle (
). He really shows how this game can be grand strategy, role playing, and/or story-generating device. It's his story that got me really interested in CK2.
One recommendation if you buy it is to download one of the many music packs available (free) on the workshop. Since you're in the game for so long, if you don't listen to your own music the CK2 theme can get very repetitive. Other than that, the game plays well out of the box.
Edit 11/27/2016: I still play this game regularly with friends, and it's only gotten more incredible. While I initially disliked the Conclave update, the Reaper's Due update provided lots of new flavor and variety to playthroughs, and I even see conclave as making playing as a vassal more enjoyable now.
More importantly, this game is extremely easy to mod - I often tweak the game with small mods that let me play exactly how I want to. Almost everything you'd want to change can be modded, as displayed by the excellent Game of Thrones mod for CKII that basically makes it a new game.

I purchased Crusader Kings because I had grown bored of Civ V and wanted a game like it that would hold my attention. Little did I know what I had in store when I started playing. Civ V is to CKII as Peek-a-boo is to Chess against a grandmaster. It took me several hours of tutorials and youtube walkthroughs to even begin to grasp the mechanics of this game, and even now I still continue to find features I wasn't aware of almost every time I play.
That being said, Crusader Kings is a masterpiece of Strategy Gaming.
Do not expect to jump into this game and master it immediately, as that is simply not how this game is played. It takes hours of careful observation and trial-and-error before you can even call yourself a competant CKII player. Don't let the learning curve discourage you, though. Once you get the hang of it CKII is one of the most entertaining games I've ever played. Paradox loads keen and funny pop-culture references into the event pop-ups and the possibilities of your own imagination and nearly limitless, especially with the great modding community for both here on Steam as well as Nexus. It's not often that I can hop into a forum and discuss my romp through Europe with an incestuous, lunatic, demon possessed monarch who is married to his own illegitimate daughter.
tl;dr: Not for the weak of heart, but once you;ve got the hang of it it's hard to pull yourself away.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery. Also, wear your seatbelts, kids. This game should be the reason why you do.
Gameplay: I'm not too learned when it comes to racing games, but I do enjoy a good one from time to time. FlatOut is what I would consider to be a good racing game. Not a great one, but a good one at least. As you may or may not know, FlatOut is a racing game more in the vein of rally-style courses than Formula One courses, where there is a great deal of emphasis on vehicle control in rough terrain as opposed to hold down gas, turn wheel every once in a while. Yes, you will definitely need to make use of your brake button in this game, as well as maybe letting go of the gas every once in a while, as all the vehicles in game are rear-wheel drive. RWD means that you can do donuts. It also measn that you may find yourself doing donuts unintentionally. Since most racing games use front wheel drive, the physics in this game may feel unrealistic to some, but if you kinda know how a RWD car works, it's pretty solid actually.
The game has an alright selection of cars, but honestly, you should just pick the car with the best power-to-weight ratio just as a matter of principle. This game also has a system of currency where you win races to get more dosh, and while it never turned into a grindfest for me, it might be if you're not as decent at racing games. Plus, the vehicles with the best PWR aren't really too much more expensive than the ones of the same class. Yes, there are multiple classes of cars in the game, which unlock one class at a time over the three series. While you can beat class two racers with a class one car, it becomes very difficult, and in some instances downright impossible. The way that you can kinda do this is through upgrades, which while a neat idea is also not that well executed, as you have to buy components through a series of parts (you can't just buy the best parts on their own; you've gotta buy the crap ones first). These parts don't transfer to other cars either, which just makes the system feel like a waste of time.
The AI isn't exactly great, and if you've got an underperforming car, races can turn into an exercise in frustration as you have to take the track perfectly. There's no rubberbanding, which is good if you're absolutely smoking your opponents, but also pretty frustrating if you are way behind. AI in this game doesn't really have any aggression either; they just take the track as they want to, irrespective of you being in the way or not. This game manages to save a lot of file size by having only six maps where the tracks are different routes through the map. While the courses do for the most part feel their own (although there are a few lazy excuses for courses just being a course from earlier in reverse), you'll find yourself seeing a lot of familiar sights. Also, as mentioned earlier, this game is more along the lines of a rally racing game, so there's a LOT of start and stop. If that's not your thing, you may wanna look elsewhere.
Overall, while this game could've done with some more work on tracks and the AI, it's still a pretty fun game overall. I managed to 100% the game with all gold medals in the amount of time that I've been playing it (~8 hours as of writing this review), and I don't regret my time. I just wish there was a bit more done for the single player. 7/10.
Story: No story.
Graphics: The game looks pretty great for a game from 2004, and it manages to have a good bit of detail for only being a 1GB download. The maps are big and constructed pretty well, things break in a satisfying way, there's a good deal of detail to the cars, and it all just looks good. While a realistic style does have a tendency to age absolutely terribly, from the perspective of a game from 2004, it looks pretty damn solid. There's no optimization issues for modern hardware either, as I was able to run it at a perfect 60 FPS with everything on max at 1080p. One issue that cropped up every now and then was that a magical fairy would show up every now and then and make the HUD go away and vomit the alphabet at me. Fortunately, this can be fixed temporarily by just Alt-Tabbing, so it's not a huge deal. Overall, the game looks pretty great for a 2005 game and not half bad for today's standards. Give it 20 years time though, and it may not look so great. 4/5.
Sound: One big draw to this game for some is the amount of very obscure bands that this game has. Most of the bands are either of a punk or metal persuasion, but the metal only goes as far as something like a rip off band of Judas Priest. In fact, there's a few bands that sound like ripoff bands; there's a band that tries to be the Beastie Boys, one that tries to be every Industrial Band from the early 2000's, and one band that tries to be as terrible as possible (I still remember Killer Barbies' Baby With two Heads as being one of the worst songs I've ever heard from when I rented this game for PS2 back in '07). While it's not bad for the first few runthroughs and while there are still a few pretty good songs, it does get kinda tiresome after a few hours, so you're likely to just shut off the music and play your own. Sound design is delightfully chunky, and I still haven't gotten tired of the guy driver's derpy scream after being ejected from the car. Again, the problem with licensed music is that it's cool for a while, but it gets old really quick. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 7/0/4/3; cumulative score of 7.0/10. Pretty fun racing game, and definitely a fun one to play with friends, but apart from that there's not much to it.

The experience, though obviously inspired by other first-person puzzle games, feels entirely new. It does the impossible: marrying relaxation with puzzles, without making those puzzles childishly simple.
Though the game relies on a relatively small pallet of environmental and graphical elements, it introduces them gradually enough that it continuously warrants (and rewards) those who like to explore, and especially those whose curiosity takes them outside the boundaries of the "normal" level path. Qbeh-1's difficulty ramps up considerably should you choose to search for its secrets. Though they're not essential, they do unlock extra levels, and the complex puzzles you must solve in order to find these secrets make them a reward in and of themselves. With or without the secrets, however, the difficulty level will increase as you reach the middle and end of the game; you are eased gently into this world, without feeling as though you're drudging through a tutorial. Once you learn the basics and begin craving more exploration, new elements (like gravity-defying jumps!) make your progress worthwhile and your journey fulfilling.
As in Antichamber, Perspective, The Bridge, and other great puzzle titles, the narrative is merely implied, and never treated to full exposition. I happen to love ambiguous stories, and if you feel the same way you'll find it very rewarding to piece the game's limited number of clues together.
Qbeh-1 is beautiful, therapeutic, and fun.

Surreal and engaging from the start, this is definitely my kind of game when I want something challenging; yet won't take me all day to progress. Qbeh-1 is certainly a puzzle game, but you are certainly not forced into a linear approach. There are often multiple approaches to resolve challenges. You can utilize hidden paths, strategic jumps, and a variety of cubes with different functions to tackle each task. And, particularly later in the game, you can be tempted into making decisions that could force you into a trap. But it's all part of the fun to learn what to do and what to avoid! The tougher challenges bring greater satisfaction when you eventually solve them.
There are also secret tokens each level to find, although they are optional. Since I enjoy these secrets, I find that these extras force me to take each world with a holistic approach (figure out where a secret might be by considering the whole map), as well as an analytical one.
The visuals, sounds, and music bring a fresh and even soothing atmosphere to the game. Yet there is also danger: Looking below you and seeing nothing but sky can tease more than a little vertigo. You must always watch your step! The controls are very simple and avoid complexity that can interfere with immersion into the game. And you build upon your acquired knowledge as you go. You learn solutions to common puzzles, and sometimes you gain inspiration to improve those solutions. And you truly feel you're learning when you are able to combine those solutions into an even greater one.
I truly recommend this game to anyone. Even if puzzle games aren't normally your cup of tea, the relaxed pace, beautiful setting, and multiple approaches may just attract both the hardcore and casual gamers alike.

It's trucks, but this time in America!
I'll be honest, it's not a whole new game by any means.
(Henceforth ATS) is
(Henceforth ETS) in a new region with a few new bells. The underlying engine is the same in pretty much every area that matters.
The list goes on but for the most part the things you disliked about ETS will still remain gripes in ATS.
There are some minor remnants of ETS that serve as little jabs for the time being. For instance, the Long Distance Hauling perk remains unchanged with a maximum rank giving you rewards at 2500 Miles and beyond. I may be wrong, but I don't believe there are actually 2500 miles between any two points on the map currently.
the descerning reader may ask. I honestly couldn't put my finger on any one reason. I find myself able to sink hours of time into driving a virtual truck down a virtual road. The change in environment from ETS is nice, and having driven there myself I can say SCS did an excellent job capturing the look and feel of California and Nevada. While those are the only states available at launch they will be expanding that selection over time. The lack of truck selection while disappointing is understandable from a business perspective. SCS has modeled several major manufacturers that they would like to have in the game but for licensing reasons they want to wait for approval before they put them in the game. Placing unbranded look-a-likes in the game was done in ETS at launch but it hurt their ability to license some manufacturers following release. For that reason I can accept their hesitence.
So what's new?
So my final word / TL;DR is this:
If you are a fan of Euro Truck Simulator already and really enjoy the gameplay it offers, I'd recommend this game.
If you are new to the series and aren't sure yet, I would direct you to purchase Euro Truck Simulator instead. I say this becuase ETS currently has a larger area to explore, more trucks available, and a wealth of mods available to expand the game and the core gameplay is more or less the same.
ATS is an 'investment' title as it were. I like what SCS has done with the series and want them to be able to continue modeling America. The only way that will be possible is for me to speak with my wallet, and with the promise of improvements close down the line and their track record with ETS I feel confident doing so.

Now, I'm not one of those people who had this game ruined by the hype that ensued around its release, nor does this game offend me, I'm just voicing what I feel is so problematic with this game. Fable is essentially an action RPG, so I'm going to hold it to my standards of an action RPG, I feel that is only fair.
Since Fable is an action RPG I guess I'd be best to start with its RPG elements. My biggest complaint is how shallow they actually are, they make Pokemon (the single player aspect that is, so the fanboys stop ripping my head off) look super in depth and complex. No thought needs to be put into leveling your character to make sure he can face the challenges ahead. The fun of RPG elements is having to make a tough call on what needs to be leveled to keep your character ready for the fights ahead. The thing is you can essentially max out the levels in every skill tree in one playthrough, this lowers replay value significantly, and eliminates the decision making aspect that makes RPG elements so enjoyable. Other action RPGs like Fallout New Vegas have max levels, so you have to making a decision as to what you're actually going to level up, this ensures the player isn't mindlessly filling all the bars on the stats screen, keeps the game interesting. All of the RPG elements are basically tacked on, and have little to do with your success in combat in any way more than how much damage you do, and how much defense you have
So if the RPG elements are rather shallow, the game must fall back on its action, or combat. The combat in Fable is rather uninteresting to be quite honest. It has little depth to it as well, as it ends up being constantly clicking to keep hitting the enemy in the face, shooting the enemy or blasting an enemy wth some spell. *Correction* Enemies do have weaknesses, but I went the whole game without noticing a real difficulty jump from ignoring these weaknesses, rendering them pointless, since they failed to add complexity to the way I played the game. Enemies don't have stats that effect the damage you do to them, like if they wear armor or are immune to certain spells or elements or weapons. So little thought is required from the player to be successful in combat. The combat is so simple that it grew quite repetitive and monotonous very quickly. An in depth RPG system and nuanced combat would give players something to dig into, invest time in and master, but this game plays more like a really uexciting beat 'em up than an RPG.
Of course there is player choice and morality, which has become a near industry standard in action RPGs. Just like the combat and level system, the element of choice is just as simplistic. Most situations have very black and white morality involved, which holds back a players freedom to construct a character that is anything other than a saint or a demon. While you are given choices, you never face serious consequences for these choices, so why should they matter to the player? One choice bothers me in particular, where *SPOILERS* you can choose to put on the mask or not at the end of the game. Instead of using some kind of prompt or better yet presenting this choice to me through the gameplay, the choice happens during a cutscene, and the way they handle it baffles me to no end. Why would you click the mouse to NOT put on the mask? Wouldn't you NOT click the mouse to NOT put on the mask? How is a player supposed to know it isn't just a regular old cutscene, this isn't conveyed to the player on any level.
Fable highlights my problem with morality systems in general. Fable tells the player what is right and what is wrong, so the player doesn't have to think about this morality for themselves. The morality system should have been a hidden aspect of the game, working behind the scenes, so the player doesn't know they are being judged on a moral scale. If the player was making morality choices throughout the game without being told which options are good or bad, their actual moral alignment would come to light, and the game would make people think about the decisions they made. But since this game tells you immediately the good and evil options, people will choose what the game tells them is good or bad rather than what they actually believe, this morality system reveals nothing about the player, and has little bearing on the direction the story actually goes. People's true moral standing comes most to light when morality isn't in their thoughts at all. Since the morality system doesn't make me question my moral alignment, or have any serious consequences story wise, why should I care about making these decisions? I make decisions in the real world because I am concerned with their consequences.
This game gets a lot of recognition for its charm, I'd credit the game's tone. While the story, characters and setting are not exactly super compelling, especially on RPG standards, the tone is handled quite well. The tone of this game lends Fable a pretty memorable atmosphere. The most prominent example of the game's use of tone is right from the beginning when a light hearted intro is suddenly cast aside by a quite jarring, uncomfortable and expectation flipping tonal shift as tragedy strikes the main character. This intro is a nice kick-off to the game's plot, and gets the player ready to start the game. Unfortunately charm alone can't hold up a game.
I feel Fable, while not as offensively simplistic as its sequels, is still too lacking in sophistication on a gameplay standpoint for me to consider it a solid action RPG, and I cannot recommend it to anyone.

This game is dumb. Very, very dumb. Putting aside little technical bugs like the compass randomly glitching out and hovering in midair, the gameplay and controls are just sloppy. The FPS elements are harmless enough, you point your gun at the Nazis and the Nazis fall down. It's not especially engaging but it breaks up the puzzle-solving well enough I guess. The puzzles have two settings, irrespective of difficulty: insultingly obvious or impossible to guess. That is to say there IS no puzzle, it's just a stylized code lock with the answer written in your grandfather's all-knowing notebook. The different puzzle difficulty levels seem to only change how hard it is to read his handwriting.
To give some very mild spoilers, the point where I lost interest in this game is the start of the Arctic Mines level. It started when after the Sudden But Inevitable betrayal, I'm suddenly in a firefight with Russians of all things. And our 'intrepid heroes' start spitting out the word "commie" like it's five years into the Cold War when up to now we've been fighting the freaking Nazis! If anything, the protagonists actually seemed to think the communists were WORSE, since they were fairly civil when they got pushed into solving puzzles for the Nazis at gunpoint but couldn't go two sentences speaking to the Russians without resorting to namecalling. It was bizarre, like one of the devs bumped into someone working on Call of Duty in the hallway and they got their notes mixed up for a few pages. Complete with an out of nowhere QTE escape sequence at the beginning of the level. If that's the case, I look forward to the inexplicable sliding block puzzle in the next CoD game.
That said, it wasn't this idiotic story swerve that made me throw the game in the bin. No, that came a few minutes later when, as I abandoned a terribly-designed platforming sequence in digust, pulled on a lever and was immediately shoved into a cutscene that pulled me past a point of no return (which the game is lousy with) AND autosaved at the exact same moment, making it impossible to backpedal without restarting the level entirely.
That was the proverbial straw. I'm done with this nonsense, the game was only getting by on C-list SyFy doofy charm to begin with - giggling at as its Indiana Jones-by-way-of-noir-PI protagonist, his designated love interest by virtue of bust size and open disgust trying to sound like sexual tension, the dialog that sounds like a ten-year-old trying to be clever - and that's stopped being cute. Don't bother with this inept piece of trash.

This is the second part of the Mass Effect trilogy, picking up where the first left off.  If you haven't played the first game yet, you should play it before starting this one.  The entire universe of the series is laid out in ME1, and this second game loses a lot in the story department (the series' strongest part) if you don't have the backstory and characterization that the first game brings.  Also, there are a number of major decisions that you make in the first game which carry over with your save into the second.
On a technical level, this game is better in most respects than the first installment.  The shooting and controls are improved, the galaxy map is massively improved, the graphics are much better, certain things which were overly complicated are simplified, etc.  They have improved the overall accessability and playability of the game greatly
Unfortunately, Bioware also seems to have decided that if something didn't work right in the first game, it's better to just tear it out instead of improving it.  So they practically removed weapon customization from the game for example.
Another case in point - the first game allowed you to explore huge sandbox style spaces on dozens of different planets throughout the galaxy.  Although this was tedious at times and the controls for exploring were wonky, the one thing this mechanic did perfectly was SHOW the vastness and variety of the galaxy you were flying around it.  In Mass Effect 2, they remove this mechanic entirely save for a couple of DLC missions which pale in comparison.  So now you play almost entirely on small map spaces with many corridors and indoor sections and makes it just feel like you are flying from airport to airport like a business traveller.  You don't get the feeling that you are really exploring the great expanse of the galaxy, and the overall feel of the game suffers for it.
Still, this is a great game, and I think more fun to replay than the first game because of the simplication measures that were done.  Taken as an overall package it's probably the best game of the trilogy.

This particular iteration of the Assassin's Creed franchise is based off a once exclusive Playstation Vita release, but has been enhanced and expanded for the PC. A much welcomed surprise, Assassin's Creed: Liberation HD (also referred to as Assassin's Creed III: Liberation) is a game that feels and controls like any other triple A title. It introduces a new and unique character that is easily more lovable than the original protagonist from the third game. In terms of gameplay, the game roughly revolves around the same mechanics found in the universe, but offers a new twist in the form of changeable personas. The main lead in the game, Aveline de Grandpré, can alter her attire fulfilling the roles of an Assassin, Lady or Slave - each providing their own incentives. Assassin’s Creed: Liberation HD shouldn't be passed up by gamers especially by those who know and love the franchise. The game's price point does draw attention since it is less than regular releases, but it's certainly not something disproportionate. It'll offer you roughly 10 hours or so of gameplay!

The atmosphere is created through level and audio design combined with a good colour palette, resulting in a solid foundation for a game.
It's serene and calm in the strange world of Qbeh. The slow and relaxed melodies combined with desolate but beautiful visuals gives a nice, pacifying feeling to the player. Playing this game relieves stress, well, personally speaking anyway, and I find that to a really nice and rare quality.
I highly recommend it. Not because of any action - there is none to be found. Not because of any electric guitar shredding - you're in the wrong neighborhood for that. Qbeh is a game of peace, exploration and a little brain work. When you're bored of blowing everybody up with explosives, riddling them with a hail of bullets or slashing zombies to bits, play this. It helps.

It's trucks, but this time in America!
I'll be honest, it's not a whole new game by any means.
(Henceforth ATS) is
(Henceforth ETS) in a new region with a few new bells. The underlying engine is the same in pretty much every area that matters.
The list goes on but for the most part the things you disliked about ETS will still remain gripes in ATS.
There are some minor remnants of ETS that serve as little jabs for the time being. For instance, the Long Distance Hauling perk remains unchanged with a maximum rank giving you rewards at 2500 Miles and beyond. I may be wrong, but I don't believe there are actually 2500 miles between any two points on the map currently.
the descerning reader may ask. I honestly couldn't put my finger on any one reason. I find myself able to sink hours of time into driving a virtual truck down a virtual road. The change in environment from ETS is nice, and having driven there myself I can say SCS did an excellent job capturing the look and feel of California and Nevada. While those are the only states available at launch they will be expanding that selection over time. The lack of truck selection while disappointing is understandable from a business perspective. SCS has modeled several major manufacturers that they would like to have in the game but for licensing reasons they want to wait for approval before they put them in the game. Placing unbranded look-a-likes in the game was done in ETS at launch but it hurt their ability to license some manufacturers following release. For that reason I can accept their hesitence.
So what's new?
So my final word / TL;DR is this:
If you are a fan of Euro Truck Simulator already and really enjoy the gameplay it offers, I'd recommend this game.
If you are new to the series and aren't sure yet, I would direct you to purchase Euro Truck Simulator instead. I say this becuase ETS currently has a larger area to explore, more trucks available, and a wealth of mods available to expand the game and the core gameplay is more or less the same.
ATS is an 'investment' title as it were. I like what SCS has done with the series and want them to be able to continue modeling America. The only way that will be possible is for me to speak with my wallet, and with the promise of improvements close down the line and their track record with ETS I feel confident doing so.

Dinosaur Hunt is a FPS centered on surviving and hunting various breeds of dinosaurs in and around various biomes. Your goal is simple: kill the dinosaurs before they kill you. There’s a story woven into the fabric of this game, but it is so mind-numbingly boring and uninteresting that I had a hard time listening to the dialogue. There’s something about genetic experiments, dinosaur breeding, and death all from the monotone voice of what sounds like someone’s father regurgitating a children’s book to their kid with little to no enthusiasm. The game only gets worse from there.
The formal campaign for the game consists of eleven levels, each with a certain number of dinosaurs to hunt in order to finish the level. Each level has what I can only assume is a boss-type enemy, but it’s hard to differentiate sometimes. When you start each level you’re dropped next to some mesh netting and three caches of weapons that hover precariously above them unless they are clipping through the containers or the terrain. Occasionally they’ll all spawn upside-down, making access to said weapons obnoxiously difficult. Once you select your weapon(s) of choice, you’ll be tasked with shooting “the world’s most horrifying animals” as the tagline to the game says. However, horrifying they are not.
The entirety of the dinosaur AI is best described as buggy and sluggish. You can outrun literally every species and maintain a relatively safe distance walking backwards as well. I cannot stress enough at how slow these creatures are, including the T-Rex and velociraptors.
In addition to the sloth-like AI, there are massive clipping issues, which allows them to walk through solid objects, which oddly you cannot. In fact, even being near objects like walls or rocks impede your character’s movement, even when you’re not touching them. Inversely, you could climb up sheer cliffs by just spamming the jump button.
Terrible AI aside, the weaponry isn’t any better off either. You’re given an array of melee weapons, various handguns, assault rifles and explosives. The guns themselves handle decently and I didn’t really notice anything terribly wrong with them. However, the explosives are another matter; there are no explosions for them. What I mean to say is, you shoot an RPG and there is no smoke trail, no animation, nothing. The dinosaur simply explodes. Any and all explosive weapons suffer from the same issues: grenades, for which you have a seemingly infinite amount of and bazookas both come without particle effects. The grenades simply flash, make a noise and then that’s it.
The worst part about the firearms are when you’re not carrying one at all. If you play multiplayer and your partner is carrying a melee weapon, say, an axe, they still have the animation to everyone as if they are carrying an assault rifle. The icing on the cake is that if you swing your axe, everyone hears them fire a gun. It’s just bizarre.
There’s copious amounts of other issues the game suffers from as well: random landmines that kill you that are laced in unexplained regions of certain levels [often by weapon drops], dinosaurs explode with some terribly rendered 1990s reminiscent blood and gore, empty level design, invisible walls, poor menu design and even worse voice acting. One of the strangest things of all is if you shoot boxes, they bleed. I don’t even know what to say to that except it doesn’t surprise me.
Lastly, there’s the multiplayer, which, to no surprise, does not work properly. Stats are only tracked by the host, so you cannot earn anything while playing online. The host and each player seem to run independently from one another; the host could pause the game, but each player could still continue the game and vice versa. There’s some massive connectivity issues that we were unable to rectify while playing. This problem was prevalent in both multiplayer and local co-op.
With just about every aspect of this game broken and poorly done, Dinosaur Hunt did not come remotely close to fulfilling my love for dinosaur-themed games.


Overall, Dinosaur Hunt, with a lot of time, effort and talent could have been something at least mindless to play. When you look at some of the dinosaur games of this nature, you see mindless shooters that I’ve invested a lot of time into because they’re downright fun, regardless of their minor problems. However, this is not one of those games and despite the inexpensive price, isn’t even worth that.

So, in 1938 Allan Quatermain's great grandson teams up with a snooty English archeologist who wishes she was Lara Croft and together they bumble around in some old ruins fighting nazis, communist Russians, Arab mercenaries and a whole bunch of zombie-mummy-type things.
If I'm being entirely honest then I'd have to admit that I did enjoy this game to some degree - after all, I did effectively finish it in two sittings and a little over twelve hours. The story is fairly typical Quatermain stuff, and makes for some simple escapist nonsense, but unfortunately the game itself is let down a little by repetitive combat sequences and overly simplistic puzzles (though in a couple of cases I found the clues that are given in Allan's legendary notebook to be more than a little obtuse).
All in all I'd have to give this game a 6 out of 10 - it's good fun the first time through but I don't see it having all that much replayability, even with the multiplayer options. Buy it if it's on sale at a really good price (60% off or better) or if you're really desperate for a game that mixes Quatermain with Indiana Jones and Tomb Raider, but otherwise leave it alone.
