This game is great, although it may take some time to like it. Graphics is so so. Soundtrack... It's been giving me a headache, literally. No fast travel, no minimap, no map at all (exept for community made maps in internet), very limited use of verbal skills, non combat skills are mostly crafting oriented (wich can in the end, only benefit combat).   So, what is so good about Underrail?
1.Setting. Game takes place in future, where people live in some undeground infrastructure, that mostly consist of metro, service tonnels, caves and underground rivers. While some locations resemble modern constructions, other just don't make sense, leaving you with the surrealistic feel of the game.
2.Tons of allusions. Some are just funny text, some add portion of surrealism into game, and some are more of adoptions of characters, creatures, ideas.
3.This game is all about combat and exploration. They are really, really great. First, stealth. Your actual stealth is derived from your skill, your armor penalty (the heavier armor - less sneaky you are) and other creatures perception. You don't have to kill most of hostile creatures. You can just skulk about, looting various containers. But if ninja warrior/looter is not your style, mediocre stealth still has great implementation, since knowing position of the enemy and being able to prepare (although, there are almost no prebuffs, wich IMHO is good) is 75% of the victory. So you will develop a habit of entering stealth every time going behind a corner. It's hard to explain in every detail, but stealth is just as it is meant to be.
Since there is no minimap, and world is actually a vast multilayer labyrinth, that you need to memorise, this game gives you unique experience.
As for the combat itself, there is great choice of styles, actually not predefined. Attributes, feats, that you choose during the game, selection of weaponary determine your style very non linearly. General rule is more tactical abilities you have - less pure power and vice versa. I found the system pretty balanced. Actually, I've played two times, with very different styles and could manage most of hostile mobs.
If you liked this review (despite my english) than you'd like Underrail.

Man, I really love this game.
Let's start with some backstory on why it appeals to me specifically. I'm a college student with a rather small amount of free time - aka maybe 2-4 good hours per night, and that's abnormally lucky. Over the past few weeks I've been rather busy with class and work, but Underrail is easy to pickup for 2-8 hours and smash some heads, cut some throats, shoot some fools, etc. My current time commitment situation lends itself to a turn based shooter, but even moreso to an RPG with the elements Underrail contains.
Now for the game itself. Underrail is a vast expanse of areas that are not all nessacery and provides ample options to how to progress your wallet and your character. The oddity XP system is a nice addition that allows characters who are not continually interested in combat to continue advancing and not fall behind on levels within the game. The areas you visit are somewhat chronologically based around your charachter's ability at that point in the game, this allows for some amount of leeway, but generally guides you toward accomplishing the goals set forth by the questgivers and other NPCs.
Character creation allows for a wide variety of combat styles, playstyles, specializations, crafting options, and personal choice. You are not forced to be able to craft, perhaps your character is adept at making a living by stealing from the NPCs in the game via pickpocketing or a high mercantile skill in order to best make use of his limited (or unlimited) loot. Stealth tends to be a recurring theme in the game, and depending on factional choices (and there are several), certain factions tend to favor certain styles of play. It is in your best interest to follow the faction that best suits your playstyle, if you're stealthy, play for the stealthy faction, if you're a ♥♥♥♥ing tank, play for the tanky faction. Despite this, the early game is fairly difficult for non-stealthy characters that do not focus on being a heavy tank. Hybrid characters are penalized early game via difficult areas that offer two distinct linear paths - frontal assault or stealthy approach - and since they do not specialize, they are easily detected or easily killed.
This game is intense, but forgiving, and varied, but still fairly linear (this could be a negative to some people, and it borders on being too linear for my tastes)
Overall, I reccomend everyone to try Underrail. Two hours may not be enough to truly get into the game, but the lore within and varied weapon and combat choices will expose themselves if you spend enough time on it.

It plays like an old-school RPG very reminiscent of fallout, but well... better i'd call it a fixed version of fallout 1 or 2:   you have feats -toats not perks-  attributes,  and it pretty much uses the vat system in combat.  Combat is hard -even on easy- but not as hard as fallout.  The lore and background appear to be well developed and it's a tad more serious than fallout but that's okay as well.  Like fallout you have options for game play, weapons stealth and psi ( i personally go with sci as when any setting lets me do magic i take it (go adepts, mages, sorcerors,psikers)
There are some issues with it, primarly that it's VERY like an old school RPG health dosne't regenerate so you can find yourself well and truly buggered if you haven't prepared, money is a limited recource and your spending choices have to be careful, there's no map and often finding your way is very hard, and selling is difficult like merchants only accept very specific items, which one one hand is very realistic in a post capitalism barter soceity but from a practical game playing prespective is just annoying.  Probably the most unforgiveable thing is you can't see enemies when there beind scenery making is diffcult to impossible to target them, i say this is unforgiveable as games of this type have been around since bg, and the 'black isle' method of getting round this was to give them outlinesso you can still see them,  there are ways round this (move so they move to get you, or my personal favourite mind napalm the area)
I suppose i should say the graphics arn't great but acctually i don't, there good enough for me
Long story short:  if your thinking about buying an old school RPG get this, it is easy a contender to the fallout games and even the baldurs gate games.  If your looking for a more casual/playable game look elsewhere, if you need good graphics leave it alone.

If your dream has always been playing an undead fedora-wearing douchbag neckbeard solving criminal cases like some try-hard Maltese Falcon reject who can't come to terms with the fact that he neither lives in the 1940s, nor understands the actual era (dress code included) - this might just be the game for you. Douchehat McNeckbeard might be laughably slow in how he connects clues, but he comes with a full package of mangst in the form of a fridged (of course) Manic Pixie Dreamgirl wife, and the attitude you'd expect from a 40-year-old basement dweller. If that is what you enjoy in a game, this will be a dream for you - albeit an admittedly short one, since the game is as the most 10 hours, and that's when you take your time as I did.
On a more serious note, this game did have potential, and I really wanted to like it. Tuning out the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ protagonist and his ridiculous and frankly embarrassing fashion sense (which is explained away in the most ridiculous 'didn't even try' manner possible in the game), parts of the gameplay, particularly in the beginning, were fun. Sadly the really fun parts are tragically underused, and for the course of the game following the opening mission, you experience practically nothing new. The first bigger investigation was fun especially through learning all the things you could do to get clues - connect existing clues in your head for new revelations, possess people and prompt them to reveal what they knew by triggering the right clues in their heads, seeing through their eyes into computer files, etc - but there it ended. You acquire a few more fine-tuned skills later on (teleporting, most notably), but nothing that really stands out. The fun experimental trying and testing which witness might have seen what and respond to which clues turns into a tedious button-smashing 'where's the one tiny object in the room that I keep missing?' adventure. Gameplay stagnates and turns into the same thing over and over and over again, only for Mr Fedora to finally come to a conclusion that quite frankly you could have told him after or even before entering the building.
The worst part by far is the writing. Not only are the main characters (most notably the supposed 'tough cops' who only come across as petty, ♥♥♥♥♥y, and whiny) utterly unlikeable, but the main story itself lacks any originality. For the sake of avoiding spoilers if you are for whatever reason still interested in playing, I won't go into the details further, but whatever 'twists' were apparently thought up by the writers have been done before and repeated to death, were foreseeable to the point I don't even want to call it foreshadowing anymore, and - due to the absolutely flat character writing - lacked any sort of emotional impact. I never thought a game centring around a murder investigation done by a GHOST in ♥♥♥♥ing SALEM could be boring, but this is. It's plain and simply boring, with slightly awkward, incredibly repetitice gameplay, and with the added disadvantage of the most obnoxious, annoying, self-centred, whiny wannabe-tough guy fedora-wearing neckbeard Gary Stu of a protagonist I have ever seen. It's like a bad '40s film noir rip off (BUT IN SALEM, WOOO SUPERNATURAL THINGS) gone completely wrong. And not even spectacularly wrong, just underwhelming, tedious, and most of all - disappointing.
There are worse games, of course, but this game stands out mainly because it doesn't - it's all been done before, been done better, and there is literally nothing that this game has to offer. It's not the worst, not a spectacular train wreck, but it's poor, and it's sad. Good for a few minutes of fun, and if you really have to kill time and have absolutely nothing else to do.
Overall, 2/5, and that's me being nice, because I enjoyed parts of the early gameplay. Suggested time to buy: at 90% off.

I have put a decent amount of time into this game and I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to play a clicker with a bit more thought into it. It has your standard cookie-cutter features that any clicker game has like upgrades and idling support but somehow it manages to draw me in and make me actually spend time playing it. The game differentiates itself from other clicker games with its stratergic features. Your crusaders have a formation and their abillites correspond to the formation. A crusader may have an abillity like "If the formation is not full increase DPS by 150%" and however simple this is, it encourages you to think about where you place your crusaders and if you could improve your formation. The game keeps you wondering if you could improve and it always draws you back in.
The crusaders are each unique, vibrant characters and have somewhat funny references to them, especially in the description for their skills. Although most of these are pretty poor jokes, they dont really have any negative impact on the game.
Another great feature is the level reset. I know this is pretty common among clickers but each time you reset, it allows you to choose a different primary objective, a different formation and different conditions like batman taking up one slot like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and not doing anything. These resets really help make it interesting again. Completing certain levels can give you different crusaders with different abillites which you can swap with the default crusaders. This is where the strategy is really fleshed out.
As far as microtransactions go, there is a few things you can purchase which give you great buffs but they are more to support the developers, the game isn't dependent on them.
Its has like no impact on computer peformance at all and can be run in the background for pretty much forever. If for some unknown reason you can't then it has a low quality mode.
Every now and then a special event occurs. These events present oppurtunities to improve your team and are often based on things that are happening at the time.
The game encourages you to idle and has features like auto-progression to assist with this. Idling is often needed when you come across later stages.
However it does have its flaws, such as the redundance of the only character which gives a clicking damage boost. He is only useful for like 50 seconds until you can get the first DPS character and then he's worthless. 98% of all bonuses go to DPS and only a few characters provide bonuses to click damage but they rely on him taking up a slot where a useful character could go.
The second biggest issue is the strategy itself. Most aspects are fine except for the fact that until you get past the first world (which takes a damn while) and get new characters, formations and special conditions, there is no strategy. Until then its just get your best guy and buff him up with everyones abillities.
Pros
Cons
It really needs an option to speed up the game. Overall, it is a great addition and a fresh breath of air to the clicker genre.

This is an okay game, which is sad, because it feels like it could have been a great game.
In brief, you play James Quatermain, the grandson of H. Rider Haggard's Allan Quatermain, a fictional big game hunter who spent most of his life in Africa, seeking to improve the lives of the native people without destroying their culture--so, Allan wasn't a terrible guy, and the simple fact is...the game should have been about him. In their desire to emulate all the Quatermain knockoffs, primarily Indiana Jones, the developers instead make an Indiana Jones knockoff. You fight Nazis who are trying to steal some ancient relics that are mysterious sources of power, bring a potential love interest along, have, for a while, a wise cracking cohort (somewhat surprisingly a German), and solve puzzles while ruining ancient tombs. So, the story is somewhat lacking.
Gameplay wise, it's nothing special. Combat works alright. There's a limit cover mechanic, though shooting out of it isn't smooth, grenades aren't devastating to you or your enemies. There's a flashlight mechanic for dealing with risen mummies that's straight out of a horror game, and even on higher difficulty settings makes them the least dangerous enemies except in occasional swarms.
There's a system for increasing your skills and attributes, but you could go the entire game without doing it and not suffer. It works based on locating artifacts that give you points, and a sufficient number of points let you up things like health, stamina, weapon reload time, the flashlight enhancing skill, and so on. But, again, their help is minimal, and it feels tacked on. Also tacked on: treasure maps that show you where the artifacts are, but without a birds eye view for location context, they're not all that useful.
The puzzles are kind of fun, but if you take too long, your female companion starts spouting off a helpful line of dialogue--just one, over and over and over, until you want to shoot her.
Things that would've added greatly: Better characterization. The sexual tension was laughable, and the script could definitely use a once-over. More back and forth between the characters would've actually been okay for those long walks between combat sessions, while the combat dialogue could've used more than the female character always complaining that the Nazis were moving closer to her. This was especially true in one hilarious context in which she was nowhere near the action, just waiting for me to take a standard slow video game elevator down while under fire. She was in literally no danger, and just kept repeating that one line over and over.
A better spread of weapons, or modifiable weapons, would've been nice.
Some sort of stealth mechanic would've actually gone a long way. You disarm occasional traps, how about setting some?
And, finally, the lead character feels wrong. If the devs wanted to do a story in Quatermain's universe, how about doing one about Quatermain?
I feel like this is one of those rare instances where a sequel could outshine its original. It's a pretty firm 7/10. Grab it on sale, play it once, forget about it.

As an avid Assassin's Creed fan I purchased the game right off the bat, having deliberatly avoided all form av spoilers of AC:Liberation. Granted, I had no objective mindset regarding the game. This proved too be both a positive, as well as a negative experience, as I shall explain below.
First off, for those of us having played AC3 and the more recent AC4 the intro of Liberations lands between the two, quality wise. It's not dragged out like 3, but it's not so much of an intro in the sense of giving the player a sense of going forward. With that said, it could've been pulled off better had they chosen to have an intro where we as the players are more curious as of giving that "what-happens-next"-feeling, which was the case of the excellent intro of Black Flag.
As we progress through the game, we are introduced to several new game modes, unique to Liberations: the three different types of "clothes" Aveline can wear, each "unique" in their own way. Without going into too much details, this idea was a good one, but I happened to find it somewhat tedious and not that much of "change", gameplay wise. It felt more like disguising in the different clothes for the sake of appearance. Once again, I want to emphasize, the idea is GOOD, but fails to deliver gameplay-wise, making it almost irrelevant and only important for those missions where you've to change in order to progress in the story.
And now for perhaps the most characteristic feature of Assassin's Creed: Liberation HD: the HD part. Yes, the game is "only" a port, and a GOOD one at that, which Ubisoft cleverly mentioned in several of their ads throughout the release of the game, which could've turned out ugly if they tried to "fool" us gamers. Nevertheless, the graphics has its own share of graphical problem. It's worth to mention that I ran this game on the highest settings possible with a GTX 770, still there were notable stutter, the occasional water turning into extacy-rainbow-colored water instead, important side-characters making faces like they're having a diarrhea and the constant failure of the game to render thing from a long distance. Furthermore the voice acting has to be one THE WORST I've ever witnessed in gaming, let alone how bad the combination is with several of the charachters, "speaking" but with their mouthes barely open. It's really sad, but the few moments the game shines is the alliance with the french smugglers, and Avelines colonial Brother Connor in the side-mission.
So APART from all of this, what good comes out of this games? Well, for one, it has definitely a more cohesive story than AC3 managed to achieve, the story of Aveline is intriguing and interesting, the FEW moments the "HD" part really lives up to the name doesn't pop up until later segments of the game (no spoilers!). I feel like Liberations as a game per say, is NOT a good game at all (read above), as an overall AC-experience is not a bad one, but not a solid one either, making it only "OK". The game is recommended for all of those Die-Hard AC-fans, itching to know more of the Assassin's Creed Universe.
I'll give this game a solid 2 out of 5!

Mudered: Soul Suspect is a very hard to sell game. It is a supernatural detective adventure game where you play as the ghost of a man searching for his own murderer. Along the way you get a partner and that's basically it for characters you meet for most of the game. It has a wonderful story but suffers from rather boring gameplay that boils down to "walk around until something glows then press the button it tells you." The best comparison I can make would be taking the clue finding sections of the Pheonix Wright games and place them in a 3rd person adventure game. The "detectiving" if you would allow me to to call it that is not hard at all and they try to place the mini-games (very loose use of the word game as you either select a picture or word from a group) as soon as you learn something new (I'm assuming this was a design choice trying to mimic how you would start thinking immediately like in real life but it just comes off as a form of forced gameplay so it isn't just a "walking simulator.") This makes it both obvious and simple as to what you need to select in every single situation. After you find all the clues to the scene you press the finish up button and more story plays out. There are forced "stealth" sections in which you try to avoid demons by mashing a jump into glob button hoping they don't get in your way. They are very boring and the biggest flaw in the gameplay aspect. The story in this game is, as stated before, wonderful. It is engaging and very well done and  you'll be able to tell if you will like this game or not if you watch the first 10 minutes on youtube. The biggest fault of the game is the fact it could have been amazing. If the gameplay got overhauled in a few ways it could easily be an 8 or 9 out of 10 but in its current state I'll have to rate it a 6 or a 7.
If you like story (and fedoras) BUY IT.
If you hate "walking sims" then stay away!

I don't get why places like IGN and other respected game sites gave such poor reviews of this game.  I find it quite appealing and quite fun.  This is not an action packed, fast paced game.  On the contrary it's a slow paced, thoughtful mystery and  ghost story with above average production values.  While this is a supernatural themed game it is by no means gory, nor does it rely on jumpscares (this game isn't really scary at all) but it does have some violent, creepy, and to some, disturbing content.
While nothing about this game will blow your mind there is very little that dissapoints.  The story is somewhat predictable, and as a mystery you'll generally figure something out before you character does so it's not a brain challenger.  There is no combat in this game, and only minimal action which is easily overcome and there are no traditional puzzles. Puzzles amount mostly to selecting relevant information from a list of choices about a specific question.
If I have any gripes about this game it's that sometimes the controls can wonk out on you where you'll be posessing a body and your controller stops functioning altogether.  There was one instance where one insignificat ghost was talking but I heard no sound.  And some of teh minor characters could have had more background lore on them.  And lastly one of the gameplay aspect, helping other ghosts, was used too little.  Started off good but fades away a lot as teh game progresses.  Also no manual saves, only checkpoint saves and that can be a problem in a couple of areas, but nothing major.  Also, the game is short.  11 hours in and I am almost finished with it.
All in all if you like creepy settings, ghost stories, mysteries,  and gathering collectible lore this game has it surrounded by a good setting .  If you're looking for something challenging look elsewhere a sther eis not much in teh way of combat and puzzles.  This is a slow paced, story focused, adventure game, not a supernatural shooter.
I highly recommended for the mystery/ghost story lover.

I have put a decent amount of time into this game and I would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to play a clicker with a bit more thought into it. It has your standard cookie-cutter features that any clicker game has like upgrades and idling support but somehow it manages to draw me in and make me actually spend time playing it. The game differentiates itself from other clicker games with its stratergic features. Your crusaders have a formation and their abillites correspond to the formation. A crusader may have an abillity like "If the formation is not full increase DPS by 150%" and however simple this is, it encourages you to think about where you place your crusaders and if you could improve your formation. The game keeps you wondering if you could improve and it always draws you back in.
The crusaders are each unique, vibrant characters and have somewhat funny references to them, especially in the description for their skills. Although most of these are pretty poor jokes, they dont really have any negative impact on the game.
Another great feature is the level reset. I know this is pretty common among clickers but each time you reset, it allows you to choose a different primary objective, a different formation and different conditions like batman taking up one slot like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and not doing anything. These resets really help make it interesting again. Completing certain levels can give you different crusaders with different abillites which you can swap with the default crusaders. This is where the strategy is really fleshed out.
As far as microtransactions go, there is a few things you can purchase which give you great buffs but they are more to support the developers, the game isn't dependent on them.
Its has like no impact on computer peformance at all and can be run in the background for pretty much forever. If for some unknown reason you can't then it has a low quality mode.
Every now and then a special event occurs. These events present oppurtunities to improve your team and are often based on things that are happening at the time.
The game encourages you to idle and has features like auto-progression to assist with this. Idling is often needed when you come across later stages.
However it does have its flaws, such as the redundance of the only character which gives a clicking damage boost. He is only useful for like 50 seconds until you can get the first DPS character and then he's worthless. 98% of all bonuses go to DPS and only a few characters provide bonuses to click damage but they rely on him taking up a slot where a useful character could go.
The second biggest issue is the strategy itself. Most aspects are fine except for the fact that until you get past the first world (which takes a damn while) and get new characters, formations and special conditions, there is no strategy. Until then its just get your best guy and buff him up with everyones abillities.
Pros
Cons
It really needs an option to speed up the game. Overall, it is a great addition and a fresh breath of air to the clicker genre.

Fable - The Lost Chapters, a classic game that originally released in October of 2005 on the original Xbox, September of the same year on PC, ported to Steam in December 2011 and recently had an HD re-release on Xbox 360. Fable is a RPG in which your decisions dictate where the story will go. You can be a Hero of purity and good or a Hero of deceit and evil. This was a groundbreaking feature when it first released because no other game on the market had that "I really control this character's life" feel to it. With a unique skill leveling system, you can make yourself a burly warrior, a gifted mage, a craft thief, or as I like to do, a "Jack-of-All-Trades" sort of build.
When the game begins, you are still just a boy in the town of Oakvale. It's your sister's birthday and you need to find her a present. Your choices start at a young age, as you decide where you want to do good or bad deeds to make the few gold needed to get the gift. Let me make something clear.
If you've grown accustomed to the Cookie cutter Monopoly that is Call of Duty, Battlefield, and even the most recent power titan;  OVerwatch.
This isn't the game for you.
There is an unrealistic amount of complexity in it's simplicity.  An aged feeling of a young lad racing home from school with only one goal in mind- To play  a great game.
I'll explain a few things that replicates the sensation of the game.  As best I can, rather.
GRAPHICS -
Astounding.  I, being a man of class, would like my outfits to match my tools.  A black, lightly dusted cloth adorns both your character, his outfit, and his weapons-  leaving only his facial features to differ.  This is not a lax of developers.  This is an ingenius method to keep you focused on the game.  Enthralled.  Entertained.  Complex designs distract from what you came to do.  Play.
GAMEPLAY -
I was able to fool a dinosuar into believing himself to be my comrade.  After standing atop his mighty form- I charged boldly into battle.  The other dinosaurs, assuming him to be a comrade of their own, refused to nip at my ankles.  This is development at it's highest asset. Games like The Stomping Lands, Ark, etc simply can't compare in the level of complexity.  A.I pathing is simply ingenius.  I've seen multiple instances of enemies rushing past my partner to attack me instead.  Now, one would assume that this was a feat of bad coding.
False.
The A.I actually factored in my superior aim, and priotitized me as a far more viable target.  This made more sense to me.  Don't target the weakest. Target the strongest. Take out the elite.
PVP -
The game has a randomly occurring PVP mode that is absolutely breathtaking.  Often times, Enemies will stop spawning.  Without rhyme or reason.  In these episodes of peace and tranquility, you are damn near influenced into firing at one another to pass the time. What was already an overwhelmingly fun experience is now an outrageously in depth combat system waiting for exploitation.  Killing a friend doesn't seem to cause a mission failure. Or being killed for that matter. Or death in general.  This doesn't make the game *Easy*- it adds yet another complex layer to the game that deserves a spot in Valve's vault of greatest hits.
Overall -
Buy this game.  Letting this opportunity pass by is insanity. When I purchase something, I usually grade a game on the hour to minute ratio. For each dollar spent, a game needs to entertain me for an hour.  At 0.50$-  I spent a whole hour plus playing.  That's nearly 200% profit of fun.  Words cannot explain the feeling of blasting the same two different dinosaurs for an entire hour straight.  The only reason I stopped playing was because my house had caught aflame from the sheer heat this game gave off.

Also, the fact that when you're in the slave persona, you can get into any plantation by picking up and carrying a crate is amazing!  It may not sound like much, but when you're in a lazy mood and need to get into a plantation, just change to the slave persona and walk straight passed the gueards.

When I pre-ordered the game, I didn't know what to expect.  I thought the game mechanics where going to be incredibly bad (as this has just been re-ported - used to be a PS Vita game).  And to be honest, ubisoft have done really well.  There will be many moments in the game where you just want to throw your computer out of the window (as I wanted to while recording a walkthough) because some things are fairly glitchy. Also, the free running (like in all Assassins Creed game) is really frustraiting.
One more bad point, this game has quick time events.  These are really annoying!  I was trying to do a mission but couldn't until I took down this crocodile.  However, it was a quick time event.  If you pressed a button just a second out of time, you will have to restart all over again!
However, over all, ubisoft have done really well porting this game over to PC!  Even though the missions may be a little short, that's fine because they're packed full of information!

Great mechanics, pity you're forced to play PvP. These mechanics would make for a great single player game. Instead, you're forced to PvP and "newbie" servers are lvls 1 to 15..... so everyone is about 10 levels higher and newbies get thrown into a sharp, unenjoyable learning curve.
I'd rather see the option to earn XP from bot games even if it's less XP than a pvp game. Simple reason being that I'd rather be having fun earning less XP than not having fun earning more XP. As it is, this game is no fun, which is a shame because it has the potential to be. Instead is a fun-less grind where you are cannon fodder for other people's amusement. Perhaps if it HAD a better matchmaking system where the ranks are better bracketed (say in brackets of 5s instead of 15 for the newbie matches and 16 to 50+ after) it would be far more enjoyable even in PvP. As other reviewers have pointed out, the problem isn't limited to just the newbie backets: get past lvl 15 and you're even worse off....
So, if you are a masochist, and you are picking only one game to soulessly grind till you get good, this is it. Or maybe if you're one of those gamers whose sole kicks come from "pwning" others.... For the rest of us normal gamers, this is sadly not it.
edit: hilariously the elitist "muhhhh i get my kicks from putting others down" crowd is already rearing their ugly head. good games encourage you to pick up a game and improve in it with a broader learning curve. bad games expect you to be an expert with reflexes that only the top 1% of players actually have(and whom those putting others down to feel better about themselves actually don't have) right from the start.

This has to be my favorite Assassin's Creed game so far. Aveline is the most interesting and likable protagonist in the series so far. There aren't many strong female protagonists in video games but Aveline stand amongst the best including the new Lara Croft( Tomb Raider 2013), Heather Mason( Silent Hill 3) and Ellie( The Last of Us).
The three persona system works well and improves as the game goes on. The parasol dart gun is a really nice touch; nothing quite as satisfying as dressing as a lady and assassinate your targets with your cute little umbrella( giving that Hitman vibe to it) There's also quite a number of puzzles and mini games littered throughout the main storyline and side quests. They range from fairly challenging to downright annoying( I'm looking at you, fragile canoe with health bar!) The updated textures looks really amazing up-close and the color feels richer than the Vita version making New Orleans look beautiful and lively. On the negative side, the water animation is so flat that it breaks the immersion a little. More sound effects could have been great during cutscenes. Controls are quite fluid and on par with the recent Black Flag.
At this time of writing the review, my pre-order bonus is having some issues( happens to quite a number of people especially those who bought from Steam) and not showing up even after registering them in Uplay so i don't recommend anyone getting the Voodoo Pack DLC until the issue is fixed. The vanilla game itself will provide many hours of entertainment for fans of the series and newcomers alike. For the low price it's offering now, you're getting a fairly large game with many hours of content. One could almost forget this is a Vita port. Highly recommended! 8.5 out of 10

What do you need to like in order to enjoy this game?
- You like dark horror or dark science fiction
- You love things like the Alien Movies or Dead Space games
- You enjoy slow paced adventure games with riddles and a dense atmosphere
- You dont mind if a game has not ultra 4k 3d roflstomp graphics (the graphics of Stasis really fit the atmosphere to my mind)
- you value a good soundtrack
- you dont mind reading quite a lot of text
- you value if somebody put a lot of detail and love into a game which is obviously not produced by a big company
- you can have fun gathering achievements for dying and then loading again (happens not often, but sometimes)
For me, these points apply and therefore I really enjoyed it. And yes, I had to look up some of the riddles, but I mainly go for story or atmosphere, anyway. I would say a lot of the riddles can be solved by paying close attention to the surroundings and the things in your inventory. And for the rest, there are online walktroughs.
Playtime without gathering all achievements is around six hours, so thats less than an euro per hour of fun if you grab it on sale. I recommend giving it a try.

Probably the most underrated title in my Steam collection, UnderRail (not to be confused with UNDERTALE) is an isometric roleplaying game very much like the Fallout games in which the world has been destroyed and humans now dwell in the underground railways organized into loose factions of scavengers, bandits and station-states. Your character is a new recruit of South Gate Station and is sent on various missions on their behalf. The game starts out in a fairly linear fashion and not much exploration can be done until you have helped SGS clear the rocks blocking the station from the rest of the UnderRail.
Once the initial hurdle is taken care of, you'd better put your best traveling shoes on because it soon becomes apparent this game is enormous and there is more of everything than you ever imagined. I'm told that this game is a one-man project, and I almost can't believe it; it would have been tough even for a team of level designers to complete the task. This may be the most controversial aspect of the game, too, because it provides no map of its cavernous depths and you must either draw one yourself or simply memorize the important connections between areas. I don't mind it, but it's something to consider if you are susceptible to getting lost in vast fictional worlds.
There are plenty of creatures scurrying about in the lawless railways who would love to decorate the floors with your sorry hide. It would be wise to have a plan for the occasion. This is not a game where you can simply walk around and socialize; it's very much focused on hostile encounters. Perhaps the feat list will clue you in on this fact; most of the available feats have something to do with either killing foes or sneaking around them. However, once you accept that you will inevitably be involved in battle, the game offers a wide variety of weapons and techniques for that purpose - pistols, sniper rifles, sledgehammers, throwing knives and all manner of psionic trickery.
My favorite feature is the oddity system, an option you can select when starting a new game (and I highly recommend you do,) which replaces the traditional "kill enemies to level up" mechanic so common in RPGs with a new system in which you level up by collecting trinkets - oddities - scattered throughout the UnderRail in barrels, boxes and cans. The genius of this feature is that it encourages you to explore the world using whatever methods you desire. If there's an oddity guarded by three monsters, it's your choice: kill them and take the loot or just sneak past them and grab it.
UnderRail is a difficult game, but it's also a rewarding one when you finally figure out how to take on the enemies standing in your way. There is no party to recruit; it's just you versus the world. The graphics are nice and the ambient sound design greatly helps the atmosphere. There's a lot of viable character builds and tons of replayability for those who like to experiment. The crafting system is substantial and allows you to create pretty much any item in the game from its raw materials. Overall, I highly recommend UnderRail for any RPG fans, and especially Fallout fans - it's a work of love from a developer who clearly has too much time on his hands.

Underrail is a RPG with a large gameworld with plenty places to explore and competing factions to interact with. However the possibilities for the player are often limited and the progress feels stretched. The game could have used a higher budget to mitigate these deficiencies but in the end offers a good price for plentiful content.
Underrail is set in a postapocalyptic world, where people are based around former railroad tunnels because the surface is no longer accessible. While this, on first glance, seems to limit the gameworld, it really is pretty large with many tunnels, caves, stations and underground rivers to explore and even get lost in. However a lot of the places are not interesting, just filled with repetetive enemies and mostly there to keep you busy till you get to somewhere else.
As the player you have a relatively high degree of freedom to take quests or leave them and to work for one or another faction in some places. The writing and options in the quests is somewhat lacking and generally follows typical tropes.
Character creation offers a variety of distinct choices in gameplay, be it stealth, talkative, relying on melee, ranged or psi abilities. There is a lack of tutorial on how to skill your character and I had to restart early on because I felt I had too many problems winning fights. After that I was happy with my casting type character. While there were too many fights overall, i kept getting challenged throughout the game.
The fights are turn based and use an action point system, that gives you time and opportunities to plan the use of your character's abilities. I generally like such a system for controling a party, but in Underrail you only ever control your own character. I did not expect the combat in this game to be very entertaining, but it was. This did develop as the character kept gaining new abilities.
While there are obvious comparisions to make to other games like for example fallout 1,2, Underrail is significantly different enough to warrant a distinct experience. I wish the game had been less ambitious in scope and more focused in detail, but in regards to its price I could not expect more.

I used to play this game a bit. I'm coming back now to give negative reviews after one of my friends has just been given THIS dialog box when running the game:
There are a number of red flags here.
Red flag #1: Why is "DirectX" referring to warframe by name? They've NEVER done that. DirectX is a publicly available and redistributable package, nobody gets special treatment.
Red flag #2: This is a non-standard dialog box even in outdated windows operating systems. This looks like a windows NT/98 dialog box, except those never asked for a username... only a password (unless you selected to sign in with a different username).
Red flag #3: "Enable UAC". Even if UAC dialogs were disabled, it wouldn't trigger a prompt or inform the application that it doesn't have admin perms. UAC would just let the program run and depending on access settings *(default admin or default non admin)*, the application would run into access forbidden messages when trying to perform certain actions.
Mind you this was all ran as an admin (right click -> Run as Admin) however even so there STILL isn't an excuse for this to appear.
There are posts on the forums saying this is a security feature, except it's not the correct way to do things. The correct way is to go through UAC like everybody else. It is this reason why I've reported the game to valve. Devs, correct this before reddit finds out, otherwise you will likely be pulled off the steam store faster than you can say "it's a feature".

Crusades, Holy Wars and Jihads, oh my! Religion and politics were never so intertwined as they were during the Middle Ages and you get to relive the entire experience from the late 800's all the way to the mid-15th Century (thanks to the Norse Gods xpac). The original starting scenario is one of the most historical battles in history: Stamford Bridge. Selecting this scenario you can either play one of the three combating forces to decide the fate of England or perhaps some other noble elsewhere in Europe while the Battle of Hastings takes place or... doesn't. The second original starting scenario is after William the Conqueror has become King of England. With the advent of xpacs such as the Sword of Islam and The Republic you can play as an Islamic lord and invade Europe from a foothold in Spain or eradicate the Byzantine Empire or play as a patrician and establish a Serene Republic. The best game I played thus far was as the ruling family of Bohemia, gaining independence from the Holy Roman Empire and through marriage and war claimed the crowns of Poland, Hungary and Croatia, creating a dynasty that eventually became greater than the HRE itself! My favorite scenario is starting in the 800s as Harald Fairhair and establishing the Kingdom of Norway through conquest before invading Finland and then Scotland and Ireland to establish a far-reaching Norse Empire that stretched from the Baltics across northern Russia. Prestige and Piety play important roles for every ruler: What kind of dynasty will you build and will it be enough to keep your bloodline safe and your titles secure from neighboring lords and ladies or the church? Best keep highly competent vassals in your court to forge claims, train troops, improve your diplomatic relations, collect taxes, convert your population, and spy on your own people or steal technology from your neighbors.If you're lucky, you might live long enough to withstand the Mongol Hordes when they sweep across the steppes or be sacrified to heathen gods when the Aztecs discover Europe. From Ireland to India you can either relive history or change it forever!

I have just unistalled the game now after playing (although it was mostly idlying with my computer open) for over 150 hours over the course of a few months and several events. Do I recommend this game? The answer is no.
And here is why:
First of all, what is important for me in games is how they are able to bring me happiness and more importantly long term happiness because I remember the wonderful experiences I had with that game. This game however has none of that, now that I uninstalled it I feel relieved because i am free from it's pressure, it's urges that it created through this kind of gaming to just play forward for the short term, one small little feeling of 'progressing' a little bit more although there is no real progress here, no story, no real achievement. The only 'achievements' in this game are robotic tasks such as achivements for clicking a certain number of times or gathering x gold and so on and so forth there are dozenz of them and at the end there is nothing really from this. All the campaigns in the game including the event campaigns (although the developer does give plenty of those in the course of a few months) are rather small, especially after spending a bit of time with the game and they only offer about 100 mini-level maps with lazy objectives with no real challenge in terms of having players play the game. They are all just about boosting your Damage per second and letting the crusaders idle.
The areas are all recycled and if you get to area 101 in any campaign it's actually area one again and it goes on like this, you just get bigger numbers for the levels.
Besides this, the game has microtransactions. Not any kind of microtransactions but microtransactions with random results. Every crusader in this game has only 3 items with 4 tiers each. This implies in reality that after you get an item you will mostly be getting lots and lots of duplicates while waiting for a random drop for the epic and paying real money for that random drop. I had my main DPS crusader get 55 duplicates. 55!!!! Imagine that. And I didn't even buy the magic jewelled chests with real money, My frustration with the game would have been even bigger had I spent 40 euros to get useless duplicates of the same thing. I know randomness has an appeal for some but for me it's a frustrating business model. This now links to my main issue with the game.
To get those 55 duplicates it took me a lot. I mean a real lot. More than resetting 60 times, and that's a lot of time actually wasted in real life. Time wasted to just grind through the same recycled levels lots of times. I wonder what that is doing to my brain really...In any case I am done with idle games. But back to the matter at hand. I put a lot of time in the game and although now I can get to a much further area than in the beginning I still don't really feel any satisfaction since it just goes on and on and on, the areas get recycled and new numbers are added. If you want to get far in this game you have to play it a lot, and reset a lot...and it takes a lot to get to the point of resetting. Especially in the beginning. Either that or you need to pay to get gold and damage boosters and items so I couldn't honestly recommend this game as a relaxing pleasant experience for other customers to relax in their daily lives. It's more of a very stressfull experience.
My next qualm is with the events. Although there were events like every month or every 2 or three weeks which each had a few objectives and some new but really not that usefull crusaders unless you decided to put real money on them, these events are really a big source of pressure. I mean, every one of these events sends out a mail to tell you the event has started. You go in but you can't really do much since on every event you need to accumulate a certain currency for that event which means you have to grind when that event is active. I grinded for a month before and didn't like it. Ok...New event is up, I have to grind again to get the currency which is only available that week. And then these events are always limited in time with achivements which are really grindy- one of them is actually to spend, that's right, spend 17.500 or something like that of that event currency. See what I mean, just earn it to spend id, big grind with no real purpose, no satisfaction. The game with its event and pressure I feel only hammers on the urge to get more achievements which in the long term gives no real gaming value.
My last claim with the game is that it automatically puts you in a game chat with other people who play. The game is not competitive so you don't need it, but still you are automatically put there and I was enjoying it for a bit when playing it at the beginning because other players shared their experience... But that went untill I asked something and some idiot decided to randomly insult me because that's the case of things especially when Steam links you into a sepparate account for this game only and you will meet lots of other people who play but don't have any real tools to interact with them and sanction them for this kind of behaviour since it's just pretty much a random chat. So that really made my experience unenjoyable, especially since it's a single player game and you have to ignore that chat. I later found out that you can disable it, but I don't know why it was on there in the first place because when the community is not solid and it's not because of these sepparate umoderated accounts, you get this behavior. That's a another reason why I like steam because I can choose who to interact with completely.
To sum up, if you are a new player who wants to try this game I would advise against it. It takes a very long time to get anywhere, the satisfaction is not really great and you might end up like me regretting the experience. If you put dozens of dollars on it and you only got duplicates and random trinkets to just get you past a few more levels you will definitely regret it. And generally I think the idle genre is just an empty marketing thing, with no real gaming value, so it will probably hook you up for a few months then make you regret you didn't play the Witcher or any other story-rich game during that time which will give you fond memories for decades to come. Speaking of that, I got more time on this than I have on each title of the Witcher...I might solve that :).

Assassin's Creed Liberation HD feels like any other AC game. You can definitely tell that it's a port because of the way missions are set up. There seem to be more checkpoints, and missions overall are shorter in comparison to other AC games.
The game also uses less areas and the story can be roughly completed in 8-9 hours. That doesn't mean you finished the game, however, there's still tons of stuff to do, like finding secrets, buying different types of properties, stuff like that.
Liberation allows you do stuff that you can't do in other AC games and vice versa. For example, there's no hunting this time. Is it sorely missed ? Not at all. That's all just mindless, but enjoyable filler. But I still missed it. Same goes for naval combat, which is not included. Liberation allows your female assassin to charm people, and switch between different outfits. It's a fun idea that's poorly executed, because it basically limits your freedom. The assassin outfit allows you to move freely, the slave outfit allows you to blend in with slaves and the lady persona allows you to be a lady that can be harrased by smugglers, which is absolutely useless. Ok, that's not exactly what it's used for, but come one, it doesn't even allow you to kill someone while wearing it. As I said, the idea is good but it needs better implementation.
Other fun new additions to the AC formula are the whip which is great for combat and also for traversing certain areas. Chain kills are also great and are very handy at times.
The graphics are hit and miss. First of all, the game doesn't run at 60fps, but around 35-45fps, which is already frustrating, because a port like this should definitely run at 60fps solid. And while most of the graphics have been improved, the faces of some of these characters are still terrible. I also missed a lot of fine detail in many scenes. But considering the price they're asking for it, I can't complain I guess.
Voice acting is pretty solid, and exactly what've come to expect from an AC game.
The story isn't as interesting as many of the other AC games but still managed to impress me, with its slave theme and female lead.
Liberation is a flawed but interesting AC game that's still very much enjoyable if you can look past these flaws. You might be disappointed because it's probably not what you've come to expect from the series, but as a game it's all good fun. Is it better/more fun than ACIII ? Absolutely !

I'm 80 hours in with my first play though of this game and I'm not finished yet, so that should give you an idea of how much there is to do. You could do it faster of course, if you just go straight through the main quests and never step off the path to explore like I did. I wouldn't be surprised if I get 100 hours of play time. Well worth the money.
The world is huge, with many different factions that you can either work for or kill (or both) throughout the various cities / bases that you visit.
You can start a fight with just about anyone. The merchants and even quest related NPCs aren't in some kind of magical protection mode like most other games do. A lot of freedom in cities, stealing and whatnot, but be prepared for the consequences if you get caught.
The quest system is pretty good. Your journal/log only gives you the vague outline of the quest, which forces you to actually listen to what the guest givers are saying, because the dialog holds a lot of hints and directions on where to go.
Crafting is useful, although getting the right mix of crafting skills is a bit hard at the start. For some items you'll need a lot of tailor skill and also some electronics skill, for example, and it's hard to find the right balance.
There is lockpicking and hacking, and you should definitely put points in those skills. It is almost never required for quests (and I think never on main story quests), because they will usually make some other way for you to get through a lock or electronic lock (hidden trapdoor / path with more enemies / etc), but it is good for finding extra loot. Hacking also lets you hack security systems sometimes, to turn off cameras, shut down robots, or open gates.

Assassin's Creed Liberation centers around a character by the name of Aveline, a woman raised from childbirth as an Assassin whom now struggles to find her way and test her faith and loyalty to the Assassin Brotherhood and her mentor - all while keeping her business afloat.
This game is a remastered version from the original PSVita release. It features MUCH higher resolution textures, some better music cues, and rebuilt lighting to go along with it all. It does, however, still look a tad blocky at times, as is the case with mobile adaptations. Aveline herself seemed to have been upgraded a bit and her animations are slightly better, but most everything around her looks fairly blocky and inconsistant, though this has almost always been the case with every single AC installation. I do have to give special mention to the lighting in this game though, as it gave a more impressive, visual look to the game that expanded upon the coloring and fidelity of the game that wasn't present in the rather monotone PSVita version, which had a more drab appearance and was less colorful.
The gameplay, for better or for worse (definately for worse) is standard AC, but this particular game has a few issues additional to what's already dreary mechanics. Aveline has 3 different "Personas" which in concept should alter the game marginally - but to me, it doesn't and mainly adds ways to further monotonize the game. The "Assassin" Persona is your go-to - You can use every weapon in your arsenal, can "freely" (more on that later) climb up structures and buildings as well as have the added nuisance of "Yellow Lighting" enemies. The "Slave" Persona is a less glorified version of the Assassin Persona except you can use less weapons and is not as easy to "Yellow Light" guards and the "Lady" Persona, which removes climbing ENTIRELY and severely limits your combat options and of course adds the random nuisance of thugs pestering you. The Persona system in general just ended up being rather underused for me because it requires the need of "Dressing Chambers", and most of the time I would rather just make do with the outfit I had on (except for the lady persona) and just be on my merry way, additionally, it doesn't bring many gameplay alterations to really warrant using any of them except to maybe add or take away certain annoyances.
As far as the standard AC mechanics go... I would dare to say some here are actually worse than they were in AC3. The combat is very random with very little indicators as to what may work or not. Until you actually pick up the "Whip" later on in the game - combat is still very "Counter-centric" except the game itself doesn't give you many options to varie what you do. Some enemies can counter your counters and there's no indicator as to who they may be, they just do - and is very annoying because it makes you keep guessing as to which one may work, only to find it that it suddenly doesn't work. Combat in this game I would say is by far it's weakest it's every been in an AC game, even compared to AC1.
The actual climbing and free running mechanics here are fine - they certainly aren't the worst it's ever been, but there's a few issues I have to point out - one is the "Sticky" issue that also plagued AC3 - where your character tends to want to scale stuff you never even pointed to, making you lose time and another where if your camera is slightly off, you have a chance to make Aveline jump to somewhere you didn't want her to do so, even if you were pointing in the right direction. These two issues aren't particularly common, but they are definately present, and it can be VERY annoying. Another personal issue I had with the game was more of a limitation than anything, but I found that this game was more linear than other AC games - particularly having "blocked off sections" that look climbable and are not.
Stealth. Well, not much to say here really. It's just as bad as it was in AC3. You can hide in certain bushes, but guard don't particularly respond well to alerts or are as dynamic. There are actual occasions where you're up in a tree and you can see the enemy looking UP at the tree, but doesn't trigger the alarm or Yellow Lights or anything, it's one of those occasions where the AI just latches on to where you are and it serves to severely break immersion. You have the option of using Poison Darts or Berserk Darts (given later in the game). Poison Darts make the enemy stumble about and eventually die, and Berserk darts make the enemy wild and prone to attacking his allies. Both of which are very helpful in situations where stealth is a must.
The game also has a number of collectibles, which honestly serve next to no purpose. You can collect Diary Pages to uncover a hidden mini story behind Aveline and her Mother - you can collect Jewelry from charming certain people using the Lady Persona, and of course the usual chest hunt for money. There are also purchases available (via in game stores or "Smugglers") that allow you to purchase weapons and pocket watches (another form of collectible), aswell as a minigame in the form of management of trading/selling goods for Aveline's business found in her Headquarters - as well as the obligatory "Abstergo" or in this game "Erudito" hunt for truth - that have you hunting "Citizen E" for added cutscenes.
All in all though, it's fairly hard for me to really recommend this game to non AC fans. It doesn't bring anything new to an already drab set of base mechanics, is, in my opinion one of the worst AC games in recent memory (Still better than AC3 due to an actual interesting character) due to the extremely limiting gameplay and linearity the story progresses at, as well as some odd bug here and there that make the entire package feel woefully underwhelming. As it stands, it's a decent entry in the AC franchise that is worth a look if you're a fan of the series or if you're looking for a different take on the series - otherwise I would honestly say skip this game, and get the much better Black Flag instead.
Pros:
-Very interesting Main Character, Aveline.
-Amazing Lighting and texture effects bring out life in a drab setting.
-The Whip. This needed to be used more.
Cons:
-Combat is weakest it's been in any AC game.
-The 3 Persona system is nigh useless and serves as mere nuisances that any utility.
-Purchases and Upgrades are fairly useless.
-Weak Collectibles and endgame. No real reason to replay the game outside of story.
-Very short. You can beat the story in around 5 - 7 hours depending on how experienced you are.
-Enemies pop up contantly from out of nowhere.
-Stealth is very weak.
Additional Note: The PC Port seems to have a few issues pertaining to AA. AA in this game SHOULD be turned off if your CPU rating isn't above 3Ghz. It WILL cause heavy lag. Not sure why, but AA in this game isn't very well optimized. VSync locks the Framerate to 30.
EDIT: I only put a "Non Recommended" because it fell right in the middle for me. It's not a terrible game either. Some people DO enjoy this game more than other AC's, that's entirely dependant on you and what you enjoy.

Underrail is, in most respects, what might've happened if we've gotten a Fallout 3 in the old isometric style, and if it'd been made by an indie.
Which this is.
And for for the most part, that's a good thing.
The game sets itself apart from it's spiritual heritage in several ways, most notably the size and complexity.
The world of Underrail is vast, with a sprawling network of tunnels and railways leading everywhere and nowhere, with secrets and stuff to find aplenty. Enemy encounters are very frequent, and combat is a centerpoint in the experience for sure.
That's not to say you cannot solve some situations by talking, but I found these instances very few and far between compared to the massive amounts of non-vocal enemies that just immediately try to murder you on sight.
To support you and to keep things interesting, the game sports a huge and complex crafting system, with tonnes of recipies and materials littered across the world. With few exceptions, every piece of gear and consumable in the game can be crafted, and the game actively encourages you to utlizise this system whenever you can. It does not guide you in this in any way, leaving you free to experiment away.
Unfortunately, this is where the game starts to stumble a bit.
Crafting in the game doesn't really come into its own until a bit later in the mid-game when you've amassed some skill in the various disciplines necessary (Mechanics, Electrics, etc) and the stuff you build is more often than not woefully underpowered compared to what your enemies are using. Knowing beforehand what skills to invest in here in order to stay competetive with the opposition is key, but this more or less necessatates you starting over again.
Some enemies are also just ridiculously overpowered, specifically the Snipers and Hunters who can frequently one-shot you from far off-screen with full health and shields, leaving you wondering what just happened. The combat log goes away the instant you die, so the specifics of the incoming attack will remain unknown, so you'll never really how how to prevent it.
This is where the combat turns sour.
Far too frequently you simply cannot fight the enemy at all on equal terms. You'll get to a point where your own armor or defensive capabilities either prevent you from taking damage completely, or do absolutely nothing and you die instantly. Survival becomes a matter of lucky dice rolls, and no matter what creative trap usage or line-of-sight exploitation you employ, the slightest mistake will leave you in just the wrong spot making the enemy able to hit you, and immediately kill you, so you have to start the whole encounter all over again. Sometimes it doesn't even come down to mistakes, as you just die before you can even act as soon as you step into an area.
The game becomes a lesson in trial-and-error, with quicksave and quickload taking such center and prime roles in the execution of the gameplay that they would've made a lot more sense if presented as actual game mechanics, like in Prince of Persia: Sands of Time. The Dark Soulds comparison has been made before to this game, but in DS dying is a natural part of the game's flow, making it part of the story. Here in underrail it more often than not comes down to dying and reloading over and over until you finally manage to push through, which isn't fun nor engaging. Thankfully, the loading times are really fast.
With the focus on combat and crafting, the game spreads the rest of itself fairly thinly. Art assets are re-used almost everywhere as a rule, and despite the caves and metros all having their own unique layouts and designs, you'll quickly come to a point where you feel you've seen all the art the game has to offer. The passages and caves blend together into same-ness, and basically only the loot and enemy encounters remain fresh.
All in all, Underrail leaves a bit to be desired.
On the one end, the game offers remarkable complexity and variety with its huge (and pretty great, I must admit) crafting system and and sprawling world to explore. On the other it relies on combat too heavily and stumbles when you cannot get past certain encounters, wondering what to do with itself when that inevitably happens. The re-used art certainly doesn't provide incentive to go too far off the beaten path, as you know all you'll find is just more of the same. The story itself is fairly weak, and doesn't provide you with much more than "go to X, do Y", so if you want to explore you have to do it on your own volition and only for the loot.
I debated this with myself for a while, but I'm having to go with a thumbs down for this game. It shines in a few aspects, but it's so samey and often needlessly hard just for the sake of it being hard, without context or explainable reason. It just gives rise to frustration, so I recommend you find your top-down RPG fix elsewhere (Like Divinity: Original Sin, hard but fair and excellently polished. As of this writing the sequel is coming out fairly soon, too)
PS: Props for the interesting "oddities" experience point system. I just had to mention it, since I haven't found it's like anywhere else before this. It really rewards exploration instead of just up-front combat, which in hindsight is both a blessing and a curse since combat is so prevalent everywhere you go. But still, neat idea.
//EDIT:
Having reached the end of the game, though not quite completing it yet, I can now thoroughly say that this game is an excercize in frustration. Despite high levels and good gear, many enemies can still one-shot me if i fail the initial initiative roll. Without prior knowledge of what you'll face before entering the the point of no return (which actually you are not informed of that you've reached) you will either luck out and have the proper weaponry and stats, or be utterly screwed with little chance of recovery. The quick-save and quick-reload fest has continued, and gotten even more frequent. Nearly every single battle (not joking) is decided by pure chance for me at the moment. Either I survive the enemy turns and kill them off instantly, or they kill me without me ever getting a chance to act for a single turn (again, this is not a joke, exaggeration or hyperbole).
This game has so much potential and enjoyment that is squandered by the binary nature of the combat system. It is truly a shame.

I recommend this because it does offer some new features, something the AC franchise has done quite well. However, while Aveline is a very unique character, I feel Ubisoft squandered their first female assassin with this half-done game. It just doesn't feel like they put as much effort into this as they did the others. The story is okay, but it's not very engaging. I also notice some of the animations are poor compared to the previous games. For example, when Avenline slows down from sprinting to walking, there doesn't appear to be an animation that shows her actually slowing down like Edward or Connor. Instead, it seems as though she's just walking, but her slowing movement speed doesn't match the animation. As well, when she is sprinting and she moves left and right, the animation is just not right. Connor and Edward's animations showed their pivot foot push them in the direction they are strafing in, and the upper-body twist responding accordingly. Aveline just turns the direction she is strafing towards. It looks awkward and unrealistic compared to Ubisoft's beautiful animation work in Black Flag and AC:III.
I have not beaten the game yet, but again, the story also doesn't appear to be well-invested. I do enjoy the features like the chain kill feature that I am still getting used to, and I think a female assassin like Aveline offers new gameplay options, such as Aveline's ability to change personas. That's a great feature, and I hope to see that be expanded into a male assassin in future games. I can only hope that where Liberation's shortcomings begin, make for a great experience in the next AC; I hope that perhaps we will see another female assassin (personally, I want to see Shao Jun's story in an AC title), and Liberation was more or less an introduction to it, like naval combat in AC:III to Black Flag. Liberation is a nice addition to the Assassin's Creed Franchise, but it seems like Ubisoft just got lazy in this title and put only half effort into it.

A lot of fun, but 'Old School' hard.
There is actually a lot of interesting little game mechanics happening here. The amount of XP for killing enemies drops as you start to level up, forcing you in some ways to start looking out for the more dangerous prey just to keep moving forward level wise. Traders aren't junk dealers, well, except for the ones that are, and for the most part don't want that rubbish you are carrying. There are also a fair few interesting things happening with damage to make things a bit more than Hit Points and dead.
The game is also not going to hold your hand. You will be given missions but do not expect quest markers, glowing icons above NPCs of importance or even little updates part way through the quest to even let you know you are doing the right thing. Even knowing if you are on the right map is going to require you to pay attention and work things out.
The main quests slowly level as part of what I am assuming is the overall story arc. Side quests pop up from time to time if you talk to enough people but for the most part are linked to what you are trying to do anyway. At time of writing I believe I have progressed maybe 1/4 of the way through, possibly less, and can't really talk about the middle/end of the game. You are allowed to explore to some extent but the game is in no means an open world sandbox and some parts of the starting map are blocked off with rock falls that you lack the equipment to move until later.
On the down side I did mention this game is Old School hard. Combat is turn based and if you get in over your head you are likely to be swamped and killed before you can get out of it. On the flip side thinking up creative ways to defeat your enemies can be very rewarding. Having been kerb stomped by one enemy three times in a row, I finally defeated him by first throwing in a molotov and then following up straight away by entangling him with a net so he could gain the full enjoyment of standing in fire for several turns. Unfortunately with other combats I have only been able to succeed by entering a map, taking one round of damage from the multiple enemies that are still there waiting for you, shooting once and then exiting the map to heal before doing it again, and again, until you finally manage to kill enough of the buggers to make it a slightly more managable one on one.
The game is also a bit unforgiving if you don't follow the 'correct' path on the skill tree. Many areas include air vents that you can, one assume, enter and crawl around, successfully by passing the bigger and badder enemies on the level. I assume as your character needs a high enough Lockpick skill to get the vents open in the first place and I have never been able to increase my skill enough to get a vent open.
Also don't ask me how the crafting system works. There seems to be a lot of crafting you can do, just not with my skill base. There are actually a fair few combat related skills I do seem to be needing to constantly increase thank you very much Mr Game Designer so I can't skill up everything.
However if you can get over the fact you are going to die alot and are willing to accept that you do need to PAY ATTENTION (one side quest involves
:P ) then you will have an entertaining little old school RPG with some interesting world building and backstory.
Great game, everyone should try it ;)

For horror fans and fans of point-and-click adventure games, this is a great title.
The story is pretty good, but not fantastic.  It is mostly a survival game, getting from one place to the next.  Story unfolds as you go.  The voice work is good, and the writing is pretty good.
The art is fantastic.  Some of the settings are truly horrible and creatively done.  Lots of gross-outs.  I think this is one of the best points of the game.
The puzzles are very nicely done.  MOST puzzles can be solved on your own with a little thinking and ingenuity.  Some are simple, some are complex, but you can figure most of them out with some patience.  There are a few puzzles (three I can think of) that don't make much logical sense, and (in my opinion) could only be solved by clicking though everything in the environment and everything in your inventory.  There were also a couple of puzzles that I had a harder time than I should have because I missed an element that could be clicked on by thinking it was part of the background art.
For a horror / survival game I was a bit surprised at the lack of timed puzzles; for example escaping from a creature chasing you.  There is one really great timed puzzle, and it is one of the best in the entire game.  I'd have loved to see more of these.
Buy this game for great puzzles, wonderful art, and a brutal horror sci-fi setting.  If you are new to point-and-click adventure games, I think this game would be a challenging and fun introduction.
Don't buy this game if you demand complex storylines and characters, or if you're not particularly fond of sci-fi horror games.  If you don't like point-and-click style adventure games, obviously you shouldn't buy this.
