A rough gem of a game for people who wax nostalgic for the old fallouts. Having just finished my first play through (60 hours to complete) I wanted to share my experiences. Overall I greatly enjoyed the setting story and gameplay, especially the combat, but I wont be rushing to start my 2nd play through!
The feel of the game world is a bit of a mix of Fallout, Metro, Avernum and Shadow Run that comes together cohesively thanks to the (mostly) good writing and atmospheric locations (once you get used to the fallout 1 era aesthetic).
Exploring the world reminds me more of the Avernum series of games than fallout as there is no abstracted map travel. You eventually have limited ‘fast travel’ between key hubs but beyond that you navigate from A to B through each and every winding rat infested tunnel and utility shaft that connects them. I find this very cool in general … but the world is maze like, and there is no map / mini-map at all! This can lead to frustrating moments.
Character creation is super important and potentially quite easy to mess up! I think almost any build could make it through the majority of the game content, but the last quarter or so of the campaign is a real change of pace / difficulty, ultimately leading to a final boss battle that some left-of-field builds might just not be able to beat (through you can jump through some *awful* side quest hoops to lower the boss difficulty). Really it’s best to go in with a clear idea for your character and the fore knowledge that it will be ‘end game viable’. Still within that spectrum of builds though there is good potential for a variety of play-styles.
Combat is definitely a strong point of the game, there are no random encounters, instead all the enemies are already on the map. Depending on your skills, perks and items you can end up with a lot of tactical options during an encounter, with many difficult encounters that encourage you to explore all your options. I wish the diplomatic solutions to some situations were better fleshed out and gave better rewards, as even playing a persuasive character I tended to use that skill to avoid enemies engaging on me, but then I’d initiate combat with them on my own terms straight after to get XP anyways – otherwise I just got nothing from the encounter.
My biggest gripes about the game, and the reasons I am not diving directly back into a 2nd play through are:
1. The back tracking – Limited fast travel and the maze like network of large locations mean you can spend ALOT of time travelling just to reach a merchant or follow up on a quest lead. It never got too tedious for me (borderline...), but your mileage may vary. It can also be quite obscure with what you need to do next for some quests, so you can end up losing time just wandering around to try out different possibilities (ultimately I started using the Wiki to avoid unnecessary travel while trying to complete some quests).
I would probably not replay the game again without using a certain ‘speed hack’ utility that increases movement speed!
2. Merchant system – This kind of ties into the first issue, merchants buy only a very limited number of items at a time (say 2 guns 1 melee weapon), meanwhile you’re trying to unload a stockpile of looted goods! Crafting is also a technically semi-optional, but ultimately important part of min/maxed builds that requires a lot of scouring round merchants when they restock looking for new and better components. Paired with gripe number 1 this leads to a lot of ‘downtime’ just handling the logistics of getting from A to B to sell something then onto C to buy something else. That being said it certainly isn't mandatory to loot everything, you probably get enough cash through quests etc to scrape through the main story - but what kind of RPG experience is that! I had *MAX* bottle caps by the time I finished my 1st fallout 1 play through :)
The same program that allows for the 'speed hack' also has a feature for forcing an instant shop refresh. Giving the merchants new stock and allowing them to buy more of your blood stained loot – I don’t think I would replay the game without this added feature! (while trying not to abuse it)
3. The Final Act – The last part of the story takes place in a separate location to the rest of the game, and the quests and mechanics introduced in this area can honestly be quite annoying. It feels like this whole section was designed to prolong the game time (going back and forth between screens looking for key cards, a huge scavenger hunt of finding random items in random places to get to the boss, constantly re-spawning enemies, etc). Ultimately I just followed a guide on the wiki - It would be an incredible time-sink otherwise.
The actual final boss battle was pretty cool in my opinion but the whole section immediately leading up to it dampened my enthusiasm for going back into the game again where I now know my new character is eventually going to have to do all that hoop jumping again.
Wow – you’re still here. Thanks for reading. It looks like my negatives kind of out weigh the positives when reading this doesn’t it? But they really don’t. It’s just the gripes of someone who other-wise had a great time exploring the world of Underrail. If the backtracking sounds like it might be a deal breaker for you then try the game with the speed hack. This game certainly has a niche audience but If you think you -might- be the intended target, then you probably are, and you’ll likely have a good time playing it just like I had.

Well done game.
Pro:
- Nice graphics, even if everything is a bit small for my taste
- Great soundtrack ... but hey, what would you expect if you read Mark Morgan in the credits?
- Voice-overs are really good for an indie game. There are some flaws, sure, but for the most part it's superb.
- Dark, gloomy atmosphere and a story that makes sense for the biggest part. Sometimes it feels a bit forced and the ending was not really that surprising, but all in all I've seen way worse stories.
- Lots of background stories which are interesting to read. Yes. Read.
Bad:
- The puzzles are so-so. They are doable because there your inventory is small and there are not very many hotspots where it makes sense to interact with. But still, many solutions make only sense in hindsight.
- The deaths. It's okay that you can die. But that the dying-sequence is unskippable and resets you to points where you have to repeat unskippable dialogs sometimes becomes really tedious.
- The unskippable travels.
- The "I can't do that"-statements. There are not as bad as in "Cayne", but still they won't fit in 50 percent of the time. "I might just break it" is my favorite, I can't recall a situation where it made sense.
- In the very ending, they screwed up some voice overs. You have scences where the protagonist is really, really down, and the voice acting in this parts is great, but in-between he talks to another person in a complete other tone.
- In general, the ending makes little sense to me.
I'ld say, if you've finished all must-plays on your gaming-list and are looking for other games which are quite good but have their flaws, you might give this one a chance.

The second installment of the ME franchise, and another all-time favorite of mine.
The gameplay, which was the flaw of the previous ME, has been massively (hue hue) revamped, making it a more enjoyable shooter, although (and is mostly the case in higher difficulty settings), you'll find yourself digging through the multiple layers of protection your enemies have (Biotic barrier, armor and shield, some enemies combine two if not 3 of them), but this is where powers shine.
Much like the first installment, the game has both tech powers (hacking, burning, things like that) and biotic powers ("super-powers" if you want), you MUST make use of these powers in a smarter way.
The inventory management part has been for the most part removed, all that is left for you to do is simply chose your squadmates' weapons and yours, and customize your own armor (you can only change how your squadmates' armor looks like now, and there ain't much choice).
The whole weapon modding mechanics has been scraped as well, ammunition mods are now powers inherent to your class (if it has any), and weapons can be upgraded through research.
Same goes for the skill trees, their size has been greatly reduced which allows for a greater understanding of what is what and what does what.
With that, the game is a lot more simplified, perhaps for the best.
The storyline and storytelling remains awesome, and the fact that choices made in the previous game get carried over is just great.
In conclusion another hit by Bioware. Do keep in mind that you'll have to count at least 30 hours + (if playing on Insanity, and if you give enough of a damn about the storyline) in order to complete this other epic journey.
Also, it is best to have played the first game, not just because you can shape up the world of the games to come, but because you get a greater understanding of what's going on, who's on and of course... What is what.
Hell, it's a must! Why play this game in the first place if you don't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the story.

This is going to be a bit of an odd review.  I DO recommend the game when it's cheaper - just for the experience, but with several caveats mentioned below.
, and any game that opens with "Press START to continue" is always a bad omen.  It's a frankly horrible and frustrating experience with keyboard and mouse (it really hasn't been converted very well).  I resorted to my trusty XBox 360 gamepad to save myself the headache...
Sorry about the long review, but for tl;dr, just scroll to the very last para...
_________________________
When I started this game, I was pretty wowed by the concept.  Think back to the late, great Patrick Swayze, Demi Moore and Whoopi Goldburg and the film
and you basically have the plot of this game - sorta (no Demi or Whoopi-alikes, and no Swayze personality).  You play Ronan, a rather bland, non-uniform detective who is murdered in the opening scene (great start!) and in that typical way (of ghosty-films) his soul rises out of his body and he looks down on himself, realising the very worst has just happened!  And it's a BRILLIANT start!  It really is.  I was so excited that I couldn't wait to throw myself right in the game.  Cops soon arrive at the scene of your murder, and there are priceless scenes like someone leaving the building in front of you, happily unaware of a ghost who slips out right behind them and then vanishes.  Absent-mindedly, you walk THROUGH a cop who suddenly shudders as you pass through them, and if you have a rumble feature on your gamepad, it too mimics that shudder whenever you pass through objects and people - fabulous!  I thought: "this is going to be GREAT!"
So, you're a ghost.  You quickly learn that you are to remain behind to catch your murderer (Swayze theme again).  You learn that you can 'possess' people and read their minds and, on occasion, influence their decisions.  You can enact 'poltergeist' activity by making phones ring, switch on desk fans and the like.  You can even possess a CAT!  That alone is beautifully done - exceptional animation and effects.  The game style is closer to a 3D point-and-click adventure with some action parts, and it's mostly themed around collecting clues and solving the "Bleeding Obvious"...  There are side missions to collect odd objects, like 9 rifles, or 5 boilers (yes, boilers) and if you collect them you will be told a very short spooky story about that area.  It's a novelty, but it could have been improved by some quick-time spooky movie to watch instead of listening to a blind reading.
What started really well soon goes downhill and I just want to scream about the potential this game doesn't quite reach!!!  It could have been so BRILLIANT but it fails pretty much throughout.  At the beginning, instead of flailing and wailing and trying to understand what's happening, you instead walk off happy as anything to just be a ghost as if you'd been a ghost for YEARS!  You died literally two minutes back but you're already fine with everything - off to do ghost-business right off the bat!  Remember
where Swayze had to learn to touch things, who encountered other ghosts of very different kinds, who badly wanted to make contact and to find his way back to life and love, dear Demi Moore?  Ronan is not like this at all.  He's now suddenly and happily engaged in not only his own quest, but solving everybody else's problems - everybody else being people who have presumably been ghosts for much longer than our dead-2-mins hero who can magically solve problems (find clues in the immediate vicinity) of these other apparently clueless ghosts who are much more experienced ghosts than he is - surely.  But they're all stupidly incapable and you must gather the clues blatantly laid all around them.  Not good for a concept, but it's doable (he's a detective after all, and maybe only detectives can spot clues on the ground around the victims' feet...).
Moving on, you will see ghostly apparitions continually.  The vast majority just do nothing.  They're not even animated - just 2D transparencies that shimmer to fade out when you approach the image.  At first, the early ones are done well, like a girl in a shower who simply vanishes whenever you try to get closer, quite eerie and clever.  But after a while you realise they're all merely static images that don't even move (very obvious when looking top-down at one from a stairway) - and often it's the same image repeated.  It would have been SO much better to have some background ghost characters just lurking around, some of them sad or lost, some angry or frightening - all of them at least
.
Your ghostly powers are okay, though the game explains to you right away that external walls are "consecrated" so ghosts can't pass through those (ergo: the boundary of the map!) but what is SO disappointing is that, beyond the opening scene hardly anyone ever reacts!  Switch on their TV, ring their phones, WALK through them!  Mostly, they notice absolutely nothing unless you reach a case where you must distract people (in which case they react predictably to you triggering a phone or vending machine).  Mostly though, your haunting torments make no difference and cause no reaction.  It would have been such a greater game to be given a moral choice whether to haunt or help, but for what it's worth you hardly need to be a ghost really.  It's a shame - it would have been FUN to cause some haunted-house things.   Possessing people soon loses its fun too when you realise that most characters only have two lines to 'say' (always about not feeling safe or the murderer being at large), and only a couple of times do you influence them.  No
random thoughts here!  It gets to be boring after a while.
You will encounter 'demons' for the action bit - nastly brown/orange things that will 'suck up your soul' (ie game-over - go all the way back to that ages-ago checkpoint...) and demon-holes (where they come from, of course).  You can hide from the demons in areas where past spirits wandered and left a timestamp (ie a blue foggy area vaguely shaped like a ghost).  You become invisible from demons when you are in these, and you can hop from one ghost-space to the next until you are behind the demon, and you can dispatch it with a quick-time event that, in a split second, expects you to register a thumbstick direction AND a button press.  As for the demon holes, they're nearly all just used as pathway blockers to force you along another route.
Finally, there's Ronan himself.  It's impossible to empathise or feel this character at all, or sympathise with his story.  A dude in a fedora, cigarette permanently hanging out of one corner of his curled lip and a cocky swagger, and as is video-game fashion, he's the gruff, growly white male as always, but not even likeable.  You will uncover snippets of his story and wonder why on earth he was ever a cop at all.  It's difficult to be interested.  He should have been confused, angry, frightened and determined, but he is for all the world like a regular guy just sauntering along to the corner store.
________________
It's a relatively short game, and for the full price I really can't recommend it, but if it comes down to a more casual-game sensible price (the $15/$10 mark) then yes, I would say it was worth buying just to experience where the game NEARLY goes, because it is such a clever and original idea!  It's worth it just for the opening 30 mins.  It's worth it just to possess the cat, for crying out loud!  But it's not a game with any real replay value, and it's certainly not
ghost-style.  It should have been, and it could have been epic, but it misses the mark in every direction and fails to deliver on everything it hinted at when the game first opened to your murder scene, and that's such a shame.

This game is a horror game, but we need to clerify what that means.  You see the horror genre is very open and there are many things that fall into that catigory.  So in this case horror will be defined to be gore and the depths of human depravity.  Think mad scientists torture porn and you'll be on the right track.  No, its not that scarry.  No, you won't really be on the edge of your seat with this one.  This is more of a "the horror...oh the horror of it all" type thing.
Next, half or more of the horror comes from reading PDAs scattered through out each area.  If you don't do that you'll be missing out on a lot of the game.  If you think, well, I don't know, give it a skip.  Its probably not for you.
One more word about the gore.  This game is pretty blood drenched.  Honestly its way over played.  You get to a point where the next "horror" to be unveiled doesn't phase you because its really a case of been there seen it or worse.  Which is a shame because there are several scenes that  would have been alot stronger if you hadn't been completely desensitzed to the gore.  That said, if gore really freaks you out or you just don't like it, give this game a skip its definitly not for you.
How about the puzzles?  Some are intuitive some are not so intuitive.  And sometimes you have to walk to the right area to trigger the next "thing".  This only happened to me twice, but I had to lookup the "solution" in a walkthrough both times.  Not a huge thing but if that kinda thing isn't you're cup of tea then you were warned.
Overall as a point and click horror game it was interesting enough to keep me going and not so frustrating I gave up on it.  If nothing I've said so far is a turn off give it a go.

Well, a lot of what you've heard about this game is true. There is a lot of clunk to its port (the menu has no mouse support and doesn't even use arrow keys). The "combat" amounts to a random key press alongside a random mouse button click. And the mystery isn't that complex.
So why am I recommending it, you ask? Because it never lost my attention. Between the atmosphere, the unlockable ghost stories, and the main case (albeit not Sir Arthur Conan Doyle stuff) it was just a lot of fun to play. I even got into the random key sequences of excuting demons (and was a bit suprised that in the beginning my nerves would betray me and I'd fail at times). It was Airtight's swan song, and you can almost feel it in there what with the brevity and all, but it
a nice tune for those seeking an atmospheric haunted noire vibe. Definitely not for everyone, but much better than the critics have given it credit for, that's for sure.

The touching saturday morning cartoon type of story: where friendship wins over all. And no, this isn't cringe like some of those cartoons are, there's actually some good writing here thanks to character interaction and actually caring about those characters. The visuals are hit and miss, with the visual novel portions of the cutscenes really working well, especially with the character models. Where the game stumbles is the gameplay. The strategy is basic but does work at first, with secret trends as well as more obvious trends then you can take advantage of. It's just doesn't have enough power over time, and becomes a bit repetitive, and yet have specific strategies that you have to follow. And it has technical problems with a lack of options as well as some performance issues. Regardless however, the game still was worth playing, thanks to that charm factor I mentioned.

Good adventure game with a good story. Not a fast-paced game and with very few action elements, but it was never supposed to be an action game to begin with. Soul Suspect plays more like an adventure game with puzzles with an occassional fighting scene (which itself is presented like an action puzzle with a small amount of strategy involved).
The atmosphere is great. Sound (voice and music) and visuals are superb and convincing and set the mood for the game right away. The story is classical detective story, obviously with supernatural elements, is well written and even though not mind blowing in its "message", it kept me completely immersed en interested through the whole game. The game world is not very big,but detailed and varying, and there are very many things to observe and find. Lots of collectibles, but these are done right: when found, they provide smaller details to the story, or tell separate smaller stories of their own.
Gameplay puzzles aren't very difficult, and failing them doesn't give any penalty. The detective puzzles will remind a lot of LA Noire, but are somewhat easier.
To sum up: not a game for people looking for action. It is rather a game for people who don't mind standing still occasionally in a game for a while to observe the surroundings and solve a puzzle or mystery. If you are one of those, you are in for a treat: the game is very convincing as a supernatural spooky detective.
PS: almost no bugs found, except cinematics graphics sometimes appeared in much worse quality than actual gameplay (which are pretty good). Also keep in mind that collectibles you might have missed can't be collected once you finish the game (the game notifies about this in the last scene).

Only recommended if you've already played Recettear and desperately want another shopkeeping game. If you haven't played Recettear, it's a superior experience for just $5 more. Al Fine involves too much clicking and not enough thinking.
The market you buy your items from has infinite stock and their prices rarely change. Exploring dungeons consists of selecting an adventurer and waiting 3 days for the game to tell you whether he succeeded or failed. And selling your items basically consists of setting the same items out at default price 98% of the time and occasionally clicking their shelves to restock them. The biggest change of strategy is during one of the 4 Commerce Battles in the game, where the easiest way to make a bigger income (not profit; spend as much money as you like) than your competitor is to sell all the expensive loot you've stored from the dungeons at a 10-20% discount.
It feels like they cut a lot of corners with this game: it only gives you information on the buying preferences of less than half of your customers, all of the information about the other stores in the Top 10 list (not to mention the Top 10 list itself) is worthless, and there's a persistent bug where after an hour or two of playing it, it'll start maxing out your VRAM and refuse to load textures (and also switch to Japanese).
The story itself is too bland and light for its own good. All of the characters are caricatures that barely get any development and the only major conflict is a plot to monopolize the town's economy that only takes up 10 days of the 100-day duration. The other 90 days basically involve the meek main character deciding he wants to be a merchant and making friends to help him. Nothing is really done with the 3 different races or the floating island setting.
It took me 14 hours to finish the game. I wish I hadn't invested that time (or my money) into it.

In Short:
An improvement of the business mechanics seen from Recettear.
Long Ver:
Recettear, a Japanese indie darling that focuses on being a merchant, years later we now find a very similar game inspired by Recettear.
In Al Fine, you play as Loius, a young man swindled by a Sprite named Alice to pay back for breaking a supposingly precious 'gem'.
But there is no giant debt hanging over our heads but in place are the guild taxes which occurs a few times per month and when there is a challenge, you have a few days to upped over your opponent's profits.
The shop is affected by what types of customers which are affected by decorations, by weather (sunny, rainy, cloudy) affecting the numbers of customers, by type of items (food *rot by days*, equipment, merch) or by the usual...price.
But within price, there are more restrictions as customer's budget are not affected by your rank like in Recettear (aka the level). Only by market trends will the price change, allowing you to sell more.
While in the shop, using Alice you can restock items as long as you have it in the warehouse. Although, I have not found anything to improve her speed in the game so far (5 hours of playing).
Improving the shop will cost you your merchant points that are gained via selling in the guild. I do find that its best to pile a few upgrades rather than 1 upgrade as 1 doesn't affect too much into the shop and you save time.
Speaking of time, just like Recettear...you will pass the time by just visiting places. Some places will give you information to be used much later in the game.
There is 1 huge con to this game, the inability to go into dungeons.
You can hire an adventurer to do so but its just bassically assigning them away missions which success depends on their level and equipment.
The game does not have any feature to change an adventurer's equipment so far...
Another con would be the character design, the illustrator seems to lack basic anatomy lessons but in return makes it very detailed. There is just something annoying about their necks and collarbones...
Interestingly there is actually another illustrator on this game as you can see on the merchants portraits via rank which are superbly better than the character designer (unless its somebody introduced in the game).
Storywise, I do feel there is far more characterization with Alice than Louis...I can't really say anything more as I'm in Chapter 2. The game does not show anything on romance, only friendship.
The music so far is pleasant and it works within the game. But is it memorable? No.
Overall:
If you're hungry for more selling mechanics aka Recettear, this might scratch that itch. I did enjoy the game with my 5 hours and it does have some difficulty to it to gain maximum profit within a short time. (The game does tell you whether you're good or terrible). There are more games inspired by Recettear but those games are sadly to be release so...so far away. It either 75 or 78/100 would be my rating.
Currently: 29 hours = Finish. It might be shorter but I was trying to get rank 1 in the Merchant rankings. Its actually pretty easy to fall from rank 1 to rank 3 or 4 after just 1 day of terrible profits. Also found out that seasons also changes the trends of items so the difficulty increases.

Though the graphics are fairly dated, this is a wonderful gem of a game. Along with your standard racing, FlatOut goes a further step and gives you semi-fully destructible vehicles as well as often hilarious bonus activities, such as throwing your character at a dart board or bowling with the top of his skull. Aside from an engine that's on fire and is still somehow propelling you, the car physics are very believable and sometimes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(such as when your wheels are all ♥♥♥♥ed up and every time they rotate they make your car bounces).
The choice of music isn't something I care to listen to, but it suits the gameplay well enough.
Oh, your car is also fully customizable, to the frame to the tires to the engine that realistically improve your vehicle (as in, there's no "super tire" that never loses grip, and there's no "super engine" with a million horsepower). In fact, the wee bit of power the upgrades give you are sometimes the only thing that keeps you in 1st place.
This is a very nice game, and if you don't mind looking at low-poly characters, definately give this game a try.

Golf with your friends is one of the best, if not the best, mini golf game you can find here on Steam (and most places for that matter). It's pretty self-explained what the game is about, you play golf, with or without your friends. (Though playing with friends will give you an overall better experience, and if not, you need new friends).
The game currently has four maps with a fifth one on the horizon, all of which has a different theme, you got your standard green forest type of map, a map set in the ancient Egypt, a map taking place in a enchanted magical forest, one in a haunted mansion and the fifth and upcoming one (as of this review) will feature a candyland sort of theme from my knowledge.
The game does get somewhat repetitive after a few hours of gameplay once you figure out how every hole works and how to do well on them. This is a problem especially if you're playing multiplayer with strangers, and certain friends (Damn it Carl) since there is a handful of guides on Steam explaining how to get a hole-in-one or the best possible score on each hole, so more often than not you will play against someone who has memorized all the holes or just simply looking at a guide as they play.
But there are a few settings you can play around with to spice things up incase you get bored such as: bigger golf balls, enable jumping (which makes the game way easier but is really enjoyable at the same time), enable gravity and so on.
I haven't experienced any game-breaking bugs myself but the game is in Early Access so chances are there are a few bugs and glitches here and there that needs to be eliminated, aswell as more content being added in the future.
For $6 this game is defenitely worth picking up, and you're able to get it for less during sales. And since it's not very expensive you can most likely talk some friends into buying it, or perhaps you can be generous and gift a copy to them.

Early Access Review:
Original Sin 2 is what exactly what every RPG gamer has been looking for - there's a potency to its' immersion that every EA title should aim to hit. This is the caliber of gaming you (EA devs) should truly attempt to employ!!!! It's an absolute masterpiece of Early Access gaming. A true game of D&D mixed with chess.......Larian said they posted this game on steam with a laugh, and I know why!! Ok I'll stop with the hype and explain.
(Graphics, optimization, controls, gameplay, sound.)
Graphics/Animations: 10/10
Right from the jump you notice how polished the world and characters look. From beautiful landscapes to fluid animations, I love it!!!! Nothing left to say here! Excellent job!
Optimization: 10/10
No loading screens.. LIKE EVER during your gaming experience! Excellent work!
Controls: 9/10
No complaints other than the restriction of your camera angles. Part of the experience is viewing a gorgeous and artistic world... You can never look at the sky....and view your character from better angles.. sad. Although, you can rebind your keys, you can rotate and zoom in - You feel like you're in control. Great job!
Gameplay: 9.5/10
This is where the bulk of the game lies. From story to combat - the immersion starts with the world appearance and story narrative, then ends with a blast with its' combat delivery. The combat is spaced out making you feel like you're not always in a chat box, and you'll be satisfied in casting, buffing or even simple melee attacks.  You can be whatever you want to be. Unless you want to be an orc...you can't be an orc - BUT what you can do from what they have to offer makes you feel like you're totally in control of your character's person.
Yes, customization is quite limited. I like my rpgs to let me customize my character to the "T" ... and this does limit you in that aspect to a certain extent...better than most games but coming from MMOs you may be disappointed. Given a more customizable character and maybe even adding a few other races .. you'll never play the same character again. Character creation is key in this type of genre - still ... Excellent work!
Music/Sound: 9.5/10
The sound and music is fantastic! ... I'd still love to hear a larger variety of music during gameplay...This will probably end up being a 10 simply because they will add voice acting and more music throughout the future acts. Excellent job!
Overall: 10/10
The story, the adventure, the combat, the scenery, the ..... oh you get it already!!!! What a phenomonal game. RPG lovers, MMO lovers...hack'n'slash lovers... VIDEO GAME LOVERS! You'll love this. I wouldn't post my first review on steam if I didn't believe this to be a game for everyone on steam. Do enjoy! Thanks Larian!

Fable is a franchise I've had a bit of a rocky relationship with. My first experience was Fable II (having completely missed the original), and it is one of my favorite games of the Xbox 360 era. Fable III, not so much. With Fable Anniversary coming out soon, the remake of the now 10 year old RPG, I figured why not just get a cheap copy of the original and see what it’s all about.
The premise starts you as a young boy in the town of Oakvale in the land of Albion, who has a loving sister and parents. But that kind of story makes for a boring video game, so a group of bandits attack your village, kidnaping your mother and sister, and murdering practically everyone else, including your father. But before you meet your own demise, you’re saved by a hero named Maze, and are inducted into the Guild of Heroes. In the world of Albion, a hero isn't just a title but an occupation, something you learn by joining the guild. The game switches over to your teenage years for your guild training and then finally to adulthood after you become a true hero. This is the first neat trick Fable does, giving your character, and the world, a real sense of growth. Seeing the world change around you as you grow and make choices is neat, and gives everything a sense of place.
Fable has the typical “your character glows if they’re good and pale skin and devil horns if you’re evil” that most games with morality like to do, but how you spec your character also affects them. If you put a bunch of points into strength, your character will become more bulky and muscular as a result, while if you put a lot of points into magic, you get glowing blue tattoos on your face. Unfortunately the options felt a bit too simple preventing me from having my character look exactly how I want. I like my characters to be a bit on the thin and scrawny side, probably because I myself am thin and scrawny, but there wasn't any way to go full on melee combat without forcing yourself to become a hulking beast. A little more variety on this front would have been cool.
In combat your main tool will be your melee, of which you are given a nice selection of fast swords like the katana, something with a bit more punch like great swords, and even more massive weapons like hammers. There’s not much in the ways of multiple attacks, it’s rather simplistic with one button for attacking and another for using a flourish attack when you build one up. It’s all about timing and avoiding your enemies with blocks and dodges. Getting in hits and avoiding them yourself builds up your combat multiplier, letting you deal more damage. It’s a system that works but by the end of the game I found myself a little tired of it. The ranged combat, bows and crossbows, I found to be rather useless. It has its place in certain situations but you’re not going to want to spec your character into a full ranged one, which is a disappointment. Magic is by far the most interesting and varied. There’s a ton of spells all put into a bunch of categories. So if you want to go full on attack magic you can throw points into lighting, fire, etc. Even if you’re melee focused like I was, it’s worth getting spells like slow time, which I found invaluable during the later parts of the game.
The core of Fable has you taking on guild quests, making choices, and being the "hero." The moral choice system is bit too black and white for my tastes. You’re never really given any grey area and it’s always very clear which is good and which is evil. Having a character say something like, "you can go do this quest for this reward, or I guess if you were some sort of evil person you could always just kill me," doesn't really leave much to the imagination. One nice thing however is the game does provide full good and full evil side quests, usually having them be on opposite sides of the same problem. Will you take the quest the farmers put up to help stop the bandit raids, or will you take the quest the bandits put up to help with the raid. Stuff like that’s more fun because it lets you put your intentions forward right away rather than giving you some black and white choice half way through the quest.
Another big component of the game is the interaction system with NPCs. You hero has a ton of different emotions they can express ranging from simple ones like laughing or saying hi, too more morality specific ones like flexing your heroic muscles or giving an evil laugh, too the ridiculously absurd such as farting and doing the chicken dance. Sadly I never found myself having any real gameplay reason to use them past their first time. For example you can flirt with NPCs and eventually have them fall in love with you. Cool idea, but no real benefit doing it. I didn't even have to try honestly. By the end of the game, every girl, and even some men, had a big enough heart above them that I could simply walk up to them, hand them a wedding ring, and be married before the sun set without even trying. The ability to interact with NPCs is a neat idea, and admittedly I got excited when they started to call me by my title I picked out and talking about past quests I did, but overall it feels more like a proof of concept than a fully implemented feature.
The story does go to some interesting places and has a large focus on family, with the hero's sister and mother coming heavily into play. This does give everything a more personal feel to it and I found myself caring in the hero's journey and his seeking revenge. The antagonist, Jack of Blades, lives up to his awesome name by being a great creepy villain. My only wish was that is motivations were explained better as I was never quite sure why he was doing what he was doing other than to just be evil.
It’s worth noting that I played the PC version, known as Fable: The Lost Chapters, which contains a bunch of extra characters, side quests, and continues the story after the final boss battle, which by the way was pretty weak. The extra content is cool, adding new characters and extra story that is welcome, but doesn't feel completely necessary. Also the new final boss somehow manages to be easier and lamer than the original.
Graphically the game holds up pretty well for being 10 years old. Stuff like faces and character animations feel a bit old and outdated however it is saved by Fable's art direction which still shines though. The game goes for a very classic bedtime story fantasy look, hence the name, and succeeds at it well. It’s a world that takes itself very seriously one minute, and starts poking fun at itself the next. It all manages to work very well; making Albion a world you want to spend time in. This is also helped greatly thanks to the music, which is quite wonderful, perfectly capturing the whimsy the game is throwing at you.
For a 10 year old game Fable one holds up surprisingly well. Moral choice in games has certainly grown in the years and in a lot of ways fable feels too simplistic in its decisions to a fault. But at the same time it all works well in the context of its storybook like nature. If you want a fun filled adventure where you get to be the hero, or villain, Fable is still a game worth checking out.

The best old Fallout game that isn't an old Fallout game.
UnderRail is about the remnants of humanity surviving within the metro stations, railways & catacombs under a ruined world. All the RPG mechanic staples of the old isometric Fallouts are here: core stats control skills & both serve as prerequisites for
feats that effect how your character plays & the special attacks & abilities he/she has. Because of this system, character builds have an enormous depth of options. Be sneaky stabby guy, soldier man, silver-tongued merchant, crafting man or psychic wizard guy. Psychic wizard guy? Yes, in addition to the standard post-apocalyptic guns, melee & crafting, there are also psi powers that let you throw ice & energy blasts at people. There are also a breadth of gizmos & gadgets to utilize, from road flares & caltrops to forcefield generators & invisibility fields.
Crafting is a very important thing to do in this, possibly more so than any other rpg I've ever played. Any weapon, armor or item in the game can be made by the player & there is a significant benefit to making stuff yourself. While npcs will sell mostly standard armor vests or leather armor, you could make a suit of reinforced riot gear with ceramic plating & a tungsten riot-shield. The crafting is just as depthful as the rpg mechanics but the skills to make things are spread across 5 different skills.
If you miss the indepth rpgs of yesteryear, UnderRail is for you.

UPDATED REVIEW
Alright, now I'm a ton of hours into this game. 50hrs in 2 weeks says steam... good thing my PhD supervisor doesn't use steam...
The game continue to be awesome and scale unexpectedly well. Just when I'm thinking I'm rocking everything I get
. It didn't make me feel bad, it made it not get boring.
Other things I liked are the small-scale combat challenges you come across break up the larger dungeon-delving type experience. The town dialogue-heavy quests also help break the game into sections, giving it a very full and satisfying feeling. It's fairly open-world (with plausible limits), that you can switch between these types of play if you want to freshen the experience, and then go back as needed.
Here's some suggestions to players to keep their game enjoyable:
Don't overthink your skills, though I gotta say I'm putting pionts where I thought I wouldn't at character inception, just because there's cool stuff that I want. Don't read wikis about everything. The open and the unknown, learning through playing the game and talking to people, that's freakin' awesome!
Do put a handful of points into throwing and carry grenades. I can't think of a reason not to do this, so don't be silly. I went forever throwing grenades with 0 points before I finally pumped it up to 10 with bonuses. Not having my grenades go all over the place is nice, but even when it was pretty random, it was awesome and useful
. If you're doing a grenade build, I think you're going to have a really fun time and I look forward to doing my own grenade build.
Do plan to play it again. Can't do something? No sweat, just tell yourself you'll plan a build for that next time. Can't craft it? Can't kill it? Next time. I can't wait to play through with crossbows.
Do play with oddities. Oddities are a cool way to go up levels. I'm finding the progression smooth. I'll try the traditional way on another build, but really I'm digging it, and I think it's worth doing for the novelty alone. Given the bloodbath/completionist approach I usually favor, I'd be overpowered on kill/skill-based experience progression by now.
Don't ruin the mystique of the game by over-researching it. None of the puzzles are cripplingly hard, and the couple times I looked, it seems I just missed something pretty obvious... and I restrained myself from perusing much further.
Don't sweat having to go back to saves. Some people freak out because they get killed without warning. It's a post-apocalyptic setting and this generally doesn't happen on the bigger maps. In
there's a bunch of places that you unexpectedly get popped before you figure out what's going on, but the map chunks are tiny, and with two levels of autosave, you're not gonna lose too much time. Still, save often. Did I save scum on a couple of dialogue generated quest rewards? Yes I did, but I can tell you after extensive research that the ranges are pretty narrow.
BUY THIS GAME AT ALL COSTS!
What I'd like to see improved (these are small things):
* When visiting a store, I want a tab for items that they vendor will buy. Or at least a filter checkbox on the existing tabs. That'd make my life dandy!
* Plot items tab in inventory is a key. Let's face it, it's really just for keys. Save a tab an exclude keys from the main inventory, putting them in the keyring tab or whatever. Put a blue/red highlight that's different from the game color scheme around the few remaining plot items in the inventory tab or classify them into the other stuff and leave it.
* Make the fishing rod easier to see. I'm light-dark color-blind, and while I appreciate the general color scheme of the game, when I fish I have to paste my face up against my monitor if I'm remotely tired. Sure, I could go find my glasses, but it doesn't cost anything to maybe make it a bit more visually apparent.
* I wish there was an icon on the item info near its price or quality to tell you whether repairing it was worth the price for either recycling to scrap or selling. I hate having to think about that, though I suppose there's evidence that the devs don't want you constantly min-maxxing... I just think it'd be convenient and wouldn't detract from the game, particularly since what you can get for selling an item is gonna scale so I'll have to redo my estimates for items when I play a more mercantile build. Some may call me lazy, but I'd rather waste my time on other interesting aspects of this game.
* That right-click context menu is good, but it should have an option to repair/charge that gives guidance on the cost-effectiveness of the repair/charge and uses the right thing.
* Add partial-charging so you don't have to waste batteries. Make a new item which is a partially charged battery, allow them to be charged be other partially charged batteries and they don't stack. It'll be so much less of a nuisance. Let auto-charging prioritize them.

You wake up to find yourself in a ship you have no memory of being on. Now, you must find your missing family and get out of a spaceship that’s home to a few horrifying experiments in STASIS.
The level of suspense & atmosphere in STASIS is well executed. Whether it’s the discoveries of the horrifying experiments that you will encounter, the numerous dead bodies strewn all over the place or even the random scream that you will hear more than once, the layout is nicely setup (speaking of a horror perspective, of course).
Another thing that should be mentioned. During your play-through, you will find PDAs that give some back story to the victims, the ship and it’s shady owner, the Cayne Corporation.
Progression in this game is made by solving a specific dilemma, or puzzle. It’ll require you to look around the area for objects to use and look for clues to help you advance. With that said, unless you are proficient in puzzle solving, issues will be presented to you. This game is not beginner friendly and it requires you to stay sharp at all times in order to make it to the end.
Looking at the achievements for this game, I couldn’t help but notice that two-thirds of them requires for you to either get killed by a specific hazard or use a specific object and commit suicide.
I can understand having 1 or 2 achievements as to poke a little fun, but in this instance where you are playing a horror game, this is not exactly an ideal setup to just die for a few laughs.
The adventure was something else. Is it the best? Maybe, maybe not. Personally, I’ve only just started playing more games of the horror genre and I have already heard of a few games that are much more scarier than this one, but this was a good game, and this is one that I will recommend.

Al Fine is a shop management game similar to Racettear, but is unfortunately inferior to in every way.
Many mechanics are similar:
- Each day is broken up into 3 time segments: morning, day and night.  You can spend this time either opening shop, or choosing to visit one of the town's locations.
- Locations are exactly same as Racettear - town center, market, pub, adventure and merchant guilds.  Access to each location are restricted by the time segment of the day (ie pub on accessible at night).
- You obtain goods to sell by either buying from market, or obtaining through dungeons.  Unlike Racettear, there is no combat or RPG element.  You just hire the adventurer and send them off.  They'll return 3 days later and bring back loot.
- You can upgrade and redesign your shop to change the mood and type of customers that visit shop.
- Every 10 days you have to pay a fee to keep the store open.
The differences
- Weather and seasons.  These affect the number of customers but in reality the effect is only cosmetic.  Even on a bad weather day, with nothing else to do, you are still going to open the shop regardless, just means you make a little less profit that day.  It does not affect your decision making hence I describe it as cosmetic.
- Commerce battles.  You have to make more profit than your rival within x days.  This is also cosmetic since you're still going to sell things and make profit anyway.  The battles dont change your course of normal actions.
Poor implements:
- cant change resolution.  there is no fullscreen option, so the game at 800x600 (i think?) is just a tiny window.
- The game allows you to speed up time, but you have to manually restock shelves.  If you speed up time, by the time you notice the shelf is empty and click on the shelf to restock, the store is already closed.  So you can either watch the slow shopping process and be more efficient in restocking, or you can fast forward the boring parts but possibly miss out on sales.  I don't understand why restocking isnt an automated process.
- unlike Racettear where all customer types will buy pretty much everything, but have individual preferences towards price of certain goods, Al Fine customers will only buy the items they are designed to buy.  It is not fun to see alot of customers walk in, look around and not like anything then walk back out and waste your time.
I also encountered a game crashing bug where an error message popped up and said something like "out of VRAM unable to load scene".  Game does not autosave, and I lost all progress.
Its another game where I wish there was a neutral button. I'll hit recommend but really Racettear is the same but much better.

For now, STASIS have mixed rating, and it fits it the best, because the game itself is a wild mixture so you can't precisely decide its taste. Simply, they did a good job to create a world, but had no idea, what to fill it with.
As you can read in official artbook and forums, game was developed by a 3-part South African team of Brotherhood in 5 years. One short surgery cut-scene (you will remember it, no matter you liked it or not) was made in 3 months.
In spite of doing trending moba-games or something catchy for mobiles, they decided to produce a sci-fi horror adventure. And, somehow, they Kickstarter-ed it and launched on Steam.
David, tiny and brave, at his finest.
And what's the result?
The most valuable part of STASIS is its visual and sound-design. Whatever you look at, it seems like something sci-fiish, whatever you hear - it's cold and terrifying. You hero is a school-teacher, so his costume is not an armor, but bare nakedness in this haunted place. Blood, mess, corpses - everything creates a believable morbid picture. If devs wish to make an isometric Dead Space - at this point they did it right, maybe even better than EA in their sequels.
There is only 2 flaws: repeatative screams in ambient sound and sometimes not obvious ways for hero to walk. But they are not really matter.
The first thing, what will disturb your involvement is plot. Its quality will range, but it's... it's not rich as it pretend to be. In texts, here and there, you can see a lot of ≈dramatic stories, but for most of them there is no way to feel something; a lot of heavy themes mentioned, but none of them covered. In spite of that, the "mainquest" itself can be described in 2-3 sentences, and God bless the man, who can avoid cliches and comparations doing this. 5 years of all-day work was sacrificed to bring us poor Holliwood tale? Seriously? The only thing they could figure out themself without tons of cash was left without notice, as an early scetch.
Plot-devices have been chosen by default. It's text, nothing else. Sometimes you can read it in PDAs and terminals by you will, sometimes you're forced to "stay awhile and listen" for a long radio-talking scenes, but there is not much you can earn yourself. Decorations are static, they can only follow the story and can't tell us something new.
As for the character-creation - you will not see any sign of it. They are grotesque images, and nothing can change them.
There is a standart point-and-click sickness:
1. You grab something barely-seen
2. Use it
3. Then return to the #1.
Some of so-called puzzles looks logical, but mostly I find myself not in a "Ah, how I missed that? Wow!"-mood. Honestly, 99% of reasons to be stuck is not obvious actions and hidden details. I bet, there would be a lot of people out there, who would like that kind of torture, but I would prefer The Talos Principle or simply chess to challenge my mind.
I've ment, that the atmosphere part is alright, but the sad thing - devs' lack of ideas, what to do in the great house they built. Enemies are screamers and waiting traps, characters are dead heads on the screen. You feel yourself not lonely in the darkness, but dropped on your own to solve tasks with no real reason. Abandoned rooms of spaceship make a good impression on the first sight, and it lasts as the only reason to walk through.
Questionable thing - is suicide\death achivements. In my opinion, they are meaningless, even harmful. In Dead Space there were a lot of cool death-animations that starts when you lose. But what if death/suicide is a things to achive? Maybe, to lay with cut-open wrists - is a thing, devs want for their auditory? I don't know and don't really want to.
Game have a 50/50 misture of win and failure. Grab if you value the "atma"-part most or like the indie-thing with all it flaws, otherwise - you'd better obtain The Cat Lady as an example of how to do everything they done wrong right. Especially, writing and motivation.
But – keep an eye on devs. They clearly have a potential, and may figure out how to use it next time.

While I was initially very keen on this game, it just falls short on too many points. For all it has a great atmosphere and really great artwork, it keeps hitting snags as it continues.
• For all John's VA is great at what he does, he spends a lot of time talking with Ti'ah, who is one of the worst I've heard in a long time. As in it sounds like the deadlines were looming, so they just called through to the front desk and got their secretary to read the lines over the phone.
• The atmosphere is really intense, which gets the game a lot of points. That is, until the game stoops to jump scares, and not even good ones; it's bad enough when the game makes loud noises to startle you, but requiring the player to inspect something just so a human scream can be blasted isn't scary, it's just annoying.
• While the scenery is great, the animation leaves a lot to be desired, especially given the player character moves in very awkward paths at times and clips into the scenery on occasion.
• When I saw other reviews complaining about copying Dead Space, I assumed they were mere exaggerations. Having your protagonist narrowly survive a tram crash, then have one of its hanging cars full of debris almost crush your protagonist, is something very specific that happens in Dead Space 2, to the point it feels like mild plagiarism.
• The writing is bad at times, but it is atrocious when you can't even skip it. Making your player sit through a terrible bedtime song for a child (sung really badly to boot) is never a good idea.
• I've come across a few puzzles that are just incredibly stupid. Like one requires breaking open machinery containing corrosive fluid, so breaking it open just gets you sprayed with it and killed. The solution? Break it open then run away, because for some reason the acid doesn't spray out for about a second (i.e. the exact way that any fluid
behave).
All in all, the best ideas in the world are wasted if they're not executed correctly. It tries, but this just isn't a good game; not to point fingers, but a lot of people in the opening credits have the same surname, so maybe this is just plain and simple nepotism at work. Save your money: even though I got it on sale, I'm admittedly disappointed I kept giving it chances as I can't claim a refund.

Even though the metascore is quite "low" and while I haven't heard anything about the game before, the game itself looked like it could be enjoyable for me. Kind of like a supernatural-thriller-movie with a few methods to interactively find the culprit behind everything. And it was almost exactly as I thought it'd be.

While you get to walk through walls/doors/cars/... in Salem to investigate the death of many young girls - and most importantly your own death - you find piece after piece to finally solve the puzzle.
The story itself starts where most others end: You are a detective getting killed while investigating a murder case. The difference here is that you're not dead-dead but rather "live" on as a ghost to find the meaning behind your death so you can get to heaven (or whatever there is...). Soon you get help of a young medium who's part of the whole case and also searching for her mother (in the end she mostly just makes it possible for you to pick things up / move things / open doors / ...).
The whole game is divided into several different "chapters" where you get from one part of town to another and investigate the place to find more clues. The game mechanics consist of recognizing sounds, answering questions with photos & connected sentences, manipulating people to tell you their "secrets" and hiding from demons / destroying them.
Also there's quite a huge chunk of stuff you can collect to get info about other case which have absolutely nothing to do with the main plot. Even though they are certainly interesting, it would probably take a lot of time to find every single one of those as many are hidden pretty well. I was often missing one part of a "story" and couldn't get myself to keep on searching another 20 minutes.
Even though it definitely isn't one of the best games I ever played, it certainly has it's own unique touch. I really enjoyed playing through the main quests and solving the case (although the final plot twist wasn't that surprising in the end) and would definitely recommend trying it out (at least the demo if there is one) to see if the game fits your taste.
Just keep in mind: It's not the mechanics/gameplay that make the game enjoyable but rather the thrilling story and the way it's told.

For those who played Euro Truck Simulator 2 will find American Truck Simulator quite familiar. The systems, mechanics, even graphics are almost the same, except this time we'll be driving through the good ol' U S of A.
Though much of the game is similar if not the same as Euro Truck Simulator, there are a few key changes. There is now 2 drop off options, easy and hard, hard giving you more XP, new traffic laws to follow, and the map is smaller. The additional drop off mechanics, as in the easy drop off, is a great alternative to the previously "skip" option. A welcomed addition for the more casual player. The new traffic laws will definitely confuse some European players but will be very familiar for North American players. Then there's the smaller map. Though the game is titled "American Truck Simulator" not all of the USA is open. Currently there are only 2 states to drive around in. California, and Nevada. The content is less than it's predecessor for the reason, but an interested side effect of this is that you'll be driving through more cities and towns than in Euro Truck Simulator 2. Since you'll be driving through towns and cities more often, the driving is a little more interesting, as there's less long stretches of highways, and the visuals are also more interesting since we'll be taking in the hustle and bustle of an active city, rather than staring at wilderness for long periods. The smaller map has both negative and positive elements to it.
For those who haven't played a Truck Simulator game the premise is simple. You get full control of your truck, the head lights, to it's wipers, to it's emergency lights, and everything else you would expect from a simulation game. The amount of control you have over your truck is extremely detailed. But other than driving trucks, there is also a career component as well, where you'll be buying new trucks, hiring employees to drive said trucks, and expand your trucking empire.
American Truck Simulator may not be for everyone. It is a simulation before anything else, and there's no explosions, or other frills. It's just driving trucks. That's it's focus and that's what you'll be doing... a lot. But even if that doesn't sound appealing to you I still would recommend it. The immersion is very high in the game, it's very relaxing to play, and it's surprisingly challenging. Not just because driving a big rig is harder than it looks, but because following traffic laws and being aware of potential dangers can offer it's own set of challenges.
Overall American Truck Simulator is a fantastic game that hits all the right notes. Though it's almost a carbon copy of Euro Truck Simulator 2, the new location itself makes it worth it in my opinion.
Pros:
- More towns and cities to drive through
- Incredibly immersive
- Accurate portrayal of it's locations
- Casual and hardcore friendly
Cons:
- Smaller map & less content overall than Euro Truck Simulator 2
- Very slow progression system

This game falls in the motto "oldie but goodie". It is a surprisingly fun game, that can make you waste hours!
The graphics aren't awesome for today's standard, it can't be compared to some AAA titles like Need For Speed, but yet, they are very good.
Don't think it is an easy game: it isn't. It requires you to acquire some skills and it is nothing like any other racing game. It is more "arcady" than a simulator. The physics of the game aren't exactly scientific, but they are meant to entertain and make you laugh, and it succeds at that, as long as you approach this game with some sense of humour.
There is a car upgrade system in the game, and it's up to you to figure out what upgrades are and aren't relevant. Most of them aren't. It is important to only get the upgrades that will give you an advantage over the AI cars (which are very good, BTW).
All in all, Flatout is still a very fun game. It is possible what other games like GRID 2 tried to achieve but never quite got it.

This is a good example of a game that just doesn't know what it wants to be; the racing aspects of it actively contradict the demolition aspects, making it downright painful to play at times. All of the modes offered each somehow find a way to sap all of the fun out of flinging yourself from a moving vehicle.
The cars and terrain look decent enough for 2004; I'd even go as far as to say the damage effects look good. The skybox texture and the background look like they came out of the '90s, however. There is an issue with models and textures not covering the full extent of their physics, creating invisible walls or bits of physics objects. The UI is abominable and after extended play it can begin warping itself around the world; it's difficult to explain, but it appears that physics are applied to the UI and it can glitch out, causing display issues.
The sound effects, particularly the car sounds, seem very budget and hollow, as if they were recorded on a $20 tape recorder from the 80's. The soundtrack itself though, is actually pretty good; most of the tracks fit the game well enough.
Your driver seems only too eager to launch himself through the windshield at the slightest brush from a sapling. Sure, it's funny the first couple of times, but when it gets right down to it, this game's poor physics and driver launching feature get in the way of both racing and, to a slightly lesser extent, the "Bonus" modes (which include a counterintuitive demolition derby in which you keep your car from getting smashed, and things like darts and bowling which utilize your driver being launched from the vehicle). The vehicle customization is scant and performance options are as vague as those of the
games of the era.
The main selling point of FlatOut proves to be little more than a tacked on gimmick to what is ultimately an average racer that seems to have assigned itself the task of trying to make losing funner
easier. If that sounds appealing to you then by all means go for it, otherwise, skip it.

As a PC port, Liberation HD is actually well done. The game works very well with the controller, plays just fine with the keyboard and mouse, and the graphics are actually HD! Be warned though: Some people have reported having trouble with the anti aliasing, myself included (though my issue was minor); others claim to have performance issues.
The thing that separates Liberation HD from the other Assassin's Creed PC games, gameplay wise, is the persona mechanic. You are able to switch between disguises: Assassin, noble and slave. You have different properties/abilities and wanted levels while wearing each of those different disguises, which gives us a nice break from the usual gameplay (from AC 1 - 2.3) that was becoming stale.
Final verdict: Worth it!

Disclaimer:  UnderRail is not a 'spiritual' Fallout sequel, is
like the original Fallout franchise, and (while a good game) can't hold a candle to either of the original Fallout titles.  Don't let the 'member berries of other reviewers talk you in to picking this up solely for nostalgia's sake.  Both Fallout and UnderRail are turn-based post-apocalyptic RPG's, but that is where the similarities end.
---------------------------------------------
UnderRail is a good (not great) game, and a worthwhile purchase - especially at (or below) the current sale price of $7.49.  As is my habit, I'm going to skip giving you the "pros" (because the reviews are canvassed with 'em), and just provide folks with the bad (and often infuriating) "cons" of UnderRail. Straight to it:
---------------------------------------------
All that said, I am still happy with my purchase, and my playtime.  Like any other turn-based RPG, you can take UnderRail at your own pace.  That means you have as much time as you need to adjust to the steep curve, and get a good handle on it.  And it's worth it.  UnderRail is pretty, has a decently strong narrative (a bit spotty on lore, though), tons of character and atmosphere, and also has several phenomenal systems in place that allow you to create and customize a character that is truly yours.
If UnderRail were a book, it would certainly be a classic - Well worth the read, but only if you're prepared to deal with being slowed down by antiquated structure and the creators assumptions on what knowledge and understanding you're equipped with prior to sitting down at the table.
For those of you looking for a similar, but more contemporary, experience; I can't recommend
enough, although I would definitely advise most people to wait on a sale/price drop, since $29.99 is pretty steep for a game of this type.

A bigger, a bolder and darker story than its predecessor, Mass Effect 2 is an excellent and worthy sequel.
This time round, the theme is alot more darker and doesn't shy away from more mature themes such as racism, same sex views, ethics on genetic sterilization etc. The set-pieces are also alot more intricate. Graphics are crisp and sharper. Characters are now alot more fleshed out, old friends and new acquaintances alike. (I LOVE the guy who did Mordin, they should give him some sort of award or something! )
Game system is now alot more streamlined and boring mechanics such as vehicle driving are removed. It now also feels alot more Action Shooter rather than ME1's more RPG feel, although i felt ME1 itself wasn't really an RPG lol! (This may or may not be a good thing depending on your viewpoint. I personally felt it was ok to play it like an Action Game.)
It also introduces some new mechanics such as planet scanning which although may be troublesome, could be ignored if you wished. There are some design choices which i didn't agree with tho, such as why can't i just go to a shop and buy guns and upgrade like in ME1? Why are all the upgrades hidden in some remote world or something? Doesn't make much sense.
As always, the music and voice acting are top notch in quality. The whole thing feels like a spectacular space opera and you won't want to miss a single minute of it. I cannot wait to continue on with the next game to see how it all ends.
Final Result after Suicide Mission:
50% crew dead, Only Jack and Legion Dead. Paragon. Romanced Tali (She's so cute ) Personally, im happy with this result. It just seems logical to me to have casualties in war rather then having everyone alive and giving each other flowers.

Look I have really enjoyed myself in this game and I have also been stupidly bored with it. Its one of those games that has so much cool content but its an absolute pain to reach that content. The game itself is designed to take forever, to be unforgiving and some people love it for that and don't get me wrong I see why but my issues with the game exist within some of the developers choices, balancing choices they made that render a significant portion of dinosaurs useless (even when playing on official servers - which use the 'at times' painfully slow official rates), balancing chocies that make some of the tools/armors (especially on the aberration DLC) break way too quickly, releasing paid DLC before its even out of early access, so many performance issues and just overall gameplay issues (building in this game is still so buggy).
It's not all bad though, as I said there is some really great content, cool items and abilities, amzingly fun creatures and really deep systems that allow this game to do some great things. I also have to tip my hat to the developers support of modders; making some really great mods official free DLC (primitive+, the Center, Ragnarok), finanically sponsoring a bunch of mod developers doing some intresting things (Castles, Keeps and Forts is definetly worth checking out in my opinion but only one of the numerous great mods that the developers support), mods on the steam workshop being able to be downloaded easily when logging into a server that uses those mods.
If you have a bunch of friends and don't mind grinding then sure go for it, this is a great game with a lot of fun to be had. I have had some good time, sespecially enjoyed the aberration dlc (on a private server) and some of the mods that exist for it, had a great time on an unofficial pvp ragnarok server and some not so great times on an official server. So as I said if you don't mind grinding for hours to reach a little bit of great new content or if you want to play something with friends that requires all around dedication then go for it.
I want to be clear that I am not hating on ark, its a good game but I just can't recommend it to casual players and even to players looking for a dedicated challenging long-term experience I have to say "it can be buggy".

This game is essentially a point-and-click Resident Evil adventure in space, and takes many of its cues from the Alien movies and Dead Space. Bought it on sale on a whim and enjoyed it more than I thought I would; here's my 2 cents:
Graphics: 8/10 - Solid for an indie title, but nothing that'll knock your socks off. Honourable mention for the great work done on the death animations (you're going to be doing that quite a bit)
Puzzles: 7/10 - Good logic behind them and satisfying to solve for the most part, but a few are duds that will probably leave you scratching your head.
Writing: 9/10 - The developers definitely didn't skimp on this; lots of well composed descriptions of various items/objects throughout the game world, with PDAs acting as diaries to provide background since you're essentially all alone.
Sound: 10/10 - Best designed aspect of the game, hands down. Music is rarely heard and you are almost always listening to noises from the background environment, which are quite frightening to say the least. Random voices crackling through the intercom, screams from the next hall over, something scampering through the vents, and many other gems to keep you on edge.
Atmosphere: 9/10 - Great setting. Everything fits together really nicely and results in a consistent experience throughout. I especially appreciated that the game was very light on jump-scares and focusses on using the environment/setting as a means of instilling fear. There are still a few jump-scares, but the few times they pop up are very effective.
All in all, if you're a fan of point-and-clicks and are partial towards horror, you're cheating yourself if you don't pick this up the next time it's on sale.

Stasis is a futuristic point-and-click adventure with ok puzzle elements and very good isometric graphics. What was eye popping for me was its atmosphere.
The environment in Stasis is one in which immorality, incompetence and corruption are rampant, making the harrowing events that take place in such a setting feel almost like a natural development. One could say that your character - a loving and empathetic family man - is the true alien.
Thematically, Stasis manages to head nod many sci-fi and survival horror references. Keeping score of the references to "Aliens" specifically was part of the metagame for me. There were also echoes of games like Project Firestart (C64), Dead Space, and others. Still, Stasis does succeed in developing its own style and personality.
After a while, unlocking new areas and stepping into each new screen becomes an exercise in anxiety, and also in morbid curiosity, as the reasons for finding yourself in such a hellish situation are slowly revealed. There’s an interesting contradiction between wanting to know more about the people and the environment around you, but not really wanting to soak in any more gore and mayhem. Frankly, I was a little sickened at times, but to each his own.
On the downside, I thought puzzles were a little weird relative to difficulty. Most are easy but then there are spikes of difficulty here and there.
Ultimately, the story carries the game through a satisfying overall experience, and there's enough meat around the bones (here we go :-) to motivate pretty involved discussions in the forums.

For those who played Euro Truck Simulator 2 will find American Truck Simulator quite familiar. The systems, mechanics, even graphics are almost the same, except this time we'll be driving through the good ol' U S of A.
Though much of the game is similar if not the same as Euro Truck Simulator, there are a few key changes. There is now 2 drop off options, easy and hard, hard giving you more XP, new traffic laws to follow, and the map is smaller. The additional drop off mechanics, as in the easy drop off, is a great alternative to the previously "skip" option. A welcomed addition for the more casual player. The new traffic laws will definitely confuse some European players but will be very familiar for North American players. Then there's the smaller map. Though the game is titled "American Truck Simulator" not all of the USA is open. Currently there are only 2 states to drive around in. California, and Nevada. The content is less than it's predecessor for the reason, but an interested side effect of this is that you'll be driving through more cities and towns than in Euro Truck Simulator 2. Since you'll be driving through towns and cities more often, the driving is a little more interesting, as there's less long stretches of highways, and the visuals are also more interesting since we'll be taking in the hustle and bustle of an active city, rather than staring at wilderness for long periods. The smaller map has both negative and positive elements to it.
For those who haven't played a Truck Simulator game the premise is simple. You get full control of your truck, the head lights, to it's wipers, to it's emergency lights, and everything else you would expect from a simulation game. The amount of control you have over your truck is extremely detailed. But other than driving trucks, there is also a career component as well, where you'll be buying new trucks, hiring employees to drive said trucks, and expand your trucking empire.
American Truck Simulator may not be for everyone. It is a simulation before anything else, and there's no explosions, or other frills. It's just driving trucks. That's it's focus and that's what you'll be doing... a lot. But even if that doesn't sound appealing to you I still would recommend it. The immersion is very high in the game, it's very relaxing to play, and it's surprisingly challenging. Not just because driving a big rig is harder than it looks, but because following traffic laws and being aware of potential dangers can offer it's own set of challenges.
Overall American Truck Simulator is a fantastic game that hits all the right notes. Though it's almost a carbon copy of Euro Truck Simulator 2, the new location itself makes it worth it in my opinion.
Pros:
- More towns and cities to drive through
- Incredibly immersive
- Accurate portrayal of it's locations
- Casual and hardcore friendly
Cons:
- Smaller map & less content overall than Euro Truck Simulator 2
- Very slow progression system
