It's a 7,5/10, I think it's more like this.
Why? The atmosphere is gorgeous, dark and, not really terrifying, maybe something like "disturbing".
Yeah, the game itself it's very "disturbing". A really good effort. And also a WARNING if you don't especially love tough horror scenes.
This is not Alien (the film franchise), or a sort of Silent Hill (I let you evaluate that this game is FAR more tough that any Silent Hill...), or an adventure game with "some" scenes.
This is simply Event Horizon (the film) put in a totally different (and better) story and with more, far more, tough moments!
It's pretty unique, and, for this, someone could have problem to play it.
But, as I said, it's unique.
It's like... you may have issues or comments with the setting and the story.
But it's really like a very good, pretty perfect, "genre" film.
You may not like it, but only because you don't like extreme horror films (totally acceptable).
But, it stand quite perfect, for what it WANT to be.
So, why not 9/10?
Because as the general setting and the story are pretty perfect, the game desing is not.
It don't have major issues, but failed to impress and often fail to have a logic of a sort.
You simply try to skip that part to achieve more incredible scenes and location, but, as themself, they're hardly worth of your time.
At the end, only be strongly warned that this is NOT for children ( :) )!
But, try it or buy it.
It's a dark, good (really good) interactive "novel", and unique in it's style.

I wanted to review this game from a Californian's perspective.
The game is generally on par with ETS2.  The parking is harder, but the physics and simulation, along with game play,  is about the same.  So in that respect its not much different than ETS2.  However, since we in America are so excited to get an American version of the game, I really want to comment on that part of it.  For me the cool part is to be able to base my garage in my real home town.
First, there are a lot of great landmark and local visuals that make this stand out, even in the smaller cities.  I found several local landmarks in my own home town which is fantastic.   It's much more "personalized" than ETS2 was, which is great.  You won't be disappointed in this.
However, the big let down for me is the immense mistakes on their map of California's freeway/highway system.  It's not that its off a little bit, it's just plain WRONG!  It seems that the map developers didn't try very hard to follow any real map, and made up their own freeways and routes.  There are so many mistakes it's really sad.  Takes a lot of fun out of  driving in "my back yard".
Another interesting thing is the cities that are included map, and the ones that aren't.  It's an odd collection of towns that are included, verses those left out, to be sure. You would expect the major cities to be selected, but it seems the developers have a hard time determining what the major California cities are, not to mention where they are located.  Must not have had access to Google Earth or Wikipedia I guess.
Then there is the missing geographic features for the road systems.  But I don't want to bore you with flat roads where there should be mountain ranges and passes.  Someone told me in a discussion not to expect too much, since it's a "simulator".  But I wonder what they were trying to "Simulate", since it wasn't California as I know it (at least not our major cities and road system)?  I bring this up because many people are hoping for maps of their own states.  I wouldn't get your hopes to high if this is any indication.
But, on the whole, it's a fun game,   Is it buggy?  Of course.  But I'm sure they'll improve on it.  Personally, I just hope they fix the map a little better.  It was still worth the $20 for me!

Obviously if you like ETS 2 you will enjoy this. That being said you need to realize what you are buying. At this point it is a little more than an expansion of ETS 2 with American Scenery and 2 types of trucks. I was a little annoyed by this then I realized that they intend to dole out the other trucks and scenery in expansion packs, which we will probably have to pay for. Outside of the scenery and trucks there is little that is new to this game, I realize there is only so much you can do as a truck simulator. However they have made things more difficult, by which I mean annoying. First there is no govenor on your truck, so police work as speed cameras have in the past. The speeding fines are $1000 a piece and the police are unforgiving, I have gotten a ticket for going 1mph over the posted limit. This makes it really aggravating in the beginning. At least there were signs for the cameras, but no way to know where the police are. While this game is very fun, it does have it fair share of problems. In some ways it feels a bit dated, but at the same time it holds up quite well. Which is not that surprising for a game that came out in 2005.
The controls really make and break this game. They are very floaty and extremely clunky. It basically feel like you're controlling a jetski in rough waters. When on tarmac, it feels good. You can drift around corners and speed through light curves and it feels like a great arcade racer. When you drive on snow and off-road on the other hand, you're sliding all over the place and have little to no control. Almost slowing down completely before big corners in order to handle them. And the AI cars will drift through like zen masters.
Which is another problem with this game. The AI. There's not much rubberbanding in this game. If one of the AI cars end up ahead of the pack, then their perfect path finding will leave you in the dust. You can never catch up. I had the fastest car with all upgrades, and they still sped ahead of me. This game is about crashing your opponents to get ahead, and then keep the lead. And if you crash yourself, you're forced to a 4 second slow-mo crash sequence, and when it ends you're put back quite a while. Usually last place. There's also a reset button. It works when prompted, and some other times as well. When you've been pushed off track and facing the wrong way though, it will most likely not work. You don't decide when to reset, Flatout does.
But when it all comes together (usually the tarmac tracks) this game is incredibly fun. But the other aggravations kept me from finishing this game. I beat the bronze and silver tracks, but I had to give up at the gold tracks. After resetting a track 20 times because the AI kept using the PIT maneuver to turn me the wrong way, I gave up. That's where the fun ended for me. But for the price and for the hours I put in, I can't complain. I will recommend this game, but be aware that it definitely has its shortcomings. But then again, it's also a 9 year old game.

Crusaders of the Lost Idols is currently the best ‘clicker’ game out there. It offers significantly better illusion of control than pretty much any other idle game I’m aware of without ever making you feel stressed, straining the brain cells too much, or introducing any kind of competitive element (there is no leaderboard, no clans and no pvp).
Of course, it is an idle game and your results will therefore vary depending on your tolerance for such things – Call of Duty or Civilization this is not. You’ll either like this style of relaxed micro-progression or you won’t and if you don’t Crusaders isn’t going to change your mind.
Like most other idle games, play consists of completing a run, resetting for boosts (idols), then running the game again to get a little bit further next time. This is a bit more interesting than many other idle games, however, as there are five different 'maps' to run each with half a dozen objectives of varying difficulty to complete (as well as short-term event-only maps at least monthly).
You start with a basic bench of 20 crusaders that you unlock as a run progresses. Depending on the objective between 9 and 13 of these crusaders can be added to your base formation in various ways to increase overall damage (dps), add other buffs (like heal or splash/aoe damage) or to generate more gold. More crusaders can be unlocked during frequent events.
A fair bit of the thought in this game is about tinkering with your formation to squeeze an extra few percent out of things, one way or another. In practice, however, the boosts gained are pretty marginal as your damage is multiplied fourfold every 4-5 zones anyway. It’s an idle game, after all, don’t expect it to burst any brain cells.
One of the particularly nice things about the game is the built in chat server. 99% of the players are really chill and helpful – it’s a lovely community – and that certainly helps to pass the time while watching the ridiculous numbers spiral up into unpronounceable multiples of infinity. (You can, however, turn the chat window off if you find that kind of thing distracting.)
The devs are extremely active, with new events at least every month, new crusaders to mix up your formation, and the occasional addition of new objectives and achievements to aim for. They also pop into chat regularly to discuss the game and are enthusiastic and approachable.
There’s been plenty enough content added already to have maintained my interest for five months straight, with more additions regularly being added – none of these are particularly onerous or complex and all of which are well integrated into the game’s basic systems (unlike, say, the tacked-on additions of some other clicker games, such as Clicker Heroes).
The game’s free to play income model is pretty reasonable. There is the option to buy additional chests for a chance at gear to increase the stats on crusaders (these chests also drop normally during play).
Additionally, every event there is also a ‘free’ ‘golden epic’ awarded for buying three chests ($4.99), and these are typically a little overpowered in one way or another.
Regular players generally see the occasional purchase as a nice way to throw a couple of bucks at the developers, although if you are a collect-the-lot type who is a little cash-strapped you might resent the implied pressure to buy so that you don't 'miss out'. The best any gear can do, however, is help you to get 3-4 zones further before hitting a wall and needing to reset.
It’s not a pay to win model in my view because, well, there’s no actual winning nor is there any direct player vs player interaction. The only ‘win’ to be had here is something to boast about in the in-game chat. But seriously, the developers have to make some cash to fund development and in the scheme of things this is pretty mild.

If you enjoyed the gameplay style of the original Fallouts 1 & 2, and like games set in the post apocalypse, I recommend checking this game out. Underrail is not just the same old mechanics with a new story. Although the overall gameplay is similar to the original Fallouts there are a few features that make Underrail stand out.
In addition to conventional weaponry your character can gain psionic abilities, and some of your enemies will be using them against you as well. Oh yes, they certainly will, and a lot of those will be bugs. I hate it when *insects* give me a mental thrashing ... how degrading.
There's a detailed crafting system for making, recycling, and rebuilding weapons/tools/items; as well as crafting medical supplies, buffs, and poisons. There are five skills that govern crafting, and you'll need levels for harvesting some componants as well as for making stuff. Which skill will depend on whether you are doing Mechanical, Electrical, Chemical, Organic, or Tailoring work.
Underrail has an interesting way of gaining experience for leveling your characters. In Fallout and  similar games you generally gain XP by killing beasties, completing quests, and/or using your skills. In Underrail this is called "Classic mode" and is not how the game is meant to be played. Instead there's "Oddity mode" where you gain XP only by either completing quests, or finding Oddities. Oddities are objects in the world that you find either in random containers or occasionally on the corpses of fallen enemies. (Perhaps in the pockets of live people, but I've yet to pick pocket anyone.) You can choose which of these modes you want to play with at the beginning of a new game.
During Early Access I only played in Classic mode 'cause that was what I was used to and wanted to wait until final release to delve into the Oddities. I thought it worked well and that my character gained levels and abilites at about the pace I would expect if I were playing a similar game. Since the official release I've been playing only with Oddities mode.
There's been more than once where I've gotten to a spot where the enemies were kicking my butt and thought, "Let me just go do some grinding and come back to you ... oh wait, I can't get XP that way ...." so it's either get by with what I've got or actually work on side quests to do some leveling and not just grinding peon creatures. This has caused me to sometimes take a stealthier approach than I normally would have and leave some enemies still alive that I would have otherwise just prefered to clear out.
With the Oddities mode I find leveling to be slower than what I'd see in other games, but not game breakingly so. It has made some things more difficult, but not impossible to get through. Instead of XP gain being something I just take for granted in the course of fighting my way through the world, the Oddities system makes me take more notice of when I'm gaining XP and how I'm going to go about getting more. And because of the effort in finding Oddities I'm more likely to read the lore in the description instead of glossing over it and moving on.
The only complaint I have about this game is also a complaint that I have with the original Fallouts ... you can't rotate the camera view. Fortunately there's a key binding to highlight interactable objects/enemies that may be obstructed from view by the walls and camera angle. Enemies only highlight if they are currently in the character's field of view.
One thing I really like that the devs put into the game is being able to get into the air ducts of buildings. Useful in general for getting around cave ins and sneaking around the enemy's attention as you'd expect, but sometimes they also help you get into locked areas you might not have skills to get past the doors to get into. While you are in the airducts you can peek into rooms/hallways to see if there are enemies about before getting out. Opening vents to get into the ducts uses your Lockpicking skill and requires it's own kind of tool instead of lockpicks. Do not expect the air ducts to be empty of hostiles, but their teeth and claws may be easier to deal with than the enemies that you're trying to sneak around.
Lastly, from the start of the game you have your own room with storage containers. Bonus, you have a keycard and can lock the door to the room.

Have you ever wanted to play a psychological horror game, but was too much of a damned ♥♥♥♥♥ to *actually* play the game? You want to experience the macabre and grotesque ambience of death and gore... but, like, without the constantly present anxiety-inducing knowledge that there might be a jump scare around the next corner? Then, this is the game for you!
I know when I'm playing games like Dead Space, Outlast, or The Evil Within, I'm too amped up on adrenaline to fully take in the atmosphere and enjoy the game.
First, the cons:
- Voice acting was meh. The protag's voice was the only one that sounded even remotely non-robotic and realistic.
- Glitches clearly have not been completely ironed out.
- There are a few puzzles that don't follow any logical sense. I was hard-pressed to peruse a walkthrough to figure out at least two of the puzzles.
- For many people, point-and-click games don't constitute as bona fide video games... so there's that. Unless this is your cup of tea, you're most likely going to be bored with the fact you can't really kill monsters.
The pros!
- Lots of dead bodies and haunting commentary on dead bodies.
- But seriously, there are dead bodies EVERYWHERE. It's AWESOME. It's like a veritable Edgar Allen Poe novel all up in here.
- Descriptive, polished prose.
- Few jump scares, LOTS of creepy atmosphere that is reminiscent of the classic Silent Hill games
- Horror game through and through. Plenty of fridge logic at play.
- Exploration was actually fun.
Thumbs up, overall the game is an 8/10.

First of all, if you're looking for something unique to play that doesn't involve zombies or first-person shooting, then this should be right up your alley. Sure Murdered: Soul Suspect has it's flaws, but otherwise it's definitely an interesting murder-mystery with a side of ghosts and demons.
The things that I liked:
The graphics and voice acting was very good, better than some of the more well-known games. All of the characters had distinguishing features like freckles and blemishes. It was easier to care about the characters when they don't all have the same wooden faces when afraid.
The story itself was interesting, maybe a little predictable at times, but there are still a few twists at the end. Investigating the crime scenes reminded me of L.A. Noire, and some of the puzzles were a little tricky, but nothing that couldn't be solved through trial and error. I also like the open world and how I could explore without automatically being pushed into the next misson.
Now the things I didn't care for:
As many people have stated, the saving system is one of the things that bring down this game. You can only have one save file, and there isn't anyway to backtrack to a previous chapter or mission. Even though it warns you at the end that you can't return to Salem, I feel like I should've gotten a warning at the museum since you can't go back for any missed artifacts. I might have been able to forgive this , if I was able to go back to a previous save. So really if you missed anything at the museum or Judgement House, you're out of luck. While I enjoyed Murdered, it didn't really have much replay value. Even though I wanted the artifacts and achievements, I didn't feel compelled to play again.
I also have to agree that the demons are repetitive and somewhat tedious. While it was a good idea, the execution wasn't so good. They were more of a hindrance than a threat. The button pressing to destroy them can be awkward, and is one of the reasons why I died so much. Along those same lines, getting artifacts can also be awkward, as I found one clue, but I had to walk around it for five minutes, finding the perfect angle before I could pick it up.
Overall, I enjoyed this game, and would recommend it. Yes, it is rather short, but still takes up some of your time. Even though I wished I wished I had waited until it was on sale, I don't regret buying this.

The appeal of Recettear is not immediately obvious. Gameplay which is a lite mesh of dungeon crawl and economic sim, limited and cutesy graphics, irritating sound with untranslated voiceovers… However, it is definitely a case of the sum being greater than the parts.
It is certainly a game which you can jump straight into – well, once you figure out how to get past the menu. For keyboard users, the select button is not obvious (for the record, it's 'z', which was only discovered after a minute of keyboard mashing…). There is regular and in-context help through the game which establishes the basics. Success, however, requires a lot of experimentation and awareness of what works.
Some parts of the game feel a bit like a cross between Majesty and Diablo. While you control them directly in the dungeon, they buy equipment and make themselves available at their own initiative. It's quite possible to go through the main storyline with several adventurers never becoming available. Also, while you can loan them items, this takes valuable loot space. It's much better to sell to them, but since that's something you can't control, it takes a lot of manipulation (or luck) to get them properly equipped.
The game's key storyline – paying off a debt weekly through profits from the item shop – lends purpose to the gameplay without completely restricting it. Indeed, the tight time limits provide much of the game's fun and challenge. Choosing to go for a last-ditch dungeon run to pick up high-priced items and risking not having enough time to sell them and make up the debt is just one example of the agonising strategic decisions to be made.
Indeed, weighing up choices is a big part of the game. Stick with an expensive and high-levelled adventurer who can work the tougher dungeons or sacrifice the bigger rewards to build up another who may prove to be more powerful in the long run? Sell a useful item to an adventurer at a discount, or get every possible bit of money from a non-adventurer? Attract a certain type of customer with a dark store, or keep things light and draw another? Sacrifice several items to forge one? For what looks like a very slimmed-down mesh of two types of game, it presents a lot of challenges.
Though failure is very possible, especially on a first run, it's possible to carry on with some of the assets you have collected. This makes the next attempt easier, eliminating a potential frustration.
The writing is generally good, with some entertaining, and occasionally quite heart-warming, dialogue. The setting is interesting enough, though there is not that much to learn about it. Bring on a sequel! Sound is probably the least impressive aspect, and it gets downright annoying in dungeons. Switch it off and put on your own music.

Space Pirates and Zmbies is a top down space shoot em up. Having not completed anything other than easy or medium, try not taking this review into account for the harder difficulty settings.
The game itself starts off slow when you are given the worst of the worst ships named the Short Bus. This thing's beam cannot kill pretty much anything. But new and better ships start coming along very soon with the player going from the worst laser ever to lasers and cannons. (For the cannon think of a rifle in those games where you can hold down the trigger or whatever, where it shoots at a moderate speed.)
Even though the guns get better some poeple may still think of them as utter crap as the better stuff comes in much later.
Also new players may find the shooting with both lasers and cannons very frustrating and have the A.I do most of the work.
The game also features 3 resources. rez, goons and data.  Rez a brightly coloured space rock that doubles as the currency of the game  as well as the raw resource that you build your ships with. The game does a very good job of allowing you to collect rez and not loose it. The enemy ships, you will be fighting, nearly always drop a nice chunk of rez for you to loot whereas your ships deposit your supllies of rez into a large pool that you (mostly) cannot lose.
The next resource is goons. Goons are workers/slaves/mercenaries that you pick up in escape pods floating around in space. Picking them up ads them to your goon pool much like your rez pool. Unlike rez, goons are used to keep your ship in tip top shape once it is flying, rather then build it. The amount of goons that join you when you pick them up depends on your crew skill.
Your crew skill is an indication of how well you keep oder/how much they like you. At first this skill will be very low, level zero in fact. At this low level most of the crew get thrown out of the air lock of your ships instead of being crewed. This could be a bit frustrating as 6 crew can suddenly turn into 3 crew as half are chucked out the air lock for being troble makers.
But there is usally so many crew pods, you rarely have this problem.
Then there's the last resource data. Data are little bits of trashed computer parts and what not, scattered about the place after you trash a bunch of your foes. Data is unique in the fact that it can generate itself as well as goons.  Every time you collect a certain amount of data, starting at about 100 (eazy to do as you collect it in tens at a time) you clone a certain amount of your current goons into new ones.
Data also allows you to progress along a tech tree of sorts as each time you level up you gain 3 points to spend. The points can be spent in things such as shields thrusters or drones. Each certain amount of points you put into a certain category upgrades it a bit. And with the best weapons upgraded to the full level (10) or even a little below it (8) you can blast and melt your way through whatever even looks at you funny without a care.
Next up(ALERT! ALERT! SPOILERS INCOMING!)
Zombies. Zombies come into the game at a very late point which is a bit weird considering the game is called space pirates and zombies. They can be a bit of a pain if faced without the right equipment, for example without a point defence system (a little red cricle that shoots a red laser at incoming zombies and missiles) they can swarm your ship, take down its sheilds, kill its crew and infect it, turning what was once your best ship, against you. Another slightly annoying thing they do, is spawn the very tiny ships called ticks that, once injured enough, will fly faster then you can to the edge of the screen causing you to retreat back to your mother ship and then warp to a new place, rather than just warping, as you cannot warp when there are enemies nearby.
2nd last on this reveiw is bounty hunters. Bounty hunters can be a HUGE pain in the backside as they track whoever you kill, causing your bounty to rack up. Once this bounty is high enough it will cause the bounty hunters to come after you for that sweet bounty on your head. If not prepared properly these guys can wreck you and your ships pretty fast. That's why I recommend for any new players to turn them down to low in the starting settings. This will make sure you are not getting smoked by them every time you warp to a new sector, but also allow you to find out what they are like and how they work.
Lastly are space stations. Space stations are big shielded things that stay in one place. But be careful who you anger in this game. As flying to a space station, when either it is to high a level for you or you are to low a level for it, can leave you with no rez or ships if it blows them all up. Also a tip for a mid level mission, in which I got stuck on for a while, where you have to shoot a space station untill it gives up its reactor for you. My tip is if you can't beat it at first just grind a bit of low level stuff first. Trust me, at first it may be boring but it defenitly is worth it when you beat the station and move on to the better parts of the game.
Well, that just about wraps up this review and my few last words are: A good game for most poeple, but better if you're patient and don't mind a bit of a grind.

Deadfall Adventures captures that 'Indiana Jones' feel that seems lacking in modern adventure games.  Throughout, I felt immersed in the environments and gameplay.  It's a fun experience overall and there are many moments that will make you feel like a true adventurer!
The story is quite predictable but that's something you want from a game like this, in a way.  Knowing what's about to happen not only allows one to focus more on the gameplay but it adds to the movie-like feel presented through the game.  Everything presented has a real feel for the most part.  A game like this can't afford to dip out of that realistic feel for very long because in the moments it did, it sometimes felt more like a saturday-morning cartoon more than an adventure movie.
Deadfall's shooting mechanics work well and the nuance of using the flashlight to make certain enemies vulnerable adds tension to fights that might feel tame otherwise.  Most of the time, one will duel wield pistols but while using the flashlight, one is restricted to a single handgun.  This allows for two very different styles of fighting which I greatly enjoyed.
The puzzles can be a bit of a mixed bag.  There is a fine line between challenging and unreasonable.  While most puzzles are are doable with a little time, there are a few that may stymy the player because the solution is unobvious and the hints provided are too vague.  It was helpful for me to use an online walkthrough for the more frustrating moments.  That said, I applaud the inclusion of puzzles like these because they can be the difference between a true adventure game and a generic shooter.
Environments in Deadfall Adventures are visceral and diverse.  The level in the jungle is a real stand out as the path winds through and each set piece is presented.
An unfortunate issue for this game is the frequency of small bugs.  Sometimes, events won't trigger properly.  A few times, I had to reload previous checkpoints because of issues such as this.
Overall, Deadfall Adventures gets my tentative reccomendation.  It's an enjoyable game with a unique experience.   The only caveats being the bugs and the possible necessity of using a walthrough.  If you're looking for a fun adventure game with challenging puzzles and immersive gameplay though, this is definitely something worth your time.

SPAZ, where to begin with this game?
It is fun, perhaps not as intuitive as could be, interactive, perhaps sometimes montonous, especially on the first play-through when 'rez' farming becomes a regular occurence as countless little ships of yours get blasted into the dark abyss of space. It's design features and artistic styling leaves little to be desired; there truly is something for everything in this game! The faction system appears bleak, with the UTA, CIV, and Bounty Hunters not being fully exploited to their potential; the game uses the excuse that different star-systems don't communicate, and as such your reputation is reset to a set level in each system, a much better idea could be to have an option of this, but also a ranking system within a faction. Right now 'respect' is the only obtainable quantity with a faction (BH), and even that has miniscule effects on the game.
The personalised feel to the game is something that draws you in and, more importantly, makes you want to stay. This game is so engaging, I can see myself losing countless more hours to it! I highly recommend this game, and though the £6.99 price tag may at first appear quite steep, believe me, the hours of fun you will get out of this game makes it all worthwhile.

I had a good 6 hours playing this game, and it delivered mostly on the expectations I had coming in. You start small, and sooner or later depending on the choices you take; you get bigger and bigger over time. I thought it would be more harsh or difficult to get big, but it actually wasn't that hard. However progressing through the different stages of your YT career felt satisfying and fun for me.
As for specific downsides; it gets repetitive, and quite fast actually. I played for about 6 hours, but it was getting repetitive before this point, and yeah I do have good patience for these kind of things (abnormal really). I would also like to point out the lack of diverse dialogue in general (talking to friends, comments on your videos etc). Even the dialogue with your closest ones was just the same over and over, and so you get to a point where you just click and don't even read anything anymore.
I missed having some kind of personalized direction on your channel as you grow, and how you would stand out from other channels. I mean the only real difference here was the category right? The last thing I would point out is that there was a lack of explanation when you joined a network, and how you could achieve the different goals. Some goals for the higher networks weren't even explained to me which eventually led me to getting banned. Maybe it was intended to be that way?
In conclusion gets repetitive but I would still recommend this game to anyone who likes SIM games, and/or wants to kill off a couple of hours.

The rest of the game looks amazing, and I love the fantasy, but even those moments are marred by the juvenile script and writing.
How could this be better? Add quicksaves, redo/remove all cutscenes, and go through and fix all the level geometry. You'd then have an recommendable game. It still wouldnt be great though.
How to move it into great? My view is remove the arcade fights (which are at best forgettable), and go for more simulated gritty survival horror combat (think Dark Corners of the Earth) - I think at this point Deadfall Adventures would be quite special.

The settings are well crafted and beautifuly displayed; each viewpoint feels unique making every climb feel different from the last. The game also loads quickly taking you straight into the action. The story develops seamlessly as it takes you into the mission area and lets you take control, the only thing slowing you down being the occasional mandatory changing of clothes before proceeding. Avelin takes up one of three personas: The lady, The Slave and the Assassin each having unique abilities. Overall this is a great installment to the Assassin's Creed series and if you missed out on this title on the PS Vita then this is a good buy.

There's enough good stuff here that I'm interested to see what these guys do in the future, but I don't recommend this one.  A lot of annoying issues that added up over time:
-- It is very dark in almost every room even on 100% gamma setting, so dark that I usually ended up clicking randomly in a new room just so I could notice my guy moving and figure out where I was.
-- There's no item highlighting, which results in occasional pixel hunting.  Pixel hunting is made worse by inconsistency in the indication of what you can interact with.  Most things you get a response to when you mouse over them have an eyeball, meaning you can get a description but usually no interaction. Hand icon means interaction.  But sometimes the eyeball things can actually be interacted with if you use a specific item.
-- The geometry can be a mess.  Lots of inacessible looking areas in varous rooms that are in fact inaccessible but some randomly aren't.  I got stuck in one area for 20 minutes before checking a walkthrough because an area with a bunch of inaccessible platforms had one that somehow was accessible via a ladder you can't see, and there was a room off of that area needed to progress in the area.
-- Pseudo cut scenes with scripted voice interactions can't be skipped.  Sometimes you die and get pulled back to a save before a lengthy dialog you can't skip.  Super dark rooms + instant death + unskippable dialog eventually convinced me to give up and stop playing the game.  There's one super dark room I walked into and died in a few seconds.  I could hardly see anything as usual, and didn't understand what killed me or how to avoid it.  Rewind to listen to a few minutes of unskippable dialog.  Walk back in, die in a few seconds, repeat.  Repeat.  Repeat.
-- The joke achievements were a bad idea.  One achievement for stupidly killing yourself, okay maybe.  The majority of the achievements for that?  It was making me deliberately play the game like an idiot, trying to find stupid ways to kill myself.  That's not fun.
-- There are some really senseless puzzles with bad cases of "adventure game logic."  The developers apparently realized how silly some of these were and inserted in game hints in scribbles off to the sides of various PDA's you pick up.  There's no reason to notice the scribbling usually and no reason whatsoever for the people who owned these PDA's to have doodled puzzle hints on the sides of their PDA's for puzzles they couldn't have known about.

I have no idea why this game gets so many good reviews, this is a walking simulator with cheap shock effects and frustrating gameplay. Don't buy.
You are awaken from stasis on a spaceship without any recollection how you got there. It soon becomes obvious that the ship is not in working order. After not too long you are contacted by a mysterious woman via radio who offers to help you. While you make your way through the ship you uncover what went down there. Turns out, the immoral experiments of an evil corporation went horribly wrong.
All of this is pretty much apparent right from the start. You fill in more details as you progress but there are no surprises. The only redeeming aspect are the PDAs you find which give you insights into the lifes of some of the people whose bodyparts you see laying around everywhere.
The game is in isometric perspective. Your character runs to where you point your mouse and you enter new rooms by clicking on exits. You get descriptions of items by hovering over them (as text at the bottom of the screen; your cursor changes into an eye symbol) and if there is anything you can interact with, the cursor changes into a hand. So far, so good.
Did I say the cursor changes into a hand if you can interact with it? Yes, most of the time, but not always. Sometimes you have to randomly combine stuff from your inventory with eye symbols to make something happen. Sometimes you even have to click stuff twice (in one case thrice) to get an effect. This all is made worse by the fact that the hotspot areas are sometimes really small, so you have to pixel hunt. There is no way to actually
what you are supposed to click because everything is so damn small in this perspective.
All of this makes the puzzles in this game incredibly frustrating because even though they are mostly logical in hindsight, you often don't get any indication what you are supposed to do and you end up randomly clicking stuff. So, it is probably a good thing that there aren't that many puzzles.
There are also a few instances where you enter a room and have to react quickly in the correct way or you die. If you have to make me die over and over again while I figure out what to do at least don't make me watch the same lengthy starting animation each time, thank you very much.
I'm not an achievement hunter and I'm usually not all that interested what the achievements are. But in this game, the achievements give you a good indication what this game really is about.
Of 27 achievements, roughly one third is story related. The rest are for different ways in which you can die in this game. You can even commit suicide in various gruesome ways, shown to you by a kill cam.
Yes, that's right. You can, for example, watch yourself drill a hole in your head or gut yourself with a glass shard.
The developers apparently expect you to make a game out of trying to kill your character in as many ways as possible. YMMV, but that's not my kind of fun and it doesn't make up for the lack of real puzzles.
There are no graphic options beyond two settings for screen resolution, that's it. On highest resolution on a 19'' screen, everything was slightly blurry. If you could zoom in to specific areas, or if there were at least a hotspot viewer this wouldn't be too bad but as it is the need to pixel hunt is probably my main gripe with this game.
Regarding the overall look, I liked the design of the ship and the different areas. Unfortunately, the developers followed the mantra that there can never be enough blood and guts. Basically every surface in this game is coated in some kind of human-derived organic matter. It is a bit ridiculous.
There's not much voice acting but what's there is decent. There are a lot of ambient noises and screaming that create an atmosphere of looming danger, at least at first. As with the blood, the developers overdid it. If you constantly hear screaming at some point it stops being frightening and becomes background.
As much fun as drilling a hole in your head.

Ok. I admit, I don't like adventure games. I often get stuck and have to resort to reading walkthroughs. I can bear this as long as there's any promise of a good story. And what a major letdown the story in STASIS is. It starts off ok-ish as you know nothing, everything is a mystery and the atmosphere created by visuals and sound do all the heavy lifting, and successfully so. But it quickly unravels and it's just a cliché-driven story with no unpredictable twist whatsoever.
It's a horror so... flickering lights, distant shouts and creaky noises all for no reason? Check.
Saving wife and daughter? Check.
Amnesia? Check.
Evil corporation? Check.
Grotesquely stupid levels of negligence? Check.
Moustache twirling mad scientist villain? Check.
Radio companion betraying you at the end? Check.
Immoral human experimentation gone wrong? Check.
At least some logs contain stories that are more nuanced.
Don't get me wrong. I'm not saying any piece of art should contain no cliché or trope whatsoever. No. I know it's hard and often counterproductive trying to be 100% new and original. But combination of all of the above? That's unbearable.

A really well designed point and click will give you hints on how to progress, but many times in this game you can be seen to interact with an object but nothing happens and your character never mentions why it didn't work.
All that said. I still recomend Stasis. Mostly because I liked the setting and the storyline. It might not be the most original and it borrows heavy from pretty much all sci-fi horror genres, but it's effective, gory, dark and disturbing. It's well paced and even manage to have a few effective jump scares in a point and click adventure. The storylines of the inhabitants of the ship before all went to hell that you read about in the text logs flesh out the backstory and help you figure out just what happend. The sound design is great, with a ton of the usual weird mechanical sounds, screams, wails and so on, that you expect from the setting.
The puzzle design is pretty ok (the above mentioned problems aside). It's not really hard since you usually have a fairly limited area and items to move around and interact with in each area, and when you move on there is little to no backtracking. Had it been much more open ended it probably would have bothered me more, as it stands it's about 7 hours long.
It's a fairly strong recomendation if you like sci-fi horror and/or point and click adventures. But be warned, it do get quite dark.

On a scale of 1-10, I would rate this game as a 6. I understand the limitations of the graphics engine and they cannot detail out every city in its entirety. That being said, This game severly fails to capture the complexities or even the scale of the california highway systems, and the scale of the cities. I wish we had this much open land as portrayed in the game. For example from San diego to Carlsbad, There is very little open land or a point you dont see a building.  Overall however, I do think they managed to capture the spirit of america in the game.
Several issues I hope the devs hear and take notes on.
1.) STOP signs should only be at intersections and directions that are NOT guarded by a light system. Most intersections in "San Diego" have a stop sign AND a traffic light. Very confusing. Do you stop, or do you go on the green?
2.) Offramps for highways have Broad Dashed stripes a ways before the off ramp to denote that lane must exit.
3.) On ramps need to be a bit longer, 90% of the on ramps here In San Diego (yes, I have lived here all my life) are longer than in game. Basically, they need to come down the hill or what not and run with traffic a little bit fore they just suddenly end to force the merge. Now, there ARE a couple of on ramps here in town that do that, but again, they are rare. We also do NOT have a merge lane like in Europe where vehicles stop coming down the on ramp to then merge when clear. Ive seen this a couple of times in teh game, and It caught me off guard. Why are they stopped?
4.) Please improve the AI, In several cases the AI has just randomly ran into me, or cut right out in front of me.... on second thought, thats california drivers for you. Cutting off big rigs does sadly happen and it never ends well. However, I did plow through a red sedan in a previous play session becuase an ambulance who was stopped at a light, turned on its siren and lights and then moved through the intersection. The problem was the red sedan suddenly stopped mid intersection in about 3 feet givng me no reaction time. The other problem was that the ambulance didnt appear to have its light flashing, at least, I could barely see them in the day light, and the siren was very quiet.
5.) Granted this is a game, however I have been fined at random for speeding when for most of the time, there are no speed limit signs. I was fined 1000 for going 66 in a 65 mph zone. There were no cameras, no cop cars, nor any other cars around at the time of the random fine. This fine does occure steadily near a split on the run from LA to El Centro.
6.) The horn... omg.... wtf is that... It sounds more like a telegraph machine than a clasic big rig horn.... Seriously, try blasting out some moris code with it and tell me I am wrong...
7.) I have seen more classical cars in this game, than I have seen in RL. Please turn down the frequency of them. Plus all americans seem to drive are Ford mustangs with a smattering of Dodges here and there. Need to have a lot more import cars like hyundai, toyota, honda ect.
Overall, my impression of the game is good, But it definately needs a lot more love. The lack of driveable trucks here at the start is disapointing. I understand the issues with licesnsing so I am hopeful we will get some more in the near future. Happy Trucking!

Let me save you the time, and let you know that while this will be a review, it is going to read as more of a rant than anything else. Understand going in that I am not going to recommend any one play this game, at all. The reasons will be detailed below, but I am writing this as a way of venting my frustrations with the game, and treating the main purpose of this as a "buyers beware" because let me tell you, I am not going to let the store page lie to you. I will get to that in a second.
That being said, Murdered Soul Suspect is the most dissapointing game of the year for me. Hands down. When it comes to expectations (what little I had asked from it in the first place) Not only did they fail miserably, they somehow managed to fail at even the BASIC expectations.  So what were my expectations? I just wanted a good mystery game. Interact with the environment/clues, piece stuff together. Learn about the mystery and basically just immerse myself as a detective. It didn't have to be a compelling narrative or anything, but for the story, I at LEAST wanted a likable main character.  I didn't EXPECT an L.A. Noire esque mystery game, and I would have even allowed a Deadly Premonition esque kind of mystery game. But this......WHAT IS THIS?
Where do I even begin with this game. I hope if you are foolish enough to read my tirade you will at least have the respect for yourself to have a snack. Buckle in boys and girls, here comes the salt.  I want to address the store page bullet points real quick. To get this out of the way now. It's a good starting point as any. I won't address them all, just the ones I object to, and you, the future buyer, deserve to know the truth of.
-"A twisting storyline supported by a great cast of characters constantly raises questions over the secrets that Salem hides."  This is cute. What great cast of characters? No. I am not being facetious, I mean what great cast of characters? Where are they? There are characters, sure, and I would have loved to learn more about them, but 75% of the cast occassionally drops in for that ol "THEY COULD BE THE KILLER" scooby doo schtick.  No in reality the game really only focuses on Ronan (main character) and Joy, his spirit medium. Every other character isn't any more developed than the last beyond fulfilling the cliche role they were intended to fulfill. There is no "constantly raising questions over the secrets that Salem hides." It's no secret. No, I want you as the reader, right now, to mentally say the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the word Salem. If you said "oh the Salem witch trials right?" then you my friend, are one smart turkey. Tadah. Oh, and there is only one main twist. I don't know where this twisting storyline business comes from. That implies it's constantly twisting.
-" Move freely from one haunting location to the next and even if you have completed your investigation, return to previous scenes to follow new leads." Sounds compelling right? By move freely they mean you are essentially in a little invisible walled off box, and boy let me tell you there are a TON of invisible walls. Yes, you can return to previous scenes, but "to follow new leads?" What on EARTH are you TALKING ABOUT? The only time you return to a previous scene is if you forgot some disposable optional collectible you wanted to collect for 100% completion that doesn't do jack for you unless you are trying to get all the achievements. None of this "new lead" bullcrap. You don't change the outcome of anything. You are merely just taking a guided tour through this game.
-"Seek-out hundreds of collectibles, side-quests and cases from Salem’s citizens past to learn facts about the town and its people, improve your detective ranking and help you piece together the truth about the killer." If there was ever a burning point I wanted to address, it's this one. This one, singular sentence on their page. It's complete false advertising. First off, while there are a COUPLE hundred (not hundreds) of collectibles, there are NOT hundreds of sidequests and cases from Salem's citizens. There are FOUR cases (not a typo) where you help out deceased citizens, and  EIGHT collectible sidequests that reveal a story of a previous murder not really tied to the main quest murders. The other collectibles that involve the main quest killer? They don't help you piece together ANYTHING about the killer other than he likes killing  and little blurbs from tabloids. How does that HELP anything? and honestly, with how poorly fleshed out and planned the characters were, you can more or less figure out who the killer is within the first 2-3 hours of gameplay.  The twist was nice, but again, you kind of expect it. The really sucky part about all this is they should have done more with the sidequests involving helping the citizens come to term with their death. But no, you get 4 quests, and the other spirits you run into, you get a two choice branch that changes nothing and it just falls flat. Or hey! hey! better yet! more of those collectible stories involving the side murders but you know, without the cheap copout collectible requirements! MAKE THOSE ACTUAL MISSIONS.  It would have been a farcry better than what we actually received.
-"Survive powerful demonic spirits who devour souls in a belief that they can regain their own. Strategically use supernatural abilities to evade and outwit them before they tear away your soul forever." HAHAHHAHA, "strategically?"  STRATEGICALLY?! Are you kidding me?! What STRATEGY? Wh-what, you mean, exploiting the terrible AI of the 3 enemies at any given moment by hiding in plain sight, waiting for them to lose aggro, then mashing a QTE prompt? Or, or, using the various distraction options available (j/king you can only distract them with one thing, a crow) and then rinsing and repeat? Get out of here with that nonsense. Stop dressing up this lazy nonsense to sound fancy. Shame on you.
Now that is out of the way, let's talk "gameplay." Well, you can basically consider this game a semi-rails game. Or, more or less, a guided tour game. You aren't actually playing the game. I mean, yes,you are controlling Ronan, and he is responding to your controls, but literally 60% of the gameplay is you collecting stuff. It's like a giant collectible scavenger hunt. When you aren't collecting things that have no rhyme or reason or impact to the game, the other 40% of the game is you "solving" crime scenes. But, YOU aren't solving SQUAT. The GAME has that covered. Look, there is no penalty for guessing wrong or deducing something wrong. All the clues are in the same room. There is no interacting with clues. Hell, the game will sometimes literally zoom in on the primary clue in a cutscene before you even start, rendering all your clue collecting pointless. AND, when you DO have all the clues collected, guess what reader? The game is like, "soooo what do you think happened" and you piece together 1-3 of the clues to "solve the scene." BUT AGAIN, there is no penalty for failing. It's as braindead as you can possibly get. My favorite moment occurs when the killer is looking at a picture, and the game asks me "Well, what do you think he is doing?" and 6+ words flood the screen and you gotta figure out what he is doing. He is clearly startled and up to no good, and literally half the options are the exact opposite of the mood being displayed. What is this, Dora the Explorer?
Agh... this game, I haven't even scratched much of the surface, there is so much I want to talk about. So much...so much rage. But I have already spent too much time talking about the game. Look, I don't like it. I think it's highway robbery they would seriously ask for $50 of YOUR HARD EARNED MONEY for this crap.
TL;DR: I  hate this game.

You are a group of mercenaries, traveling through randomly generated galaxy, gathering resources - actually there is only one main resource - "rez". You're trying to reach the galaxy core to discover the origin of "rez". That's how the story looks like, pretty simplistic, but by no means boring. SPAZ is almost completely non-linear - You can visit a lot of galaxy sectors without touching the main storyline.
Gameplay reminds me of another great game "Escape Velocity Nova". You build ships, gather resources, research new technologies, fight against 4 game factions - Civilians, UTA, Zombies and sometimes Bounty Hunters. Built-in tutorial is all You need to learn basics of SPAZ.
SPAZ features top-down 2D graphics, and I find it a big advantage - everything is nice and simple. Sounds are also good, music nicely blends into the gameplay.
To sum this up - If you're a fan of space games, at least try SPAZ - it's a true gem among the genre.
PROS:
Nice 2D graphics
Non-linear gameplay, high replayability
Easy to learn, difficult to master
RPG elements
Lots of ships to discover
CONS:
Combat can be frustrating at higher difficulties
Becomes repetitive at times

This game is really hard to recommend and not recommend, because it does so many things right, and few things wrong, but the few things it does wrong take away immensly from the experience. So, as most people do, I will go through the different aspects of the game, and giving my final verdict
Graphics
What you first see upon starting the game, and they are pretty decent. Nothing really caught my eye, but I wasn't disgusted by them. They were good. The animations were the same. Didn't catch my eye like mocap usually does, but they're still decent.
Gameplay
The gameplay is where the majority of the issues lie. The shooting is very good, the controls are very tight, and shooting the guns feels impactful. However, the problem is in the game not being clear on where I need to go and what I need to do. I had to look up multiple walkthroughs just to finish this game. And that really frustrated me. Aside from that, some very cool ideas were put into the game, like needing filters for your gas mask. It puts the player in an interesting situation; Do I look for more supplies and risk having less time later or do I keep going for more time later? However, I had a problem with this feature, since it autosaved 10 seconds before I died of suffocation (because I wasted time not knowing where to go) and I had to restart the chapter. Other than that, the gameplay was solid
Story
I didn't play the original Metro, because I didn't think I'd have to (thanks, AngryJoe) so trying to folow the story was difficult. I still don't entirely get it, but upon reflection, I'm sure I will. But, from what I did understand, the game is well written, the players have clear motives, and nothing happens for no reason. Aside from Annas attachment after being with Artyom for a total of about 5 minutes. Yeah, Anna was not well written. But, Pavel was one of my favorite characters to hate, a much better villain than Handsome Jack, since the player is given a reason of their own to hate Pavel, for putting us in a dangerous situation.
Overall
This game, as you can tell, does so many things right. But the amount of times I said "WHERE THE ♥♥♥♥ DO I GO" is almost unacceptable for a recommendation. Almost. I find it ridiculous to not recommend this game because I couldn't figure out what to do. But, even when I was watching the walkthroughs, they had trouble figuring it out too. And it's because the way to go wasn't made clear enough. That is a huge problem. Other than that, the game is fine. Don't get me wrong, this is a good game. Just be cautious. Overall, 7.5/10

Writing this review as of the Plains update, as someone who has played since the game came out.
Warframe seems to be getting farther and farther away from the formula that made it entertaining to begin with, which is mindlessly killing things in fun and fast ways. While new concepts in Warframe have always started off rough and gotten polished over time, the latest additions are doubling down on concepts that many players resent.
First, the story in Warframe has become mandatory. Early Warframe you barely had to worry about any story, which is what many people look for in a somewhat mindless shoot and loot game. Now, you are forced to partake in story quests if you don't want to severely limit your potential. And why they still don't allow you to skip cutscenes is beyond me. Being forced to sit through the entirety of what I find to be an uninteresting story is painful.
The grind in Warframe has also become insane with the newest Plains patch. I enjoyed knowing I could log on, do a sortie and maybe an alert or two, and then I could choose what to do with my time. Maybe that is farming materials, maybe it is void missions to get parts for a new weapon or frame, maybe its a credit farm, but whatever it was, its because I wanted to do it. With the current update, accessing any of the new content requires that I now force myself to run bounties and kill the same enemy over and over for the new reputation gains. If I want to use my archwing, I am forced to fish. Because thats why I play a game about space ninjas... to go fishing. And in what is basically like a big middle finger to their players, you can spend 45 minutes doing a high-level bounty, and assuming a bug doesn't ruin it, the reward at the end can be a common item found in a 5 minute alert.
I could go on and on about things that don't make sense to me... why are they forcing operators down our throats which just feels completely uninteresting after we have spent years working on frames and weapons. Why do riven mods require  such stupid tasks to unlock, instead of something fun like kill 300 enemies. Why is the Plains patch described as an open world and completely new way to play Warframe, when ultimately it is just the same map over and over with a slightly larger tileset, and really not open world at all.
It seems like the devs need to hire someone who listens to every idea that they pitch or discuss, and then asks "but is it fun?" Because many of their current designs seem to be lacking in that. The game has become more of a chore for me than something I can play at my own pace and in my own way. It is days after the release of a major new patch and I find myself uninterested to log on at all.

10/10
After a long hard day of killing monsters and slitting the throats of my enemies in the shadows like some kind of badass Russian ninja, I can sit back and admire this game's superior jiggle physics and, at times, really bad Russian humor.

I'm mixed in reviewing this game.
I love tower defense games, they're probably my favourite kind of games when it comes to Flash websites.
And this one has cute graphics, good settings and well, the usual variety of tower weapons that you can place only in the marked spots. Then the enemies will go from one or some paths to your castle (being the whole game in a medieval setting) and so on.
It works like the most classic tower defense game ever. The main problem is that I've already seen hundreds of games like this one, and this one has literally nothing else to add.
Plus, even if it's free, there are lots of microtransactions like Royal Defense (same developers) or other games not on Flash websites but here on Steam. And this is a very negative point, since tower defense games should be free when you buy or install them.
And for the rest of the game well, it doesn't pose a threat. There are no difficulty options (no options at all apart from windowed or fullscreen and regolating sound volume), no other challenges (like the iron challenges and the defense challenges of the Kingdom Rush franchise for example).. so you just go from one level to the other one and, like Royal Defense which has been created by the same devs, you can just add some upgrades but really.. it's super boring 'cos the levels look all the same, the customization isn't that good, you don't have many towers to choose from and if you're going for free you won't last that much.
Apart from the transaction theme, it's really a weak title in the tower defense genre. There are lots of them way better and for free on Flash websites and not only there. This one gest boring after half an hour, all the levels look the same even to me that I've been playing tower defense games for years so I should be prepared for everything.. but this thing is very boring, I liked the graphics but really I played too many games similar to this one and this one is definitely ripped off and adds nothing to what you've already played.
I'd rather recommend to check other free to play tower defense games on Flash websites for much better experiences. It's clear that this game was made with little effort (mainly in the settings and in designing the towers and the enemies, 'cos then in the later levels it's all the same) and for the purpose of making money with microtransactions.. I don't think the developers wanted to make a solid tower defense title like series such as Cursed Treasure, Kingdom Rush, Bloons, Invasion, Gemcraft, there's plenty of them.. they just took from a little bit here and there and put together a game which seem cute and free but it's in reality boring and needs real money to progress.

Okay, so everyone says it's a pay to win game, and that it's a microtransaction based game. In all reality it's not, sure spending elixir (which you get from beating levels might I add) give you plots with with bonuses to them. You CAN spend money on the game but you don't HAVE too. Sure the waiting a half hour for another atempt after exerting my other 5 is annoying, but guess what? It's nice to take a break from a game now and then.
The game actually gives you a nice challenge, actually starting a few levels off with no money and having to use spells too kill a few units to get enough gold for a tower.
Yes the game confines you to specific plots but that helps with the challenge, you have finite places to place towers and
have to chose wisely which to use when and what towers to put in.
The game even has a pause, play, and fast foward button that lets you micro spells and placment of towers.
It also lets you put a target over a specific enimie by clicking them focusing all the towers in range to shoot it.
There is the topic everyone who is negative to it brings up and that's its pay to win aspect, it's not the only option. The game allows you to spend money too help yourself during a level. Like Bloons Tower Defence 5 has the special agents and perks you can buy with monkey money, this game does the same. It's a challenge if you want to take it, but it's not a game for everyone. Call it what you want but at the very least accept that you can win it by playing it completely free.

Underrail is easily the best game I have ever played, and I suspect that it will hold this title for many, many years to come. I cannot recommend it highly enough. To list the reasons why Underrail is an absolute gem of a game and an exemplar of its genre would take ages, so I'll be relatively brief.
As an "Isometric Turn-Based Western Indie RPG", Underrail clearly fits itself into a very unique little niche in the gaming market--and for this reason it has existed in almost total obscurity from the main gaming limelight. However, it is in this niche that Underrail truly thrives as a unique game and an even more uniquely captivating experience.
If the 300-something hours I have (as of the writing of this review) happily dedicated to the enjoyment of this game are any indication, Underrail can really suck you in. The world of Underrail is incredibly fleshed-out, and is beaten in this regard only by the impressive amount of solid characterisation that goes into crafting literally every single noteworthy NPC in the massive (and I truly mean
) overworld of this game.
The music, while lacking in the number of actual tracks for the game, does a good job of furthering the atmosphere of Underrail by being, you guessed it, almost purely atmospheric. However, this isn't to say that Underrail doesn't have any action music! It most certainly does, and the combat music can really get you head-banging. (And the final boss music, hoo boy, talk about ♥♥♥♥ing awesome!!)
The mechanics are easily the most impressive part of Underrail, since they are arguably even more complex and thought-out than the overworld is! Combat works in a turn-based manner, similar to the early Fallout titles (of which Underrail has taken much inspiration, and only in a good way) and feels very intuitive to anyone who has touched a turn-based title in the past. Although I will admit that new players to the turn-based genre may have some difficulty developing their skills, as the tutorial for the game is rather... lackluster.
Bartering and crafting can take pretty significant roles in playing Underrail, and while these systems are excellently handled, bartering especially can be rather confusing--if not downright aggravating--for new players. Merchant NPCs aren't just going to buy every single piece of junk you have on you like in every other game out there. Instead they have very specific kinds of items that they are looking for; one merchant may be looking to buy two firearms and a pair of boots, another may only be willing to take an electronic device or up to 3 grenades. Of course, all of the merchants are more than happy to take your cash, so you can feel free to buy everything they have if you can afford it (and can carry all of it).
And don't even get me started on the story; best I've ever seen in a game, hands down. Beyond perfect.
So, yeah, as you can see I have a lot of good things to say about Underrail. The only bad thing: no shotguns. But, hey, you get awesome crossbows and throwing knives and massive sledgehammers which can zap people with electricity when you hit them and stun them for a turn. Oh, and you can craft grenades and explosive traps that shoot out napalm onto people, and if that doesn't sound awesome then hell if I know what does.
tl;dr: buy Underrail. It's $15, and for a game this perfect it really ought to be $60.

Let me say before anything else that this really surprised me as much as the first game. The side quests and the anomalies, newly introduced in Mass Effect 2, in the first game the side quests and some of the main quests required you to use your Mako to travel around the landscape and go to the where the action really began. In Mass Effect 2 you don't need even to travel around the planet, I really enjoyed watching the landscape while driving in the first game but after you got inside the buildings where the quests were taking place the level design was always the same and after some missions you would probably get bored, but in this game they totally improved these aspects. Every single quest has an an unique level design and there are so many backgrounds which look ABSOLUTLY GORGEOUS. Doing the side quests was in no way boring but completly a pleasure for me. Now, you certainly remember that in Mass Effect there was little micro-management or perhaps you can say that there was none at all, you had credits, medi-gel and omni-gel, nothing more and you could just get TONS of creds by selling pretty much everything you didnt needed on the stores. In Mass Effect 2 there's alot of stuff added to the "resource management", for example, remember that quest in the first game in which you had to survey several planets for resources for the Alliance? Well now you actually have a mini-game other than just clicking "SURVEY" one that is actually entertaining and requires you to purchase probes at the fuel depots, which of course, cost credits. Those resources that you acquire from mining/surveying can be used to acquire new upgrades for your weapons and/or research new weaponry, this ended up excluding the looting of weapons which was possible on the first game. Other than buying upgrades for yourself and your squad you can actually purchase upgrades for the Normandy which actually will help you in the end game. Each member that you add to your squad grants you with new upgrades for both your squad and your ship. Now the combat, it is pretty much like the first one but in my opinion you don't really feel as much "overpowered" as in the first game because there's no mods for the weapons and the guns have alot more recoil in Mass Effect 2 and you also have limited ammo making the use of your powers a must, making this way, the combat alot better than in the first Mass Effect. The space exploration has alot more depth into it now, with the adding of fuel using while travelling, you can also purchase fuel in fuel depots for credits. The story continues where the first game left of and it is just incredible in my opinion, one of the best I've seen and experienced in a long while with the soundtrack keeping up to par with the cutscenes and the emotinal moments which are capable of making a sensitive person cry. The character design is as good as the story as far as I'm concerned didn't really noticed someone "where it doesn't belong". Every single squad member has their own unique personality and even the geth,  "Legion", and EDI have a very interesting dialogue. There's also the love story in which you decide you want to take part or not. The Codex keeps up the great job in providing you with aditional information and "lore" which you don't find in the characters dialogues. And of course, surprisingly enough the choices you made on the first game carry on to this one and the ones that you make in Mass Effect 2 will carry on to the third game. I honestly don't know what more I can say about it, it's an awesome game and experience that both role playing and shooting fans most definatly will enjoy but I judge this game by it's storyline so the 2 games I've played so far are for me only one and for that I can say it is really a hell of a game that you should try.

Seems fair to me. I totally recommend this game.

So, I was a little torn on whether to recommend this; I enjoyed it, but it honestly didn't feel worth full price to me.  I got it for 50% off during the Steam sale, and I would have still preferred it went a little lower.
I love horror games, and I enjoy good adventure games.  This beast tickles both of those urges, but not as much as I would like them to.  The horror is fairly light, mostly featuring gore and a couple tense situations.  The adventuring is fairly standard fare; there are a couple creative situations, but mostly it's just pick up everything and use all the things until you find the right one.
Still, I did enjoy my time.  One caveat: if you want to get the achievements, most of them come from dying.  Usually, the checkpoints are not too bad; however, if you kill yourself, make sure to make a manual save first, or you may find yourself thrown back much farther than expected.

This may just be the best racing game I've ever played on Steam. But, it may also be the most fun platformer game I've played here, too. So how could it be both at the same time?!? Well, this my friends, is what SpeedRunners is.
The high-speed platforming is a lot of fun on its own, running around at the speed of sound while doing parkour moves like the best of them, and swinging around like you're in the greatest Spider-man 2D game that never was. But then you have online multiplayer opponents to race against, and an array of weapons that make the race exhilarating to compete in and win. It may be "Sonic meets Mario Kart", but you'll soon realize you need skills to make it to 1st place.
For a fast-paced online multiplayer romp it plays very smoothly, though you may find a few connection hiccups here and there. However, it's been on Early Access for a while now and it has progressed a LOT since its early days. In fact I wouldn't be surprised if it comes out officially by the end of the year.
BTW you can play as the Scout now (as in TF2 the scout). So add that to the already long list of reasons you'll want to get this game NOW. :3

I seriously cannot recommend this at all. This game just flops, specially compared to its successor. Ignore this and get FlatOut 2 instead.
Flaws:
• The cars feel weightless. You barely nudge a curb going 15 and your car just tumbles. You slam into another car and it doesn't really feel like you've done anything to it.
• Cars have no grip/traction, you seem to be constantly sliding along. This would be fine on snowy tracks, but not on every track. Braking basically has no effect, trying to slow down before a hairpin turn and NOPE! just keep on sliding off the course!
• Courses are very bland. They are wide and empty feeling with no character to them. Theres also very little in the way of different paths/shortcuts.
• You get flung from your car if you barely tap anything.. most of the time. The game is really inconsistent as to what makes you get flung out. Barely scrap a sign? AWAY YOU GO! Slam head on to another car? Nah, you're fine!
•
With how easy it is to be tossed out of your car, theres no point in going after the other racers. You get boost for crashing into things, but it also increases your odds of being thrown from your car, and the fact most things you can break to get boost are also very heavy when hit and will slow you down. Boosting is also something you'll only use to correct coming out of a turn, because going to fast and barely scraping something (and one time nothing at all) will send you flying!
• If you drive ever so slightly off the course, even though you can easily correct yourself and get back on, the game will nag you to reset, often respawning you behind everyone else! With how slippery your car handles, this is more common than it should be.
• The sound design is poor.. very poor. With how amazing it was in the 2nd game, I truly was surprised how crummy it is here.  There are almost no sounds for hitting things. Your tires are next to silent, with how slippery the cars already feel, the lack of sound makes the cars feel like they are floating. The engines sound weak, like you are driving a go-kart or lawn mower.
• Unsatisfying driving. Managing to get a perfect run on a track felt more like a test of patience than skill.
• Upgrades do nothing, atleast they feel that way. My thinking was to upgrade my tires and suspension to have better grip. Well it did nothing at all, the car was just and slidey as ever. You often feel like your car is under powered compared to the computer. Eventually after buying a few upgrades you can beat'em easily, even though the upgrades feel like they've done nothing at all to improve your car. You just suddenly starting keeping pace with the computer. There was no noticable increase in speed, durability, grip or anything.
The few Pros it has:
• The cars look nice again, being mostly muscle cars and having a nice demo derby look to them.... Now if they only sounded like muscle cars.
• Music seems a bit better than the 2nd and there was a noticable amount of female vocals.
• My controller worked on the menus! Not the way I would of liked it to, but it worked fine enough.
While its not the worst racing game I've ever played, its certainly skirting the line. The game is at odds with itself, not knowing what it wants to be. Is it an arcadey smash everything demolition derby game? Its too easy to be pinged out of your car and everything you crash into slows you down. Or is it a technical driving sim? Well it has boosting, very simple upgrading and far to slippery controls. What does this game want to be?
Ignore this and get FlatOut 2, they really improved EVERYTHING in the sequel.

This game has a lot of cool Ideas but the execution is just lacking in too many ways to make it worthwhile.
The Good:
The premise is pretty sweet. You are a descendant from Alain Quartermain in what is a story heavily inspired by Indiana Jones. Which is a very nice Idea. It's not the imaginative of stories but it works.
The overall look of the game is also quite good. Bright desert, moody lighted tombs, blinding sunlight in the frozen glaciers...
Voice acting for germans actually made by german native speakers. Yes! So many really big games and movies fail at this. Big tumbs up!
The Journal, helping you with the puzzling. You don't need it but it gives hints.
The Bad:
Combat is mediocre at best, usually ending in "wait for enemy to pop up and then shoot him in the face" or "point flashlight at mummy then shoot it in the face".
Voice acting. The effort is appreciated but Quartermain comes through as a chauvinistic loudmouth instead of the laid-back adventurer he's supposed to be.
Puzzles are so-so, none of them are complex or challenging but some are frustrating because you have to wait for ages until an object finally moves into position or until you have finally turned that statue 180 degrees.
The scripting of the action Cutscenes isn't too bad but they just look so... awkward. And sometimes they just don't make sense. Quartermain jumps on a hook, slides through a tunnel, onto another hook, out the other side of the tunnel.. and his companions stand right beside him. Huh?
Consolified controls. Keys are rebindeable (and there's a FOV slider~) but the controls still are very console-y in the way they are laid out.
Textures are pretty bad. Rocks tend to be a grey smudge, snow is just a white mess.. meh. Not too distracting but it just looks unfinished.
Also the animations on the AI look ... strange. And some sounds are disconnected from the motions. While cycling the K98k the sound plays a much faster bolt-action sound than the model shows..
The Ugly:
Leveldesign. It seems very rushed. Sometimes you can jump on boxes, sometimes you can't. Some places just outright kill you without the slightest warning setting you back to the last checkpoint and force you to go through the motions of another deadly trap.
The game itself presses exploration, stating exploration is key for this game, go explore and find treasure.
(As it should be!) But then you are running into invisible walls everywhere. Boxes that you clearly should be able to effortlessly step on are insurmountable barriers all of a sudden. Some rooms that are difficult to find are just empty. What the hell?
This game just didn't know what it wanted to be. Action-Adventure? FPS? Puzzle-Game?
In the end, it tries to serve too many masters and fails. And it feels very rushed and unfinished, to boot.
