Murdered: Soul Suspect is quite a good game. Square Enix tends to publish games with good to brilliant story telling and Murdered: Soul Suspect makes no difference. The main story as well as the shorter "cases" that could be solved are interesting and sometimes quite emotional, that is, at least as far as I've played it now...
Unfortunately there's also something that lessens the fun a bit. The
. It seems that the developers were concerned, that the game wouldn't be successful if they didn't add some daemons that would tear you apart if they saw you. To "destroy" them you have to stay unseen and get behind them. Then you're able to attack them, what you can also do from some hiding spots. At some point you'll even learn how to distract them that it get's easier for you... I think it is a sad attempt to implement something to achieve a larger (or different) audience. In my opinion it would have been totally unnecessary.
On the technical side it's a solid piece of work. So far I haven't experienced any bugs. The graphics are quite good. I was surprised that the ghostly appearances have no unwanted, doublesided surfaces shining through. I've always been a fan of FPS, and Chivalry has to be one of the most brutal, unforgiving and rewarding games I've played. One night, about fifteen years ago, my girlfriend came home with a surprise: she had rented me Turok: Dinosaur Hunter for the N64.  She made a good call: a game about hunting dinosaurs would be sure to rock.  When I opened it, the cartridge inside was for Pokemon Snap -- a game where you walk a linear path and take photos of Pokemon and the professor grouses at you if they're not framed exactly center.  That was pretty disappointing but not as disappointing as it would have been if that cartridge had Dinosaur Hunt on it.  Everything about Dinosaur Hunt is terrible.  The AI is awful with enemies often standing in place or spinning in circles, the maps are boring, the graphics are bad (especially gun and corpse effects), the guns are boring to fire, the music loop is nearly as grating as the rare voice effects.  It stands as a mysterious testament to how you can make a game about shooting dinosaurs not even a little bit fun.

Lots of ambition, poor implementation.
What initially drew me in was the premise of the game:  A murder mystery ghost story who-done-it.  Instead, you find yourself trapped in a luke warm, predictable storyline with little flair.
The investigation system, the setting and the like?  They are good ideas poorly implemented.
There's only ever one soulution for each investigation, you know exactly how many clues they are, and it's very easy to figure out what happened in each situation before you conclude each investigation.  Solving a case means finding all the clues and then selecting the "correct" ones to move on.  The only difficulty in each investigation comes from trying to figure out which clues the developers wished you to reference in each investigation (the objectives aren't always clear).  After a few investigations, you pick up how the devs intended things to go, and it's basically a no-brainer from there.
There's much more that I could go on about:  enemy encounters that can't decide if they are confrontational or stealth based, the very limited "open" world, and more.  Instead, let's take a look at what might have been.  The most depressing fact about the game is that you can easily see how this could have been a much better, very different game if they simply refined the experience.  Imagine:  a realized world with multiple fully fleshed out characters and places to explore.  Imagine:  being able to guess incorrectly on an investigation and wasting precious time following a false lead while there's a killer on the loose.  Imagine:  characters changing (killed, alienated and the like) based on your decisions.  Imagine:  multiple endings based on the decisions you've made.  Imagine:  meaningful sidequests that, while optional, might also give you access to different powers, resources and people.
All of that just serves to make the whole experience more depressing.  If I could think this up not even halfway through the game, how could have the developers missed an opportunity like this?  Lack of budget/time/inspriation/testing?  Such a wasted opportunity!

Youtuber's life is about as fun as watching minecraft let's play videos for hours. The gameplay revolves around repeating the same actions time and time again, intertwined with real life lessons such as:
-Give up studying as early as you can, it's not worth it
-Building a relationship with someone is as easy as asking them a question about fashion, 10 times in a row, until your love is unseparable
-Is that your friend? Who cares! Everybody looks the same and acts the same.
-Making good youtube videos does not require any amount of talent whatsoever. It's just about putting random bits of clip together, buying better microphones, and getting a PC that breaks down every 3 days instead of every 2 days.
The gameplay is sluggish. your character moves slowly and there are some incomprehensible delays, for example your acions can take 5/10 seconds to register, but if you think it did nothing and try to repeat the action you will then repeat it multiple times in a row.
It doesn't help that the game mechanics are not well explained so you never know if what happens is as intended or if it's a bug.
A lot of things happen, but they're all extremely boring and also seem to be affected by those sluggish delays. For example friends hit you up on your computer when you cannot use it, or you're just about to walk out of your house with your friend and suddenly another friend texts you "Do you want to chat?" Whether you say yes or no, nothing happens, or maybe it does, or maybe that guy isn't your friend, or maybe it's all inside your head. Who cares. I don't want to talk about fashion anyway.
There is absolutely no fun to be had outside the box either. A lot of  "life simulation" games allow you to enjoy yourself doing whacky stuff. If you thought that Youtuber's Life would allow you to make videos about space nazis, kill your friends, draw inappropriate doodles, or anything just a little bit fun, you were wrong. Everything is so scripted that there is absolutely nothing you can do apart from eating, sleeping, buying stuff, talking to friends, and making youtube videos. The last one being the least interesting of the lot.
Whatever...I'm out of here...

You'll also find a social aspect with in-game chat, daily activities, and a very good soundtrack. I decided to check out this game during a promotion, and it was definitely entertaining.
It does contain some steam achievements, but the in-game achievements are much more attainable. For those who specifically look for games with the intention of maxing out achievements, keep in mind that you're in it for the long haul.
If, however, you're looking for a casual game that you can play at your desk over a lunch break without becoming too involved in a campaign, or a game that you can build up to the point where it pretty much functions on its own, then this is a game you might enjoy.

Fallout 1 & 2 were just about my favorite games of all time. I never really found another game that captured that play style until I bought Underrail. It has a great turn-based combat system, a very unique xp mechanic, great leveling system, cool post-apocalyptic atmosphere, and an unfortunately lack-luster story. This game is drenched in atmosphere but the locations just aren't that interesting; there's never a town, ruin, or cave that makes you say 'wow this is cool'.
Quest descriptions can be annoyingly vague at times. 'Get 5 things and bring it back to Ezra', if it just said 'get 5 things and bring it back to Erza on the 8th floor cyber-lab' it would have saved me a lot of wiki searches. I don't want the game to hold my hand and give me a big arrow on the floor telling me which way to go, but I don't want to have to write a bunch of directions down on a piece of paper just so I remember where to go back to hours later.
There's no map system which was annoying, but not a huge deal. There's no running in Underrail which is annoying and is a huge deal. Getting from place A to place B takes a lot of time in this game. There's a pseudo-quick-travel system later in the game but it doesn't help that much. There's a quest later in the game with The Beast, which requires nearly an hour of just walking back and forth talking to person A, person B, etc. I just about quit playing it was so tedious, but I'm glad I didn't because despite all it's flaws this is still a really really fun game. If you're like me and you loved Fallout 1&2, this is the game you've been waiting almost 20 years for.

Stasis is an isometric adventure game, with a bleak, sci-fi horror theme. Storywise, you're John Maracheck- and you've just woken up out of Stasis in a strange facility floating in space (Read: Like Weyland Yutani + Shodan decided to make a research facility and compete in escalating crimes against humanity).
Between the gore spattered surfaces, skittering creatures, and apocalyptic PDA logs, the story of the game is played out with a distinct focus on building a dread-inducing sense of suspense. Though, despite it's focus on exploration and puzzle solving, it certainly does present a few jump scares here and there- and the opportunity for more than a few 'Industrial' accidents, and self-destructive options. Where, Thematically, the related game to Stasis (Cayne), played out with a characterization that focused on the sort of unpleasentness you might have expected in Demento/Haunting Grounds, Stasis' main theme and unpleasentness tends to have a far less sexual bent/squick factor- instead focusing more on the very real adult fear of a parent looking for their child, and wife in a strange hostile place. And the story does provide a few interesting twists here and there.
The presentation for the game is slick, with the spaceship you navigate being lovingly rendered in all its dark gore & aberration filled glory. Animations are smooth, and there's even cutscenes for certain distinct moments (and deaths).
The voice acting was uniformly good, and the soundtrack definitely helped in building up ambience. (Also, I might have cracked up at the lounge).
Gameplay wise, the puzzles are fairly forgiving, as though the game lacks a hint system, and I did get stuck a couple times when at the 'surgery' section- The games otherwise fairly good at clueing you in via contextual data found in the PDA's, and just by a bit of experimentation- and it does tend to slightly illuminate many items you need to grab, which avoids tedious as hell Pixel hunting. (That, and the cursor changes to a grab icon- this is so very helpful). That said, whilst the puzzles are forgiving, in a sense, they do remain pretty clever, and are also immensely satisfying. Plus, if you ever do find yourself stuck, you can just kill yourself off with the games suicide options as a way of relieving stress. ...Or being morbid. You know, whichever.
All in all, I'd definitely recommend this game.

Stasis is a wonderful little gem of a game. Even though it is best described as a point an click adventure game, Stasis is NOT your typical adventure game. The mood of the world that Stasis paints for us is dark, brooding and unfogiving, like a H.P. Lovecraft story set in space. Some parts of the game really caught me of guard in that regard and I got a similarly uneasy feeling when playing Stasis as I got from System Shock 2 back in the day. What makes Stasis stand ouf from the crowd of adventure games in my opinion, is the amazing attention to detail in every aspect of the game ranging from the visuals and music to how and in what form the story is presented to the player. You could probably play through this game in a rather short time if you are a cunning and experienced adventure game player and completely ignore the story elements, but you really shouldn't. This game should be enjoyed much like a dinner at a fine resturant, in order and over time. Take time to read through all texts you will encounter throughout the corse of the game and you will have a much more rich game experience. I like that no part of the story is served for you straight up in Stasis, you need to connect the dots and see the big picture for yourself. I like when a game developer put faith in the player to discover the story inside the game as a part of how the game is played. It reminds me a little of how the old 90s game Bioforge handled the story telling, where you found log books and journals to read ingame and find clues to how all disjointed parts of the story hangs together.
If you like sci-fi horror and enjoy a game that doesn't shy away from ethics and moral dilemas, set in a gameworld that feels like a plasusable dark future, this is a game for you.

Okay....
I have to be honest, I came into this game with one very simple, stupid goal: I wanted to play as teh Roman Empire in EU4.  That's it.  I didn't really care much about it beyond that.  Now, I know what you're thinking: what were YOU thinking, buying a game you're only going to play for a little bit, especially when it's going to cost 80 bucks (not on sale)?  And truth be told, I really wasn't thinking very much at all, but playing as Rome in EU4 sounded like a ton of fun.  That's it.
Oh, and the Game of Thrones mod looked really freaking cool.  MUCH better than the actually GoT licensed games (grumbles for a bit).
So, I bought the game, booted it up with the GoT mod, and played for about an hour before going back to EU4.  I was in the middle of a pretty intense campaign as France, though to be honest, I'm still pretty new to Paradox's games.  I was always a Total War fan, and I only heard about Paradox recently when a couple friends insisted that I HAD to play these games.  I refused adamantly for about a year, and then eventually I caved - and thank goodness for that!
Anyway, I really enjoyed EU4, and then I bought this and basically forgot about it because of other gaming exploits, finals, the works.  Then, I finished my France game and thought "You know what?  I really want to play as Italy." And my Naples game went pretty well for about 50-100 years.  I got free of Aragon, allied with a few of the other powerful Italian factions, and had a pretty good time until I was completely decimated by three back-to-back wars in the midst of a very powerful internal struggle over some Pretender to the Throne.  Long story short, I wasn't out, but I was down.  So I said, "What the Hell.  May as well try that Rome super-game I was thinking about doing..."
NOW COMES THE IMPORTANT PART: So I picked up CK2 again, and decided to actually play the game.  And the crazy thing is that I absolutely, positively LOVE it.  I only have about 50 hours on record currently, but that's 50 hours over the past week and a half - and I have other stuff to do (a job, research... OH GOD WHAT HAVE I DONE?).  This game is absolutely spectacular, and it's much, MUCH better than EU4 in my humble opinion.  Which is saying something, because I really, really enjoyed EU4.  A lot.
Now, for the game itself.  CK2 isn't for everyone.  I say this because there are people that have very, VERY precious time, and they will end up wasting all of it on this game.  Not healthy.  But as a game, it's just terrific.
I see CK2 as being very akin to a giant, highly complex board game that takes care of most of the fiddly bits for you and makes sure you don't break the rules.  That comes as a supremely high compliment from me - I love board games with a passion.  Now, that isn't to say that it plays exactly like a boardgame, or that I think it should be a board game; just that it has the same feel.  I mean, it isn't turn based, but it's real-time with pause, which is pretty great and helps a lot with people that like to micro (like me).  I have some reasons for this comparison that are a bit esoteric, but some are very practical.
First, the game has a ton of complexity, but you can ignore a good portion of it (at least at first).  Anyone who's ever played Twilight Imperium 3 or the Civ board game knows that huge, empire-building board games can have tons of fiddly bits, and lots of them can be ignored, at least for the first couple play-through's.  Second, the game has a lot of open-endedness to it.  You set your goals.  You can only play within a certain number of years, but you really set your own goals and do whatever you like.  Unlike most set-piece games that hand you a to-do list, this game really lets you choose.  While this isn't a feature most people think of about board games, I'd like to point out that board games are by their very nature modular.  You're playing with others, attempting to achieve SOMETHING.  That something isn't necessarily the same thing for everyone. Sure, with most games there's a 'win condition' (there is one here, too, which is victory points), but the truth is that you can set your own path and just ignore the conventional victory rules.  You very seldom get a screen that says "YOU LOSE."  And when you do, it's pretty darn interesting and fun.  Anyway, that reminds me of playing board games.  A lot of times, when my group gets together, we'll set our own mini-goals for a game.  One time, when we were playing Monopoly (not a game I'm particularly fond of), I made my goal to get every single in the game so I could run around the room "making it rain."  I can "make it rain" in CK2.  I can't in most games.
Now for the inevitable comparisons: Total War and Civ.  Total War is a great series.  Seriously, everyone should play it.  But their latest title is pretty lackluster, and the games lack a certain complexity.  The title says it all: Total War.  All you do is war.  There is no peace option (for all intents and purposes).  You fight a ton of battles, and to be honest, it's pretty fun.  But the games are really about their battlefield simulation.  Don't let the campaign mode fool you - it's a ton of fun, but the games are really at their best on the battlefield.  Otherwise, it's just a bad, super simplistic rip-off of Padadox.  Honestly.  That campaign modes are hyper-simplistic.  There's very little intrigue, and I feel like Rome 2 kind of sounded desperate when it sent me pop-ups saying "LOOK AT ME PLEASE I'M INTRIGUING!!!!"  All I really wanted to do was get to the next battle.  Also, the turn-based nature kind of messes with the strategic decisions sometimes.  So, how do these compare?  Truth be told, they don't.  If you want *tactics*, play Total War.  If you want *strategy*, play CK2 (or other Paradox games).  If you want both, play both, and don't forget to delineate which is which.  Also, side note, TW is ALL about painting the map.  CK2 is DEFINITELY not (though you can play it that way if you want to).
Now, the Civ comparison is much closer.  The two games are both more "Grand Strategy," and as such they're much closer cut.  I'm a big fan of the Civ series, and I've been playing since Civ3 came out, but I have to say that I prefer Paradox's games.  In Civ, you take an empire through history, whereas Paradox has much closer-cut timeframes.  That isn't really THAT important, but I feel like Civ simply has to water down the experience because it tries to cover so much.  Paradox games, on the other hand, are much more immersive (though you theoretically get fewer options with each).  The issue  have with that is that every culture in Civ feels pretty much the same.  You get a few special units, a new color, a few stat boosts here or there, but it doesn't FEEL that different.  Sure, there's some difference, but everyone is starting with one city, everyone has the same techs, and everyone uses the same units.  In CK2 and EU4 (at least, among the Paradox games), the nation/character you play is wholly unique.  The starting conditions are completely different - there's no semblance of balance.  Want to play as a single-county Count in the middle of HRE?  Good luck.  Have fun.  Want to try to paint the map as Ryukyu in EU4?  Wow.
In Civ, 'Hard' modes are accomplished by making the AI more aggressive, or giving numeric advantages (mostly).  In CK2, Hard mode is trying to survive as an inherently lesser nation - but one that is handicapped in a way that feels more or less natural.  Now that isn't a judgment of how difficult it is to play either game - there are definitely people that would feel very strongly if I were to say that Civ wasn't a hard game (it is - I've never won on anything above Prince, so I can't imagine how hard Deity must be).  This is just to say that the difficulty feels more *natural*.  It just feels right.
Wow.  That was long.  Tl;dr - BUY THIS GAME.  NOW.  WITH ALL DLC.

This is one of those bad games that I personally enjoyed for some reason. And I do mean bad.
I've noticed a silly argument on it being based on a book series vs. ripping off a movie series. It is based off a book series that also happened to inspire a movie series some. BUT, the game also draws direct inspiration from the movie series. It doesn't "rip it off" or anything. But it directly references the movies on multiple occasions. And clearly draws inspiration from the movie's scenes. Which isn't a bad thing! It is based on the book series but also inspired by Junior. I just don't even know why its a discussion But it is. And I just kept it going! Woops, haha.
Lots of bad stuff; Graphical glitches*, frame rate drops*, downright silly character animations*, plot holes, plot jumps, invisible walls, places to get stuck, clunky puzzles to get to areas our adventurer could clearly just leap or climb to, mindless AI, and more I can't recall. But worst of all is the silly saving system. Checkpoints that activate after killing certain enemies or triggering certain puzzles. Rather annoying on a game with hidden side treasures and traps that insta-kill. Upon death it reloads you to the checkpoint and you have to get all the side stuff again. There just happened to be a few long distances, with high chances of death, between a few checkpoints that made this a fatal flaw. But for the most part the checkpoints do come often enough. Another time I killed a boss with minions still running about and it triggered a cutscene that, when over, had me standing right in the middle of the surviving minions! I soon died. You can read all the negative reviews that elaborate on all the problems and more I didn't mention.
But in the end, I had fun. I really did. This game has some sort of weird charm to it that got a hold of me. Maybe it was the over the top adventure, or the cheesy one-liners, or the puzzles that actually took thought, or a little bit of all of it. It was a fun casual game that took just over 8hrs to complete. I just simply had fun. And you might too! So that's why I recommend it. Do buy it on sale though, it'll ease the rough sections.
*I guess I should mention that despite the bad animations, graphical glitches, and frame rate drops, this game does look pretty damn good overall. And then also, I only play single player games and didn't even attempt the multiplayer.
EDIT/UPDATE (March 2015); I just would like to mention since playing this I have read a decent handful Allan Quatermain books by H. Rider Haggard and it makes me appreciate this game even more. Just for turning me onto the books! But, that said, I wanted to mention that any fan of the books shouldn't expect anything close to them in the game. Like I mentioned in my review, it borrows from Indiana Jones regardless of being inspired by Quatermain. Now I can flatly state; Beyond the name and it being an adventure, it borrows 95% from Indiana Jones versus 5% from Allan Quatermain. Which makes that whole discussion/argument even more silly. Regardless! I enjoyed the game standing on its own and as a bonus it turned me on to the books! Which I enjoyed for their own reasons and separately. To reiterate though, "don't expect a Haggard inspired romance from this game at all" is the supposedly edit worthy point I wished to make.

Ah Elsword, I gotta say, this is one of the best Anime MMORPGs I've played in my experience as a gamer.
Don't throw your F grenades yet, (and by F i mean F@%*) I do know about LOL, Diablo, WOW, and destiny, so hear me out and take your fingers out of the pin hole.

Now I don't know about you guys, but when I'm about to jump into a new MMO, I tend to do research.
I start with the little things, is it visually appealing? Does it have PVP and if it does is it well ballanced? Can I see my character fully instead of just the top of it's head? and most important, is it fun?
In my opinion Elsword has everything an MMO should, awesome fast paced gameplay, unique character styles and combat, beautiful scenery, and blood pumping PvP action. And this for free!
Dispite the gender locked characters that all start out the same, you are somehow able to still feel unique and different from any other player. Be it cosmetically or combat wise. You don't ahve to spend DAYS!!! trying to level up just to get past a stage. And admittedly, the dungeons can and will get kinda repetitive, this happenes in all gaming, the only way to avoid it is to keep coming out with new missions and updates. Which, as far as I know, Elsword does.
Remember what I said about balanced PvP? Well this isn't exactly the best example. While it may seem impossible for a level 4 to absolutely destroy a level 70, I gotta say in Elsword, this isn't all that uncommon. What I like about ES's PvP is that it gives all players a chance, if they are skilled. What I don't like is that the new characters are automatically stronger and more efficient, which, outside of context makes perfect sence right? New meaning improved and more efficient. But honestly, its like you don't even need skill anymore, I normally play as the star character Elsword himself, but I tried one day as a new character named Ara. at level 10 I effortlessly conquered a level 64. and don't get me wrong, this was an A class player, he had experience! but Ara is absolutely unstoppable and has seemingly endless combos, thats absurd to me. But like I said, if you are more skilled than the other you will win.
All in All, Elsword is a great game to play if you have patience and are a wiz at combos. I'd always recomend it to anyone who calls themself a gamer.                                                                   Gameplay: 9/10
Story: 7/10
PvP: 8/10
Visuals: 9.5/10
Community: 9/10

I don't usually write reviews, but I do like this game and hope it could be better.
Pros:
This game is fun.  It would be worth paying money for if they fix the problems.
Cons:
There are a lot of bugs that indicate a lack of polish
* I can't set my screen resolution for fullscreen to anything but my native desktop resolution.  Workaround is to set game to windowed mode with a set resolution via steam launch options then set to fullscreen after login.  There is a change resolution option in the game, but it doesn't have any options but my desktop res.
* When attpempting to join a game that is full, a chunk of code error shows up rather than a message saying the game is full.  Not a problem, but seems like something that would be trivial to fix.
* Game objectives that show up on the map sometimes have game error text rather than actual names
* There is apparently a known bug on arena team matches where you sometimes don't spawn.  Based on other posts it has been around a long time and is quite common.
* Players in team matches can apparently have skins/colors that override the team color, so the only way to tell what team they are on is to mouse over them and see if the dot is red.  This is rediculous.
* Performance on a lot of maps is terrible, mainly because they make them large with tons of detail.  We don't really care how pretty the game looks, we'd rather it not chop.
* Archer is quite frustrating to play.  Quite often shots go right through people without hitting them.
* Block seems to be able to block attacks even from behind if attacking with a slash, and from multiple opponents.
* There is no cost to being blocked.  If two people keep blocking/attacking each other, it will continue endlessly, pretty much regardless of weapon speed (dagger might be the only exception.)  I've heard it's supposed to attack faster after you block (riposte) but if it's there it's too miniscule to matter.  Think Assassin's Creed swordfighting without having a counter attack. This also applies to blocking multiple enemies simultainously.

What can I say, utterly brilliant apart from some niggling flaws.
Graphically: Dated obviously, but the art direction is so good that it doesn't matter.  It looks lush.
Combat: A bit too much stun locking from certain mobs, dodging is not well implemented.  Mostly good though.
Combat styles: There's lots of variety, go the caster path, the ranged path or the tank path.  They all work and there's room for variety within those styles as well.
Story: Excellent, beautifully scripted, brilliantly voiced.
The World:  Here is where this game excels.  It's vibrant, funny and interesting.  In no other game, other than maybe other Fable games, is it such fun to just wander round listening to the splendidly insane chatter.  There is just an incredible amount of superb voice acting, often for purely throwaway world detail. Silly side quests like the books for school kids are just perfectly done and just add to the overall entertainment.  The depth of the interactions is sometimes just amazing, one minor niggle is that many of these interactions are only available to naughty people.  The good guys don't get to poke around in the game mechanics so much.
Save System: God awful, mental.  Why?  I guess it works well enough once you are used to it, but it is certainly strange.

Youtubers Life
Released
U-Play Online
U-Play Online
3D Simulation
18th of May, 2016
Singleplayer
Have you ever wondered what it’s like to be an internet celebrity? Of course you have, only that unlike the lucky few that actually reach that status, you probably lack the charisma, self-confidence, good looks and so on and so forth. Hey, at least look on the bright side of things: you’re not a Steam review writing loser! Youtubers Life is the promising debut of a dev team that nailed the hardships of trying to please an ever critical online crowd. Not to mention severely lacking in common sense since this is the internet, right? We can act like the animals we can’t impersonate in real life, because of society and other reasons.
The game was nowhere near as buggy as some reviews pointed out. It is true that I focused on the Gaming Channel since the other two channels for Music and Cooking, don’t count among topics I’d feel the need to write about. I listen to almost any genre as long as the current mood fits it and as far as food is concerned, I never understood “the art of cuisine”. At least in gaming’s favor I can vouch with my nearly 18 years of experience while playing almost daily on PC. I was still dismayed by the limited selection of activities you start with in Youtubers Life. For example, as a novice Gamer on “U-Tube” (that’s how the website is spelled in-game), you can only make and publish gameplay videos. I would have started with reviews directly but the virtual powers that be, decided that you must start your promising career as an infamous gamer, by screaming in your microphone while you’re recording yourself. If some Swedish dude got away with it, surely this must be the formula for universal success!
I’m almost surprised you don’t kickstart your path to internet stardom, by living in your parents’ basement, but that might have been one stereotype too many. No father figure is present but at least there’s a mother to pester you about “minor” things such as studying or getting a job. It would have felt really meta, if I wasn’t already “enjoying” adult life at its fullest. But as any good story, it is best for the exposition to contain a rags to riches element. Nevermind that most YT celebs in real life, are never average joes recording themselves from their trailer-park homes. We’ll play along the idea that you can start small and once you dream big enough, it will come true. George Carlin summarizes it perfectly: “It’s called the American Dream, because you have to be asleep to believe it.”
So we shall dream big and earn in-game a lot of cash. Apparently enough to afford yacht parties after 100 uploaded videos on “U-Tube”. The game does have an air of nostalgia to it. Why? Because I stopped playing The Sims around its second installment, so I never bothered with how they were milking the third and fourth one. But I do miss the house building and design aspects that have made the Sims franchise famous in its own right. Youtubers Life tries to emulate some of those elements, through the implementation of upgrades that you can “buy online” in-game on some mock-up sites with names similar to their real life counterparts. So the sense of progression is firmly embedded, not just in skills (you can call it experience gain too) but also new objects and hardware that increase your popularity yield and allow players to personalize the living spaces as well, not just the characters themselves.
How well you manage to compete on U-Tube, is not quite as random as reality can be. As long as you put sufficient effort in the post production part before uploading the videos, you will soon find yourself with a steady supply of virtual cash. As far as I’ve noticed, ultimate success for the gamers/streamers in Youtubers Life, seems to be the attention you receive at Gaming Conventions. Talent Shows are the pinnacle of success for aspiring musicians and last but not least, Cooking Shows for those that start out by filming themselves as they burn the food while adjusting the focus and zoom level on their streaming cameras. A lot to experience for a game, I agree. The price tag might be ultimately justified, given the attention to detail. I won’t mark it as a weak point, that’s for certain. The hybrid mechanics which feature the economic simulation aspects are balanced enough so you cannot claim the game is punishingly difficult. The start is the only rocky part of your journey to online fame. At least until they add the IRS in a future DLC or something. Better not, U-Play Online. Just focus on making more games such as Youtubers Life. Steam surely needs more quality 3D simulators.

Underrail is a ton of fun.  There are many "old school" rpgs being released these days after kickstarter became so popular, but along with the Shadowrun series this game came the closest to making me feel like I was playing Planescape or BG2.
That's not because it's an extremely similar game, mechanically.  In many ways Underrail is more like a turn based Deus Ex than Baldur's Gate, but there are a few things about it that I didn't know I was looking for when I backed Pillars of Eternity, Wasteland 2, etc.
What makes Underrail so special, besides the awesome and absorbing combat/character build system, is the great immersion of the setting.  The music is fantastic.  I enjoy walking around the maps listening to the janky, mechanical and ominous soundtrack (serious fallout/planescape flashbacks).  The lore is presented as background, not through infodumps or encyclopedias, and is all over the place in small, rewarding tidbits.  The monster ecology is cool.  The visual design is unbelievably good for a game created by one person.  The drawn 2d look with dynamic lighting is just as interesting to look at as a AAA 3d title.  The sounds are satisfying, from the punchy gunfire to the weird glug of my purple telekinetic wrecking ball.
This is not a party based, or even a particularly story based, RPG.  But it is crafted so well that it doesn't matter.  There are no companions, but every character that you speak with substantively has some detail about them to flesh them out.  Motivations make sense and the moral landscape of the game is very dark.
Can't recommend it enough if you enjoy detailed turn based combat and interesting settings.

Title: This is not a bad review
Before anyone starts yapping ‘hey skoom this is a bad review’ or ‘why do you play for thousands of hours if you don’t like it Grakata?’ blah blah blah.
Do I like Warframe? Yes. Do I recommend others to try this game out? Double yes, no one should miss a great game like this. Then why do I not recommend it? There are reasons, partly because good reviews aren’t nearly as eye catching as bad reviews, and since there’s no mixed review option on steam, so I chose to pick my stand and not side with Warframe. On top of that, there are also some general and personal reasons, also there are some bad things that can outweighs the good. So, before you want to say anything, please read on.
Overview:
Warframe is a free MMORPG game that can easily rival most of other AAA titles with similar aspects. Warframe is not just a game for people with grinding fetish, it’s not just a game for those who can’t afford other AAA titles, Warframe is a game with depth and huge content, providing diverse experience for those who with too much time to waste and those who don’t.
With 4 years of development, Warframe has racked up an incredible amount of contents, and has built up amazing lore alongside with one super friendly and loyal community. In combination, the vast content and interesting lore Warframe provided can totally get you hooked and wanting to dig deeper and deeper into the game, and with the help of countless helpful vets and players, you will have no problem swimming through most of whatever this game has to provide with ease.
Most people’s first impression with Warframe is amazing graphics, endless customization, and ocean deep combinations for your mods, weapons, frames, and as you progress further, you will come to realize there are even more customizations, mechanics, playstyles, stories, deeper lore and more maps to explore, and all of that are brought to you via constant bi-weekly updates for free. The fact that I’ve always been inclined to write a review is because of this exact reason, with over 1000 hours devoted into this game, I can still learn new things, come up with new build combinations, and expect more updates to come, and writing a review too ‘early’ I fear I won’t do this game and its community justice.
However, nothing in this world is perfect, Warframe is no exception, so here are my breakdowns on a few major pros and cons of Warframe.
Pros:
1.	Huge content
2.	Amazing community
3.	Deep lore to dig into
4.	Constant updates
5.	Great customizations
6.	Mature mods system
7.	Resource balance
8.	PvE balance
9.	Vast build options and melee
10.	 Diverse missions and playstyles
Humongous amount of contents, satisfying anyone who wants more to dive into.
A consistent community that’s always ready to provide any information, or help you out whatever and whenever you need.
Deep lore with interesting characters like Clem and Stalker, the deeper you dig, the fonder your will get for the characters, and further you get, the more you will be amazed by the story.
Due to Warframe’s beta development status, constant updates are being rolled out every other week (U22 as of this review), bringing new weapons, frames, quests and cinematics, and even new maps and game modes, and all of these are accessible for all players for free, new or old alike.
Countless of customization options are also provided for us players ranging from color pallets, cosmetics, skins and community created items ready for the grab, enabling you to create your most unique looks that suit your fashion sense the best.
Mature mods systems with thousands of mods for each type of weapons, frames, sentinels, archwings, and even for your dogs and cats. You can customize your builds with whatever mods you want to suit your own playstyle. Modding your weapons for raw power, elemental, physical damage or AoE damage to eliminate waves and waves of enemies. Modding your frame for power strength, efficiency or duration to build your own mass murderer or a silent assassin. Countless build options, you never need to submit to any meta.
A highly balanced resource system, never makes you feel bored to keep farming a single resource in one single place or in one single mission type, great resource yield rate making players feel satisfied over time. Granted some building requirements are painfully unfair, but those are the only few items that differentiate new players from the old.
Focusing solely on PvE, Warframe has created a gap from other MMORPG series, not caring a wee bit for PvP, making this game feel incredibly balanced considering how many weapons and frames out there and all the combinations there can be, almost any weapons and any frame you use, with enough investments, can make you feel like gods walking on the surfaces of all these different planets, this is the exact reason why we play video games after all and Warframe has nailed this part.
4 years of contents, not just the universe is growing, your arsenal is growing bigger and bigger in almost every update. With over 300 items available, you can create thousands of ways to torture a grineer, to humiliate a corpus, or to disembody an infested. With Warframe’s unique melee system, which other games tend to disregard, you are free to combat any enemies from any range, combining with different enemy types and hitting mechanics, it even brings out a somewhat authentic feel despite being a space ninja shooting aliens game.
Lastly Warframe also provides very diverse enemy types, with new enemies introduced every now and then making your combat feel refreshed, and adding more challenge and playability. Vast maps and mission types meaning you never have to do the same objective in the same tileset every time, increasing the replayability.
Cons:
1.	Total lack of explanation
2.	Objective designs
3.	Mission reward system
4.	Weapons and warframe nerfing and constantly changing builds
5.	Sinister developers
This week, the highly anticipated Plains of Eidolon released, I created a new account as per my dearest clannies request, only to find out that my new account is also banned, as it turned out I was IP banned just for replying to support tickets with open status. I would completely understand their action if I have ever created any negative posts about them on social media, just like I would understand them if I was truly wrong and deserved my ban, but their action to disregard a single player because they have the other 30 million fans who don’t know their mischiefs, is simply outrageous.
Before all this, I loved Warframe and DE wholeheartedly and admire their courage of being different from the other developers and being consistent for their fans, and I snuffed every reddit post and YouTube video presenting DE’s injustice, but right now knowing how it feels to become one of the few people who I thought I would never become, I have to recognize the facts and pick my stand towards DE’s egregious measures.
Conclusion:
Do I recommend this game? Sadly yes, it is a shame not to try out one of gaming industry’s best products for free.
Is it a good game? From performance to player receptions, it is 9/10.
Does this game deserve more effort and attention than any other game? Yes, due to its nature of being a loot based MMORPG game you will need to sink more time into it to achieve a satisfiable result, and needless to say, if u decide to do so, the result can definitely satisfy you.
Does this game worth pour money into? Yes, despite the fact that almost all items in Warframe can be obtained through farming, and you can also earn in game currency via farming, but spending a little money to buy some cosmetics and speed up your farming process will definitely improve your gaming experience. However, do bear in mind that although low, but there are still chances for you to get banned and have you account erased regardless of whether you are a new player with under 100 hours or a 5000 hours vet. So do be careful when you do.

A somewhat impulse play Medieval Defenders appeared on my Steam Suggestions and I was appalled by the greed involved.
Created by Creobit and published by 8floor Medieval Defenders is a very basic free to play tower defence game that relies on its cute graphics and outright devious limitations, to make players purchase microtransactions.
Elixirs are the ingame item used for enhancing turrets and spells and can be earned in small amounts each level, however in later levels the best tactical turret locations also cost Elixirs to use.

To give a full example of the game I've played through the first 10 of the 40 levels.
To Summarise:
- Elixirs are needed for nearly everythig in the game from specail tower placement, putting down towers when out of gold, upgrading towers and spells. You get a very small amount of Elixirs per successful level and the rest you must pay for.
- No way to refund upgrades so if you choose poorly you will become stuck or need to pay money.
- You get one life charge per 30 mins but there is no way to go back to the level select screen which forces you to lose one life and forcing you to get more life charges with money.
- The death noises of the various units you kill and the firing noise of the turrents quickly grow annoying.
- Lackluster in general
- Little real option for tactics and cheap difficulty spikes.

How do you describe a game that is so extraordinary as Mass Effect 2? Where do you begin? With the superb graphics, that stand with the best today? Do you go with the gameplay that feels a thousand times more polished than the first with absolutely tons of available sidequests as well as Downloadable content? Maybe with the fact that this is the first story game that has allowed a player to carry over player-made decisions onto another game, and with this comes a promise that the character you crafted to YOUR expectations would be waiting for you in this story. (That alone is something that gamers like myself have been waiting years for.) And don't even get me started on the story and where the team at Bioware is taking this series. Not only are your character relationships you made in ME1 still intact, but now they have new and truly exciting avenues that they can take. This is doubly true for the Lair of The Shadow Broker DLC with character Liara T'soni. (Highly recommended, along with all the other DLC) Then there is Shephard. The hero who has a bit more personality than before, is forged through player decisions that can alter the state of your party dramatically. And forging him or her is another matter altogether. How exactly do you craft a character who is the most important human in the galaxy? And more, a character who knows it? These elements are sheer brilliance and the amazing experience gifted to us in the first is grossly intensified. The action feels real and livid. The romantic stories feel romantic (particularly with Garrus, Thane, Jack and Tali Zorah, who seem the slightly less than obvious choices) And the music (yes, I'm yet again, going into the music) composed by Jack Wall fits the situations of the game even better than the first entry. Some take issue with the mining and doorlock minigames because of their repetitive nature. To me, it is small potatoes considering the rest of the experience. By the end, you feel the weight of your decisions and their consequences on your shoulders, be they good or bad. The brilliant thing, though, is that you've felt this all along.

Not really sure why this game is getting such high reviews. I mean, ok it works well as a horror game with some truly horrifying situations and rather nice pre-rendered isometric graphics and good sound. The abundant writing is decent and the various characters you read about are usually well linked together. Voice acting is sparse but of ok quality. The puzzles are reasonably logical. End of positive points.
On the other hand, I find playing it infuriating. Somehow this game ignored 5-10 years of adventure game evolution:
- cheap deaths and a sloooowwwww "you are dead" screen before you can try something else. The more you progress in the game, the more timed puzzles you're gonna encounter. You often have mere seconds when being presented with the situation to react or die: more repetition.
- non-skippable dialog, and of course sometimes the game autosaves right before that dialog in a section where you're gonna die a lot, forcing you to listen to it over and over. You can save manually but the game autoloads its last autosave before you can manually load, forcing you through at least a part of that dialog.
- pixel-hunting for some items, in very cluttered environments. No hotkey in sight to show all interactive hotspots like The Book of Unwritten Tales or Black Mirror II and III.
- imprecise controls, bad pathfinding, and when a screen overlays the game to show an object or even the save/load menu, your clicks are still registered as movement! Goes great with the aforementioned cheap deaths which trigger by stepping at the wrong place.
- if you have a dual-screen setup, there's no way to lock the mouse cursor to the game window, so expect sudden jarring interruptions as you accidentally click off the edge when accessing your inventory. Unless you disable your second screen. Of course the game keeps running while it lost focus, which can cause you to miss a crucial moment.
- No options menu, no resolution options. If you have a 16:10 monitor the game has black bars at the top and bottom
On top of that the story is really run-of-the-mill and predictable, and you see the "plot twists" coming a mile away. The game also explains some of the stuff that happened too early and in an unexciting way. It's also completely linear, which is pretty standard for adventure games, but sometimes the main character does something if would really have preferred not to do, like (minor spoiler)
. Multiple paths for some solutions would have been appreciated in cases like this.
I ended up finishing the game (with a walkthrough at hand to avoid repeated cheap deaths) to see what other morbid sights they had in store, but I was rather heavily disappointed given the high expectations I had formed from the reviews and early impressions videos I watched. The ending is a nonsensical mess leaving many things unexplained... and in a sloppy, contradictory way, not a good way. Some of the horror is completely gratuitous and doesn't help the story, like (huge spoiler)
The bad guys are one-dimensional and stereotypical, and the whole thing just leaves a bad taste in your mouth like after having read a low-grade sci-fi novel.

Stasis is a dark, isometric point and click sci-fi horror adventure which really excelled in creating an immersive atmosphere. Through the sounds, the gorgeously drawn environments and the well fleshed out lore (through crew journals, dialogue) I felt like I was on board the Groomlake space station with John Marachek.
The story is good, though perhaps not great. It is clearly well thought out and has been well put together. John Marachek wakes up aboard the Groomlake, an empty, broken space ship, with no knowledge of he got there. A simple enough opening premise but it evolves and develops quite nicely. I think the story is a wholly traditional sci-fi tale and should be especially pleasing for purist fans of the genre.
Controls were simple enough. Point and click. Find objects, use them appropriately. Sometimes combine objects to enhance function and solve more puzzles. There are small puzzles to be solved in the game, some of which aren’t immediately obvious. A nice touch, adding some welcome distractions from the horror of the Groomlake. I think I used a walkthrough a couple of times.
It seems to me that THE BROTHERHOOD, the devs, picked one an aesthetic and focussed much of their design efforts around this. When I say it is a dark game, it truly is. The environments, as striking and well made as they are, are dark. They use dark muted colours, the story they tell is a grim one of suffering and death. The look and feel of the world has a direction and this shows, and the game is successful for it. The audio is an unnerving, far from comforting affair – truly hitting home the point that this is a horror experience. The sounds of the ship, pipes, vents (yes, those are vent sounds, I refuse to believe they’re anything else) and computers synergise with the visual aesthetic to paint the doom laden, oppressive atmosphere of the Groomlake.
Overall, I feel the various components I have discussed come together very nicely to produce the finished product that is Stasis. I feel it is a complete game, albeit not particularly long. For a game that is very much a game of the horror genre, I did wish there was more horror-based challenge. Not a major bad point as this does allow one to enjoy the ambience somewhat but many of the horror elements struck me as being part of the background. There certainly were threats in the game, but I wonder if there could have been more. Furthermore, the story, which was fine and had some very good moments, did feel a little unoriginal at times. Yet again, not a major point but I think this took away some edge. It was a good story, but not a riveting one. Perhaps a tiny bit unadventurous given the scope of the material it was working with but overall, a solid game with a beautifully designed world that I believe is definitely worth a play.

STASIS is a point-and-click story set in a sci-fi setting, with a dark and streamlined narrative. Without spoiling anything, let me give the rundown:
Overall, STASIS succeeds in telling a compelling story of a man in search of his family, but it is nothing particularly mind-blowing. This looks like it will unseat New Vegas as my new favorite RPG. 10/10.
There are many changes and improvements from Divinity: Orginal Sin 1, all for the better. The biggest changes are in the way stats are handled.
Instead of being a flate or percentage damage reduction like in most RPGs, armor is now an extra healthbar that has to be worn down to 0 before you can take damage or status effects. You have separate armor bars for physical and magic damage. There are abilities that can regenerate your armor and also a few abilities that can penetrate armor and damage vitality directly. This is a pretty simple change but the tactical considerations are wide-reaching. Nuking the enemy with status effects turn 1 (or being nuked yourself) is much more difficult now. You will have to prioritize targetting, as enemy soldiers have lots of physical armor, mages have lots of magical armor, and some enemies have no armor but large HP pools. On your own characters, you will have to decide whether they should wear more physical or more magical armor, and whether they should learn armor-regenerating skills. Another fortunate side effect of this change is that minor traps are less tedious, as your armor protects against harmful surfaces like ooze and electrified water.
The skill system has also been greatly improved. DIVOS 1 had a great concept for a semi-classless system, but it had some flaws. An INT character could invest a point or two in each school of magic and learn twenty skills easily while still kicking♥♥♥♥♥with wand and staff basic attacks, but STR and Finesse characters had a limited skill selection outside of the few spells that didn't scale with INT. Both of those problems have been solved. There is a greater variety of skills available for the non-magical characters and they can dip into magical classes more easily too. Getting access to class skills only requires a single point now, with any additional points simply providing secondary stat bonuses (+10% damage to magical armor for example). The new Polymorph school allows even a  10-int fighter to literally bull-rush enemies, or your archer can sprout wings and take the high ground. A real plate-clad, ax-wielding battlemage is a viable option now.
The maximum number of skills your character can know at one time is now limited by your Memory stat, so no more mages putting 1 point into every magic school and buying up every skill book you can find unless you're willing to put a lot of points into Memory. You aren't lacking for options though, since your class skills + race skills + bonus skills + potions, grenades, magic arrows and abilities from gear still adds up to a lot even with nothing invested in the memory stat.
The companions are pretty cool as well. There are going to be six when the game releases and each one has a unique model, skill, dialog options, and quest. You can even choose to make one of the companions your main character.  When you meet them in-game, you can make them any class you want, so the Red Prince can become a mage or archer instead of the default fighter/geomancer. Only four of the characters are out now, but they're all cool and likable, easily on par or surpassing Bioware and Obsidian companions.

This is a fantastic simulation game.
That being said, this isn't a game where you are the hero and it revolves around you - you play as the head of a royal family somewhere in Europe, and your primary goal is actually pretty simple - survive!  If your lineage dies out, the game is over.
Beyond that, you can attempt to do whatever you want - grow the family titles and lands they control. from a Count to King to Emperor - or not; participate in Crusades or not; or just sit back and watch as the various other Lords and Ladies make their own attempts at expansion.  The game does not care what you are doing or not doing - everyone is busy hatching plots, scheming, and making their own moves.  If you choose to sit on the sidelines, the game and history will move on without you.  Choose to get involved, and you might just be able to bend a corner of it to your rule.  For a time.

Askutron is a fun little quiz game, best enjoyed with up to eight friends on a big TV screen. A nice touch is that smart phones can be used as controllers with a free app and most common game controllers work on PC as well. Since the latest update even the good old “Buzz” controllers can be used. The gameplay is solid with four different game modes and a finale per round. The players can choose between standard quiz (massive question catalogue) and themed quizzes with a smaller amount of more specialized questions. A feature I really enjoy is that themed quizzes can be created by users with the help of the Askutron quiz editor. So potentially there will be a steady stream of new questions for different topics. At the moment, there are already some quizzes in the Steam workshop. All in all, the game is “you get what you expect” from an indie quiz game. No fancy graphics, not the prettiest user interface, and some occasional bugs, but does the job. It is early access and receives constant updates, so hopefully the weak spots get addressed.

I can only barely recommend Deadfall Adventures..and if you're thinking about getting it for Linux, you'll benefit from excessive loading times and some graphical glitches (though you can still complete the game).  Given that these have been around for most of a year, I wouldn't hold your breath in the hope that they'll be sorted soon.
More generally (and I'd imagine that this would apply to the Win version too), puzzles are often weak and some can be solved quite simply by spamming switches if you're too lazy to consult the in-game game guide (i.e. the notepad).  Dialogue between characters varies between dull and cringeworthy and is not helped by the rather awful voice acting.  Combat is so so, neither types of enemy will surprise you in their tactics and weapons, whilst generally doing what you expect, are rather limited in variety. The different shotguns also seem a little on the weak side when they should be at their best (limited range / spread).
Cutscene animation was like watching hover-handed people with parkinsons and often combined well with the aforementioned dialogue to make for awkward watching.  Thankfully, you can just click on ahead,
Soo, why recommend?  Well the backdrops are nicely done, but more importantly, the game is just well-paced fun - an easy game you can just go back to and be pretty sure that you'll make progress without it being a complete gimme.  Probs best to get it during a sale or in a bundle as the original price is steep..and I can't guarantee you'll get your buck / hour value, but it will be an non too taxing experience that doesn't take itself too seriously.

Deadfall adventures isn't going to amaze you or stun you with its original story or dialogue. It is really quite the opposite.
That being said, it's a  fun, OK game, resurfacing the Indianna Jones atmosphere that has been deeply missed. However, it is full of glitches with a crappy checkpoint save system. Yes, a checkpoint save system in an exploration game. Who would have thought.
In the beginning I attempted to collect all the treasure via my handy compass treasure-pointer, yet, once I ran off to collect my treasure to only be killed instantly it was a bit frustrating. Nevertheless I try again, and again. Fixed on getting this one piece of treasure, but each time I was killed instantly I was forced to run all the way back (roughly 4 minutes)  purchase my upgrades again and THEN attempt the puzzle again.
My character kept getting stuck in ridiculous places, forcing me to restart from the nearest save and collect all the treasure I had collected previously ... again.
The dialogue, oh the dialogue. Filled with corny, primary school aged teasing-flirtatious remarks that make you facepalm while having to endure it throughout the entire campaign. I could get past this, if it wasn't for the crappy save system or the glitches but sadly, it all comes together, ruining my experience as a player.
To add some positive in my otherwise negative review, the settings are beautiful and gorgeous to explore and the action isn't bad.
I recommend picking this game up on a sale of at least 60% off or more, the asking price of $40 is a bit over the top.

Deadfall Adventures is basically what happens if you combine Alan Wake, Resident Evil, The Mummy, and Indiana Jones together into a game. It features puzzles that have to be navigated in the same way as Uncharted - by physically looking ingame at your notebook to determine the solution. These include puzzles like your classic Elder Scrolls/Indiana Jones floor tile puzzles, light-mirror puzzles like The Mummy/Resident Evil. lighting the right symbols or pressing the right buttons in the right order, slider puzzles, platforming type puzzles and more.
Like any good archaeology-fantasy story, it takes place in the early days of the Nazi regime. The Nazi's have, of course, obtained the services of experts to navigate ancient ruins in search oif ancient powers that can ostensibly help them rule the world, etc. etc. Did I also mention Russians? So within minutes, what does your character end up doing? Evidently awakening all the mummies and other ancient beasts. All of them.
This is where Alan Wake comes in. In order to actually damage and kill said beasties, you need to hit them with the flashlight enough so that shooting them matters. The mechanic made sense in Alan Wake because of the light and the dark being a permanent theme. I'm not sure it makes sense here, but I'm not complaining about it. I think in the Mummy movies the light wasn't kind to the mummies either. Other than shooting Mummies, though, you get to kill your fair share of "Nazis" - and really that's all you need for a game, right? As well as Commies.
The voice acting is bad, I'm not going to sugarcoat that. All of the VA's said their lines far too quickly and didn't seem interested in putting effort into it. In addition, a lot of the dialogue is very B-movie, generic, absolutely expected drivel. It's unfortunate, because this game had the potential to be quite awesome if the presentation had been pulled off with a bit more polish or experience. Presentation can turn a horrible game like Uncharted from a generic shooter to a phenomenon, and it looks like Nordic stopped somewhere in the middle with this one. Other than that, the game is also gorgeous. It doesn't have the best graphics ever that will melt your eyeballs, but it uses Unreal engine and looks quite good. There's a lot of epic scenery like the pyramids and Sphinx, but you may get tired of seeing it if you aren't into ancient cultures or Egyptology or any of that.
The only thing to really complain about other than the overall indie-ness of this game is just silly stuff like bugs where you get stuck ffor no good reason behind or inside objects. I actually fell like 100 feet when you rescue Jen from the Russian colonel guy, and didn't die - which I thought was hilarious. Other than that, the Steam store page is full of bullshots. I'm playing on as ultra graphics as possible with a GTX 1080 and the game simply doesn't look like that in most of those scenes.

The easiest way to describe Underrail - an all underground Fallout2 style RPG.
If you haven't played Fallout2 then this review isn't for you.
If you don't like Fallout2 then Underrail isn't for you.
Underrail has great story telling. The text is short and efficient and the quests are somewhat diverse. It's not at the Fallout2 level of storytelling (the pinnacle of RPGs) ** but it rivals the other Fallout games and most other RPGs. The characters are colorful and well defined(except for the protaganist) and the overarching plots well formed and motivating.
** edit- fallout2 AND Mass Effect are best story telling for an RPG.
Underrail takes a few hours to get used to.
The design of the world in Undrrail is self limiting because everything is underground and almost every turn is  a right angle.
In every fallout game, you happily open your shelter door and greet the sun. In Fallout, every dungeon crawl ends with you back on the breezy surface cruzing to base and hitting the bar. In Underrail you will NEVER see the sun. When I first started playing UnderRail I thought it might be too constrictive.
After playing 5-10 hours you realize that there  is a lot of subtle  variety in the maps, and especially the feel of the different towns.  The world is well thought out and it has it's own gritty feel.
And you can get lost in the map. The maps and the way they are connected is not made obvious. There are only a few signs and no in game maps, at least not so far. It is up to the player to piece the world together.  There are no quest markers on a minimap, unless I've missed something for 50 hours. Not having markers and maps is fine in this game because exploring stays entertaining and is somehow relaxing. And it doesn't feel constricting. The map opens up to underground lakes, rivers and a railway. Boats and trains offer quick-travel points.
The Skill tree is excellent. The balance seems almost perfect. I'm playing for my second time , on normal , (first was a rage quit). I've messed up a little bit in my allocation (I started a crafting build but didn't stick with it) so I struggled a bit but 30 hours in I'm matching up well against the mobs but still dying once in a while.
I usually play these things on hard but this game's normal is actually hard. I wouldn't play this on hard. It's not DAO where if you play on normal you aren't getting the whole game. Or Fallout2, KOTOR... where there isn't a true hard option. This game is tricky the first go through. YOU CAN'T RESPEC unless you use game cheat. Lot's of enemies can  kill you in one round.
Which brings me to combat.  First, there is an immersion breaking flaw in the combat. It seems that the game often wants you to fight part of the battle, leave the combat map, recover, go back and continue the fight.
The way I think about this is it's like a  long assault on the enemy base but doing this over and over gets absurd at times.
Otherwise, combat is well done. Psionics(magic) is seamless, interesting  and feels balanced. It looks like there are plenty of different builds to play.
Another negative is there are no companions so you will always fight solo.
I didn't play a crafting build and the game seems to want you to commit a lot of skill points to make a viable crafting build. Crafting looks like it's well developed. Certainly , crafting and skills are at least as good  in Underrail as they are in the  Fallout series.
The GUI is simple and easy. Sometimes clicks don't register correctly (or the hit box is faulty) and you can ruin a long battle with one bad click but it was the same in ShadowRun HongKong(I just played before UR).
The music is low key , sad violin synth to scary violin and synth with lots of industrial ambient ... it works. Fallout 1-2 had some of the best scores in RPG so it's hard to compare.
As far as story, the biggest problem is the start. Your character has no back story. You wander through the world as a blank slate just doing the whim of others. Sure, all RPG are fetch quests for others but you usually have more reason and purpose then in Underrail. ie You are trying to recover your memory, you need to find your dad/son/wife , revenge for what they did to your clan, save your home town etc. From the very start of this game everyone is a stranger and you are immediately their main go to guy.
Otherwise, like I wrote, the story telling is excellent and efficient. The characters are evocative, even the unknown bosses that you dispatch have personality. The world is different and makes sense. The inner politics of the various factions are actually interesting and easy to follow. I usually skip most of the background text by mid game but I read it all in Underrail because they don't bore me with long winded writing not meant for an RPG (see Skyrim, which I still loved, and many others).
Also, the game implements a novel and well done experience system(called oddities).
10/10 - though it has a few flaws it's so creative with it's art design, writing  and game rules that it gets a 10.

Why I like Warframe:
* Good gunplay and large variety in powers for various warframes.
* Excellent selection of gameplay modes.
* It is a genre-hybrid with some unique gameplay mechanics.
* Free-to-play done right with incentive to purchase, but with no requirement.
What I dislike:
* Long development cycle has resulted in numerous content patches that are designed for longevity with the install base. As a result, some of the content is gated behind activities that are more tedious than fun like codex-scanning or finding all the caches in a large level.
* Itemization is all over the place with relics being random drops and having a long list of possible drops when you run missions to unlock them. This results in a process that is basically RNG except that you have to read menus. This could use some simplification and more player-autonomy.

I have to agree with other reviews that this is much more of a "thinking man's" idle game. Every crusader has his, her, or its own special active or passive skills as well as equipment that can augment those perks. Furthermore, the effectiveness of those skills changes based on your team's positioning or even on which crusaders you're using. For example, the Hobo does way more damage if nobody is in front of him, but he's not very sturdy; or Queen Siri gives a hefty damage boost to all female crusaders. If you use the hefty gold-find bonuses and special active abilities that come with pairing Detective Khaine and Gold Panda, can you find the best spots for them to maximize that gold gain without too badly hurting your DPS?
If you play it a lot you risk making the frequent seasonal events too easy, which is too bad because the enemies and quests are pretty funny but they move by too fast. I'm curious to see how they balance out the limited-time heroes with regards to when/if they come back and how often it'll be possible to find new equipment for them. Currently, filling the holiday heroes with rarer gear seems to be somewhere between impossible and improbable without spending money. The game is in no way competitive, though, so I suppose that's not so bad.

Out of all the clicker/idle games I've played (Clicker Heroes, Adventure Capitalist, Time Clickers and Tap Tap Infinity) I am pleased with the progrees in the genre this game has made. Along with choosing characters and equipping them with gear; the player has the option of many different quests to partake in after resetting the world. Some quest runs require an amount of strategy, while others are just level runs. There are different formations in each quest tier for the characters to be placed in as well.
On top of the frequent updates, there are seasonal challenges to partake in. While fun, they are limited to a few days and if you're not quite up there in experience, you'll only be able to make it past the first two missions in the quest. Idol collection is a big part of the game and the player cannot proceed far without obtaining a fair amount. It's a grind but I find it to be pleasant.
Overall, I would say it's a new take on an increasingly popular gaming genre. With RPG elements added; it's definitely worth trying it out. You should know within the first hour or less if it's something you'll enjoy.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is by far this year's biggest contender for RPG Game of the year. The original Divinity: Original Sin shook the RPG community and will forever stand in the Halls of our hearts. The sequel looks to improve on just about every aspect of original.
At the time of writing, the game is in Early Access and players have access to the first act of the game along with most of the gameplay mechanics.
Character creation is deep and highly customizable. You will choose from numerous races and classes. You will also choose an origin story, ambient music instrument preference, as well as starting skills and abilities within your chosen classes skillset. This along with a selection of numerous talents that will aid you in your journeys, you really get the feeling that your character is your own.
Gameplay is absolutely glorious. The movement is much like any other RPG dungeon crawler as you explore the vast world of Rivellon. When you find yourself in combat things start to get interesting. Combat is turn based and played over a number of rounds. Players will spend their action points casting spells and using abilities. Some may damage your opponents while other aid you and your companions. There are way too may skills here to discuss, but suffice to say that there is always something exciting going on in combat. Once combat is over (preferably with your team still alive) movement returns to normal and you are free to openly explore the world and interact with characters to continue the story line.
The game has a robust crafting system as well as a number of other inner workings that can keep you busy in town for hours if you so desire, though players who desire more action and less crafting/fishing/customizing can still play without needing to sink time into extra activities.

Crusaders of the Lost Idols is a clicker game, well, unless you're recruiting characters that will deal damage for you. Set in a fantasy world, your goal is to pass through levels, with your party which is moving by itself and with enemies coming to you. Complete the quest of the level to access the next one. Every five levels, you get a boss to kill, which gives a chest. The latter hides cards with permanent bonus, new gears, new clothes or buffs to use during a quest.
The money you're collecting will serve to upgrade your characters, to recruit new ones or to unlock new abilities. Some of them are specific to your character, others will affect those next or in front of you while special ones will be used during the levels. In other words, each character can be useful.... if only you weren't stuck to 10 characters maximum.
That's the core of this free-to-play. Only chests are for now a paying item if you want to advance faster.
The graphics are quite cheerful and colorful, the soundtrack is nice. I must say that you don't need an account somewhere to play it. However, you can play it elsewhere and link both accounts.
I'm just disappointed that in-game achievements aren't counted here. Apparently, you need to reset the world (where you don't loose your acquired trinkets for example) so that Steam is considering that achievements can be unlocked. I don't know as I need to reach the requirements for it.
Anyway, the game is surprisingly addictive and simple to handle. Cards are just bonus, you don't have to build a deck, which is a relief for me. Given the fact that it's free, without account to make, give it a shot. Be warned though, you may find it slow without chests. I could enjoy the potential of this game thanks to orly and its key giveaway.
EDIT: I had to uninstall the game - apparently, it was causing a problem with launching games freshly updated or uploaded.

Fantastic fantasy sci-fi rpg that makes your choices, and decisions throughout the game matter. The game itself does storytelling right, by starting off with a high-octane beginning bordering on cliche. This is where the game differs from most other games, where others would continue with the cliche beginning of starting with your charecter dying, then revert back to the present with some sort of prophecy garbage. On the other hand, Mass Effect 2 rolls with Shepard dying and bases the game behind this trillion dollar man, creating a exiting beginning that leads into a solid mid-game. The way they present the beginning story means that the player is independant to the council's wishes, in contrast to the previous game, meaning a greater degree in this open RPG. The choices you make in the mid-game regarding charecters, items, and ship upgrades influences how the game ending will proceed.  The late game provides a final mission, no spoilers for you, that all I can say is epic and worth you playing throught his masterpiece to see.
Besides the way the story is told, the game makes many changes from the previous game which include: a revamped weapon system, a simpler level up system, a planet scanning mechanic instead of the mako vehicle mechanic, fully customizable armour, and no mako vehicle sections of the game, plus many more. The game also changes on the graphical front, with higher resolution testures than the previous game, that still run very well on lower quality machines.
There is much more I can say regarding this game, from the charecter progression, the amount of content, the pitched battles in the game, the fitting and well-done soundtrack, the fixed combat system, and many, many more. This game is one of the  best games I have ever played, from a production values persective, to a content and personal perspective. I give the game 93/100 an A+, plus the CDFW seal of approval, I highly recommend it to everyone who likes good video games.
tl;dr : Buy this game, it is good.
