I really have mixed thoughts for this game...
Essentially you race around in clunkers and beat up old muscle cars. The cars are supposed to handle like clunkers too, which they do. At least for the first couple of races. Once you're past like the fifth or sixth track, you'll realize that even though you're driving the same exact car with all the upgrades, all the AI cars start handling like exotics which doesn't seem right.
Second, this is one of those "make one mistake and you're done" racing games, if at any point you come to a complete stop you might as well just restart the track because everyone will get so far ahread if you weren't first..
Another strange flaw is the  turbo/nitro system. The game will give you turbo not for driving good, but the opposate. Instead of getting boost for drifting corners successfully or maybe jumping something, it will give it to you for smashing things around you which seems really counter prodcuctive. If I slam through a stack of tires to get boost, the speed I've lost will is almost always more than the speed I'll get from burning all my boost. Also, most of the things required to get huge amounts at a time will slow you down almost to the point of stopping.
Another huge flaw is the reset button. I find that I use it every single race. Want to drive through a fence or buliten board? sure smash it up. What about this wooden pole or small tree stump? Nope, that will wreck your car completely causing you to  need to reset. But, this wouldn't be as bad if the game didnt make you sit there and watch your driver ragdoll around for 3 seconds before you can get back on the track. On top of the 3 seconds you just lost watching your ragdoll, the game sets you back a pretty good distance away from where you wrecked. This alone will send you from a decent first to last in seconds.
For me I just can't be happy and play this game with these flaws. I can drive like a boss the first couple laps then screw up once and be done for the rest of the race. If I cant get at least third then I just reset it because theres no money awarded below that. Now, I'm not saying I want the game to be super easy because this isn't a pull ahead and win game by design, It's just the objacts that you'd think would be breakable and arent, or having to reset the race because I crash at the last second and lose my standings, and the terrible reset, I just can't enjoy the game without getting mad.
Now if you want to just get the game to drive backwards on the track and smash stuff or play the demoliton derby minigames, then get it, But if you want a fair driving game that you can have fun and progress in this isn't the game you want.

After hearing bad reviews about this game, I was a bit hesitant to even buy it. But the more I read into the reviews, the more I realized that this game was just never given a fair chance from the start. A lot of people came off as jaded as to what they wanted and expected with "Murdered: Soul Suspect". In truth, I feel as though they were wrong.
"Murdered: Soul Suspect" is what you expect out of a good ghost story, or even a Noir movie. You have many different characters that fit the roles they were supposed to play. The story keeps you guessing until the very end, and manages to keep you on the edge of your seat the whole time. While it is not like a sandbox game like many had hoped and desired, you still have plenty of places to explore and little nooks and crannies to find within the game's structure.
This game is not for a player who wants a sandbox world, who wants to shoot up bad guys, or that has to really put some effort to unlock, discover, and solve the many puzzles within the game. This is the kind of game that is for those who enjoy the journey it takes you on. For those who loved games like "Gabriel Knight" or "7th Guest". Good horror stories that make you want to discover everything that happened and why.
While the replay value may not be as good as some other games, it is the sort of game you will play, try to find all the artifacts in the first run through, and then put away when you are finished. You will then pick it back up after awhile, and play it once more for the amazing story it tells.

Deadfall Adventures is an exploration-oriented, first-person adventure game with some shooting and puzzles, including puzzles that involve shooting and shooting sequences that require solving puzzles to survive them.
The story is a typical Quatermain-style adventure - while it won't win a Hugo, if you like punching Nazis, shooting Commies, immolating mummies, or applying dynamite to irreplaceable archeological treasures, there is something here for you. The fighting sequences are mainly creative and well done - I enjoyed them more than, say, Bioshock Infinite's. The puzzles are generally straightforward, but they establish a nice, relaxed pace between the high-tension action segments. I took about 20 hours to play through the single-player campaign - I attempted to collect most of the optional treasures, at least the ones that were semi-obvious, along the way. "Normal" difficulty combat was perfectly doable with a gamepad - if you're using a mouse, I'd bump it up to "Hard."
Thanks to The Farm 51 and Nordic Games for porting this to Linux - I played the complete game on Ubuntu 14.04 x86-64.
There are a couple of technical issues, but I'm not sure if they're Linux-specific or not: Load times are massive, over 5 minutes for a "cold start"; the gamepad mappings are odd - "Jump" and "Use" are mapped to the same button, so you need to hold LB to interact with things (or perform mêlée attacks), which simultaneously toggles your flashlight.
Overall, I would recommend this game to fans of the genre.

The game was one of my faves when it was released. Unlike most RPGs, there were immense amounts of choices on how to build, and essentially, how to play as well. There is a main storyline, of course, and a presecribed path to take, but the game does sell on its promised choose your destiny format.
That said, gameplay is quite broken in general, and takes adjustment if you wish to scrape by without the broken aspects. For instance, you can make money simply buy buying and selling stuff to the same shopowner, as his stocks of items fluctuate the cost. Additionally, the most broken skill in the game is Physical Shield, as it not only keeps you from taking any damage at all, but you don't get thrown around, and you never lose your precious combat multiplier, so long as you chug mana potions, and that helps break the game wide open for you. But, in general, any character can grind to the point of being all-powerful, with some time invested, of course, as any build path is open for any character, as even though "Being good" or "Being bad" does influence your skill pool minimally, it's even more minute because fluctuating between good and bad is not difficult (especially for being bad...).
All that aside, the game was pretty much the first game to give a hero any type of plotline choices that I saw, and I must commend them for that. However, the game has a poor look for being released on Steam nowadays, and only diehard plot enthusiasts or general gamers who want to experience it all will enjoy this. I had to buy it for old time's sake, and while it has managed to accrue a bit of playtime, I don't see many out there enjoying this for what it's worth in this age of gaming. I really don't know of anything like Fable still, and I enjoyed it more than Fable III (haven't played the others...), but getting through the early game will be hard to weather through to get to the better parts of the plotline and become strong enough to feel less than some shrimpy character at times. In my opinion, casters are very underpowered, partly because Physical Shield is so overpowered, and will sap your mana if you don't kill things fast enough as a caster. The other paths get so much more powerful, and I don't see why you'd even bother. Still a huge step in the right direction for a choose-your-own-path type adventure, but there is still a clearly prescribed path, like any adventure with an adversary. It just has good areas you can stray from the path a bit, and they will effect your destiny in various ways.
I checked... I played it on Steam for 2nd most hours compared to any reviewer, and that's not all that much... I don't know what that could mean for certain, but I'd guess that the majority of reviewers who upvoted it are in it for the nostalgia. It was a good game in its heyday, but I believe that the strengths of this game would be overshadowed too much by its weaknesses in today's gaming environment, even at its lower price. There are a number of games that deserve being carried over into today, but while this one is on the fence for me, I'm leaving my opinion where it was; This game doesn't hold enough appeal to stand out amongst today's games.

Metro 2033 Redux + Metro: Last Light Redux:
About The Game:
"The Metro" series is a book based game, that is all about the life in the underground metro station of Moscow, Russia.
The story is all around the metro because this is the only place where survivors in the game could have survived the atomic bombs and the radioation that is all around the city as a result of those atomic bombs explosions.
In the game, the protagonist is Artyum, a young man who wants to join the "Rangers" squad in the metro and help fighting the Nazis, the Communists (AKA The Reds) and the most common and dangerous enemys, the Mutants. Yes, there are mutants in the game.
Gameplay:
In the first 5 minutes into the game, you'll feel as everything is moving very slow, literally, and you'll feel weird and uncomfortable to play, but you'll get used to it.
The movment of the game are nice, it lets you feel comfortable enough to be able to combat and fight your way trough the metro and use any weapon that the game will offer you such as on any other fps game, nothing to special about the mechanics of this game.
Voice Acting + Soundtracks:
Well, I have to admit that the voice acting of some characters in this game are really weird and awkward. like, when a little kid approches you, you'll expect him to sound like a child, right? Well apparently, Metro is a game where kids sound older than their own father. so dont be surprised if you hear an adult calling you in the game, and when you'll look at him you'll see a little scrub begging for money (BULLETS, in the game). Also it seems like ''4A Games'' haven't put a lot of effort into the voice acting of the game....
Now the Soundtracks, thats another story. The soundtracks of the game really fits to the environment of the game. Creepy ghosts, moaning monsters, Injured soldiers and battle-crys. Weapon shells droping, scopes zooming in and out, and your heavy breath as you're using the gas mask. Every sound that a good horror game needs to be perfect.
Ok, So, After all, Metro is great horror game and I cant say to much bad things about it. Its fun and intresting, it has a good story and its also a long game. I highly recommend playign this game to everyone who likes a good long story.
P.S: For the non-russian fellas who wanna get this game, dont buy the normal Metro 2033 game. It has Russian language only in it and it can't be switched to any other language. So do yourself a favor, and get the Redux version (The gameplay, graphics, everything is the same).

Have you ever played cookie clicker? Clicker Heroes? Loot Clicker? A Dark Room? The Monolith? Adventure Capitalist? Or maybe none of any of these? Clicker games are almost a loophole in each human bieng's mind, while playing it, the numbers of your "atk" or "econ" grows higher and higher, and then you "unlock" areas which are typically non-game changing in terms of play style. and with each "level up" you feel accomplished, which is way so many people feel inclined to play these games. Usually with these games, the player will play quite far into the game and then end up deleting it because they finally realize how pointless it is. Trust me, so many of my friends have raged. But Im here to tell you, this game will not make you rage, or feel like its pointless, so, what makes Crusaders of the lost idols stand out as a game?
Crusaders of the lost idols is an idle game, but it breaks multiple boundaries. Not too many, as there is still the core gameplay of a clicker game, where after awhile clicking isnt worth it and its more based around idoling, where you can reset your current game in exchange for something to help you on your next run. However, this game adds a much needed aspect to clicker games. Strategy! And thats not all! It also adds a very nice loot system with different rarity based items, events that ACTUALLY AFFECT your runs even AFTER the event has concluded! With me having spent 240 hours on this game, i can tell you personally, its a really fun game, it may take up a bit of your time, but its well worth it.
The actual physical gameplay is simple. There are hordes of monsters coming in on the right side of the screen. Your Crusaders, Like the heroes from Clicker Heroes, are the ones that can kill these beasts! Each crusader has custom abilites that can help benefit your other Crusaders or stick it to the monsters. As you play, bosses will drop silver, and other types, of chests! These chests can contain loads of different items that help you get farther through objectives. There are 36 objectives, more constantly bieng added, that give you a certain goal you will have to accomplish. As you continue to go through each of these, you will be givin idols! These idols give you a small atk boost so you can go to other objectives more prepared! The game may seem a tad overwhelming on paper, but once you get in game, it all is quite simple really. Here are a few aspects of the game drawed out.
Strategy is a huge part of this game. You start out with 1 crusader, that you have to click with to kill the monsters, as you get more gold you will start unlocking more crusaders. There are a total of 24 crusaders (not including event ones). These crusaders each have a special ability to give to the team. You can arrange them in a way so that your front line of crusaders takes barely any damage and heals quite fast so that monsters cant destroy you, you can arrange them so that you give tons of extra gold per kill, you can arrange them so you have massive attack. Each Crusader can be upgraded which increases thier health and attack by using the gold you get from monsters, but some are worth more to upgrade than others. So, each arrangement can offer pros and cons, moving, or upgrading, one crusader could be the difference between 100 atk and 100k atk, so you must use logic and problem solving to figure what is the best formation to suit your playstyle.
The areas in this game are amazing. Like alot of idol games, the areas repeat, the background for area 22, will be the same background for area 122. However, each area has a unique quest, it has nothing to do with the gameplay, except that you need to either retrieve X amount of items or kill X amount of monsters, but each of these quests are often references to games, tv shows, movies, fairytales, and more worlds are still bieng added! Its an amazing little extra thing the developers through into this game, but makes it that much enjoyable, the background are nicely colored and the bosses fit in with thier environment
This game has MONTHLY EVENTS, thats right FREAKIN HYPE! Each of these events introduce 1 more, limited time, world, that is totally unique, a new currency (in which to buy event chests and do event quests) TWO BRAND NEW CRUSADERS, that you STILL KEEP even after the event is over with, items for these crusaders, objectives for the world and its amazing. Fantastic fantasy sci-fi rpg that makes your choices, and decisions throughout the game matter. The game itself does storytelling right, by starting off with a high-octane beginning bordering on cliche. This is where the game differs from most other games, where others would continue with the cliche beginning of starting with your charecter dying, then revert back to the present with some sort of prophecy garbage. On the other hand, Mass Effect 2 rolls with Shepard dying and bases the game behind this trillion dollar man, creating a exiting beginning that leads into a solid mid-game. The way they present the beginning story means that the player is independant to the council's wishes, in contrast to the previous game, meaning a greater degree in this open RPG. The choices you make in the mid-game regarding charecters, items, and ship upgrades influences how the game ending will proceed.  The late game provides a final mission, no spoilers for you, that all I can say is epic and worth you playing throught his masterpiece to see.
Besides the way the story is told, the game makes many changes from the previous game which include: a revamped weapon system, a simpler level up system, a planet scanning mechanic instead of the mako vehicle mechanic, fully customizable armour, and no mako vehicle sections of the game, plus many more. The game also changes on the graphical front, with higher resolution testures than the previous game, that still run very well on lower quality machines.
There is much more I can say regarding this game, from the charecter progression, the amount of content, the pitched battles in the game, the fitting and well-done soundtrack, the fixed combat system, and many, many more. This game is one of the  best games I have ever played, from a production values persective, to a content and personal perspective. I give the game 93/100 an A+, plus the CDFW seal of approval, I highly recommend it to everyone who likes good video games.

Stasis feels like a love letter to Dead Space, Event Horizon, Alien, and countless other stories of terror in space. Waking from stasks (roll credits!) you find things are not as they should be: the space ship is badly in need of some overhead lighting, industrial machines clank in the darkness, and the floor has been painted in red and giblets. Looking for items to use with other items, your job is to work your way through the ship, find out what happened, and rescue your family.
Unfortunately the appeal of this enduring horror premise quickly gives way to padding, pixel hunting, and cliches. Obtuse objectives are a hallmark of point and click adventure games but feel very out place here, your character often reacts to things on screen but that are indistinguishable from the background environment. The biggest problem though is that while the game exists as a homage to the properties above, it adds nothing new to the table, and I found it both predictible and dull after about an hour into the game. Stasis is a dark & twisted horror story relentless in its dishing out of dread. It features, without question, some of the most eff'd up scenes I've ever witnessed in a horror game. However, this is not necessarily a criticism. Bleak stories can be very effective in provoking thought and in leaving a lasting impression on their audiences. Unfortunately, they also run the risk of going too far, and depressing their audience to the point of losing investment in the characters or story. There is certainly a threshold relative to each person on how much dreariness they can take. Judging where Stasis lands in this regard is kind of difficult, though. Much of the dark narrative twists were very effective in drawing me further into the story and intriguing me, but some just seemed flat out unnecessary. One scene in particular, that I won't spoil, really stands out, in this respect. Ultimately, the narrative in Stasis is competent and enthralling, so these moments do not detract from the story too much.
On a mechanical level, Stasis is a classic point-and-click adventure, with all the connotations that implies. Progressing through the story will require you to think critically about the tools you come about, and how they might interact with your environment. The game will take roughly 5-8 hours to complete, based on how quickly you can solve the puzzles.
Overall, I was very pleased with Stasis. I love both horror and science fiction, and Stasis is a proficient melding of those two genres. There's plenty of backstory loaded on to computer terminals and personal PDAs found throughout the ship, but you can glean a great deal just by playing through the game. It's also nice to see successes like this come out of Kickstarter, proving that crowdfunding can be a viable method for delivering quality games.

Good game with enough complexity to keep it interesting for a long while, although this does make it more difficult to understand and get used to at first. A lot of new players might find it too difficult to bother with and give up, but if you keep playing you will eventually have a moment where it all 'clicks'.

John wakes up from a pod on a deserted spaceship without knowing where he is. He only remembers going to sleep with his wife and daughter. Moreover, the rooms on the ship contain a lot of bloodstains, intestines, corpses and malfunctioning equipment. What happened? He soon finds an aid through radio; Te'ah will accompany us and tell us what to do and where to go. John sets out to find his family; priority number one in this horrible nightmare.
I was thinking all the time that John was similar to Isaac from Dead Space. His voice, his reactions and the spaceship somehow had the atmosphere of Ishimura. Minus the necromorphs, of course. First and foremost this is an adventure game so action sequences are set to a minimum. Our inventory cannot really hold more than 5 or 6 items and beside using these on each other we interact with objects in the surrounding area.
Now, the game has a sprite-based graphics engine so while it looks really nice it gives no graphics options for us. First, I found this strange but then again it really has a '90's vibe here. Some of the animations look great and we have a couple of cutscenes as the story progresses. This is slow at the beginning but later on it gets more and more interesting; some rooms only have PDAs for us to read. Employee logs, reports and e-mail correspondences shed more light on the background story.
This all is accompanied by great music and sound effects. While reading the PDAs a loud scream is often heard. The creators truly accomplished something great here! I would say a headset is a must for the optimal horror experience! The deluxe edition of the game includes the soundtrack in a separate folder under our Steam library (mp3 and flac formats are both available).
The game has a rather interesting achievement system. While many of these are granted automatically as the story progresses the rest are related to death or suicide. The former is obvious; whenever Te'ah says we should be careful we just need to do the opposite. The latter, however, means that we have to experiment with the items in our inventory and see if they can be used for suicide. Using them twice on ourselves results in a small - and often gruesome - cutscene showing John's last moments.
Stasis is an excellent horror game! Sometimes puzzle-solving is not obvious (we also often do pixel-hunting for some hidden objects) but apart from the increased difficulty it is a captivating horror adventure that is a great purchase if you like the genre and the good-old isometric perspective.

I picked up Murdered: Soul Suspect because a good friend kept stressing how good it is (in spite of all the negative reviews), and I wasn't at all disappointed with the game. In fact, I enjoyed it a lot more than I ever thought I would! The game relies largely on its characters and the murder mystery that's central to said characters' lives. If you're looking for a fast-paced, highly action-driven game, it doesn't deliver on that front - but that's what made it such a great ride for me as a player.
I wasn't sure what to expect of the game from the premise alone, but it does atmospheric horror really well, along with the splashes of detective fiction and noir, too. Investigating, gathering clues, questioning witnesses, and making deducions are all important to the game. It even has an historical angle that I first thought would be somewhat canned, but actually surprised me a bit by the end.
Collecting is an important part of the game and, although it's "optional," a lot of the story content depends on how well you can scour a map for all of the items - some hidden and some not. Even with ~10 hours play time into my first "completed" game, I still didn't track everything down! So if you're a completionist who enjoys searching and interacting with maps, M:SS definitely appeals on that front.
The other main challenge of the game is demon encounters, and they can be tricky to master at first, since some of the combinations are a little awkward. Still, by the last few maps it seems easier (as the difficulty doesn't really go up much during the course of the game) ... but it's definitely anxiety-inducing sometimes! All in all, the demon encounters kept the game from feeling extremely linear (i.e., like a visual novel).
So if you're into mysteries and crime fiction, love spooky stuff, and enjoy a game that burns a little slowly, definitely give it a try.

I wish there was a middle of the road button in Steam, not just the basic yes or no.
When i first saw this game i was really impressed and 100% in on the first day as far as picking it up goes.
I've stuck a no on this, but my last comment is pretty much a yes, just for the right price.
One of the problem's with this game, is that i perhaps didn't find out enough about it before buying it.
I do like my puzzle and mystery games a lot, i sort of had it in my mind that this would be a bit of a hybrid.
(Which it is, just not fully developed i think)
The whole marketing side was gearing you up for playing an epic murder mystery, but what you get instead is just very linear.
I'll point out the bits that really were poor, and then some of the bits i did like.
1) Fighting enemies - This is both a chore, and yet few and far between too.
It's almost like you "could" fight enemies in some areas as there are hiding spots and things to possess -There just aren't any.
(When i say fight, basically all you do is sprint up behind them and do a poor QTE)
2) Uncovering evidence - Not really uncovering, much more like clicking on things in the vicinity, with a running tally telling you how many you are missing. (This also leads into the next point)
3) Detective score - 0 reasons for this to be there, every investigation will rank you out of 5 stars.
Trying to jolt someones memory in the game? Well ignore the stars and just click on everything, as you wont get penalised.
(Same with the uncovering evidence, just get the main parts you need and move on, the only reason to listen and view all parts is for the story - i have a positive for this later as well)
4) Bugged side quests - Meet a ghost and solve their tale, only for the large amount of times that you exit and reload the game for them to be still wailing on about something when you return.
(They are supposed to go to heaven... i think after you do the mission - Though it never really says, they just get ingulfed by a white light and float off)
5) Masses of the same character models all throughout the game.
6) Map hub world -  I can see what they were tryng to convey, what with the ghost buildings... almost like a tear in time.
It's just a shame that theres not much acually happening, just a lot of weirdo human NPC's hanging around in parks and on benchs in the middle of the night complaining of a murderer hanging around (Your in a park in the middle of the night... errr)
7) Lack of locations.
8) Possessing people - It wears thin, especially when they only have two lines of internal monologue to listen to at best.
(Most people also have set paths if they aren't just sitting)
Ok, what i liked
1) Character development to a degree was pretty good, the main characters are fairly well fleshed out throughout the game.
2) The story, although you know it's going to be a supernatural sort of tale, it actually just ignores most of the witchcraft side of Salem until about 70% of the way through.
3) The ghost stories and tales are fairly well done.
4) What little locations are in the game are nice enough to look at.
5) Some times the random ghosts freaked me out a bit.
What could have made it better -
1) More sections with the whole "Cat" possession :-)
2) The ability to scare people and freak them out with possessions.
3) More locations and places to explore.
4) More... way more, NPC's and things to interact with.
So, thats all i got, i think when i was playing it i came up with a lot more negatives, but the story was pretty engaging.
If i had to give a score and some final comments i'd say -
6/10 - Only buy if you can pick it up for less than £10.00

First, let's get one thing out of the way: this is not an Indiana Jones clone. Indiana Jones was himself based on and a tribute to Allan Quatermain (H.R. Haggard, 1885) and Professor George Edward Challenger (A.C. Doyle, 1912). And the protagonist of this game, James Lee Quatermain, Allan Quatermain's great-grandson, has a completely different personality (and a couple of jokes in the game point out those differences).
But the feel, the mood and the ambiance are the same, so Indiana Jones fans WILL enjoy it.
The good:
When Lucas created Indiana Jones, he was trying to recreate the feel of 1930s action serials. This game succeeds in re-recapturing that feel and it's the main point in favor of this game. The scenery is beautiful and even the ceilings are worth admiring (not to mention that they also sometimes hold clues or things with which you can interact). The plot is unoriginal, but still engaging. The puzzles are logical and well integrated in the flow of the game. There's an interesting selection of weapons and they feel well balanced. You can kill an unarmored human enemy with one or two bullets, but they can return the favor, so you can't play this game as if you were Rambo. The journal, a very obvious copy of Henry Jones' journal, is not interesting to read, but it is very useful. Sometimes it just provides a hint for a puzzle. Other times, it's a key part of the puzzle and you can't solve it without consulting the journal. A nice touch is that the foreigners you meet speak in their native tongue, which makes it feel more authentic.
The bad:
The game is so linear that you might not notice a difference if they put it on rails. Backtracking is impossible because your entrance is invariably blocked every time you enter a new zone. I can't see this game having a lot of replayability. It uses the lazy, antiquated, and much hated checkpoint mechanism. Sometimes, the chekpoint is so far back that it can take 10 minutes to replay the part leading up to your death. Movement and shooting are ok, but in almost every other part of the interface, it feels so much like a console port that it's practically a slap in the face to PC users. You can only scroll back and forth between your weapons; you can't select the one you want directly. The POV is very strange and gives you the impression that you're only 4 feet tall. This feeling is exacerbated by the fact that you're unable to  jump on a crate that your grandmother could jump over. The jumping is so sluggish, in fact, that it's more irritating than useful. There are glitches that will let you get trapped between two objects and your only option is to restart from your last checkpoint.
The acting is a bit on the campy side, but not so much that it ruins the game.
But for all the little irritants, this is a fun little trip into an Indy-esque world and I still recommend it, though not at the ridiculously high full price.
One odd thing: the optional Allan Quatermain revolver that comes with the Deluxe edition is worse than the default Webley; it's just prettier.
Two suggestions: (1) don't swap your basic revolver for a better one you find. The basic revolver has infinite ammo, your new one does not! (2) If you're so inclined, you can change one of the ini files to give yourself infinite ammo for all weapons (instructions are on the web). A nice side-effect is that you end up keeping almost every weapon you find (you can usually carry only two), but you occasionally get stuck on one of them until some random event in the game clears the buggy state and you can switch weapons again. It's a fun way to run the game a second time.

What's good?
Movement is smooth, you won't very easily get caught on corners.
Controls are intutive for switching weapons and turning on/off various items you own.
Varied gameplay, you're not stuck in one place for too long. You'll see a mixture of the tunnels, the surface and even experience weather effects.
What's bad?
Inconsistent tutorial system, some things are referred to over and over again, but switching grenade requires you to hold the Y button which shows up in neither game.
Artyom (Protagonist) has a terrible method of speech. The only time you'll ever hear him speak is between levels, however during gameplay, people talk to him as if he's told them his entire life story. Everyone knows his name despite never being told. While this might be for immersion, it seems to take it away for me.
Overall, the game is good and is definitely worth playing though I probably won't be playing again unless a sequel is released. The game is less atmospheric than Metro 2033 and easier (this could be good or bad) while less of the gameplay is about surviving mutant attacks and more fighting your way through.
One thing I really miss from Metro 2033 was the feeling I got while alone and someone would shout "Artyom? Is that you" to give me a sense of safety.

The game is unforgivingly difficult at times, although that is simultaneously one of its greater strengths, as it is a wonderful game of "figure it out" rather than "====---> !!! QUEST MARKER HERE !!! <---====".  It does have the same questionable lack of interaction, like such as in the third mission having two very-well armed men sitting around doing nothing while you are pitted against no less than two heavily armed robots, a half-dozen armed bandits, and over a dozen ferocious rodent hybrids, but if your character is the lone wolf type that's not necessarily a bad thing.
At times I feel as though the Classic XP system is probably the way to go after wasting a literal crapton of resources killing yet another azurida with a low-leveled character, although the oddities system is certainly a fascinating design decision and it's hard to decide whether it's worth the effort (it rewards tediously clearing out every area rather than simply getting things done), but I avoided rerolling a character in favour of the concept and I'm not convinced it was a bad decision.
All shortcomings aside, this game holds me like few others do.  This is quite possibly the best CRPG made in the last ten years.  It's up against some pretty good contenders so it's hard to say that definitively -- especially as it wouldn't be fair to some of the other contenders, which I haven't gotten around to playing yet ;-) -- but egads, I can't believe I didn't jump on this the moment I found out about it half a year ago.

CRPG Gem that seems to have received far less notice than it should have.
First a few bullet points, and at the end of this review, a conclusion.
The good parts:
- Post apocalyptic setting (yes, I regard this as universally good in its own right)
- Interesting story with very good storytelling techniques. Starts off slow, and gradually builds suspense.
- Diverse and interesting combat build choices
- Retro graphics that are just ugly enough to look like actual old-school grapics, but good-looking enough that you never have any trouble understanding what you are looking at
- Tons of characters with lots of dialogue, for the most part very well written (though I have seen other reviews say the exact opposite)
- Fun and challenging combat system
- Crafting skills that are actually good
- Very cool and immersive atmosphere
- Very good soundtrack, think Fallout1&2-esque ambient music(sorry, Fallout had to be mentioned eventually)
- Diverse quests, ranging from "kill these guys" to "infiltrate a base and help a prisoner escape" to "do detective work to solve a murder", and everything in between
The parts you might not like:
- Large and at times maze-like underground layout with no ingame map. Some people like this, some people don't. Expect to get lost every now and again, but also expect to discover flavourful nooks of the game world that aren't necessary to progress, yet offers something
- Backtracking, lots of it
- Quests that really do not hold your hand, with somewhat limited information on the wiki should you get stuck
- Min-maxing of attributes and skill points to some degree mandatory for a successful character
- Endgame can be confusing, daunting, and has even more backtracking, but is very interesting in atmosphere and dramaturgical escalation. I spent a good hour reading computer chatlogs in an abandoned research facility, completely absorbed by how each conversational fragment shed more and more light on what exactly was going on there, but never quite giving it away. The best stories are often told by having your imagination fill in the blank spots. This is a cool storytelling technique that has every player end up with their own favoured interpretation of events.
The conclusion: If you are looking for a CRPG with a very good story, good atmosphere, good and challenging combat, no hand-holding, no quest markers, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, get this game.
If you are looking for a game with any of: polish, modern graphics, fast travel, clear unambiguous quests, forgiving combat, voice acting, cinematics, not having to read a lot of text, realtime combat, this game might not be for you.
Seriously though, buy this game. It might be my personal GOTY for 2015.

I found Mass Effect 2 to be less satisfying than its predecessor.  It has its fun moments, and in some ways the gameplay was improved over the first game, but I also was annoyed with a lot of the seemingly arbitrary changes BioWare made.
The most irritating thing for me was how they dumbed down the RPG elements so much that this game hardly qualifies as an RPG in my book.  The experience and inventory systems were reduced to next to nothing, and grinding and tweaking the inventory were two of the things I really enjoyed in the first game.  I've read that BioWare thought that people wanted more of a combat-oriented game, but I think those people have plenty of other third-person shooters to choose from.
Making the weapons require clips was annoying, because I was constantly searching for more ammo for my sniper rifle.  One thing I liked about the combat HUD in the first game was how it showed every weapon that was available.  In this game it only shows the current weapon, so it requires more time to change weapons.  Also, having the space bar assigned to use, run, take cover, and skip dialogue is kind of annoying.  I wound up skipping at least one line of dialogue, because I was trying to run when it popped up.
The reputation system seems like it was dumbed down as well.  Whereas the first game just about always had a conversation option leaning paragon, neutral, or renegade, a lot of the time in Mass Effect 2 those options are missing.  I also hated the quick time events.  Since they give no indication of what Shepherd is going to do, they just felt cheap.  The first game made me feel like my decisions actually counted for something, while the second game made me feel like I had limited interaction in displaying someone else's choices.
The soundtrack was not as good as the first game, in my opinion.  The first Mass Effect's soundtrack helped create an atmosphere in the game that made me feel like I was discovering some long-lost 1970s sci-fi movie.  Mass Effect 2's soundtrack seems more run of the mill.
The story never appealed to me the way the first game's did.  It's obvious BioWare was going for something "darker," but the whole time I just felt like I was forced into situations with characters I didn't care about and didn't want to deal with.  I was glad to see the few characters from the first game show up, but those encounters were few and far between.  The game also seemed like it just abruptly stopped at the end.  It seemed like there was going to be an epilogue, but all it amounted to was one throwaway line from each of the squad members.  In all, the story seemed largely arbitrary, given where Mass Effect 1 ended, and the implied conclusion to the series.  Perhaps it will seem more relevant after I play Mass Effect 3.
There is a lot of complaining in this review, but didn't hate the game.  It just didn't appeal to me the same way the first game did.  One thing that BioWare did improve over the first game was having the side quests seem like more than an afterthought, as they did in Mass Effect 1.
Despite not being entirely satisfied with Mass Effect 2, I am going ahead and playing Mass Effect 3.  So far it seems more RPG-like than ME2, which is a good thing.

First off. I know people are going to read this and go "You have 1.2k HOURS IN THIS GAME HOW CAN YOU GIVE IT A NEGATIVE REVIEW?"
Easy. I've played the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. I love it. Interacting with dinosaurs? Amazing. Building a base? Amazing. The overall concept of the game? Amazing.
The difficulty? There are so many times in this game where something stupid happens and it literally has a domino effect on everything else. It's immersive. You take ONE moment for granted while you're mining, or picking some berries and out of NO WHERE you'll get bum rushed by a large dinosaur who's hungry and wants YOU and your TAMED animal for dinner. Within moments the flying mount you've spent HOURS taming can be gone. It's infuriating. You get so mad, and then you go back, and you rebuild. You go find another dinosaur to tame. YOU won't get beat by the game. Even at higher levels it's difficult. It's unforgiving, and for that I appreciate the game itself.
Why can't I recommend this game? It's broken. I've been playing since Alpha and there are STILL snapping issues with buildings. You have structures that have clipping issues and make it difficult building things next to each other. You know minor things that can be fixed relatively easily that have just been overlooked.
Some of the dinosaurs are incredibly unbalanced. MicroRaptors are hands down the worst thing ever introduced to this game. You literally have no way to combat them and they often come out of no where and are found near numerous other dinosaurs that have no issue taking a nibble out of you and your mount while you're stun locked for 10 seconds. It's hard enough being knocked off of your mount. This is just one of the examples I can give as far as how over powered some of the dinosaurs abilities are.
Constant bugs. This game had NO business exiting early access. I can honestly say that. Every single time you roll out a patch you're breaking something within the game. It doesn't necessarily have to be a large patch like the recent one with aberration. Often times it's small little patches that cripple the game system to the point where it's unplayable. I recall a patch not long ago where anytime you went to harvest stone the game would just hard crash each and ever single time.
Stuff like this shouldn't be happening to a game that's out of Early Access.
Quite simply. This game was not ready for a full release. It still is not ready for a full release. You shouldn't have game breaking bugs every single time you release a patch. A proper game that is ready for release is Polished. It functions. This game does not fit either of those criteria. It's understandable to have SOME issues with each major patch, and we appreciate how often Wildcard releases patches and adds things to this game, but this game is still by all means an Early Access title.
For that reason, and that reason alone. I cannot recommend that others buy this game. Not until Wildcard fixes some of the glaring stability issues that it has.

Absolutely no spoilers in this review.
*Edited review now that I have finished the game. It took me about 7.5 hours(played it offline and steam doesn't track offline play) to complete this game and that is including time spent searching for collectibles and finding probably about 85-90% of them. So the complaints that the game is short are pretty valid. Had I skipped the collectibles I probably would have completed it in around 6 hours. That said, I loved every second of this game. The game probably doesn't have a lot of replay value either unless you want to go back through to finish the collectible stories or help any ghosts you passed up on your original playthough (there are only 3-4 of them though I think unfortunately.)
So I played this game until 3 am and could barely drag myself away from the keyboard to go to sleep. I am absolutely enthralled by this game and I love it. If the rest of the game is as good as the first 4 hours I've played of it then it will easily be contender for my GOTY.
The voice acting is awesome. A lot of the random civilians share the same voice actors but thats a minor thing. I recognize most of the random civilian voice actors from other big budget games. They are all great voice actors. So it seems the devs went with quality over quantity.
The visuals are great. I feel like most unreal engine games have models that look like they are made of clay, but this game does not. The ghostly effects are really cool. The way the demons move is absolutely terrifying. Animations are great all around with the possible exception of some lip syncing here and there on the minor characters.
The gameplay is fantastic.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the demons and being forced to run and hide until they lose your scent is pretty terrifying. Finding collectibles is awesome because once you find all of a set you unlock an audio short story with a piece of art and the stories are really REALLY good so far. Your ghost powers are pretty freaking awesome and the game rewards exploration with collectibles littered all over the levels.
Helping other ghosts solve questions regarding their deaths and helping them move on is a great feeling. These little side mission stories are very well written and acted.
Finding clues is somewhat similar to but much more enjoyable than it was in LA Noire. Once you find all the clues you do a little solving... puzzle I guess. You get three attempts to solve the puzzle. I don't know what happens if you fail all three attempts yet. But they are generally pretty self explanatory for the most part. It asks a question on the screen and you answer it by selecting the proper clue(s), sometimes in a certain order too.
The game actually makes me feel like a ghostly detective. And the story itself is amazing so far. The 63/100 metascore completely baffles me because this game is great and easily one of the best gaming experiences of the year so far.
I loved the ending. It wraps everything up in a smart way. I immensely enjoyed this game. If you have any interest in ghost stories or detective mysteries then you will love this game.

This game cuts a lot of corners, and in a bad way. I will start off by saying that you shouldn't expect anything innovative in terms of gameplay and story because there is literally nothing to this game. Have you played Heavy Rain or Beyond Two Souls? Remember how there was some gameplay in that? Take that,  but remove more of the gameplay and make it a noclip simulator 2014 edition because all you'll  be doing is walking around and looking at things. Slight spoilers ahead.
The detective bits? Bland, and obvious as the story is. Sure you won't figure out who the killer is but you will pick up what the deal is with the Killer and still have the protagonist and everyone else bumping their heads into the walls being clueless. Anyone could of picked up the patterns since it was so obvious but near the end of the game that you'll be eager for it to end. Unless you're easy to please. Oh there's a twist to the plot but it doesn't make any gatdam difference to the plot nor does it change anything at all for the later part.
Now let's get to gameplay, aka wonder around a building trying to navigate and occassionally posessing people just to influence. There's no point in posessing other people that aren't vital to the "INVESTIGATE ZONE" since they all have two lines in mind read and that's it. Reused model heads on different bodies and that's it, find a creeper ghost in some kid's closet only to find five more of him with multiple jobs. Investigate zones are what I like to call areas that you'll be trying to search every nook and cranny to find enough clues to conclude the level, and that itself is also really annoying. Most of the clues are hard to see, and I understand how it is but if I have to look hard through one big room just to realize I need to examine some bloody cat prints for no reason that aren't even remotely related to the case then what's the point? This game is more hollow than how I felt when I beat it.
As for the supposed combat? Horrible. There's nothing to it, and it's the most bland thing you'll ever experience. The demons that you face are always set on a path, they won't hunt you down unless they see you nor explore any rooms other than the patrol paths that they'll never stray from. Killing them is also a chore. Press direction + button = instant victory. That's all to it. They're just there to hinder you and nothing else. They'll arrive in the area you just left and have to backtrack to because they can. You can't get by them either so you have to fight them. You can hide and wait patiently. It just feels like they threw them in there just "because." They don't have any real point to them other than to add more than just walking around and "examine" things.
There are side quests though, and that's just more INVESTIGATE ZONES for you to burn time away in to make the game last longer. Will you get anything for it? No. There are collectables, will you get anything for it? No. Only thing you will get is achievements, and  that's it. There are no rewards, there's no good feeling having to help ghosts and frustrate yourself in INVESTIGATE ZONES that are so damn open or have clues so hidden that you can't complete it. No one in that area, not even the Taxi cab driver who was probably called the other night. There's no point in any of these side quests, nor the collectibles to find out "Salems history" or backstory.

A fun premise: solving your own murder, possessing cats and being able to walk through walls.
Too bad investigation is simply a treasure hunt followed by a guessing game.  Walking through walls sounds like it should be freeing, but the majority of walls in this game are unpassable which makes the entire experience strangely claustrophobic.
This feels like a game whose design had many more elements, but wasn't given the resources to expand much beyond the primary gameplay elements.
For a game whose plot is so central I would have hoped to have more twists and turns.  Instead I guessed the ending halfway through the incredibly short storyline.
I hope whoever did the visual design for the characters gets put on another project as their work was one of the few saving graces.

I'll start off by saying this isn't a game for everyone.  If you're all about being a big badass and toting around guns shooting everything, then you're probably not going to enjoy this.  Murdered: Soul Suspect feels like a watered down version of Alan Wake - thriller with a story that tends to pull you along with the "I need to know!" vibe.  I play games a lot for the story and this definitely gave me one.
I enjoyed the take on some of the history of the Old Salem witch trials; a lot of their information being factual.  The witch trials were a huge interest for me as a kid, so it spurred a lot of nostalgia in me for that alone.
The graphics were pretty.  Not OHMYGODNEXTGENBEAUTIFUL, but very pretty and fun.
Controls were simple enough.  It's a very point and click style game.  You don't get story-determining choices as you do in TellTale games, but you're actively searching, interacting with the enviornment for clues, hiding from demons, or possessing cute lil' kitty cats to get you into places you couldn't go otherwise.
My main gripes were very minor.
- You can complete the game easy in a day.
- Some of the cutscenes were distorted and compressed - which I felt took away from the appeal of the otherwise pretty graphics.
- Not much of a soundtrack.
- Some of the clearly older ghosts wearing modern clothing, which like choppy cutscenes, will yank you out of the "mood".
- Glitches.  Holy moly.  I didn't have crashing issues or "sticking" problems as some people have reported, but it absolutely infuriated me that some areas/quests were not accessable once you left that area... ala; girl on the beach being the main culprit.  So unless you're willing to sit through a game twice or have the manual on hand, this will more than likely agitate those who are achievement hunters.
7.5/10

Almost the thematic opposite of Magicka, this is a fantastic RPG for those of you who love classic RPGs.  Where Magicka strips every element of from a traditional RPG other than combat, Recettear does the opposite.  Extensive item management, a wealthy economy system, and a fairly standard J-RPG storlyline greet you in this game.  While there is a combat / dungeon crawling aspect to the game, you can 100% skip it and focus on the buisness of the game, which is item management and running your own store in a fantasy game world.
While the only complaint I have is that you really need a joypad to play this well, you can't use a mouse/keyboard combo.  Using the keyboard alone to navigate works, but feels clunky.  So if you don't have a joypad, it can be tedious.  However despite this one flaw, Recettear is ultimately enjoyable and worth the price of admission, I reccomend this game to anyone who likes the olderschool RPGs.

This game *is* a bit overpriced for what it is, but it's a very good game. I got it though a humble bundle deal and got like 95% off, which is well worth it.
You can basically boil this game to a lower budget Uncharted with basic FPS combat circa the late 90s, some good and sometimes involved puzzles that are varied enough to keep you interested, and a lot of content for a game in this specific genre. The main thing that will make you notice the low budget is the mediocre and sometimes downright awful voice acting and script, not to mention the two generation old animations and models.
That said, it's a fun game that *is* worth some money, I would just wait until it's on sale for $15-20 like it probably will be again during the holidays. If you like shooters with some exploration and adventure, this is one of the better, allbeit dated, ones that is currently on Steam.

I have to say I wasn't to exited to play this game when I first started. I previously played Fable III and only bought the game after hearing the poplar complaint that Fable II and III had failed to live up standards of the first game. Firstly,  the opening tutorial was painful at times and the graphics are not the best thing this game has to offer, but once you get past that, Fable: The Lost Chapters is a truly enjoyable game. The combat system is fluid for melee, ranged, and magic alike, the leveling/experience system rewards you XP for not only defeating monsters and completing quest but also for which skills you used to do so. For explain, if I used magic abilities, whether they be combative or not, I would receive Magic XP, which I then could spend on buying or upgrading my magical talents.  Thus the more I use my skills, the better I will be at those skills. Another feature I liked was the ability to Boast. Just after you take a quest you have the ability to Boast about what you will do on said quest, for explain doing the entire quest with no clothes or without taking or doing damage, doing so increases gold you will receive at the completion of the quest while also providing a challenge for the journey ahead.  In order to truly get the Fable experience and better understand the series you must give this game a try.

I felt the need to write a review for this game as the critics gave it quite a severe hammering on release and I wanted to put a few things right. First, I'll get the negative points out of the way. The game won't win any awards for originality, the story is pretty run of the mill, the combat mechanics are a little clumsy and the voice acting ranges from average to comical. To be honest though if anything these enhance the fun I've had with the game as I figured right from the start that it doesn't take itself too seriously.
You play as wisecracking adventurer James Quartermain hired to find a powerful artifact sought after by the Nazis. Sound familiar? Yes, it bears many resemblances to the Indiana Jones movies. It's primarily a first person shooter but with puzzle elements which might not be the most smartly designed and occasionally border on stupid but again, that's half the fun. The locations range from hostile looking temples through Arctic wastelands right through to lush Jungles and ancient cities. The game looks fairly pretty in most places and it all runs very smoothly with no lag or fps drops to be found. There are one or two glitches and some occasional pop in on loading but that's it really. It certainly isn't the buggy mess that some critics would have you believe.
One of the main additions to the game is the constant hunt for treasures which act as stat boosters if you find enough. These will enhance things like your health, rate of fire, reload speed etc and while they don't appear to make a significant difference it is however quite fun to hunt some of these down.
Obviously being a first person shooter the main selling point for many will be the gunplay. As mentioned, this can be fairly clumsy and the aiming feels like it's on some kind of grid if that makes any sense. It doesn't really take much getting used to and it certainly doesn't ruin the game. As I said, this is a pure old style game which takes me back to when first person games were enjoyable and Deadfall Adventures doesn't try to be anything other than a good fun game. I can't comment on the multiplayer aspect though as I simply have zero interest in multiplayer or online games. I have had a lot of enjoyment out of the single player campaign however, and while it's probably not worth full price I would urge anyone to give it a go if it's on sale.
Deadfall Adventures is far from original and it might not be the most polished game but it's still a very enjoyable shooter. If you have any interest in Indiana Jones or the Uncharted games then I'm sure you'll find something you like here. Critics were overly harsh on this in my opinion. Then again if it's not Call Of Duty or Fifa most critics don't seem to want to know these days anyway. I think there's a lot to like here. Sure, it's flawed but at the end of the day it's good old fashioned fun. Something most modern games overlook in my opinion. Give it a try. You may just be surprised.

If you have fond memories of playing Subspace back in the day, but always wished the game had a single-player mode, SPAZ is the game for you.
A top-down shooter, your ships handle like the one from Asteroids, with thrust and momentum affecting your crafts as they goes flying across the battlefield. You have an entire squadron at your disposal, but can only directly control a single ship at a time. The others are handled by the AI, but you can and you swap between ships with the press of the button. Each ship can be upgraded or swapped out for different ones better suited to the challenges at hand.
Instead of flags and bases, the game pits your squadron against varieties of enemy ships. Your squadron jumps from system to system in the galaxy, mining for resources to upgrade your ships while completing different missions. There isn't too much variety in the gameplay, with most of the missions boiling down to "blow up everything that isn't yours." There is a story, too, but it is pretty thin.
I got a kick out of the game, mostly for the nostalgia of playing something similar to Subspace. The lack of variety and paper-thin story hurt the game, and give little reason to grind your way to finish. But for the price, it's fun while it lasts, and I'm hoping for a sequel or add-on that fleshes out the core gameplay further.

As a game, DA is a fair one.  It's probably not going to be one of the titles that you will remember with nostalgy 10, 20 or 30 years from now, but it's not horrible either.
In terms of game concept, the main shortfall is its
: there's not a distinctive feature that sets it apart from other titles, not in terms of mechanics nor progression, or characters.  The fact that the game is inspired by the H. Rider Haggard novels (the same that inspired Lucas/Spielberg for Indiana Jones) makes the game feel like a knock-off of the glorious franchise from the '80s.  There's the fedora, the rolling rock ball chasing you, the ride on the mine cart, the female sidekick, etc...
At this point I would have still given it a "thumbs up" though: afterl all, not every single game must be ground-breaking and innovative.  However the execution is also unimpressive:
I should also mention that I played DA on a linux box (64bit, brand new nVidia card with proprietary drivers, CPU 8 cores, 16Gb RAM) and
.  In particular there is some issue with shader compilation, so that even on my machine (which is quite top-end, hardware-wise), just to boot the game requires ~3 minutes.
In-game transitions between different segments of a map are affected by the same problem, although at a much smaller scale (5-10 seconds of waiting).  This is acceptable while roaming on foot in the map, but it totally breakes the experience in fast-paced transitions like those in the mine cart run (basically you are left with a fixed screenshot and the music background, and when animation resumes you are much further down the railtrack than when you last were playing.
Again: the game is not horrible.  It's "ok", but the world is a big place, and I would rather recommend something else to a friend.

Deadfall Adventures is somekind of a mix between Uncharted, Tomb Raider and of course, Indiana Jones. A piece of warning though... this is a true BUDGET TITLE, so I tried to keep that in mind even though, the game falters in so many ways but somehow, I still wanted to keep going and finish the storymode.
The story is very cliché from Indiana Jones, The Mummy, Uncharted, Tomb Raider, all mixed together. The game involves the player into finding some major artifact but unfortunately, it was split into three parts and guess what, you have to search from them until the very end, where you realize that it was all for nothing.
The gameplay is lacking. Linear corridors after many invisible ways and glitches aside, the exploration aspect is as rotting as the mummy rot!
I'll put the good and bad aspects so you can have a better preview of the overall game.
PROS:
+Visuals can be good at times but not the characters though.
+Diverse geographical locations.
+Pretty lenghty for a FPS game.
+Weapons variety.
+Collectibles found are used in upgrading your skills divided into three categories.
+Soundtrack is quite average but does the job for a budget title.
CONS:
-Poor retelling of a story we've heard countless times before.
-Repetitive combat.
-Level design in this game is really bad. It's filled with glitches and invisible walls.
-Boring puzzles.
-Laughably bad voice acting.
-Dead or non-existent multiplayer.
RECOMMENDATION:
Honestly, I'm sure the developers tried their best to make a fun exploratory treasure hunt game but it failed on so many aspects that I find this hard to recommend. The game is lenghty and you do have a few collectibles to find around but beside that, once you do finish the main story mode, there isn't much else to do. The multiplayer portion is like a ghost town although, someone wouldn't had bought this game for the MP! At 39.99$, I truly CANNOT recommend this game for all its CONS but if you can manage to get it around 10$ or less, you may want to give it a shot!
The best recommendation I can give you though is to stick with Tomb Raider and Uncharted games. They deliver the stories more professionally and are more enjoyable in the gameplay category.
PS. I can't find much of a reason to recommend you the Deluxe Edition as the goodies included can't justify the price, IN MY OPINION! You do get the soundtrack with it and if you're a soundtrack sucker, then get the Deluxe!

Ok, It's Fable... We have mostly played it before. I picked this up simply to scratch a nostalgia itch. On the whole I found that it was good... still! Yes there are a couple of issues as it's an older game so the port hasn't aged particuly well, no controller support and as the magic system relied on three buttons on the xbox version it now relies on 2 (left and right mouse) which can make it a little difficult with all the scrolling to find the apropriate spell. you could of course get very wow style and have a million hotkeys buuut meh, its not really designed around it.
Anyway back on track, the port is actually good, 1080 supported (which looks quite lovely!)  AA is supported as well as some basic visual sliders and such. The only thing i found didnt work properly was the refresh rate, is seem to stick at 60fps, not terrible at all but i have a 120hz monitor sooo, well it would have been nice.
On to gameplay! Yes the game is flawed... it does feel a little like "babby's first RPG"  but it has bags of character and you will remember your time with it. i found on my recent playthrough some more annoyances... such as indestructible barrels, having to run MILES to pick up rent and a slightly janky inventory. Seriously when you pick up a book you cant find it in your inventory.... its in your hero's logbook UNLESS it is a note/letter given by a non main story NPC and then it turns up in the "other" section of you inventory.  Yes the attack cycles will get repetative you will get bores of the 4 or 5 different unblockable "flourish" moves, ranged combat feels slow and you become super powerful very quickly. and then you feel like all the experience you have aquired is useless (it is) But with all that being said, Albion is a fantastic world to inhabit, a lot of thought went in to contextualising the world, everybody has a life that you can see being lead, they will react accordingly... if you raid Oakvale, and murder people (even as a good guy) you will find that for some time the inhabitants will cower and run away from you... even though you have a halo....
THE BOTTOM LINE.....

TL;DR
For being a free, this game is completely worth what you get. You have agility beyond belief which allows for more than a 'CoD like shooter', and extensive modding which doesn't "dumb down" the player at all. Quite literally billions of mod combinations! This game has a fluidity which doesn't allow for a review to do it justice. What does that mean? Well, the nearly monthly, FREE updates, can completely change this game. With the Plains of Eidolon just on the horizon, this game will go from mission based to open world. This is the sort of game that gets updates which seem like Warframe 2. Imagine Destiny, but Destiny 2 was a free update. It's a great game, honestly. Not P2W at all, and is SO generous you'll probably spend money just to donate to DE! I highly recommend this game. Why not try it? It's free!
Intro
Warframe, a universe thriving with lush, hidden lore. The place where a species of technologically crude, and industrious Grineer have made home. The place where a plutocratic, advanced, and money greedy Corpus have made home. The place where a technocyte plague known as the Infestation has made home. Ah, and of course.. the place where you, the noble, honorable, Tenno; have made home.
Warframe Pros
Warframe is a free to play done right, everything in this game can be earned for completely free. You know how I know? Well, I've been getting EVERYTHING for free, and have spent a fair amount of hours to get this info!
This game has thousands of mods. Unlike its 'comparable' Destiny, this game has more than a dumbed down skill tree. This game has a modding system. One which lets your power have billions of stat combos.
This game allows for player to player trading. Whether you're looking for 'prime' gear, or platinum (premium currency), trading has you covered. There are people willing to trade you for mods, gear, and platinum.
The UPDATES, now this is a big one. This game Warframe has had so many updates, nearly on a monthly basis that it could EASILY have had a Warframe 2 by now. For a game being completely free, these updates are WELL worth your time. I mean hell, for the first time, we're getting an enormous expansion adding open worlds! (which we all know will be expanded to every planet).
The memorable moments. One, undeniable fact, is that this game gets sweeter as time goes on. With monumental quests such as The Second Dream and The War Within, this game will blow you out of your socks. Though, for some, this can take up to 100-200 hours to get to. It's crazy, but gives you the best feeling and memory afterwards.
Your Space Mom. Every Tenno needs to feel like they have someone.. SOMEONE! For the longest time, in the game, I was closest to my dear space mom. The Lotus!
The soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous, I know this is a random one but it can really hit you in the feels later on. Try looking up "This is What You Are - Keith" <- It'll bring you to a Warframe song that is too good..
Warframe Cons
The grind can be unrelenting for some. For people like me, the grind was never bad because of my constant progression, but for people who aren't patient or want things quickly (in a progression system) this might be a bit too much.
The lore is very hidden. There is a story, but for some major lore, and theories on it, you'll have to look it up on YouTube. If you'd like a good series I recommend StallorD
The enemy scaling. For some people who love a hard challenge, the enemy scaling might be too much. Not exactly the ENEMY itself, but more specifically the ARMOUR on an enemy. It can be insane to even damage an enemy after level 100.
Improvements?
These are simply opinions on minor things...
Dojo improvements. I think Tennogen should be introduced for the Dojo, more decorations should be added, AND massive group builds. I'm talking about decorations that require a load of resources. That way if you have a large and active clan, you'll have special things that show your true power, and riches!
On 'Finisher' animations for the Nikana backslash, a mark/bodysplit hould happen. What I mean is that you do a diagonal slash across the enemies back, yet no deep cut appears, or body splitting? I dunno, just a request!
Please add a flashlight we can toggle. Especially with the release of PoE, seeing in the dark is crucial. Either an option to turn on and off the flashlight manually or nightvision would be greatly appreciated. I don't know about anyone else but seeing in the dark hurts my eyes sometimes, oopsie!
Final Words
Now please, note that this is all speculation and pure opinions! I love Warframe! If you have any questions, need help in game, a clan to join, or notice anything spelled wrong, or anything I should add.. please feel free to drop a comment in the space below!

I'll say straight-up that not everyone is going to enjoy Underrail, but that doesn't mean its only for grognards that miss Fallout 1, 2, and Arcanum. I've never played any of those game (though not for lack of trying), and I LOVE this game. There are so many different ways to play, it's insane. It almost makes me sad that I'll never be able to build all the characters I want to make. Gameplay is solid, easy to pick up if you've played any form of turn-based strategy. Quests don't hold your hand, but with the exception of one optional quest at the end (which, to be fair, is supposed to be hair-tearingly difficult), it doesn't bother me, and the world is wonderfully fleshed-out.
Gameplay is solid, especially crafting. I'd be hesitant to approach a playthrough that DOESN'T invest in the crafting skills, they are THAT fun to use. The only downside, for me, is that in retrospect, the characters, while not always flat, I never had a connection with any of them. There are no followers in this game, true, but that doesn't mean all the NPCs have to be that way. However, the dev team are still active, so who knows, maybe that will be invalidated?
But, flaws and all, this game is one I heartily recommend to anybody.

Pros:
1. Two endings, and both are good in their own way. I got a "bad" ending, but I felt entirely satisfied and happy with the result.
2. Interesting, motivated characters all with their own stories.
3. A world with lots of detail jam-packed into it. The setting feels very "real".
4. Good voice acting.
5. Many difficulty modes and gameplay options to help with replayability.
6. Stealth options. Not perfect, but it was there.
7. Nice gunplay, though the enemies are a little bullet spongy in spots. (Not much, though)
8. Long campaign. My first run through took I think 10-11 hours. For the price, that's a nice deal.
Cons:
1. Level design. For me, I had an enormous amounts of time when I went "Where the ♥♥♥♥ do I go?". It was incredibly frustrating to finish killing everyone in an area only to run around in circles for half an hour trying to find the exit. Even more frustrating if you're wasting precious gas mask filters while you're doing so. It felt like they did an incredibly poor job of alerting the player where to go and how to get there properly.
On top of that, there were some sections (like a marsh) where I swear to god I just couldn't see anything. Fog, enemies, water, tall grass, everything. It was all piled up so high that I just couldn't freaking handle it.
2. Performance. I know my computer isn't the best, but I had all the settings cranked as low as they could go and I was *struggling* in some spots, which really took me out of the experience.
3. The way the "moral points" system is calculated. At every opportunity I spared people. I listened to conversations. I helped people when I got the chance. Still got the "bad" ending. :/
4. The lack of communication with the player about key information. It never mentioned the moral points system. Or the fact that when looting a body, you can strip an enemy's gun of its clip for their ammo. Or the fact that in order to buy a gun you need to swap one of your current ones. (and the fact that you get a discount on the new gun since you're trading in) Or the way that you take down certain enemies, especially towards the end of the game.
5. A little too much of the game is locked away in conversations you need to overhear. Cool mechanic, but overused.
6. Stealth felt impossible to maintain. Remaining compeltely undetected just seems impossible. There are some enemies who just stand right next to each other, and if you kill one the other is alterted.

3rd generation Clicker/Idle game, with some very novel new ideas bringing the whole genre forward, 9/10!
Time Clickers (2nd gen) brought the aiming part to the genre, and this game brings formations and that you can actually die/wipe with your team to the genre!
There are different campaigns, each tells a simple story with x numbers of stages, and the # heroes, all with unique skills, you can take with you varies between the missions. What is even more important, they have special goals (e.g. only 1 hero, or double speed of monsters, or double monsters, or less gold earned, or random slots blocked...) which makes each mission quite unique. And that is because of the formtions... as DPS and other skills depend, who is next to whom, and who is in front... and even after 100h, you are forced to try new combos and discover new optimal order how to place them to get max Dps or max Gold... New chars can be played for in special, timed missions... which adds even more variety.
A small warning to the devs/new players... these new char events are almost getting too many/frequent, as some of the normal missions take several weeks to complete, and I dont want to cancel them just to be able to play in a timed event (normally 1 week), as its the only way to get the new chars! 2nd warning: After ca. 1500 Idols, a lot of grinding is required, and the remaining missions take forever to complete (prediction you need min. 15000! but each playthrough gives you ca. 50-70)... this will soon make me stop the game... but I have more than 200h+ in it with a lot of fun, likely currently the best and most complex idle/Clicker game out there... so get it if you like this kind of games!
