One word can describe Underrail : Tedious.
With that out of the way, I would say that the first part of this game is very enjoyable and I really thought it would become a game that I would play over and over. The quests are a reasonable introduction to the world and it's mechanics and early fights are a decent challenge. The oddity system is really fresh and encourages exploration and makes looting random places really exciting and rewarding
All of that changes after you find the drill parts and the world becomes fully explorable. For some strange reason, the writing takes a huge turn for the worse. Quest motivation is essentially non-existant beyond "This is a generically dangerous situation and you're the new guy so you have to do it." There is no world map so the exploration all of a sudden becomes incredibly overwhelming and turns into a save scum fest. The only way to continue exploring the rest of the world is to bring inventory space killing TNT charges wherever you go and hoping you didn't accidently waste one on a place you can't explore because then that would mean walking all the way back to town to get more. Walking back to town is tedious in itself because a lot of the wild-life type monsters respawn and if you don't invest in stealth, you have to fight them all over again, both ****ing ways.
Speaking of going back to town. There is a lot of backtracking and unncessary traveling in this game. The merchants only buy so much of your loot, so even if you bring a whole fresh batch of loot to town, you more likely than not still need to bring it back to whatever place you designate as storage. In addition to that, their stock is determined randomly. Despite having a great crafting system, the extra tedium in trying to find a crafting component of good quality quickly becomes frustrating. It's huge lost potential for a game that focuses so heavily on crafting.
The combat is rough. Very rough. If you again, don't invest in stealth early, prepare to save scum a lot. Many of the enemies pack stuns, immobilizes, action point reduction skills or a combination of all of them. One unfortunately timed stun usually means a quick reload. The only way to circumvent that is to always have the jump on your enemies, which you need to rely on RNG for. It's fun to get challenged, it's tedious to constantly reload a fight just becuase the game is unbalanced.
Even if you slog through the entire game. You'll find the final encounter is one huge **** you. It is a backtracking hell for a puzzle that makes the boss bearable, assuming you've built your character correctly from the start of the game.
Underrail has great potential but it definitely needs a whole slew of quality of life improvements to cut back the immense amount of tedium before it can really be a great game.

This looks like it will unseat New Vegas as my new favorite RPG. 10/10.
There are many changes and improvements from Divinity: Orginal Sin 1, all for the better. The biggest changes are in the way stats are handled.
Instead of being a flate or percentage damage reduction like in most RPGs, armor is now an extra healthbar that has to be worn down to 0 before you can take damage or status effects. You have separate armor bars for physical and magic damage. There are abilities that can regenerate your armor and also a few abilities that can penetrate armor and damage vitality directly. This is a pretty simple change but the tactical considerations are wide-reaching. Nuking the enemy with status effects turn 1 (or being nuked yourself) is much more difficult now. You will have to prioritize targetting, as enemy soldiers have lots of physical armor, mages have lots of magical armor, and some enemies have no armor but large HP pools. On your own characters, you will have to decide whether they should wear more physical or more magical armor, and whether they should learn armor-regenerating skills. Another fortunate side effect of this change is that minor traps are less tedious, as your armor protects against harmful surfaces like ooze and electrified water.
The skill system has also been greatly improved. DIVOS 1 had a great concept for a semi-classless system, but it had some flaws. An INT character could invest a point or two in each school of magic and learn twenty skills easily while still kicking♥♥♥♥♥with wand and staff basic attacks, but STR and Finesse characters had a limited skill selection outside of the few spells that didn't scale with INT. Both of those problems have been solved. There is a greater variety of skills available for the non-magical characters and they can dip into magical classes more easily too. Getting access to class skills only requires a single point now, with any additional points simply providing secondary stat bonuses (+10% damage to magical armor for example). The new Polymorph school allows even a  10-int fighter to literally bull-rush enemies, or your archer can sprout wings and take the high ground. A real plate-clad, ax-wielding battlemage is a viable option now.
The maximum number of skills your character can know at one time is now limited by your Memory stat, so no more mages putting 1 point into every magic school and buying up every skill book you can find unless you're willing to put a lot of points into Memory. You aren't lacking for options though, since your class skills + race skills + bonus skills + potions, grenades, magic arrows and abilities from gear still adds up to a lot even with nothing invested in the memory stat.
The companions are pretty cool as well. There are going to be six when the game releases and each one has a unique model, skill, dialog options, and quest. You can even choose to make one of the companions your main character.  When you meet them in-game, you can make them any class you want, so the Red Prince can become a mage or archer instead of the default fighter/geomancer. Only four of the characters are out now, but they're all cool and likable, easily on par or surpassing Bioware and Obsidian companions.

I can't believe I'm doing this because I genuinely wanted to love this game. I watched it slowly develop for nearly six years and I was ready as hell to play it. Sadly I can't recommend it for reasons I'll go into. The important point is that I don't hate it or the developers, I'm merely hoping that with feedback their next game can be better. There is a lot of promise here. It is getting a thumbs down only because the bad ultimately outweighed the good for me personally.
First the good stuff.
-Atmosphere was superb. This was something that hammered out years ago and it survived into the finished product. It's grim and gross and lived in - and I loved the visuals for EVERYTHING.
-Graphics are great. The style is a bit dated but that's not a problem when you nail it.
-Good music for about 90% of the game.
-Protagonist was a decent voice actor.
-World building is fantastic. There is a lot to pick apart in the PDAs and I love how much texture there is and how many different angles it's explored from.
-Puzzles could use more than a single solution but for the most part the clues are there if you are paying close attention or even taking notes. I like the complexity of some of them - especially one involving chemical compounds.
-Overall interface and layout is servicable for a point and click and I could see future games made in the same engine and interface being excellent...
But... On the other hand. I just screamed in frustration at my monitor and quit - possibly for good because...
-Without spoiling things: You can die in this game. While in some situtions it works to elevate the tension - further in there are sequences where you can easily die over and over and over. It quickly slides from dread into tedium.
-All dialogue and cutscenes are unskippable. This is a small annoyance normally, but given the sequences where you may perish multiple times; hearing the same exchange of dialogue over and over can both drain the tension and draw attention to flaws in the writing or delivery.
-Even if you save Right before you run into an area where you die - it automatically reloads to your most recent autosave. So then you have to listen to the dialogue you were hoping to skip AGAIN before you can reload your save.
-Look the overarching story is fine but it might be a good idea to bring in more writers next time. While the PDAs are meant to represent a wide array of people and backgrounds; they quite literally all read like they are diary entries from the same person. With the notable exception of the mad scientist which brings me to-
-Seriously the villain is just a mad scientist? The whole story just swings into pure anti-science mode. Like; I don't want to dig in too deep but some nuance and complexity... some characters who were actually trying to do good would have been nice. The logs seem to show people who are either comically amoral or comically ignorant. Neither are that compelling.
-I did not finish this game so admittedly some of these things might be resolved; but Te'ah never convincingly seems like someone trying to Help John. This is simultaneously because of how she is written and the fact that the Radio helper turning on you has been a major trope in games since the year 2000.
-Numerous interface nitpicks like the above. No options at all at main menu. You cannot adjust audio channels, subtitles, gamma or contrast, etc etc. There is also no key to summon your inventory - or if it is there is no keybindings in options to see it or edit it. On multi-monitor setups there is no mouse caging, so it's easy to accidentally click on the border trying to open that inventory and minimize the game. It can often be difficult to distinguish usable objects as sometimes they have a glint and sometimes they do not. Since the PDAs also glint there are often simply rooms full of lens flares and picking apart what is important is more tedius than it needs to be. Different colored cursors for PDAs, usable environment, and inventory items would be more than enough without the glint.
I intend to revisit this game in a different state of mind. Perhaps I'm just too tense to slow down and enjoy this one properly. I'm not sure. But After being gunned down 10+ times by a robot who's detection radius is impossible to gauge without dying over and over again - and listening to the same string of dialogue with dramatic music trying to rush me along... I'm just tired and angry. I can't in good conscience recommend this one to anyone given the state it's put me in.
I am hoping that the developers sharpen their teeth on some of the criticisms pointed out by me and others. There is so much promise in the complexity and unique horror of the world they built here. With some more passes on the gameplay and writing this could have been a masterpiece.

I have absolutely nothing but praise for this game. I just want to start this review by saying that.
I'm not a massive horror video game fan. Hell, I can't even get through the first level of F.E.A.R. So when I first saw Murdered: Soul Suspect pop up as a pre-order at my local games store, I was fairly hesitant. Upon release, I was still hesitant, and decided against it. Then it popped up in the Steam Summer Sale, so I figured for half the price, why not? If I don't like it, no harm done. Luckily for me, I loved it.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic, the characters extremely well fleshed out (or spirited, I guess), and the story is amazing. You play as Ronan O'Connor, a detective with the Salem Police Department. The opening cinematic sees Ronan fall from a fourth floor window to the street below. After desperately trying to align his spirit with his body, the person who threw Ronan from the window, known only as the Bell Killer, appears. Using Ronan's own gun, the killer fires 7 round into him, and ends his life for good.
Only, he doesn't end Ronan's afterlife, and this is where the fun begins. You play through the game trying to solve the mystery behind not only your own murder, but the murder of several young girls throughout the town. What follows is one of the most brilliant gaming experiences I have ever had the pleasure to play. Using an array of otherworldly abilities, and the assistance of a girl who can see and interact with Ronan, you embark on a mission to find the killer, and put your soul to rest.
A special mention goes to the collectables throughout the game, especially those required to unlock short horror stories. These just upped the atmosphere of the game, and I felt really immersed in the world of modern day Salem. Whilst the game isn't overly long, it has been thoroughly enjoyable, and I recommend it to anyone who's played L.A. Noire, and seen the movie Ghost (with Patrick Swayze of course). This game, to me, felt like a mashup of those two instances of media, and Square-Enix really pulled it off.
So, after all that text, do I recommend this game? Yes. Yes I do. And shame on all those who don't.

I'm writing this mainly for the Steam Summer thing, but it also happens that I never got around to recommending this for some reason.
On the surface, Recettear looks like a cutesy little animu game - and it is - but below the uguu~ exterior lurks a solid, incredibly addicting, surprisingly deep, seriously awesome gem of a game.  Store management is what it's about, and that includes buying low and selling high, decorating to attract specific clientele, playing favorites and garnering favor, and dungeon runs with a colorful array of customers-turned-companions.  The gameplay is simple, forgiving, and above all, fun.  50+ hours I've spent on this, and there are still personal goals I've yet to achieve.
The bottom line: Recettear is a fantastic little game that can easily occupy tens of hours of your time, and you'll love every second of it.

An obvious labor of love, and a love letter to Star Control 2... and a leading candidate for exemplifying the necessity of polish in games. It is so mind-bogglingly dull thanks to really poor pacing and a nasty set of balance issues that I really can't recommend it at all. Supposedly it's still being worked on, and I can see modders fixing almost all the problems with the game, but right now it's just garbage. There are ideas and systems in place that could almost certainly be fun, and they simply aren't, thanks to some bad math, for the most part.
As an addendum, I feel the need to point out that combat is mindless and broken. Examples: AI is brainless and employs its weapons for minimal effect, often failing to use their full complement of weaponry. Enemy AI uses a simple tactic of running away when their health is low, which can lead to endless chases if you happen to pick a slow set of ships. Your own AI is almost impossible to control precisely and loves to wander into range of enemy weapons, and shoot your allies. In a late-game mission, you are tasked with defending four generators simultaneously: attempting to do so will get them all blown up. But, if you concentrate all your ships at one generator, the enemy completely ignores the other three. The list goes on. DON'T BUY THIS GAME IN THIS STATE.

Of all the appeals: shooting, hacking, sneaking, lockpicking, I played through the tutorial and although they have a large amount of customizable stats, it didn't seem worth investing time into this game because shooting was: click gun, click target. Lockpicking: click lockpick, click door. Hacking: click hacking tool, click thing that needs to be hacked. Sneaking seemed awkward as well. You need to hide behind walls to avoid camera angles, but because you're behind the wall you need to put yourself in the open to see where the camera is looking.
Also during combat, if you didn't read those clunky paragraphs of text, you need to know that space ends your turn, and enter ends combat mode (under conditions like: all enemies are neutralized, or you have avoided line of sight long enough to escape.) It doesn't really prompt you the way some games do (think Civ V; a large button glows saying "END TURN" once you've taken all possible actions.) So even though I did read the text it felt awkward at the end of turns because it didn't feel right. Hard to explain, maybe it's just me there. But at the end of battles: all enemies are neutralized but you're still in combat mode. I feel it should just end; or even just use the same button (spacebar, instead of enter.)
I couldn't let this dry gameplay go, because dialog is also dry. Explanations of the above processes (click gun, click target) took entire paragraphs, sometimes several. The writers for this game need more experience. Mostly, it just wasn't gripping for me, in the way a game like Undertale, or Tales from the Borderlands (even just the Borderlands series in general). The writing lacked humor; they had a few jokes that were okay (in tutorial you ask: How do I hold this gun? Guy answers: Good one. *then a huge awkward paragraph that was hard to read.)*
I would not recommend this game: gameplay was weak, writing was also weak. Character creation was fun though; I got to imagine all the cool things I would be doing. Except it's all click this click that, without cool animations to make it feel satisfying.

All the most popular positive reviewers have spent about 20 hours ingame and were not even close to finish the game. But the people who gave the most helpful negative reviews did and thereby spent about 150 hours ...
First: besides the setting Underrail has not much in common with the old Fallout series. The NPCs are forgettable, the story underwhelming and the humor almost non-existent.
The gameplay consists of mainly three parts:
- Most of the time is to be spend on safe scumming since you are fragile and weak throughout the game. Wrong dices mean an instant reload. Not seeing the mines scattered everywhere means an instant reload. Bumping into an enemy while sneaking means an instant reload.
- Besides this, you will spend hours with with walking around. There's no map and the quick travelling possibilites are very limited, so you have to get to the next town and back by foot.
- The rest of the time goes into the clunky vendor system.
In total the game does not reward your specialisation but punishes you for all the skills you did not invest in. On the other hand, a "balanced" build will just fail in every regard and is no viable option either. I feel that this game is only enjoyable for hardcore gamers who seek challenges and won't get frustrated by trying over and over again. It's not like in Fallout where you where just miss stuff due to the drawbacks of your build. No, you will constantly die here, just because of everything. This is a game for min-maxer.
I appreciate the work and the heart the developers put into this game, and I value some innovations regarding the mechanics (i.e. the oddity system). But all in all it's neither interesting nor fun to play, just tedious. I feel sorry for voting it down, but I really can't recommend it.
Edit:
Ye, I can see the irony of being top listed with far less then 100 ingame hours. But well, that was obviously not the case when I asked myself "Will it ever become more enjoyable? Will my issues dissolve later on? Should I continue?" and therefore dediced to check out the (negative) reviews. I trust you still get my point.
Edit2:
I've just played Age of Decadence. This game is everything Underrail attempts to be but fails. It's  hard, but in a rewarding way, it presents a post-apocalyptic scenario (in a different setting), it offers different ways to solve quests (with consequences), and it makes you curious about all the content you've missed due to your build/stats. Even if there isn't any jury-rigged smg or mutant in the whole game, it feels more like a sequel to the old Fallout series than any other game out there, including Underrail.
Really enjoyed this game, a lot of the small details are fleshed out and was a pretty good point and click survival horror-ish experience.

Post-apocalyptic gaming fans rejoice, for this is another gem in the ever expanding genre.
UnderRail is packed with content from its complex story arcs and decrepit scenery, to is piles of guns, bullets, armor, and plenty of foes to use them on. Not to mention the Mind powers. Fill your pockets to the brim, loot, kill and quest your way across a rather massive complex of caves, tunnels and subway systems. Experience a society twisted by apocalypse, choose from factions or pave your own path. As in any RPG the choice is yours, and boy are there a lot. Though, a word of warning, don't expect to be a "jack of all trades" in this game. You must find a specialty and perfect it, otherwise the game will beat you down like the sniveling indecisive worm you didn't know you are.
Unfortunately I was unable to complete even the games main story due to my hard drive frying. Although with 60+ hours on record I can say I have an accurate impression of the game. Although it goes with out being said, this is not a game that you can sit down and beat in a day, or even a week. At least if you plan on experiencing anything, I suppose you could speed run through the game in a 24 hour play through. You'd have to be damned lucky though, because there is more than one spike in difficulty throughout the game. If you want a game that you can deeply invest yourself in and still feel some bit of sanity at the end of it all, this is the game for you.
The gameplay mechanics don't come with out their learning curves, but what respectable turn-based game doesn't? There have been patches out for the game since I played last. So I'm sure a lot of the bumps have been smoothed out, not that there were a lot to begin with.
All in all the game is well rounded and well worth the price, though it doesn't come without its cons. I 100% recommend this game.

I have played Divinity Original Sin Enhanced Edition, It has to be one of the best games I have ever played in terms of provided content, coop, exploration and level of adaotation required in many of the opponents you encounter.
Despite Early Access being limited with content release, voice overs, maps and skills, the game has still successfully impressed me, there are so many variable options that allow you to make the story fit to your playstyle, you can so choose to go about quests however you choose....i.e if you need a key to save someone, you can pickpocket the person who has said key, instead of follow through with their demands.....and similar like things, combat is fantastic, the reconstruction of the AP system is amazing and works brilliantly, the way you memorise skills for fights and have the option to use any  combination of weapons you want is also a really nice touch. I personally find that the start can be very off-putting to players perhaps seeking a more casual playthrough, simply because good gear at the start is hard to find and it takes many hours to sift through enough quests and objectives and even area's just to progress to a stage where you feel "comfortable".
The only bad point that comes to mind after playing just under 30hrs, is that combat seems to be heavily based on a need to be the same or higher level than your opponent, I have found that despite having fairly good gear, if an opponent is even 1 level infront of me, the battle is very challanging and any hits you land seem to do very little damage...where as if I return, being the same level with the same gear, I can breeze through them, I am unsure if this is just early access stuff or the way they have chosen to go about combat.
Overall, I recommend both, they are extremely fun with friends and fit a varying style of game types like a mix of rpg and rts, stealth...all out, magic, melee, archery. And I enjoy that the game is not a straight line, sometimes you have to turn back and find the right gear, or adapt how you enter combat or return with skills that counter the enemies. If you made it this far....I only write reviews for games Im extremely impressed at...so for me - 10/10

Its been a long time, but with CAYNE coming out I thought I would give this game a review. Stasis is a theird-person isometric horror game with a very strong focus on the story. There are a few light puzzle elements, but nothing that should really try your brain.
I will not mention any details about the story, so don't worry about spoilers. The story is well written, hitting on all the points you want a space horror game to hit. If I had to describe it, I would say that it is a mixture of Alien: Isolation and Dead Space. There are a few moments where it feels like the developers where trying to shove their lack of cliches in my face, which was unnecessary, and there were a few strange moments towards the end that could have used more explanation. Overall, the story of the game was solid, and the ending left me with chills.
The horror aspect of the game is what really drew me to Stasis. Stasis is extremely atmospheric, with high quality graphics and excellent ambient sounds. Everything I saw and heard served to add to the tension, which was capitalized on with a few well placed scares. I never felt that the protagionist John was ever in a truly safe place and it kep me moving and jumping at shadows. Stasis did not scare me as much as Dead Space, another top quality space horror game, but it gave me a greater feeling of dread. Also, peering into the labs on the ship creeped me out like nothing I can remember.
The art style of Stasis deserves mention too. It serves its purpose well, adding to the atmosphere of the game. However, when played on a large monitor, some of the backgroud textures get stretched and warped. In a game that depends so much on the visual aspect (espically when some of the gameplay functions like a hidden object puzzle) this can be a problem. In addition, graphical options are lacking. I have heard that some people experience major graphical problems, so if you plan to buy Stasis, find out if it will run well on your machine.
Stasis is gamplay light. I didn't "play" it as much as I observed it. I was stuck only twice, once because I didn't know I could pick up an item on the ground and once because I didn't know that I could use one item on another. If you have ever seen an adventure game, then you know how Stasis plays. The item interactions for the most part make perfect sense, and those that I found confusing could quickly be solved by process of elimination due to the small inventory size. Occasionally background objects obsucured items to interact with and occasionally I thought something I needed to click on was background. However, these only occured 2-3 times in my 6 hour playthough. Minor spoilers for the rest of this paragraph. If anyone remebers the eyeball scene in Dead Space 2, there is an equally gruesome self surgery segment in Stasis that was one of the major highlights. I actually winced several times in my chair as John screamed his way through... very well done!
Stasis took me just under 6 hours to beat. I found every item and data log on my first playthrough, and I have no real desire to go back to see all the (incredibly gruesome and entertaning) death scenes. If I had run through without reading every bit of text, I think I could have completed it in just over 3 hours.
Overall I give Stasis one thumb up. By no means is it my favorite game, or even in my top ten. I would not reccomend it to anyone who has not played and enjoyed slow paced adventure games and space horror games. If that sounds liek your cup of tea, definently get Stasis. It is great to kill an afternoon with (I expected to only play 2-3 hours of it and beat the whole thing in one sitting). I don't think I will ever play it again, but I loved my playthrough and I am looking foreward to CAYNE next year.

Personally, I enjoyed the experience that was Deadfall Adventures, because this game is meant for people who are fans of the Adventure/Fantasy genre, but with archaeologists.
Sadly this means not everyone might enjoy this, as this follows the usual "Get to the artifact before the badguys get to it and use it for world domination" cliche. Also, since the game is focused in the first person, some gamers might expect alot of good action in a first person perspective environment, but I will say that the shooting bits of the game are pretty generic, along with the usual cliche armies of Nazis and Russians (yes the two most cliche kinds of badguys in shooters are in the same game together.)
In my opinion, I did not mind the cliches as they were exactly what I wanted and expected from the game, because the game does take place in the eyes of an archaeologist, and I always like adventures involving such a profession. This game does it's best to recreate the kind of Indiana Jones like adventure we expect in a game involving archaeologists, so I understand why the shooting sections seems generic, because the game wants to focus more on the actual adventure and not just drown it in FPS heaven... which can be a bad thing if overdone.
I heard a bunch of people complained about some of the puzzles in the game, saying it was either too confusing, too straight forward, or the hints of the ingame journal seem too vague. I played through the game myself and only once did I have to look up a walkthrough for a puzzle, turns out that certain puzzle I was stuck on was super simple as all I had to do was shoot a lever. Some puzzles in the game did seem confusing at first to me, but after some thought and looking around I did actually figure out what to do, and the journal only seemed very vague to me just once in the game, which was at that one super simple puzzle I mentioned. There was indeed some simple straight forward puzzles, but I felt these puzzles were a simple relief to the bigger and more complex puzzles I encountered previously. Overall, I felt the puzzles were fun and it felt good just to finally solve each one.
My only complaint in the game is character animations in the cutscenes. Characters move awkwardly in cutscenes, which reminded me of how bad the character animations in the game Dead Island were in cutscenes when I used to play that.
Other than that, I pretty much enjoyed myself with the rest of the game.
My favourite part of Deadfall Adventures was the very cool and well done minecart chase scenes were done in the Mine level of the game. That part of the game made me feel very nostalgic as this seemed to be a clear reference to the minecart chase scene in the film Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.
Sadly I could not try out the multiplayer portion of the game, since nobody was hosting anything. So I shall skip this part of the review since I was late for the party.
Overall, I enjoyed this game. I really liked the adventure it let me experience, as I also had alot of fun with the characters, even if our archaeologist hero seemed awkwardly animated in cutscenes along with everyone else. I got through alot of fun puzzles and moments in the game, just feeling the nostalgia of older adventures touching my heart with each step.
Now, I recommend this game to people and fans who enjoy adventures starring archaeologists, travelling, exploring temples, avoiding traps, solving ancient puzzles, and recovering mythical and genuine artifacts for fortune and glory. This game is not as bad as Metacritic says on the store page, as I feel it deserves more, because the game is based for a certain kind of audience who would enjoy this, no matter how cliche the things in this game sound. I missed playing a good adventure starring an archaeologist in the 20th century, and that is exactly what I got to play once again with Deadfall Adventures.
Thank you Farm 51 for giving me another adventure to play. I hope the next adventure you guys make will be a successor to Deadfall Adventures, because you guys deserve more than that cruddy 53 out of 100 Metacritic gave you for it.

A lovely doujin game, part strategy, part tycoon, part dungeon crawler. You play as Recette Lemongrass, a clueless young girl who is given 4 weeks to pay off a loan her father took and disappeared with. You take over his shop where you can buy and sell various items to earn money. You can buy and resell items from the marketplace, or from people or you can go and do dungeons to get items without having to pay for them.  The idea of the game is to earn a profit while keeping your customers happy so that they will return for repeat business. The game gradually introduces gameplay mechanics until you realize that there is a fairly deep game hiding behind the cute exterior presentation.
Don't be put off by the Japanese style, the Anime look or the fact that it's made in Flash. This is the reason we play games... to discover new and wonderful experiences that can be had through this medium. I thought it was worth full price, but it's definitely worth getting in a sale.

Recettear: An Item Shop’s Tale, or Recettear for short, is a very intriguing time/money management game with some interesting mechanics to boot. Essentially, you play as Recettear, a young woman living alone in a home that apparently has a huge mortgage on it. Your father took out the mortgage (or loan, whatever) but has yet to pay it back – and he mysteriously vanished! Yeah I didn’t really get that and could have probably thought of a better back-story myself, but hey, it doesn’t really matter!
A fairy comes to pay you a visit one day to take the home away from you (Hey I thought Fairies were nice?!) because the loan is outstanding, but then takes pity on you (Oh right, yep, Fairies are nice) and develops a plan for you to pay back the loan – Turn your downstairs into an Item Shop. Apparently you live in unnamed (Maybe it has a name and I missed it) RPG village where all manner of NPC characters live! How convenient! The intention is to buy cheap goods from the local Guild Master or market, when things are on sale, and resell them at your Item Shop for a markup. Using these funds you’ll of course buy more and buy and sell more and more. An endless circle of buy low, sell high.
But wait, there’s more! Should you be so inclined, the RPG village also has a dungeon! Should you choose to enter the dungeon, you’ll take an adventurer with you (And you’ll unlock more as you play the game) to slay monsters and descend deeper into the depths of the dungeon. Essentially you’ll get free items from killing the baddies, assuming you make it out alive. The dungeon is a very neat feature, and you need to use it in order to unlock more parts of the story line or other adventurers – however I found myself not using it because I could make a much greater profit from buying cheap goods and reselling them normally. You would think that getting something for free and reselling it would be better, but in my experience, I was getting rather junky items even when I went further down the dungeon in any later play through. Also it doesn’t help that it uses 2 pieces of the “daily pie” so to speak (A day is not endless. Going to market, opening the store, adventuring the dungeon or progressing the story takes a portion of the day) and also I really sucked at it. I am a video game pro, but found myself frustrated at the difficulty of some of the boss battles at times. But hey, that’s the challenge and charm of Recettear!
So as you earn money, at the end of each week, you have to pay back a portion of the loan. It starts out small, but then becomes exponentially larger! Week one you may have to pay back 40,000 (Not exact figures, pulling from memory right now…) and week four you find yourself needing 1,200,000! Say WHAT!? It’s achievable… …once you play through another time! If you fail to make a loan payment, the game ENDS! Game over, done, finished, ka put. However, not all is lost! You may get to start the game over from day 1, but you get to keep all the items you have in stock. So when you lose the game, you somehow go back in time (Not really, just my way of thinking how this works…) and have a huge stock of expensive items that you wouldn’t have had on your first play through. It took me three game overs before I was able to make all the loan payments and finish the game. I think it’s a very nice addition to the game, a handicap if you will – if you lose, not all is lost and you can try again with a little help.
Overall, Recettear has an extremely cute (I can’t believe I used the word ‘cute’…) visual appeal and has a great sound and music score included. The story line is interesting to say the least (Some of the dungeon adventurers are odd, but hey, that’s part of the charm!) and has lots of replay ability (Not just replaying when you lose, but once you win you can continue to play and unlock more items and upgrade your store to be better yet!). Overall great game, well worth a play through if you’re interested in JRPG’ish style stories and business sense.

I loved this game when I had it on Xbox. I have heard and seen it as being one of the most disapointing games of it's time, but I loved it. I went into the game blind, and loved it. I think it was because it was expected to be much more, but I was very happy where it was. It had plenty of action, a good story, great characters, and a lot of humor. It had a quite ElderScrolls feel to the leveling up. Instead of like most RPGs, where you get EXP from killing enemies and used that to level up, Fable is a bit different. You do get EXP from killing, but you also get it from doing the killing. You shoot something with an arrow, you get skill EXP. Blast them with lightning, you get will EXP. Bash them with a hammer, you get strength EXP. They do not mix together, so you can't play as pure mage and have a high health. Not from Will EXP, at least. This is where the General EXP come in, the stuff you get from killing and quests. That can be put towards anything.
Also, what you do in the game effects your appearence. Like to crunch on little newborn chickens (yes, you can do that) and kill people? A red mist will rise from your feet and eyes, you will become pale, flies will be drawn to you like the corpses you leave behind, and you grow horns (also destroying the majority of your hairstyle). People will run in terror from you, and hate you though your power will keep them from doing anything. But if you play as good, people will flock to, you will get a halo and a beam of light when you stand still. I think your eyes change color, though it has been a long time. Max out strength and you will look like a bodybuilder. Will will make you glow. I can't remember what Skill does. Fighting badly leaves you with scars.
I could keep going on, but you should play it yourself. My only complaints are that the GuildMaster gets annoying "Your health is low. Have you any potions, or food", and I am having trouble getting the game to run on my computer even though it should be able to run it no problem. But once I get it up and running I won't be doing much else.

Deadfall adventures is a FPS/Action Adventure/Puzzle hybrid and it combines and mixes up these elements extremely well to keep the game from falling in a rut.  It's essentially an Indiana Jones type adventure, complete with many familiar tropes, and the story is extremely cliche and predictable.  However it does give you an excuse to visit several of really cool looking exotic locations.
The gunplay is solid with the weapons feeling quite different from each other and the weapons that should pack a punch feeling appropriately meaty.  The game even occassionally gives you a fun toy like a MG 34 to play with for a short while.
Puzzles aren't overly challenging, even on hard difficulty (you can set combat and puzzle difficulty seperately), but a few of them will at least make you think for a bit.  Most puzzles are thinking puzzles, though there are a scant few that rely on quick reflexes.
Overall it's a very fun game if you're looking for an Indiana Jones-esque adventure and can get past subpar production values.

Warframe has really become something beautiful, before you were always completing missions in the galaxy but now you can focus on eidolon when you have nothing else to do, this is what people have really been looking for in warframe, a open world of which to share with others and explore to their hearts content.
Likes: The crafting system - I enjoy being able to craft something being able to get the satisfaction of building it from scratch instead of getting it in a whole package and not just right off the bat having it, there's that little something of being able to build the parts and then the whole product.
The Farming - I know many may get at me for this but its fun, you find mods, you can combine them, you can break them for materials for other mods, and if you're lucky you find one that is JUST your playing style, plus farming materials is actually really fun in this game because of how they go about it. I love farming the mat's in this game because of how satisfying it is.
The combat - It really is interchangeable, you can either stealth, Go guns blazing, or use nothing but your warframes powers depending on which you choose to dominate the battlefield, or you can support your allies with the powers your warframe has depending on which you choose as well.
The possibilities are endless in warframe of what you can do to make your experience better and fresh, all I can say is step into the world and see what you like to do the most, experiment with builds that you think can fit your playstyle, and maybe get prime parts to the extent of getting a full gun from the relics.
Cons: I cant really think of anything truly right now. But I guess one can come up here.
The prime parts are sometimes very hard to come by and to get anything prime it costs a fair amount of platinum which in turn costs a fair amount of real life cash, but in turn people can argue they have the money for this that they can use it because they have the jobs to pay these bills. I dont know, You guys decide on this front.
But that is all for this review, but dont take it from me go into warframe and explore on your own look to what you will like in this game I wont take away the satisfaction of it because you deserve to see this game for yourself, not through others' eyes.
I do hope you found this helpful in what you may like or dislike about the game and I know that I did miss a few but, I cant cover everything.
So, with that I wish you good luck in warframe, and see you on the battlefield, Tenno.

A flawed gem.
If you start reaching for your wallet whenever you hear a sentence like "oldschool isometric turn based RPG", chances are you'll enjoy Underrail a lot. Like really a lot. I know I did.
"Fallout-esque" is a word that gets thrown around a lot when people try to describe Underrail, and while the classic Fallout vibe is felt throughout the game, there's a huge difference between the two games. Fallout focused on dialogue, Underrail focuses on combat. Hard, brutal, save-scumming combat. And that's just fine, because the game offers you a wide variety of interesting ways to approach said combat, which helps to keep it feeling fresh throughout the game (mostly) . The dialogue is serviceable, but nowhere near the standard set by classic Black Isle/Bioware titles.
The game world is enormous, and for the most part interesting to explore, and although many of the cave areas feel a bit samey,  lacking in detail and generally "un-lived-in", the towns and cities are spot on what I'd hoped for and the highlights of your journey. The in-game graphics are fine, and what you'd expect from late 90's RPG, if a bit lacking in variation at times. The interface however... is clunky. Needlesly so. And the icons look awful and undetailed, as well as tiny if you run the game at higher resolutions. The music is amazing though, and really helps sell the game's atmosphere.
The game's non-combat mechanics can feel pretty rough at times, the crafting system in particular could do with more polish. And why there's no in-game map of some sort is beyond me, considering the size and complexity of the game world. The level cap feels really low and I reached it a lot sooner than I expected, which limited what I was able to do with the crafting system just as I was starting to take full advantage of it. I wish I'd known more about the mechanics when I started the game, I would certainly have spent my skill points more wisely had I done so.
I didn't enjoy the last part of the game. Instead of culminating crescendo, it's a slow deathmarch collectathon that spams you with trash mobs over and over again. This is by far the game's biggest flaw, and probably the one that's hardest to correct.
I've brought up a lot of negative points, but I've also put over 100 hours into this game, and just started another playthrough. I criticize because I care, otherwise I would've spent those hours on something else, and I wouldn't have bothered to write this review. Underrail scratches my classic RPG itch, even better than Wasteland 2 did.

I first downvoted the game because its ending drove me insane.
As it is the first game that ever manage to put me in such raging mood, I thought it was logical to downvote it, despite having a great time with its content otherwise.

Ill establish my opinion of the game through this review, but the first thing that need to get done is to explain what is Underrail ending.
Underrail Ending is its own game. And it can suck a large amount of your time if you are not prepared and did not read a guide before hand. It might also very much be a sequence of the game that you can't finish (because 1-2 puzzles are completely delirious); it might also prove impossible to beat to certain character builds; and the possible worst part is the crazy backtracking that it will ask you if you don't help yourself with a guide of sort.
A little spoiler before the end game  is actually a good thing, so, at some point in the game, when you believe you're near a major turning point in the ending, try to gather as much info about DC (the end game zone) as you can before jumping in.
Now that we are past that, the game is great. And its ratio play value / price might be one of the very best out there for single player games.
It starts very slow, would it be gameplay-wise or writing-wise, but after 15-20 hours play time gets a lot better (fallowing the main quest), and it only gets better, and better, and better in all aspect.
To a certain point where you'll notice that its questlines are very linear and do not offer any alternative that the player might think off.
After beating the game, you'll get those awesome sliders that will tell you how things are for the various stations that you visited, but sadly, it suffers from the same ''narrow'' writing than the quests, the author interprets your actions, instead of just stating the state of things.
I personnally loved the plot, even though I think there and there are some holes, but I can objectively say that Underrail offers among the most memorable moments that video games can offer.

I have played turn-based tactical combat games for ages.  Oh, those glory days back in 1994 with Jagged Alliance.  Oh the wait for JA2.  Oh the disappointment of the subsequent JA licensed titles.
But Underrail, I dunno.  I'm not going to play any more after being unable to compelte the first mission.  From some searches online as I encounter problem after problem with basic things, it seems if you don't happen to pick a perfect set of opening stats and perks you just get stuck.
The rathounds?  _So_ hard.  I have never seen a game with an initial enemy so hard to kill.  It'd be fine if you could, you know, use cover, or otherwise exploit the landscape to outsmart them.  But nope!  They can run further than you, and then they always have enough AP to attack you three times.  They almost always hit you.  They get critical hits that are in the range of 20% of your health.  They swarm in packs up to _four_ and they get _multipliers_ for more than one attacking you at once.  And all you have is your trusty piece of garbage pistol that takes at least 2 of your turns to kill them.  So it just becomes a game of hoping you can make only one find you at once, because if two or three get you, you're dead, or so close to dead you're using your precious stimpacks to heal.  (No, you can't use the other type of healing available to you, bandages, because you're less than 40% health and they don't work in that case.)  You have to spend every once of AP on firing your peashooter at the weakest one, hope you kill one every 2 (but probably 3 or 4) turns, while sweating out the attacks from his three buddies all chomping on your with increased "Pack Hunting" damage.  You can't move because they swarmed you in one turn and you are now surrounded on all sides.
Lucky me, I found a machine gun.  It does . . . no more damage than the pistol.  In burst mode, it does actually have a chance to kill them in one turn, but it probably doesn't.  But it doesn't matter because I could afford 11, yup, 11 bullets for it.  And I had all kinds of junk, but I couldn't trade for it.  (The barter/trading system is too hard to actually use because you are always "trading" instead of, you know, using the invention of CURRENCY.  Even credits are an item you must "split" in the inventory and trade for other things.  And some vendors don't seem to buy some stuff, or at least I think that's what the faint pink X through an item means on the barter screen.  So tedious.)
So, is it fun?  Not one tiny bit.  C'mon.

What can I say about this game that other reviews haven't said already?
In broad strokes, Underrail is what you'd get if you mixed "Fallout" with "Metro 2033" and "The Ice Company" (a series of novels by Georges-Jean Arnaud, dealing with a post-apocalyptic winter and conspiracies). It's a post-apocalyptic world where the apocalypse was so long ago noone remembers how long it has been since it happened, and the surface is a mythical place that might as well be Shambhala, since noone's seen it or knows how to get there, and as far as anyone knows is uninhabitable.
You start out as someone who has just passed the admittance tests for one of the most important stations in the Southern Underrail (which is the name for the whole underground rail and stations complex) and soon after making yourself home you are asked to start carrying your weight. Your work for the station (or for youself) will send you into a web of danger, conspiracy and conflicting interests upon which the fate of the whole Underrail will rest.
Now, onto the specifics: having played the game for about 150 hours at the time of writing this review (one botched playthrough with an unoptimized character which left me stranded in the boss fight, and a melée-specced one which allowed me to breeze through), I have to say that the attention to detail in this game is staggering, especially considering the small size of the team. The writing is spectacularly good, and this game does reward the players who bother reading. There are many characters telling their own stories, and logs, messages or e-mails telling the stories of those who aren't there, many of which are written from several points of view. The big picture often comes as a portrait of a world in the throes of death and war, to which its inhabitants are often oblivious - it might as well be Carcosa.
Regarding the worldbuilding, there are plenty of likeable characters, as well as memorable locations (many of which you don't have to visit even once), and not even once have I felt that by choosing a side on a conflict I'd been shortchanged (by having chosen the "wrong" side, as it happens in other games). Exploration is its own reward, moreso if you are using the oddity XP system, whereby most of the XP you get are from "oddities", collectable items that tell a small story about the Underrail, be it in the shape of antiques, trophies, bizarre things, artifacts from before the war or forteana (as opposed of getting XP from combat and skill usage).
I have to point out that, in regards to game mechanics, the system if fairly simple but flexible enough to grant a wide array of options. When generating a character, not specializing for a build will spell doom in the long run, but the game has the option to display all of the feats on character creation and on level-up, so that planning which ones to obtain and  how to distribute attribute points is feasible even on the first playthrough. All weapon categories are viable for the end game provided the character is specialized, so one needn't worry about whether knives or guns will be useless by the end.
Crafting is present in the game, and will allow a character with enough points on the respective skills to make equipment far superior to that found in loot or shops. Virtually any equippable item is craftable, except for the unique ones.
As for the sound, the game has great ambient music that sets the mood for each location, and the sound effects, while not out of this world, are good. My dog even barked back to the game's dog sounds.
Regarding graphics, while I liked them very much as they suited the game style and the setting, if you are looking for eye candy á la Fallout 4 you've got another thing coming. If I had to compare it to other games, it'd be between Fallout 2 and Van Buren.
If I had to say something that didn't feel right to me in this game, it would be that the social skills are almost useless: Persuasion and Intimidation are useful at specific points in the game, but if you spend enough points in them you'll miss those skill points somewhere else later in the game, and if you don't spend enough in them, you might as well spend zero or you'll be wasting points. Mercantile is outright useless, as you'll be swimming in cash (especially if you run a melée character, as you won't spend ammo), but in general it's not a big deal, as you could say the same about Fallout 1.
All in all, even if it's not Ultima VII, still a game so awesome I'd buy it again. Hopefully, the developer will make Underrail 2.

I have played the game for the day and I have tried to give it an objective review.
Here is my feedback to all;
It’s an okay game to play once.  There is no reason why anyone would play it a third time.  The first time you play it you can finish it in less than 4 hours and the second time to get all the achievements will also take about 4 to 5 hours.
The game is too linear and if you figured it out the first time there is no surprise the second time you play it.
It makes the game very boring and grindy, because the second time you play it for the achievements as the story does not change in any way.  Then with the Suicide and Death Achievements the place from where you start is more irritating and unrewarding than the time it took you to get the achievement in the first place.
However that being said the atmosphere in the game is very nice.  There are some instances where I was surprised at what I saw on the screen and that was nice to observe.  The story was compelling however short it is.  The characters needed more depth and character but even that was not so bad.  The dialog was a bit lacking and the narrators of the voices could have added more to the atmosphere had it been done better.
The graphics really did not do the game any favours.  I was not able to change any settings and the gamma on my Screen was very low and this did result in me only moving the mouse over the screen to see where I could interact without being able to take in the ambiance.
The interactive missions and puzzles were very nice however once you got the hang of where to look it became very easy to overcome the obstacles.
Overall I would score the game a respectful 6 out of 10 and would recommend people who enjoys the genre to buy it on sale.

After many hours of playing this game I can safely say it's the world domination strategy I dreamt of. People often compare it to the Total War series, but there is a crucial difference. Total War is played in a turn based system, making it a bit annoying to play longer campaings for me. In Crusader Kings II, it all happens in front of your eyes, sped up or paused.
I originally bought the game for multiplayer and was disappointed, as the multiplayer was not that flowy. If you have the patience for your friend to pause, then for you to pause, and then to speed up... Play it, it's good fun. For me, not really.
What I like about this game is it's endless options as to what you will do. You can start out as the count of who-knows-where in God-knows-what-country and end up as the supreme ruler of Europe. Sure, it's a bit hard, but possible!
Here's my most recent expirience: I started out as duke of Jylland, and thanks to the elective law for sucession I ended up the king. A few generations of kinging later, I conquered Pomerania. The whole country (Not big, at the time it had like 6-8 counties) and I created the title 'Kingdom of Pomerania'. Scared that I would lose my titles, I changed the law to ultimogeniture (Youngest child gets the kingdom) as I couldn't get my oldest to lead. The law in Pomerania, however stayed elective. I gave my son the title 'King of Pomerania' thinking he'd be the king, while still in my country. Like a vassal thing. I know, I'm an idiot.
So at this point, my son is a 16 year old independant king of Pomerania, where election laws exist. I am not nominated as the heir, logically, so I, a 44 year old king of Denmark do my DAMN BEST to die. (If I die, my son inherits Denmark and I play as him, king of both kingdoms) I go hunting, I go to impossible wars, I anger everyone powerful hoping to be assasinated... After one hunt, I remain maimed. Even that doesn't kill me. My son dies at age 22 and Pomerania is forever lost. It is now officially catholic and I cannot go to holy war against it, which I used to get it in the first place.
Anyway... I would highly recommend this addicting game, and if you like these kind of games but hate turn based systems, check out Knights of Honor. It's an outdated game but it's really fun. I'd write about it, but just go check it out.

Recettear: An Item Shop’s Tale, or Recettear for short, is a very intriguing time/money management game with some interesting mechanics to boot. Essentially, you play as Recettear, a young woman living alone in a home that apparently has a huge mortgage on it. Your father took out the mortgage (or loan, whatever) but has yet to pay it back – and he mysteriously vanished! Yeah I didn’t really get that and could have probably thought of a better back-story myself, but hey, it doesn’t really matter!
A fairy comes to pay you a visit one day to take the home away from you (Hey I thought Fairies were nice?!) because the loan is outstanding, but then takes pity on you (Oh right, yep, Fairies are nice) and develops a plan for you to pay back the loan – Turn your downstairs into an Item Shop. Apparently you live in unnamed (Maybe it has a name and I missed it) RPG village where all manner of NPC characters live! How convenient! The intention is to buy cheap goods from the local Guild Master or market, when things are on sale, and resell them at your Item Shop for a markup. Using these funds you’ll of course buy more and buy and sell more and more. An endless circle of buy low, sell high.
But wait, there’s more! Should you be so inclined, the RPG village also has a dungeon! Should you choose to enter the dungeon, you’ll take an adventurer with you (And you’ll unlock more as you play the game) to slay monsters and descend deeper into the depths of the dungeon. Essentially you’ll get free items from killing the baddies, assuming you make it out alive. The dungeon is a very neat feature, and you need to use it in order to unlock more parts of the story line or other adventurers – however I found myself not using it because I could make a much greater profit from buying cheap goods and reselling them normally. You would think that getting something for free and reselling it would be better, but in my experience, I was getting rather junky items even when I went further down the dungeon in any later play through. Also it doesn’t help that it uses 2 pieces of the “daily pie” so to speak (A day is not endless. Going to market, opening the store, adventuring the dungeon or progressing the story takes a portion of the day) and also I really sucked at it. I am a video game pro, but found myself frustrated at the difficulty of some of the boss battles at times. But hey, that’s the challenge and charm of Recettear!
So as you earn money, at the end of each week, you have to pay back a portion of the loan. It starts out small, but then becomes exponentially larger! Week one you may have to pay back 40,000 (Not exact figures, pulling from memory right now…) and week four you find yourself needing 1,200,000! Say WHAT!? It’s achievable… …once you play through another time! If you fail to make a loan payment, the game ENDS! Game over, done, finished, ka put. However, not all is lost! You may get to start the game over from day 1, but you get to keep all the items you have in stock. So when you lose the game, you somehow go back in time (Not really, just my way of thinking how this works…) and have a huge stock of expensive items that you wouldn’t have had on your first play through. It took me three game overs before I was able to make all the loan payments and finish the game. I think it’s a very nice addition to the game, a handicap if you will – if you lose, not all is lost and you can try again with a little help.
Overall, Recettear has an extremely cute (I can’t believe I used the word ‘cute’…) visual appeal and has a great sound and music score included. The story line is interesting to say the least (Some of the dungeon adventurers are odd, but hey, that’s part of the charm!) and has lots of replay ability (Not just replaying when you lose, but once you win you can continue to play and unlock more items and upgrade your store to be better yet!). Overall great game, well worth a play through if you’re interested in JRPG’ish style stories and business sense.

Warframe is quite the game, not just because of it being free-to -play, but the fact that despite it still being a beta, it is incredibly polished, fun, and with tons to do.
So what is Warframe, you may ask?
Warframe is a Third-Person Shooter with elements of class-based gameplay and a very high emphasis on movement.
The amount of things you can do to get about levels is large and mastering the movement does actually make you feel a bit like a ninja. Rolls, slides, "bullet-jumps", wall-jumps, and this is enhanced by the wide variety of classes/Warframes avaliable.
From the energy sword wielding Excalibur, the anti-matter flinging Nova, the tiny fairy Titania, the amount of frames is staggering, and all of them can be aquired for free, although some are harder to get than others.
Despite this variety, I will state some things that can turn people off.
1: The game IS somewhat grindy. Treat it like a co-op MMO style game. There's lots of weapons to level, resources to get, things to craft, and this all can take a decent chunk of time. Remember that practically everything minus most cosmetics CAN be aquired for free, however, just in exchange for time.
2: It's still not done. There's no real end as of yet in terms of story, there can still be plenty of bugs and things change or are added all the time. Don't expect the most polished gem.
3: Early-game tutorials kinda are bad. There's a lot of things left out that may come as a surprise later on. If you're confused, i'd recommend asking others. It can be a little daunting at times.
That's most of what I have to say about the game. There's plenty  to do, lots to kill and collect and the game just feels good.
I highly recommend this game if Shooters are your kind of thing.

After five long years in the making, sci-fi horror isometric point and click title STASIS finally hit the Steam store in 2015. It went on to win several awards, including 4th best in both horror and adventure at the Global Game Awards. On top of its chilling visuals, the game also has a soundtrack that was composed by Mark Morgan, who worked on Fallout. Developed by The Brotherhood and published in conjunction with the highly acclaimed Daedalic Entertainment, it's surprising that STASIS isn't a more popular title, having only sold roughly 30,000 copies on Steam.
A man named John Maracheck is violently awoken from his suspension in a stasis state, with no knowledge of where he is or how long he has been unconscious. The last thing he remembers is boarding a travel vessel with his wife and daughter, their destination intended to be one of leisure and vacation. Somewhere along the line, something went horribly wrong, and it's up to John to not only find his family but also to uncover the terrible secrets that lay hidden within the blood-drenched corridors of the Groomlake; a massive spacecraft that is orbiting planet Neptune. The majority of the story is told through found PDAs and computer terminals, from the perspective of now deceased, on-board staff. The remainder is conveyed via radio communication with a woman named Te'ah. If you want to understand what is truly going on, reading the PDAs is absolutely essential, and the writing within them is very entertaining and well done.
STASIS is a very difficult, slow moving game; this could be a con for some, and a pro for others. Even while using a guide, the hours clock in around the beefy 7-8 mark, which is huge for a point and click title. Without a guide, a lot more time could be put in to solving the complex puzzles and hard-to-find items that are needed to proceed. In certain situations, an event has to be triggered by standing in the appropriate spot to be able to move on. Needless to say, it's very easy to get stuck, and the game is overall very challenging and thought provoking; the latter not only in terms of enigmas, but also the compelling yet chilling story.
The visuals here are, by far, some of the most horrific and gruesome that are available in any 2D isometric game. Nearly every screen is filled with blood, fog/steam, rotting corpses, and terrifying abominations that've been being genetically manufactured on-board. The game is quite dim, but not so much that it's too difficult to see. There's also a great use of lighting to make many of the scenes even more spine-chilling. The graphics can be compared heavily to the FPS title Deadspace, in terms of the amount of blood and gore, coupled by the fact that both take space on an isolated, abandoned spacecraft. The aesthetics marry well with the jarring sound effects, which include the blood curdling screams of victims far off in the distance. Likewise, the atmospheric soundtrack by Mark Morgan really ties everything together.
Buckle up and get ready for one of the most immersive and bloody 2D isometric games of all time. STASIS is truly a title that shouldn't be missed, and it's very much an underrated horror gem. The only downside for me could be an upside for you; the story and overall game just seemed to move incredibly slow. However, the end result was completely worth it. Right now, The Brotherhood are working on a post-apocalyptic adventure game, as well as a free follow-up to STASIS about the Cayne Corporation; both should be exciting stuff, and I greatly look forward to playing both of them, and you should too.

I wanted to like this, I really did, but I found it to be a below average example of a point and click adventure.  The setting and artwork was great...beyond that I really can't recommend it.  The story was extremely cliched, particularly the ending, and I really didn't feel anything for the main character.  More importantly, the puzzles, beyond a few really good ones, were very simple, consisting mostly of "use the only one or two objects available in the area to proceed" type of scenarios.  Like a lot of adventure games, they got increasingly lazy as the game went on.  This is sometimes okay if the story is good enough to carry it through to the ending...this one wasn't.  There were also a couple of parts where you had to walk to a certain area of the room in order to 'trigger' an event, before you could proceed.  This is okay if you make the area one which the player is unavoidably bound to walk over...but due to the unique system of mouse over automatically giving a description of items and areas in Stasis (which is a fantastic and welcome addition btw), there are times where this just isn't going to happen.  The only time I got stuck in this game were on these bits, because I never walked over the right area and so the story never proceeded.  That's just sloppy design.
Overall, it's just not a very good example of an adventure game.  Like a lot of modern examples of the genre, the puzzle design is poor and too easy, but the ones that still manage to be enjoyable have a good story and/or humour that makes up for it.  I can't say Stasis had either of those for me.  So I wouldn't recommend it to more hardcore point and click fans, and I can't recommend it to the more casual fan either.

Like many succesful Kickstarter projects, STASIS went for nostalgic value, for doing something people wanted to see more of and didn't lately. I feel, a lot of people expected from STASIS was something close to what good old Sanitarium was going for - a psychological horror point and click adventure with isometric view and a nice mix of pre-rendered and real-time elements. But with a more sci-fi horror twist to it all.
It looks good, has fantastic Mark Morgan (Fallout, Planescape: Torment, recent Wasteland 2 among other projects) writing music for the game. Has some great looking pre-rendered backgrounds. On top of that, there is an intriguing universe and a story that fits just a perfect balance between disgusting and spooky at first, creating a certain sense of dread that not a lot of games manage to do. There's a bunch of backstory text scattered around the game and the protagonist is given a lot of nice sound detail - a lot of his grunts, breathing and other occasional things are recorded and nicely used to make him feel alive and vulnerable.
But then, it also has surprisingly badly written story, which at times also feels like a complete rewrite of Dead Space 1 (including environment, backstory and character design ideas). Pretty dreadful voice acting, including use of text to speech not just for AI characters, but seemingly for one secondary character as well. Horribly looking animations and rather bad cinematography. Bad pathfinding. Bland gameplay design, with puzzles never being "bad" as much as just "okay, they're here".
In the end, STASIS is not as much a bad game (it isn't), as much as it is simply a waste of fantastic art and sound design the game has, the atmosphere it builds up in the beginning. Those first 30 minutes of the game or so at the start are better than everything that happens afterwards. Everything that will simply leave you disappointed.
TL;DR  As it stands, don't buy till the game is on a 50% sales, and hope the bugs are fixed. It has some redeeming graces.

So, you're thinking about buying Golf With Friends. Here are some things you need to know:
PROS:
Golf With Friends is very addicting. You will find yourself staring at your computer screen for hours on end, lining up perfect hole-in-ones.
Contrary to the name, you don't need friends to play this game (or rather friends that play the game. Hopefully you have friends.). You can play online with people you don't know, who tend to be nice (and also probably better than you). Alternatively, you can play by yourself and practice the heck out of this game.
You can customize matches insanely. Want to play with giant  jumping bouncy acorns in moon-like gravity? Of course!
Want to only have 3 shots and 30 seconds per hole? Why not? Want to turn on collision mode and spend the whole time trolling your friends instead of trying to shoot your own ball into the hole? Sure.
This game is still in early access, so new maps, features, and bugfixes are still coming out.
CONS:
Only 4 maps. However, at least two more will be added.
Lots of bugs. These are gradually being fixed, though.
And the worst part: the game crashes. A LOT. For me, it crashes when opening it around 75% of the time. However, this problem will hopefully be fixed. EDIT: It doesn't do this anymore.
All in all, this is a great game. I rate it 9/10, with a point taken off only because of temporary issues like bugs and crashes.

Absolute classic... if you were unlucky enough to never own the original Xbox and to play this gem of a game, I apologize. I remember this game receiving some hate simply because it did not live up to the hype that the infamous Peter Molyneux made it out to be. I have beaten Fable several times, and I have recently decided to give it yet another go since its been a few years... it never becomes any less entertaining. Despite all of the things Mr. Molyneux promised and failed to implement in this game, it still accomplishes tons of things modern RPGs never even come close to. There is a very real sense of character development in this game, and you'll find your Hero evolving as the game progresses. He will age as time goes by, and he will even grow physically larger and more physically fit as you accomplish more in your heroic lifetime. You can decide to walk the path of evil, and your body will change as a result of it. Not only that, but the world will react to you as well. You will either have people fleeing from you in terror, or rushing to see you in excitement, hoping to give you gifts to show their appreciation.
The original Fable actually has quite a short main storyline, but thanks to The Lost Chapters, you'll find that there is quite a bit more to do. Despite all of that, there are more than enough entertaining and interesting sidequests to keep you going. This game is very detailed, and if you're into it, you can find the woman (or man) of your dreams and get married and move into a home. Once you are bored of this house, you can sell it or rent it out and move into a new one. Again, there are just too awesome features to list. You simply have to try this game out for yourself. I know some people did not enjoy it, which is really a shame. Without a doubt, Fable is a very entertaining RPG. It's not the deepest in terms of "stats" or "phat loots", but there is an incredible charm and addiction to it, especially when you find your Hero actually growing stronger and more powerful as you progress through the story.

Recette's deadbeat dad has gone and disappeared and left the poor girl with a bunch of debt so she's forced to trade items from her shop to pay off the Loan Sharks represented by business-like fairy, Tear, who makes sure you keep earning.
The game's ultra compelling as you organise your time making a nice little earner scalping the mug punters all to avoid losing your home. Explore dungeons, kill monsters, find items, upgrade your shop, take orders, buy low and sell high, all to manage your cash to meet the escalating weekly payments to the shyster fairy's bosses.
The game's very Japanese and has a 16-bit sound and feel to it, so much so that playing with a 360 pad it's like 1992 on the SNES. You may need to play it windowed as large resolutions aren't available. There is a lot of text, but it is entertaining.
Interestingly the game also seems to be an allegory on the enslaving nature of debt and the empowerment of the individual with free markets. 'Capitalism, ho!'

One of the best Isometric RPGs I've every played in a long while. I played and beat it before the final release and I think that says alot about the game. My first impression of the game was, "Why are there not any games like this anymore?" Underrail really scratched that itch I had for a turnbased rpg.
Underrail has a pretty decent story (something along the lines of Metro and Fallout), and the gameplay and character building is one of the most fun I've had in a game. I built a melee psionic bruiser that just punched his way through the entire game.
There are two ways you can progress in levels in this game and they are oddity or classic. Oddity is a really interesting idea where you gain experience from finding unique items from monsters or looting through junk (The way I played), and then there's the other way that most gamers are probably familiar with which is classic (where you beat up people or monsters and gain exp). Either playstyle works very well depending on your interest.
The game progresses very well and it never felt like I had to grind my way to progress. This game is a must play even at full price, but if you can get it during a sale, please do! It is one of the most fun and enjoyable games I've ever played! Totally support this developer!
