Underrail has an immersive atmosphere, excellent character creation and growth, high multiple play through potential and will keep those players who have to search every nook and cranny busy for 100+ hours.
In short I would highly recommend the game to fans of the genre, if you enjoyed the early fallout games, Arcanum or even Balur’s gate, I would say with a high chance that you may enjoy this game too.  It has a great story, great customisation, interesting characters and rewarding combat with interesting dynamics when it comes to planting traps and sneaking about.   There are hundreds of doors and boxes to lock pick and hack, characters to meet and converse with and areas to explore, also some of the chat dialog options are awesome.
I would however be hesitant to recommend the game to people unknown to this genre, I feel the mainstream gamer would be betrayed by the issues in the late game section when the first ¾ of the game are very entertaining.  Furthermore the black screen transitions between areas get tiresome very quick and make large connected areas like corecity feel sliced up and disjointed.
Upon entering the last section of the game, it feels like a call back to a bygone era of gaming where progressing through the plot is done by only the devoted few- you would hear of how to progress from those who had stuck through it or like some Nes games, go buy Nintendo Power and discover it wasn’t so straight forward as the rest of the game was.  The last part of the game is unforgiving- not via combat as other may say(A stealthless character is not recommended!!), but with your time.  If you were unlucky such as I, you will be walking back and forth for some time (granted I did it at 2x or 3x speed with an external program, explanation below) which adds up to poor gameplay.  I was truly frustrated with the obscure late game plot quests (mainly the worm tunnel + spore jungle + powering the mutagen door, I made that journey about 8 times after selecting the wrong power) that I feel it has let the entire game down and will turn any new people to the genre away.
If you’re patient however, the first ¾ of the game are great, the last ¼ not so much- but I did enjoy the boss battle and final wrap up- A good solid ending to a game means a lot to me and I was pleased with this game.
Thanks to the devs for making this game, it’s quite a rare experience and one that I very much enjoyed.. mostly (deep carverns i'm looking at you!)
*******************************************************************************
Technical issues and other stuff.
If you get mouse lag on full screen, I would highly recommend ‘Borderless Gaming’ a steam downloadable app which I got after almost giving up on this game… The program removed and fullscreened the games 1920*1080 window and removed the borders.. as described :D, also works with other programs, does a good job of it and is very light.
At around the 20 hour mark, I simply got fed up with travel times, it was starting to hurt my enjoyment of the game so I hunted for a program to speed up and slow down the game.  After my first play through, I have negated 20 hours, of a 100 play time by simply speeding up and slowing walking around (Not exploring new areas-just getting from A to B).
(Calculated from steam game play time-100hours, vs borderless gaming play time 80 hours, ran them both always).
Be prepared to walk everywhere, like I said- I cut out 20 hours of just walking.

Crusaders of the Lost Idols is an incremental clicker/idle game featuring a customizable adventuring party and a simplistic tower defense playstyle.
Click to deal damage to enemies as they advance from the right toward your party on the left. Kill them and they drop some cash, which you'll automatically pick up if you don't do so manually. Spend that cash on upgrades to your click damage. Purchase automatic damage over time, and upgrade that. Unlock special skills and use them to defeat enemies faster, or earn more cash per kill, and invest that cash into more upgrades so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest so you can kill faster and get more cash to invest...
Yep. It's one of these types of games. There's a prestige system that gives you Idols, which increase the damage your Champions deal, and increases the value of cash that you pick up.
Each Crusader has gear that can be found within chests that randomly drop from boss waves. Crusaders have skills that can be purchased. Gear and skills can improve single or party dps, gold find, provide an activated skill, or have some interaction with other Crusaders. The position you place each Champion into changes the overall effectiveness of your party, and the best formation will depend on your gear.
It's an idle/clicker/incrementer with a twist. If you're embarassed for liking idle games, give this one a try.

I really, really, really wanted to give UnderRail a positive review despite a number of issues that occurred throughout the game.
However, all of these were completely overshadowed by the final area.
Without giving away too much let's say it involves A LOT of wandering around, limited supplies, often difficult opponents to rapidly drain said supplies, and an impossible final boss that can only be defeated by reading way too many journal entries (hints buried in way too much text) and deciphering a (unique to each game) chemestry puzzle that will weaken the boss enough to defeat (Thank you to those who posted the puzzle solving tips).
The very annoying thing about the chemistry puzzle (once you even figure out/find out how to solve it) is that you don't get all the pieces to the puzzle until just before the final boss, and then you have to return to an earlier area to analyze those pieces to get all the information you need.  While that may seem trivial, the thing that pushes it into a negative review is that all of the baddies you've killed along the way have respawned because you opened the final area.  At this point, low on everything and just tired of all the wandering back and forth (a recurring theme in the game), I gave up and deleted the game (after 132 hours of gameplay, holy @#$% I played this thing for 132 hours!?!) .
In the end you have what could have been a very enjoyable game being ruined by several end stage "challenges" that are just end up being annoying and frustrating.
P.S.:
While the following few items were not enough enough for me to dislike the game, they did detract from the game.
> And we're walking...
> Level Cap: While I'm not a big fan of level caps, I can live with them.  However, if you are going to impose a level cap then you have to cap the rest of the game as well.  Example: "Wow, I could make this really cool <whatever> but since the crafting requirements are random and open ended and I didn't put OVER 150 POINTS into the needed crafting skill I can't" or "I thought a lockpick skill of 119 would be enough but look, a door that needs a skill of 120 to open it."
> And we're walking...
> Weapons Don't Keep Pace:  As you move through the game the bad guy's toughness out paces your ability to inflict damage.  This is especially true if you don't craft the right items.  This means you have more and more difficulty with the bad guys despite any increase in level.
"Well that's the challenge." you say?  To that I say "No."  A combat against three different types of bad guys that requires three different types of defenses (and you can only wear one) and without the proper defense any one of the three can easily kill you in one round and your weapon can only dish out enough damage to kill one opponent each round...oh, and there's two of each type of bad guy.  Not a challenge, just a death and reload.
> And we're walking...
> Being Stalled By Quest Requirements:  This happened a few of times.  In order to complete a quest a specific skill at [X] level was needed.  Didn't think pickpocketing was important?  Better go wander off and find anything to level grind on for several hours to get the points needed.  Included in this would also be quest items that are difficult to find due to any number of reasons.
> And we're walking...
> Finally, and I admit this isn't a hardcore problem, if you are going to put something behind a 100+ difficulty lock then make it something better than some @#$%ing scrap metal.
> And we're walking...

Not enough game there for the money. The game parts aren't tuned and playtested enough IMHO. Needs more QA playtesting. Too many cutscenes.
There's two basic games within this game. The first is easter egg hunting. Do you like panning your camera around to find every single easter egg around you? Do you really like doing that over and over and over? Then you'll love this game. Pan and click, pan and click.
The second game is sneaking up behind monsters that can 3 shot you if you don't kill them first. And you have to kill every monster with a really twitchy 2-step attack move. If you fail, you have to run and hide or die and try try try again.
That's it. Everything else is cutscenes tying it all together. It has a horror theme, but that's like saying the ice cream is strawberry flavored. It could be set on the Ishimura or in Azeroth for all it matters.

MILD SPOILERS ALERT
My review might be biased some what. The reason why, is that I love Indiana Jones movies and for a game that some what recreate that experience for me to live it is utterly SPECTACUILAR.
The GOOD:
The game is beautiful, its not the best graphics but still amazing to look at.
I loved how you have a book in your hand which shows you how to tackle puzzle but not make it like a piece of cake for you.
The gun fights is decent but not challenging, still loved the variety of guns and how the game forces you to chose new guns rather than stick to what you like.
The game also links the puzzles to upgrades by having you solve side puzzles to earn treasures which can be used to upgrade various abilities.
It is good to see that the game has a variety of enemies as you will fight mummies, German, Russians and Arabs. each with unique weapons at your disposals as you will tend to pick up their fallen weapons as there are plenty of ammos thus.
The BAD:
The game is linear in a way that is somewhat cluster phobic, don’t get me wrong for a game that requires you to solve puzzles it requires narrow areas, but since the game itself was able to achieve by landscape for its last puzzle, it led to wonder why this wasn't the case for all the previous puzzles.
The game is also very short, I mean looking at the number of hours I have played it above would give you a hint as how short it is, not to mention that I have collected all treasures in one play through.
Boss fights are a bit easy and boring, I enjoyed fighting mummies more than fighting bosses.
The main character is funny, but I have a Deja vu as if I am playing Duke Nukem all over again, the reason why this is a bad and not a good thing is that, first, I like Duke Nukem to be left alone to be seen only in his games, and two, don’t mix two things I love and expect it to impress me, you are lucky its not in the ugly.
The UGLY:
The voice acting is, well, UGLY. It is so bad that it over shadows Merritt Weaver Emmy award speech in terms of worseness.
The character modelling would take you back to the time when you first played Metal Gear Solid. I mean for a game that was made on Unreal engine they could have done way better than that.
Given the two UGLY things above, resultantly, the cut scenes is something that would take you off of the experience, so much the case that you would dread watching a cut scene. In fact, come to think of it, I believe the game would be way better if there is something that would skip all cut scenes. It is this bad, sorry, this UGLY.

OVERALL:
As a fan of Indiana Jones, which the game, to some extent, was successful in mimicking certain aspect of it, I can but only recommend this game as I enjoyed my time playing it and solving the puzzles. The fights is nice way to take you off puzzles and puzzle time is a good way to relax from all the fighting, while mummies, they are there to always keeps you on your toes whether you are solving puzzles or fighting enemies.

This game is great! And a ton of fun!...but not worth full price. The game game has a lot of mechanic related improvements over 2033 Redux and is a lot less buggy. It also has a longer campaion, but it just doesn't deliver as good of a quality of story as the first one does, nore does it really seem to care about your actions like the first. Let me ewxplain:
1+) Mechanics - Like 2033 Redux, Last Light Redux uses the same HUD display that can be removed based on the style you choose to play on, and no real changes have been made to that. The real improvements have come in the stealth system wich is noticalby more advanced (or at least more sensative) and which does a better job of really kepping you on your toes as you play. Its honestly a nice improvement.
2+)Buggs - While this game is by no means perfect, a lot of the buggs from the first are no longer an issue. Don'e get me wrong, there are bugs, and if you look at the community forum you'll see about 10k ways to fix them all, but its better than 2033 Redux.
3+/-) The campaion - In last light the campaion is much longer than in 2033 (about 2x) and there is another probably 0.5x in bonus material added on as well in the main menue. That said, the campaion gets a bit flat about half way through and at some point starts dragging along. It's still good (a lot better than some big tittles out there) but it just isn't as good as the first and that's kinda a let down coming from playing 2033 Redux.
4-) The Moral Point System - Alright, I'll be honest, this system was annoying in 2033 Redux as well, but the issue here is that the longer campaion means there is more of these points to look out for and more ways to screw them up. It also doesn't seem to matter too much at the end as there is still almost the exact same play sequence regardless of ending, just a different 20sec clip plays after it. Also, while talking about this, the ending doesn't care how you played. Regardless of if you went sneaking or if you went guns blazing, you get the same fight sequence (event for both endings) and while it is crucial to the plot...it just seems sorta cheap. The game reards you the whole time for playing a certian way, and then doesn't really care at the end. It just takes some of the fun out of it.
Final thoughts on this game are that one should try to get it when its on sale or part of a combo with 2033 Redux. Its not bad, but I don't really feel its worth the full price they charge for it.

DISCLAIMER: This review is out of date and will be updated post scale update. This is also a reminder for myself.
Big things come in small packages and this holds true for every aspect of American Truck Simulator.
As of mid February, you are given two states to travel through along with the choice of three trucks to do the driving in. It doesn't sound like a whole lot of content, and many people will argue that Euro Truck had quite a bit more during its launch. Don't worry, more states and trucks are being added in due time. In my 110+ hours of playing, American Truck has a more detailed map and hand-woven map than Euro Truck did. Unlike a lot of the Western European roads, the roads of American Truck doesn't feel like they were cut-and-pasted at all. In American Truck, you are given a beautiful sense of exploration and discovery as you're traversing unique little roads that have a riding-the-wave sort of feeling with its dips and bends, tumble weeds rolling towards you, and narrow alleyways that you must maneuver your truck and trailer through.
While you're driving, you will see police cars parked on the side of the road, much like you would find in the streets of the U.S. Not only are the police cars parked on the shoulder, but they will also patrol the roads and ping you with fines if you were to be caught speeding or ramming into the car ahead of you. In addition to this, the game is programmed to allow you to turn right at a red light, which is a beautiful tid-bit of realism that was added into the game. Additionally, American Truck Drivers will often be required to pull into a weigh station to have their trucks and trailers weighed. This, of course, carries over into American Truck Simulator.
Aesthetically, the game is incredible. The state of California is very dense with civilization and traffic whereas Nevada is very barren and open. Whether you are in Las Vegas or San Francisco or anywhere in between, you will be gifted with the presence of familiar landmarks, like the golden-gate bridge or the casinos in Vegas. There is a plethora of realistic moments in this game, and a few hidden goodies as well.
Finally, the game play. As one might imagine, American Truck Simulator is very much the same under the hood as Euro Truck Simulator, with a few differences that sets American Truck apart. Most noticeably is the ability to choose the difficulty of parking your trailer. You're given three options with the harder options rewarding the player with more experience. Within the gameplay settings, you can have the game always choose one of the three settings, or pick one at random for you. Coming from well over 440 hours in Euro Truck, I found the trailer parking in American Truck Simulator to be quite a but more challenging than that of Euro Truck, which is something I very much appreciated. Those who play with a wheel controller (Like a G27) are given a treat as well, and that is the ability to float the gears. Floating the gears simply means you're shifting without the clutch, relying on listening to the trucks engine to match the revolutions of it and the transmission before you shift. This adds another level of difficulty and realism to the game as many truck drivers use this method of shifting in the real world. Under the controller setting, having your shifter layout behavior set to advanced will allow you to float the gears. For added realism, setting your shifter layout to 'Eaton Fuller' will bring the realism as close as you can get.
Lastly, this game will undoubtedly bring with it the modding community over from Euro Truck. Being the same under the hood means that mods will easily be ported over to the new game. If you're not happy with the selection of trucks you have or the way you can customize them, or that the game looks just a little off to you in that one slightest way. Maybe you're looking for a longer drive. Give this game a week or two, you will be smothered in mods that will meet your desires.
To conclude this review, I'd like to state that I believe American Truck Simulator will help to further the significance and presence of the trucking simulator community. American Truck Simulator, as it stands, has opened its doors to a wider audience of fans who want to drive a truck, but not necessarily in Europe. The game can essentially be split into 3 parts.
The first, tending to the shop - involves selling, haggling, decorating. The entire story is based around this.
The second, gathering, talking, evolving - involves visiting other shops for stock, leveling up and quests.
The third, the RPG - involves hiring an adventurer to visit a dungeon; you control who you hire and it becomes a good ol' dungeon crawler with lots of loot you can sell in your shop.
There's alot of content, alot of things to find; not alot of unique features but enough to keep it installed.

SPAZ is one of those oddball games that is just surprising. It has surprising amount of depth due to the variety of random bits and pieces it offers you. The premise is simple: you have a mothership, and it builds these tiny remote ships (of 4 different size classes) that you can take out to do things with. You start with the tiny-size and mine asteroids. Soon you'll mount attack lasers and armor and other components as you take on tougher and tougher missions while you encounter the threat to humanity... Space Zombies! Different systems have different factions (government, rebels, and bounty hunters) who have different feelings toward you! Attack, defend, ally, betray, it's all up to you. Depending on relations, some will trade, others will not. The actual game is just pretty much "asteroids" as you control one craft but due to different components on the ship (you outfit yourself) it can feel very differently. AI ships will fight against you or be on your side. Give fleet orders while you do your own things... it's all up to you. Don't let the 2D graphics turn you off. This game has some serious depth into it.

Wow. I've spend about 5 days straight playing this one, and I still hungered for more.
SPAZ, or Space Pirates and Zombies (And Bounty Hunters) feels unique. You've got a small fleet of spaceships, and your objective is to reach the center of the galaxy, in search of a fabled load of Rez, an exceptional element discovered in the future capable of being transformed into any metal you need - starting ALL THE WAY BACK from the edge of the Perseus arm, where Earth is currently situated. You can assume direct control of any of your ships at any time in the field - being able to switch back and forth at a moment's notice, while the AI takes care of your other ships for you. You also have a Tactics panel, from which you can evaluate the situation of the entire battlefield and give orders to your fleet, set action stances, order reinforcements, etc. You can also DESIGN each and every one of your ships - you can unlock different hulls, weapons, modules, you name it.
You'll find yourself dragged into a MARATHON once you get a hold of it. There's only one problem, though: the game is a bit grindy. The Milky Way is ENORMOUS, so there can be quite an expanse between your location and your objective in it. You'll find yourself battling through a load of star systems just to reach your next mission or unlock the newest upgrade, and that takes time and resources - most of which you'll be grinding out of mining stations/enemy fleets if you're careless. If it weren't for the grinding, this game would be perfect on my book. But still, it's VERY enjoyable.
Has a great story - but I don't want to spoil it. Play your cards right and the game will go easy on you. Screw up, and expect to spend a few hours grinding for Rez.
DEFINITELY recommend. You'll need some patience, though.

Yes yes, I know, you came for that Fallout 1 feeling you've been reading everywhere this little gem here has. So did I. Well, you know what? Jackpot baby.
I've spent some silly amount of time in this title right here and... damn, the goodness is almost omnipresent. It will hook you more potently than Jet and keep you strapped, aching for more.
Let me get started quickly. I simply love the atmosphere. I get lost roaming the rails, the caves, the tunnels, the abandoned warehouses - for no particular reason, just waiting for the next interesting encounter or nasty surprise down the road. I revel in the ambiental music, which picks up the pace smoothly when combat starts. The general theme is bizzaro-techno-cyber/steampunk depending on which area you're on. I fool you not, I had the feeling I was exploring the Hub, the Glow or some dark alley in Necropolis more often than not. There is also a strange coolness and attention to detail that usually defines everything: stylish art direction and intentional retro fitting. The gunshots have just the right kick to them, the echoes and screeching sounds in the caves are exactly the right fit. Even the neon flashes in the dump, gritty, grimy, depressing dread dystopic metro stations have the right sound to them.
"More often than not" is the word to remember here. More often than not, Underrail gets things right; it delivers on atmosphere, combat and mechanics, exploration, inventory system, stats, skills and "perks" and quests. But let's not get ahead of ourselves.
The highlight piece of the game (but you should know this already) is the turn based combat system. Take Fallout's combat system and reimagine it into a more complex counterpart. Add cooldowns, movement points in addition to action points, interesting cloaking and hide in shadow mechanics and we've got a winner. To be honest, this is the most maturely developed turn-based combat system I've seen in a while in an isometric RPG. Hats off Styg, you've managed to outperform even established developers - Wasteland 2 for example doesn't even come close, in my view. Well, if you were to be extremely picky, you could say that a proper cover system is missing. Also, multi-level combat a la Jagged Alliance 2. Or, from the same game, ducking or going into prone positions. To Underrail's defense: remember this is not a tactical game with RPG elements (as much as it may seem at times :wink:) - but quite "au contraire".
I'd like to say at this point that no matter what builds you'll be experimenting with, you are going to miss a lot without being at least partly invested in PSI abilities. Needless to say that mind-affecting abilities aside, those fire, ice, electricity and telekinesis attacks will just come in handy when dealing with a large variety of enemies, each packing a different flavour of resistances. The usual archetype builds you'll meet are the PSIchopath, chiller, firestarter, electronist, gunner, cutter or invisible stalker with a crossbow. Expect to meet anything in between. There are mostly two approaches when talking about defense: one, you can pack the heaviest suit of metal armor that you'll find and become essentially a tank (and try to resist almost every attack) but suffer movement, evasion and stealth penalties. Two, go as light as possible and invest in actually evading the bullets and dodging the cranium-targeted sledgehammers. By going with light armour, you'll keep your ability to be effective at stealth and make it your life's purpose to actually avoid getting hit in the first place. Now, the plus side to this approach is you'll attack first and surprise your enemies more. On the down side, expect to risk being put down by a single, well-aimed sniper rifle bullet, simply because your armour doesn't have the stopping power to withstand the mechanical impact. My views on defense are quite biased - to quote a line from a favorite game of mine, "neither view is balanced, but one is less unwise".
Speaking of enemies, a scavenger named Marty once told me that there be bandits around; robbers; raiders; outlaws; marauders; gangsters; criminals; crooks; thieves; railroadmen; thugs... his own words you know. Don't get me wrong; packs of rathounds, bugs, giant insects, lizards, spiders, or even robots - can be menacing in most situations, especially when they surround you or surprise you. However, *nothing* really compares to dealing with a roomful of human enemies, no matter what faction or allegiance. The fact that they can and *will* use the entire arsenal at their disposal and all the offensive capabilities that *you* yourself can, well, that makes them downright dangerous. At most times you'll have a chance to prepare for assault, which is tactical goodness right there. You can position yourself, hide in shadows or trap the room if your skill is high enough. Attacking first allows you to pick targets close together and blast them with grenades, EMP their energy shields or simply mass PSI them with fire, ice, electricity, telekinesis or mind-control abilities, instilling fear or mass enrage. Carnage is guaranteed and a lot of itemy swag will be left on the corpses, for pillaging purposes.
Now, I don't know about you, but I love the an*l detail of items and inventory in general. If you've liked that in Jagged Alliance 2 for example, you'll know what I'm talking about.
So many items and none of them are really useless (pun intended: Wasteland 2). Pick 'em up, steal 'em, stack 'em, store 'em, trade 'em. I've been running around locker rooms managing items, choosing weapons, repairing and crafting. Not to mention selling in order to sit on mountains of ca$h. However, in no way is the game unbalanced on this (if more, it is very well thought, with merchants only having a limited amount of money at all times, refreshing the inventory every once in a while)
It is true that I would have liked more dialogue choices and consequences and it is unfortunate there aren't so many, as the potential for those to tie into the storyline is immense. There are, however, some events related to quests that offer multiple solutions and different approach routes, depending on skill and ability. Without spoiling it, I'm going to tell you that at some point you pick up a side quest to look into a particularly suspicious death. If a certain skill related to science is high enough, you will discover aspects of the death that would otherwise remain hidden. In turn, that generates additional dialogue lines that will offer quest closure via a fulfilling path. Thanks to true detective work and dialogue options, you must complete an entire puzzle: the suspect's background and affiliation, the weapon of choice used at the scene and a solid motive for the assassination.There will be areas in which you'll have the chance to explore multiple-path approaches a la System Shock II. For example, you could break into a rather important mansion at some point. High Agility allows for a climb via a steep balcony, overriding the need to hack the high-level electronic panel, which was kind of nice. I also sneaked my way into a metro station full of lunatics, in order to recover a stolen item for a faction. Not a single shot was fired, as the alternate route was to level the entire station in a gruesome battle. It's too bad that Underrail only offers these approach paths from time to time, so do treasure them when you see them because there aren't so many.
Conclusion time: just pick up this piece. You'll remember it for a long while and never regret it.
Word on the street is there's also new content headed our way - maybe, just *maybe* Styg will play a riskier hand and it will turn out to be more content that develops interesting characters, quests, stories and dialogues. In my opinion, those are the areas most underdeveloped, but also full of potential to add more value into an already shiny gem.

The idea of this game is fantastic, and the story is interesting enough to make you think about it when you stop playing.
Overall, the atmosphere helps the immerision, so it had everything to be one of those games you never forget.
But...
There are 3 things that were VERY annoying to me:
1. "Combat": The demons that appear once in a while and can actually kill you, forcing you to restart from the last checkpoint were simply unecessary. It is not a challenge, hiding and waitng for the right time to kill them is just an annoyance. They're also not scary at all. They just kill the tension when they appear as you are exploring somewhere, finding clues, wondering what the hell is going on, or just admiring the nice graphics. They kill the atmosphere. If at least the encounters were better developed, with real stealth strategy, it could be cool. But no, it just makes you wonder if continuing playing is worth the trouble.
2. Collections: It is nice to search for hidden items, that help you picture the background story of the characters, and understand the history of the city (which is very cool, made me think about visiting it someday). But there are just too many, some of them really hard to find (specially when the cursor has to be at a very specific position to collect it), and each one adds almost nothing to the story. The fragments are just too small, and that makes you lose interest in finding them after a while. Some of them are directly connected to the story, and can hint you at what is really going on (it is very easy to figure out the whole mystery if you pay attention), but after some time you just say "nevermind, let's continue with the story", and forget about them.
3. "The most relevant Clue": This made me stop playing the game after the first minutes of gameplay. (But of course, after a while I gave it another shot and finished it). There are times during an investigation that you have to select the most relevant clue you found at that place to continue, or link an older clue to new developments. The concept is very nice, but it doesn't work. You can't think logically to find out which is the correct one. You have to wonder what the writers had in mind when they created that part. Sometimes it just doesn't make sense (and apparently you have infinite tries, so what's the point, anyway?) I'll just give an example: At the beggining, there is a part where you have to select which information in a cop's notes is the most important one. I selected the one that to me was obviously the most intriguing detail, and any cop in the world would immediately investigate that. But no, the "correct" answer was somthing obvious, with nothing really interesting about it. After some minutes, guess what happens? Yes, Ronan (the main character) decides to investigate that thing that the game wanted you to think was not relevant at all.
Anyway, even with these flaws, I loved the game, and definitely recommend it to everyone who likes mysteries, and investigative games in general. It is worth it.

I had high hopes for this game, and it certainly lives up to the hype I had after looking at the trailer and screenshots. I am generally a big fan of well-rendered isometric games and am glad they've been making a comeback with the likes of shadowrun, pillars of eternity and xcom. The whole premise of this - a sci-fi horror isometric point and click - is brilliant, and well executed for an indie game.
The setting is very obviously dead space and event horizon-inspired. Reminds me a bit of Pandorum as well in many ways. When you're first thrown into it, the voice acting can be a bit offputting, you do get used to it though so don't let it spoil a great game. It's not terrible really, just...a bit clunky to say the least...
The gameplay is that of a decent and challenging point and click. What added to the horror and excitement of this for me was being able to die in it in several situations.
Music is brilliant, a bit reminiscent of McCann's for Deus Ex at times in a good way, as well as decent sci-fi horror atmospherics. the ambient and sound effects design I can't fault either, I never really got used to hearing at random the genuinely tormented sounding shrieks in the background.
The graphics are beautiful, every screen is a memorable work of art. Occasional FMVs were a nice bonus, I found my game could occasionally lag, which I wouldn't normally expect from a point and click. Overall though this wasn't an issue, and may have just been to do with what I had open at the time.
The plot is very well-written, the ending felt like a lot to take in at once, not rushed as such but....I still liked the ending of this though, a suitably unnerving and grim ending to a consistently grim and unnerving game. Plenty to read in PDAs on here for backstory and characters, can get too much at times but draws you in to that world.
I was sad when I finished it, was a delight to play, would definitely recommend to any sci fi/horror/point and click fans, and the good news is they're supposed to be developing a follow-up to release for free to the public.

All around great game. You can tell how much thought and effort was put into making it, and that's only going off of what I can see so far in Early Access. The soundtrack is amazing (real orchestra), the character customization is already great with seemingly MUCH more of it to come in the full version, the combat is challenging where it needs to be (with some pretty tough beasties out there) and makes your victories feel like they were earned rather than freely given. And now in a recent video they've announced that they've secretly gone and fully voiced the entire game for the full release (sneaky rascals) with 80 voice actors for the world at large and 14 different voices for the various player character options (6 premade characters + 4 custom males + 4 custom females).
All in all I can't fully describe everything that makes it great here in a quick review, but I can say that with some of the games nowadays that are seemingly just made in a rush for the profit (with 'real endings' and the other half of the game behind paid dlc), it's nice to be able to look forward to a game like this, one 'made with love' you could say :P If you like the genre and/or miss this style/quality of game than Original Sin 2 might be just what you're looking for. Honestly the September 14th release date can't come fast enough for this guy!

In many ways, a significantly improved game than ME1.
Controls were much simpler, albeit, not in a bad way. Some may argue that the weapon customizing feature was watered down in ME2. But to be honest, it was much more concise and sensible.

Next, the storyline, once again, proved immersing. The fact that your decisions count could make it as if you're in control of a story, a feeling that you don't usually get in today's games other than TWD and most of Bioware's games.
There's also huge replay value since you can embark on the paragon/renegade course with either a male or female character. Take for consideration also the plethora of choices that you can decide throughout the whole game. If you loved ME1, KOTOR, Dragon Age, and the like, this game is a must.
I would also suggest those who adored TWD 1 and 2. ME2 may be more FPS-oriented, but the story is always the game-changer for me, no matter what the game genre is.

In general this is a good game but it does have one glairing flaw that I'm a bit supprised has not been addressed earlier.  Outfits.   Outfits are not just a personal preferance.  Each party or outing has a dress code and if you don't meet that dress code even the person who invited you will have a chance of getting mad at you when you talk to them as they tell you that you are not dressed correctly.   What is worse is if someone invites you to an outing or party you go straight to the outfit selection with no way to find out what the dress code is.   Then to make it even worse, if you go to one you could look the dress up ahead of time there is still a good chance you are wearing something that people could complain about.   I went to a Disco that was casual and green with every item either casual or green and still got yelled at.  They don't even tell you what piece is offending.  Eventually you can unlock perks that make this less of a problem but that is many hours in.  Oh and apparently if you wear glasses or jewelry you will also need to have these be the correct style which makes me wonder if they have a negative effect if I don't wear them.
The social scene is quite important for even non social people but you can work on the relationships online and at home and then go to the party for the one or two things you really need.   However the party and outing aspect of the game looks like it could be very cool and useful and the best advice I saw online for dealing with parties was never accept an invitation to go.
The second biggest complaint I have with the game is that it doesn't handle distratcions well.  The first part when you live at your parents is not too bad as very few people come by and you mom will wait until you don't have anything queued to talk to you briefly.  However the second place you get interupted all the time and it's obvious they didn't design that system well.   I will often be doing a video and have pop ups that just need yout to click OK that block things I'm trying to do.   Or get invited to a party by someone walking in while I'm talking to someone else, click No to the party then have the person I'm talking to walk out and the game start the party dressing action (I said NO).  It happens a TON at the second place.  So far the third place seems better but it was agravating.
In general this is another place I would like to see a neutral vote.  I'm voting down becasue these flaws REALLY iritate me.  One makes the whole going out aspect of the game something to be avoided,  the second makes the game agravating being at home.   The rest of the game is rather good and after 6hrs I'm mostly still willing to play but I'm feeling I paid WAY to much for this game (And I didn't pay full price for it).  Lets hope that they do some work to clean up the game even after it's out of early access.  If they can clean up at least the going out problem (Just give hints to what piece is wrong and the basic hint on what the party needs when invited and let the fan base work it out would be fine with me) I would likely change my vote.

I did finally get the perk that says it makes any outfit good and gives bigger bonuses and people still hate what I wear and I still can't tell why.   I'm mostly to the point where if I want to get colaberators I have to go to a party, make everyopne mad at me so I at least get their contact info.  Then go home and chat with them online until they like me enough to come over.  Then I can talk to them to find out if they can help me.  I'm done with this game until they fix this.

Where to start? My steam stats aren't helpful, because I originally owned the GamersGate version of it and only recently had it migrated to steam. Nevertheless, I would estimate that this is the single game I've played the most since its release a couple of years ago.
2 important things have been the main contributors. The 'roleplaying' element is strong in this one. Taking the heritage of the original Crusader Kings, where the characters and their family relationships, rivalries and complex courts helped shaped the success of your dynasty in its rush to acquire titles, CK2 has let the concept blossom. You interact with characters - whether those in your own court and demesne or other families and title-holders, plotting against them, marrying them, sending assassins to help a title pass closer to one of your dynasty. There are lots and lots of events, random and semi-random to guide the freeform story taking place.
Secondly, Paradox have a fantastic DLC/update structure in place. Supported by paid DLC of two types, they have improved the game for two years already (and going strong for more), adding new mechanics and refining old ones. Major DLC usually involved adding a category of playable characters (originally only Christian feudal rulers available), but many of the core mechanics have just gone into the patches which have been going strong all this time. Cosmetic DLC has also been good and now well-priced for a quid or so.
It does take a little bit of effort to get into, and a Let's Play from youtube is highly recommend to get started, but if you're up for some personality-laden strategy, I don't know why you haven't already given this a go?!

There are those indie games that truly captivate your attention and keep you engaged for hours on end, and you know it's a gem when you find yourself spending the whole evening mining, collecting, running and blasting your way through zombie space.
MiniMax Game's Space Pirates and Zombies was developed by two blokes in Canada and boy, for two guys this game sure does outstand in the indie pool. You start out as a little 4-hardpoint ship, just plunderin' the good plunder. As you progress through the story you'll find out something crazy has stirred up at the centre of the universe. Something that allows flesh eating monstrosities to biologically enhance and drive their own ships, despite being mindless husks. The story has an enormous gravity to it; as the plot progresses, your fleet of AI-controlled ships, blueprints, hull types, weapon types, subsystem effectiveness, mining ability and the like go on the up as well. Doing this makes the player feel the gravity of the situation: there's a huge threat of space zombies capable of surviving without oxyen floating about at the center of the universe and you're going to need all the help you can get.
I suppose the reason why I find this game so enjoyable is an amalgamation of perfect game dynamics; the tactical RTS-like command of your own ship, with a main player-controlled ship and up to 4 other AI controlled ships, all of which are available for the player to directly take control of any time during flight. Missions are undertaken for either the civillians of a star system or the UTA - the universe's private military force, and doing favours for one faction often angers the other. The ever expansive tech tree is a delight, as well - research data, the space equivalent of experience points become increasingly important to get that rank of weaponary, subsystem, engines, or armour that you know you're going to need at the current system. As time seems to go forward when you jump from planet to planet and star to star, the players get used to planning a route according to a star systems ecosysem, 'difficulty' (measured in civillian or UTA strength) and managability.
With the addition of vicious money-hungry bounty hunters to the mix, I've never enjoyed any space-sim-top-down-physics-based-shooter as I have with this. I've found myself dedicating chunks of my gaming sessions to mining, exploring, trading, or fighting in this game. And when you finally get all the blueprints, all the ship hulls, and high-tier tech skill upgrades,  you're still finding yourself having a blast dealing with pesky space zombies. In a nutshell, I haven't quite experianced any game like this but I can sum it up into two expressions: YARR and BRAINS.

I've had this game for the past couple of years and the progress made throughout development was excellent. Lots of content was added and a lot of performance issues were fixed. I have played over 1200 hours and still have not done everything there is to do. A little of my experiences so far:
I wake up in an unknown land with a weird implant in my arm. As the world comes into focus, I realise that I am not in my own time anymore. Somehow, I was transported to a land where time seems to have reversed. I look around to take in my surroundings. I am on a beach. There are these big birds walking around making cute sounds. What are they? I get closer. They are Dodos. They are supposed to be extinct. Suddenly the earth starts shaking. I turn around and I see a Triceratops right behind me! What the hell? Run away! Luckily it is not hostile. O crap, I am very hungry. What can I eat? Aah, I can pick berries from the bushes and eat those. There are these small little things coming to look at me. What are they? Compies? They are soo cute? Here comes another one. And another... o Crap! They are eating me alive!!!
I wake up in swamp area. This looks interesting. I'm dead. Eaten by a Titan Boa.
I awake again, staring up at a Brontosaurus towering above me while the ground shakes. This is awesome.
Eventually I start making sense of my surroundings and start harvesting materials. Build a few tools, build a bow and arrow, start hunting. Build better tools, build guns, tranq darts, armor. I tame flying mounts and rule the skies. I tame a T-Rex. I investigate the obelisks and transfer to another world! I tame a Griffin. I steel a Wyvern egg. I hatch the egg and feed the baby untill it is a fully grown. Now I rule the skies and breath fire on my foes! Then I accidentally fly into the Lava of an ative volcano. We both die... :(

Ark is a very pretty and immersive game.  You will be entertained, frustrated and satisfied by the wide variety of creatures and things to do.  A good deal of time has been spent by the devs to make creature models and balanced game mechanics.  Once you have spent some time on the island map you'll want to explore the other maps... craving more.
The first official DLC map was "The Center", free to download.  A very pretty and interesting map... nothing really new, just different, interesting and fairly satisfying.
Then came "Scorched Earth", $20 US to download.  Nothing pretty here.  A couple new dinos with some interesting abilities and some new things to learn, new resources and such.  Nearly impossible to survive the environment.  Very frustrating, very little satisfaction.
"Ragnarok" came along, free to download.  Everything available in Scorched Earth  (except the chainsaw engram and the Pheonix) without the impossible environmental hazards.  The rich landscape, plentiful resources and diversity of creatures is very satisfying.
"Abberation" is $20 to download.  Much anticipated this map is easily the worst of the series.  The new dinos are lame.  The old dinos are boring or simply not available.  The landscape is difficult to navigate and become familiar with due to the overwhelming colored lighting and lack of a horizon. The environmental hazards are extreme although, to be fair, they are not as global as in Scorched Earth.  A huge dissapointment.
My conclusion is if they are charging money for a DLC its gonna suck.  If its free its gonna be a lot of fun.

The Survival mode is very good to play alone or with friends wich give a more extense to the gameplay, or if you are more of a competitive player, the multiplayer is also satisfying with some fun modes you dont find in other games, but in that regard you have better options for the classic modes.
Conclusion, it is fresh experience from what we have in the market about shooters, with the adventure touch that make Deadfall a diferent game from the others, and if you fan of QT adventures, you surely feel the similarity betwen them, so id give it a try.

I don't often write reviews for games, but I felt like this game deserves more attention than it's getting.
This is the classic Fallout-like game that I've been waiting for a very long time. Gameplay feels quite a bit like the first 2 Fallout games, with Action Point turn-based combat making a comeback.
It's astounding how many different ways you can play through the game with different character builds. You can smash your way through the game using melee weapons, take out your targets from a distance with sniper rifle or sneak up on them with a dagger, craft and use traps, bombs, cloaking and shield devices. Heck you can even use your mind powers to bend the enemies to your will or burn them alive. It's all up to you.
The underground world is pretty big and full of dangers, shady characters, competing organizations and political powers, gangs and cults. the dangers you encounter range from mutated rat-hounds and weak, mind-broken humans to psychotic, mindless androids with psychic powers. The richness of the writing in this game is astounding, which is proven even by the items you find, notes you read, people you talk to, or even just the paths you walk. Everything is nicely bound together to bring you a living, breathing, atmospheric and believable post-apocalyptic game world.
I could go on and on, but now I feel like getting back into it and squeezing another few dozen hours out of it.

///// A DAY LATER, IN AWE...
OK, the fact that this game is SO much more than a masterclass in happy hypnotism is amazing. there are actual systems at play here.
you will get attached to characters the longer they click for you and keeping some of them in line with the abilities of ones you can pick up later can be a very expensive (but wonderful) habit to keep. (i squealed in glee when my Insane (for real this time) ageing hermit wearing tiny little antlers on his knit cap dealt 103B DPS the first time - worth every one of the hundreds of trillions of gold coins it cost to get him there).
playing with character upgrades and skills with their formation is so smartly set up and left for the player to explore and play with, swapping gals and guys in and out of your lineup to see what changes occur is so deep it's like spinning around a gravity well.
and they don't stop marching onward (in place. ahahaha)
that adorable voodoo doctor owl and THAT GRIFIN - hug them and kiss them and give them anything they want because you will lose count of the times they save those you place ahead of them.
i seriously expected NOTHING from this game. (it's possible i actually started playing it by accident with an errant double click). BUT it's a magical combination of mindless not mindless, non-click clicking, grind that grinds itself while you're away - it has cute quest goals and cute monsters (that kill you) - my little ponies ON FIRE charging through your front lines, casper the VERY unfriendly ghost tearing through your entire party with a goofy smile and googely eyes...
last i checked i have over 9,000 pieces of pumpkin pie and so many other reasons to just play and laugh (the game is brilliant enough that you can also NOT play and still progress - (the non-SRS BSNS version of EVE online's skill queue?).
five words i never thought i'd write: a clickfest grinder of joy.
last words:  i've NEVER liked this sort of game before, let alone loved it.
(i'm 200+ hours into The Wild Hunt since august, Nobunaga's Ambition 14, am loving keeping my own notes while getting lost in Serpent In The Staglands, etc)
give it a shot.
you can always make more dopamine later.

This game is absolutely awesome. It delivers everything that I expect and love as a fan of old school turn-based RPGs while being modern in just the right ways (especially UI).
Of course this style of game might not be for everyone but I would still recommend it wholeheartedly even to those who don't usually play these kinds of games because it is way more accessible than many of them, since skill- and inventorymanagement are much less of an issue than is often the case I think.
Hit-chances can be a bit annoying at the very beginning but that gets better very quickly. But if u hate the idea of hit-chances I recommend going purely for Psi-abilities since they will always hit (except for very few abilities, but they have high chances as well).
Pros:
-Great customization in terms of skills, items, weapons, crafting etc, allowing for many different and all viable characterbuilds

This truly is a gem of a game. One of the best adventures I have ever played since the 'olden days' of Lucas Arts adventure games such as Monkey Island.
STASIS combines all that is great about the Sci-Fi/Horror genre, and in atmosphere, storyline, and presentation definitely can be described as an amalgamation of several franchises such as Aliens, Event Horizon, The Thing, Dead Space, and others. It's not as downright terror inducing as some movies or games are, but the subtlety behind the story, the way it is presented to you, and the almost casual way you end up dead in random situations, are definitely a novelty.
As far as difficulty is concerned, some of the puzzles require a little thinking, and I do admit that I did get stuck for a bit in one or the other area, but none of the puzzles are illogical, and the game does provide all you need to solve them; just read, read, and re-read the pads, don't skim or skip any of those, otherwise you may miss some vital clue on how to progress. Plus it is essential to the storyline.
So, in short, if you like Sci-Fi and Horror, and don't mind a little, good, 'old-skool' point-and-click adventuring, then whatever you do, don't skip this. And remember: In space, no one can hear you scream!

STASIS is exactly as described, a sci-fi point'n'click horror, but for people that have an overactive imagination (like me) you wont have to worry about any scares from an isometric perspective. Unfortunately it's not as great as it sounds.
The storyline has been used sooo many times, in games, in films, probably in books I haven't read, that it's actually frustratingly annoying to see it again. It screams lazy. We cannot be at a place in time where we have explored every fictional idea in the vastness that is space! Alas this is only part of the problem.
I've seen some people criticize the voice acting but I'd say it was the script/direction. There is extreme emotion trauma in this game which isn't really reflected by what "John" (the protagonist) says. His feelings seem inconsistent; he gets seriously disturbed at the atrocities he sees then couple of scenes later it's as if he has forgotten. On the bright side (if you like reading), a lot of what gives this game depth is written on PDA's found throught the game. You will need to read them as they give clues to puzzles. Thankfully, they're easy to see, well-written and give a lot of backstory. To the puzzles!
The puzzles are all pretty logical and not overly hard. The items are distinguishable from the art in most cases with only a few being the sort of small that makes you say out loud "REALLY?". What I would of liked to see is some timed puzzles to enhance the horror aspect of the game.
The art is great as can be seen in many of the screenshots.
Music didnt really fit well.
And animations need a bit of fine-tuning when interacting with objects.
I feel like I've been overly harsh, as I believe most of the work was done by a small group of family members. And it shows a lot of potential for future games if they use this one as a learning experience. It's not one of the greats but it's not a complete waste of time either.

After an earthquake destroyed you and your sister's home you both find refuge in a small fishing village. You decide to help the people in the village and the surrounding areas as a show of gratitude when pirates suddenly attack and kidnap your sister. Determined you vow to search the world for her.
HotK II has its own story which is not related to the prequel (there's only one small reference at one point) but the game works exactly alike. You meet new people, complete jobs for them, find items and trade items for quests and improve your skills. The story is more complex but it's still full of clichés with pirates and damsels in distress. The kingdom is a bit larger and seems to have more areas than previously. It's a clear homage to the King's Quest games and other, similar point-and-click adventure games.  You can die in several very stupid ways, and there are even ways of killing yourself added as little easter eggs.  There are even achievements for each method of death.
Be aware that this also means it has gameplay elements that might not be endearing to people looking for an old-school adventure game.  While MOST objects have a little glow on them, some items are maddeningly hard to find and require a bit of pixel hunting... or just checking a guide.  None of the puzzles have completely bizarre solutions, but I did have to use a guide in a few places.  The solution made sense in "adventure game logic", but never quite to the level of ridiculousness some of the old King's Quest solutions were.
The plot is pretty decent, with a twist here or there.  Voice acting is generally well done, particularly for the protagonist John.  The general setting is also fleshed out fairly well with the typical "apocalyptic log" stuff found in text form via various PDAs and terminals you can flick through.  The writing is generally high quality.
I did encounter two game-breaking bugs in my playthrough, but the developer was quick to offer a workaround after contacting them via their support section in the game's Steam forums and even offered me a free deluxe edition upgrade.  Something to be said about indie developers genuinely caring about their customers.  I wouldn't worry too much about bugs.  It seemed like I was just about the only one running into these problems, so most players will probably have a smooth ride - I just got lucky, it seems :)
If you like adventure games, it's worth picking up, although $25 may be a LITTLE high.  I snagged it for $12 (including the soundtrack and other deluxe edition goodies) and found it to be a real bargain.

Where to start? My steam stats aren't helpful, because I originally owned the GamersGate version of it and only recently had it migrated to steam. Nevertheless, I would estimate that this is the single game I've played the most since its release a couple of years ago.
2 important things have been the main contributors. The 'roleplaying' element is strong in this one. Taking the heritage of the original Crusader Kings, where the characters and their family relationships, rivalries and complex courts helped shaped the success of your dynasty in its rush to acquire titles, CK2 has let the concept blossom. You interact with characters - whether those in your own court and demesne or other families and title-holders, plotting against them, marrying them, sending assassins to help a title pass closer to one of your dynasty. There are lots and lots of events, random and semi-random to guide the freeform story taking place.
Secondly, Paradox have a fantastic DLC/update structure in place. Supported by paid DLC of two types, they have improved the game for two years already (and going strong for more), adding new mechanics and refining old ones. Major DLC usually involved adding a category of playable characters (originally only Christian feudal rulers available), but many of the core mechanics have just gone into the patches which have been going strong all this time. Cosmetic DLC has also been good and now well-priced for a quid or so.
It does take a little bit of effort to get into, and a Let's Play from youtube is highly recommend to get started, but if you're up for some personality-laden strategy, I don't know why you haven't already given this a go?!

I have just started the game, but I want to add my insight.
First off, I love this game. I am a huge Euro Truck fan and I am glad that SCS finally brought trucking to the United States. Reminds me of the good ole days from 18 WOS.  I know it is only a starter, but this should be an Early Access than a full game.
Pros
- Beautiful graphics.
- Fun/addictive.
- Love the cities.
- Police Cars
Cons
- Only two states. (I know they are adding more as the game progress. Can't wait until New York is added, to truck across the country, which could take god knows how long.) The lack of states make me feel and know that the game is incomplete. Some signs say closed, but I know once they add expansions they will open. I know when they add more cities, those routes will be opened.
- Only two trucks. One Kenworth and Peterbilt. (They are adding more soon, when they do I will take this line off)
- Fines. $1000 fines for speeding is much. I was worried about fines in Euro truck, now it is high. I had $1700 at the start, and a speeding ticket and I accidentally crossed the stop line, left me with only $53.
Overall great game. As time progresses, this game is improving, especially with the small staff at SCS. Kudos guys. Some persons are mad because this is the same as Euro truck. The President of SCS said this in an interview already that the two games will be similar. Same tasks, game mechanics but different location. And of course the cities are going to be small and not exact to par like in the real world. It is a $20 game. And this is a game, not real world. I am certain that the game will change some of the things. over time. But that is it, OVER TIME. I love the game as is, but if you want more content, I would wait. SCS is really working hard and remember they are not a huge corporation, so they work at a slower pace. The states themselves are small, but thats what happens when we have to drive across statelines for a delivery. What were you expecting a real 5 hour drive from LA to Las Vegas?
8/10 - Great game that will improve over time. Can't wait for Arizona and the upcoming states and trucks.

Here we are, yet another review on this game. I'm not gonna go so deep into things but I'll make this enough to know what's going on.
Been playing this for 2 years before I joined Steam and it used to be a fun game, but went downhill ever since CBS was released. There's been less and less balance between the characters since then and it's nearing a breaking point. to avoid most of the headache, don't do PvP. You won't be able to get a few items by avoiding it, but it's all mainly for looks anyway.
Dungeons to me are fine at first, but get really tedious after a while because it's the same tactic. Beat the crap out of everything as fast as possible, rinse, repeat. Very few bosses either need a strategy or force you to divert your attention. They have fixed the leveling issue a bit with the new random missions, but it's still a long grind in order to hit the level cap, which needs to be done if you wanna be as powerful as possible.
Speaking of power, this game is free to play, but is so Cash Shop geared that you can put tons of money into it and become nearly unbeatable. There's also players that pride themselves on this stuff, so that's even more fun removed from the game and the reason why no one really does another thing called Ereda Island despite there being less hackers in the game.
What I do like however is very little. I like how the game looks and some of the gameplay, but it's (again) overshadowed by the pay to win crap and lack of balance. The soundtrack isn't bad, but hearing it after a while, you may just mute it and get your own music. Most impressive looking places are the Hunting Fields and trust me, you'll see a lot of them given the grinding issue. I do like how the characters are designed too, along with the various looks you can give them even without putting a single cent into the game.
So, what do I think overall? It's decent if you don't mind the grinding and don't play PvP. But it's gone downhill so much that this is mainly to kill time or play dress-up. You can make friends, but you WILL make enemies too given the community. And in game crap is expensive, but smart players can get around that. All in all, it's a good idea gone bad and I can't really recommend it. Trust me, there's a lot more negative things I can mention about this game that I didn't put in...

Having almost 100h on record for this game, it is obvious it delivered for me.
The game is very old school in most regards. No map, no quest markers, minimal guidance. But I consider this an asset. It actually reminds me very strongly of Arcanum.
For me the combat is the best part of the game. It feels incredibly balanced. Although I was probably playing a strong build (pure PSI) I had to really use all tricks in my arsenal. Lay out traps, ambushes and use all sorts of mind magic (aka Telepathic PSI).
The graphics are OK, the soundtrack could use a bit more variety, but it adds to the claustrophobic feel.
The story is unfortunately pretty linear and if you side with the "wrong" people, events still play out the same, but you get punished by being told less lore. You will only know at the end of the game, which path to choose to get the most information and make the right decisions on the second playthrough. Considering one playthrough was ~100h for me, a second playthrough is not going to happen. This is a pity in the game design department, because you can very easily block out big chunks of questlines by some "roleplaying wise" / "information at the time given" sane decisions.
I am recommending the game as the overall experience was very enjoyable.
Only the story related design decisions mentioned above left a sour aftertaste. If you are easily offended by this, I recommend waiting a few month until all the secrets have been revealed in the wiki and than choose your path appropriately.
Otherwise, by all means, buy this game.

Absolutely wonderful, played at least 6~ different builds and spent countless hours.
Before reading further I'll give you a TL;DR of my review
TL;DR: Probably one of the best isometric turn based fallout esque roleplaying experiences to date, interesting setting, countless dialogue choices, clever writing, conversations and events that change depending on what you have done as a player. This is one of the best games I have played in years.
**THE GOOD**
- Combat is insanely difficult: this is a game where it expects you to play smart and plan ahead or it gives you a rude awakening. This is the Dark Souls of isometric turn based RPGs. When you beat an encounter that seemed impossible it is extremely satisfying. Don't expect to waltz your way through even the simplest of encounters.
- Combat is varied: you can beat encounters with magic (psionic skills), traps (landmines and the like), melee, ranged combat, etc. With some skills you can make enemies fight each other, run away from you in fear while you hurl icebolts at them or avoid combat completely by using stealth. I'm not sure how much of the game you could complete without having to resort to combat, but I'd reckon you could stealth past 95% of content instead of fighting it.
- Oddity XP system: This is probably one of the most clever XP systems I've seen in an RPG, you are rewarded for finding oddities, items which when found reward a static amount of XP. You can find some oddities on the corpses of enemies, but most oddities are found by exploring the environment, breaking into locked doors and opening containers, basically you are rewarded for your skill build rather than only being rewarded for killing enemies. If this doesn't sound good to you don't fret, the game includes a classic XP system where you gain XP from killing enemies if you prefer that. With the Oddity XP system you will reach maximum level right around the end of the game.
- Crafting: I wasn't expecting an interesting crafting system when I bought this game, but I was surprised to see you can basically construct items and equipment for specific situations. All items are made of components, things like leather and fabric, and these leather and fabrics come in many varieties with bonuses exclusive to them. For example when you use kevlar cloth as your fabric then you will be more resistant to bullets, if you swap that out with black cloth instead you will recieve huge bonuses to stealth. Expect to always be on the look out for higher quality components as you play to improve your gear, even at the end of the game you are always finding better components.
- Story: I won't say much since I don't want to spoil anything, but there are multiple ways to proceed in the games main storyline, you can murder everyone in your path or ally yourself with the bad guys. In the end, its up to you and the choices you have made.
- Immersion: If you do things that would make you famous, character and NPCs will react realisticly to this. I once leveraged my importance as saviour of the town to get alone time with a prisoner in their private prison, little did the prison warden know I had ulterior motives and was actually there to silence this prisoner. But it's not just that, say I didn't convince the warden to let me see the prisoner.. I could've broken into the prison completely stealth and accomplished my goal that way, and you can even break this prisoner out of jail instead of killing him. There are multiple ways to tackle a lot of the quests in this game, which is what makes it so interesting and in my opinion a good game.
- The World: This is basically the Dark Souls of isometric RPGs in more ways than one, almost every area you explore seems to lead to two or even three more areas. It really feels daunting and endless, you can get lost in caverns, subway tunnels, and other places for hours. It is AMAZING. When you beat a quest that has you clearing out a dungeon for lack of a better word don't be surprised when you find two more paths that can lead to interesting places at the end of said dungeon. This game rewards exploration, and I'd almost say you're playing the game wrong if you don't spend hours exploring for the sake of exploring, especially with the Oddity XP system.
** THE BAD **
No game is perfect, and I feel I'd be doing a disservice if I didn't share some of the things that might turn you off.
Difficulty: This is both the selling point of the game for me and its biggest problem. This is such an immense huge RPG and you won't even see but a fraction of it if you don't play the game right. Early on in the game is a quest which leads you to a place called Depot A for example, this place will rip you a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you aren't ready for it, and you most likely are not ready for it. It took me hours to clear this place the first time I came here, I even had to make a new character because I realized my build wasn't combat oriented enough upon arrival here. The difficulty persists throughout the entire game, nothing is impossible but most encounters you run into will have to be avoided and returned to later when you are stronger. Some people may not like that, but it adds immersion to the world, you are not the biggest badass in the universe and the game lets you know, you can eventually become a power house but you will not be one for a very long time. I'm currently on my 5th character, and I think my odds of completing the game at this point are pretty good. But I rerolled a lot just to get to this point. You can spend skills wrong, you can make your character wrong, there is no respec available. Play carefully and plan ahead. With all this said, I'm playing on normal and there is an easy difficulty, hell there is even a hard difficulty...
Deep Caverns: Now I don't want to fuss too much about this place since it would be spoilers, but at the very end of the game there is a quite long section of the game which is so different from the rest of the game and so much harder than anything before it that it might just drive you mad. With that said you won't be anywhere near the end of the game for at least 20-40 hours.
** IN CONCLUSION **
Do you like difficult isometric RPGs with heavy story and great writing?
Yes?
What are you waiting for?

An extremely basic twin stick shooter with very little to recommend it - the controls work fine, and there are a few bonuses to pick up that mix things up slightly, but that is about it.
There are four (?) enemy types - the large ones that shoot at you and move more slowly, the medium sized ones, the small ones that mostly are the ones to kill you (as they are fast, harder to hit, but still take a few shots to down), and another medium sized one that spawns two more smaller aliens when you kill it. You will also be killed by the walls any time you get too close.
You are relying on luck for your weapons/powerups - your starter gun and the triple fire gun are poor and semi auto so you will need to click a lot to stay alive. The beam laser gun is better but easy to miss with, the pulse rifle is okay (and shots richochet regularly which sometimes helps). The two best weapons are the green flamethrower type weapon and the chain gun, with the flamethrower probably the best because although the range is only half the screen, the little aliens are far less likely to dodge between the bullets and get to you.
There are a few non-weapon powerups - a shield that doesn't last long as it increases your hit box a lot, some sort of bomb that clears the screen when you pick it up, a bot that sits near your shoulder and adds a bit of firepower, and another bot that circles about you (didn't work out what that one does).
There are two game modes that don't really have any meaningful difference, survival you chose your arena, which basically affects the background colour, the size of the square arena you are in, and where the powerups are located. One Life mode just seems to be the same but without the choice of venue, and a probable bug where your score doesn't reset when you die, and even seems to multiply up rapidly.
If you want to play a game like this, better to try Crimsonland or Ubermosh.

Stasis is a fun point and click adventure game. In it, you play as John Marachek who, setting out for vacation with his family, somehow awakens from cryogenic stasis aboard a huge, deserted, and deteriorating shape ship.
The real prize of this game is the writing, which is vivid, yet as cold and harsh as the ship you find yourself stranded on. The story is not conveyed through interactions with characters, but through PDAs which log the experiences of many crew members as their comfortable life on the ship becomes a living hell. Because the narrative is all text-based, people who don't enjoy reading may get frustrated pursuing the story.
Gameplay in Stasis is not its strongest point. Progressing through the story consists of solving a small amount of puzzles ina hub. The puzzle hubs are not connected. Once you solve the puzzles in an area and progress to the next, you are prevented from backtracking. Because of the small area associated with each puzzle hub (generally up to 5 rooms at maximum), the puzzles are mostly easy to solve. The puzzles mostly consist of combining items in your inventory and using them on the proper environmental objects. If you are looking for logic based puzzles or puzzles that will challenge you, STASIS wont satisfy.
Finally, the graphics are something I really appreciated in STASIS. Though they aren't full HD with amazing textures and quality, they do a great job at projecting the right mood and environment. Without giving away too much, there are definitely a lot of gruesome scenes in STASIS and the designers did a great job at making it a very unnerving experience for the player.
In conclusion, STASIS is a great, spooky sci-fi adventure game with fantastic writing, but lacking in terms of gameplay novelty and puzzle design.

Stasis an isometric point and click adventure game, with paralells to Dead Space.  It’s not a bad game, but there are a number of areas where it falls short.  I’d rather talk about what it does right, to start with.  The sound design and art style are solid, as is most of the writing and acting.  There are some great body horror scenes, and the plot is fairly well put together.
But it also falls flat in a number of areas.  Firstly, the isometric perspective isn’t great for an adventure game.  Mechanically it works fine, but adventure games are primarily about characters.  The isometric perspective keeps you distanced from the characters, so you never get a good look at them, making it harder to get invested.  It also seems to run at a pretty low resolution, and suffers for it.  The puzzle design is largely average, with objectives sometimes unclear, and occasionally obtuse solutions.  As a seasoned adventure gamer, I have a pretty good feel for when I’m bumping up against this particular type of wall, and almost every time I consulted a walkthrough, I found myself vindicated as the solution was usually an obscure one.
It’s not a bad game, but I have a large gaming backlog, and I don’t feel it justified the time it took to play through it.  That being said, these developers definitely have some promise.  I’ll keep an eye on their future work.
