~~TL;DR: Don't buy. A great game ruined by an awful community, rampant exploitation, and some questionable tweaks. ~~
God, how I used to love this game. The objective-based maps were a blast, the Team Deathmatch was fun an a cut above the usual TDM you get in games, and the main draw - the combat, obvioulsy - was exceptional and fun, and I felt for a very long time other first-person melee combat games should be taking notes from this game.
This game is not nearly as fun to me as it was anymore, and I, personally, find it difficult to play for extended periods of time, like I used to be able to. To refer back to what I mentioned above: Team Objective is still good, I think, and they've added more maps (that were free updates, to boot); they changed Team Deathmatch to be faster and, to my mind, more generic - there was no longer a last man standing, and they tweaked the reinforcements meter to not even allow for such a thing to happen; and then, of course, the combat, which warrants itself a whole new paragraph for readability's sake:
It hasn't changed, it just came to be that more and more people found out how to exploit it. Without going into detail, it's why you see why level players doing this odd dance with their weapon, where it appears, among other things, that they're swinging at nothing, before they kill you. Of course it's possible to beat someone who plays like this, but it's more difficult and just plainly not fun, and removes the tension that was present in a well-matched duel between two skilled players, and replaces it with a general annoynace that you're probably just going to flatly die if you engage a player like that or, if you do beat him/her, it's, very plainly, not going to be a fun match. I was - and not to be arrogant - but I was at one point a reasonably skilled player, with an excellent dueling record and frequently scoring near the top in TO and TDM matches, and I still found it difficult to beat these players and, to reiterate, when I did, it was not a fun match. Mind you, I haven't played in some time, but I can only imagine it has grown even more prevelant, as it has been doing since those few handfuls of people discovered this dreadful exploit.
To be sure, there's a lot of different tricks you learn with the combat system, as it has a lot of depth and nuance, and there was nothing like a well-matched duel between two playerse of equal skill, or taking on three opponents and winning by using a combination of well-placed strike, the proper attack (there are three different attacks), and superior footwork. But the way that many high level players play now - with this odd dancing moveset (I'm not sure if it has a proper name, it's been some time since I've played) - is a clear exploit. Many of them will defend it, of course, but there was no way the developers ever intended their combat system - which was good enough that I would have called it (and probably still would call it, were it not for this awful exploit) the best melee combat system ever. It truly felt like you were in a swordfight (or axe fight, spear fight, etc.). It's not fun and it's not fair, and since this is a purely-combat based game, even in the Objective Mode, this is a huge problem that it has overtaken the community. It completely destroyed a well-balanced combat system (or at least the game was well-balanced at one point; I will comment on this further below).
And the community itself has only grown worse. I, for one, still find it baffling that players will condemn people for feinting - a move that was coded into the game (therefore being the developer's intention that you use it, integrate it into your fighting style if you so choose, and learn how to fight against people who use it) that allows you to cancel your attack within a certain timeframe of you swinging your weapon, which could cause an opponent to prematurely parry, leaving them open for attack. No doubt that this can be a frustrating move, but it also highlighted the importance of proper timing in this game, as someone who was adept at parrying would not be foold by a feint most of the time. But, at least the last time I played, this move that the developers explicitly put in (it has it's own key) is maligned and hated; and the dancing fighting style is met with a general: "meh, that's a pretty good player."
That was, perhaps, a digression, but I feel it's a valid complaint against the greater community of this game, and shows how accepted this exploitive fighting style has become. Other than that, it's a general awful community, with the sort of comments and idiocy that come with that. I don't care to go into detail here - I think we've all played games that have had garbage communities, so you'll forgive me if I neglect to mention the general nonsense and hate that is spewed by this one. How it compares to some of those games notorious for terrible communities - DotA, LoL - I couldn't tell you, as I've never played this game. Not all people are bad, mind you, and I've met some fun and skilled players; but as a whole, it's pretty bad.
Now, these are my main complaints against the game. The following complaint I cannot confirm, as I am unable to give specific details on it, so take it as you will. Some context: I have, throughout the years, gone in and out of playing this game. It's gone through some pretty extensive updates throughout this time, some of them wholly welcome, of course, like the UI changes and the new maps. There were those that I can clearly point out that I didn't like, like the changing of the excellent TDM mode that made it far less enjoyable, and my relatively minor personal complaint of no longer having your death animations play in first person. But with these updates came something indefiniable, at least to me. I've never been one to pour over patch notes, and I never looked to closely at the numbers behind a weapons speed rating, reach, hitboxes, etc., etc.; I mostly just learned the general feel of the weapon. But I felt like, somewhere along the line, the developers made some subtle changes to the game that had a drastic effect on it, and have - and again, forgive me, because this is where my review grows more vague - but have simply made the game less fun, even against those players that don't exploit the combat system. I can't put my finger on what it is, but the game at it's core, exploits notwithstanding, has changed in some way. Perhaps the balance has been off? The game was very well-balanced at one point, but it was constantly tweaked, and perhaps it was tweaked to the point of no longer being enjoyable and feeling proper. Or, perhaps this is a result of me having played this game to death, and no longer finding the enjoyment in it I once did.
I am, however, not going to let that above possibility factor into my recommendation; or at least I will try not to, as it may color it somewhat at this point. But the combat system - the ideas behind it, and largely the execution of it - was, and is, exceptional. There game boasts a good variety of game modes, all of which are find enjoyable in their own way. The graphics are excellent, and the game has received free map updates, most of which were excellent. There's a fair bit of humor in the taunts and other voice commands you can make your character say, and the voice acting behind it is equal parts comical and exceptional. These are all plusses, of course. Do I recommend this game?
This is hard for me, but I cannot recommend this game now. I wish there was a third option other than "yes" or "no," but I suppose that wouldn't be very helpful. It's a shame: I loved this game, and it had a lot going on for it, but a horrible and exploitative community deconstructed this game at the expense of others.

Stasis is a pretty decent point and click, isometric adventure game. Think of this like a horror setting for an isometric adventure game without any combat. The lack of combat makes it a very "relaxing" game, if the theme of the game itself does not unsettly you duly. There are a few, namely two, locations where timing is an issue, but that's about the height of gameplay-related stress you'll experience.
The game itself features a fairly interesting, if slightly standard, story. The puzzles involved are fairly straightforward, except for a few that suffer from the usual "combine everything with everything and hope it works" approach. As such, is not a particularly challenging game in itself.
With regards to the game itself, it is rather short - I'm guessing anyone but the most inexperienced players will be hard pressed to tickle a two-digit playtime count.
So, in summary, a fairly enjoyable, straightforward adventure game with a somewhat decent story. If you want a low-intensity snack of an adventure for an evening or two of slightly distracted gaming, go for it. If you want something with meat behind it that consumes your time, you'll be better of elsewhere.

First off, what a truly remarkable game by SCS; they’ve outdone themselves again with another great trucking simulator. Some might say it’s a re-skin of ETS 2, but it really isn’t; they share similar aspects, but it is
a re-skin.
It shares the same graphical details and even the graphical options in the graphics options as ETS 2 which is convenient enough if you’ve played ETS 2 before. They did however make a few changes here and there for added characteristics to the area and environment. This includes cracks on the road especially near farm areas, different cars on the road (More American style cars, like a station wagon), “rebranded” company names and dusty looking buildings in some areas. This is a graphically amazing game.
All gameplay aspects from ETS 2 is also present in this game, which is nice to see. It has been changed slightly, just very miniscule changes like: The turning circle for the trucks, this has been widen up a bit as these trucks are longer, making it harder to park, there is now a weighting system for the trucks to see if you’re load is overweight or not. The engine and horn sounds has also been changed. Other than that, this will feel right at home if you’ve played ETS 2 before as it has 99% of its gameplay aspects.
I would like to see more slight changes however, like a CB system to communicate with nearby truck drivers; better speed change mechanics. The speed limit changes waaaaaaay too often and sometimes you miss them, this can mean speeding in an area and getting fined for it. Taking about the fines, they are painful to the wallet if you ever get one, reducing this as early levels would make the game flow a lot better. Also, it would be nice to have more trucks, as there is only 2 brands of them in the game, I know they will add more though. Another one would be more cities and unlocked states. I can see that some of the states are greyed out, so I’m just taking this as a future state later on in the game maybe? I really want to see it as I’m probably only going to spend around 10 hours in the game until I unlock all the cities (I’ve unlocked 11 already).
Other than that, it delivers a solid gameplay just like ETS 2. But, it really needs a bit more attention on some aspects.
Nothing too fancy to show off here, I mean I’m not saying the sound is “bad” in any way or form, but it’s also not “good” either. Starting off with the moment you open the game…sounds pretty similar to ETS 2, which I like. Then, the “American Truck Simulator” logo comes up with a different sound from ETS 2, I wasn’t really impressed by this, but it’s certainly a nice touch. Once you get into the opening menu, you’ll hear a familiar soundtrack that almost sounds and feels the same as the one you hear in ETS 2, this is because some of the menu soundtracks from ETS 2 are “remastered” as I say it in ATS. They’ll sound similar, but not quite the same. I would’ve personally liked them to have changed the soundtrack completely so it wouldn’t feel like a “remastered” soundtrack, but it’ll do for now I guess.
In terms of engine noise, it’s all good, no problems there. The horn is really crap though, it sounds like a car horn which make the truck feel “unreal” whenever you press the horn. Yes, I know there is an air horn option, but you have to unlock it in order to use it *sighs* oh well.
I know you might be saying, “Why only a 5, c’mon, it deserves more than that surely”. Well, let me tell you something, not it doesn’t (As of this day). There is only 2 trucks (Kenworth and Peterbilt) and there is only 2 states with very limiting cities, you can potentially explore the whole 2 states under 8 hours of gameplay making it not worth the money right now. If the game gets free map and truck updates, then sure, I’ll bump up the price score; but for now, it only deserves a 5/10.
To warp it all up. It’s a solidly built game that shares very similar aspects to ETS 2 with a few changes here and there. It needs a few improvements in some parts and an addition for a few more states and new trucks, but other than that, it is a truly amazing simulator experience. This is a must buy for any simulator enthusiast.

For those of you who are wondering, SpeedRunners is basically Mario Kart meets Smash Bros. The goal? Race ahead of other players using items, speedboosts, and grappling hooks until one by one your opponents fall behind, touch the edge of the screen, and die.
This game is a blast both local and online, and run pretty smoothly for the most part. I do occasionally run into weird bugs where the game will randomly kill everyone, refuse to kill someone, or follow someone other than the leader, but it's never much of a problem.
The single player time-trial-like mode isn't that great, but you'll probably have too much fun in the multiplayer to notice. There aren't as many items as a Mario Kart game, but most of them are pretty cool: a hook to latch on to a player in front, a bomb that can be remotely detonated, a homing missile, a drill to speed you up and make you invincible, and crates to block incoming missiles and hooks or to trip up opponents. The stages are also great, featuring hard to reach shortcuts and alternate paths that can be closed off. Also, I have to say, once you master the grappling hook, getting around the stages feels so good.

Being a keen player of ETS2 and playing it for multiple hours at a time on my stream, I was excited when it was announced that on the 3rd of January the American Truck Simulator would be released to us all. And boy, has this been an exciting release. With over 90 hours in ETS2 before even purchasing a wheel I think it is pretty obvious that the uniqueness of what SCS have achieved pulled me in beyond what I thought imaginable. The ability to not only truck and deliver your hauls, but to run a trucking empire with a fleet of 50 trucks, multiple staff and millions of pounds in the bank.
After cruising down all the motorways in Europe in my trusty Volvo FH16, it was time to step out of my comfort zone and move into the Kenworth T680 onto the highways of America. SCS, I'd like to congratulate you on getting America to look, well, just incredible! The cracked rounds, dusty builds, rough textures and smooth skies, all make for a true American feel. But, and yes unfortunately there is a but! When ATS was announced it was also announced that the game would be released with California & Nevada, Arizona will be coming soon as a free DLC, so it was no surprise to me to load up the game and see a fraction sized map compared to what we are presented with in ETS2. But for the dedicated trucker who will be putting countless hours a day into the game this is nowhere near enough, having nearly 5 hours already and covering close to 20% of the map. To most fans this comes across as a lack of content and dedication from the SCS team, but after hearing the plans that are set we can stay hopeful that this drought won't last long.
Trucks, quite literally plural, yes, two trucks. Again, to be fair to SCS this was announced and the reasoning for this is very fair, it boils down to "Licences". Truck manufacturers aren't common with independent game companies like SCS asking for a licence to use their truck in a video game. But even still, this game has been in the making for over 2 years now. With those 2 years they managed one truck a year. We are presented with the
&
, Kenworth being my favourite thus far, but then again it's only between the two. I'm really hoping that more trucks are added very soon, but then again like ETS2 we can rely on the modding community.
Much has changed, ranging from parking your trailer, sirens from the coppers, weigh stations, oh and did I mention actual police cars! Finally SCS has given us the option to choose how to park; you can go with the full armature route of no parking at all, the intermediate which is a straight forward park and advanced, which is where it gets tricky. These different parking options result in different experience gains. Police cars, yes we now have coppers in the game! Now when you're at a junction and the AI decides to take ages to turn leaving you stuck behind a row of cars and you decide "Hey, let's just go round", nope. As you go out and accidently hit that Prius in front, you'll hear and see sirens 5 cars behind as you get fined a painful $1,800. Nice new addition, yes! But SCS what were you thinking? There is almost more police cars than normal cars, no longer can I speed down the highway and slowdown before a speed camera because there seems to always be a police car on the road next to me or directly behind me, or even BOTH! Weighing stations, now, when requested you have to pull in to get you truck weighed. If you refuse to do this and carry on your journey, expect a nice little fine coming your way, so turn in, get on the scales and drive off.
Being a trucking fan since ETS2 this was a must have for me this year. After being a follower of the blog posts to keep an eye on what's happening I am not disappointed. SCS Software has developed a great game! Now I can get that incredible feeling from Europe and now have it in the vastness of America, with much larger trucks and more features. As of right now the game is a solid 8/10 and will stay that way until the promise of more features comes our way, the day that comes this game is an easy 10/10 from me. So SCS get making more states and give us more trucks!

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a detective puzzle(?) game, with some action(?) elements.
You play as Ronan O’Connor, a cop whose wife died. That's all the back story the game has to offer. Though there was a bunch of collectables, each one had around 2-3 sentences of boring info. So I never bothered to read them, as it wasn't engaging or well wrote at all (much like this review).
Ronan is murdered at the start of the game by the Bell-Tower Killer, who Ronan was hunting down. He soon discovers he is a ghost, and he must solve his death to move on to the afterlife.
The game is open world, in the sense it has a hub of sorts between missions. It's literally just filler to add time to the game as you walk a short distance to the next area. The hub is littered with collectables to find, but they glow up so it's easy to get them all quickly.
Investigations are poorly done. The only game I could compare this to is L.A Noire. But this feels like the poor man's L.A Noire. It's a total cheap knock-off. Asians are not only making fake American clothing, but games now too.
You are thrown into an area and must walk about looking for clues. There is no indication of what might be a clue, so sometimes you could be spending upwards 10 minutes looking for the final one. Only to stumble upon by sheer luck, Whereas in L.A Noire, the controller would vibrate, or a jingle would play.
The clues are also really badly thought out. Most of them are just one word, or a little phrase. Instead of finding proper evidence, you'll get one word like "damage", or "scratch". It's as if no thought was poured into the game.
The only action in the game consists of you running up behind demons and holding a key, then pressing a QTE prompt that's displayed. There are no more than 20-30 demons in the entire game, so this was very lackluster.
Concluding investigations was poorly done. You'd be shown all the evidence you have found, and must select 1-3 different pieces you think are most relevant to the question asked. But this could be rather arbitrary. As the clues were poorly explained, it was hard at times to figure out the most relevant ones. There are 3 badges displayed at the bottom of the screen. I at first assumed these were lives, and that if I messed up 3 times I would have to start again. But it turned out they are not. There is no failing. If you get it wrong, there are no consequences at all. As there is no point/scoring system, or achievement for getting all 3 badges in every case.
Overall, the story was pretty meh. There was not much to it, and it was rather cliché. Nothing was really explained either, or made much sense. The main focus was figuring out the murders, but there were random things to do with other people tacked in, which seemed silly.
Gameplay was pretty bad. Being a ghost was cool, but there were issues with walking through walls. Investigations were poorly done. Again, if you expect another L.A Noire, you're gonna be seriously disappointed. Most actions were performed with pressing a key or two, and there was just nothing to it. You walk up to an item and hit E. There was no examining it, or any of that jazz. Action was non-existent. The whole demon business was stupid and pointless.
The game takes around 9 hours to complete 100%. Rushing the story and ignoring the collectables will probably reduce that time by around 3-4 hours.
I do not recommend this game, even on sale. It was a drag to play, and I only did so because of the Playfire Rewards.
If youre looking to play L.A. noire, get it on a console. optimization issues cripple the pc version.

An isometric sci-fi horror game with some of the best art and art direction you will ever encounter.  The authors did not use tiles or sprites.  Every inch of this game:  the overheads, the cut scenes, the close-up, functional views of various tech is thoughtfully, painstakingly hand-crafted.  In terms of creating a plausible-feeling atmosphere for what it might be like to live and work in space, STASIS has set a new high bar.
Unfortunately, the art is paired with fairly lukewarm gameplay and a story that's disjointed and boring.  I could live with the bad point-and-click gameplay, but by the end, I was just anxious for the thing to be over.  The unskippable voice acting snippets add little.  There is a lot of background reading that's intended to fill in the background, but most of that is even more boring than the main story.  By the end you will be briefly skimming the contents of the NPC diary entries, if that.  It was an interesting idea, but just seems silly after a while.
The gameplay and puzzles -- all of it -- can be summarized with one question:  what thing in this room do I need to click on next? If it wasn't immediately obvious what to do after 10 seconds, I usually looked it up because there really is no point in trying to figure anything out.
STASIS stands out among isometric games for its brilliant art and dark, horrific atmosphere.  Coupled with its pedstrian gameplay and weak story, it was less fun than I would have liked.  I still recommend the game for the glimpses you will get about what day-to-day life on a doomed research vessel would actually feel like.

So many little annoyances with this release of the game that made me return it.
TL;DR If you like your steam controller, you won't like this game. Also, plenty of other stupid annoyances.
Long version:
1) Even though the game is single player, you must be online and create a "Social Club" login to play the game.
2) It seemed to work with the Steam Game Controller initially, but then after an update to the game rolled out the controller support went all wonky, from working badly to not working at all. Even when it was working badly, you had to contend with controller prompts that were apparently for the Playstation version, and sorry I can't always remember that Green Triangle is Yellow Y during those quicktime events. F
3) After the update if you were using Steam's Big Picture interface, the startup screen pops under the Big Picture interface, making it impossible to start the game without exiting big picture and breaking out a keyboard and mouse.
4) Even  if you can get the controller mapping working, some of the button combinations are awkward, and the game isn't much help as it's flashing up Playstation control instructions to help you, which doesn't work as you aren't on a Playstation.
5) No way to exit most cutscenes. So, if  you fail a mission or need to reload you might be watching the same two to five minute cut scene over and over and over before the game allows you to move.

7) The dialog in the game is repetitive. It seems that they must think the people playing this game aren't very smart, because every cutscene seems to spend a third of the time repeating the protaganists backstory.
Overall, can't reccommend, too many obvious problems with it being a Playstation port. I'm sure it worked at one point, but as they like to change things when they re-release a game some of the older reviews may not be valid anymore.

(THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS! YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED)
There are some minor complaints, but for the most part this is an adventure game every adventure fan should have in their collection.
PROS:
- Great atmosphere that portrays perfectly the feelings of isolation and depression
- Great musical score
- Beautiful 2D hand drawn isometric backgrounds
- Great voice performance by the main character. The voice performance in general was very good and the only character who souned weird was John's daughter, but she doesn't have too many lines, so its not a gamebreaking.
- Very logical puzzles, although they could be a bit harder in my opinion.
- Interesting and engaging sci-fi-horror storyline with a shocking ending.
- Many surprises and small touches that make you appreciate what the developers did with limitted tools they had at their disposal. For example, almost seamless transition between the game and video sequences, crawling in the air ducts,  riding various vehicles, the operation part, etc. There is so much variation between the areas and how they are presented to you that the game never becomes boring.
CONS: (Most of these things are minor gripes, but I need to mention them):
- DEATHS. This is a personal preferance, but I do not like deaths in adventure games. This is because most adventure games use cheap unpredictable deaths to kill you. Stasis is a bit better and you get hints you are about to die, but still it feels a bit cheap. For example, when I opened the furnace, the computer starts talking to warn you of the dange, but you die even before the computer is finished. So I died not because I was too stupid to run away, but because I didnt realize I have control over my character while I was waiting for the computer to finish it's sentence.
- The game seems to be divided into different sections, so when you clear one section you never can go back. This results in puzzles being very localized and as a consequence much easier to solve. You will never have more than 5 items to work with, which makes progression much easier. Not a big issue (if an issue at all), but I wish the game forced you to go back a bit.
- Majority of puzzles rely on you noticing details around you and then putting them together in order to solve a puzzle. As long as you are observant, you will not have any problems with any of the puzzles. I wish there were at least 1 or 2 puzzles that required genuine intelligence to go further.
-The game did an excellent job in keeping puzzles logical. However there is 1 instance that does not make any sense. When you need to look at the corpse in a cage in order to trigger an event that leads to your capture by the mad scientist. There is no way to figure this out! The problem is that you trigger the afore mentioned event by using the eye symbol, which took me completely by surprise and it felt like a very artificial way to move the storyline forward. Unless you walk by or press on that cage by accident or curiosity, you will get stuck for no apparent reason.
- I liked reading the logs and they are very well written (am ignoring a few typos here),  but 2 complaints:
1. The whole premise of the game is to save your family. This creates a big sense of urgency which makes you want to skip over the logs.
2. Also, why does nobody on that ship ever lock their journal entries with a password? Even when they talk about things they dont want other crew members to find about!
- The game seems to build this huge story about SAMANTHA, but it never goes anywhere with it.
- Pathfinding can be awkward from time to time.
I know I have mentioned quite a few things in my CONS section, but quite honestly they are not huge issues and some of them stem purely from my personal preferences. I give it 8/10 and recommend it warmly. I also hope we will get a sequel or more adventure games from this developer!

This is basically a copy/paste from my previous post (which went ignored) regarding my original post 6 months prior.
Tried giving this a go since way back in March when I played. I had forgotten just about everything from my previous play through, but it all came rushing back pretty much immediately. So much seems exactly the same.
Things that jumped out right away:
o Camera (or lack of) to see an overview of the hole you are on. I'd say by far this is the biggest annoyance of this game. Maybe I'm in the minority, but I feel like 100% of the enjoyment is lost when you sink the ball into a hazard that you don't even know is there. This trial and error is extremely frustrating. There should be an overview (top-down) button that is always selectable at the very least A flythrough camera would also be nice at least for the start of the hole, but a birds-eye view would at least give you an idea where you are even shooting for. It is a fundamental of the game to be able to see the course/hole to know what you are aiming for. This is so much more important (in my opinion obviously) than additiona courses or ball shapes at the moment. It is the one thing that makes me not want to play the game again.
o No sound for striking the ball. Not only should it make the sound of hitting the ball, but it should also be louder based on how hard it is hit. Without this sound, it just seems weird (especially since hitting the ball into an object makes a sound). Very sterile and like the game is muted. The sounds could be realistic (like a ball actually "pinging" off the putter).. or more arcade-like with the sound of a swoosh of air and the driver whacking the ball. Just something to give it a little "life".
o No visual or audio cue that the turn is over and the ball is ready to be struck again.
o The stroke counter resetting to 0 immediately after sinking the putt. While yes, the score card is shown at that time, it still would be nice to leave the current stroke count at the bottom right of the screen until the hole is advanced. Since that is where you normally are keeping track during the game, it always seems odd when you sink the putt and glance to see what you got (something that is just natural), but just see a big 0 instead of your actual stroke total.
o Ball is routinely covered by world geometry. While you can still see your power indicator, it is very jarring (and just plain looks odd) to try and aim a ball you can't see.
I know this is still EA and you guys have been working on it quite a bit. Just giving my opinion again for that very reason...

To break up the monotony of dungeon crawling is an item shop system where you hawk the items you buy or find in dungeons for phat cash. In order to meet your quota every couple of weeks, you've got to learn how to buy low and sell high, and the game teaches how to do that, though a lot of it boils down to luck.
Finally, the characters are pretty entertaining, but hardly anything original. If you're looking for an action/RPG and don't mind the SNES graphics or the dungeon grinding, then Recettear is worth checking out.

First Impressions review of UnderRail (Edited due to more play time)
Pros
-A lot of choices for you to make your character, like plenty of skills and traits to choose.
-Writing is pretty solid, not remarkable but better than most modern games.
-The oddities system of leveling up is a pretty fun scavenger hunt in my opinion
-good item variation and crafting keeps the world interesting
-some unique areas have interesting stories when you piece the shattered remnants together
Cons
-Bare bones tutorial in the beginning that fails to teach you some fundamental aspects
-Some choices in the game don't have their consequences explained very well (for example not taking the psi pill in the beginning)
-The interface is crude and not very customizable, game is also missing a map which takes off some points.
-While the variation is a good thing some traits are clearly a waste of your precious points
-This game has the worst merchant/barter system I've ever seen in an rpg, merchants for an entire settlement only wanting 2-3 items.
-frustrating backtracking and mazes (looking at you damn Rathound King) made much worse to get out of by the lack of map
-Tons of loot drops you can't carry because the weight limit is too low
-rocks only being breakable by tnt charges is very stupid, there should be another way to break them after you get strong enough that is quicker.
Overall I will definitely continue playing this game despite its tremendous failings in some areas. No game is perfect and if you can ignore the problems this game is definitely worth picking up.
However I  just can't recommend it to the average pc gamer due to the unforgiving difficulty and lack of intuitive game design.

I have never played the 1st Divinity. Having being a D&D fan, the play style of this game reminds me of D&D but just with a graphical interface and no dice rolls. There is something new at every corner, you have no idea what to expect.
After understanding how the game works, I CANNOT quit playing it. It's immersive and hard. If you are someone who does not like failing at anything, don't get the game. If you are up for a challenge this is the game for you.
Some tips for you if you are just starting to play.
1: SAVE, SAVE, SAVE. Save a lot, you will regret not saving, trust me.
2: Don't get discouraged if you die, it's going to happen... A lot.
3: Pay atention to the dialog. Choices you make will effect the outcome of the dialog and actions.
4: Slow down. This game isn't meant to be cleared in a few hours. Take your time and look through and at everything.
5: READ, READ, READ. If you don't read, you may find yourself on a simple quest that takes 6 hours, because you didn't read, "Just teleport me over to that ledge beside that stump."
There are a few pros and cons to the game that I have found so far.
Pros:
Fun
Co-Op Play
Challenging
Cons:
Quite Expensive Game
Auto-saving doesn't save at the best times (You could go two hours with progress and not get an auto-save just to die and be set back 2 hours)
No voice dialect (There is A LOT of reading to do, granted the game is still in early access)
However, in a nut shell, I would easily rate this game a 8/10 just for the gameplay and mechanics alone. On top of that, I can't put the game down. I don't know what it is about this game. I just enjoy it.
Note:

Of all the recent-ish rpg remakes, comebacks and spiritual successors I'd say UnderRail is the purest. It takes the single character rpg formula seen in Fallout 1/2 and truly refines and improves it without compromising the complexity and depth expected of an "old school" game.
Combat in Fallout 1/2 was fun thanks to its colorful gore, npc taunts and that falloutesque
quirkiness but it very much lacked in tactical depth and tools that would add diversity and options to one's violent encounters. In addition, old Fallouts had loads of skills but many of them (namely non combat ones) felt underutilized and therefore unsatisfying to take. There was also no crafting in a post nuclear wasteland where survival, salvage and improvisation would've been very important.
UnderRail resolves the above flaws by adding a vast array of tactical options like activated and passive abilities, weapons that really work differently and require building your character around them, psychic abilities, equipment like combat drugs, tasers, NV goggles, cloacking devices, shield emmiters, mines, flashbangs, poisons, etc., a functional and useful stealth system that has both combat and non combat utility as well as a robust and detailed crafting system that is actually useful but not necessary in case you don't like crafting (it's yet another thing that becomes part of your character build or not).
Skills are all useful (not equally of course) but also require careful consideration not just in terms of the skills themselves but also how they synergyze with your feat/perk and equipment choices. Long term planning is important. Character building is very detailed and definitely a strong point of the game. You don't just make a melee character or a ranged character. You make a specialized sledge hammer wielder, or a pistolier that combines one handed firearms and riot armor with shields or a sneaky, trap laying crossbow using poisoner, or a "monk" that combines unarmed martial arts and psi abilities. How about a scary, paranoid, crazy scientist with acid firing pistols, plasma guns and mind controlling psi who melts both bodies and minds? It's a character builder's dream with skills, feats and equipment all beautifully designed and integrated to allow for all sorts of specialized and hybrid builds.
Writing in UnderRail tends to appear functional and spartan at first but as I explored the game I found quite a bit of humor and elaborate descriptions of characters many of which are interesting in their own way. It's a post apocalyptic, underground, cyber-punky setting so many characters are pragmatic and to the point but not all and the game is not unkind to fans of text and story. There's a good amount of quirky characters and setting specific colloquialisms and expressions and bits of lore and background to discover if you care to. It's just that immersion requires a bit more of one's own effort like rpgs used to, it's not served up with voice acting and fist person perspective. The writing does suffer from a large number of typos though (at least at the time of me writing this).
One very interesting aspect of UnderRail is it offers two experience systems at character creation. The "Classic" one is what you see in almost every rpg out there but with the "Oddity" system you get no xp for killing or using skills like lockpick, only for solving quests and collecting oddities which are all sorts of strange or old world objects that you can study to advance your character. The oddity system rewards stealth, exploration, social skills and non-combat solutions and works remarkably well, both systems do and make for a welcome option.
UnderRail is not an easy game, normal difficulty actually provides a stiff challenge. There are no quest markers, no maps (only a compass), charging recklessly into battle will often get you killed. It's a game where secondary tools and consumables are actually useful and required, not just something you hoard and never use and it's my top RPG for 2015.

Reminiscent of Fallout 1-2 with a twist of a "modern" feel of the cave crawling of the Avernum series. Character specialization building is a must to progress without running headfirst into a brick wall. I started over several times because I wasnt familiar with the game world. It will happen to you as well. Min/maxing your character comes with experience of what to expect. If that bothers you then you will have to make a descision if that is a deal breaker.
Oddity/Classic experience system. Oddity means you find things to "study" that give experience instead of the "classic" way of killing things to earn exp. This essentially means that you do not have to build your character solely for combat, but combat is still a focus. You will fight, but it allows for more varied play-styles.
Graphics are retro, but well animated. Quirky, but I would argue full of soul. The devs really put their heart into this game.
The story was well thought out. Very logical and consistant, but only truly makes sense if you take the time to do things properly and I mean that certain outcomes of questlines will yield different results. You can fail quests and you can come across surprising results.
Endings change base on your actions. Similar to the Fallout 1-2 games.
Music repeats itself retro style over and over, but I found the music designed very well. It was made in a way that fits where you are. Very well done.
Game is very long. Seriously. 50-100h on average depending on how quickly you do anything, but rushing is actually detrimental for a first playthrough in this game. You WILL miss things and it WILL screw over potential gains for the ending and for quests. I know this firsthand.
This game is built for nostalgia and for a new adventure. It is well worth the cheap price of 15 dollars. Frankly, I think its worth more. The game isnt for everyone, no, but if your tired of the crappy hand-holding experience you get with the more modern RPGs and want to try something a bit oldschool, but still modern concering isometic tactical RPGS, then give this one a try.
Hell, taking your family out to the movies would be more expensive. That alone makes this worth the price.

Better than expected! Even though the engine is the same as ETS2 SCS Software put a lot of work on it to optimize it and give "Truck Simulator" series a whole new difficulty level.
"Oh, it's only nevada and california"
Don't go with that. This isn't Euro Truck Simulator 2 where states are pretty much 2 to 3 different roads of endless repetitive content (Like those gas stations and hotels that are always exactly the same). In ATS you'll have to think beforehand on your fuel and also care to know which exit to take to get closer to the Gas Station, as most of them are inside cities and not spread on whole map on the roadsides.
Driving through city with a huge truck really feels like driving in a city with a freaking huge truck. Trust me, it's MUCH more immersive than ETS2 in this aspect. To be honest I wouldn't feel a difference in ETS2 as most cargos were likely to be the same size only with weight differences. In ATS you'll notice every aspect of the cargo you're hauling. Be it the disposition of the axles, weight and also size. I'm not sure if it's because I'm not used to it yet but driving in and out of cities can be REALLY difficult. You'll have to be careful at all times because, also, the tickets and fines are a thing now. They are something you should be really worried about in the early game as two fines and there goes all the money you'd get for this trip in the first place.
I give this game a big yes. Can't wait for the 2 new states they promised to be free. And if they meet the same quality level as Nevada and California I'm certainly buying /EVERY/ DLC they ever release for this game.
Props to you, SCS Software!
(On a side note, even though this game has only two trucks right now you'll barely notice it. There's plenty to change and plenty to work for. I really hope they release new trucks soon, but seeing how much you can modify your trucks right now I don't even mind there being only two.
You have several engine and transmissions to choose from, 3 cabins and multiple types of chassis. And of course, custom mirrors, handles, exhausts, tires, wheels, etc, etc. )

Stasis is Dead Space reimagined as a point and click adventure. There is a tremendous amount of detail put into this game. Almost every piece of each part of the levels has a unique description, describing even the way a shadow cast by a slow spinning fan makes your character believe he's seeing things move in his peripheral vision. The pdas you stumble across flesh out a large deal of the story. Each one belongs to a unique npc, and is filled with backstory ranging from why he got on the ship, whom she’s in love with, to how they are coping with the dubious experiments taking place. It's all the best things about an interactive story, and neither the puzzles, nor the horror overtones, go out of their way to interfere with your progress through it. Highly recommended to fans of dystopian space drama.

Awsome game!
It's something new and original, something you won't see often these days.
I played for about 16 hours to complete it with all it's side quests and most of the collectibles, that reveal some nice story elements.
Didn't find all of them yet, though.
While the graphics are fantastic, the textures and animations of all non story relevant characters are pretty low.
Their movement is kind of stiffm their textures low res and on that many of them even share the same textures.
Since Salem, the town where everything will tak eplace in, is pretty small, you will have the feeling to run across the same five npcs the whole time.
That said, it might even hurt the game concept if it was bigger.
Everywhere in the open explorable town, are notes and similar collectibles hidden. Despite Salem's small proportions, those collectibles can be pretty tough to find, since you won't come across them if you aren't searching for them.
Among notes and ghosts and humans  with trivial conversations, you happen to meet some ghosts with their own problems.
If you find one, a side quest opens up and you can help them to get rid of their problems and move on.
The system to help them is the same as in the main story line.
The Main story line uses a puzzle system which repeats itself with every quest, but does never get old at the same time.
Since you are a former detective, you will investigate each place, lokking for hints and combine them to find where to go next.
Those hints are aquired and combined by many different actions to assure varied gameplay.
The story itself is very atmospheric and intense with a good soundtrack alongside.
The story characters have all an own personality which is intentionally used to drive the players sympathies.
All of them are important in their own way and no one of them is forgotten quickly.
Technically is some room for improvement.
There are some minor bugs, graphically and not affecting but common.
I came along one game breaking bug which forced me to reload an old checkpoint. Saving is done automatically and fair placed, though.
Hitting some walls will let Ronan twitch around for a second while some other walls, intended to vanish at will, can't be targeted to do so. Luckily, there is always another way around.
In the end I would give this game a 7 out of 10, strongly recommending it to experience something new.
Overall a VERY competetive game to have fun in. Very simple mechanics, but surprisingly unique. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys competition

Great Game. SCS have drastically improved this game since the release below and as such I have adjusted my below review to reflect this here:
The game has a much larger map now thanks top the rescale under way and also advanced systems new to series such as coupling of the trailers and new physics. The modding community also have expanded options now thanks to the support of SCS and the game is soi much more satisfying to play. Relax, chill out and explore the open world of ATS.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SCS have certainly improved since the making of Euro Truck Simulator Series and this is just the beginning for the American alternative.
So far I have enjoyed every moment playing the game. The new engine, typical American environment, the trucks, traffic, police, economy. It all ties in nicely. Sure there are some things that can be improved, as always, but as a release I see no issue.
(Especially for such a reasonable price of £14.99, where can you go wrong with the investment if you are not 100% confident!)
Key features:
- New American setting covering 2 states at the moment
- New American themed trucks 2 at the moment
- New Police system that matches the environment of the states. If you are speeding and the police see you they will fine you and alert you to there presence by turning their sirens on and driving on.
- Different physics and truck handling to represent differences in the cab types.
- Much more challenging parking system and locations
- Longer trailers which in combination with the cab adds a new challenge to driving these monsters.
- Slightly enhanced company management and improvements.
- Integration with World of Trucks and profile.
- Much more!
Now I imagine over time the game will get better. The licensing issues with trucks and so on will come in time hopefully but it is a start. The free-dlc will most likely be all the states that are finalised over time and trucks that are approved.
When you first look at the map, it may seem rather small, but when you are driving the routes and roads, it is a whole different scale. With only 2 states it is quite extensive and when more are finished it will only grow and get better.
*On a side note: The community always enhance the series with mods and before the game was even released, modders have already created some nice new additions. From more trucks, standalone, to physics, traffic and economy related mods.
As time goes on I will update this review to reflect the changes that are made. :)

I love my space trading/combat simulators, I love my gory first-person shooters, I love my stealth action over-the-shoulder games just like the next guy, but there's something special about a good point-and-click adventure title. I think it's the potential the genre has for narrative.
STASIS really doesn't disappoint in that regard. It does a whole lot with a very barebones start, no less. The story is a bit tired, the voice acting can occasionally be grating, there are three characters in the entire game and they're all pretty trope-heavy. Despite this, it's an excellent game.
The PDA logs were an unusually interesting experience. While I will usually skim these pretty religiously for clues and information, I found that the plentiful PDAs were slightly redundant, offering very colorful and diverse persoectives on what was sometimes overlapping information. Each of the characters' stories were fascinating, which is probably part of why the whole experience was so riveting. Perhaps what was best, was that in the event you missed one, you weren't screwed in the long run. You will not want to miss them, though, because they're half the fun.
The puzzles were not overly difficult. I'm by no means a master at these things, so I had to walk away for a few minutes from time to time, but I was able to negotiate the entire game without ever resorting to a guide, in a pretty reasonable amount of time, about ten hours. None of the puzzles was difficult enough to really break the narrative pacing, I felt.
The imagery was great for such a simple media. THe game does a lot with a little, again, in this regard.
Voice acting was a little bit rough in places. The daughter in the first flashback, for example, was so bad that I was convinced briefly that there was something wrong with my computer or with the game. It worked beautifully whenever it counted, though, and was never really grating.
If you're not the patient sort, you may want to give this one a pass, because it is extremely sluggish, as these games can some times be. If you enjoy a very dark narrative with some very cool puzzles and imaginitive design, you'll want to grab this one in a hurry.

I've played, or at least ATTEMPTED to play, quite a few point-and-click adventures in my time, and the sad truth is I either give up on most of them before I reach the end, or I cave at some point to the temptation to look at a walkthrough, and from pretty much that point onward, find my lazy♥♥♥♥♥♥returning to said walkthrough so frequently that I probably could have just watched someone else's YouTube video and saved myself all that RSI from clicking.  There's only a few point-and-click adventure games which I've seen through to their conclusion WITHOUT constant deference to a walkthrough, and Stasis is one of those games.  (Well, okay...a few walkthrough consultations, to be sure, but not THAT many considering, haha!)

A lot of people downright believe that this genre of gaming should have gone the way of the Dodo a long, long time ago.  I mostly agree.  But it's the rare game like Stasis which completely validates the genre's ongoing existence.  STASIS is just modern enough - with its gorgeous graphics, atmospheric sound, excellent voice acting and generally high level of immersion - while still evidencing the kind of story-telling and puzzle-solving logic which surely only the very best point-and-click games, of any era, are able to boast.  It's completely "real-time", you CAN die, and on the whole it's about as "cinematic" as a point-and-click adventure can be without ever fully crossing over into the "action-adventure" stakes.  It's even a tiny bit scary, in its way, but not enough to make it a tie-breaker as to whether or not one should purchase it (i.e. don't buy it expecting Dead Space 1, but likewise don't be discouraged from trying it if you "don't normally like" scary games).

So who would I recommend this to?  Anyone, anyone at all, who thinks they might be in the market for a high-quality, moderate-difficulty, ultra-atmospheric, surprisingly emotional and, okay, rather "dark" point-and-clicker.  If you don't like reading and/or don't like games where you don't get to shoot loads of things, then please, KINDLY ♥♥♥♥ OFF.  Then again, if you don't like reading things, WHY ARE YOU READING THIS REVIEW?!  So, er...if you managed to get all the way to the end of this review, I guess I'm recommending it to YOU, whoever you are.  It's damned good.  Trust me.  I don't even usually dig this kinda game all that much, and even I think it's staggeringly good.  That's gotta count for something, surely...

Having played the first title, I would have to say that this game improved upon what the first one did, at least ever so slightly.  A simple improvement was not having levels to the skills you learned, as it made you have to retrace your steps and return to all of the early areas in the game multiple times as you'd find something else to collect.  For instance, in the first game you would collect the hidden mushrooms, starting off with the brown ones, then the red ones, and lastly the blue ones.  So at the start you'd only be able to gather brown ones and it wasn't until you leveled up the skill that the other ones would even spawn in.  This was removed entirely, so once you learn how to collect them, you can get all of them in one go (more or less; if the screen is still partially greyed out you can't get them there of course).  There are still times where you do return to earlier screens, but it's not nearly as tedious this time.
Early on in the game, you'll come across a goblin in a cave, with two options on how to address it.  You can either lure it away or take it on in combat.  I was quite excited when I saw that because I thought it meant the game would have these sorts of options throughout, with you having different options on how you wanted to progress.  Maybe instead of getting health potions you'll stockpile weapons to blitz through or instead of giving them X amount of gold you give them X amount of rarer items.  This early encounter was misleading though as this only comes up one other time and has no impact on the gameplay or events.  I have to wonder if they started implementing it in but either hit a deadline or just didn't want to put in that much further effort for an otherwise linear progression of story events.  It is a disappointment either way.
I think the one aspect of the game that felt underdeveloped to me was Salamander Island.  It's a late-game area that you do almost nothing with, which is rather ironic later on.  Since it's a peaceful island they don't have much conflict, so you only need take care of two simple quests and you move on.  Even with the optional task you can complete there the island has very little to offer, giving the overall feeling that they had less content in the late game.  In the first game it seemed like you had several areas that needed to be worked through at the end before moving on, but here it was more direct.  I suppose that is the downside to not having skill levels and maybe others don't see it the same way as I do.
The achievements weren't quite as demanding as last time, which required you to find every last hidden mushroom and egg.  There was more leniency and it seems like they were easier to find this time around as well, though I may just be a bit more inclined to know how this game works having played the first one.  Only two items in the game really threw me off while I was looking for them.  One was a shoe on a cliff while you're searching for a missing man (that one was completely unexplained and too integrated into the picture for you to notice) and round stones near the end-game (they are optional and once I knew what they looked like it wasn't too hard finding them).
Simple flaws I brought up from the first title are still around.  Like last time, as you click on hidden objects, you have to wait for them to process and then collect them before going to the next item, which is a bit annoying with the game being so basic and you'd think quick to process.  You also have to click each individual time for every increment of item you wish to buy or sell, which can get old fast, especially if you're doing a bit of grinding.  On that note, the best time to do so is after the king gives you money for the ship, as you'll have plenty of gold to turn it around into more money.  I recommend checking the guides on how to do so with the poison method, as it's what I used.
If you were like many individuals who enjoyed the first game you are getting more of the same here, with a bit of improvement in a place or two.  However, it's fundamentally the same game and they didn't expand it as much as they could have.  I don't see it being worth anymore then the first game ($8 instead of $6), so I wouldn't buy it at its full price, or at all if you got your fill from the first title.  Despite how it sounds I did like the game though and do recommend it, I just wish they had done more then they had, especially when they hinted at more versatility that didn't end up delivering.

I enjoyed both games but accept they may not be for everyone. They can be repetitive, extremely casual to the point of boring, and it can be argued that the most boring quest in most rpg's are the fetch quests .... pick up item from point A and deliver to point B ... and that's what most of this game consists of, but the game did enough in terms of storyline, and quest variation to keep me interested.
So if you want to try something a little different as a casual time-sink, play the original. If you like it, the sequel is more of the same, but better.

First off. I know people are going to read this and go "You have 1.5k HOURS IN THIS GAME HOW CAN YOU GIVE IT A NEGATIVE REVIEW?"
Easy. I've played the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. I love it. I split the time playing it between myself and a family member. Interacting with dinosaurs? Amazing. Building a base? Amazing. The overall concept of the game? Amazing.
The difficulty? There are so many times in this game where something stupid happens and it literally has a domino effect on everything else. It's immersive. You take ONE moment for granted while you're mining, or picking some berries and out of NO WHERE you'll get bum rushed by a large dinosaur who's hungry and wants YOU and your TAMED animal for dinner. Within moments the flying mount you've spent HOURS taming can be gone. It's infuriating. You get so mad, and then you go back, and you rebuild. You go find another dinosaur to tame. YOU won't get beat by the game. Even at higher levels it's difficult. It's unforgiving, and for that I appreciate the game itself.
Why can't I recommend this game? It's broken. I've been playing since Alpha and there are STILL snapping issues with buildings. You have structures that have clipping issues and make it difficult building things next to each other. You know minor things that can be fixed relatively easily that have just been overlooked.
Some of the dinosaurs are incredibly unbalanced. MicroRaptors are hands down the worst thing ever introduced to this game. You literally have no way to combat them and they often come out of no where and are found near numerous other dinosaurs that have no issue taking a nibble out of you and your mount while you're stun locked for 10 seconds. It's hard enough being knocked off of your mount. This is just one of the examples I can give as far as how over powered some of the dinosaurs abilities are.
Constant bugs. This game had NO business exiting early access. I can honestly say that. Every single time you roll out a patch you're breaking something within the game. It doesn't necessarily have to be a large patch like the recent one with aberration. Often times it's small little patches that cripple the game system to the point where it's unplayable. I recall a patch not long ago where anytime you went to harvest stone the game would just hard crash each and ever single time.
Stuff like this shouldn't be happening to a game that's out of Early Access.
Quite simply. This game was not ready for a full release. It still is not ready for a full release. You shouldn't have game breaking bugs every single time you release a patch. A proper game that is ready for release is Polished. It functions. This game does not fit either of those criteria. It's understandable to have SOME issues with each major patch, and we appreciate how often Wildcard releases patches and adds things to this game, but this game is still by all means an Early Access title.
For that reason, and that reason alone. I cannot recommend that others buy this game. Not until Wildcard fixes some of the glaring stability issues that it has.

Believe the hype. The learning curve is as steep and high as the Empire State. You can get grossly unlucky with random events, or if the AI makes good decisions, or itself gets lucky with events. There's a million complex systems that you have to learn intricately to play even semi-competently. There's no clear plot or goal to this game. You can lose for reasons entirely beyond your control. Married your daughter to a neighbouring King for an alliance? Well his son, your grandson, comes into power and now he has a claim on your title. This game can be brutal for newcomers. However, if you manage to learn how to play, you will have endless hours of fun in this game. The depth is ridiculous. Whether you love medieval politics, history, or are just a fan of Game of Thrones (there's a total converstion mod), you'll love this game. If you're the kind of gamer who loves Total War games, but hate how historically inaccurate they are, then Paradox Interactive is the company for you.

THIS IS NOT A CITY BUILDING GAME.
My friend and I bought this game on sale thinking it was a simulation/city building game, and then neither of us touched it for months. I was pleasantly surprised to see it's nothing of the sort. I'm not quite sure how to explain it, I guess the best explanation I can think of is "Point and Click". It's in a medieval/fantasy setting. You and your sister are homeless and looking for a place to live, you come across a kindly old man who lets you stay with him, in exchange for a piece of bread. One day pirates attack your cozy little village and kidnap your sister, and you have to rescue her.
This is the basis of the game.. sort of. The game basically takes place in still images.. or maybe a GIF would be more accurate, but don't let that deter you. It is a very relaxing game. No pressure. At the point I'm in (About 1 hr into it) it isn't difficult at all, but that's okay. This is a nice game to chill and relax and play. There's no time limit. You basically click between maps doing favors for towns people, usually in exchange for what you need to get further in the game. I came across a friendly troll who would let me pass in exchange for 25 pieces of bread. Don't worry, the game isn't all about bread, but it is all about clicking one thing in order to do another. The story is simple, but it's soothing. This game isn't going to blow anyone's mind, but for the low price tag it is absolutely worth it.

What ships you use, how you equip them, what tactics you employ, where you go, who you befriend/betray/fight, it's all up to you.
If you enjoy Sci-Fi and shooters and a simple but great game with a rather twisted, grim-dark universe, all for the low price of 9 EURO's that don't demand a monster of a gaming PC, this is for you.

This small review is based on limited free weekend gameplay. After finishing the first part of the story I wasn't allowed to continue, so practically, what I played was just a 7GB demo. Ouch.
The camera nearly made me nauseous at times, but the game is pretty. It's a linear game, but you're allowed, and encouraged, to roam around the places. There are hidden treasures that upgrade your abilities, spread around in nooks and crannies. That's a plus. However, one big room that begged for exploration didn't seem to hold anything, and ending up in the water, that was everywhere, made you drown. In fact, most places you would expect something hidden, you would find nothing.
The first taste of combat felt quite awful, but it might just be that the pistols you start off with are bad. I couldn't really hit anything properly. It seemed to improve later on though. There's a nice variety of weapons to use. Some enemies requires using a flashlight in a certain way (like in Alan Wake), but it wasn't explained well, forcing me to look it up.
The story seems a bit thin, but alright. The voice synching and face animations could be better though. The puzzles seem fairly easy, but the notebook that is supposed to help you is a bit frustrating to use. It doesn't help that it's bound to the middle mouse button by default, which is also the melee attack button, which I found out by chance. Some of the notes I couldn't figure out where I was supposed to use.
All in all, a fair adventure/puzzle FPS game. Honestly, it's quite overpriced (even at 50% off). I suggest picking it up during a sale, if you like this kind of stuff.
Notable alternatives: Tomb Raider, Adam's Venture.

It's one of the best cRPGs in over 10 years and the closest game to Fallout 1/2 than any other game (including New Vegas). Still, it's a worse game than
which is the best cRPG ever (only Fallout 1 can compete).
The exploration here is superb (if you think exploration in Gothic was great you should play UR, you can even blow up rubble that blocks your way and make your own passage), fights are fun and often challenging forcing you to use your brain instead of mindlessly clicking on an enemy, crafting is quite complex and well developed, character creation is well designed and allows for different builds and different playthroughs (not as good in AoD though). The plot and dialogues are decent and even though most quests are fetch/kill quests there are many very interesting ones so that the player wouldn't get bored.
The game isn't without flaws of course. My main gripe with this game is that you can't run here and travelling is so slow. Due to this about half of your gameplay time will be spent on walking from point A to B. It's not as bad as in Bethesda games though where locations are bloated so that the world would seem bigger. In UR there is also a form of fast travel so after first few missions it gets much better. The other thing that annoys me is that font is too small. There are some more minor annoyances but all in all pros outweigh the cons in overwhelming proportions. Because of these cons however, I consider Age of Decadence a way better game despite the fact that Underrail is one of the best games I've played in 10 years or so. But UR is cheaper and it has as good value for money as AoD.
tl;dr
This game is worth way more than it's being sold for and instead of wasting time on reading reviews just play the demo and see for yourself (same goes for Age of Decadence),

Better than expected! Even though the engine is the same as ETS2 SCS Software put a lot of work on it to optimize it and give "Truck Simulator" series a whole new difficulty level.
"Oh, it's only nevada and california"
Don't go with that. This isn't Euro Truck Simulator 2 where states are pretty much 2 to 3 different roads of endless repetitive content (Like those gas stations and hotels that are always exactly the same). In ATS you'll have to think beforehand on your fuel and also care to know which exit to take to get closer to the Gas Station, as most of them are inside cities and not spread on whole map on the roadsides.
Driving through city with a huge truck really feels like driving in a city with a freaking huge truck. Trust me, it's MUCH more immersive than ETS2 in this aspect. To be honest I wouldn't feel a difference in ETS2 as most cargos were likely to be the same size only with weight differences. In ATS you'll notice every aspect of the cargo you're hauling. Be it the disposition of the axles, weight and also size. I'm not sure if it's because I'm not used to it yet but driving in and out of cities can be REALLY difficult. You'll have to be careful at all times because, also, the tickets and fines are a thing now. They are something you should be really worried about in the early game as two fines and there goes all the money you'd get for this trip in the first place.
I give this game a big yes. Can't wait for the 2 new states they promised to be free. And if they meet the same quality level as Nevada and California I'm certainly buying /EVERY/ DLC they ever release for this game.
Props to you, SCS Software!
(On a side note, even though this game has only two trucks right now you'll barely notice it. There's plenty to change and plenty to work for. I really hope they release new trucks soon, but seeing how much you can modify your trucks right now I don't even mind there being only two.
You have several engine and transmissions to choose from, 3 cabins and multiple types of chassis. And of course, custom mirrors, handles, exhausts, tires, wheels, etc, etc. )

Lets start of by saying the obvious - This is a console port. The graphics as such aren't too great, and I was actually let down by them personally. I was expecting much more.
Now, lets talk about one of the more important parts - gameplay. It has some good gameplay mechanics, and feels somewhat unique to begin with, but then starts to feel repetitive. The clues/puzzles/quests - whatever you would like to call them are nearly just as easy at the end, as they are at the beginning. So if you love real detective games, this may not be for you.
Story wise - it's okay, but short and dragged the hell out. I like the idea of the optional quests bt I think they should have been mandatory to begin with to make thw base game not as short.
Lets talk demons next. Through-out most of the game they are easy to aoid, and then the number increases more and more and they get more challenging. Now, nearer the end of the game there are so many that it is just plain ANNOYING, and almost immersion/game breaking. Sure, having 5-7 is a nice challenge, but if you go above that number its just pure annoying as you have to break out of the actual story feel and just keep teleporting CONSTANTLY to get behind 1 and kill it before the other 8 catch up to you.
Overall, it was a good game story wise, and the game mechanics were okay too, but the demon side, and the fact the story was dragged out to more than it needed to be let it down.
I think a divorce would have solved all these problems...

Stasis is a point and click sci-fi adventure game with hades of Dead Space and Event Horizon. Taking place on a research ship called the Groomlake, a man named John wakes up from Stasis in a mysterious and dangerous situation and must find his family and escape from the horrors aboard.
To get the bad out of the way first, this is definitely a flawed game. The animations have really jerky transitions which are jarring, there's a lot of "adventure game" logic where you do unintuitive things to progress, and the pacing at times is gods awful slow. When you're walking across a room at a crawl, possibly literally, it's easy to get bored or frustrated. The isometric viewpoint occasionally makes it difficult to tell where you can go or what you can interact with.
However, it does a lot of things right. It's creepy. It's disturbing. It makes you want to know more about the setting and the events. There are a lot of interesting setpieces. Some of the puzzles actually are really clever or interesting when they're not running on vague logic. The voice acting, music, and sound effects are pretty good as well. The graphics and visual design is fantastic, top to bottom, and you definitely feel like you're in a derelict spacecraft where something unspeakable has happened.
The game runs about 7-8 hours, but aside from achievements, there's not a ton of reason to replay it. There are no story branches. There are no secrets really to miss (again, outside of a handful of achievements). But many adventure games share this same problem, so it's more of an issue with the genre as a whole than Stasis in specific. I did enjoy my time with the game and would recommend it to people who like their horror mixed with sci-fi or like their adventure games with a darker shade.

Hero of the Kingdom II is about a personal shopping assistant, who is routinely sent out to buy stuff with his own money: going from fetch quest, to fetch quest, until there's no more, at which point he suddenly comes to the realization, he's become the hero of some non-descript fantasy kingdom.
The gameplay is similar to a time management resource gatherer, where the time constraint is removed, and replaced by hidden object game elements instead. Its main challenge lies in the bartering system: as the world opens up, the player will have to remember where the things needed for the quests can be obtained, and which bartering sequences are available, and provide better profit, so to buy the items required by the larger quests; speaking of quests, after the intro there may be too many to keep track of (it's Trello time). That, predictably, does not lend itself too well to true casual play, and the game is best played in closely-spaced together sessions, to minimize the time wasted rediscovering things. Other games, typically hidden object, sidestep this problem through the use of a hint system, which is present here too, but has way too few hints and is mostly useless as a result.
The story is formulaic to pedestrian, delivered through generally planar, but correct, English, interspersed with some typically Eastern European brokenness; there is some paper-thin pretext about a kidnapped sister, pirates, a princess who inevitably falls for the goody two-shoes PC, a lost brother too; it's mainly there to keep you clicking, and yet, somehow, manages to spit out the occasional pearls of (often patronizing) wisdom that could be good for a laugh, if viewed as simply naive rather than normative.
One could also see some humor in having friends, loved ones, and relatives handed out universally, and unironically, as
and stored as
, which are then
or
. Everything is flattened and objectified: adventure games sometimes do this, too, the good ones, however, don't miss out on the chance of laughing at the absurdity of it.
The pleasant 90s look of the art doesn't do much for the world, which is very static, unimaginative and ultimately joyless; while it's ...pleasant enough again, the music seems lifted straight out the first game, which overall is basically the same as this one.

Do you like Game of Thrones?
If the answer is yes (which it is), then play this game.  It's all about intrigue, backstabbing, assassination, and just being an all around jerk to your fellow man.  Jolly good!
This game isn't like EUIV or Civ or Total War.  By that I mean, it's not just about getting a huge army and steamrolling around the map.  It's more about building up your political dynasty, making sure you have strong heirs, making sure your relatives marry into powerful families in order to gain more territory (through inheritances), forging powerful alliances with other powerful dynasties, etc.  You always have to keep an eye on your vassals' opinions of you:  the higher the opinion, the more taxes they will pay, the more troops they'll give you, etc.  On the other hand, if their opinion is low, they will revolt and plot against you.  Of course, there's a good deal of warmongering too, it's just not as big of a focus IMO.
The variety in the nations you can play is also great.  You can play a Western European power and wage Crusades on your Muslim enemies, while trying to stave off aggressive neighbors.  Or, play as a Viking warlord, going around on nice pillaging expeditions, raiding coastal areas, whilst making lots of gold and prestige.  Play as a Merchant Republic and build a big trading empire.
As far as DLC goes, I recommend the Old Gods for the extended timeline and Vikings, and Legacy of Rome for the ability to have standing armies and enhanced flavor for Byzantines.
