You take control of one of three mercenaries for hire and carry out various paid missions concerning SICON, usually by shooting everything in sight. And no, it's nothing to do with Christian fundamentalists.
Westboro is played from an isometric-style viewpoint, but in full 3D. It's a shame it's not a fully controllable 3D camera, as it would have been great fun to rotate and zoom for a customisable view of the action. Instead you can toggle between two preset zoom levels, and you can't rotate at all. The game makes everything between your character and the camera fully transparent, so you can see where you're going. Partial transparency would have been a better choice, in my opinion, to provide a bit more environmental context around your character.
Graphics are reasonably detailed, but the colours are bland and boring. This is obviously a conscious choice from the developers, as they're wishing to portray the game world in a certain way, but a bit of variation in the interface, at least, would stop everything on the screen from blending into a drab greyish-brown. There are some good filters and special effects, and nice graphical touches like smoke from gun barrels, while at the same time some basic details have been missed, such as cars driving past without their wheels turning. The game has a pretty high DoF effect, which may not appeal to everyone.
Level design and models are good, as are textures, but there are a few too many sharp edges. Character models are fine, but you'll notice their textures are a bit lacking when you zoom in. Animations look a little bit wooden, but they're good enough. Valkyrie, the female player character, has some 'jiggle' to her, too, which is either a nice touch or completely unnecessary, depending on your point of view.
The UI is basic and only explained very briefly, making it rather confusing at first. The player character FPS camera that you can open in place of the minimap is an interesting addition. The quality is poor enough as to make it not very useful in most circumstances, but it's a nice idea.
The title music track is great: very atmospheric and mysterious. In-game music is pretty good, too, with slow, ambient sounds blending together nicely for a good background sound stage.
Game and UI sound effects are also good, and appropriate for the setting.
The game features some spoken sections, with variable quality voice acting.
Westboro plays a lot like a simple science-fiction Diablo with guns. Everything is controlled using the mouse and hotkeys. Hold down the mouse button and you'll move towards it, at a speed controllable by scrolling the mouse wheel up or down. Click on an enemy and you'll shoot at it, with some benefit provided by holding ALT to crouch behind cover. Press assigned hotkeys to use one of your skills or abilities, or to change weapons or take a health-restoring drug. Everything is very simple, once you work it out.
It's unfortunate, then, that it's so frustrating, and I mostly put this down to pathfinding and movement controls. Your character will sometimes move when you only click the mouse, and sometimes won't. Sometimes he or she will stop moving immediately if you've been holding the mouse button down and you release it, and sometimes won't. Sometimes you'll spin around on the spot when you try to run from an enemy, losing precious time (and health) in the process, and you'll almost never be able to walk automatically around a corner -- expect to have to micromanage your character's movement.
All of this makes for some very annoying combat. I can't count the number of times I've died from charging into a room full of enemies when I expected to stop outside or been mowed down while turning slowly to try to escape. And the amount of ammunition I've wasted shooting walls when I thought I should have a clear line of sight to my target, well, it would fill a rubbish truck. And for some reason, reloading is much slower than changing weapons; be prepared to die a lot because you don't realise you've run out of ammo, and it's so awkward and slow to reload.
But it's not all bad. You can find and buy weapons and different ammunition types, and handle them all in a slot-based inventory container, which works well. There's a basic collection of active and passive skills, some of which are pretty good fun, unlocked using skill points from levelling up your character. But that's the only allusion to role-playing games, here. Hotkey assignment is quick and easy, too. And it's strangely satisfying to chew through your ammunition, mowing down unsuspecting police and corporate lackeys.
There are only three character classes in Westboro: Recon, Valkyrie, and Spectre. These provide a bit of variation to play style at the beginning, at least, based on their starting skills and equipment, but after gaining a few levels and spending your skill points as you wish, the differences between them become less meaningful.
There's no indication of progress through the story, so I don't know how many different missions are available, but there aren't any save points mid-mission; the game only saves when you leave an area and enter a new one. You should expect to die a handful of times on the first mission as you come to grips with how the game works, but once you get the hang of it, survival becomes much more straightforward.
The in-game text has been translated from Russian, I believe, and has error after error. A bit of proofreading, or at least running the text through a grammar checker before release, would have done wonders for the quality of the writing.
Pros:
+ Great graphics, with some caveats
+ Interesting dystopian future setting
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Unresponsive controls make combat awkward and frustrating
- No in-mission save points
- Graphics are bland
- Poor writing quality
- Role-playing elements are very limited
Westboro is an interesting game. On the one hand, the unresponsive interface and frustrating combat, coupled with lack of in-mission save points, makes for an experience that sometimes ends up with yelling at the screen and rage quitting. But then, once you get used to dealing with the game's quirks, it's actually quite fun in spite of all of that.
It has a lot of rough edges, and the price is a bit steep, but it's definitely worthwhile taking a look if you're a fan of the genre and you have enough patience to come to terms with its quirks.

The Grandfather is a very short (less than 30 mins), story-driven puzzle game.  It's a dark tale about The Grandfather and his wife (thats all Ill say about that to avoid spoilers).
The game boils down to basically, a short voice segment telling parts of the story, followed by a short walking segment thats just strictly walking forward, followed by a short point-and-click puzzle.  Rinse and repeat 5 or 6 times and that's the entirety of "The Grandfather".
PROs
- It's short and cheap, the game is perfect if you want to go through a random game completely, but dont have a lot of time to spare.
- The artwork is nice, some twisted and mildly grotesque drawings.
- The puzzle's are very obtuse, but simple enough that it's not too frustrating (the puzzles will be under CONs too)
- The story is interesting enough for you to want to see through to the end.
- The overall game has a creepy ambience which I am a fan of.
CONs
- The sound quality and the reading of the voice-over is pretty bad.  It sounds muffled and the ladies voice doesn't have the needed eeriness or conviction to the mood of the story.  It heavily detracts from a decent, creepy story.
- The segments where you walk forward before every puzzle is a complete waste of time and if taken away would turn this game into a 10 minute game at most.
- The puzzles are just a point-and-click-and-see-what-happens-next situation.  Only a few times I had to think a little bit about what I should do next.
- No replayability at all.  Once you finish it, then you'll probably never pick it up again, unless you want to show someone else the game.

A wonderful isometic role playing game, and you do play a role. It has a great soundtrack as you scour the ruins and caverns of an otherwise inhospitable world filled with rats the size of dogs, beetles with psychic abilities, your own shadow; and much worse. While at the beginning you are forced to do several introductory quests within the main storyline {mainly to progress to the open ended gameplay which takes about 40-80 minutes depending on your initial statistics}; you find yourself immersed not only in the questlines but also finding the proper crafting materials to improve your gear.
Your gear does eventually break down, but can be repaired by sacrificing other gear to become scrap hunks and making repair kits or simply buying them from the plentiful traders though their stock isn't near as plentiful. Though there are many easy routes to take to most civilizations; some of the best are hidden from plain sight and must be found within the labryinth of abandoned subways and caves. You end up facing a unique selection of factions as well depending on how you interact before and after certain quests. The Faceless are a group of cybernetically enhanced secret society who hides their face under masks and hoods while mapping out the world. The CoreTech group is a protection service for the largest civilization in the game called Core City. But these are only two of the many and I mean at least two dozen plus factions you will meet, interact, and even may eventually kill off depending on your choices.
But wait, that's not all! You can fight in an arena against animals and humans to earn fans and coin; you can buy a house underground and furnish it completely for an absurd amount of said coin, you can steal dogs and cats, you can pour lava on enemies, YOU CAN EVEN CRAWL AROUND VENTILLATION SHAFTS if that's your thing. All that and more is available in this wonderful game.
Now for the cons, and my probably biggest pet peeve with this game at the moment is the abusrd cost for attempting to get some end-game gear. It's up to the god and goddesses of RNG {Random Number Generator} to determine what quality you get for this otherwise adapatable material but it is expensive and literally time consuming to do so each time. But that's just the way the ball bounces.
In short, this game deserves your attention, your admiration, and quite possibly; your money. It's an astounding game that will make you continue to play it wanting more. There's even a WIKI on the main website that is being updated constantly. Thank you Styg {Developer's Name}.

follows a male protagonist through a campaign of 11 missions, spanning throughout a variety of locations and climates. During this time you become solely responsible for an exodus of dinosaurs taking them single-handedly from the realms of the living, to what I can only assume is a fate worse than hell, or so you are lead to believe by both the main character and the voice over in the mission briefing. Seriously, I cannot figure out what the dinosaurs have done wrong and in fact most of them don’t even attack first.
The campaign is relatively low in content; however this is matched with a low price tag.
The game also hosts a survival mode & a multiplayer version of this aforementioned mode, which feels like faster paced versions of the campaign missions, in which the dinosaurs are constantly aware of your location and running towards you, less Dinosaur Hunt, and more Dinosaur I wish I reloaded faster.

+ 11 Campaign missions with different, relatively pretty locations.
+ Low price tag.
+ Multitude of weapons & a store to purchase ammunition and further weaponry.
+ Controls are smooth; the game feels fluid and guns respond as expected.
+ Two game ‘lab’ choices provide a mildly different feel.
+ Active Developer (as of this review).

- Repetitive missions, each mission requiring you to kill X dinosaurs, a variety in challenge or objective based missions would be really beneficial.
- Terrible voice for protagonist providing a Duke Nukem type feel, often saying things unrelated to the games theme, and also suggesting that he is aiming for world domination... No, seriously.
- A lot of the game is in briefing narrative before mission start, instead of playable content, or viewable via cut-scenes.
- No obvious reason to play survival mode other than to massacre dinosaurs, levelling up and/or unlocking weapons/character upgrades would provide a purpose to play this mode more than once.
Overall this game can be recommended due to the low price tag, I wouldn't expect anybody to get countless hours out of this, however it may indeed be worth picking up due to it being a short, yet playable set of content. As more updates are announced I am confident that this game will only increase in quality and content.

If you enjoyed Fallout 1/2, then I would reccomend checking this game out. Sure I had fun roaming around and shooting things in Fallout 4, but after that game its refreshing to play an RPG where stats, skills and feats (perks) make a difference again.
Graphics are 2D and if you played Fallout 1/2 you have an idea of what to expect. Sound is good, with some decent music too. It's not on a Fallout 1/2 level, but definately not bad. Control is good, although be careful when clicking to attack, sometimes you'll miss click and WALK all the way to the enemy if you aren't careful. Writing is pretty straight forward, nothing mind blowing but not awful either. The game had some typos but they are getting fixed. The writing is more straight and to the point, so don't expect a Planescape Torment-like tome here.
It has an interesting method of gaining XP. You can either do the usual kill enemies to grind XP. Or you can get what are called oddities, basically items in the game that when you loot them give you xp and a bit of story depending on what they are. Now that is not to say if you take the oddity system, that killing enemies is a waste of time. Because enemies can drop oddities as well (with a limit on how many times they give xp), plus they also drop loot, and crafting materials. And it has a fairly deep crafting system, you can craft many items, weapons, armors, weapon mods, consumables, and components in the game.
Stat checks are in the game although not a lot in dialogue from what I've seen so far (but they do exist). Things like perception can reveal hidden things (trap doors, etc) that let you bypass areas more easily, or agility that lets you climb over an otherwise impassable route. Nothing mind blowing but nice to see after playing Fallout 4 and missing them.
If you enjoy old school turn based CRPGs, I would give this one a whirl.

If you love old school CRPGs, stop whatever you're doing and buy this now.
It's a wonderful homage to games like Fallout and Arcanum, all the more impressive given that 90% of it was made by a single person.
Pros: Deftly executed CRPG in a novel underground setting. Sprawling world that feels dangerous around every corner. Wide array of skills and items. A novel 'oddity' EXP system (you level up by finding items as you explore; there is a traditional skill-and-kill based EXP system as well but play with oddities enabled, you'll love it.) A bit more accessible in terms of going new places than a lot of old CRPGs, but not enough that it's a total A-to-B fest.
Cons: It can be unforgiving at first, and you should either be prepared to restart more than once or research your character before building. (You won't get far without lockpicking, for example.) The crafting system is cumbersome and really for advanced players. The font can be tiny and hard to read. But otherwise this is a fantastic title.
I can't recommend this highly enough if you like the old school RPGs. If you've never played an old school CRPG you may find the learning curve a little steep but if the screenshots and reviews grab you, give it a shot - you may find you love it anyway.

This game would be great if it weren't mechanically broken beyond the point of playability. The story is great I'm sure, good characters, good graphics, etc.
But the line of sight/line of fire system is extremely critical to the tactical combat, and it's extremely broken. You will not spend five hours playing before you will find yourself in a situation where you do not have line of sight or line of fire when you absolutely should, or when the enemy is able to attack you when they absolutely shoud not have line of sight/line of fire.
When this basic aspect of a tactical combat game is so totally arbitrary and senseless, it makes combat feel totally stupid, unbelievable, and unfair. Even if you win, it just feels stupid.
If you're looking for a great deep CRPG with dystopian overtones, this is your game. It's a lot of fun to explore. The game is tough as nail, even on normal difficulty, so be ready for a challenge.

Maybe you play one of the many Call of Duty games, or maybe you used to.
Maybe you're interested in medieval combat and want to find out what it's like.
It's skullcrushing, disarming (literally, arm dismembering), bloody madness. I cackle maniacally while playing this game. I can't even get angry at other players, not even at archers (the largely hated class among non-archers). The many game modes are fun including one-on-one duels, standard FFA and TDM, as well as a fun team objective mode.
The weapon selection is great with anything from a quick bashing quarterstaff to a giant Zweihander and everything in between. Javelins and stone slingers, flails, daggers, axes, and halberds, it's all here. Weapon control is pretty spot on. Don't go swinging wide into a group of your buddies unless you're looking to slay them all.
Even fighting the bots is fun alone or with a friend, however one downside is poor AI and they cannot successfully function in any mode besides FFA. Any other mode and they're just running into walls aimlessly or unable to leave spawn properly.
Even so, this game can provide hours and hours of enjoyment and the basics have a pretty short learning curve, although using all the combat tactics at your disposal in a fluid way could take some getting used to. Just hack, slash and stab your way to victory, and apologize for killing your teammates, a quick 'sry' goes a long way to stop you from getting kicked.

Chivalry is a very fun Multiplayer based game with first person combat in a similar vein to The Elder Scrolls: Oblivion and Skyrim, albeit a bit more focused and varied in my opinion, most likely because the game is a lot smaller in scale and the amount of things you can technically do as you'd expect.
There's a variety of classes to pick from each with different weapons (Including two handed swords, basic swords and shields, Bows, Crossbows, Halberds etc.), damage outputs, abilities and HP and it's fun to experiment and try all of them, personally I settled on a ranged class using Heavy Javelins for the most part and I had a lot of fun with that playstyle, there's also some basic character customization that allows you do look the way you want.
Weapons feel visceral and combat feels heavy and satisfying, getting into a lengthy duel with someone can be extremely fun, or going solo against a pair or a larger group of people can be very satisfying as well, particularly if you're able to pull off a victory.
In terms of map and game mode variety, there is a nice mix, plenty of environments ranging from medieval castles and large structures towering over the ocean, forests, deserts, fields, medieval villages and more, game modes are varied and are mostly team based, with your traditional team deathmatch, King of the Hill, Capture the Flag, and a Team Objective game mode in which one team attacks by doing a variety of things, and another defends, this mode reminds me of Assault from the original Unreal Tournament and UT2004 in quite a few ways.
It's also worth mentioning that the game has always run very well for me, it's not a very taxing game and you shouldn't have much of an issue playing it with older hardware, it is an older game at this point in itself.
Overall I definitely recommend the game, especially if you can group up with some friends, you can have a lot of fun with it.

A friend asked me, "HOW IS THIS GAME SO FUN?" I replied, "It is kind of impressive how fun it is being an NPC, isn't it?" And it is. You can't really summarize this game; it's got too many great things going for it, and attempts to do so generally result in disbelief that a game like that can be as entertaining as claimed.
The game's about running an item shop. Initially you have to pay off your debt but once that's done you enter "Endless Mode" and can enjoy being a merchant (and also running through dungeons to get loot!) to your heart's content. Don't be disheartened by failure; even if you fail to pay off your debt, you'll still get a second chance.
Good luck getting 100% completion; the post-endgame content is ridiculously beefy, and filling out your item encyclopedia requires at least six or seven playthroughs. And even when you've got that sorted out, you STILL have Endless Mode to challenge yourself with.
Also it's an indie title, if you like that sort of thing.

I'm not much of a horror fan -- at least not when it comes to playing them.  I can live without the jump scares and the frequently limited perspectives most games in the genre restrict you to.  I thought Stasis would give me an opportunity to test the waters, so to speak, and visually speaking, the game delivers quite a bit of quality.
Unfortunately, where it falls flat is in an overly convoluted backstory that you have to piece together from scattered crew logs.  Further, I never once felt anything for the main protagonist.  His personality was inconsistent -- tossing his cookies over a pile of bodies, collapsing into a weeping heap over someone he has to put out of their misery after having accidentally killed someone else probably only an hour before hand, watching perhaps the most horrific event he could and then telling his companion to get a grip a few minutes later.
Even after finishing the game, I'm still completely at a loss as to what happened on the Groomlake before my character woke up other than a perfect storm of events that would give Agent Mulder nightmares.  The end game is one mindf*** after another with an overall depressing conclusion that left me wondering why I had bothered in the first place.  I would have to say, on a scale of 1 to 10, the game rates a mediocre 4.

I played through most of this a few years ago on the xbox360. I remember quite enjoying it, but struggling with the interviews... When I saw it for 6 quid on PC I fancied giving it another go - maybe see if I was missing something.
I've only played a couple of hours of it this time through, but it's just as I remember it. Decent graphics (although I played through the original Mafia recently and for my money, that looks far better despite being 10 years older), decent controls, quite interesting premise... But the interview system is a joke. I'm meant to "read" the expressions of characters faces, but it's entirely hit and miss - people can look shifty but be telling the truth, they can look you dead in the eye and by lying...it's just an infuriating nonsense. There's no skill to it, it's all guess work. It doesn't work in a game. You can accuse them of lying when you have a piece of evidence to back it up (although the logic of this isn't always clear), but choosing whether to doubt or believe someone...! Flip a coin! Seriously, it's a terrible gameplay mechanic, if it can even be called gameplay.
And that applies to the whole experience - can you even call it a game? Is it actually fun?! There's this big open city, but you just watch the map the whole time or let your partner drive. It might as well not exist. The cases (which is all the game is - there's little side crimes to do too, but they're all just little shoot outs) are actually just dull. Walk around in circles until you hear a musical phrase, press button, look at thing you've found, repeat half a dozen times. Interview people/flip a coin for a bit. Drive somewhere, inevitably shoot or fight or chase someone. Interview some other people. Maybe some driving or chase or shooting, done. Repeat. And I find it really difficult to keep track of names I've only heard once or twice, and during interviews you don't actually know who you're talking about - the in-game notebook is limited during interviews it seems..
I love the idea of a detective game, but this just seems awfully hamfisted. Compared to old adventure games (what this most reminds me of interestingly is Blade Runner on the PC!) it's simplistic and without skill. Trial and error isn't a thing, which just makes it tedious. And you can't skip cutscenes, which is massively annoying.
At 5 quid or so it's maybe worth a play, if just for the interesting idea, but it's not all that entertaining in my eyes.

Despite having its flaws,
is quite possibly one of the most enjoyable single-player games I've played this year.
The Pros:
· A unique story that feels like a combination of Silent Hill and L.A. Noire, and the beginning does a great job of introducing you to its atmosphere.
· You start at the point where Ronan O'Connor (the game's protagonist, of course) starts the hunt on his murderer, the Bell Killer. This makes you feel like you know as much about the afterlife as Ronan himself does and creates a sort of connection, right from the get-go.
· The town of Salem is pretty small, but its yours to explore... and it's worth exploring. Tons of side missions and collectibles can be found in Salem, and the eerie mood that constantly lingers around really immerses you into Ronan's role.
· The atmosphere is incredibly unique and satisfying. The ghostly white glow around certain object make the bridge-world connect with the world of the living. Seeing the flickering souls of dead children sitting next to a swing or a dead corpse dangling from a tree by its neck is oddly disturbing and makes you feel uncomfortable, which a bridge-world should.
· Pretty cool characters. Ronan is your typical rebel-turned-cop tough guy, but his tattoo's reflect his life and the sins in it, and the detail to him is quite impressive. Even though he's partially see-through (because you know, he's a ghost and stuff), the orange bullet holes give Ronan a distinctive look from the other ghosts in Salem.
The Cons:
· The mechanics feel a bit underused at times. As a ghost you could be able to do so much more, like possessing and controlling others for example. Sure, you can influence people and read their minds and control a cat (10/10), but it limits the player.
· For a detective game, it doesn't really require too much thinking. You have to find clues and connect the dots (sometimes those dots connect in an unlogical way), and that's basically it.
· The NPCs are mostly the same. Salem doesn't have many people walking its streets, but two of the same people might be sitting a few feet from each other. Plus, they have the same thoughts, which is weird. Like freaky weird.
· The combat is there, but its simplistic and repetetive. You hide in lost souls, sneak up to a demon and quickly rip him apart. It's satisfying and it even feels as if you're helping those tormented souls, but it's just too much of the same.
The Visuals:
· Most of its atmosphere comes from the visuals. Ghostly white silhouettes and detailed environments may not look next-gen, but they're stunning none the less.
Final Verdict:
·
sure has its flaws, but it's a unique and highly enjoyable experience and easily one of my favorites of the year. 8/10

The truth is I am sure that some will like this game, those who know the tricks and tips to kite enemies perfectly and the exact skills to invest in, and has a high tolerance for fail, try again moments. I'll start by saying that ninety-nine cents is not a great deal less than this game is worth to a player. It was incredibly short, and the content was dubious (which I will get to in a moment.) enough to give me pause. However at just under a dollar, the fact that it has a beginning, middle and end with gameplay in between makes it at least worth the price of admission.
I appreciate what the developer of this game was trying to do, and I appreciate oblique, surreal or mysterious storytelling. A peice of work just needs to have a solid sense of itself, and steady direction to not have it be an unrelatable mess. This game does not have a solid sense of itself. It wears it's Lynchian influences embarrassingly on it's sleeve without realizing that what makes his movies so good is that the symbolism, while impenetrable, is consistent and resonant. It never got around to developing it's own set of symbols for the player to relate to (The umbilical cord was a literal umbilical cord, for goodness sake.). The story is a straight line from start to finish, with no conflict to speak of. Even the antagonist is revealed to be such through a series of flashbacks which do not relate to the surreal gameplay, which one can assume is the "present" in the narrative timeline.
The gameplay is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzles. They're meant to be non-logical puzzles, I realize, but that makes them ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzles.

I have a hard time speaking in a balanced manner about Mass Effect 2 because it's one of my single favorite video games of all-time. There are so many good things to gush over, but the bad pieces are really, truly bad and do a lot to ruin the experience of actually playing the game. The most concise way I can describe it is 'flawed masterpiece'. It's a game propped up by fantastic art and sound design and far better overall writing than the much maligned Mass Effect 3, but at the same time, the gameplay is nowhere near as tight and the overall design is way rougher -- To the point where I'd criticize the combat as being unfinished.
To start, the graphics and the engine run pretty smoothly on the PC. It runs easily enough -- I see around 110-120 FPS on my 120hz 1440p monitor, but the textures are often muddy and low-res, a curse of the title being designed with far outdated consoles in mind... Even back in 2010. I had a similar experience with the first Mass Effect, though that game is even rougher-looking than this one is. The textures here are, on average, higher res. It helps that the lighting is far better designed than the first game (goodbye, ham-fisted lens flare!). There are a great many visual bugs, though. Far more than the console version. Glitches with the eyes, characters model inexplicably spinning, etc. But it's saved mostly by the beautiful art design. The use of colored lighting really adds a great touch, and the environments are unbelievably vibrant. There's a lot to 'feel' here just by looking at skyboxes. It's indicative of good art design and adequate design on the technical side to support it. The art team is the MVP here.
The sound! Where to start? Jack Wall is absolutely fantastic, almost up to the level he was in the first game. He's at his best when he's laying down eerie music for the tense missions (Collector Ship, anybody?), but he does a great job with handling the huge change in tone from the first game. Mass Effect 1 was carried by a super-techno, futuristic style soundtrack, whereas this one has touches of futurism but mostly just feels brooding and dirty. It fits the art direction of the game perfectly, and even a minimalist track like the droning that plays during the loading screen really does a fantastic job to impart and augment the overall 'feel' of this game, which is a big part of what I find so enticing about Mass Effect 2.
The writing is probably the games single strongest aspect. I don't mean to exaggerate, or to gush too much here, but there are some of the most well-written characters in any video game I've ever played. It's clear that Walters, Karpyshyn, and the rest of the writing staff were going for a Dirty Dozen, Wild West type feel with the characters and settings here, and they've succeeded in spades. There are a lot of characters that might even fit into a cliche, but the dialogue is so well-written and the voice acting is so superb that the game manages to skip that pothole and cruise along. Thane Krios, the spiritual, regretful assassin, is a stand-out among a cast of solid personalities. His discussions with Shepard and his dealings with his son Kolyat are excellent. Garrus is far more fleshed out here than he was in the first game (in which I found his character to be disappointingly underdeveloped), and the writing here creates a bridge to his being so likable in the third game. Legion, a character who arrives unfortunately late in the game, is another stellar twist and an amazingly well-written and impresses in unexpected ways. It's hard to go into detail without spoiling anything, but suffice it to say that his obsessive 'complex' is wholly unexpected and goes on to completely destroy any expectation I had when I initially learned of the characters presence in the game.
There are some pitfalls here, unfortunately, mostly in the form of Jacob Taylor. He always came off as completely unlikable to me, though that's more a personal feeling and not a general criticism. I think he's a poor character simply because there's not really much there to dig into. He's got some father issues to deal with that feel crammed in mid-game and seem to hover around the outside of his character rather than fleshing out his core, like so many of the other characters side missions are intended to do.
Now that I've gushed over the good things, let's talk about some of the bad.
The game plays as if its half finished, particularly during combat. There's a nice idea and an adequate core design here, but it seems like it could have used far longer in the QA process than it actually had. The core mechanics of taking down the enemies shields/barriers, armor, and then health are really excellent. Each is weak to a different type of weapon, ammo, and power, so each encounter becomes a sort of puzzle where you're evaluating which enemy is the most threatening and thus must be dealt with first, and by using which power or weapon to do so. It's incredibly complex but relatively simple to learn, and getting through some of the more difficult encounters on hardcore or insanity difficulty is amazingly satisfying.
Sounds great, right? Unfortunately, while the game is at its best on the two hardest difficulty modes, it also suffers the most on those modes due to extremely buggy cover mechanics and unbelievably poor friendly AI. The AI is absolutely abysmal, and if you want that Insanity trophy you better be ready for some frustration. It's necessary to completely micomanage your allies by controlling where they're taking cover at all times. The problem with cover also manifests itself here, as there are many times when allies simply refuse to listen to you and wade out into enemy fire only to die immediately. It's so frustratingly idiotic that I find myself wondering how the game ever shipped in this fashion. It's a mess, and having to babysit your idiotic, suicidal squadmates really destroys what would have been an otherwise fantastic gameplay system. The general design is there, but the technical execution is utterly terrible and enough to make you bash your head against a wall. It's much more passable on Normal and Casual, but if you're gunning for Hardcore or Insanity, get ready for a headache.
The overall design of the game, despite these poorer aspects, is excellent. The episodic style of gameplay in which you're recruiting allies just feels right, and the game feels far more organized and direct than the first game ever did. On the harder difficulties you really get a sense of it being a race against time. You've got to plan out what missions you're doing at what time, because upgrades are incredibly important and if you find yourself trying to take on Horizon or the Collector Ship without the good ones, you can actually get completely stuck and be forced to start over. While this sounds frustrating, it actually does a good job to suck you into the situation that Shepard and the crew find themselves in. They've got to get all of this done, and quickly, because the Collectors are on the move and they aren't waiting for you. This episodic style is paced perfectly, and you never seem to experience any of the drag that you see in the first game when you get dropped onto the Citadel after Eden Prime only to find yourself immediately bogged down with a huge area to explore and dozens of sidequests to tackle. It does a far better job with making sure you never feel overwhelmed than the first game. It's open-ended enough without stranding you in a sea of objectives -- You've always got a handful of options of what to do next, and it's up to you to decide which seems to be most important.
All of the gameplay here comes to a head in a fantastic final act that sees everything you've done so far in the game build up to one massive conclusion. The suicide mission is truly excellent, and caps off a must-play game for everyone interested in RPGs.

Here is my shortcut; the hole in one for this review.
It's Golfing - as easy as it gets - you hold the mouse button, move the mouse to change the strength and direction of your shot and release to hit the ball.
Additionally, you can choose to play a kind of basketball, where jumping (default 'Spacebar') is enabled and the holes become hoops.
You can also zoom in and out to get a better idea of the location of your goal. Beyond that, even if something obscures your vision you can use the free camera (default 'C') to get a better idea of your position.
Currently, there are 6 different levels: Forest, Desert, Moonlight Park, Spooky Mansion, Candyland and Jurassic Park.
Something I really enjoyed to see is the progression you can observe going from level to level.
Each map contains 18 holes and at least in the forest level you can finish it with 18 shots - but this will take a lot of practice.
The design is really neat and most of the time you can take more than one approach to hitting the ball.
With to the many possibilities comes a big part of the replay value and the whole fun of the game. If you manage that one insane hit, none of your friends even thought about and you leave them wondering how you managed the hole in 2 strokes when they are on the 7th.
Creating and joining a lobby is super easy, as well as setting up modifiers.
Another big part of replaying this game will come from setting up different modifications - such as 'random ball shapes'. When the unlucky one with the acorn hits the hole in one - a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm will be unleashed :D
before even going into multiplayer, I advise you to paint your ball under 'Customize' - so you can be recognized by your friends. Just don't take the same colors.
Press 'L' to light the way for your friends.
All the levels are really neatly designed and have a really cool air about them, to match a certain theme and bring you in the mood.
I really like the sweet melody in the background, my friend, however, turned the volume way down because he couldn't stand it - so it's really a preference thing.
If you have friends willing to play this game with you - by all means you can have a good time.
, there isn't that much content in the game yet. Of course, you can aim for the hole in one on every map (if this is even possible; I don't think it is), hone your skills by trying new hits and playing with funny settings but it depends on how long you and your friends will stay motivated together - because if the first one loses the interest, the others will probably follow.

A beautiful exercise in Cronenberg-like body horror, this is a narrative whose pacing might be too slow for some, but creates an effective sense of dread and sorrow without resorting to jump scares or other spooooooky tactics. It's a fairly flatfooted commentary on eugenics, gene manipulation, ethics of cloning and human experimentation, but it's executed with steady-handed, thoughtful style.
Though it appears to be a real-time strategic puzzle-solving game, there are actually very few time-sensitive events and could be considered a fluid turn-based adventure. The isometric style reminds of Satellite Reign or Shadowrun, but the textures are more organic and atmospheric, and the cutscenes mesh pretty well with actual gameplay.
As the game progresses, there are longer cinematics/cutscenes that are repeated and unskippable if you happen to die at that checkpoint, so I started saving after every scene.
As an aside, until the *procedure* (don't want to spoil), I was convinced John was running around naked in all sorts of filth and rot. I'm going to just continue to imagine that he's traveling through this subterranean network for hours in the nude.

Despite the rumoured shoestring budget, 4A games managed to deliver the best first person shooter in years, which directly challenges and beats the triple A competition. Instead of wasting the graphics budget on meaningless spectacle with little substance and thin-at-best relevance to the experience of playing the game, the developer concentrated all resources on making the world beautiful from the point of view of an armed eavesdropper who carefully sneaks through the metro system of post apocalyptic Moscow. Here, reactivity to the world with special animations from the first person perspective, immersion building effects such as condensation inside of a gas mask and subtle uses of lighting (including breakable light sources) makes all the difference.
The game is still a first person shooter at heart, but it supersedes your expectation of how a first person shooter should play again and again. The majority of areas have a parallel design, where enemies can be tackled completely with stealth or with tactical shooting at your discretion. Both designs are well developed with a steady increase in difficulty throughout the game, and I felt encouraged to use both depending on the circumstances (for example, sparing pathetic guard duty foot soldiers, but mercilessly killing the aggressors who followed me to the surface).
The way the game handles exploration deserves special praise. Basically, the main path of this linear game is full of optional areas. You are encouraged to explore these optional areas because they contain valuable assets from the in-game economy, but you will surprisingly often find elaborate scripted sequences such as an ambush by monsters or some stray soldiers hunting down and attempting to♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman, or even more frequently subtle environmental story telling based on items, marks and bodies lying around. Even when you are funnelled down a linear path, the game requires your attention and your ability to analyze environmental cues to progress forward. There is no overuse of x-marks-the-spot waypointing or sequences where you are following an ally (I was sad to see gaming journalists embarrass themselves by indicating the opposite, presumably based on only playing the introduction of the game).
Finally, despite being a game with so much freedom, where a playthrough can last anywhere from 10 to 30 hours, the game is better paced than any of the 6 hour Call of Duty-likes costing tens of millions to make. For example, early in the game, a tactical section against humans is followed by a horror section where vicious spiders are trying to eat your brains, which is followed by downtime taking in the beautiful sights of the post apocalyptic Moscow, which is followed by psychotic hallucinations, and where the experience finally ends with an overwhelming mutant ambush and a desperate escape to the closest metro station. The game just continues to throw varied situations at you like that, and it is even more impressive considering that the game is grounded in a single location, without the generous use of air travel or teleportation devices that makes the “good pacing” of some other titles possible.
Metro: Last Light is simply one of the best first person shooters ever made. Sadly, too few people seem to be willing to give a first person shooter from an unknown eastern European developer a chance. I personally can’t recommend this game highly enough for those who enjoy first person shooters and I sincerely hope that more people get a chance to try it.

- If clicker games are your thing, you'll enjoy this one.  It has most of what made Clicker Heroes so great, with a little more strategy.
This game has everything that has made similar games of the genre so successful: heroes, skills, levels, addictiveness, and the never-ending loop of getting stronger, beating quests, and trying to overcome that next boss.  But it takes it a step further with main quests.  Before you begin the game, and each subsequent time you perform a world reset, you will have to choose a main quest before you start.  A main quest is an overall goal set for you for that particular run, and it comes with a nice reward of the in-game currency that can also be bought with cash.  There are also a few worlds these quests take place in, so you won't always be seeing the same backgrounds and monsters as you progress, which helps freshen up the environments you will be seeing over and over.
This game is also more strategical in how it's played versus other clicker games.  In most clicker games, you can buy every hero and they all add DPS to your total.  In Crusaders, each world that you visit requires a unique formation that varies in shape and quantity/size.  For example, the initial formation you will use allows for 10 heroes.  From there, you will unlock other worlds, that require different formations.  This is where the strategy comes into play.  Sometimes you will have to swap out multiple characters to see what gives you the best DPS.  There are also quite a few heroes that offer nice DPS bonuses to heroes in the same row, in front of them, behind them, or all heroes.  You'll also get a few heroes that give you insane gold bonuses, but at the cost of low DPS.  You will soon be testing what works best between heavy hitters, and weaker units to bolster those powerhouses.
There is a Halloween event up as of me writing this, which has a formation allowing for 12 in a unique Halloween world. It's a limited time event so I've recently reset and chosen that world.  What the game failed to tell me was that in 1 of the slots, I have a Witch that screams, giving all adjacent heroes -2% or -4% DPS for each monster on the screen.  The reason I mention this is because this Witch is in the middle of my formation, causing me to be a bit more selective with who I put around her.
There aren't many negatives to the game.  The sound is nothing memorable, but not awful.  I was going to say the graphics are mediocre, but compared to games like Adventure Capitalist, whose only animation is bars, or even Clicker Heroes, whose only animation is the monsters when clicked, this game actually has animation.  So that's a plus.  All in all, it's a pretty good clicker with more depth than most. I don't usually write reviews for games. But I thought my experience here was much different from the norm. I want to talk about Dinosaur Hunt: Africa Contract. I love Dinosaurs. I don't feel there are enough games out there that use the theme, and those that do don't usually do well. I saw this game, on sale for half off none the less. I thought a game for fifty cents? With Dinosaurs? I can dig that.
Please note, I'm listing my complaints with it first off as I go, then I'll tell why I loved it. To start, the menu's are messy. Things need to be organized better, and the game does suffer from it. All of the basics you would see in a PC game are in the options, such as quality, resolution and so on. I fiddled with it, and jumped into picking the game. I had option left, or option right. I learned later on the main difference was the weapons you had access to. I chose the right one, it had a cooler looking gun. I started up right away with the campaign, and things started getting hairy.
The story is really basic. Dinosaurs escape a research lab, and are running havoc through Africa. You're there to kill all of them. Fair enough, I started in the first level and was given a good amount of money to start with. Those messy menus I mentioned? Yeah, the weapons menu is, well. Barf. Buttons are missalligned, quality control here is really questionable. It wasn't a pain to figure out, though. I bought some weapons, and got started.
I looked at this big map in the upper left corner. The hud was a bit messy, too. Arrows represented where Dinosaurs were on the map, so I started running towards them. I encountered my first Dinosaur, a raptor! And, began shooting at it. It ran towards me, and I quickly began to dump my clip into its face. And then? He blew up. Needless to say, I laughed! His body went flying over me, in seperate pieces. It was so unrealistic and silly that I loved it. I noticed something as I continued. I had a strange glitch where if I stopped sprinting and aimed down my sight, sometimes the model would aim off center. I still shoot straight, but the gun would aim to the left until I fired off a round. It was quick to get used to, though.
I ran around the rather empty map, and found one weird thing. A pile of health, and ammo. Tons of it, loads. I scooped it all up really quick, not knowing if it would disappear or what. This brings on a new issue, though. This health and ammo is very random, and not placed so well. You see, this is also where the exit marker is. If you finish the objective, and run back towards it, you can't actually pick up any of this stuff if you didn't earlier. You'll run towards it, and end up right in a loading zone. I found myself looking for this pile in each start of the levels. I also found that buying ammo became pointless. All weapons seem to share the same ammo pool, even if the game shows multiple ammo types. And even if you bought ammo, the money you get for killing Dinosaurs is next to nothing. You know what a headshot gets you? One dollar. That's right, one. Completing a mission gets you fifty, but when you look and see that you need 7,500 dollars for one of the better weapons? That's a lot of grinding.
Sadly, I began to get bored. The Dinosaur variety was very slow to change, and the missions were very tedious. Kill the Dinosaurs, leave the area, kill the Dinosaurs, leave the area. That's all to it, nothing different. Between each level is a single picture with dialogue explaining what happens next, but it's all the same. Bad grammar, and a picture that changed a few times before seeming to become just the same image for each level. Glitches were becoming more apparent, getting stuck on enemy parts in the ground sometimes.
Eventually in the missions, I did get killed. That was enough campaign for me. It was a slog, it got boring fast, it was tedious and didn't bring any changes to gameplay. It was the same thing asked of me, over and over. So, you ask. Why do I enjoy this game? It's messy, it's buggy, quality control got tossed out the window. Sorry dev, not to insult you with this stuff. But anyways, why did I enjoy it? Well... I played survival mode.
It promised a wave based battle, see how long I could survive. Okay, sure, why not. It seemed to be the last game mode, so I decided to try it out. I saw that the game carried over everything from the campaign. Weapons I purchased, ammo count and my collected money were all brought over, which was nice. Then I noticed a little blip show up on my map. Far distance, a Dinosaur was running toward me. Much out of my range, so I closed the distance and killed him. But from there? Four more showed up. This wasn't wave based at all, not like it said. This was an endless horde of Dinosaurs spawning from the edges of the map. I was able to pick them off, getting headshots made it easy. Then, a Triceratops showed up! I had never seen one in the game yet, but it was just munching on my bullets like candy! It took a load of headshots to kill it, but by the time I did, the game literally showed there were 9 Dinosaurs spawned on the map. I made distance to try and line them up, gunning them down quick to have to fight another Triceratops. Things were getting insane, seriously. Raptors were popping up everywhere, and things were getting out of hand. Then, next thing I knew it? A Tyrannosaurus. Oh God, they don't care about bullets. I had to burn through so much ammo to kill one, and he outpaced me. I took a good chunk of damage, but did manage to kill him.
I was on the edge of the map. I could literally look out in the distance, and see a horde of maybe twelve Dinosaurs running straight at me, including another Tyrannosaurus. This was it, I was a goner. I pulled out my sniper rifle for one last stand, and began railing the Rex over and over in the head. It wasn't enough though, and I got overrun. The game immediately started back over, and I paused it to get a breather.
That, was exciting. I had an absolute blast fighting off those Dinosaurs. It brought me back to the times of playing Doom, or Painkiller. Games that weren't about defending an objective, or doing fetch quests. No, it was about firing bullets every which way, and unleashing absolute chaos. The glitches didn't matter anymore, the graphics didn't matter anymore. This was what I paid for, and I loved it.
This game needs a lot of work, trust me. Look past it, and you'll find an over the top run and gun shooter. If I had to put out my biggest issues? It would be the menus, the weapon damages, the hud and the campaign. Honestly, I would love first to see the campaign be altered. Or maybe even dumped, to just focus on adding variety to survival. To the developers, keep doing what you're doing. In the short time I had with it, I ended up loving its unique charm. Easily the best dollar I've spent in years, and I'll be coming back for more!

The game is difficult to review because it contains a great deal of intentional unpleasantness.  In a way, that's the point.  Your character was not a happy man, and this is a dark moment.
Several design choices are structured to make you uncomfortable.  The whispery narration volume forces you to strain to hear it over the jarring background sounds.  Background images subtly shake out of sync with foreground images, leaving you feeling queasy.  Puzzles include no context or clear goals whatsoever, leaving you disoriented.  The game opens with the most difficult puzzle, which adds an element of frustration on top of that.
But, again, that's the point.  All of it matches up perfectly with the dark story, the dark art style, the tense ambient noises.  Most likely, you've read this far because you enjoy art games that go to dark places.  This one does.  If, having read all that, you're still curious, this is probably the game for you.

Well. What can i say about this game.
Visuals/atmosphere/sound: 5/5.
Controls: 0/5
That's probably it. The game by itself is something Fallout'ish / Deus ex like, but it's got completely different game mechanics.  It's all real time. You control character by mouse only. No tactical time stop, no bullet time. And i should say - the controls are STIFF. It takes an eternity before character starts to do what you want it to do. And that what gives this game it's difficulty. Your ability to react in combat is significantly limited. This turns every combat in to a roulette. If you're lucky enough, you can bring down a bunch of enemies and don't get a scratch. It not - you are dead. However - you have stuff to mitigate it - active abilities. But they have really beefy cooldown times. Now multiply that by: no saves through the mission, not even on game exit, no checkpoints. You died - you start it over. And missions are pretty big if you do all the side stuff. Add limited supplies. So your win strategy is: run into bunch of enemies, use cooldowns. Wait for cooldowns to reset. Repeat. That makes game reeeally hardcore.
So at a time i have pretty mixed feelings about this game. Visuals are really good. Combat is actually satisfying. It's got a lot of RPG in it, and i really like RPG. But difficulty through controls is really killing most of the fun for me. A good example of great indie cyberpunk/RPG is Dex. And that game is not easy either. But the big difference - it is really responsive. I actually enjoyed playing it. And it's really sad about this game. It has really big potential in it. Fix controls, add saves/checkpoints - 5/5.

I've always been a big fan of the cyberpunk and post-apocalyptic genres. From Deus-ex, to System Shock, the original Fallouts and Wasteland. I've played and loved them all. Underrail is a great hybrid of these genres, it's like a spiritual successor to the original Fallouts, with the same kind of humor and attention to detail.
Pros
-Great Soundtrack that will remind you of Fallout, Deus-Ex and System Shock 2 (But still very unique and fitting)
-Skill system is very well done and balanced
-Combat is challenging and allows for very creative strategies based on your playstyle
-The UnderRail is an interesting place and exploration well worth it
-The Stealth system is very well done and allows for even more tactical planning, from sneaking through vents, to Hit-and-Run strikes as well as insta-kill sneak attacks and trapping.
-Lots of great references and humour
-Great crafting system with a huge amount of variety and options
Cons
-The story while interesting, is a little generic
-The RNG can be aggravating, causing you too miss an 80% chance-to-hit strike 4 turns in a row or turning an easy fight into a tense situation by giving the enemy a 10 hit string of criticals for no apparent reason
-Quest direction can be incredibly vague sometimes, barely giving you an idea where to start looking, or giving you♥♥♥♥♥♥poor directions to the location you need to reach
In summary, if you are looking for an old-school RPG experience or are a fan of the original fallout games, UnderRail will become a classic for you. So much care and balance has been put into this game that it now has a permanent place along-side the classics.

The Grandfather is just a strange a ride as the screenshots suggest, so know that going into it. Be prepared for some elements to not make sense or even feel random. Also be prepared for an interesting exploration of ideas and a fairly strong story, though, which helps balance out the sheer weirdness of the imagery/gameplay.
Visually, the game is amazing. The audio ties the strangeness together with almost alien sound effects. Initially, the voice over was too quiet, but apparently that issue has been addressed already, so good to see the devs responding quickly and positively to relevant feedback without compromising anything vital to the game's creativity.
The game play is fairly straightforward puzzle solving, but the puzzles are not always logical and the game does not hold players' hands at all. I found myself clicking on random things in random order to progress at least once, which was the only time I became frustrated.
The game lasts about half and hour or so, and the conclusion to the story is satisfying. This game probably won't blow your mind, but it will take you to places that no other game can. If you can stand a bit of confusion and frustration while valuing unique experiences, then this is the game for you.

Five hours into the game, I was saying to myself, oh, well, this part is good, this part is kinda meh, this part may be interesting...
Fifteen hours into the game I was saying to myself, more Underrail. More Underrail! MORE UNDERRAIL!
It takes a bit to get rolling, but this is a really good game.
This is a develop your character, explore, and solve tactical puzzles RPG. It doesn't have a lot of character interaction, lots of description, or intricate story. It DOES have a very well conveyed atmosphere. Underrail feels like a real world.
The systems (character building and crafting) are deep. Exploring the systems is a game in itself, and you can't do it all in one playthrough. I am sure I will play this game at least twice, maybe more.
There are some warts. Walking speed is too slow (I usually think this about RPGs) and there is a lot of it. Barter is kind of clunky, and there is a lot of it, too. Barter is getting better as I get farther along.
The game is hard (I'm playing on normal). Expect to quickload a lot, expect to walk away from some things to (maybe) come back later. In my book, this is a plus.
All in all, if this kind of game is the kind of game you like, it is an absolute steal at $14.99.

One night after going to sleep in his bed, separated from his wife's (wow that woman is a total ♥♥♥♥♥), he wakes up, none of his body parts present OR attatched to his body! Only his head, which also can float, he begins his venture to find his body parts, what he ends up with though, is better than what a paint brush could ever do.
The puzzles in The Grandfather were, honestly, not very difficult. Maybe I got stuck two times trough the whole game, the puzzles felt sort of meaningless as I just clicked at things, but they were fun to figure out when figuring out was needed.
The game was made in Unity 5 (which I highly suggest to any devs who are starting out, for real, get it, it's free) which most people enjoy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at, however thanks to games like Firewatch, The Forest and the development hell beaut' Raindrop it's slowly getting a better reputation after it got slaughtered by the billions of Slender clones.
The Grandfather though, it's weird, it has this ugly yet pretty, cool looking style that gets accompanied by some nicely done lighting. It also has these short segments that are first person where you walk forward, these are also very nice. The illustrations of The Grandfather are done by the talented SaintYak, the art is very well done and characters have a nice artstyle going on, objects in puzzles look sort of sketch'y like if they were drawn quickly, really adds to the creepy atmosphere of the game.
There isn't really any music in The Grandfather, if there is then it's some sort of saw being played on, it's very weird and sounds kind of creepy... Or funny. Other than that there is omnious ambient noise going off most of the time, which works and fits the rooms you solve puzzles in. Whatever is there of soundwork is interesting and adds to The Grandfather's already creepy atmosphere.
All in all, I pretty much enjoyed The Grandfather, it was way cheaper than I expected it to be and it totally came out of nowhere as I forgot it's release date, I hope it does well and that more people will try out this little enjoyable, creepy game.
I give The Grandfather a 8/10

I've been waiting for something like this to appear ever since playing Fallout 2. If you're a fan of the Fallout series in general, you won't be disappointed.
Let's go over some pros and cons. Keep in mind, this list is not all-inclusive; just some of the plusses or minuses that immediately come to mind.
Pros:
-Old-school feel with isometric camera
-Interesting combat system using initiative to decide turn order
-Many different character builds available, such as guns, crossbows, melee, unarmed, psi, and throwing. Within each weapon category there are different weapon types, and specialized feats assoiciated with them
-Ability to avoid most or all combat situations if one wishes to play a diplomat-type character
-Three difficulty settings, and two choices for how the main character gains experience. One favoring experience via exploration and quests (which reinforces the ability to play as a diplomat), and one favoring killing and quests.
-Comprehensive crafting system
Cons:
-Debatably difficult at the start of the game due to the tutorial only breaking the ice of the way combat mechanics function
-Lack of in-game map
Yes, I have only listed two cons, the first of which is easy to over come with a little play-time. The second con, which is my only real gripe about the game, is that there's no in-game map.
This is an issue because there's very many zones in the game, which aren't labeled, and once you get away from the city and start transitioning through many zones, it can begin to almost feel like you're in a maze.
Hopefully something regarding the map will be addressed sometime in the future.
In conclusion, the amount of content in this game is staggering. The amount of value for the price of this title is off the charts. I HIGHLY recommend you pick this up if you're a fan of the older Fallout games, or are just a fan of isometric turn-based RPGs in general.

It's so sad that such a cool looking game gets completely ruined by one of the worst systems I've seen in any videogame. The interrogation system is easily the most frustrating garbage I had the bad luck to come across. It doesn't make any sense and all it does is completely destroy the experience for the player.
You're left with a system that apparentaly makes the player decide depending on the characters expressions, but that's a whole lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Sometimes characters will make expressions, gestures and even small pauses when they talk, yet apparentely they're telling the truth.
Then sometimes you call on their lies, but even when you have pieces of evidence that clearly incriminated them and proved they were lying it's apparentely not good enough because the evidence is inconsistent. It apparentely isn't the one magic piece the game chose as the 'right' evidence, so the player fails.
And then, sometimes they say something that either is pretty much true or you can't prove them to be wrong, yet the option "truth" is not the right one, but "doubt" is without any clear indication as to why. Makes absolutely no sense.
The game tries too hard to make the player feel like he's an awesome detective from the age, yet it does the opposite completely. By determining your next move based on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ interrogation system, all it does is completely frustrate the player and break the immersion, since it's not intuitive at all and it's outright confusing.
It wouldn't be so bad if the game allowed you to repeat the interrogation sequences, but obviously that's not the case, so if you ♥♥♥♥ up you're not even allowed to try something else.
It's really depressing, really. This truly looked like an awesome game, and I still think it is, but I just can't cope with how insanely bad the interrogation system is. I don't even know if I can finish it, I don't feel like wasting my time over such a frustrating feature.

This game is great because you can do anything you want. Sadly lacking in a controllable battle mode, this game requires a large degree of imagination to be fully enjoyed. You have the choice to control a nobleman in the early middle ages from a lowly count (town mayors and bishops answer to you) to a duke (who rules over the counts in his duchy) or even a king who rules all the dukes! The goal is to expand your domain using clever diplomacy, marriage, fabricating claims and, when all else fails, war. Utilising a complex and truly amazing diplomacy system, every single character in the game (and there are thousands) has a pre-determined opinion of you based on your culture, religion, prestige, traits and the council you employ. It is very important to maintain good relations with your vassals as they ultimately decide how many men they will lend you in your wars, i.e. Laws dictate the minimum men they MUST give you but opinion is more important in how many they WANT to give you. Truly a great game.

Of course you are required to think a little outside the box, but I would not say any of the puzzle are devoid of logic. If every item I picked up instantly said "hey, I go here and this is why" it wouldn't be much of a puzzle. Obviously there are a lot of individuals that probably don't care for riddles in the least. And what's a good riddle if not to tax your brain for the answer.
I had a lot of fun, had to rack the old brain for an answer or two, and was creeped out to boot. Also makes you ponder some of the heinous stuff people do in the name of science.
Final words......I enjoyed the game immensely.

Just finished the game. Over all, it was pretty neat. The graphics were nice and the story was pretty interesting. I enjoyed playing a ghost detective and getting to posess and influence people to get what I needed. Also, the demons you come across in this game are pretty terrifying. There are just a couple cons about the game:
1. No map. While you can play and beat the game no problem without a map, it was still annoying at times trying to navigate without it. Since the game took place at night and a lot of the buildings look similar, I found myself lost a lot and running around in circles. The game DID come with a code for an interactive map, but I could never get that to load for me and thus never used it.
2. Retracing your steps. Partly due to the lack of a good map, you also have to retrace your steps a lot in this game. That can get tiring. You can also get a bit dizzy from walking/running through walls etc. while retracing said steps.
So yeah. The game was pretty awesome and worth the money. I give it a 8/10.

How to say that and not to repeat myself? Well, what a pleasant surprise!
This game is a mixture of L.A. Noire, Alan Wake and Heavy Rain, but it took only the good from them. If you are a fan of adventure, stealth, detective and mysterious games, this one is exactly what you look for.
This game has great story, quite original plot twist, brilliant and believable characters and more than satisfying ending. Plus, graphics is eye-candy, music and sounds are anxious and the atmosphere is exactly how you would imagine in game like this.
I finish this game almost in one turn and I enjoyed that since the beginning till the very end.
Unfortunatelly, although this game is long enough for this kind of gameplay, the replayability is probably a no-no as it is common for the most of story-driven games. Even if you are a collector freak, you will probably not get over 12 hours of gameplay. So it is up to you if it is worth of 40 euros .
Also, this is just another fast-cooked PC port, and even I haven't faced any technical issues like crashes, glitches and bugs, inability to remap your keys is a crime against humanity in 21st century - I strongly suggest gamepad.
Last but not least, this game is not for everyone - if you are an action-oriented player, this is not for you. The pace is slow and it requires focus on details to solve the investigations. For someone like me it is an advantage, for others it can be a disadvantage.
But for me, along with Wolfenstein New Order, this is another big "YES" this year.

I've been playing on and off for a long time.
The game makes a ridiculous effort to cockblock my attempts at progress. There's a stamina bar that limits how many monsters that can be killed in a day (it's
, especially with unlimited stamina weekends), but more importantly the EXP rates screw you over around level 45. I've been forced to grind several times in between dungeons around Velder for that reason, and it appears at the same spots on every character.
The progression itself doesn't feel very spectacular. You only get a skill every five levels which isn't too often when the cap is 70. Once you finally do get a variety of skills, you're locked to only using four at a time unless you pay $10 for an expansion. Changing jobs is what pathes the way to more skills, but it also gives you new combos to use in addition to your character's base ones. The problem here is that most of these combos can be impractical to use, so having more than one of a character can feel incredibly repetitive.
You mostly play the game by using combos. You also have to practice catching opponents in PvP and knocking them down wastes a good opportunity. Knocking down monsters reduces the damage they take and they may retaliate with a strong attack. Combos are pretty easy to do in PvE, especially since you can just obliterate the first 20 dungeons without a care. btw don't solo. Love yourself (and your stamina). Monsters tend to be more aggravating than they are challenging.
The art is pretty and the outfits have a unique style, but the characters have been driven to almost exclusively fan-service. This is most apparent in the recent customization options (cash only) that have appeared in the Korean server. Most (if not all) of the new female art is sexualized.
There haven't been many efforts to upgrade the "anime" quality to the game. They've stuck to the same assets they've had since the beginning which is ironic when I see ads saying "Play your manga!" as if that were the main appeal.
The characters weren't amazingly unique but they had their own things going for them. Effort has clearly dropped in development, however, and this is most apparent in their most recently released character, Add, a blatant ripoff of Accelerator from
. Although it makes sense to try to appeal to anime fans in this way, it exhibits the disrespect the game has for its own storyline. The character preceding was an imitation from their previous game--a callback and a bit of respectable fanservice--so it was no foul, but, to be fair, it also wasn't the pinnacle of creativity.
The worst part is I'm going to keep playing.

When even idling requires a strategy, you get this game.
CotLI is one that stands out among others in the same genre of idle games. It is an idle game with a twist - one that transcends beyond the same old cycle of beating monsters, advancing and levelling/upgrading heroes that is present in other games of this genre. The formation system present in this game is what mainly brings it to the next level, as the game is no longer solely about that cycle, but also about strategies to maximise the team's efficiency. And that is not all. You get to restart, choose from a list of various different objectives, each one possibly altering your formation or imposing certain limitations that pose a certain level of challenge in this game. It is as if the game is telling you 'So you are able to reach this far without any limitations... what if I say you must reach this area within a limited time/you cannot use certain spots?'
To top it off, the game itself is F2P, and even when in-game spending is involved, this game is by no means harsh towards players who opt not to spend their money on it. This game also encourages people to discuss various strategies to optimise damage output (or formation DPS) or to complete objectives with a built-in chat, which has already formed a diverse community as of current. As if this isn't good enough already, the developers enter the chat from time to time, ready to receive feedback from the community, ready to hear from the players on how to improve the gaming experience, a really rare sight in most games nowadays. As far as the record goes, they have already implemented many changes from the many feedbacks and comments received.
If you think negatively of idle games, do give this game a try. Perhaps it will give you a new impression on how a truly immersive idle game is like.

Youtuber’s Life is a simulation strategy type game. It has tons of endless replay ability with all the constant updates the devs are providing, I hope to see a bright future in this early access game. As far as 1/2/2017 There are only 3 different channel types you can have, which are gaming, music and cooking, with lifestyle and fashion on the way. I have currently only tried the gaming channel, which I’m assuming is the best one, as it should be the one worked on the most. But I’m sure all other types are decent. The core mechanics of the gaming channel is make RELEVANT videos, build friendships, don't mess up on the video recording and editing, and do your best to make quality content videos. Once you reach about 30k subs and so on the gameplay gets repetitive, as all I found myself doing for 3 hours of gameplay was recording videos, going to events, making friends, leveling up my tech tree, upgrading my computer, and doing jobs for bulk cash. My status in the game with 6.5 hours was 270k subs and about 5 million views. Making more than 1k for my income. And that has been my whole experience so far. As my type of playing style, I don't mind the repetitive grindy gaming style that this game extremely caters too. Overall I really don’t mind the setbacks this game has as it is still in early access and has lots of opportunities to fix itself in areas it needs help. One of the useless mechanics I find annoying and intolerable is if you have a mate, she or he buys furniture and clothing using your money. One time she bought a 50 dollar ninja sword hang, it was really inconvenient as I was trying to save to get triple monitors. Overall I recommend this game to any friend knowing what I just said, it will get really cold at some points of the game especially when you’re working towards the luxury apartment, but as I said if you like that kind of stuff, get it but if you want nonstop action, then this game isn’t the greatest option for you.

Cliched plot, naive protagonist. You know where the plot will lead 30 minutes in, but the game is mostly interested in showing you a lot of dead bodies on the way.
Ugly environments. The art style reminds me of Sanitarium (1998) but that game had a lot of different areas to render, here you just have multiple rooms in a grimy spaceship. Some of the screens try to have vertical depth but end up looking borderline undecipherable.
Log entries redundantly explain the events that happened in each area two or three times. Then, after you've read the logs, the voiced characters will have a discussion where they reach a conclusion without acknowledging that you already understand what's going on from those entries.
A couple of the most illogical puzzles I can recall in an adventure game. Some of these puzzles only seem possible to figure out because you have a very limited amount of items and a very limited amount of rooms to try them in. Even then, it's frustrating to try out several near-solutions and get no feedback from the protagonist other than misleading default actions ("I
do that, but it would break...").
A lot of the puzzles seem like the answer was determined then mapped to whatever random objects they felt like giving the player that had the slightest chance of achieving that end.
If you tried Stasis and you love it, I won't begrudge you that. But I think this is a dour, arbitrary exercise and you could spend your time better.
